Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Salutation to Durgā.
Homage to the gurus; homage!

Worship the lotus-feet of the Guru, which surpass the ordinary lotus, which possess a constant luster, and whose seat is the *bindu* emerging from the corners of the qualities within the unfolding Brahma-lotus of the hundred-petaled [sahasrāra]; worship them for the sake of pacifying the impurities of the heart.

For the sake of illuminating the meaning of all scriptures, we worship that which transcends body, speech, and mind, within whom the three worlds appear like a bracelet upon gold. Having extracted from various tantras, I shall here present the worship of the Kula in brief.
Then, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the goals of human life, he [approached] Menā, who was devoted to the family tradition,
while all people were being consumed by the forest fire of the suffering of saṃsāra.
Desiring to uplift [the world], I, whose essence is compassion and who am full of bliss, respectfully undertake this work,
even though there exist here many treatises and compendiums composed by learned scholars.
Nevertheless, a logical argument will be stated here:
"This girl belongs to a noble family; she is given in marriage to one of noble lineage."

Just as one of noble birth should nurture [the self] according to the scriptures for the attainment of happiness, so indeed here, all goals—ranging from wealth, sons, and the like, up to heaven and even liberation—are accomplished through ritual action (*karman*). For it is said:
"One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma; that very same [heaven] [is attained] by the study of the Vedas."

"Through sacrifice they desire to know. Thus, from the knowledge of that [sacrifice], there arises engagement in ritual action (*karma*), because the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the cause of such engagement. In this regard, since wealth, sons, and wife are impermanent, they are to be abandoned; whereas the primacy of liberation (*apavarga*) is heard in scripture. As it is said in the *Gītā*: "Having obtained which, one considers no other gain..."
"Greater than that."
And in the Kalpasūtra as well.

There exists nothing higher than the attainment of one's own Self; there exists no other. Even the Śruti, which is all-knowing, lives by depending upon that very Bliss, saying, "In this [Bliss] all these [other] pleasures are but a part. Now, what indeed is the reality of the Self, whose preeminence is thus declared in the Vedānta? It is the Abode of the Universe.

The reality of the Self is that which transcends the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; whose nature is gross, subtle, and beyond them, eternal, pure, and enlightened; which is the illuminator of the phenomenal world and devoid of the qualities of the three *guṇas*; and which is without middle or end.
Furthermore, it is so because of its very nature as the Self.
One should ascertain that which is full in all directions—across, above, and below—which is existence-consciousness-bliss, immutable, infinite, eternal, and one; that is what truly exists.
And in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:

"Having meditated upon the stainless, pure lotus of the heart, one should contemplate within it that which is luminous, free from sorrow, inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite in form, auspicious, tranquil, and immortal."

The source of Brahman; for thus the Śruti says: "The one, all-pervading, wonderful Being, devoid of middle and end, consisting of consciousness and bliss, formless"; and also: "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss.

Likewise, he is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra, he is the Imperishable, the Supreme Sovereign of the gods; he alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, Fire, and the Moon. He alone is everything that has been and all that is to be, the Eternal.
Knowing him, one transcends death; there is no other path to liberation. Thus, everything is indeed in me.
Whatever has gone forth is established in me;
everything goes to dissolution in me. I am that non-dual Brahman.
I alone am subtler than the subtlest; likewise, I am the Great One, I am the universe, I am the manifold, and I am the Ancient One.

"I am the Supreme Person, I am the Lord, I am golden-hued; I am the very form of Śiva. Without hands or feet, I possess inconceivable power; though without eyes, I see; though without ears, I hear. I know all, being of a distinct nature, yet there is no knower of me; I am eternally Consciousness. Thus, those who are portions of Brahman, whose true nature is such, are nevertheless afflicted by beginningless ignorance.
"Having entered my body, living beings experience the enjoyment of pleasure and pain.
And in the *Tattvasāra*:
"Indeed, no one was bound in the past; therefore, liberation does not exist."
This conceptualization of bondage and liberation is characterized by a certain degree of ignorance.
Bound by the snare of conceptual construction, which arises from merit and demerit,
he endures all sufferings and various kinds of pleasures.

And thus it has been said: "The individual soul (jīva) is one who possesses the excessive conceit of being an agent and an enjoyer. Among those [factors], the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) directed toward the constituent of *sattva* that has become the cause—through the firm superimposition (*adhyāsana*) of "I am He"—is called the Lord (*īśvara*). Of that...

Because it has the quality of being a sentient being as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is omniscience, omnipotence, and the capacity to perform all actions. Just as the darkness within a womb or a jar,
by virtue of having that [jar or womb] as its object, attains the nature of concealment and projection.

Just as an object situated nearby appears reflected in a mirror, so too its reflection in consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is reflected within *vidyā*, which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*). But that which is other than this [reflection]—
the form of the cause dominated by the quality of *sattva*— is [distinguished] by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the portions of *rajas* and *tamas* which constitute the effects of *māyā*.
When that consciousness which has been realized, by virtue of the influence of karma,

assumes various limitations of space, time, and substance, abandons its true nature, and undergoes differentiation from things of its own kind and of other kinds, resulting in the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "I" and "mine," then it is called the individual soul (*jīva*).

Because it has the effect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the *jīva* thinks: "By means of that [adjunct], I am the agent; I am happy or miserable; I do not know myself. According to the Śruti, the *jīva* has the effect as its limiting adjunct, while the Lord (*īśvara*) has the cause as His limiting adjunct.
Furthermore, the Lord, through the differentiation of the three qualities of the limiting adjunct, appears in the forms of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra by means of *avidyā*.

Having attained the two forms of obscuration and projection, [the Self] creates, sustains, and withdraws the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. Brahman is the manifestation of its own modifications. Now, regarding the individual soul (jīva) who desires liberation:

For the sake of achieving liberation—that is, for the purpose of removing the obstruction of beginningless ignorance—ritual actions (*karma*) must be accepted, since one has attained eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman through them. One who is eligible for Brahman-knowledge has, in this life or in a previous birth, studied the Vedas and understood the meaning of the Vedic scriptures as auxiliary branches (*aṅga*). [In such a person], that which is prohibited by the scripture...
Having abandoned [worldly attachments], his inner self is stainless because it is free from impurity through the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*);

he is thus endowed with the fourfold qualification (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*). Regarding this, even the Śruti says: "By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil. Also, in the *Ātmabodha*: "For those whose sins are exhausted by austerities and who are peaceful..."

Regarding the phrase "for those free from passion": this self-knowledge is enjoined for one who is indifferent toward favorable objects. Thus, the fourfold means [to knowledge] are: discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities; dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter; mastery over the six internal and external acquisitions (such as tranquility and self-restraint); and the desire for liberation, and so forth. As for discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities: Brahman alone is eternal.

"Everything other than that is impermanent. This refers to the enjoyment of sense objects such as sandalwood paste and the like in this world; and because they are produced by karma, they are impermanent. Likewise, since even the enjoyments of the afterlife, such as those in the celestial nectar (amṛta) realms, are impermanent, detachment from them constitutes "dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next. As for tranquility and the others, they are: tranquility (śama), self-restraint (dama), withdrawal (uparati), and concentration (samādhi).

Faith (*śraddhā*), tranquility (*śama*), control of the mind (*manonigraha*), equanimity (*sama*)—which is the restraint of the external senses (*bāhyendriyanigraha*)—cessation (*uparati*), renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*), and concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration (*samādhi*) is the complete absorption of the mind upon the objects that are its final attributes. Faith (*śraddhā*) is confidence in the teachers, the Vedas, and the Upanishadic statements; this constitutes the definition of the qualified seeker (*adhikārī*).
And it is said in the Kulārṇava:
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, performer of the fivefold acts!"
O Lord of the Kula, Supreme Sovereign, ocean of the nectar of compassion!
In this essence-less and terrible saṃsāra, defiled by all manner of suffering,
there exist infinite living beings inhabiting various kinds of bodies.
They are born and they die; their end is not found.
Afflicted by great suffering, one does not attain happiness.
O Lord, tell me by what means one is liberated here in this world, O God.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, a man is liberated from saṃsāra.
O Goddess, there exists the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, who is the very embodiment of his own nature,
partless, self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, and higher than the highest.

He is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (sac-cid-ānanda); the portions of Him are known as individual souls (jīvas), conditioned by beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyā), just like sparks from a fire.
Bound by their own actions from beginningless time— actions consisting of merit and demerit that bestow pleasure and pain— they are divided by the limiting adjuncts of the body and so forth.
In each birth, they obtain a body endowed with its respective species, as well as a lifespan and experiences born of karma; and thereafter, yet again, for them...
O beloved, that subtle body, the *liṅga*, is imperishable until liberation;
[through it, beings become] stationary things, worms, blood-red creatures, domestic animals, and wild beasts.
In the same way, the lustful gods and the birds,
having assumed fourfold bodies in due order, were released by the thousands.
If one who has become a knower, having attained a superior self through well-performed deeds, should obtain liberation,
it occurs after eighty-four hundred thousand bodies among the embodied beings.
Nowhere else can the knowledge of reality be obtained except through human birth;
even after thousands upon thousands of births, O Pārvatī, it cannot be attained elsewhere.
Sometimes a living being attains human birth through the accumulation of merit;
having obtained this rare human state, which serves as a staircase to liberation.
There is no one more wretched than that man who,
having attained a human birth and obtained the excellence of the senses, does not save himself.
He who does not seek his own welfare would be a slayer of Brahman;
for without the body, no human purpose whatsoever exists for anyone.
Therefore, one should accomplish merit through the body, wealth, and kingdom;
one should protect the self with all one's being, for the self is the vessel of everything.
One who lives with the senses subdued beholds auspicious things:
again a village, again a field, again a livelihood, and again a home.
Furthermore, pure and impure karma does not repeatedly produce the body;
rather, it is always by people that means for the protection of the body are employed.
Even those afflicted by leprosy and other such diseases do not desire the casting off of their bodies;
therefore, that [body] should be maintained for the sake of dharma, and dharma exists solely for the sake of knowledge.
Knowledge, however, is for the sake of the yoga of meditation; through that, one is liberated without delay.
If there were no self, it would not restrain [the mind] from things that are not to be honored.
Who else is more beneficial than he who provides a cure for the disease of hell in this very life? Who else will deliver himself from it?
Having gone to a body devoid of medicine, what can one afflicted by disease do?
As long as this body remains, so long should one meditate upon the Reality.

Like a blind man digging a well while his house is on fire, the evil-minded one remains indifferent to the splendor of the Kāśī, which shines with radiant light like water from a jar of a different kind.
Disease destroys like an enemy; therefore, one should practice what is beneficial while suffering is not yet known and calamities have not yet arrived.
As long as there is no impairment of the senses, one should practice the reality;
in time, it is known through various bodies born within saṃsāra.
For the heart of a great soul is indeed filled with the joys and sorrows of all people;
he is grieved by seeing those afflicted by torment, those who have died, those seized by calamities, and those who are suffering.
The world, having drunk the wine of delusion, is never afraid;
its prosperity is like one asleep amidst lions, and its youth is comparable to a flower.
Life is as flickering as lightning; who can find steadfastness in it?
A hundred years of life are exceedingly short, and half of that is stolen away by sleep.
Though it is afflicted by the sufferings of childhood, disease, and old age, that [life] is nonetheless fruitless;
indeed, one is devoid of effort and remains fast asleep when one ought to be awake.
What man here, in a place of fear, can be trusted?
For this body is like the foam upon the water, and life is established in sorrow.
In a dialogue with Anityaśrī, [the Buddha] asked: "How can one remain fearless?
How can one perceive what is harmful as beneficial, and contemplate the permanent in what is impermanent?"
Perceiving what is not beneficial as beneficial, he does not recognize his own death;
though seeing, he stumbles, and though hearing, he does not understand.
Even while reciting it, O Goddess, he does not understand, being utterly deluded by Māyā;
this world is sinking into the deep ocean of Time.
No one at all perceives that death, disease, and old age are like crocodiles;
though time flows away moment by moment, it is not noticed even while one is living.
Like a raw clay pot submerged in water, it is perceived as shattered;
the wrapping of the wind is undone and the sky is rent asunder.
The binding together of waves is possible only as long as life endures;
by that [same power], the earth is consumed and even Mount Meru is shattered.
The waters of the ocean dry up, yet the talk of divine women remains in my body; "I have no son," "I have only one wife," "May there be wealth for me," and "May I have kinsmen."
They smear themselves excessively with death; Death, like a man-lion, forcibly slays them while they think, "This has been done, this is to be done, and this other thing is half-finished."
O beloved, death approaches the man who is thus engaged in such efforts;
he does not even perform his own duties, whether they pertain to the morning, the midday, or the afternoon.
For death does not wait to see whether [one's work] is done or yet undone;
it is like a butcher waiting for the path shown by old age along which one must set out.
Do you not see that Māyā has entered the domain of Death,
pierced by the needle of craving and sprinkled with the clarified butter of the sense-objects?
Neither passion nor hatred stains, nor does death seize the human being—
whether they be children, those in the prime of youth, the elderly, or even those still in the womb.
Death thus enters into all this world of beings,
as well as the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, and all other classes of living creatures.
They pursue only destruction; therefore, one should practice what is beneficial.
[One should avoid] transgressing the conduct prescribed for one's own caste and [avoiding] the acceptance of improper gifts.
The destruction of men occurs through desire for another's wife or wealth,
as well as from the neglect of the study of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, and likewise from deceiving one's teacher.
For men, the depletion of their lifespan occurs due to the lack of restraint over the senses;
likewise, disease, mental anguish, poison, weapons, hunger, serpents, predatory beasts, and wild animals [bring about such depletion].
O Śivā, all living beings go by that path which has been described; the individual soul, like a leech on a blade of grass, moves from one body to another body.
Having entered within by means of a portion, it abandons the body for worship,
just as childhood, youth, and old age follow one after another through successive bodies.
Likewise, the attainment of another body is like going from one house to another;
having performed various actions, people experience happiness and suffering.
O Goddess, those who lack knowledge go and return again and again to the other world;
whatever action is performed here, that is experienced there.
Just as the fruit of a tree watered at its root is seen upon the branches,
so too do poverty, suffering, disease, bondage, and calamities [arise from their source].
These fruits of embodied beings are the transgressions of the self;
liberation comes only through detachment, for all defects are born of attachment.
Through attachment, even a knower falls downward; how much more so one of little wisdom?
Attachment must be abandoned with all one’s being, yet it is not possible to abandon it.
One should perform actions together with the virtuous;
association with the good and discernment are the two steady eyes for attaining perfection.
How could a man who has no sense of shame not become a follower of unrighteousness?
For as many connections as a living being forms with those dear to his mind, [so great is his bondage].
O Goddess of caste and family, as many as these [impurities] enter his heart, causing the thorns of grief,
so much this living soul abandons even its own body.
For saṃsāra has suffering as its root; he who possesses it is one who suffers.
O beloved, he by whom that [attachment] has been abandoned is the foremost among the happy;
it is the source of all sufferings and the abode of all misfortunes.
O beloved, one should avoid saṃsāra, which is the abode of all evils,
a terrible bondage from which there is no release, and a great poison that has not been neutralized.
O Goddess, for those whose minds are powerless against the cycle of existence, this entire world is a weaponless shattering;
it is suffering from beginning to middle to end.
Therefore, having completely renounced worldly existence, one who is established in reality shall become happy;
even one firmly bound by fetters made of iron or wood is liberated.
One who is constantly attached to women, wealth, and the like is never liberated;
for one occupied with the concerns of the family, virtues such as tranquility and moral conduct do not arise.
The world, having accumulated all its remaining wealth and possessions, constantly perishes with its limbs, like a lotus whose beauty is destroyed by mud and water.
Alas! I, who feed upon sense-objects, am being devoured by the thieves of the body and the senses, just as a fish greedy for meat perceives a hook made of iron as bait.
Now, the greedy embodied being does not perceive this affliction;
ignorant of what is beneficial and harmful, he constantly follows the wrong path.
O beloved, the final state of the wise is like that of the ignorant;
for all living beings, sleep, sexual intercourse, and food are the same.
O Dear One, a man possessed of knowledge is called a human being, while one devoid of knowledge is a beast;
[the former is afflicted] by excrement and urine at dawn, and by hunger and thirst at midday.
O beloved, during the night, human beings are overcome by passion and sleep; all living creatures are devoted to their own bodies, their duties, and their wives.
All living beings, though devoted to the conduct prescribed for their respective castes and stages of life, are born and die, alas! deluded by ignorance.
O Pārvatī, those who do not know the supreme Dharma perish;
among them, some are intent on ritual action for themselves and others, while others are devoted to vows.
Those whose souls are shrouded by ignorance wander about as deceivers;
satisfied with mere names, such men are devoted to the ritualistic section of the Vedas.
But those who follow the practice of mantras are deluded by elaborate sacrifices such as fire-offerings (homa),
and by various rules for bodily purification, such as residing in forests and so forth.
Deluded and bewildered by your māyā, fools desire that which is beyond perception; for those lacking discrimination, what liberation can there be through the mere punishment of the body?
O Goddess, where has the great serpent been struck down by the Valarīka? Among those who plunder wealth, there are hypocrites who merely wear the outward garb of religion.
They wander in the world like those possessing knowledge, delighting in what is dear to people;
they are incapable of worldly happiness and claim, "I am a knower of Brahman."
One should abandon this bond of karma which has fallen away through fear; just as she who has cast off her shame and wears no garment looks upon the house and the forest as equal.
And donkeys and other such animals also roam about; would they too become solitary?
O Goddess, if human beings were liberated merely by [smearing themselves with] earth, ashes, or dust, [then so it would be].
O beloved, how could those who dwell in earth and ashes, who endure cold and wind, and who are indifferent toward what is fit to eat and what is not, ever become intoxicated?
Do donkeys and other such animals become wise simply because they constantly subsist on grass, leaves, and water, and do not dwell [in houses]?
O Goddess, do those deer such as the *hariṇa* become ascetics,
having taken refuge in the waters of the Gaṅgā from birth until death?
Do those who observe vows, such as the frogs and fish, speak?
Do parrots and mainas recite that which gladdens the heart?
O Goddess, what do those gods say in the presence of people?
O Supreme Sovereign, they are pigeons, stone-eaters, and cātaka birds.
"Do those who observe vows not drink the water of the earth?
Why is that?"—such [questions] are merely for the purpose of pleasing the world through ritual action.
O Goddess of the Suras, the direct cause of liberation is the knowledge of reality; O Beloved, those who fall into the great well of the six systems of philosophy are like corpses.
Constrained by the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), they do not know the ultimate truth;
therefore, they become deluded in the terrible ocean of the Vedas and Śāstras.
Here, the wicked logicians remain swallowed by the suppression of their knowledge;
he who does not know the supreme truth from the Vedas, Agamas, and Purāṇas [is likewise lost].
All that was spoken by the crow regarding Viḍaṃvaka—
such as "this is knowledge" and "this is what is to be known"— was filled with anxious reflection.
O Goddess, those who are averse to the supreme reality recite day and night [these texts],
which are bound by the constraints of prose and verse and adorned with poetic ornaments.
Distressed by anxiety, deluded, and with their senses agitated, people remain in this state;
they strive for the supreme reality in one way, yet they suffer in another.
Otherwise, they explain the existence of the scriptures in one way,
yet they speak of the state of the Unstruck Sound (unmanī-bhāva) while not experiencing it themselves.
Some, overcome by egoism and deprived of instruction and the like,
study the Vedas and Shastras and dispute with one another.
They do not know the supreme reality, just as a ladle does not know the taste of the food it stirs;
the head bears the flowers, but the nose perceives the fragrance.
They recite the Vedas and the Shastras, yet that single discernment of true being is difficult to find;
not knowing the Reality residing within the self, the fool is deluded by the scriptures.
It should be known that the dull-witted person who digs a well while standing within the scriptures is like one digging a pit;
for a mere partial understanding is not capable of destroying the delusion of saṃsāra.
Just as the wick of a lamp can never dispel darkness,
so too is the recitation of one deficient in wisdom like the sight of a blind man.
O Goddess, for the wise, the scripture is the means to the knowledge of reality;
some [follow it] from the front, some from behind, and others from the sides.
They indeed dispute with one another, saying, "The truth has been declared by me";
yet that man is renowned for his virtues such as true knowledge, generosity, and heroism.
"Such and such," O beloved, is how one who is far away is described by people; there is no direct perception of him, only the report of his existence.
Thus, those who are utterly deluded regarding the scriptures remain far from certainty;
they desire to hear everything: "This is knowledge, this is the object of knowledge."
O Goddess, one does not reach the end of the scriptures even in a thousand years;
indeed, the Vedas and numerous other treatises are millions of obstacles to life.
Therefore, the wise person, having studied all the scriptures and having realized the truth, should discern the essence from them, just as a swan extracts milk from water.
One should abandon all scriptures like straw for the sake of grain;
just as one who is satiated by nectar has no need for ordinary food.
O Goddess, for one who knows reality, there is no need for scripture;
liberation comes neither from the study of the Vedas nor even from the recitation of treatises.
O Goddess praised by heroes, liberation arises from knowledge alone and not otherwise;
neither ascetic stages nor philosophical systems are the cause of liberation.
In the same way, knowledge alone is indeed the cause of all actions;
the words of the Guru alone grant liberation, for they are the sole remedy for all ignorance and crookedness.
The state of wood is the supreme life-force of the venerable one;
indeed, non-duality is declared to be Śiva, devoid of all ritual action.
It can be obtained through the mouth of the Guru, and not otherwise, even by means of millions of scriptures.
Knowledge is declared to be twofold: that which arises from scripture and that which arises from discernment.
Some desire the Supreme Brahman to consist of the scripture of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma) born of discrimination,
while others desire it to be dualistic.
They do not know that reality which is equal and free from duality and non-duality; they are bound by two states for the sake of bondage and liberation: "mine" and "not mine."
A living being is bound by the thought "this is mine," and is liberated by the thought "this is not mine.
That action which leads to bondage is karma; that which leads to liberation is knowledge.
All other action is laborious toil; knowledge is something else entirely, as is the practice of the arts.
This continues only so long as one is not liberated from desire and so long as the latent impressions of worldly essence persist.
As long as there is fickleness of the senses, so long is there talk of reality;
so long are there vows, pilgrimages, recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and the like.
Therefore, with every effort, at all times and in all circumstances, one should investigate the truth as it is found in the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Agamas.
O Goddess, if you desire liberation for yourself, you should be established in reality;
for it is the true flower of dharma and knowledge, and its fruit is the enjoyment of heaven.
Tormented by grief for her son, she took refuge in the shade of a tree.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Purāṇa], there is the speech of Vasiṣṭha.
All this that is seen—the entire world, both stationary and moving—is like deep sleep; it perishes at the end of the kalpa, when even the waking state has vanished.
Then there remains something existent, neither light nor darkness, pervasive, beyond description,
and without a second.
This name of that Great-Souled One was devised for the sake of conventional usage.
Scripture also [states this].
Brahman alone is one without a second; here there is not even the slightest thing that exists as a name.
Thus it has been stated by way of direction through the Vedas, Āgamas, and other sources.
Once the falsity of saṃsāra is known, human awakening is required.
Cognition is indeed verbal in nature and not mental; for it is precisely this [verbal cognition], being contrary to the mental [misconception], that possesses the capacity to destroy doubt. (p.

[This is] by way of being an error and by way of being a specific perception produced by the mind; however, that which is produced by an external sense-organ is not so, because the relationship of destroyer and destroyed has been established as being between an error and a specific perception produced by an external sense-organ.
But mental cognition [arises] from that.
It has already been stated that the mind is purified by means of actions,
and that [purity] is its very nature.
Therefore, for the sake of destroying the delusion of saṃsāra, the worship of Śrī Bhavānī must certainly be undertaken.
Thus ends the auspicious first chapter in the independent *Kulavṛtti*, composed out of devotion for the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha.

Although there are many views and many types of liberation, nevertheless, devotion to Prakṛti is essential, because liberation is something to be accomplished by removing ignorance (avidyā). For even the Vedāntins maintain that when ignorance has ceased, what else remains but the Self?
This has been established. As it is said in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi: "Liberation without Śākta-jñāna results only in ridicule. [This applies] to other causes.
* * * * Neither by yoga, nor by cognitions, nor by scripture, nor by the lineage of gurus, nor by primordial nature (prakṛti) is that [liberation] produced for anyone.

The Puruṣa is known by his nature; he has become insentient in every respect within this existence. That very cause is indeed Prakṛti. Thus also says the Śruti: "He, through Māyā, transforms himself into the form of the world. Now...
"By illusion alone one pursues a corresponding form; by illusion alone are bondage and liberation [experienced], according to the nature of the object.
Thus it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*.
Just as ignorance itself is the flood that destroys one's own self,
so too is that wisdom attained through equal means and by the desire for it.
Even regarding the vessel for worship, many varieties have been prescribed for those of extensive vision;
yet among these, one must adhere to the path of one's own family tradition, as that is necessary.
This has been stated in the Kulārṇava:
What is the use of much speaking here? Listen to the secret, O Pārvatī:
there is no liberation apart from the Kula path; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the exposition of the family dharma (*kuladharma*). In that regard, the definition of the family dharma is as follows:

it is the very practice of the fivefold substances (*pañcamakāraka*) performed by an agent endowed with the divine-heroic state (*divyavīrabhāva*), preceded by the respective mantras prescribed in the system of the Siddha-Yogīśvaras; this alone is the virtuous dharma.
The meaning of the word *kula* is as stated in the *Kuloḍīśa*:
"Wine is *kula*, meat is *kula*, the perfected one is *kula*, and the menstrual flow (*rajas*) is *kula*.
The power *Kuṇḍalinī* is *kula*, while *Akula* is said to be Śiva."
This has been stated in the Kulārṇava:
The illustrious Umā said:
O Lord of the Kula, ocean of compassion for all living beings, I wish to hear about the attachments to the Kula-peak; though indicated by the God, it was not made manifest.
O Supreme Lord, if you have any compassion for me, tell me of the greatness of that Dharma which has been proclaimed as superior to all other Dharmas.
The Lord said:
By the mere recollection of him, you shall become very dear to yogins;
this was previously told by me to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Guha, and others.
I speak out of affection for you; listen with a one-pointed mind.

Transmitted through the succession of the lineage, established within the words spoken from the mouth [of the teacher], it is inexpressible in terms of ultimate reality; nevertheless, I shall speak of it.
You too must indeed keep this secret; it must not be given to just anyone.
It should be given to a devotee or a disciple; otherwise, there will be a fall.
The gods are superior to all others, and among the gods, the Vaiṣṇavas are supreme;
the Śaivas are superior to the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Dākṣiṇyas are superior to the Śaivas.
The Left (Vāma) is superior to the Right (Dakṣiṇa); the Siddhānta is superior to the Left;
the Kaula is superior to the Siddhānta; and there is nothing higher than the Kaula.
The meaning is "from among all those worthy of worship. *Vaiṣṇava* refers to Viṣṇu himself; *śaiva* refers to Śiva himself by virtue of his own nature.
It is the same here as well.
The "right" [path] is the worship of the Goddess according to the manner prescribed in the Śruti.
On the left, below, is worship according to the Buddhist sequence as taught in the oral tradition (āmnāya).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that you are [the goal]; the meaning is that one should not engage in worship that is inconsistent with the intended sense of the words. "O Goddess, [this is] more secret than the secret, the essence of essences, higher than the high;
O Goddess, make this manifest Supreme Śiva pass from ear to ear."
"Passed from ear to ear" means it has been transmitted from ear to ear; the meaning is that it is fit for the disclosure of secrets.
O Goddess, having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Agamas with the staff of knowledge, I—who am a knower of the essence—have extracted the Kula-dharma.
On one side are all dharmas beginning with sacrifice, sacred fords, and vows;
on the other side is the family dharma (kuladharma), O beloved, for the reality of the Kaula is superior.
Just as rivers with winding courses enter the ocean,
even so do all traditions enter into the Kula alone.
Just as all the footprints of living beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant,
so too, O Beloved, are all philosophical systems contained within this alone.
When iron is found that is equal to the Yamunā and the Narmadā rivers,
then another may become equal to the agreement through the law of the family.
Just as the waves of the sea are not all equal in their size and form,
even so, all people are not equal by virtue of their family dharma.
Just as there is a vast difference between Mount Meru and a mustard seed, or between the sun and a firefly,
so too is the great difference between other systems and this [teaching] of the Kula.
O beloved, if there should exist a man equal to me who loves a woman equal to you, and if he were of equal lineage and equal virtue, then he might speak thus.
For that evil-minded man, through delusion and by practicing an improper act against his family dharma,
would speak of a false sārikā bird as if it were a real one, like a person who has fallen away from truth.
O beloved, he who out of ignorance speaks of a duty that exceeds the requirements of his family lineage incurs a sin greater than the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Having ascended the path of the lineage from the mouth of the Guru, O man,
and having gone from this difficult island to another, one attains the jewel of liberation.
In all philosophical systems, men attain liberation through long-term practice; however, in the Kaula system, they attain it immediately—of this there is no doubt.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen, O beloved of my life!
O Mistress of the Kula, there is no dharma equal to that of the Kaula, even in a fraction of a part.
If one is a yogi, he cannot be an enjoyer; if he is an enjoyer, he cannot be a knower of yoga.
Therefore, O Dear One, the Kaula, which consists of both yoga and enjoyment, is superior to all.
O Mistress of the Kula, when the Kula-dharma is present, enjoyment itself directly becomes yoga, sin becomes merit, and even worldly existence becomes liberation.
O Goddess, even the gods such as Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the foremost of sages, are devoted to the dharma of their own lineages; what then need be said of human beings?
Having abandoned all phenomena and the various systems of the teachers,
one who desires his own welfare should indeed know the Kula alone.
Through the practice performed in previous births, the Kaula knowledge manifests, like the recognition of one who has just awakened from sleep, even without instruction or the like.
Whatever intellect has been cultivated by human beings over a thousand previous births, that very same intellect the creature practices again; thus, instruction is rendered useless.
Through those born of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Daurga, Ārka, Yāta, Patya, and Indu traditions,
as well as through Manu, those whose minds are purified by knowledge reveal the Kaula wisdom.
For one whose mind is pure, who possesses the qualities of a spiritual seeker, who serves the guru,
who is extremely secret, and who is devoted, the Kaula knowledge shines forth.
In those Śrīkula scriptures, in the Kauliṣuka texts, and within the Kula lineage,
the knowledge of Kaula dawns upon him whose devotion is firm.
Through pure discipline, joy, and other virtues, through right conduct, firm vows,
and the observance of the guru’s commands, the Kaula knowledge is revealed.
One who is unworthy never abides in the knowledge of the lineage;
therefore, having examined [the recipient], the knowledge of the lineage, which brings great prosperity, should be spoken.
One should impart the Śivadharmas to the worthy and the teachings of Śiva to those who are worthy; he who causes a violation of this command out of malice shall incur the wrath of the deity.
If, after having fulfilled the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*), one should speak of the *kula*-dharma,
that teacher as well as the disciple shall become an animal (*paśu*) in the eyes of the excellent Yoginīs.
Having awakened the disciple, the Guru should reveal the family dharma (kuladharma);
both of them immediately obtain the assembly of Yoginīs and Vīras.
He who crosses the ocean of saṃsāra without effort—having understood this family dharma—is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.

One who has entered the great path of the Kula-dharma shall go to the city of liberation; there is no doubt about this, and it will happen without delay. Therefore, one should take refuge in the Kaula tradition.
He who disregards the Kula scriptures and practices the scriptures of the fettered (paśu) is like a fool who abandons the milk-rice in his own home and goes out to beg for alms.
He who, abandoning his noble lineage, seeks out the low-born out of childishness, is like one who casts aside a heap of grain and desires to grasp a heap of dust.
Afflicted by thirst, one indeed runs toward ponds as if toward a mirage;
likewise, the illusions of Indra’s net bring pleasure for only a moment.
O Mistress of the Kula, other observances are not equal to the Śrīkaula; the dull-witted person who desires liberation without knowing the Kula-dharma is deluded.
He who desires to cross over the near shore and the far shore, as well as that which is shoreless, and who seeks both worldly enjoyment and liberation from other philosophical systems; |||
O Pārvatī, if one were to become wealthy through wealth obtained in a dream,
it would be just like the delusion of silver that arises in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Likewise, enjoyment and liberation are praised as resulting from other observances;
such a person is free from all ritual actions and devoid of the distinctions of caste and stage of life.
O Mistress of the Kula, he who is devoted to the Kula is a worthy vessel;
even if he is devoid of the knowledge of the Kula, if he is a devotee of the Kula, he shall become so.
Even he attains a good rebirth; how much more so one who is devoted to him!
O beloved, even if his livelihood is destroyed by the customs of his family, he protects himself from harm.
Therefore, one who has been honored should quickly abandon the body through worship;
let all kinsmen, as well as wife, sons, and others, abandon it through censure.
O Haṃsa, people may constantly revile me, or kings may punish me;
yet I shall serve, I shall serve, and I shall serve again, O Supreme Deity.
I do not abandon that dharma through the actions of mind, speech, or body;
such is the well-ascertained intellect of even a foremost ascetic like this.
He is worshipped by the gods and shall become auspicious in the next world,
O beloved, even if he is constantly afflicted by poverty, suffering, disease, and the like.
Whoever worships you with true devotion shall attain your state;
whether they chant your praises, offer hymns, or even criticize you, let Lakṣmī come to them and remain there.
Whether liberation is attained today or at the end of an eon, one should never abandon the Kaula path—
not out of desire for wealth, nor out of anger, nor out of fear, nor out of envy.
One should not abandon a member of one's own family out of desire or even out of fear;
for he who, knowing you, does not worship you while relying on the family dharma, [is a transgressor].
He is despised by that enemy, the well-burdened one, merely by his arrival here—
like a grain of chaff among grains of rice, or like a creature blind from birth among living beings.
Those who are devoted to the Kaula path are like pure drops in the waters;
for even trees live, and beasts and birds live as well.
He whose mind is established in the family dharma truly lives;
for one devoid of the knowledge of his lineage, the days merely come and go.
Like a blacksmith’s bellows, he does not live even for a moment,
whether he is moving or standing still, waking or sleeping.
O Kulīśvarī, for this bound soul, the Command of the Kula is its very life;
whether he be learned or utterly ignorant, righteous or unrighteous.
Whether one is established in a vow or not established in a vow, those people who are averse to the Kaula path are indeed merely creatures born in this world who live as virtuous men.
O Goddess, those devoted to the family dharma are the remainder, like aged donkeys;
he who is devoted to the family dharma is liberated by the virtuous as one possessing such splendor.
But another, O beloved, though possessing firmness and covered [in learning], is ignorant of his own lineage despite being a knower of the four Vedas; he is a low-born man and destitute.
One who possesses knowledge of the Kula through his own practice excels even over a Rākṣasa;
he is purified by the compassion of the Guru and has shaken off all impurities from his body.
O Goddess, he who delights in the life-force of the Kula is a Kaula, and no other.
Cursed be the life outside that belongs to that Kaulika who does not perceive, does not find, and does not worship the knowledge of the Kula; he is like a crow.
Those of meritorious deeds who cross over are knowers and they are yogis,
in whose minds the knowledge of the Kula has arisen as it was proclaimed.
Those people who are indeed doers of good deeds enter that family and dharma which is constructed by all sacrifices and entered through righteousness.
Furthermore, they never enter a mother's womb;
nor does anyone who speaks of "knowledge of the lineage" ever praise them.
O Goddess, O Mistress of the Kula-sacrifice, by your grace her family becomes a true Kula; for her, no other dharma serves any purpose.
Likewise, for those high-souled Kaulikas who are devoted to the Kula, no other dharma serves as a purpose, even the command of the Kula itself.
I shall bestow the supreme knowledge and mantra upon you in due time; there is no doubt.
O people, wait for that moment which yields the fruit of the Self, consisting of pure consciousness, as you desire it.
Alas, he does not know the Kaulika doctrine which grants all fruits through the mouth;
yet he considers himself a knower of the Kula, a knower of the Parvas, or even one who observes Vedic scriptures and vows.
Even one who knows the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Agamas, if ignorant of the Kula, is indeed ignorant;
only your devotees, and no others, know the majesty of the Kula.
Only those who know can discern the true luster of the moon, and none other;
O beloved, only those of noble lineage are satisfied upon hearing the stories of their own kin.
Do those who know the Pārā [Vidyā] and follow the Kaula path increase their infant-like nature through the moonlight like the ocean? They do not look toward the doctrines of others.
The bees, who frequent the fragrance of that mandāra flower, honor its transition to another blossom; for those who possess all-knowing wisdom do not disregard the dharma of their lineage.
Alas! Siṃhikā swallows even her own head when it is ablaze at the end;
indeed, those who know only their own vows do not understand the vision of the lineage.
Only a bird like the swan knows how to drink milk mixed with water;
likewise, in this world, only one established in the Kaula tradition knows the world as consisting of Śiva and Śakti.
Therefore, how can the Kaula, which is superior to all, be common to everyone? The six philosophical systems are its limbs: the feet, the belly, the head, and the two hands.
For whoever should create division among them, who indeed would he be?
These very six limbs belong to the Kula as well.
Therefore, O beloved, the Kaula is identical with me and I am identical with the Kaula;
it yields the single fruit within all philosophical systems and possesses a single deity.
O beloved, in this knowledge which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
even that which is contrary to worldly dharma is [accepted] according to the Siddhayogīśvarīmata.
O Dear One, because Mālaya bestows visible fruit, it is worshipped by the family;
and among all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the foremost.
By the power of his realization, all those false dialecticians were defeated;
for who knows what may happen in the future to anyone?
Or rather, O Supreme Deity, that vision which bestows direct perception is the sight [of You];
having known this family dharma, all human beings are liberated.
Thinking thus, O Maheśānī, I have [spoken] what is censured in the world regarding those who are devoid of your compassion and who oppose the knowledge of the Kula.
The family custom of the ignorant among the *paśus* is censurable;
for him, in another birth, there will be the obstruction of sinful karma.
The teacher’s compassion does not arise for one who lacks knowledge of the Kaula;
just as the blind do not see the sun, the illuminator of all.
Likewise, those deluded by your māyā recognize you through their lineage;
even those belonging to the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, and other systems do so out of devotion.
Human beings constantly devote themselves to those [paths] which yield only fruitless results;
whereas that which is proclaimed in the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas is the sole means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Alas, alas! The fools who revile the sight of you, my beloved, are like beasts, O Goddess, though they are experts in the scriptures; they have been deluded by me."
Those who pride themselves on vain knowledge know only by means of their family traditions;
indeed, all the scriptures of the beasts were spoken by me alone.
But having entered into another mode of existence for the delusion of the wicked-minded,
a supreme desire for great sins arises in living beings.
For them, there is no way out even in hundreds of millions of eons;
though it is being examined, the evil-minded person does not engage in knowledge at all.
By preserving the dharma, a righteous soul saves his entire lineage;
by means of the family dharma, the gods have attained divinity, as the deities themselves have declared.
To the Lord of Sages and Yogins, from whose lineage those who have attained supreme perfection have emerged—
those on this earth who have desisted from the vows of the bound (paśu), who are free from hypocrisy, and who possess ease.
Those who serve the Kaula deities are indeed great and rare;
there are many men who speak falsely, claiming to teach the true reality.
O Maheśānī, those humans who are experts in the Kula-tantras are difficult to find; O Goddess, O Mistress of the Kula, they are forever free from disease.
They do not employ divine medicine that destroys great diseases; instead, they consume unwholesome food which increases those very ailments.
In that very same way, those devoid of your compassion constantly perform the worldly activities of birth and death, even though they are capable of better.
They do not follow the family tradition that liberates one from the bonds of existence,
just as merchants do not follow the saltiness inherent in salt, pepper, and the like.
O Mistress of the Family, human beings request ordinary objects with affection,
yet some indeed do not request priceless jewels.
"In the same way, they ask about the animal sacrifices, their purposes, and their fruits; for these fools are indeed deluded by your Māyā."
They do not inquire about the family tradition that bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
regarding musk as mere mud and desiring camphor and salt instead.
Just as a common person perceives sugar as gravel, a gem as glass, or gold as mere clay, so too does he regard even that which is held in his own hand.
Likewise, those devoid of your grace do not know the Kaula tradition.
O Goddess of the Gods, what indeed shall I say regarding the greatness of this delusion produced by Your Māyā, which can delude even the immortals?
"Wine is to be drunk, meat is to be eaten, and the face of one's beloved is to be gazed upon"— this is the veil [of delusion].
Having attained the supreme,
O compassionate one, such [a state] is seen in this family.
Only those devoted to you know [this] as the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, and not others;
yet some, though intent on the instructions of their gurus, do not understand devotion.
Some people, having been previously deluded themselves, delude others; some base individuals, devoted to wicked conduct, indeed cause others to read [their works].
Tell me, how can Bhūtodbhavasvāmī have such servants?
They are numerous followers of the Kaulika path, mocked by their false knowledge.
If men, devoid of traditional lineage, were to imagine this through their own intellects, and were to attain liberation through the drinking of liquor; [then so be it].
If those addicted to drinking liquor all attained their desired success merely by eating meat,
then [merit would likewise follow from such acts].
O Goddess of the Gods, if all those who behold this world become meritorious by means of sexual union with women, then they must surely attain liberation.
O Goddess, all living beings in the world would be liberated simply by serving women; yet, I have never at any time disparaged the path of my lineage.
Those who are devoid of proper conduct are censured by that [teaching];
otherwise, I have described the obstruction regarding the Kaulika doctrines.
O Goddess, those fools who consider themselves wise wander about,
clinging to the thorns of logic and the scriptures of the disputants.
O Goddess of gods, the Kaula doctrine cannot be grasped by those who hold onto worldly attachments;
drinking [alcohol] in vain is called the drinking of *sura*.
That should be known as a great sin (mahāpātaka), as well-defined in the Vedas and other scriptures;
it is something that must not be smelled, looked upon, touched, or drunk.
Alcohol, meat, and the fruit of animals constitute the doctrine of the Kaulikas.
But this attendance has been indicated.
The impure intoxicants of the twice-born are elevenfold;
however, the twelfth, the liquor of fermented rice (surā), is recorded as the most base of all.
Surā is indeed the impurity of grains; having seen it, one is released from sin.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra may drink surā.
Upon the mere sight of liquor, one should perform the visualization of the sun;
upon the mere smelling of its fragrance, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
From this, there shall be protection for you both; there shall be a crossing over the obstacle.
May there be refuge; may he dwell in the settled place, and may he bestow strength upon us.
If one touches liquor above the navel, the rule is a three-night fast;
however, for drinking liquor intentionally, one should drink molten, blazing liquor.
Then, once it has been completely burnt away, he shall attain purity;
such is the traditional teaching regarding the expiation for the fault of contact with liquor and the like.
O beloved, he who kills himself or a living being without authorization shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the animal's body.
Those who sell meat and those who sell weapons are reborn as short-lived beings, of wicked conduct, and in the animal realm.
They are full of trust in falsehoods.
The preparer, the enjoyer, and the eater—these three are equal [in merit].
Regarding the term "enjoyer" (*upabhoktā*), it is derived from the prefix *upa* combined with *bhuj*; since this word has multiple meanings, here it signifies "one who causes to eat" (*bhojayitṛ*).
Through wealth they kill by means of purchase; they are killed through consumption;
and the killer kills by means of beating and binding—thus killing is said to be threefold.
Having touched something similar [to meat], one should perform the ritual gaze at the sun;
therefore, one who consumes meat without following the prescribed rule does not truly consume it.
O Goddess, if you are pleased with me through my devotion, then destroy those other wicked ones; O Truthful One, that is for the sake of this evil-souled man.
Or by sowing grass according to the prescribed rite, one who has killed [the victim] will be bound with nooses.
One should never cause it to be cut.
Even a twice-born man who has committed many sins is not stained by them when [he follows] this rite;
O beloved, what is the use of saying more? Listen to this one thing.
O Goddess, this bliss of liberation while living is hidden within the Buddha scriptures; it is the fruit for one seeking liberation, possessing the fragrance of golden lotuses.
O Pārvatī, the knowledge that transcends the Kula is that supreme state;
all the Kula scriptures are endowed with the Māyā.
There is no doubt that the offerings should not be withheld from the deities and the ancestors with logical arguments; for the *madhu-vātā* [verse] is extended as an *arghya* offering.
With most excellent and desirable offerings of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water.
O Ambikā, because he possesses a golden vessel, the man who has shaken off all impurities (avadhūta) instantly consecrates the sacrificial animal;

the scriptures are the authority for what must be produced, as it is said, "He is dear. Thus, O Mistress of the Kula, I have told you something of the greatness of the Kula. O Queen of the Kula, what more do you wish to hear?

By these words, the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) has been demonstrated along with the procedures spoken by the illustrious Mahādeva. Therein, having first described the Tantric scriptures in general, it is now appropriate to specifically determine the authority of the *Kula-tantras*. First, there is the description in the general scripture regarding that *Kula-tantra* which is included therein; here [it is as follows].

Although fools and beasts lack discernment, and the Kaulikas are scholars who know [the truth] by themselves, nevertheless, because he was a candidate for the first level of authority, they examined the disciple. Now, how is the Tantric scripture an authoritative means of knowledge? Because it is rooted in the Vedas; like all the Smṛtis and the Mahābhārata, it is authoritative.

The authority of the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other such works is rooted in the Veda; for this very reason, there is no lack of authority in the various scriptures of the Kāpālikas and others, nor in the Buddhist doctrines, which prescribe practices such as striking water and worshipping stupas,
as these are established by their respective intellects and set forth specific rites.

The state of being rooted in the Vedas means having the capacity to convey the meanings established by the Vedas. Although there is a censure of the Tantras in the Purāṇas, O Paśupati, nevertheless, in the Padma Purāṇa it says: "By means of fabricated scriptures, turn those who are devoted to me away from the truth."
Likewise, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Gaurī and Himavat:
The enumeration of those tantras that have not been respected is here declared;
it is indeed for the sake of protecting the followers of the Vedas from sinners.
"O Bull-bannered One, I shall compose treatises for the purpose of deluding [people].
Thus was Rudra enlightened by Mādhava, the embodied one.
Keśava also, impelled by Śiva, composed treatises of delusion known as Kāpāla and Bhairava—
the former Bhairava and the latter [Bhairava].
O Lord, the Pañcarātra, the Pāśupata, and other systems such as the Vastrasvara were created by you,
O Gods, for those who practice what is enjoined by the scriptures.
Those who are devoted to the Kāpāla, Pañcarātra, or Yāmala systems fall again and again into terrible hells for many eons.
And other such [texts] as these have been brought forth for the purpose of delusion;
therefore, by means of the scriptural tradition (āgama-śāstra), they possess authority because they are rooted in the Vedas.
However, the authority of the Veda consists in its being the cause of what is not eternal and its being the cause of what is desirable.
It is not another [cause], because that cause would lack pervasiveness.
Wherever there is being rooted in that [desire], there is no causality;
for there is a deviation [from this rule] in the case of prohibited eating and the like, which are prompted by passion.
Not the other [the Smṛti], because even if it is rooted in the Veda, it produces *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) in matters such as eating and the like.

Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that 'not being a producer of *adṛṣṭa*' must be stated as the non-common [distinguishing feature]? Therefore, the Tantric scripture does not produce *adṛṣṭa*, whereas the Veda..."
Because it would be rootless. Even if the truth were rootless in the Veda, the Veda itself produces unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
There is a double deviation: even if it is not rooted in the Veda, there is the [authority of] Bhoja; and if the Veda is rooted in the Veda, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
As for being authoritative (*āptatva*), it consists in the absence of error, the absence of contradiction, the absence of a desire to deceive, and the absence of defective instruments.
"Because of the excellence of its clarity," meaning that as it is in the Veda, so it is in the Tantra. That the Tantras are rooted in the Veda has already been shown.

As for what is stated in the scripture (*śāstra*), its meaning is as follows: by the word "Mahādeva," Mahādeva himself is addressed. O Mahādeva, by means of the Āgamas, Śāstras, and Tantras spoken by you, people are rendered two-faced through their connection with me.

Pure consciousness is called *mukti* (liberation). Therefore, turn those who are averse to pure consciousness away from it by means of *tantras*. What kind of *tantras*? By those that are "imagined" (*kalpita*), meaning they are conceptual constructs; the word *kalpa* is derived from the root *kḷp* (to imagine/construct), and thus refers to those which subsequently desire the four aims of life (*caturvarga*) and so forth—that is, those which enjoin worldly desires. For this very reason, the latter half of that same [verse] says: "and not in that which consists of the *goddess*."

Thus, recognition itself is the Supreme, consisting of all powers;
she is one with all the differentiated forms beginning with Brahmā, which are composed of the power of Śiva.
He is indeed the agent, the enjoyer, and the destroyer; he is the totality, consisting of pure consciousness.
The power of will is the cause of Brahman, and she too has the nature of Brahman.
The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) has the form of Viṣṇu, and she too is of the very nature of Viṣṇu;
the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is creation (sṛṣṭi), and she too has the form of Rudra.
The supreme Śiva-śakti, characterized by inseparable union,
is the all-pervasive, omnipresent power of undivided pure consciousness, whose very nature is consciousness.
Possessing a reflection that is the nature of all principles,
she illuminates the multitude of worlds and acts like a great rain.
Puruṣa and Prakṛti, and the Lord who is beyond Prakṛti—
these, including the twenty-three principles, are said to be the supreme Prakṛti.
They say that the Puruṣa, consisting of twenty-five principles, is beyond Prakṛti; he who is beyond that Puruṣa when it is dissolved in Prakṛti is Maheśvara.
Because its nature is dependent upon that [Puruṣa], Prakṛti is inferior to Puruṣa; it is like a mother who, though great, is less than her son.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and possessing ears everywhere in the world, He stands encompassing all.
Alternatively, the partless Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss,
is distinguished as being present in women more than in males or neuter beings.
O Beloved, through the distinction of higher and lower, this supreme power (para-śakti) is indeed endowed with all states of being, especially within women.
Śiva does not exist without Śakti, nor is Śiva devoid of Śakti;
there is no difference between them, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight.
"It is remembered that this is not a woman, this one is serene, and this is not a eunuch;
nevertheless, the word 'woman' is applied here, just as it is to a camphor vine."
For the benefit of practitioners, she assumes both formless and embodied forms;
she is manifested within all living beings and consists of the very nature of universal consciousness.
The Goddess consists of all the gods; she is beautiful with all auspiciousness;
she is eternally composed of all prosperity; she is the supreme, consisting of all mantras.
For it is said in the *Viśvasāra*: "She consists of all tantras, she is full, and she abides in all mantras. (p. 14a)
One should manifest the gross, and having relied upon the subtle-gross, one should take recourse to the subtle object;
for indeed, O Goddess, without the gross, there is no illuminator even of the subtle.
The Lord assumes a fourfold form for the liberation of embodied beings;
it is certain everywhere that these are Śakti, Hari, Śiva, and Sūrya.
In the Vāsiṣṭha: "In some places it is the mind (manas), in some the intellect (buddhi), in some knowledge (jñāna), in some action (kriyā);
in some it is this ego (ahaṃkāra), and in some it is considered the purifying fire (pūryantaka)."
In some places it is called *prakṛti*, in others it is conceived as *māyā*; in some places it is declared to be *māna* (the measuring mind), and in others it is established as *karman* (action).
In some places it is called "ignorance" (avidyā), and in others it is accepted as "will" (icchā);
this is so even by virtue of the meaning [of the syllable].
Regarding the single-syllabled *oṃ*, there are the four Vedas and four quarters (*pada*).
The supreme Brahman consists of four feet and sixteen syllables.

With the first syllable, *pṛthivī* (earth), together with the letter *a*, there is the threefold fire, the *Ṛgveda*, Brahmā, the Vasus, the Gāyatrī meter, and the Gārhapatya fire. With the second [syllable], *antarīkṣa* (the intermediate space), together with the *Yajus* formulas, there is the Yajurveda, Viṣṇu, the Triṣṭubh meter, and the Dakṣiṇāgni fire. With the third [syllable], *dyauḥ* (heaven), together with the *Sāmans*, there is the Sāmaveda, Viṣṇu, and the Ādityas.

The Āhavanīya fire is the earth; the fourth is the power consisting of lightning. He is the Atharvaveda with its great mantras; he is Saṃvartaka, Avirāṭ, and the divine Svadhā. Brahmā is Brāhmī, whose deity is Brahman; Kṛṣṇā is Vaiṣṇavī, whose deity is Viṣṇu.
The Kapilā is in the northeast, having Īśāna as its presiding deity; the fourth is the lightning-like, which is divine.
"He who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and he who is Brahmā—to him, salutations again and again."
"He who is Rudra is the Blessed One; he who is Viṣṇu is the Blessed One Sūrya; he who is Rudra is the Blessed One; and those who are the months are Mahādevī. Thus it is stated in the Brahmopaniṣad.
Brahmā is awake; Viṣṇu is in the dream state; Rudra is in the deep sleep state; and that Prajāpati is the supreme in the sun.
Thus, Brahman shines as everything.
The Śruti also says:
Indra, by means of his powers of illusion (*māyā*), manifests in many forms within primordial nature (*prakṛti*). [From the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: The words of the Goddess:
"Listen, O son, supreme bliss, you who consist of the aspects of the higher and lower (*parāpara*)."
O Maheśvara, the knowledge of all remaining tantras is sealed by my māyā.
I am Prakṛti by nature, whose ultimate refuge is consciousness and bliss;
you are Brahmā, you are Hari, and you are Śambhu—where then is that god who eats in sequence?
Where is vision? Where is stability? Or where is the stage of contraction?
Where is action? Where is pleasure or pain? Where is liberation? And where is goodness?

Where is faith and where is atheism? Where is the state of being a teacher and where is that of a disciple? Having concealed her true self through *māyā* and divided herself in two, she who is intoxicated by the fragrance of the passion for both the forward-facing and the averse, sports as one who delights in abandoning [all distinctions].

The five elements, the subtle bodies (*liṅga*), and their qualities increasing by one at each stage; Brahmā and the others, the worlds of *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*; as well as essential nature (*svabhāva*), manifestation (*vyakti*), and genus (*jāti*).
When all things manifest therein, the conceptualization of existence and so forth arises;
through the differentiation of Śiva and Śakti, the emergence of the qualities (guṇas) occurs.
All those beginning with Brahmā, who have arisen as portions of my own self,
are families equal to the lunar mantra, though they appear mutually distinct.
Having brought about the state of dissolution (pañcatva), those who are cherished in the state of Nirvāṇa manifest once again; thus, O dear one, the Puruṣa is beyond Prakṛti.
The ego, the five subtle elements, and the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas— this entire universe, consisting of these powers, manifests once again.

"O Omniscient One, if you know me, tell me where are the scriptures and where is the officiating at sacrifices? O Omniscient One, tell me where are the scriptures and where is the officiating at sacrifices? Therefore, for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should resort to the divine and heroic states (*divya-vīra-bhāva*) and practice *prakṛti*. This practice consists of the regular (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites; this is the summary thereof.

The term "vivṛyate" (is explained) refers to the state (*bhāva*), which will be written about later. Now follows the exposition on the section concerning the states of the Divine Heroes (*divyavīra-bhāva*).

In that regard, the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) everywhere are those who possess the knowledge that the specific [practice] to be described hereafter is the means for accomplishing their own desired goal, according to the statement from the *Kulārṇava*: "For all four castes and stages of life," and so forth.
The specific details are as stated in the *Kulārṇava*:

"Free from attachment, free from the sense of 'mine,' steadfast, shameless, and devoid of curiosity—one who has determined the meaning of the Kula scriptures may drink the boon-granting wine (*vāruṇī*). Having practiced the Kaula conduct for a year and having offered the sandals of the Guru, whoever [practices] in this Tantra..."

"You surely cause suffering by engaging in this; [namely] the knowledge of the Kaula conduct and the worship of the Guru"—these are the two qualifications. O Goddess, he who, though unaccomplished in Kaula knowledge, desires to speak of that substance, is a great sinner, excluded from all dharma, fallen from the observance, and of evil intellect.
For one who acts according to his own whims, there is no success; rather, there is a fall from his lineage. Therefore, one should avoid association with such evil-minded persons.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, conducts himself according to his own desires, [attains neither perfection nor prosperity].

He who lives according to his own will, devoid of the purificatory rites of initiation (dīkṣā), shall not attain perfection in this world, nor the supreme goal in the next; for him, there is no good rebirth anywhere,
despite austerities, pilgrimages, vows, and the like.
One who forcibly consumes unprepared substances, engages in sexual intercourse by force,
or eats meat killed for one's own pleasure, shall go to the Raurava hell.
If those belonging to the Kaula tradition abide in the vows of the fettered (paśu), they are mockers of both sides;
for as many hairs as there are on their bodies, so long shall they remain in the Raurava hell— those who, having resorted to other doctrines, consume the substances of the Kula.
Equal in number to the hairs on my body, he is born among the sources of beings;
yet, being uncreated and undisturbed, he indeed consumes nothing at all.
In the Kaulika tradition, there is no meditation, no austerity, no worship, no dharma, and no virtuous action; there is no Veda, no guru, no self, and no discursive inquiry.
One who is addicted solely to sense objects falls without a doubt;
likewise one addicted to liquor, one who is intoxicated, one who consumes meat and the like, and one who serves women.

He who is devoid of the Kaula instruction shall go to an inexhaustible hell; for one who is unrefined, due to the force of worldly attachment, [there is no attainment] even through the initiation into the five mudrās.
One who knows the distinction between the three genders and discerns the divisions of the six supports (ādhāras) attains the state of Brahman through the realization of Śiva.
Having reached the yellow locations, one should proceed to the Great Lotus Grove (Mahāpadmavana),
moving again and again from the root-support (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
One should become intent on drinking the nectar of the motionless lotus in the sky, arising from the bliss of the state of equilibrium between Consciousness-Brahman and the Kuṇḍalinī power.
This is declared to be the drinking of honey; others who drink liquor are sinners.
Having slain the animal of merit and demerit, the knower of yoga [consumes it] with the section on knowledge.
By whatever means one may remain firm and non-violent—that is the conclusion—one should restrain that collection of senses within the self.
One should not be a meat-eater, O Goddess; for all others are indeed destroyers of living beings.
Unawakened, it is the power of the bound soul (paśu); awakened, however, it belongs to the Kaulika.
One who serves that Śakti becomes a servant of the Śakti;
such, O Kulanāyikā, is the definition of the five mudrās.
O Goddess, having learned this from the mouth of the Guru, he who practices it is liberated;
so too are those men who have cast off their sins and perform meritorious deeds.
Those endowed with the knowledge of the lineage and firm in their vows worship you;
you are accompanied by offerings and consecrations, and you are the knower of the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras.
O Dear One, one who is devoted to the deity and the guru, self-controlled, a knower of the secrets of the Kula tradition, and desirous of propitiating the deity, should perform worship.
O Mistress of the Kula, one who is endowed with the teacher’s instruction should perform worship;
being pure in soul, free from anger and greed, and devoid of passion.
Averse to animal sacrifices and the like, he should worship with his face turned toward [the deity].
O Dear One, when the meaning has been refined by means of the extensive Kula tradition, [he attains success].
By my grace, as long as your firm devotion remains,
you should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the oblations prescribed by Śrī Bhairava after that time.
By the method of the Guru’s instruction, and not otherwise, there shall be no downfall;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the Śrīkrama worship through the application of mantra.
Therefore, knowing myself to be Bhairava, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the rest, I myself shall respectfully receive it together with you.
Having reflected thus, the lord of yogis should perform the Kula-worship;
endowed with such characteristics as these, the Kaulika is one whose vows are constant.
O Goddess, he who worships you shall become a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
But surely, how can women and Śūdras have the right to initiation?
The prohibition is stated in the Saṃhitā,
as for example in the Mahākapila Pañcarātra.
The Veda does not exist apart from the Praṇava, and a mantra is endowed with the Veda;
therefore, the mantra is considered superior to the Veda, and the Āgama is known as a limb (aṅga) of the Veda.
Rites such as subjugation (vaśya) and so forth, which bestow both visible and invisible fruits,
are all indeed accomplished through the Vedas by means of planetary conjunctions and other such methods.
There are no sacrifices without the Veda, nor are there sacrifices devoid of the Veda;
therefore, the mantra is supreme to the Veda, and there is no mantra devoid of the Veda.
Śūdras have no entitlement to mantras; for them, there is only the observance of rules. Indeed, every ritual act is performed through the mantra by means of its internal disposition.
Likewise, in the *Tāpanīya-saṃhitā*:
"For as many leaves of mantras as one might impart to a Śūdra, for so many instances of Brahman-murder shall he be liable; thus Prajāpati himself has declared."

It is true that by these words, it is generally established that there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) for those born of the four castes, including the *śūdras*, to the Vedic mantras of the three *karmans*.
In that regard, there is indeed no entitlement to the Vedic mantra. However, for some, it is heard in the case of the Tantric mantras;
as it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those who are base-born (*malāḥ*)."

Regarding the teaching of mantras to those of mixed castes, such as farmers (*kṛṣīvala*), it is stated in the *Devīyāmala*: "In this context, the word 'mantra' refers to a specific type of mantra; a twice-born man who gives a mantra joined with the *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra shall go to hell, and the twice-born man shall attain the status of a Śūdra. This is from the *Padmapurāṇa*.
The Vedic or the mixed [path] is prescribed for Brahmins and the other [twice-born castes];
the Tantric path is proclaimed even for a Śūdra who is devoted to a Brahmin.
Women and Śūdras should also perform the worship of Viṣṇu with faith, following the path taught in their own scriptures, while keeping their husband in their hearts.
Women have the right to perform the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites, provided they are devoted to the pleasure of their husbands; this is the eternal Vedic injunction.

The mention of Viṣṇu is an illustration for all deities; this is the meaning. "Or she should meditate" refers to a woman whose husband has died, who is devoted to her husband, and who is joined with an auspicious support.
And she receives the mantras from her husband with his permission; for neither the son nor the wife has authority, as the *Tantrajāmala* states: "The wife [acts] by the command of the husband."

Whatever [practice] other than one's own dharma— such as worship of deities according to ritual injunctions and so forth— is proclaimed for the sake of the next world, it perishes in an instant like a palace built of sand.
And because of the statement in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"For women and Śūdras, a mantra ending in 'namaḥ' brings happiness," as stated in the *Rudrayāmala*.
O Mahāsena, having recited this, one should not initiate a Cāṇḍāla.
In the Yājñavalkya Saṃhitā:
"A Śūdra or likewise a woman should never recite Vedic mantras;
however, wise men consider it desirable for them to recite either the Śiva-mantra ending in 'namaḥ' or the Vaiṣṇava mantra."
The phrase "ending with *namaḥ*" means that it exists or is situated with the word *namaḥ* at its end. Here, the word *vā* signifies a conjunction;
by this, it should be understood that there is eligibility even for mantras such as those belonging to the Śākta tradition.
As stated in the *Yāmala* and in the *Tantrarāja*.

"One, two, three, four, or five years—thus [he described] those joined with yoga and the qualities of the *muktā* (pearls) in succession according to their color, O Śaṅkara. Herein is the conclusion: women and Śūdras have no entitlement to Vedic mantras alone;
they have no entitlement to the Tantric [mantras] that end in *svāhā* or *puraḥ-mukti*.
The authority over the arrow joined with the *praṇava* and the *svāhā* [belongs to him].

[Objection: But how could there be the *praṇava* at the beginning and the *svāhā* mantra at the end if the *praṇava* were excluded by that prohibition? [Response: That is true; however, according to the principle that for Śūdras and others, the rule applies to the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) just as it does to the principal part (*pradhāna*).
