Even when that [mantra] is joined with it, there is eligibility for the ancillary mantra (aṅgamantra).
And likewise, it is not the case that [the recitation] is connected to the subsidiary parts merely because of its connection to the principal act.
Now, one might object: just as in the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*), Śūdras would have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) for the chanting of the Rudra-mantras.

It is true that, according to Gautama, there is generally no entitlement [to Vedic rites] for those who lack the Vedic mantras, because he prescribes the mantra "namas" as a substitute for the primary auxiliary Vedic mantras. However, in the case of Tantric practice, there is no prohibition regarding the primary connection itself. This is because the mantra "svāhā" does not exist as an auxiliary part of this heart-mantra (hṛdaya-yantro).
No application [of *svāhā*] is observed. Without the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*), there is no recitation of mantras.
Therefore, due to the qualification for the specific mantra, there is likewise qualification for the application of the word *svāhā* and so forth in the limb-mantras.
Thus, now, a specific rule regarding the mantra excluding the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is heard: *svāhā*.
As it is stated in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*: The Goddess said:
"Among the Śāktas, Śāmbhavas, Sauras, and the Vaiṣṇavas;
among the castes beginning with Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, and especially among the Śaṅkaras—"
I wish to hear about the ritual application for the benefit of practitioners;
O Śaṅkara, tell me that distinction regarding which mantras belong to which [deities].
Īśvara said: Umāmāheśvara, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Aghoraka, Hayagrīva, Vārāha, and thereafter the Aṣṭākṣara.
One should bestow either the supreme [mantra] beginning with *praṇava*, or one's own deity, or likewise Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
it should be given to those of the three [higher] castes, but never to one of a lower caste.
The Pāśupata, the Nārasiṃha, and likewise the Sudarśana [mantras] should be given to those of two castes, and never to any others whatsoever.
Whatever mantras of Agni there may be, as well as those of Sūrya,
and the mantras of Tārā beginning with *ghṛṇi*, should be bestowed upon one who possesses the three castes.
The *anuṣṭubh* meter, the *śakti* mantra, and likewise the *Vindhyavāsinī* mantra,
as well as that of *Nīlasarasvatī*, should be assigned to the first letter.
Matenī, Ugratārā, Kālikā, Śyāmalā,
as well as Chinnamastā and Vālā, should be assigned to every color.
Tārādi, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the one named Haridrā—these should be bestowed only upon those of the three castes; they are said to grant all perfections.
Those mantras of Tripurā, as well as those of Vaṭuka and the others,
should be imparted to all castes, and especially to virtuous women.
Regarding mantras whose presiding deity differs from the [standard] deity, it has been stated that everyone is entitled to them provided they are seedless (*nirbīja*).

Concerning the specific case where they possess a seed (*sabīja*), he says in that very same place: "The *praṇava*, *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, *vāgbhava*, and the seed-syllable of Caṇḍī—joined with these seeds, they should be given at the beginning of the rite."
Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Vāgbhava should be given even to a Kṣatriya;
Lakṣmī and Vāgbhava alone are prescribed for the Vaiśya caste.
The Vāgbhava seed-mantra and the final seed-mantra are proclaimed for Śūdras;
for Śaṅkaras (the twice-born), the mantras beginning with *hṛdaya* and ending with *hūṃ phaṭ* are praised.

The meaning is that these mantras are either those whose seed-syllables (*bīja*) have been uttered, or mantras that are themselves the nature of seed-syllables; according to the specific distinctions of their respective classes, they are deities.

These [mantras] are devoted to the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*) under restrictive rules (*niyama*). However, in the divine (*divya*) and heroic (*vīra*) states, there is no longer any restriction regarding caste and so forth.
As it is said in the Bhairavī Tantra:
"When the Bhairavī-cakra is active, all castes are twice-born;
when the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, all castes remain distinct."
"Bhairavī, when the authority over the wheel has commenced" means [she is] Bhairavī when there is no authority over the wheel.
This is also because of the statement in the Kulārṇava: "Even for all four castes," and so forth.
And in the Kulārṇava, regarding the knowledge consisting of the bliss of Brahman, I shall speak, O fair-faced one:
"One is not a Brāhmaṇa by birth, nor likewise a Kṣatriya."
O Supreme Goddess, we are not Vaiśyas nor Vaiśyas; we are not Śūdras nor Śūdras;
we are not Cāṇḍālas nor Cāṇḍālas, and we are not Puṃsakas nor Puṃsakas.
"Understand all [methods] equally in the compendium of the ultimate truth.
Thus it was stated previously; those who possess knowledge of the means for accomplishing their respective desired goals are the qualified practitioners (adhikārin).
Thus, it is complete.
Thus [ends] the *Gurubhāvārthakulavṛtti* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānandanātha.
Having bowed to the stainless lotus-feet of Gaurī, and having bowed to Mahābhairavī...
Having bowed to the two feet of Vighna, and having bowed to the virtuous gurus and the learned scholars;

The venerable Pūrṇagiri has taught that entire ritual action pertaining to the limbs of worship— enjoined for the sake of liberation within the Tantras and directed toward the Śaktis such as Sakalā and others— in the divine and heroic states (*divya-vīra-bhāva*). Therein, he demonstrates,
preceded by an exposition of both, how there is at times equality through ritual action and at other times distinction among these two states.

A brief exposition [of the subject] should be made. First, there is the definition of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Its characteristic is the reception of mantra from a guru preceded by the respective ritual procedure. For the etymological meaning of the word "initiation" follows after this.
In the tradition of Śiva’s teaching, for those who are ignorant, there can be no liberation without the initiation of debate and without a teacher; such is the supreme lineage of conduct.
Thus, according to the statement in the Kulārṇava:
"The future is the cause of liberation; the mind is the cause of existence;
worship is the cause of mantra; and the Guru is the cause of worship."
And because of this statement from the *Tantrarāja*: "Since initiation,
which is obtained according to one's specific qualification,
is dependent upon the teacher, it must first be performed by the guru."
This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
That best of Brahmins is capable of both uplifting and destroying;
he knows the reality of mantras and tantras, understands their vital points, and is a knower of the secrets.
One who has accomplished the *puraścaraṇa* rite attains mastery over the mantra; such a knower of application is devoted to the welfare of others, intent on recitation and worship,
pure in heart, and possessed of an exceedingly peaceful body and mind.
One who is inwardly awakened, a celibate student, and of noble birth is called a guru.
And in the *Sāradātilaka*:
"Pure in descent from both mother and father, pure in disposition, and having conquered the senses..."
He knows the essence of all scriptures and understands the true meaning of all treatises.
Devoted to helping others and intent on the practice of recitation and worship, his words were unfailing; he was peaceful and had mastered the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas.
One who follows the path of yoga, who has reached the heart of the deity,
and is endowed with such qualities as these, is recognized as being identical in form to the Guru.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Those Śāktas who, abandoning the Lord of the Kula, serve another,
their initiation and sacrifice lead only to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*)."
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in a guru of noble lineage;
for it is proclaimed that one of noble lineage is qualified for all mantras.
In this matter, the master of initiation alone is the authority for all mantras, and no other.
It is stated elsewhere in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
"Those Brahmins who are Śivas and Śaivas are also preceptors in every respect."
Gaṇeśa is considered the lord of the Gaṇas, the one initiated by Śvamedin, and the father.

Sūrya, Saura, and likewise Vatsa, Viṣṇu, and those devoted to Viṣṇu; and in the Vārāhī Tantra: "One should accept [the mantra] as prescribed in one's own ritual manual (akalpa), provided one is free from hypocrisy and other such faults. A Vaiṣṇava should take [the mantra] from a Vaiṣṇava for Viṣṇu, a Śaiva from a Śaiva for Śiva, and a Śākta from a Śākta; or from a Guru who is all-knowing. One should never resort to the opposite."
In an odd-numbered year, one should rely on the Tantric tradition beginning with Śuddhācāra;
in this matter, knowledge of the successive lineage of gurus is essential.
As it is said in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
"Without knowing the teacher's family (gurukula), one will lose the path to the deity;
and for one who has lost the path, there is no attainment of such a range of fruits through mantra and vidyā."
If there is no succession of lineage among gurus and their disciples,
then the tantras, mantras, and vidyās will undoubtedly become fruitless.
Or even twenty persons, or perhaps three who have been heated by worldly existence.
Without knowing the gravity of the *śānas* and the disciples, the lineage is not properly maintained.
And in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Lord of the Kula, ocean of the nectar of compassion, I desire to hear [this]."
Therefore, you should now explain to me the characteristics of both the teacher and the disciple.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask of me; by the mere hearing of it, the state of being a Guru arises.
[It concerns] one who is base, devoid of qualities, and deformed, born from the influence of the Kali age.
Do not honor the fierce heretic, who is violent and fancies himself a wise man.
One with deficient limbs, foul-smelling, with deformed limbs, possessed of defective members, lame, blind, deaf, soiled, and afflicted by disease.
O beloved, one who is ill-composed or has a foul countenance, who is covered in perspiration,
and who is possessed by sleep, lethargy, old age, laziness, messengers, and the like;
Always concealing his body behind doors, walls, pillars, and the like;
adopting the behavior of a cat; and intent on hatred toward his kinsmen.
One who is ungrateful, whose inner heart is burning with malice, a betrayer of trust, a traitor to his master, and a doer of evil deeds— even though he possesses a physical body— is [condemned].
One who causes harm, one whose mind is full of doubt, one who desires success through improper means,
an assailant, one who is most wicked, one who is enraged, one who is cruel, and one who is inexhaustible in malice— [these are those whom one should avoid].
O Goddess, [he is] one who strikes at all, one who is arrogant due to the desires of the wicked,
an outsider disputant, and one who praises the path of thieves like lightning.
O Ambika, [protect] the virtuous who endure [hardship], the honored, and the afflicted;
[and punish] the Cārvāka, the friend of the wicked, who is censured by all the world.
One who is slanderous, who causes distress to others, who delights in dispute, who speaks unrighteously, who is cruel, treacherous, and who seeks out evil paths.
The meaning is that one should abandon such a guru as well. [This is stated] in the Yoginītantra.
One may receive instruction from one's father, likewise from one's mother or maternal grandfather,
from a younger brother, or even from one who belongs to the side of an enemy.
In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*:
"The initiation of a mother, the initiation of a father, the initiation of one who dwells in a forest,
and the initiation of those who have retired to solitary hermitages— such initiation does not bestow auspiciousness."
If one performs the initiation of the ancestors through negligence or lack of knowledge,
one should then perform an expiation and undergo the initiation once again.

The expiation consists of the recitation of the Gāyatrī ten thousand times; however, for a Śūdra, this must be performed through a Brāhmaṇa. This is because there are counter-exceptions (pratiprasava) such as "the mother" and so forth. Likewise, it is stated in the Yāmala:
"O Goddess, O Beloved, if by the power of fortune one should obtain a perfected Vidyā..."
Having abandoned the deliberations of the Guru, one should be initiated into oneness with That.
One should give it to the eldest son, who is the ornament of his own family.
In the *Matsyasūkta* [of the] *Ditiphetkāriṇī*:
"The mantra of the father becomes powerless and is corrupted by the Śaiva and Śākta [mantras]."
She was indeed virtuous, of good conduct, self-controlled, and obedient to the words of her teacher.
She who knows the true meaning of all mantras, is virtuous, and delights in worship,
is indeed fit to be a guru, provided she is free from widowhood.
The initiation of women is declared to be auspicious, and that of the mother is remembered as being eightfold superior.
Herein is the summary:
from the mother and others [are obtained] the Śākta, Siddhavidyā, Kulavidyā, and other mantras of the Śaiva-Śākta traditions.
One should not accept it; this is the meaning.
Now, the definition of a pure Guru is given in the Kulārṇava:
"O Īśānī, the venerable Guru [should be] dressed in pure attire..."
He was captivating, endowed with all auspicious marks, and beautiful in every limb;
he was a knower of the truth and the meaning of all scriptures, an expert in the application of all mantras,
and possessed a form that enchanted the world like a god.
He is free from doubt, knows the truth of gestures and facial expressions, has kept wicked people at a distance from afar,
is inwardly focused while appearing outwardly looking, is all-knowing, understands place and time,
possesses the power of command, knows the three periods of time, and is capable of bestowing grace.
A beloved knower of the Vedas and Vedānta, devoted to compassion for all living beings,
with his senses under his own control, he followed the method for conquering the group of six internal foes.
He is profound like the full moon, discerning between those who are worthy vessels and those who are not;
he is free from the sense of "mine," eternally contented, beyond the pairs of opposites, and possessed of infinite power.
Affectionate toward true devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and one whose speech is preceded by a smile;
dear to his devotees, generous with all his possessions, and one who has brought his disciples to perfection.
The best among the learned, wise, eloquent, and devoted to honoring [the teacher],
he should be intent upon blameless rites— whether daily, occasional, or optional.
Free from greed, impartial, non-violent, eloquent,
and full of wealth, learning, and other such qualities, he has mastered mantras, yantras, and the like.
Free from conceptual construction, he expresses meanings that have been definitively determined;
equal toward blame and praise, silent, indifferent, and self-restraining.
O Dear One, the Śrī Guru endowed with such characteristics as these has been described. Now follows the praise of the Guru. (p.
In the Kulārṇava: "O Dear One,
how is that Śiva— who is all-pervading, subtle, beyond the mind, partless, immutable, and infinite—
worshipped within the form of the Yoni?"
Therefore, O Goddess, one who has directly taken refuge in the form of the Guru and worships him with devotion, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess, Śiva’s divine form does not indeed move about in accordance with the [ordinary] state of perception;
therefore, in the form of the venerable Guru, he protects his righteous disciples.
Bound by human skin, Paraśiva himself is manifest; having restrained his excellent disciples, he wanders hidden upon the earth.
That very action is characterized by true devotion; though formless, Śiva, the ocean of compassion, manifests in the world as a worldly being and acts through external movements.
Having placed the eye on his forehead and the digit of the moon upon his body,
he remains upon the earth in the form of a Guru.
O beloved, it is said that the Śrī Guru is directly Atri with three eyes, Śiva, Acyuta with four arms, and Brahmā without four faces.
In this world, the glorious Guru is seen as a mere human by one of sinful deeds;
he is seen as Śiva himself by one of meritorious deeds through Śiva’s grace.
Those of meager fortune do not see the glorious Guru, the supreme reality, standing right before their eyes, just as the blind do not see the risen sun.
The Guru is Sadāśiva himself; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Śiva alone is the Guru in this world; who else bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation?
O Pārvatī, there is no difference between the Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Guru; he who makes a distinction between the two is a sinner.
Having resorted to his creative power, the Lord completely severs the fetter of the bound soul;
having cut it, he leads [the soul] to the supreme state—such is the sacred revelation.
The Lord, a treasury of compassion who acts for the benefit of all,
having assumed the form of a teacher, shall liberate the bound souls (paśus) through initiation.
Just as "ghaṭa," "kalaśa," and "kuṃbha" are expressive of the same object, so too are "mantra," "deva," and "guru" expressive of the same reality.
As is the deity, so is the mantra; as is the mantra, so is the guru.
The fruit of the worship of the deity, the mantra, and the guru is identical.
O Pārvatī, assuming the form of the Guru, I accept the worship;
the Guru is said to be the one who always bestows uninterrupted grace.
O beloved, he who transcends the various castes, who is never established in the self alone, is a yogi belonging to all castes and stages of life; he is declared to be the Guru.
He whose vision remains steady without an object to see, whose mind is stable without a support,
and whose breath is firm without the two [nostrils], is dear to the Guru.
O Mistress of the Kula, he by whom that reality— consisting of the bliss born of consciousness and arising from supreme bliss— is known, is the Guru.
O Goddess, he who knows the sixfold division— consisting of Bhūta, Bhāva, Mātra, Raudra, Śākta, and Śāmbhava— is indeed the Guru who effects penetration (vedhakara).
He should offer into the fire the worlds of the planes, the phonemes, the digits, and the mantras.
O Dear One, that Guru who should purify you within the six paths is thus described.
O Dear One, he who correctly knows the pentad consisting of piercing, the jar, the restraint, the seizing, and likewise the releasing— he is declared to be the Guru.
O Dear One, he who understands the determination of the sixteen supports by means of the sixfold support or the single support according to the prescribed rule, is called a Guru.
O Goddess, he who knows the fivefold states— waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turyā), and that which transcends it— is proclaimed as the Guru.
O Dear One, he who correctly knows the fourfold— namely, the Piṇḍa, the Pada, the Rūpa, and that which transcends form— is declared to be a Guru.
O Dear One, he who perceives the supreme and the non-supreme, as well as the intermediate and the manifest speech, and understands this fourfold division— he is called a Guru.
O Supreme Goddess, he who knows the fourfold reality—that the Self, Knowledge, Śiva, and All—are one—is called a Guru; O Beloved, he is celebrated as such.

O Dear One, he who is capable of purifying the three bonds— the bond of action (*kārmika*), the bond of illusion (*māyika*), and the bond of knowledge (*vidyā*)— as well as the pillar, the piercing initiation (*vedhadīkṣā*), and the very grasping [of the soul], is declared to be the Guru.
O Great Goddess, he who understands the latent impression (vāsanā) is proclaimed as a Guru.
O Dear One, he who thoroughly understands the threefold secret convention— the convention of the *cakra*, the convention of mantra, and likewise the convention of worship— is declared to be a Guru.
O Dear One, he who knows the inner sacrifice, the outer sacrifice, the abiding state of the knowledge of time,
and the method of preparing the yantra— he, O Dear One, is a guru.
O beloved, he who knows the oneness and the state of the microcosm and the macrocosm,
who is skilled in the eighty-four various postures,
and who is a knower of the eight-limbed yoga beginning with restraint (yama)— he is declared to be the Guru.
Compassion, shame, fear, apprehension,
[and so forth], as well as family and caste— these eight are proclaimed to be the fetters (pāśas).
One bound by fetters is called a *paśu* (bound soul), while one liberated from fetters is Sadāśiva; therefore, O Dear One, that friend who removes the fetters is declared to be the Guru.
Bondage consists of the *yonimudrā*, and liberation is the realization of the consciousness of the mantra.
O Dear One, he who knows that nature beginning with the Mātrās is the Guru.

O Dear One, that Guru [teaches] the fourfold [movement]: the cast-out (viniḥkṣipta), the gone-and-come (gatāyāta), the joined (saśliṣṭa), and the well-restrained (suvinīta). * * * (? within that very [practice].

O Dear One, he who knows the fruit of the movement of the individual soul (jīva) within the seven lotus petals, from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), is the Guru; no other is such.
O Dear One, that Guru is said to be the very essence of the unmanifest reality (avyakta-tattva), transmitted through the lineage of succession from Śiva down to the earth.
Or, O Dear One, he by whom reality is shown such that one becomes identical with it at that very moment,
and who considers himself as having spoken [that truth]— he is declared to be a Guru.

Those gurus who, having bestowed innate bliss (sahajānanda), remove the ground of obstacles, are to be served by disciples; those others who are deceivers are to be worshipped [only as objects of avoidance].
Those who transfer that which resides in the mind into well-polished mirrors by means of the form of Śiva are blessed gurus; others are deceivers.
For that disciple who is weary of saṃsāra,
the guru is considered to be the restrainer with respect to vows, fasts, and observances.
One should recognize that he who, with his gracious eyes, bestows the fortune of liberation upon this noble woman,
is a rare teacher capable of delivering one from the great cycle of existence.
O Dear One, that Guru who indeed bestows upon a worthy disciple his own power at every moment— power which is without beginning in its activity— is truly difficult to find.
O Goddess, that teacher who imparts the instruction of knowledge— which produces immediate conviction, is easily accessible, and bestows the bliss of one's own self— is rare to find.
O Goddess, just as one lamp may pass its light to another lamp,
so too he who bestows knowledge is a guru who has transcended practice and the like.
Just as satisfaction quickly arises for a hungry person from food, so too does [satisfaction] arise merely through instruction; such a teacher who bestows knowledge is difficult to find.
There are many teachers on earth who are of little consequence for one’s own self;
but this teacher, O Goddess, is rare, illuminating everything like the sun.
There are many gurus who have mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras;
however, O Goddess, this guru who has reached the further shore of the ultimate reality is difficult to find.
There are many gurus— lineages, mantras, medicinal herbs, and deities—
but a guru who knows the mantras declared in the Vedas, Agamas, and Shastras is rare to find.
O Goddess, those on earth who are devoted to the conduct of their caste and stage of life are gurus;
however, he who is free from all mental constructs is a guru difficult to find.
A wise man should listen only to that very teacher from whose resolve supreme bliss arises, and not to anyone else.
He whose intellect proceeds toward reality until it culminates in direct experience is liberated by the mere movement [of that realization]; of this there is no doubt.

O Goddess, he by whom the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, has been consumed with suspicion, and by whom even that suspicion has been consumed— he is a Guru who is difficult to find.
Just as butter situated near fire melts away,
so too does sin melt away in the presence of a true teacher.
Just as a blazing fire may burn even a piece of wood the size of a testicle in an instant,
so too does the Guru’s sidelong glance burn away the disciple’s sins in a moment.
Just as cotton blown by a great wind would rise up toward the ten directions,
even so the mass of evil is dissolved through the guru’s great compassion.
Just as great darkness is dispelled by the mere sight of a lamp,
O Goddess, so too is ignorance destroyed by the sight of a true guru.
One who is endowed with all auspicious marks, proficient in the Vedas and Shastras, and skilled in the application of all means, yet devoid of the [highest] reality, is not a true guru.
[Such a person cannot grant the fruits of] worship, fire-offerings, hermitage-duties, conduct, austerity, pilgrimage sites, vows, and so forth.
Knowledge of mantras, scriptures, and so forth is fruitless for one who is devoid of reality.
Today, this person has no certainty regarding his own self in the supreme reality;
since there is no grace for oneself, there can be no grace for another.
How can he who does not know the sixfold nature of the mind and his own state as it is perceived, grant liberation to another?
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, a teacher who knows reality is remembered as such;
therefore, on this earth, he alone is indeed one whose self is united with the divine.
O Great Goddess, he who knows reality even oppresses the bound soul (paśu);
for how can one devoid of reality be awakened, and how can there be the grasping of a self?
O Goddess, that which is taught by those who know reality is known as the knowledge of reality; that which is taught by the ignorant is remembered as being like the ignorant.
O Goddess, one who possesses the hand of consciousness is a piercer; one who is not pierced becomes a piercer.
One who is joined may liberate the bound child, but how could one who is not joined be a liberator?
One who possesses the wisdom of intellect may rescue a fool, but a fool cannot rescue a fool;
for a boat might carry across a stone, but that stone cannot carry the boat across.
O beloved, a man who serves a teacher devoid of reality, being motivated solely by shame and intent on worldly existence, shall obtain no fruit whatsoever in this world or the next.
O Śauri, three gurus are prescribed for a Vaiṣṇava, five gurus for a follower of the Vedas and Śāstras,
and one guru for a hundred [teachings] according to the Kula tradition.
The inspirer, the indicator, the expounder, the demonstrator, the dryer,
and the awakener— these six are remembered as the gurus.
These five are the effects, and the one who awakens them is the cause;
he who performs the full initiation is the Guru, and his sandals alone are the authority.
O Maheśānī, they are worthy of worship even in their great number; there is no doubt of this.
One should [seek] the Śrī Guru, endowed with the proper characteristics, who is the cause for cutting through doubt.
O Goddess, one who has obtained [the teachings] should not rely on a teacher who bestows knowledge but lacks the essential reality;
rather, one should seek a teacher who, though perhaps unlearned, is capable of cutting through doubt.
A disciple, having gone to another guru, is not tainted by that person's faults,
just as a bee, greedy for honey, may go from one flower to another.
Likewise, a disciple who craves knowledge, and a guru as well, shall attain a state of even greater excellence.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the true guru.
Now, since initiation involves the bestowing of a disciple, the disciple is defined. In the *Tantrarāja*:
"A disciple should be of noble birth, pure in soul, and devoted to the goals of human endeavor."
Having studied the Vedas, he was skillful and had long since cast away all mental attachments.
Always seeking the welfare of living beings, possessing faith and having abandoned atheism,
devoted to his own duty, he was a devotee ever intent on the well-being of his father and mother.
Devoted to serving the teacher with the wealth of speech, mind, and body—one endowed with such qualities is a disciple; no other is so.
In the Rudrayāmala: "One who is well-steadfast, pure, of purified soul, with firm resolve, free from greed, steady-limbed, observant of the gaze, and one who has conquered the senses."
A disciple who is faithful, firm in devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity—
such a one becomes a remover of the guru’s suffering.
In the Kulārṇava: "O Mistress of the Kula, a true disciple is one endowed with all auspicious marks,
possessed of the practice of the restraints (yamas) and so forth, virtuous, and endowed with good character."

One whose body is pure, who possesses the ninefold qualities of a perfected practitioner, whose mind is pure, who is firm in his vows, who is always a support for others, and who is endowed with faith and devotion.
One who is endowed with favorable actions, vigilant, discerning,
speaking words that are beneficial, truthful, gentle, and affectionate, and who is free from ornaments.
One who grasps the meaning upon being told once, whose intellect is expansive, who remains free from agitation when lifted from the floor onto a couch or into one's lap, and who is a devoted servant.
One who censures his own interests for the sake of another's, who is pleasant-faced yet averse to worldly pleasures,
who has conquered his senses, who is well-contented, wise, and a celibate practitioner (brahmacārī).
Having abandoned mental anguish, physical illness, and restlessness, and being free from the stain of wicked suspicion,
one should be eager for devotion through the practice of meditating upon the Guru, offering praise, wearing the patched garment (kaṃthā), and serving Him.
He was a devotee of his guru as a deity, eager to worship the Kāminī,
always remaining in the presence of his guru, and bringing satisfaction to his guru.

O Goddess, he is constantly devoted to the activities of recitation, meditation, and the like, with body, mind, and actions; he is ever intent on the service of the Guru, observes the Guru’s commands, proclaims the glory of the Guru,
recognizes the authority of the Guru’s words, and is dedicated to the service of the Guru.
O Mistress of the Family, she follows his thoughts and observes the reasons for her conduct;
in the presence of the Guru, she is free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like.
One who is indifferent to worldly things, who desires the grace of the Guru,
who is devoted to recitation, meditation, and the like, and who proceeds along the path to liberation.
The Guru should accept as a disciple one who is endowed with such characteristics as these.
Now, the characteristics of a disciple [are described] in that very same [work]:
"One who is born of corrupt lineage, corrupt, devoid of virtues, and misshapen..."
Nor one who is a disciple of another, nor a heretic, nor a rogue, nor one who considers himself fallen.
One who lacks the qualification due to being inferior or superior, one who possesses deficient limbs,
one who is lame, blind, deaf, impure, or afflicted by disease.
One who is impure, foul-mouthed, or even one who is clear-minded yet a devourer of others; a lecher, a wicked scholar, one of evil conduct, crooked, and of terrifying appearance.
One who is possessed of sleep and laziness, prone to drowsiness, gambling, and the like, clothed in rags, always standing behind doors or walls with his body constantly concealed.
What is the use of one who is devoid of faith, who has abandoned devotion, who is base, stubborn, a mere messenger, sent by another, and deceitful— though he may be eloquent and free from attachment?

O Goddess, [one should avoid] that which lacks purity of bow and armor, that which is devoid of prohibitions and injunctions, that which reveals secrets, or even that which is merely discursive regarding worldly affairs.
One who behaves like a cat or a crow, who is intent on seeking out blood,
who is full of deceit, ungrateful, and a hidden burner within.
One who betrays trust, one who is treacherous toward his master, a doer of evil, one who is untrustworthy, and one who desires success by going to the enemy— [these should be avoided].

O Goddess, [one should avoid] an assassin, one who seeks to seize [another's] name, a contemptible person, a false witness, one who acts in every possible harmful way, and one who possesses the pride of being superior to all.
One who is untruthful, harsh, deceitful, vulgar, and a talkative chatterer; one who engages in evil deliberations, fallacious reasoning, and the like, and who is fond of quarreling.
One who acts as a deceiver behind one's back—whether by causing delusion, leading others astray, or mocking them—but who speaks kindly when face-to-face; such a person is a rogue.
O Ambika, he who claims to be the first speaker of speech, who is a thief of knowledge, who praises himself,
whose heart cannot endure the virtues of others, and who is afflicted and wrathful— [one should avoid such a person].

O beloved, [abandon] the Cārvāka, the wicked man, the rogue, who is censured by all the world; the slanderer, the one who causes distress to others, and [any intimacy] with those lacking true consciousness.

O Goddess, [one should avoid] one who is fair-skinned, a corpse-eater, a traitor to his master, a deceiver of his own self, one devoted to the tongue and genitals, a thief, and one disguised as a beast.
One who causes suffering through groundless hatred, servility, anger, and the like;
one who speaks what is harmful, performs no [virtuous] action, and mocks others at their vital points.
One who is lustful, utterly shameless, deceitful, of wicked conduct, and a slanderer,
yet who is free from envy, intoxication, malice, hypocrisy, and egoism.
One who is empty of envy and the like, harsh in speech, prone to malice, angry, and arrogant;
who is lacking in fortitude, afflicted by suffering, fickle, incapable, and devoid of reality—[such a person is not fit].
One whose mind is dull and of unpraiseworthy intellect, with a heart agitated by anxiety.
O Dear One, he is possessed by craving and greed, wretched, discontented, and a cooker of all things; he eats excessively, wears a single rag, is crooked, and is a deceiver.
He who possesses devotion, faith, compassion, and tranquility, yet is devoid of righteous conduct,
and who acts as an agent for his father, mother, preceptor, the wise, and great beings.

O Mistress of the Kula, [one who is] loathsome regarding family property and the like, who is conceited about serving the Guru, who hates women, who has fallen from the observances, and who has slept with the Guru’s consort— [these are the ones to be avoided].
One should accept as a disciple a teacher who possesses such characteristics as these.
If, however, one accepts or initiates [a disciple] out of affection or even out of greed, [it is a fault].
While that teacher was with his disciple, he removed the curse;
for how could a wise man ever accept such a disciple?
If, through delusion or greed, that evil is obtained— just as the evil of a minister reaches the king, and the misconduct of a wife reaches her husband—
so too, the evil committed by a disciple generally touches the teacher as well.
Thus, because one hears of the faults of a censured disciple, one should not accept such a non-disciple.
Thus are the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple. Now, regarding the examination of the disciple, it is said in that same [text]:
"The teacher should examine the disciple either through his knowledge or through his ritual practice."
For a year, or half of that, or even a quarter of that, with diligent effort.
For a superior person performing an inferior task, or for an inferior person performing a superior task, the instruction—
including the prior provision of wealth and other such matters— should be given in brief.
Furthermore, his mind was repeatedly afflicted by those of cruel conduct,
as well as by worldly people who were either partial toward others or indifferent.
And even one who has been afflicted by misfortune does not experience despondency;
thinking, "The Guru shows compassion," he always accumulates [merit] with joy.
Whether in the remembrance of the glorious Guru, or in his glorification, in salutation, service, invocation, or even in sending him forth,
there arises supreme bliss for me, as well as transformations of the voice, eyes, and other faculties.
Those who are suitable for the initiations and purificatory rites therein—
the disciple also, by means of these characteristics, should perform an examination of the Guru.
O Īśvarī, through recitations, hymns of praise, meditation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth,
one attains the capacity for the instruction of knowledge as well as the perfection of mantras.
And having understood the capacity for awakening, the disciple shall become [enlightened] and not otherwise;
furthermore, the status of disciples as being among the best of those in the higher stages of life is established in that very same place.
O Goddess, disciples are proclaimed as inferior, middling, or superior according to their fitness at the beginning, middle, and end, based on the descent of power (śakti-nipāta).
O Goddess, at first there is devotion, and they speak for the sake of initiation; yet those devotees whose devotion has again been lost are declared to be unfit for the primordial [practice].
Those who have attained the convergence of initiation and the observance of vows, being free from both ignorance and non-ignorance,
are remembered as the "middle ones" (madhyama) due to their pure vigor even through mere devotion.
In the beginning she was devoid of devotion; in the middle her devotion was merely verbal;
and at the end her devotion became abundant, as she reached the state of being worthy.
O beloved, the designations for the supreme gnosis and likewise the instruction are such that the food is for the ant, while the fruit belongs to the tree.
One attains the instruction on karma only after a long time, and the eye is likewise;
just as a monkey, having leaped from one branch to another with great effort, [reaches its goal].
O beloved, by devotion to this [teaching] of yours, one attains the fruit in your state just as a bird quickly settles upon the very fruit.
Likewise, O Mistress of the Kula, the instruction on knowledge has been taught;
thus, for the three kinds of disciples, there is a threefold instruction on knowledge.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, as recorded, in the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru. 4.
Now, since initiation depends upon both the teacher and the disciple,
initiation is described immediately after the definition of the teacher and the disciple. As it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
Since it bestows divine knowledge and thereby effects the destruction of sins,
it is for this reason that it is called *īkṣā* (the vision) by the preceptors who are knowers of the Tantras.
Alternatively, because it brings about the perfection of mantra through the proper initiation by a guru,
initiation is described by all as that which effects the destruction of sins.
Whatever sin has been committed over ten million lifetimes, whether done knowingly or unknowingly, flees at the mere taking of initiation; of this there is no doubt.
By taking refuge in initiation, a person destroys the sins of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, and so forth, as well as hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (upapātaka).
Upon initiation, a Brāhmaṇa goes to the abodeless world of Brahmā;
a Kṣatriya likewise goes to the world of Indra, and a Vaiśya to the world of Prajāpati.
By the power of initiation, even a Śūdra goes to the city of the Gandharvas;
in the descent at the root of the lineage, he receives both knowledge and realization, and the heaps of his sins are destroyed.
Therefore, those who investigate the reality of these [teachings] have declared them to be liberation.
And in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Goddess, everything is bestowed, perfectly united with the life-force of the Guru."
The wealth there consists of gold and other such items, together with silk garments.

Through that state, one attains destruction [of impurity]; thus, O lady of excellent vows, it is called "dīkṣā" in all the scriptures because it is a collection of [the meanings of] "dā" (giving) and "pada" (attainment).
Now, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is indeed obligatory,
because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for failing to perform it without cause. This has been stated in these *Āgama-kalpas*:
The wise hear of the fault of mortals who have not studied:
their food consists of excrement and their water is urine; indeed, this is their destruction.
Whether one performs that śrāddha for him, or accepts it, one goes to a very low state—
even if it is filled with devotion and offerings of every kind of flower.
Neither the gods accept worship, nor do the ancestors accept [offerings from] a maiden;
since all ritual action is in vain for one who is uninitiated, such a person is a mere beast.
And in the Kālottara:

"Likewise, for those who have been initiated, there is no entitlement [to practice] without the worship of the mantra-deities; one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva through the recitation of mantras."
And in the Vārāhītantra:
The entire world has initiation as its root, for initiation is indeed the supreme austerity;
by relying on initiation, one attains the state of a lord of the worlds, wherever one may dwell.
If one dies without initiation, one does not return from Raurava;
therefore, one should diligently resort to the initiation taught in the Trika.
The meaning is that one should perform [it]. In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"It is taught to be fourfold, according to the divisions of Kriyāvatī and so forth;
namely, Kriyāvatī, Varṇamayī, Kalātmikā, and also Vedhamatī."
These, which bring about prosperity in this Tantra, are described in their proper order;
furthermore, each one is threefold.
Thus it is stated in the Kalpasūtra:
"All sciences such as grammar and the Vedas are hidden within the Sudarśanas; this [science] is like the bride of knowledge.
Therefore, a wise person should initiate [others] there in every respect."

Initiation (dīkṣā) is threefold: Śāktī, Śāmbhavī, and Māntrī. Among these, the Śāktī [initiation] results from the entry of the Power (śakti); the Śāmbhavī from the placement of the syllables (caru-vinyāsa); and the Māntrī is that which is taught through mantras. Some maintain that one should perform all of them, while others say one may perform each individually.
And in the Kuloḍḍīśa:
"In the Śiva-āgama, the initiation intended by Śiva, the Supreme Self, is threefold: namely, the Śāmbhavī, the Śaivī, and the Māntrī."
If the Guru, having manifested the chosen deity according to the path of the mantra, should awaken the disciple, that is called initiation (dīkṣā).
Alternatively, by means of mantras, worship, and the like, through meditation,
and by the teacher via the path of yoga, in accordance with the scriptures;
"May the mantras be effective, preceded by the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the mandala;
others, however, maintain that initiation (dīkṣā) consists merely in the instruction of the mantra."

Indeed, initiation (dīkṣā) is traditionally taught as being common to all, whether it be through the recitation of mantras, or likewise through the essential parts of mantras; it resides in syllables, O twice-born one, as well as in the primordial [principles], in the Śaktis, and in the Vaiṣṇavas. Having observed the power inherent in the Siddhas, you have performed for this child a Śākta initiation that is entirely free from bonds by means of Śakti alone.
Thus they have been fully proclaimed.
Now, there is the initiation of knowledge (*jñānavatī-dīkṣā*) and another known as the initiation of power (*śakti-dīkṣā*).
There is indeed attachment for both Vaiṣṇavas and non-Vaiṣṇavas alike, even without a teacher.
The Śaiva [power], which possesses the nature of Śiva and manifests in a visible form through the destruction of the fierce teacher, is called Śāmbhavī;
it effects the immersion (āveśa) into Śiva.
"By the mere sight of the Guru, even the doubt regarding touch [is removed];
through the mantra, there arises the realization of truth known as the Śāmbhavī," so it is said in the Āgama.
Thus concludes the exposition on initiation.
Now, for the sake of initiating a disciple, one should bring the guru.
The form of the guru is the root of Dharma; the ritual action of the guru is the root of worship.
The root mantra is the word of the Guru; therefore, one should first worship the Guru.
Thus it is stated in the Mahogra-tārā-kalpa:
"That lowest of men who seizes Tārā with his hand while she is within his sight shall undergo no purification for a thousand Manvantaras."
One should receive from the mouth of the Guru the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) which destroys sins;
here, "Tārā" is merely an illustration, meaning any [such] knowledge whatsoever.
Thus it is said in the *Tantrarāja*:
"First, service to the Guru must be performed with body, speech, mind, and wealth;
having bathed on an auspicious day and having fully worshipped Gaṇanāyaka."
Having bowed to Sūrya, Hariśiva, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kamalālayā, and having likewise gratified his mother, father, and the Brāhmaṇas;
Having taken fruits, flowers, excellent food, and so forth, and being approved for the cooking,
a virtuous disciple should resort to a guru in order to attain the supreme state.
One should worship with devotion the Siddha who bestows the fruit of one's desires as if he were Śiva;
having performed three circumambulations, one should prostrate like a staff before the Lord of the Earth.
Having descended from both [vehicles] to the earth,
he joined his palms in reverence and prostrated once more before his guru.
Then, as the divine words were being spoken,
he, showing great respect, said, "O Goddess, please grant my wish," and she replied, "So be it."
Having approached the king of gurus, one should desist according to the prescribed rules;
one should never act contrary to the guru, even in thought.
A person whose mind is thus restrained should always attend upon a resident of the same village with action, mind, and speech, and by means of his own countenance.
One should meditate upon the Guru, preceded by his name, as having three eyes and two arms, bestowing boons and dispelling fear, peaceful, seated upon a white lotus on the crown of one's head.

One should not speak the name of the Guru at the time of reciting [the mantra], nor ever in jest; however, one may utter "O Śrīnātha" in times of distress or during the performance of spiritual practice.
One should salute the Guru every day with the thought: "May I obtain that same fruit which results from the worship of Brahmā, Śiva, and the other deities."
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
for one exhausted by the ocean of worldly existence, the Guru alone is the supreme refuge.
If a person should worship [the teacher] as "Guru" [in this manner],
he shall fall into a miserable state; this is the truth, the truth— there is no doubt.
But he who, having approached his guru, treats him with contempt out of delusion, is cooked in hell like a dog bound for heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Those most wicked and lowest of men who disregard the command of their guru shall never, by any means, be delivered from the sufferings of hell.
Those who, out of delusion, revile their teacher and speak ill of him,
will surely be born as pigs even for hundreds of lifetimes.
Those fools who are betrayers of their guru and are constant evildoers—
there is no doubt that for them, whatever merit or demerit there may be [will follow].
For one whose intellect is steadfast toward the guru, liberation is held in the palm of his hand;
by day and by night, he should carry out the guru’s command like a servant.
One should not transgress the words spoken by the liberated regarding that which is impossible and impure;
those who possess pride should not harbor conceit on account of wealth, birth, and the like.
One must never consume the teacher’s property, even if it has been given by him;
likewise, one should not perform the worship of deities, the recitation of mantras, sacrifices, hymns of praise, and so forth [on his behalf].
One should not engage in jesting or idle chatter in the direct presence of the Guru;
nor should one treat the sandals, the meditation belt, and other such emblems of the Guru as mere ritual implements.
One should never touch [the deity] while standing, nor should one ever prostrate with the feet;
likewise, one should avoid sitting upon wooden planks and ascending vehicles.
One should not lie on a couch, nor stretch out one's feet, nor perform stretching of the limbs or playful gestures in the presence of the guru.
Having prostrated before the sandals of the Guru, one should perform coming and going;
having reflected, one should carry out one's duties, graced by the favor of the Guru’s word.
One should not step over the teacher's shadow, nor should one walk ahead of the teacher;
rather, one should exit from behind the teacher's feet and leave the teacher's house after having prostrated.
One should effect the dissolution ordained for the disciple at the feet of the Guru;
when the Guru is satisfied, Śiva is satisfied; and when Śiva is satisfied, the three worlds are satisfied.
When Śiva is pleased, the guru is pleased; when the guru is displeased, no one is. Therefore, with every effort, one should not cause displeasure to the guru.
In this manner, one should perform the service according to the prescribed injunctions and ritual procedures.
And in the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*:
"The progenitor is more venerable than Brahmā and Rudra; he is the father who bestows Brahman. Therefore, one should honor the Guru, who is even greater than the father."
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, it is said:
"The auspicious and inauspicious nature of the lineage of the Guru should be known as superior to one's own lineage;
and the bestower of mantra should be known as superior even to one's father, O Maheśvarī."

And in the Muṇḍamālātantra: "In the morning, one should meditate upon the Guru—two-eyed, two-armed, peaceful, with hands in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness—upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name:
'Salutation to that Guru, who is the very form of the chosen deity.'"
The nectar of whose speech destroys the poison known as saṃsāra—he is the Guru;
the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara.
The Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman; therefore, one should worship him first.
For when the Guru is pleased, all accomplishments (siddhis) are said by the wise to be attained.
As is Śiva, so is Vidyā; as is Vidyā, so is the Guru. Once it has been shown by the Guru, one becomes identical with that very essence in that instant.
He who worships in the presence of the Guru while he is nearby falls into a miserable state, and his worship becomes fruitless.
When Śiva is angry, the guru is the refuge; when the guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Whether he is unlearned or learned, the guru alone is the deity.
For one who stands on the path, the teacher established in the scriptures is indeed the true refuge;
yet he who, having approached the teacher, falls into delusion and acts contrary to the teaching [is lost].
That lowest of men is cooked in hell for ten million kalpas;
he who goes before the funeral pyre must follow it as it proceeds.
Whether on a seat or in bed, one should not stand before the guru;
one may stand only after receiving permission, for by acting otherwise, one incurs sin.
Whatever food, drink, or other pleasing and delightful substance there may be,
one should offer it to the guru first and then consume it oneself every day.
Just as the sun shines in the midst of great darkness,
so the Guru alone is the illuminator for one afflicted by the cataract of ignorance.
Just as gold is produced from the touch of lion’s bile in the *Sparśatantra*,
so too does a disciple become identical with Śiva through the mere presence of the Guru.
Devotion to Viṣṇu must always be practiced toward the mantra, the deity, and likewise the guru who bestows the mantra; for that is indeed the primary means of accomplishment.
For one whose devotion to the mantra, the deity, and the guru is unwavering,
and whose mind is free from doubt, spiritual accomplishment is not far off.
"The deity should be known as the essence of the mantra, and the deity is in the form of the Guru.
One who desires their own spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) must not create a distinction between them. Thus [it is said].
Now, the characteristics of devotion to the Pādukā:
In that regard, in the *Kulārṇava*, the Śrī Devī said:
"O Kuleśa, I wish to hear the characteristics of devotion to the *pādukā*. Thus she spoke, O Queen of the Gods.
[To] the treasury of compassion.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain that which you ask of me.
Merely by hearing it, devotion quickly arises.
Or, in the *Gurumūlavali*, the objects [of worship] are described as being sewn together and swallowed;
thus, in the *Kulārṇava*, the installation of the sandals (*pādukās*) of the knowers is established.
The remembrance of the auspicious sandals is superior to ten million times ten million great gifts, ten million times ten million great vows,
and ten million times ten million great sacrifices.
O Goddess, the remembrance of the sandals is superior to ten million recitations, to bathing at ten million sacred fords,
and to the worship of ten million deities.
In times of great disease, great calamity, great suffering, great fear,
great misfortune, and great sin, the *pādukā* is remembered as providing protection.
The sandals are remembered as protecting one from misconduct, from evil means, from bad company, from improper gifts, from difficult ascents, and from wicked thoughts.
By him, the learned, the wise, and those established in knowledge have been honored;
O Dear One, he upon whose tip of the tongue the *Śrīpādukā* always resides.
Whoever worships the divine pair’s auspicious sandals with devotion even once,
being freed from all sins, attains the supreme goal.
Whether pure or even impure, whoever remembers the sandals with devotion shall effortlessly attain virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
O Dear One, one should daily offer salutations with devotion toward that direction in which the feet of Śrīnātha and Bhoja shine, as a response to their grace.
There is no mantra higher than Pādukā, no deity higher than the Śrī Guru;
indeed, there is no mantra higher than Śākta, and no merit greater than the worship of the Kula.
The root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of mantra is the word of the Guru; the root of liberation is the grace of the Guru.
O Mistress of the Kula, in this world all ritual actions have their root in the Guru;
therefore, those endowed with devotion should always serve the Guru for the sake of liberation.
Affliction, fear, suffering, and delusion— which grant undesirable objects—
persist only so long as one does not seek refuge in the glorious Guru, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
O Goddess of Devas, embodied beings who are devoted to their guru do not experience the mental suffering of all the miseries of saṃsāra.
This is indeed the fruit of mantra-siddhi; it is adorned by the mass of mantras.
This Great Sequence (Mahākrama) of the supreme reality has its root in the grace of the Guru.
Just as one who is satisfied bestows the boon-granting mantra at the end of the age,
so should one diligently honor the Guru with devotion, wealth, and even one's own life.
When one offers oneself as one's own property to Śiva, who is the self of the Guru,
then that disciple is truly such that there is no further rebirth for him.
When the disciples maintain their practice with devotion, and when there is peace through dreams,
the preceptor being pleased, all the sins of the disciple shall be destroyed.
Even in their minds, those who live for the sake of desire do not long for [worldly things];
yet the Lords, who are compassionate toward their devotees, bestow all such prosperity upon them.
The gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as sages and yogis, are pleased when all three worlds are pleased; there is no doubt that they are pleased when the Guru is pleased.
Indeed, when instructed by a compassionate Guru who is satisfied by his devotion,
the disciple becomes liberated from karma and becomes a vessel for both devotion and liberation.
That which is to be accepted from the teacher by the disciples is when the teacher has been satisfied;
therefore, they should act kindly toward the teacher through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Or, O Dear One, if he has been instructed by his preceptor— who is fully satisfied— anywhere whatsoever that "you are liberated," he too, being liberated, may perform sacrifice.
Or else, by some non-manifest power,
the Lord effects the liberation of the great beast through the form of a Guru.

Salutations to him who possesses the three and fourfold dress; even if he is a dog-cooker, if he is my devotee, from him [the teaching] should be received, for he is indeed to be honored just as I am.
Even a Brahmin, though endowed with virtues, is not praised if he lacks devotion;
whereas even a Mleccha, though devoid of virtues, is called a disciple if he possesses devotion.
O Vakuleśānī, refuge of all, for one devoid of devotion to the Guru, austerity, knowledge, vows, and noble lineage are merely ornaments that delight the eyes of the world.

One whose impurities have been burnt away by the fire of true devotion to the Guru is worthy of worship, whether he be a follower of his own tradition or another; however, neither a learned man nor an atheist is worthy of worship.
O Goddess, what need has he for dharma, artha, and kāma, since liberation stands directly before him— he whose devotion to the Śrī Guru, the source of all goals, remains steadfast?
"He is Śiva, the abode of the Guru, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon me"—
for one who remembers him with such devotion, spiritual perfection is not far off.
O Kuleśvarī, for him who possesses supreme devotion toward his guru just as he does toward the Lord,
all these goals indeed become manifest.
O Goddess, just as devotion is due toward Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, and one's own father and mother, so too should it be practiced toward one's own guru.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, Girijā and Giri,
the venerable Guru and the lineage of Gurus, and my parents.
O Goddess, just as all perfections are obtained through the mother-of-pearl shell,
O Beloved, so too are they obtained through sacrifice, charity, austerity, pilgrimage, vows, and the like.
O Mistress of the Kula, as unwavering devotion toward the Śrī Guru increases,
so too does his realized knowledge increase.
Of what use are pilgrimages and the like, or great yogic powers, or vows that wither the body?
For those who possess sincere service and devotion toward the Lord of Gods and toward the true guru, these are indeed sufficient.
O Goddess, whatever fruit is obtained even through great physical hardship and asceticism, that same fruit one obtains with ease by serving the Guru.
O Goddess, for those seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation, and for those desiring the supreme state, devotion to the Guru alone is the path; there is no other—so says the Śruti.
Inauspicious deeds and those arising from the great sins—
devotion burns them in an instant, just as fire consumes a heap of grass.
Salutations to that Viśveśa, the mind, the bestower of all perfections,
by whom even the sight of you yields a sorrowless fruit.
Neither yoga, nor austerity, nor ritual worship, nor any sequential practice whatsoever dissolves [the self] here;
in this illusion-free Kulamārga, devotion alone is preeminent.
O Goddess, in everything that is directly composed of the Guru,
one who possesses intelligence yet forms the notion of a mere human toward the Guru, or the notion of phonetic purity toward the mantras, or the notion of a well-polished stone, shall go to hell.
If one should fail to recognize the Guru, or even if one were to recognize him,
there would never be accomplishment for that person through mantras or through the worship of deities.
O beloved, for those who remember and speak of the glorious Guru together with common folk, their merit indeed becomes their every sin.
In this world, one's parents must be worshipped with great effort;
however, the preceptor is especially worthy of worship, for he is the bestower of both dharma and adharma.
The guru is the father, the guru is the mother, the guru is the god, and the guru is the refuge;
when Śiva is angry, the guru is the protector, but when the guru is angry, there is no one at all who can save you.
Indeed, one should do what is beneficial for the guru through the actions of speech, mind, and body;
O Goddess, by practicing what is harmful, one is born as a worm in excrement.
Those who abandon their body, mind, and vital breaths for the sake of the venerable Guru fall into the state of worms, insects, or moths; of this there is no doubt.
By abandoning the mantra of the Guru, one becomes impoverished by death;
one who abandons the Guru and the mantra shall go to the Raurava hell.
O beloved, reflecting upon the supreme words spoken by the Guru as a blessing,
one should remember even when struck by him that it is his grace.
One should offer the various foods and edibles;
or, O Mistress of the Kula, one may do so while reflecting, "This is the remnant of that."
Furthermore, one should completely purify the most grievous sins against a guru;
one should perform a pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*),
and likewise [perform] the giving of a debt, the release of a slave, charity, association, and buying and selling.
Having become a disciple, one should never act [inappropriately] toward the gurus,
nor [should one occupy] their place.
Having observed [the teacher], one should go some distance away and sit with companions;
for the teacher’s [instructions] exist, and one should mutter the mantra of the Guru.
That worship should also be performed seven times daily;
one who bears the lotus feet of the Guru should carry the burden upon his head.
Therefore, that which must be done by the disciple is the command; the Guru is traditionally remembered as being of the nature of that command.
Whatever has been heard elsewhere, such as from mantras or the scriptures (āgamas), one should not report that to him.
By the command of the Guru, one should take that liṅga... [text missing].
