And he should perform everything according to the command of all; O beloved, he should not embrace a woman who is not his wife.
Having prostrated with devotion, O beloved, he should rise with his palms joined in reverence.
After departing from the teacher's house while bowing, one should exit with the right foot first;
then one may sit on a single seat together with the teacher or those equal to him.
O Goddess, there is no restriction regarding seats for the deity or the guru in their presence;
however, the lion-throne should be offered to the guru, and the best seat to those who are senior.
A divine seat is for the youngest [of the brothers], while the others share a common seat;
or, one who is superior by birth, learning, or wealth may joyfully look upon the elder from a distance.
Having performed one prostration like a staff, one should perform three circumambulations;
then, having bowed down three times, one should offer ten oblations with clarified butter, beginning with the eldest, or even just one.
"O Dear One, one should salute that Guru with the formula 'Gurutadguruyoga'; then he should state his own name before the Guru, and the Guru should then restrain him."
In the presence of one's preceptor, disciples should not even think of their own teacher;
through the perception of the preceptor, they should regard everything—whether it be a deity or a blade of grass—as the preceptor himself.
However, one should indeed bow to images made of stone, metal, or clay with the mind alone;
one should perform three prostrations to the guru and only one to the elders.
Likewise, one should offer salutation with joined palms to those worthy of worship, and verbal homage to others;
[one should honor] the gods, teachers, women, those who uphold [the dharma], the wise, the enlightened, and those whose wealth is austerity.

O Mistress of the Kula, one should bow to those who are superior in knowledge and established in their own duties; likewise, a woman [should bow] to a twice-born man, to one who has honored his guru, to a heretic, and to a learned man, even if he be deceitful.
One should not bow to a performer of forbidden acts, nor to one who has strayed from the path of truth, nor to one who remains in a state of impurity;
likewise, one should not bow to a teacher who eats alone while residing in the same village.
Because of that, his food would become impure and he would be born as a wild boar in the forest;
therefore, a disciple residing in the same village should bow to the guru at the three junctions of the day.
Standing even at a distance of one *krośa*, one should bow to the Guru daily with devotion;
a disciple should prostrate from half a *yojana* away on the five sacred festival days (*parvan*).
Whether the forest extends for one yojana or up to twelve yojanas,
a disciple situated in a distant land may, through devotion, come into his presence.
One should bow to the Guru within a distance of that many yojanas;
however, if the disciple is situated very far away and so desires it, then he may go [to him].
One should not see a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, articles, and so forth, according to one's ability.
O Goddess, he who does not act in this way shall become a brahmarākṣasa;
the Guru’s consort, his son, and the Guru’s eldest brother are equal to the Guru himself.

O Mistress of the Gods, one should behave toward the family leader like a son, and toward the preceptor of the lineage, as well as toward the elder and younger gurus, with the utmost humility, avoiding self-deception.
One should perform the *gurukalpa* (the ritual of honoring the guru) and prostrate just as one does to one's own guru.
The first is the word-command (*vākya*), the second is the elder of the lineage (*kulajyeṣṭha*), and the third is the elder of the family (*kulajyeṣṭha*).
"O Goddess, the fourfold [nature] of the Guru is thus the fourfold nature of the Eldest;
as long as one is liberated through the supreme discourse on the Eldest, by means of the eight-limbed yoga."
One should perform salutations according to the prescribed rite for the guru, the family tree (kulavṛkṣa),
and for all venerable kinsmen such as one's father, mother, and others who occupy the highest rank among those worthy of worship.
One who is unable [to perform duties] due to reasons such as rising from one's seat or lack of physical capacity does not incur fault;
however, one should not falsely represent oneself by assuming the form of a teacher.
If one,
having become [the deity], should perform prostration toward the fettered beings (paśu), then he would be like a deity in terms of rising to greet them, measuring them, and so forth.
He who has obtained a stationary Guru by means of a count of sandals is called a "great beast" and shall incur the curse of the deity.
O beloved, he should be regarded as a guru and honored by the elders;
thus, I have told you something regarding the characteristics of the conduct concerning the sandals (pādukā).
In brief, [this concerns] the Lord of the Family and so forth; what more do you wish to hear?
Now follows the rule regarding the time for service (*sevā*).
That has been stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
Furthermore, by what means does a Brahmin become [subject to] agitation, or a Vaishya likewise, or a Shudra by women, or similarly after four years?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, auspiciously, in the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru. 5.
Now, since mantras consist of the nature of sound (*śabda*), the creation of sound and meaning is first described.
As it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*:
He is remembered as "Ña.

Its meaning is as follows: he is both devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)—meaning free from attributes—and possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*)—meaning endowed with attributes—in that dual form. [The qualities are...]
Because it would contradict the Vedic scripture which states: "Brahman is indeed one, without a second; there is not even the slightest thing else."
It is true that Brahman is one alone; its own [nature] is such that,
just as there is no multiplicity in the sun when it is reflected in various objects during worship for various purposes,
so too [is the case with Brahman].

There are two delusions in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. O Aṅkura, all beings are rooted in the immutable; through the various forms of Māyā, this Indra assumes many shapes. Thus [is] the oneness... *Note: Due to the significant textual corruption and lacunae in the source fragment, the translation reflects the recoverable portions of the philosophical content while acknowledging the gaps.*

O Supreme Goddess, from the totality of manifestation (*vebhavāt*)... [the following is the meaning: the discussion regarding the arising of the *bindu* from the *nāda* is as follows: *kalā* refers to *prakṛti*, because it is the counter-principle to that which begins with the *śruti* (the ear) and *avidyā*.
From the Supreme Lord, through the sequence of ignorance, [proceed] the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

From Him, who sustains sovereignty, there arises this power consisting of both existence and non-existence; even in the world, it is observed that "this one is capable" and "this one is incapable. Its conduct takes the form of the Puruṣa, and because it is considered as such, it is therefore known as Prakṛti.
Consisting of the Puruṣa, having the nature of the syllable *Oṃ*, and composed of Śiva and Śakti, it is directly divided threefold; its divisions are proclaimed to be Bindu, Nāda, and Bīja.
The meaning of the word "asu" (life-force) is that this Bindu, being composed of Śiva and Śakti, becomes divided into three parts.
The syllable *ha* is Śiva, consisting of the three Vedas; the syllable *sa* is Śakti, joined with *tā*.
This has been stated in the Yogatantra: [p.
"Haḥ" is the Puruṣa, and "saḥ" is Prakṛti.
Among these, the name of the first bindu is *bindu*, the name of the second bindu is *nāda*,
and the name of the third bindu is *vāja*.
The bindu is Śiva, the seed-syllable (bīja) is Śakti, and nāda is the union of these two;
this is declared by those who are experts in all the Āgamas.
From that *bindu*, Raudrī was born; from the eightfold source of the intellect, she arose. She was produced from Vāmā and the others, and she is superior even to Rudra and Brahmā.
The natures of perception, will, and action consist of the three fires whose forms are the two suns;
Raudrī, Rudrotyā, and so forth belong to Bhadra, who is of the nature of Śiva.
Raudrī is so called because she is the cause of Bindu and is of the nature of Śiva;
Jyeṣṭhā is the power whose feet are Viṣṇu, for Viṣṇu is of the form of Śiva’s power.
She is the cause of the eldest [Brahmā], because she consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti;
she is the power (śakti) beginning with "samā" and "brahmā."
In that [state], there is the nature of power (*śaktyātmakatva*),
because the seed-syllable (*bīja*) that has become the channel for the form of Rāma is of the nature of power.
Thus say Kātyāyana and Mātraya regarding Brahmā, the lord of Rudra and Rāma.
These consist of knowledge, will, and action.
The meaning is that these powers— knowledge-power (*jñānaśakti*), will-power (*icchāśakti*), and action-power (*kriyāśakti*)— are of the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*).
They are the seed-nature of the lights that are about to arise, which possess the form of the three eyes.
And in the Jñānārṇava:
O Supreme Goddess, know the nature of the Self to be the *haṃsa* within this very supreme reality,
adorned with the three points (*bindu-traya*).
The meaning of "that which exists as a union (saṃpuṭa) and has come [to me] as 'mā' belonging to me" is that it exists as the true Mātṛkā that has been spoken.
It is accompanied by the *uccāra* because the *bindu*s are of the nature of Brahman.
The state [of consciousness] resides in the domain of the exhaled breath;
for this very reason, it is called "carrying the yoga" (yogavāha).
O Maheśvarī, I shall now describe the three drops (*bindu*) in the form of seed-syllables (*bīja*), which abide through the union of vowels and consonants.
O Pārvatī, know that within the syllable *haṃ*, in the form of the *bindu*, is Brahmā;
in the letter *sa* and by means of the *bindu* of emanation (*sarga*), there is Hari and I, O Sovereign of the Gods.
In this world, due to the connection with their respective states of being, they are called Hari and Hara;

however, for one who has realized Brahman, there is an abiding in absolute independence, while for one who has realized Viṣṇu and Rudra, there is an abiding together with them because of their auspicious renown.
O Maheśānī, Brahmavindu is called Vāmā-śakti;
because she vomits forth the universe, she is proclaimed as Vāmā-śakti.
Jyeṣṭhā is indeed the Vaiṣṇavī power, protecting the world by her own nature, because protection is the foremost duty;
thereafter, O Supreme Goddess, she becomes Raudrī, gradually devouring it.
Because it causes fear for those who swallow [it],
know the three drops (*bindu*) to be thus adorned by the three qualities (*guṇa*):
the drop of Viṣṇu is the quality of *sattva*, the drop of Brahmā is the quality of *rajas*, and the drop of Rudra is the quality of *tamas*.
By the word *bindu* is meant the void (*śūnya*), which likewise indicates the [three] qualities (*guṇa*).
Nevertheless, according to the sage Māsa, its meaning is "not in reality" (*tattve na*).
It consists of will, knowledge, and action, and has the nature of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
Know, O beloved, that the three principles are identical with the three cities.

The meaning is that the threefold reality consisting of the three cities (puratraya)— namely, the gross, the subtle, and the supreme body— is composed of the three principles (tattva) of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
O Great Goddess, all this is established within the three *bindus*;
O Goddess, Ambikā, through the *bindus*, is both the supreme and the non-supreme of the three qualities (*guṇas*).
The state of the union of the *bindus* is *Aṃvikā*; there is no connection with the qualities (*guṇa*) of the root *bindu*, because the qualities arise from the three *bindus* alone.
The meaning is that they are superior even to Rāma and others who have transcended the three qualities (guṇas).
O Dear One, the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states arise from the three bindus.
The waking state is to be known as characterized by the quality of sattva, consisting solely of the nature of power;
it is the expansion of mental activity, characterized by the desire for pleasure and pain.
Deep sleep (suṣupti) is of the nature of Śiva; it is the destroyer of all mental fluctuations (vṛtti). This means it is of the nature of tamas.
In deep sleep, those [fluctuations] are absent; at the beginning of waking, the dream state consists of rajas.
She is described as possessing both sets of characteristics, yet marked by the characteristics of a *kṛṣṇā*.
The meaning is: by means of the characteristics of waking and deep sleep.
Even in the state of dreaming, craving persists for the individual soul (jīva).
When that is spoken, it is heard:

even in a dream, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the experiencer of pleasure and pain within the world of the universe imagined by its own *māyā*; at the time of lack of satisfaction, the entire powerful one [is]... [the rest of the passage is obscured].

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement that "it carries away all functions," because [in that case] only pleasure would exist. Furthermore, through the connection with the karma of another birth, that very same [state] becomes new again...
At the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking, it is characterized as mere throbbing radiance.
Having reached the state of being fully ripened,
she is liberated from the qualities (*guṇa*), transcendent, and eternally free; O Goddess, having spoken thus with compassion, she departed.
Sleep occurs at the beginning and end of your recitation, while wakefulness may also occur;
elsewhere, there is the throbbing [of consciousness],
which is the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).

The meaning is that they are of the nature of echoes. Devoid of the knowledge of "is" or "is not," where conceptualizations and mental constructions (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*) do not exist due to the absence of the mind (*mānasī*); likewise, she who is beyond the mind (*amanas*), consisting of pure consciousness (*vidyānuvālīya*), and free from the mind, is Rohiṇī.
Liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), the innate state, and the fourth state (*turyā*) are the wheel.
The Śruti says: "In that which is spoken of... [The seed-syllable] beginning with the Śrīkrama is the seed;
it is not the Moon because it is captivating to the mind. Its seed-syllable and so forth...

The autumnal [scriptures] are the Mervāgama and others. "Word-Brahman" refers to the meaning of the word; others say it is the Word itself, the supreme Bindu, which is established within the body as the perfection of form and the intellect. The Unmanifest Self, whose nature is not grasped as "this-ness" or "that-ness," is the resonance (*dhvani*) that is the cause of sound.

In reality, however, it is *dhvani* itself, when conjoined with consciousness (*caitanya*), that is called *Śabdabrahman*. Its detailed exposition under the names "unstruck" (*anāhata*) and so forth is found in the Yoga scriptures; this should be verified in the section on Yoga.

Having attained that form of Kuṇḍalinī situated within the bodies of living beings, she manifests through the nature of phonemes (varṇas) according to the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth. As stated in the Jñānārṇava: "Born from the three points (bindus) and the resonance (nāda), she takes the form of the Kalpas."
The detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the sequence of the dawn [chapter].

Now, Śambhu—the soul of Viṣṇu, whose own self is a digit (kalā), the witness of the world, the all-pervading Sadāśiva—is the binder of Time (Kālabaṃdhu). [The phrase] "for the sake of the staff" (daṇḍāya) refers to the binder of this Time—past, future, and present—who is its progenitor; thus, there is no origination of Time from him.

In some versions, there is the reading *sūcitādantaraṃ mattetvotpattiṃ kalāvandhoriti*. According to that view, the phrase *kamātmānam* is redundant, because its identity with that [power] is already obtained through the principle that "there is no difference between power and the possessor of power" (*śakti-śaktimator-abheda*). Furthermore, since time (*kāla*) is also included within the word and its meaning, there is the arising of that [time].
Therefore, because of the affection for this commentary, the recitation occurs at that very time.
From Sadāśiva comes Nadīśa, and from him the emergence of Rudra;
indeed, the manifestation of the fundamental stage of the self-substance has been accomplished.

It is said that from Mahat, which consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the qualities (*guṇa*), arose the uncut *ahaṃkāra*. From that, due to the distinction in creation, there is a threefold *ahaṃkāra*.
From the *vaikārika* (sāttvika) *ahaṃkāra*, the eleven deities arise.
The directional deities, Vāyu, Arka, Nabhastā, Śrī, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, and Mitra;
From that, the sense organs beginning with fire (tejas) were established through the application of their respective mantras;
from the ego (ahaṃkāra) characterized by the quality of being (bhūta), the five elements were produced.
From sound arose space; from touch, air; from form, fire;
from taste, water; and from smell, earth—such is their origin.
And likewise, in the Sāṃkhya system: from *prakṛti* arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-sense, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*);

from the five subtle elements, the five gross elements (*bhūta*); and from the five gross elements, this world—namely, the clear ether (*viyat*), the wind (*marut*), and here it is said, the pure water (*payaḥ*).
The earth is yellow; the five elements arise one by one from the support of the Bindu.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are known as the qualities of the elements.
The circle marked with six dots belongs to the Moon;
the triangle accompanied by a svastika belongs to Vahni (Fire); and the upward-pointing *dhenu* mark is associated with Indra.
The wise ones should fashion mandalas upon the ground according to their respective natures: the lotus-shaped for the Moon, the square for the Earth, and the double-vajra for Vajra.
They say that these are indeed adorned by mantras and enveloped by their respective names;
the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti are known as belonging to the five elements, starting with earth.
That [state] is Nivṛtti; it shall be established as Vidyā, followed immediately by Śānti;
and that which arises from the body of Nāda is to be known as Śāntyatītā.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, is composed of the five elements.
The non-moving is divided into many kinds, such as the distinctions between cows, trees, and so forth.
Mobile beings are divided into many types: those born from sweat, those born from moisture, and those born from a womb. Those born from sweat include worms, gadflies, and the like;
those born from eggs include birds and the like.
Old age, birth, and so forth are declared for those humans;
their emergence occurs from the union of male and female through the combination of semen and blood.
The single drop, possessing the essence of both, sequentially bestows two natures:
when blood is predominant, it becomes female; when semen is predominant, it becomes male.
Constrained by the fetters of delusion in accordance with past karma,
a certain self then assumes the state of a living being within that [womb].
Then, nourished by food, drink, and other necessities provided by his mother, the embodied being gradually develops over days, fortnights, and then months.
Now follows the exposition on the origin of the body.
As it is stated in the *Yogārṇava*:
"The *kaulika* [stage] occurs in one night, and the *budbuda* [stage] in five nights."
A layer of flesh is washed away in ten nights; in fourteen nights, it is completely removed.
On the twentieth day, when the state of the *pelī* is observed, there is dense flesh;
on the twenty-fifth day, at the time of the *puṣṇa*, a *pala* [of weight] develops all the sprouts.
When one month is fully completed, one should sustain the five elements;
when two months have arrived, the dissolution into Śiva occurs.
The marrow and bones [are purified] in three months; the ankles and feet in the fourth month;
and the ears, eyes, and nose in the fifth month.
In the seventh month, his mouth, face, belly, thighs, arms, and ears are formed;
by the eighth month, all his limbs are fully developed.

Thus, through the faults [of the humors] and sufferings, one who has attained happiness becomes manifest; he perishes along with those devoid of sense-faculties. Due to the faults of wind, bile, and phlegm, the seven bodily constituents (dhātus) become painful.
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these are pierced by it.
The eyes, tongue, and nose are known as the organs of perception; sound and the others are considered their objects. The organs of action are likewise [to be known].

The wise call the hands "pāka" (the cook) and the feet "pādya" (the one who goes); from these [terms], they declare the objects of the organs of action. The internal organ of the self is proclaimed as fourfold:
mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness.
The ten sense organs, the five elements, and the mind constitute the sixteenfold mahat.
The unmanifest, the Great Principle (mahat), and the eight elements—these are the mantras, and the Great Principle as well.
Those who know the seven principles understand the transformations to be accompanied by ego (ahaṃkāra).
In the lotus, that which consists of fire and moon is the Bindu;
the right side is known as the sun, and the left side is the maker of night (the moon).
The channels are of ten kinds; among them, three are proclaimed as the principal ones.

In the center, there is a channel (nāḍī) whose nature is that of Agni and Soma; these are known as Gandhārī, Hastijihvā, Svapūṣā, Lambuṣā, Yaśasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, and Kuhu—these are the seven channels. From them, infinite channels have arisen, as well as the vital winds beginning with Prāṇa, within the five joints of the Suṣumnā; thus say the followers of the Ātharvaṇa.
Having attained the state of branches and sub-branches beyond the Śivanakṣatra, those who investigate the meaning of the body say there are one hundred and fifty thousand [channels].
The root-support (mūlādhāra) has reached them; indeed, they proceed toward that very source.
The winds are said to be tenfold; here, ten fires are remembered.
The vital breaths and other winds are five: Nāga, Kūrma, Dhanañjaya, [Kṛkara, and Devadatta].
The exposition of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth is found in the Yogārṇava.
Padmā is that agent; she is prāṇa, apāna, and likewise vyāna.
Because of the upward movement of the fire, she is samāna; because of the upward movement [of breath], she is udāna.
Because it moves upward, its path is not at the mouth of the channel;
the Kūrma [wind], which is the Uddhārakṣāraka and the Nāga, causes [the eyes] to open.
The Kṛkara wind performs its function through yawning; then, O Devadatta, the Dhanañjaya wind performs many kinds of actions within this body.
In the *Śāradā*:
"Due to the faults and sufferings of the fires, embodied beings are dissolved into the ten [senses]."
The names of the fires are given in the *Yogārṇava*:
Bhrājaka, Rañjaka, Kedaka, Snehaka, Dhāraka, Bandhaka, and the seventh is called Drāvaka.
Pāvaka, Pācaka, and Śūyaka is recorded as the tenth; and in the Śāradā [Tantra]:
"Hunger and thirst are recorded as the two servants of Prāṇa."
Grief and delusion, as well as the decay and death of the body—these are the six evils.
From semen come the flesh, bones, and marrow; from blood come the skin and the membranes.
This sixfold composition, O Kauśika, is said to exist in the bodies of all embodied beings.
Thus situated within the womb at that time, remembering the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of his previous birth, he remains there, miserable in nature, his body concealed by old age and impurity.
And in the Yogārṇava:
"If my exit should occur through the narrow opening of the birth canal, may I constantly contemplate with a virtuous mind the realization of Brahman."
I shall practice the knowledge of Śiva, which delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra;
then, having become a yogi of Śiva, I shall attain that supreme liberation.
In the course of time, that infant even causes distress to his mother;
then, having developed a solid body, he becomes one who finds no pleasure in the realm of Yama.
For a moment he remains motionless, wishing to weep out of fear;
she, whose nature is that very consciousness, is all-pervading and possesses every form.
Having attained proximity to Śiva, they are characterized by the arising of the quality of eternal bliss;
initiated at the beginning, they are unimpeded, auspicious, and followed by all the gods.
Through the distinction between the higher and the lower, she is remembered as this Supreme Power (Paraśakti),
dancing perpetually and effortlessly within the lotus-heart of the Yoginī.
In the *ādhāra*, the Goddess exists in the form of lightning, vibrating through all beings;
she stands encompassing everything by means of the successive whorls of the conch.
The Goddess, who consists of all the gods and whose speech consists of all mantras, has entered the body of the coiled serpent, which is dear to her.
The Goddess, who consists of all reality, is manifest, subtler than the subtle, all-pervading,
the mother of the three abodes, and whose nature is the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
Consisting of forty-two syllables, yet having the form of the fifty letters;
the possessor of qualities, present in every limb, Kuṇḍalinī is the supreme deity.
Awakened as the soul of the universe, she gives birth to the world consisting of mantra;
by this sequential yoga, the beloved of Śiva is multiplied.
He composes thirty-six Śaiva principles (tattvas),
as well as other auspicious mantras and yantras that bring forth blessings.
The pervasive Viśvanāyikā, multiplied by forty-two,
gave birth to the all-pervading Kuṇḍalinī, who consists of the Śabdabrahman.
From that [Parā] comes Śakti, from that Dhvani, from that Nāda, from that the Niḥvodhikā;
from that the Ūrdhvaretas, from that the Bindu, and from that arose Parā.
Whether it be *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, or *vaikharī*, sound is produced from the *mūlādhāra* after being multiplied forty-two times over seven births.
Regarding the sequence therein: first, the power consisting of sound [is] that *kuṇḍalinī*; [then] *taṃ*, *bhā*, *dhanyā*, and so forth.

The preceding and succeeding states of sounds arise from Kuṇḍalinī alone; therein, Vaikharī— which consists of the manifestation of articulated speech— is impossible to describe specifically as something distinct, because its nature is that of the primordial state of sound.
Consisting of will, knowledge, and action, and having the nature of the qualities of fire,
this Kuṇḍalinī creates, in this sequence, the garland of phonemes.
The meaning is that the "elemental script" (bhūtalipi) consists of forty-two [phonemes] beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
When multiplied by fifty, it becomes the garland of fifty letters; it is the differentiated power (*bhinna-akalā*) belonging to that which possesses the elements.
The Rudras and so forth, in sequence: (p.
28b) the Rudras are Śrīkaṇṭha and the others; "kalās" means portions, being parts in the form of divisions of Maheśvara.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), Pūrṇodarī, Keralikā, and others are included.
The fire becomes the destroyer; the half-moon becomes the moon.
From the union of both the sun and the moon, there arises the moon, the treasury of splendors.
From that [source], the phonemes (varṇas) emerged as consisting of Śiva’s power (śakti).

They remained composed of the nature of fire and moon (agnīṣoma), having attained their manifestation through that fluid essence consisting of Śiva and Śakti, and thus they took on the forms of the moon, the sun, and fire. This establishes the essential nature of the phonemes as being fire, moon, and sun.

The fire situated in the *giro* syllable is in the form of a half-moon, and the moon situated therein is in the form of a bindu; the sun is likewise situated there. For this very reason, it is called the "threefold state.
Therefore, I shall now declare the manifestation of the phonemes within the mouths of men.
Constantly impelled by the vital winds, they flowed forth from the cakras.
In the organs of articulation beginning with the throat, they manifest sequentially;
among these, the vowels (svara) are remembered as gentle, while the consonants (sparśa) are powerful and bring auspicious results.
In the beginning, all were pervasive, having the forms of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni;
the vowels are renowned as sixteen, and the consonants (sparśas) are twenty-five.
The letters beginning with *a* are known as the essence of reality (*tatvātman*), since the Puruṣa consists of touch (*sparśa*);
pervading all, they bestow desires, wealth, and grain.
In the Vārāhī Tantra:
The vowels are renowned as sixteen, and the consonant groups (vargas) are twenty-five;
the reciters (japakas) are said to be ten, and they are proclaimed to be the trees.

In the first [state] they are said to be *sāttvika*, in the second they are remembered as *rājasa*, and the pervasive ones are declared to be *tāmasic*; one should apply those three according to what has been described.
Among the vowels, the first is short and the subsequent one is long according to the sequence;
these [vowels], ending with the bindu and the visarga, are Śiva and Śakti respectively.
The bindu is declared to be the male sun, while the night-maker (moon) is the power of emanation;
that which is the first of the vowels is the neuter *caska*.
The short vowels situated in Piṅgalā and joined with Iḍā should drink [the breath];
Suṣumnā is to be known as the middle [channel], and these four are neuter.
Without vowels, the manifestation of these [consonants] does not arise clearly;
therefore, the wise declare those letters to consist of Śiva and Śakti.
Since the Mātṛkā is produced from the five elements as its cause,
therefore the letters, which consist of the elements, are divided into five groups according to their respective parts.
Fire, earth, water, and space—these five powers and their essences follow in sequence;
they are the five short vowels and the five long vowels, ending with the nasal bindu and produced through their combinations.

The twenty-five [principles] and so forth, along with the secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), have been proclaimed; they arise from the letters of the Mātṛkā by means of the left, the sun, and fire (i.e., the vowels, consonants, and semi-vowels). Those thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) are the digits of their respective mandalas.
Now, the digits of the moon, the sun, and fire, as well as the arrangement for the installation of the Śrīpātra vessel, shall be explained.

From the various divisions of the letters of the *mātṛkā*, all mantras emerge. Through the classification of mantra-vidyā, there are diverse types of mantras. Mantras are to be known as having male deities, while vidyās are remembered as having female deities.
All mantras are declared to consist of female, male, and neuter natures; [among these,] the male mantras...
Those ending in *haṃ phaṭ* are for purification; those ending in *śūḥ* are considered feminine;

and those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter. Thus, mantras are joined with these three types [of endings]. These three kinds of mantras are recommended for the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent magic (*abhicārika*).

The mantras for both cruel and gentle rites should be understood as having Agni and Soma as their essence; for those performing rituals, they are generally said to consist primarily of the elements fire, stars, earth, and space.
The Manus are fiery and lunar; they are mostly gentle, full of the moon, and free from cruelty.
The fiery ones are fully awakened when the fiery one moves within the vital breath as its protector.
The Vidyās and Mantras are declared to be, respectively, female and male deities; for the sake of wisdom, the mantras are of three kinds, having the forms of female, male, and neuter.
Feminine mantras end with the "fire-born wife" (svāhā); those ending with the "heart" (namaḥ) are neuter;
the remaining are said to be masculine. Furthermore, feminine mantras are used for rites of pacification (śāntika).
Mantras are recorded as neuter for the rites of inciting enmity and causing possession; all mantras are recorded as masculine for the rites of subjugation and eradication.
Indeed, all the mantras whose nature is fire and soma consist of the syllables *re*, *o*, *vi*, *yat*, and *prāya*;
they belong to the fire-god and are used for cruel rites.
They are gentle, like the moon, and abound in the *svadhā* offering; they are remembered as performers of lunar rites.

When the breath has entered the *iḍā*, they are perceived as having the nature of the moon; when it has entered the *piṅgalā*, they are perceived as having the nature of a well, a pond, and a blazing fire.
Indeed, when the Piṅgalā and the downward-moving breath (apāna) are awakened, all [the channels] are awakened;
all the mental faculties (manas) are awakened, and these are the fruits for practitioners.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti*, composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha with devotion toward the Guru, this is the tenth chapter.
For the sake of his own purification, the teacher should satisfy his disciples;
having deliberated long and with effort, he should bestow the mantra, but once given, he should not have second thoughts about it.
Thus, because [this] has been obtained through the extreme grace of the Guru by virtue of the words of the King of Mantras, the defects and qualities of mantras are now being examined.
As it is said in the Śāradātilaka:
Those [mantras] corrupted by defects such as being "cut" (chinna) do not protect the practitioner;
they are described as being cut, obstructed, devoid of power, or turned away (parāṅmukha).
Deaf and sightless, as well as pinned down and paralyzed;
burnt, fallen, terrified, soiled, and insulted.
Bhedita, Suṣupta, Madottata, Mūrchita,
Kṛtavīrya, Hīna, Pradhvasta, and again Bālaka.
Furthermore, a mantra may be a "boy," a "youth," an "unmatured," an "old," or a "cruel" one; likewise, it may be "seedless," devoid of accomplishment, or even "fraudulent."
One who is *niraṃśa* (partless) is devoid of essence; one who is *kaikarī* is seedless.
One who is *dhūmita* (smoky) is marked by signs, and one who is *lohita* (red) is afflicted by hunger.
If it is described as excessively greedy, one becomes deficient in limbs;
if excessively angry, one is said to be cruel; if excessively modest, one is full of shame; and if excessively tranquil, one is likewise [so described].
One who has fallen from his position and is incapacitated is proclaimed as "bound" (baddha);
I shall now describe the specific characteristics of those who are devoid of affection and those who are afflicted.
That mantra whose beginning, middle, and end is released from its own *vāyu* (the letter *ya*),
whether conjoined or disjoined, is furthermore threefold when occupied by a deity (*surā*).
That mantra is designated as "severed" (chinna) when it appears fourfold or fivefold;
whether joined or separated, the seed-syllable of Vāyu (ya) is placed at the beginning, middle, and end—this is one characteristic.
Furthermore, that same seed-syllable, when joined with vowels, is seen to be threefold, fourfold, or fivefold—this is another [characteristic].
[This refers to] a single moment; the meaning is that it is the fault of one alone.

That [mantra] which is marked by the pair of *bhū* (the earth-seed syllable) at the beginning, middle, and end, and whose mantra is obstructed, should be known as being devoid of both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*).
A mantra that lacks the three principles (tritatva), the venerable seed-syllable (śrīvīja),
and the downward-moving breath (vāvahīna) should be known as being devoid of power (śaktihīna), provided that these do not exist within its middle portion.
*Māyā*, *māyā-bīja*, the *tritatva*, the *praṇava*, the sun (*ravi*), and the seed-syllable *phreṃ*— the connection with the subsequent [words] is that these are in the middle of which.
The *kāmabīja* is at the beginning, followed by *māyā*, the disciple, and likewise the *kuśa* grass.
This letter 'ha', when joined with the bindu, is declared to be turned away (parāṅmukha).
If [the mantra] lacks the syllable *iṃ* at the beginning, end, or middle twice over, it is considered deaf;
for the five-syllabled mantra is devoid of the sun (*pha*) and the moon (*i*).
One should know that [a mantra] lacking the *netra* (the eye-syllable) bestows suffering, grief, and disease.
Furthermore, those mantras originating from the *prāsāda* [mantra] are produced at the beginning, middle, and end.
I bow to that which consists of the letter *i* with the *bindu*, the syllable *śrīṃ*, or likewise the four-part *ravi*; he in whom this resides is firmly fixed.
The word *kalā* signifies four parts; its inherent nature is the fourth vowel.
This means the fourth vowel (*au*). There is one in the middle, two in the *tū* [of *tūrjita*], and in this *asva*, there are *puraṃdara* (the letters *a* and *ra*).
That mantra does not exist which, when its head is joined with fire and wind, would be paralyzed or cause the accomplishment of fierce deeds.
The knower of the thread should consider that [mantra] as being seen in seven ways:
by two, three, four, eight, or ten syllables; it is most excellent when accompanied by the face [the seed-syllable] and established with the Praṇava.
Whether it be Śiva or Śakti, that [mantra] is proclaimed as being "from fear" (*bhītataḥ*).

A mantra composed of two, three, or eight syllables, beginning with the word *astra* (weapon), is [so called]; in that case, if the word *astra* is seen, it is [the meaning]. As for the phrase "whether Śiva or Śakti," Śiva here is indeed the letter *sa*.
That mantra which possesses four "ma" syllables at its beginning, middle, and end is stainless; one should avoid all other types of mantras.
He in whose head the threefold form of pride or anger remains as the weapon of the mantra is said to be "overwhelmed."

If a mantra has the syllables *hya* and *dva* in the heart (*hṛdaya*) and head (*śīrṣa*), and *vaṣaṭ* and *vauṣaṭ* in the middle, it is pierced; such a mantra should be abandoned by the wise when seeking spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
I am composed of three syllables; that which is deficient is declared to be "svatyupta.
Alternatively, it may be a mantra or a vidyā consisting of seventeen syllables.
That mantra which begins with the five *phaṭ*s and so forth is declared to be "slow" (*manda*);
that mantra in whose middle the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) of reality (*tattva*) resides is "fainted" (*mūrchita*).

"Likewise" means in five ways. "The mantra of a limb which has departed from its potency is called *visaṃma*"; this means that for which there is no specific *aṅga-mantra*. The application, however, is through the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

The cessation of the mantra is "virā," and that [mantra] is new. A mantra joined with four squares at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the head should be known as deficient; such a one would consist of eighteen syllables.
The mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables is joined with the Tāhaṃ.
Hṛllekhā is declared to be situated below;
it is known as the seven-syllabled mantra, consisting of the letters of Kumāra and Unnata.
The mantra of sixteen syllables is that of a youth, while the mantra of forty syllables is mature;
the thirty-syllable mantra is [the age of] thirty,
and the six-syllable mantra is [the age of] six.
Furthermore, that which consists of four hundred syllables is called "Vṛddha" (the aged).
A mantra of nine syllables joined with the *dhruva* is declared to be "Nistriṃśa" (the sword).
That mantra whose end is the *hṛdaya* [mantra] and whose middle consists of the two *śivau*,
or which is devoid of *śiva* and *śakti*, is known as "seedless" (*nirbīja*).
This is the *phaṭ*-kāra which is seen sixfold in these positions within the *ṣoḍhā*.
That mantra would be devoid of accomplishment;
or that twelve-and-a-half-syllabled mantra is said to be "smoky" (dhūmita) and is therefore censured.
If it consists of twenty-one syllables situated with three seed-syllables, it should be known as "afflicted by hunger"; however, one of twenty-four syllables [is likewise afflicted].
That mantra which consists of thirty syllables is called "embraced" (āliṅgita);
a mantra of thirty-two syllables is proclaimed as "deluded" (mohita).
That which consists of twenty-four syllables and that which consists of twenty-seven syllables;
when afflicted by hunger, the twenty-four-syllable [mantra] is for the Yakṣas.
A mantra consisting of eleven syllables, or known as having twenty-five,
or twenty-three letters, is declared to be "satisfied" (tṛpta).
A mantra of twenty-six syllables is proclaimed to be delusive;
one of thirty, twenty-nine, or nine syllables is likewise prescribed as being deficient in its limbs.
That [mantra] which consists of twenty-eight syllables, or even twenty-one,
is said to be excessively wrathful and is censured in all ritual acts.
Beginning from forty and continuing up to sixty-three,
that number of mantras is declared to be designated as "with shame" (savrīḍa).
Those whose mantras consist of fifty-five or sixty syllables are of tranquil mind;
[this applies] from fifty-five syllables up to ninety-nine syllables.
Those mantras which have fallen from their place in the scriptural tradition are considered by the wise to be defective;
likewise, those mantras that consist of thirteen or fifteen syllables are also [considered flawed].
They are considered to be deficient by eighty, or one hundred and fifty,
or two hundred and ninety-two, or even less than that, according to the [measurement of] Meru.
Or three hundred; their number is declared by you to be without affection (niḥsneha), beginning from four hundred up to a thousand syllables.
One who is excessively aged should always be excluded from sacrifices by the wise. Mantras consisting of more than a thousand syllables are known as *daṇḍaka* and are considered difficult to master.
This mantra of two thousand syllables should be received in its hundred parts; these mantras, as they truly exist, must be understood in their form as hymns.
Likewise, the sciences should be understood by ministers in all undertakings;
the fool who resorts to spells that cause harm and mental affliction [is lost].
"Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons"—
one should apply such mantras, which are tainted by defects like these, to oneself.
One should purify [the area] above with the fire through the *yonimudrā*;
however, the *yoni-mantra* bandha must be explained in the section concerning the morning ritual.
In the Gautamīya [Tantra]: "Abiding in the state of being a beast, the mantras, consisting merely of the forms of phonemes,
having been awakened from their deep sleep, attained the status of sons."
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as the power of consciousness (cit-śakti) within the corpse;

having revealed one's own true being (ātma-sadbhāva) within that very power in the supreme sky (paramavyoman), which is nourished by the supreme nectar (paramāmṛta), there shall be the performance of fire-offerings (vahni-homa) and so forth.

Now follows the examination of the wheels (*cakra*). Regarding that, it is said: "The wheel of division, the wheel of Hara, the six-petaled wheel, the wheel of the Siddhas and so forth, the wheel of the zodiac signs and lunar mansions, and likewise the wheel of one's own *kula* and *akula*."
The Aḍakaḍamaṃca, the Kaḍaṃva, and likewise the Vargacakra.
The nine cakras have been described, which bring about the accomplishment of mantras;
by meditating upon the self as the lord of the nine cakras, one becomes fit for the desired goal through the mantras.
O Dear One, even the deliberation regarding the *gaṇacakra* is the consensus of some;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the highly auspicious *haracakra*.
Having understood this, one becomes a man of knowledge in this world, the most excellent among those who know the mantras;
otherwise, one should avoid the mantra—so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Therefore, with every effort, one who is wise should arrange the *tārākoṣṭha* (star-cells) endowed with the *devakoṣṭha* (divine cells), but not those of the *kṣatra* (warrior) class.
The collection of Āgama scriptures does not constitute a [separate] scripture; thus, there is no birth [of such a category], and so forth, in nine ways.

By this, the four quadrants in the four directions for the refined ones are indicated; in those directions are four quadrants, with one central quadrant. In the middle of that, one should divide the quadrants into four using diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*).

The term "tetrad" (catuṣka) means that there is no omission of the laying down of the central thread; thus, it constitutes a set of four. Otherwise, there would be only two diagonal threads (karṇasūtra).
When the four diagonal threads are applied to the arrow [of the grid], the meaning is that a square cell consisting of a wheel (cakra) comes into being.
One should cast Durgā, Vāṇī, Tārā, and Bhairavī into the directions; one should join them at both ends of the ear-line within the [cardinal] points beginning with Indra.
Tripurā and Bhuvaneśī, likewise Tryambaka on the sacred seat (pīṭha),
Vāsudeva and Priya, as well as Chinnamastā and Caṇḍikā.
Beginning with Īśāna and ending with Vivasvān, they are likewise arranged in sequence; then Indrāṅkī, Heramba, and immediately after, Pitāmaha.
One should draw Mahāmāyā and Kālī, as well as whatever other gentle deities there may be; one should write the fifty letters in sequence, beginning from the square of Īśa (the northeast).
Here, by each successive step, there is the grasping of the squares through diagonal movement.
The mantra performed by the mother and father, refined for all rites as appropriate, is used for the inspection of that [specific] mantra.
Beginning with the salutation "Namo," one should perform the formal acceptance when it is within the range of the deities and when they are completely pure; never when they are impure.
Wealth, a son, gain, and even loss;
agitation, liberation, happiness, and righteousness; as well as the boat that grants all desires.
One should contemplate the determination [of the letters] in the *koṣṭhacakra*; this is what has been stated.
Here too, the sequence is from right to left.
Thus ends the *haracakra*.
Now, the *akahaḍā-cakra*. This is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"One should draw five lines with their tips pointing east, and likewise [five] with their tips pointing south."
Then, by means of four sets of four, there shall be four compartments.
The northeast (Īśāna) consists of four squares, as do those in the southeast (Āgneya);
likewise, there are four squares situated at its end and four situated to its left.
These are declared to be Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddhi, and Ripu.
Of these, [the first] is in the first squares, and after that, in the second ones.
In the third and fourth [sections],
the wise one should again write the letters from 'a' to the visarga and from 'ka' to 'kṣa' respectively in reverse order.
Having drawn the [mandala] of the peaceful deities, one should then write the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*;
this is stated in the *Rāmārcanacaṇdrikā*.
O Rudra, at the beginning of the Indu [1], then seven, three, twelve, ten, six, eight, sixteen, fourteen, and fifteen;
in these squares of the Bhūta-cakra, the wise man should place the letters starting from his own name in their respective order, wherever the letter of his name shines forth.
From that [central] square, the practitioner should count up to the final letter of the mantra.
Then, in the *maru* (desert) grid, one should write in sequence: *siddhasiddha*, *susiddhāri*, *arisiddha*, *mariṃ*, *sādhya*, and *marisvasi* within the *sādhya* square.
One should then count the *sādhya*, *siddha*, *sādhyasādhya*, *susiddha*,
and *sādhyāri* in their proper sequence.
Susiddha is at the beginning of Siddha, while Susiddha is indeed Sādhya;
thereafter is Susiddha, and Susiddhāri has gone to the desert (maru).
One should know the *ari-siddha*, *ari-sādhya*, *su-siddha-ripu*, and *ari-ari*;
these four should be avoided. (p. 31a)
A *siddha-siddha* [mantra] is accomplished according to what has been stated; a *siddha-sādhya* is accomplished through two qualities.
A *siddha-siddha* becomes effective through recitation (*japa*), while a *siddha-sādhya* becomes effective through twice the number of recitations for its kin. However, a *siddha-sādhya* is useless.

From the *triguṇa* (three-fold) calculation, one becomes *sādhya* or *susiddha*; a *sādhya-ari* (enemy of the *sādhya*) destroys [the lineage], and a *gotrajā* (born of the same clan) is a *susiddha*.
Half of the *jarā-sādhya* results from the authority over wealth; thus, a *susiddha* [enemy] destroys [the lineage] in an instant, and a *susiddha-ari* destroys the caste.
The *arisiddha* [mantra] kills one's sons; the *arisādhya*, however, causes leprosy. The *susiddha* brings about the death of one's wife, while the *nirmūla* destroys everything.
Others say that [the mantra] is liberated in the Mālinī-tantra:
"That which is well-perfected at the beginning and the end bestows the power of all desires;
that mantra whose enemy ends in the letter 'ā' (ākāra) should be concealed."

Those that are already perfected at the beginning are accomplished by doubling [the recitation]; O fair-faced one, in whatever mantra the perfected syllable occurs at both the beginning and the end, it is mastered.
In a very short time, he shall become the bestower of all accomplishments;
however, one who is joined with a *sādhya* or similar [sign] achieves success only with great difficulty.
In the beginning, the Siddha-mantra is "Śatrughna," and the Sādhya-mantra begins with "Satya"; these are taught by the best of mantra-knowers.
Through the recitation of these mantras, which possess the three qualities (guṇas), one attains perfection according to the established conclusion (siddhānta).
That which is "unsuitable" (āsādhya) is well-established; it is accomplished by the prescribed method.
First, that which is "suitable" (sādhya) is below [the neutral]; one should avoid the "enemy" (śatru) with great effort.

The *siddhānta* beginning with *susiddha* is as previously stated; through it, the deity is accomplished. Furthermore, that which begins with *susiddha* and is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) observes the four groups.
The *śuddhādi* (pure-beginning) is proclaimed as the middle;
the *ādhāri* (supporter) is the *antasiddhāri* (enemy of the end-perfected), and that too must be abandoned in the ritual procedure (*prakramaṇi*).
That which is established as yielding auspicious results in the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end,
or that which is declared in the Tantras to be neutral toward all objectives, is [the Sādhya].
One who has fully mastered the three positions shall accomplish all objectives;
for one whose enemy has entered the three positions, the mantra is death—of this there is no doubt.

The wise declare that a mantra beginning with *siddha*, having *sādhya* in the middle and *asādhya* at the end, is useless. A mantra beginning with *siddha*, having *siddha* in the middle and [another] *siddha* at the end, accomplishes all desired objectives. A mantra beginning with *siddha*, having *ari* (enemy) in the middle and [another] *ari* at the end, is proclaimed to be destructive.
However, when an enemy is at the end and the *siddha* is in the middle, it is a mantra for the practitioner.
Success in one's undertaking will come with great difficulty, and the fruit will be extremely meager;
if it occurs at the end, it will be in the presence of enemies, whereas if it occurs at the beginning or the middle, it is a pair of achievable results.
The task will be delayed, and he will quickly perish;
when the goal is to be accomplished at both the beginning and the end, that which was to be accomplished becomes successfully achieved.
Indeed, both the sādhya and the siddha [mantras] are accomplished through an abundance of recitation;
likewise, one that is encased by the enemy [mantra] may become either a siddha or a susiddha.

It should be known that this mantra causes the total destruction of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt. However, when the goal (sādhya) is separated by a *siddha* syllable, and likewise when separated by a *susiddha* syllable, this mantra becomes quickly effective even for one who is naturally dull-witted; so he said.
Furthermore, the enemy may be intercepted by a Siddha planet, or perhaps by one that is Susiddha.
He is not an enemy to the kingdom, but rather he succeeds only with great difficulty;
whereas those who are *sādhya* are quickly successful, and even one who is *susiddha* is like a father.
The mantra is accomplished only with extreme difficulty for the practitioner; otherwise, it is like an enemy hidden within, and such a mantra should never be imparted.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
"But that mantra which is wicked and always censured— [this is] the consideration of the enemy and so forth."
As it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
"The line from east to west is twelve in number, and likewise five [lines] situated between south and north."
One should write the letters from *ma* to *ṇa* in the middle;

from the northeast (*īśa*), one should write two consonants each in five squares for the five vowels, the remaining vowels in six squares (one each), and the remaining consonants starting with *ka* in eleven squares in their respective order, one by one. [The numbers are] eight, twelve, and two.

The Sādhya syllables are multiplied by fifteen, five, four, four, three, and eight, and nine respectively; then the practitioner's syllables are multiplied by ten, three, two, eight, eight, seven, five, six, and two. From the remainder of the sum of these two [products], when added to "namo," "jvala," and so on, up to "śeṣāt," the greater remainder shall be the debt or the wealth.

Now, another method for that same [calculation]: the letters of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are indeed the sky (0), fire (3), ocean (4), Vedas (4), space (0), void (0), fire (3), and sky (0). The letters of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) are indeed the mouth (1), fire (3), five (5), vowels (16), mouth (1), moon (1), sky (0), fire (3), Vedas (4), and moon (1).
And in the Mālinītantra:
"Six, two, four, one and a half, zero, fire, four Vedas, and sky; sky, fire—these are the numbers for the target syllables in the purification of the mantra."
Fire is your mouth, the arrow is your own; the sky is your eye, and the ether is your ear.

The number of ears and moons (two) is proclaimed by the Tantrikas as the "sādhaka" mark. That which is greater is to be known as "sakrāṇī"—this is the opinion of those who know the Tantras. In every case, the square (koṣṭha) is the same. Another method:

This has been stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "Taking one’s own name and adding one syllable to it, one should count it all around until the end of the first syllable of the mantra. Having multiplied it by seven on the left, the wise man should divide it by seven."
Whatever measure remains is declared to be the debt;
this very [measure], up to the middle, I shall now describe.

In the reverse method (*viloma*), one takes the first syllable of the mantra and counts up to the first syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). When this is divided by two, the remainder indicates the result: if the number of the *sādhya*’s syllables is greater than that of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), he is known as being in debt (*ṛṇī*). Thus say those who know mantras; [furthermore], the name of the *sādhya* is doubled according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, as is the number of syllables in the practitioner’s name.
Adorned with vowels and consonants, one should double the [number] of the practitioner's [name] as well, combine them, and subsequently divide by eight for the practitioner.
That person is to be known as a creditor; this is remembered as another method.
A debtor planet bestows auspicious results, whereas a creditor planet and others produce inauspicious effects.
"It is declared that [the result] is auspicious when the rising is equal; such is the opinion of those who know the Tantras. Now follows the exposition of the Nakṣatra-cakra according to the Yāmala.
Aśvinī is formed by a pair of mouths; Śravaṇā is said to be from three;
Kṛttikā is from three; and Rohiṇī is from four.
Ekāśa shall be Mṛgaśīrṣā, and Astrā shall consist of one letter;
from here I shall fully explain the constellations according to the division of vowels and consonants.

Furthermore, Punarvasu is declared by two [letters], and Āśleṣā is said to begin with the letter *ka*. Maghā is said to consist of two [letters] beginning with *pa*, and Pūrvaphalgunī likewise consists of two [letters] beginning with *ka*. Then, Uttaraphalgunī arises from two [letters] beginning with *ta*; thereafter, Hastā is proclaimed to consist of two [letters] beginning with *ca*. From that...
From the letter *sa* comes Parva; from *kṣa*, the next day, Tāviṣā; from two letters, Lipi; Anurādhā from three letters; Jyeṣṭhā occurs from one letter;
then Mūla from three letters; and Pūrvāṣāḍhā from the letter *va*.
From the letter *va* comes Uttarāṣāḍhā, and from the letter *ca* comes Śravaṇa.
From that, Dhaniṣṭhā consists of two [stars], and Śatabhiṣā consists of one hundred and eight;
Pūrvabhādrapadā consists of two, and Uttarābhādrapadā should consist of three.
Revatī is proclaimed by means of two vowels as the indicators; thus,
in this sequence of the lunar mansions, the conjunction with the phonemes is declared.
Starting from the first letter of one's name and ending with the first letter of the mantra,
the best of practitioners should repeatedly count the births and other such cycles.
The hosts of gods and men are traditionally said to reside in Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Puṣyā, Punarvasu, Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Revatī, Ārdrā, Svāti, and Jyeṣṭhā.
Rohiṇī, Bharaṇī, and likewise the three Pūrvas and the three Uttarās—these are known as the hosts of mortals among the stars; the remaining ones are remembered as the hosts of Rākṣasas.
And in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"Aśvinī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, as well as Puṣya, Punarvasu, Hastā, Svātī, Anurādhā, Revatī, and the asterism whose deity is Viṣṇu [Śravaṇā]."
Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, as well as Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī; Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā; and Pūrvabhādrapadā and its younger sister, Uttarabhādrapadā.
O beloved, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Citrā, Viśākhā,
Jyeṣṭhikā, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣā belong to the hosts of Rākṣasas.
Viṣṇu is the deity of the Śravaṇa constellation, belonging to the class of divine beings;
Ahirbudhnya is the deity of Aśleṣā, belonging to the class of human beings.
Now, regarding this *Prītiśātrava* in the *Rudrayāmala*:
affection for one's own group is excellent; toward a god, it is middling; toward a human, it is inferior;
toward a deity, a Rākṣasa is death; and toward a human-Rākṣasa, it is likewise death.
This investigation, however, is indeed distinct from the [treatment of] constellations; it has been written here by way of connection to the constellations.
And in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Due to the desire for attainment, the first [letter] is *pa*; the hand of Rudra is *ru*; the first [hand] is *ru*;
[the letters] are *lo*, *ka*, *lo*, *pa*, *pa*, *ṭu*, *pra*, *ya*, *ṅ*, *kha*, *la*, *ghā*, *te*, *śu*, and *bhi*."
When the last two vowels proceed from the sequence of letters up to the end of Revatī, then this is its meaning:
the letters are those beginning with 'a' and so forth, within those asterisms.

The vowels (uditāḥ) are presented as constituent parts in successive order; this is the convention (*śaṅketa*). Regarding the consonants (*prādīnām*), for whichever letter the final consonant occurs in a position corresponding to a certain number, that many letters beginning with 'a' are to be placed in the grid (*koṣṭha*) in sequence according to that same number. This is the convention.
Birth, attainment, adversity, security, progress, decline, death,
and supreme friendship— these states, beginning with birth, recur again and again.
Furthermore, in the *Yāmala*:
"In the auspicious [nakṣatras], there is one, two, or eight [letters]; in others, it is according to the number of stars.
However, if the name does not correspond to a nakṣatra, one should investigate a nakṣatra based on the name."
In the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"Ten lines should be drawn from east to west,
and one should likewise draw four lines extending toward the south."
One should write the letters to be accomplished there, protecting them in their proper sequence:
two, one, three, four, one, moon, moon, pair, pair, bearer of digits (sixteen), pair, pair of itself, earth (one);
wing (two), three moons (three), Hara’s eyes (three), earth (one), Indra (four), wing (two), one wing (one), Śiva’s eye (three)—these are the letters of the God.
One should write the remaining letters, excluding the vowels 'vi', 'du', 'va', 'sva', 'rga', 'svara', and the final letter 'au'.
The names of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī have been declared in their proper sequence. A wise person should write [the name] starting from the first letter of the birth asterism,
up to the final letter of the name to be accomplished (sādhya), repeating the cycle of birth and so forth again and again.
Birth, perfection, adversity, security, enemy, accomplisher, and death.
*Mitra*, *paramamaitra*, and [the others] bestow fruits equal to their names.

On the tenth day, there will be royal fortune; on the eleventh, purity shall prevail;
on the twelfth, all success will be attained; and on the thirteenth, poverty shall occur.
On the fourteenth day, there is birth as an animal; on the new moon day, there is loss. At the end of the fortnight, there is an increase in merit; one should avoid Vedic study [on these days].
One should avoid these and other days mentioned in the Śruti— such as the twilight hours, the day of a defeated army, a thunderclap, an earthquake, and the fall of a meteor.
Thus, according to the Vaiṣṇava tradition, initiation is said to be supreme; it is auspicious even during censured months and during eclipses.
There is no time on earth equal to the moment of a solar eclipse.
In that regard, whatever action is performed there, one shall obtain infinite fruit. As stated in the Śaktiyāmala:

Then, it is declared that [the merit] is a hundred-thousandfold during an eclipse and on one's own birth-day.
During the sun's transit into a zodiac sign and likewise during a solar eclipse,
one should never consider any matter such as the ascendant or other astrological factors.
Especially on the Mahāṣṭamī, for the sake of accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth,
there is no need here for the purification of time, nor the calculation of lunar days or constellations.
At the time of the hand-grasping of the glorious Guru, likewise at Kāśī, Prayāga,
the holy pilgrimage site of Kurukṣetra, and in the four Devī-pīṭhas.
Likewise, on Śrīparvata, a practitioner of mantra should not distinguish between the proper and improper time;
for if it falls on a Sunday, there will be suffering, whereas on a Monday, it bestows peace.
One should avoid initiation on a Tuesday, for it destroys longevity;
on Wednesday one attains beauty, while on Thursday there shall be wisdom.
One attains good fortune under Venus, while there is loss of fame under Saturn;
likewise, the fourth, ninth, fourteenth, and eighth lunar days [are unfavorable].
The full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh,
as well as the thirteenth and the tenth, are praised as bestowing all accomplishments.

The auspicious initiation should take place during the bright fortnight, or according to the fifth chapter, during the dark fortnight; likewise, those desiring liberation should perform it in the dark fortnight, while those desiring worldly power should do so in the bright fortnight.
The rite of initiation performed on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight bestows auspiciousness;
under the asterism Aśvinī one attains happiness, and under Bharaṇī one becomes wealthy.
Under Kṛttikā one will be miserable; under Rohiṇī one becomes a master of speech;
under Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; and under Ārdrā there is the destruction of kinsmen.
In Punarvasu there will be the acquisition of wealth; in Puṣya, the destruction of enemies;
in Āśleṣā, one will become miserable; and in Maghā, one will meet with ruin.
Indeed, on the two Phalgunīs, the mind of the animal becomes agitated;
under Hasta there will be loss of wealth, and under Citrā and Svātī one shall become happy.
In Viśākhā there is happiness, and in Anurādhā there is the destruction of kinsmen;
in Jyeṣṭhā one's intellect becomes impaired, while in Mūla there is an increase in fame.
If it occurs under Pūrvāṣāḍhā or Uttarāṣāḍhā, those two bring fame;
under Śravaṇā one becomes miserable, and under Dhaniṣṭhā there is poverty.
If birth occurs under Śatabhiṣā, there will be intelligence; under Pūrvabhādrapadā, poverty;
under Uttarabhādrapadā, happiness; and under Revatī, an increase in fame.
In the signs of Taurus, Leo, and Virgo, or in the ascendants known as Sagittarius and Libra,

seventh, sixteenth, or eighteenth [counted from the lord of the year].
One should avoid performing auspicious rites under the nineteenth, twentieth, twenty-third, and twenty-fifth lunar mansions.

In the Kuloḍḍīśa [Tantra]:

Then, the best of mantra-knowers should worship, in order from top to bottom, [the deities] beginning with Vahni (Fire) around the squares to be accomplished by pairs in the upward direction.
"Koṇa," and so forth: by means of the diagonal lines (*koṇasūtra*), [the squares] become halved within the pairs of double-squares (*dvandvakoṣṭha*).
In the Brahma-square, there are two squares each situated above and below within the four corners (*koṇacatuṣka*), following the sequence.
The meaning is "in them. The wise man should recite the Sāvitra [hymn], Savitṛ, Śakra, Indrajaya, Rudra, Rudrajaya, and likewise the Āpaḥ and Paratsaka— these five.
That ear-thread is effective at both ends within the pairs of squares;
it is Śara, Guha, Tāryamāna, Jaṃbhaka, and Pilipicchaka.
Then one should worship Carakī, Vidārī,
and Pūtanā in the four directions starting from the east, in the squares at the beginning and end of each half.
The wise one, following the procedure for the Lord in eight divisions,
should worship Īśāna, Parjanya, Yama, Śakra, and Bhāskara in due order.
Sadyojāta, Vṛṣākapi, Antarikṣa, as well as Agni and Pūṣan; then Vitatha, Aya, Asaṅga, and the one known as Gṛharakṣaka.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga, then Nirṛti;
the two known as Vārika and Sugrīva, Varuṇa, and Puṣpadantaka.
Asura, Goṣava, Gau, Dharma, those known as Nāga and Sukhya, Soma, Bhallāṭaka, Vakula, Āditya, and Aditi.
Having recited the Sāman for the gods and filled their footprints with the five types of dust, one should then offer oblations (bali) to those deities from within them with these [verses].
It should be provided with milk-rice and other offerings, accompanied by incense and flowers,
prepared with sesame seeds, and adorned with black gram rice and similar foods.
O Brahman, accept this offering and destroy the defects of the site;
[herein are] perfumes and other substances, camphor, cakes, and milk duly prepared.
Truly, accept this state of nobility and utterly destroy all faults. || 1 ||
O Lord, accept this universe honored with sandalwood and adorned with camphor and agallochum;
destroy all its defects.
O Lord, accept this pleasing offering consisting of jaggery, milk-rice, flowers, and other items; grant me peace from my friends.
Accept this essence-offering, including the master's portion, along with perfumes and other items mixed with milk;
having made me the earth, destroy all my defects.
"So be it. Having offered the bali-oblation, one may take [the remainder] from others according to one's will;
this is the general rule for the bali-offering performed in a clockwise direction.
Indeed,
for all types of sites, there is a specific determination of the location;
[one should offer] flowers and the like, water with *kuśa* grass, and [incense] adorned with camphor and *agaru*.
"O Sāvitra, indeed, take hold of this person; grant him peace here. || 6 ||
O Lord, accept this offering of flour-cake mixed with jaggery and filled with red sandalwood paste, incense, and other perfumes; destroy the obstacles and mantras of Sūrya. || 7 ||
O Lord Śakra, accept this white food, as well as flowers accompanied by saffron and other offerings; take this pleasing bali; salutations to you, O God. (8)
O Indra, accept this delightful offering adorned with *udana*, clarified butter, and other [substances];
victory to you! Homage be unto you!
O Lord Rudra, accept this pleasing bali-offering consisting of cooked and uncooked meat, along with cloth, flowers, and other items; salutations be unto you!
O Rudra, accept this offering consisting of meat, cooked ghee, and various perfumes, flowers, and so forth; be victorious and grant me well-being. || 11 ||
Accept this pleasing oblation, joined with milk and sugar and adorned with flowers and other offerings; O Waters, grant me peace.
O child, accept this offering of curd mixed with jaggery and endowed with perfumes and other ingredients; destroy the obstacles here.
O Goddess of Gods, accept this offering of ghee, rice, meat, and perfumed food, well-adorned; protect us and destroy all obstacles.
O Skanda-rākṣasa, accept this offering consisting of fish, flowers, and other items, placed upon a bed of black gram; destroy all obstacles.
O Aryaman, accept this ball of flour mixed with meat and accompanied by cooked meat and water; O sole Rākṣasa, destroy the obstacle.
O Jambhaka, accept this offering of blood, flesh, rice, and fish, accompanied by perfumes and incense; protect us and destroy all obstacles. || 17 ||
O Rākṣasa, accept this meat accompanied by goat and Kaṇva, combined with red perfumes and the like, along with Palipiccha; destroy this obstacle.
Accompanied by red flowers and joined with red garments and the like, O Vidārikā, accept this; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa! || 19 ||
O Rakṣas, accept this bali offering brought to you, which is endowed with yellow garments and the like, and joined with red perfumes and the like; destroy all obstacles.
This meat, prepared with clarified butter and endowed with flavor, fragrance, and other qualities—O Carakī, come to this house; O Rākṣasī, destroy the obstacles!
O Lord, accept this bali offering— consisting of clarified butter, unbroken rice, and adorned with red cloth and other ornaments— which removes all defects of the site.
Accept this pleasing offering consisting of blue lotuses joined with milk-rice and accompanied by garments and other gifts; O King of the Gods, salutations to you!
O conqueror of spirits, accept this five-cubit long, bright yellow banner adorned with rice-offerings and the like; take this pleasing oblation, salutations be unto you! (24)
Oṃ! Accept this pleasing bali-offering of rice mixed with ghee and adorned with the five red substances and so forth; O King of Gods, homage be to you!
Accept this pleasing bali-offering, accompanied by red flowers and endowed with red perfumes and other offerings; O Bhāskara, salutations to you! (26)

O Satya, accept this canopy, which has the luster of smoke-colored [saffron], adorned with the beauty of perfumes and other offerings, and these red flowers; accept this bali-offering; homage be to you!
But take this meat-offering, indeed filled with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
accept this bull-oblation and destroy the defects of the site.
But this tiger-flesh, combined with offerings such as oblations, accept this pleasing bali and grant me peace from the sky-demons. (29)
O Seven-Tongued One, accept this excellent substance, whether it be a lump or combined with garments, perfumes, and so forth, as well as clarified butter and the like; salutations to you!
O God Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering consisting of milk mixed with parched grain and adorned with red flowers; salutations to you! || 32 ||
O Vitatha, accept this offering endowed with curd, fragrance, and other such items, along with yellow flowers; destroy the obstacle to our food.
O Lord Yama, salutations to you; accept this pleasing offering brought from the house, consisting of food soaked in honey and adorned with red garments and other ornaments.
O Lord of the House, come to this house which is adorned with red meat, rice, and new yellow garments; it is pleasing to you; salutations to you!
O Gandharva, accept this offering combined with various fragrances and red flowers; always destroy all evils.
"O Bhṛṅgarāja, take this tongue of the Nākulī plant placed upon the meat; grant me auspicious peace. (37)
Thus, accept this pleasing offering (bali) accompanied by ghee and sesame seeds, and joined with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; O Root Deity, salutations to you! (37)
Accept this offering of sugar-cane pieces mixed with sugar and adorned with red sugar-candy and the like; being pleased, destroy all defects.
This mantra, however, belongs to Nairṛta. || 38 ||
"O Gatekeeper, salutations to you; accept this pleasing offering consisting of sandalwood, agallochum wood, and various fragrant flowers. (39)
O Lord, O Sugrīva, please accept this milk-rice adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; take this oblation and grant me peace.
O King of Waters, accept this pleasing offering, beautifully adorned with barley, rice, and wheat upon the cooked food; salutations to you.
O Puṣpadanta, accept this offering consisting of kuśa grass, a heavy monthly meal, clarified butter, and perfumes; grant me peace.
O Lord of the Gods, accept this offering, ground together with honey and adorned with perfumes and other ornaments; destroy all defects.
"Accept this offering (bali) consisting of ghee and honey combined, along with camphor and other ingredients; O Śeṣa, grant me complete peace. (44)
O Lord, accept this offering of water-born lotuses, rice, and ornaments such as fragrant flowers;
destroy this disease and all its defects.
Accept this pleasing offering, adorned with garments, ghee, food, and other delights; O you who have a deer for your vehicle, salutations to you! (46)
O Lord of Pātāla, accept this rice mixed with meat and adorned with the scent of milk and other ingredients; destroy whatever obstacles are here.
"O Lord, accept this primary offering consisting of coconut water, cooked rice, yellow garments, and so forth; destroy the defects of the site. (48)
Accept this offering (bali), consisting of fermented liquor mixed with honey and accompanied by fragrant flowers; O Nema, destroy all defects. 49.
O Bhallāṭha, accept this offering of *udana* mixed with honey and accompanied by fragrant incense; receive it with joy, for salutations be unto you! 50.
Accept this pleasing offering of black gram cooked with rice, anointed with ghee, and accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; O you named Maṅgala, salutations to you!
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this pleasing offering of wine mixed with honey and joined with red perfumes and other substances; salutations to you!
Combined with milk and sugar-candy, and adorned with various offerings of worship,
O Mother of the Gods, accept this and destroy all defects.
Alternatively, one who knows the mantras should perform the offering of the *bali* with mere mouthfuls of food, placing the *praṇava* at the beginning of the name and ending with "namas."
This bali offering is declared to be the destroyer of all obstacles;
yet he who undertakes the construction of a house or similar works without having worshipped the deity of the site (Vāstudevatā) [is guilty].
In that place, everything would become empty and surrounded by demons, obstacles, and the like;
therefore, those who desire all prosperity should perform the worship of the Vāstu deity.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha, the eighth chapter is thus recorded.
And in the Kuloḍīśa: "Now,
when the ascendant is auspicious, on ground cleared of husks, charcoal, and the like,
free from the movement of people, and devoid of grass and such."
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should construct the mandala according to the rule,
using either the "lotus-hand" gesture or the hand as previously described.
Furthermore, having caused [the disciple] to recite, one should construct an auspicious maṇḍala with five, seven, or nine [deities]; such is the opinion of other authorities.

In this regard, the following is the calculation: one fortnight consists of five times seven; by that, one fortnight consists of twelve times seven; by that, one [year] consists of sixteen [fortnights]. This constitutes a single syntactical unit with the beginning of the speech [of the Kula-udḍīśa], where there is a conjunction. And in the Kuloḍḍīśa:
It is square, with four doors, endowed with a railing and other features,
joined by sixteen pillars, four of which are situated in the center.
Vedīs eight cubits in height stand all around;
those pillars are five cubits in measure, and there are twelve of them.
Regarding that, the supreme teacher of the earth, Likhita, states in the *Vāstuśāstra*:

"One should place the five-finger-breadth mark on the ground; this is the procedure for all essential [constructions]. On both sides of the door, there are two [units] each, as well as the corner and the customary practice."
A wise person should construct a mannequin measuring two cubits;
this site for the pavilion is said to be twelve arka-angulas (twenty-four finger-breadths) in area.
One should wrap it with colors on coconut leaves from the left side,
making it symmetrical with four doors and adorned with four arches.
The Nyagrodha archway is in the east; in the south, the Īśvara [archway] is prescribed;
in the west, it is produced from the Aśvattha tree; and in the north, the Plava archway.
All [the trees] originate from floating seeds, and likewise the *nyagrodha* tree is in the north;
in the absence of these very trees, however, the *samī* tree may be used.
The *jaṃtu*, *khadira*, *gāra*, *gremya*, and *lā* [trees] are situated at the archway (*toraṇa*).
The mantra is also the archway; the outer gate is the city gate, and the inner gate is the *gopura*.

Thus says the *Koṣa*; nevertheless, the meaning is that the garland serves as its substitute. Therefore, the circumference of those [measures] is declared to be seven cubits each, measured separately by the standard of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) per foot, [and] transversely.
