The measurement of the lintel (phalaka) should be two and a half cubits in length.
One should fashion tridents (śūla) in the middle of the archway (toraṇa), measuring one cubit. The central prong (śṛṅga) should be slightly longer than the others; it is not so on the sides.
Both of those are declared to be two finger-breadths thick;
then one should install the ritual components made from their own wood, O Nārada, according to the Saṃhitā.
O Goddess, from the Vaiṣṇava-kalpa, [one should take] the conch, discus, mace,
and lotus; right there, one should place into those jars the fragrant flowers that have been offered.
One should worship Dhruvadharī, Vākapati, and Vighneśa there; these [deities] are to be worshipped in sequence in the jars at the corners of the pavilion,
which are filled with water that has flowed down and placed upon lotus leaves.
One should place two golden jars each at the two doorways of the temple.
Amṛta, Durjapa, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala—
the practitioner of mantras should worship these in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should place the mantras and other elements into the jars situated at the gates of the worship area using those supreme mantras;
then, one should fasten banners, possessing a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors (Lokapālas), upon the directions.
Banners should be made from cloth two cubits in length;
alternatively, the banners may be seven cubits long and twelve finger-breadths in width.
The staffs and goads of those elephants shall measure ten cubits; the practitioner of mantra should draw the directional elephants, well-adorned, in the middle of the banners.
Whatever worship, fire-offerings, recitations, and other rites have been performed by the wise—
all that perishes for the owners of the field if it is without protection.
In a dispute, the banner and likewise the house are utterly destroyed;
therefore, what deity indeed should not be associated with the banner?
The banners should be seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide;
and in the *caṃdrikā* [the central area], the banners all around should have the colors of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*).
"Could the banner of honey (the bee) be adorned with a ritual peg? [Thus he asked. It was beautified by canopies that dispelled the rows of mango sprouts;
in the middle portion of that field measuring three parts, there was an altar.
It should be one cubit in measure and height, and square;
it should be constructed with bricks or with clay, and the altar should be like a mirror in its smoothness.
In the Tripurāsāra:

"Then, one should construct its center as being provided with four doors; on one-third of that [area], one should fashion an altar (vedī) measuring one aratni in height, beautiful and resembling the interior of a mirror. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that the length should be equal to the width of the middle portion. And in the *Śāradā*:

"In a field measured by three threads (or cubits), provided with a span (ratni), one should then prepare a square altar within the pavilion. Here, there is an option according to one's desire regarding the measurements. Regarding the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), [it is said] in the *Kulaḍḍīśa*:
In the consecration, the initiation, the installation, and likewise the festival, as well as in protection, there is efficacy; [so too] in marriage and the tying of the sacred thread.
Upon entering a new house, during the rite of consecration,
and in all auspicious ceremonies, one should perform the offering of a banyan tree.
The offering of the speech-vowels (vācām kurārpaṇam) should be performed on the ninth, seventh, third, or fifth day prior to the daily rites, or even immediately;
it is performed in the northern part of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), facing north and extending eastward from the northeast corner.
One should construct a secret chamber ten cubits wide and five cubits deep; then, within it, the wise practitioner should fashion the maṇḍala.
One should lay down five threads measuring five cubits each;
these should extend from east to west, with an interval of twelve finger-breadths between them.
In the same manner, one should lay down eleven threads from south to north;
thus there are four rows, four paths, and two quadrangles on both sides.
From the street [of the mandala], four squares are distinguished;
one should color those squares with white, red, yellow, and black.
The practitioner of mantras, following the traditional injunctions, should fill the pathways with the syllables beginning with Īśāna in due order, using the *rājābhis* and *śyāmalā* [mantras].
They say there are three types of vessels for the rite of sowing the sprouts:
the *pālikās*, the five-faced [vessels], and the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*), following this fourfold sequence.
Those who are learned in all the tantras declare that Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva are essentially one;
the vessel’s mouth-width is said to be sixfold, which is called the auspicious [measure].
Its neck-hole should be one finger-breadth wide,
and the width of the footstool is declared to be six finger-breadths.
The height of the four-fold base should be four finger-breadths, and its joint should be one finger-breadth;
alternatively, that joint may be omitted, or it may be half the measure of the footstool.
A five-faced water-clock (ghaṭikā) indeed grants all desires;
others say its faces should be four finger-breadths in width.
There are four [pillars] in the four directions and one above, according to the rule;
the length and width of the pillar is said to be twelve finger-breadths.
The teachers, however, declare that the mouth of the śarāva is remembered as being sixteen aṅgulas long and twelve aṅgulas wide.
The base is said to be four finger-breadths wide at its bottom;
it is fashioned by drinking [the measurement] according to the available dimensions.
O Dear One, the wise man should fashion [the image] from gold, silver, copper, or clay;
having prepared it, he should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread while reciting the *sambhūti* mantra.
Having washed those [vessels] and covered the groups [of deities],
one should place them, starting from the west, upon sacrificial grass (kūrca) that has been properly prepared.
One should fill those vessels with dried cow-dung, sand, and earth. Once those vessels have been sealed, one should worship Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva;
like Śrutakarmā and others, a wise person should perform this at night.
The sowing of seeds should be performed at night with cow-dung and dust,
because the moon is the constant lord of seeds and the friend of the night-lotus.
The knower of mantras, preceded by the fivefold wisdom, should wash the seeds with water using the seed-syllable *Jala* (Va), having repeatedly recited the root mantra.
One should offer auspicious blessings for the twice-born;
facing north, one should pour [the offerings] into the vessel.
For the brother-in-law (śyāla), there are black *āḍhakī*, mung beans, sesame, *iṣyāṣa*, and mustard seeds.
Kulotthaka and kumāṣa are used for the purpose of sowing seeds and sprouting.
One should worship Skanda and Skanka in Niṣpāra; Vāyu and Agni in Kulotthaka; Nirṛti in Moṭakī; Soma in Mudga; and Vasu and Aṃśa in Tila.
One should worship Prajāpati with rice seeds, Indra with mustard seeds, Māyā with beans, and one should sacrifice to Varuṇa with black gram.
One should worship Soma daily until the day of the perfuming (*madhivāsa*).
Having sprinkled [the image] with turmeric water, the wise preceptor (*deśika*) should protect it by covering it with *astra*-mantras.
One should scatter the offering (bali) for the three types of vessels in the directions starting from the east,
using mantras beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, and at night, using the names of the Night.
The five elements, the Yakṣas, the Nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva,
and Hari are declared to be the deities of the seven nights.
For the spirits (bhūtas), parched grain, sesame, turmeric, curd, and barley-meal are prescribed; for the ancestors (pitṛs), rice grains mixed with sesame are traditionally declared to be suitable.

One should offer *karaṃbha* and parched grain (*lāja*) along with coconut leaves to the Yakṣas; flour and ground meal to the Nāgas; and Brahmā, represented by a lotus and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
In the ritual of the nine nights (navarātra), the practitioner should offer a cake as food for Viṣṇu Sarva, rice with jaggery for Īśā,
and furthermore, milk-rice for Kṛṣaka.
In this manner, one should offer [the oblation] to the Vaiṣṇavas with milk-rice (pāyasa);
then, one should present an offering of milk-rice food to all the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Then the sacrificer should examine the sprout for its auspicious or inauspicious nature;
those that have grown straight upward, are spotless, and are well-formed are auspicious.
Those skilled in the tantras know that auspicious sprouts are said to be excellent;
however, those that are smoke-colored, incomplete, or growing horizontally are not so.
One should avoid those that are dark-colored, humpbacked, or otherwise inauspicious;
and to counteract those defects, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa).

The Guru should perform one hundred oblations with the *mūla-mantra* and one thousand in the hundred-faceted [fire-pit]. Now, on the day prior to the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should prepare the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles, and the mandalas. Among these, first is the construction of the house for the pit, as described in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*.
Having taken up the ground for the dwelling to the east, in the northeast,
and to the north, the practitioner of mantras should mentally designate the pavilion of the Fire-god.
It should be nine cubits in measure, or seven cubits, or even five cubits; it must be perfectly symmetrical and four-cornered.
It should be without gaps, with four doors, adorned with a raised altar,
encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass, and wrapped around with thread.
In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
"The wise man should construct the pavilion in the northeast quarter of the site,
measuring six, twelve, eight, or sixteen cubits, and being symmetrical."
It is provided with four gates and adorned with arches and other ornaments. In the *Tripurāsāra*:
"Now I shall describe the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); one should first perform the worship of Śivā and Śiva at the house of the Lord (*īśa*)."

In whichever direction the fire-altar (vittaya) of Vibhāvasu is located, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should have its corners aligned with it; it should be nine cubits in measure, or else measured by the arms of a mountain-dweller (nine cubits), or considered to be measured by the hands of a sage (seven cubits). It should be excellent, provided with four beautiful openings and without gaps, adorned with auspicious arches (toraṇas) made of kusha grass and a white canopy, and equipped with four doors; then, in the middle of that [pavilion]—

The altar (vedī) shall be one-third of that [measurement], elevated to the height of a cubit (aratni), resembling a mirror, and likewise captivating to the mind. Thus, in the case of a single sacrificial pit (ekakuṇḍa), the house should be five cubits in size. As it is stated in the *Homanirūpaṇa*: "In the opinion of those who maintain a single pit, there should be no other [dimension] than a five-cubit house; that [house] is for the sake of the pit."
To the north of the house. As it is stated in the Gaṇeśvarasaṃhitā: "One should construct a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the north of the house;
however, for a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma), one should do so in the middle of the house, as this [other] house would be defiled. This, then, is the house.

Because of the statement, "A house devoid of the Veda is a source of defilement," the meaning is that an altar (vedikā) should be constructed in the middle of the area designated for the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).

Now, regarding the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). This has been stated in the Śāradātilaka: "The wise man, having divided the area outside the previously mentioned pavilion into three parts by means of an altar, should demarcate [the directions] starting from the east within the central portion."
In the eight directions of one's own [residence], there are sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the form of a pillar, respectively:
square, triangular, semi-circular, pentagonal, and perfectly circular.
The six-cornered and eight-cornered [fire-pits] are designated by name;
the preceptor’s fire-pit should be in the center, between Gaurīpati and Mahendra.

One should mark out a square plot of ground measuring one cubit on each side, as described previously; from that, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is equal on all sides and quadrangular, which brings about auspiciousness.
The wise one should divide the square field into five parts;
he should place one part in front, measuring half of a half of the corner.
Having measured the corner with the measuring cord in that manner, the knower of mantras should then apply another pair of cords so that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) takes the form of a womb (yoni).
The wise knower of the Tantra should divide the accepted field into ten parts;
he should omit one part each time, moving downward, until he reaches the bottom.
One should drop the bowstring at the front and then rotate it according to that measurement;
thus, a beautiful pit resembling a half-moon is described.
When the field has been divided into four parts, one should place [the marks] on both sides;
then, starting from the front, one should mark each part by a third.
The wise one should draw two lines; the triangle is declared to be his own *kuṇḍa*.
In a field divided into eighteen parts, the wise one should place the Lord of the Field in one part outside.
One should rotate [the cord] by that measure to form an excellent circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa). One should divide the field into eight parts on both sides of the central line.

One should place the *bhoga* (enjoyment) one by one in the center according to this proportion; the best among those who know the *tantras* should form a set of four *matsyas* (fish-designs) on both sides.
One should understand the group of six sūtras; thereafter, one should provide the excellent hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Having divided the square field into ten parts, [one proceeds].
One should set aside one part outside and fashion a square; with that [line], one should draw a circle.
One should fashion three circles outside for the pericarp and so forth.
This is declared to be the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (padmakuṇḍa), which is captivating due to its opening.
One should divide the previously mentioned field into twenty-four parts;
having set aside one part on the outside, one should fashion a square.
The inner square should be one-half the measure of the [outer] corner;
one should mark from the two corners of the outer square along the corner-lines.
One should lay down eight lines according to the rule toward each direction;
this is indeed declared by those who know the mantras to be the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

The explanation of their meaning follows in sequence, beginning with "the teacher’s pit" (*ācārya-kuṇḍa*) and so forth. Because it is established first and because it is common to all, the pit is indeed square (*caturasra*).
Therefore, there are two additional types of square pits; however, according to the opinion of some, on the other hand, for all [pits] it is simply square, as follows:
In the *Śāradātilaka*, some Tantrikas desire a square [maṇḍala] for all [deities]. Also in the *Kulasāra*:
"O Maheśānī, one should accomplish all rites within a square. And in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"For all castes, in every rite and in every respect, one should fashion a square, or else those [other shapes] prescribed by rule."

It should be understood according to the distinction between those who are capable and those who are not. The eight sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) are now being explained, beginning with "one cubit in measure" and so forth.
Here, they draw the diagonal lines and form the "fish" diagrams (*matsya*) and other such figures.
This is because even in various Tantras, when heard, we see such statements as "for the sake of measurement, [one should perform] in a crooked pit, with mental anguish," and so forth;

thus it should be understood regarding the mandala and other elements as well. It is not for the sake of an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha), since when an explanation can be established through a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha), it would be redundant to assume an unseen purpose or a specific fruit, as that would imply a different intent.

Regarding the phrase "the square" (*caturasri*) and so forth: having marked the fifth [line] as the square by means of an additional [measurement], one should, from the corner facing [the center], rotate a thread measuring a fourth part [of the side] toward the right and the left. By that, the place which is obtained is formed through the intersection of both threads on the sides.

The meaning is that one should unify the two threads within my mouth up to the limit of the additional portion. For this very reason, there is agreement with the measurement of Rudra as being four parts, not exceeding the thread from the northeast corner to the southeast corner.
One should mark the thread measuring one cubit all around; then, having made it consist of four squares—
One should drop the diagonal cord;
thus the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) becomes square, bestowing all accomplishments.
The field is fifty [parts], with one part facing the east.
Therefore, one should lay down the threads from the sides up to the middle;
then, one should rotate each pair of squares upward from that point.
When it is done separately according to the rule, extending as far as two corners,
the pit will become stable, like that of the Aśvattha tree.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) facing north, known as the "womb" (yoni), bestows success.
Having measured the square and so forth with the bow-string (jyāsūtra), one should chant the mantra while measuring the extent with the cord;
the bow-string falls in the shape of an arrow, thus it is equal to the bowstring. One should cause the remainder to fall.

The meaning is that one should draw a line on the central line with its tip ten units further out. From the point where the thread falls by those same measures, one should place a level thread across the remaining portions and rotate it forward toward the right limit, or likewise toward the left. [The one] situated in front...

The meaning is "up to the line. And there is a corroboration in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having divided the field into parts, one should set aside two portions; having lowered the cord from below and prepared the bow-string, one should then rotate it. By that same measure, one should make [the shape], and it will become like a half-moon. Regarding the phrase "into four parts" and so forth, both...

On the right and left sides, having marked one-fourth of the *kṣetra* (area) in excess—one part on the right and one on the left—then, having unified two threads reaching toward the front, one should draw a triangular staff (*daṇḍa*). This is corroborated by the *Yāmala*: "One should cast a thirty-two-finger thread all around."

The wise one should draw the eastern opening in the form of a triangle; this is declared to be the triangular *kuṇḍa*, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Regarding the phrase "eighteen" and so forth: as for the word "outside," O Goddess, since there is no specific distinction, one should take the additional portion, place a thread in the center, and [draw] a circle with the measurement of that additional portion.

The pit (kuṇḍa) is formed according to the agreement in the Yāmala. Having divided the field into eighteen parts, one should cast [the cord] from the beginning of the first part. Having placed the cord in the center, one should rotate it along that path; thus the pit becomes circular, facing the east, and unsurpassed. Regarding the phrase "in eightfold" and so forth, it is not by means of the eighth part.
The width: having marked two fish on each of the two sides in sequence by dividing that width from the middle, [one proceeds] from the middle of the vertical line. (p.

One should draw a single line from the right fish to the [central] point, or a single line from the [central] point to the right fish; sequentially, one should draw a single line downward from the right fish to the [central] point, and likewise a single line upward from the lower fish to the [central] point;
from the right fish downward, a single line to the right fish, or from the left fish upward, a single line to the left fish—thus, O Wrathful One!
The meaning is that there is a single line from the fish (*matsya*) up to the head (*kūrca*), and another single line from the non-fish (*amatsya*) up to the lower fish (*adhamatsya*);
thus, eight lines are cast upon the eight threads. The corroboration for this is found in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"This [is] the earth-noose here, outside... from the center... (the remainder of the verse is omitted).

Having applied one's own pure intelligence to the width of the field according to that measurement, one should cast six lines across the two sides at intervals of one *ṛṣi* each; thus, this becomes a pleasing square altar (*kuṇḍa*) with diagonal corners.
Regarding the reading "one hundred and eighteen" (*aṣṭādaśīśata*) found in some texts, there is a contradiction with the *tantras* therein, as follows: [The rest of the passage would follow here.]

In the *Tripurāsāra*: "Having laid out ten parts, one circle is drawn; one should likewise fashion an outer [circle], a middle [circle], and a pericarp. Beyond that, the wise man should construct the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (*padmakuṇḍa*). 'Outside' means outside the square; it refers to three circles. Thus, there is one circle.

For the purpose of delimiting the pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should draw a circle for the pericarp; for the purpose of defining it, another circle two cubits in extent for the filaments (*kesara*) and petals. The meaning is that the pit (*kuṇḍa*) consists of the pericarp itself, while the filaments and so forth serve as the ornaments of the lotus. Furthermore, one obtains the Rudra-yāma [measure] for the pericarp and the filaments.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is indeed for the sake of the petals. As stated in the Yāmala: "Having constructed a circular pit with equal divisions, the practitioner should fashion three circles in the center, a pericarp in the middle portion, filaments outside of that, the centers of the petals further out, and the tips of the petals even further out."

The supreme preceptor should fashion it; having drawn the pericarp (*karṇikā*) with a height of three finger-breadths, he should then draw the filaments (*keśara*) in the lower portion—this is what is called the lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*). According to this view, the pit consists of the filaments and the pericarp of a lotus, as there is a rule for arranging three circles in the center. By the word "middle" (*madhya*), the very center of the circle is meant.
Now, regarding the construction of the *nala*: in the *Candrikā*, it is said that one should leave aside the central circle (*karṇikā*) according to its full extent and dig it deep;

the remainder, however, one should dig inside for the filaments (*keśara*), and one should dig the area of the petals in that same shape so that the petals may be properly formed by a skilled craftsman. Thus, according to this system as well.

The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) consists of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) itself; this is because, when the area is equalized, the pericarp is drawn [within it]. Here, the traditional method is the path. One should divide the previously mentioned field, as stated in the passage beginning with "the field" and so forth. The word "one" means "in some way. The word "square" means "having four sides. The phrase beginning with "half of the corner" refers to a fourth part of the corner.

The meaning is "by means of measurement. From the two corners—that is, from the two sides of the corners—there are two fish-marks (*matsya*) in each direction; this is the meaning. Having cast eight threads across as many fish-marks, an eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsri*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is produced; this is the meaning. "Square" (*caturasra*) means on the outside; this refers to its [shape].
In the *Tripurāsāra*, it is stated: "Having cast [the thread] here into the field toward the directions beginning with the east,
and having made one [mark] at the twelfth part, the wise man, taking again from the upper corner, [should draw] a triangle by means of this."
p.

41a) From those two corners, one should indeed draw [lines] all around with that same measurement; from the mark, extend the eight lines for the entire extent of the fang [of the deity]. Thus are the eight sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*). The Teacher...

There are nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) including the central one. Regarding the excavation of the pits and their girdles (mekhalā): at Laliteśvara, the measurement for the width of the pit should be the same as that for its excavation;
furthermore, one should make the altar-mound (maṇḍapa) of that same measure, and the girdle should be shaped like a lotus.
And in the Śāradā:
"The depth of the excavation of the pit is exactly equal to its width;
and whatever the form of the pits is, such is the form of their girdles."
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should have three girdles (mekhalās);
they should be one fist (muṣṭhi) wide, and their height and width should be known as two, one, and half a finger-breadth (aṅgula) respectively.
In a kuṇḍa of this [smaller] measure, the lines shall consist of three, two, or one aṅgula;
likewise, in a kuṇḍa measuring one cubit, they shall be four, three, or two aṅgulas.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring ten fingers, they should be made of mercury;
in a pit measuring eight cubits, they should be eight fingers long and made of copper.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring ten cubits,
the wise should know that the girdles (mekhalā) on all sides are ten fingers in width and depth.
And in the Siddhānteśekhara: "The knower of the Tantra should fashion five girdles for every fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
Alternatively, there may be three, two, or even just one girdle.
According to the sequence of the Vedas, the fires, the eyes, and the moons, there are three girdles respectively."
And in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"In this [system], the height of the primary girdle is said to be nine finger-breadths;
the height of the subsequent girdles is traditionally recorded as five finger-breadths."
Outside of that, the girdle (mekhalā) should be three finger-breadths in height;
and the width of the three girdles should be four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively.
Having cooked [the earth] in that manner for one finger-breadth, the girdle (mekhalā) should be at the edge of the pit;
however, in a pit of one cubit, one should increase it by another [finger-breadth] for each subsequent pit.
And the best of those who know the Tantras [should fashion it] at the neck with a measurement of half a finger.
And in the Jñānārṇava:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the square."
The wise one should construct a square, level area measuring one cubit.
O Goddess, listen to the excellent characteristics of the girdle (mekhalā) along with the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
so that it may be beautiful and fifteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure.
O Dear One, leaving one finger-breadth at the region of the neck, a girdle (mekhalā) nine fingers wide and five fingers thick should be fashioned, provided with the [nine] Kulas.
The first girdle should be six finger-breadths in width;
O Goddess, the second girdle is four finger-breadths in width.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, the third girdle should be made seven finger-breadths high and two finger-breadths in width.
Regarding what was stated as "the digging [should be] only that much," it should be understood that it is performed with the girdle (mekhalā).

One should cause the pit for the digging to be measured at twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in depth; O Goddess, one should fashion the girdle for that site (vāstu) at the end of those twelve [finger-breadths], measuring four finger-breadths in width and likewise one finger-breadth in height. At the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], [it should be so].
The meaning is that its height should be equal to that [diameter].
Alternatively, one should indeed dig all the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) to the measure of one cubit;
or five girdles (mekhalās) should be made with measurements of six, five, four, three, and two [cubits respectively].
Alternatively, it should be made with three [girdles] consisting of four, three, and two finger-breadths;
or else, there may be a single girdle provided with four finger-breadths.
The meaning is that one should cause it to be raised. There is a distinction regarding the single girdle (*mekhalā*).
Likewise, listen as I shall describe the characteristics for the alternative of a single girdle:
a wise man should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a depth of eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The girdle should be four finger-breadths in width and extend six finger-breadths; it should be fashioned as before, and the *yo* [the cord] should likewise be so.
The triangular pit should be thirty-two finger-breadths in extent, measured separately;
its depth should be known as being as before, and likewise two finger-breadths at the neck.
As before, the girdle should be made; it may even be just one, for in the *Jñānārṇava*, the triangle and so forth are mentioned because of the liberation [attained] through the triangle.

That pit is fifteen finger-breadths [in depth] as before; the girdles (mekhalā) are as before: the principal girdle is nine finger-breadths, the second is five finger-breadths, and the third is three finger-breadths in height.
Including the excavation and the girdles, it measures thirty-two finger-breadths. This indeed is the rule for all fire-pits (kuṇḍa).

"And even one [girdle] may be thus; one should visualize it as seventeen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length," such is the meaning, since the measurement of a cubit (hasta) has already been stated. This is also understood from the word "api" (even/also). Now, the explanation of the girdles (mekhalās): that has been stated in the Śāradā-tantra:
Let there be a line extending from the southeast (Agnikoṇa) over the Nairṛta (southwest) corner like a leaf;
this is declared to be the *yoni* of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) whose hands have reached the end of the fist.
The raised portion, however, should possess a length, width, and height of two finger-breadths;
one should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth wide, facing downward toward the northeast.
In other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the rim (nemi) by one finger-width at each stage;
likewise, one should also increase the tip of the yoni by two barley-grains at each step.
And from the Jñānārṇava:
"On the western side of the staff, one should fashion the characteristic of the womb (yoni),
twelve aṅgulas in length and likewise eight aṅgulas in width."
The wise one [should fashion] either the form of an *aśvattha* leaf or a triangle;
this applies to a single-hand-span sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), as well as for other pits, as previously described.
The meaning is that one should cause it to increase.
And in the *Kriyāsāra*, regarding the first girdle (*mekhalā*):
"One should fashion the womb (*yoni*) at the front of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), with lips like those of a goat and possessing the characteristics of a pit."
The vulva is six finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.
The wise have declared that in a pit measuring one cubit, the elevation should be two finger-breadths.
And in the Homasāra: "To the south, east, and south, water should be placed... [text fragment].
According to the established doctrine, it should be twelve finger-breadths in length and likewise eight finger-breadths in width.
The practitioner of mantra should fashion the vulva-shape; its tip should be two finger-breadths thick.
One should increase it gradually as before until it reaches a distance of ten cubits.
In the *Koṇakuṇḍa*, it is said: "One should [visualize] that womb as the essence of the mind of the Tantra. And in the *Yāmala*:
"One should fashion a cavity in the center of the womb; indeed, the mantra is the sacrificial butter for the sage."
Now, the description of the stalk (*nāla*). In the *Śāradā*: "One should fashion it starting from the position of the girdle (*mekhalā*).

This was stated by the teacher Bhāskara: "That which is on the stalk is the perforation. * * * "The base and the tip are desired to have an extent of three and two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) respectively. Thus ends the description of the stalk. Now, the navel (*nābhi*).

The Vivaraṇa [states]: In the Śāradā [Tantra], it is said: "One should cause these pits (kuṇḍas) to be made; their form is like a lotus, or they may be according to the dimensions appropriate to each respective pit.
The height is declared to be one fist, one cubit, or one hand, and the width is likewise."

In auspicious sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one of noble intellect should increase the measurement by two or three finger-breadths; however, one should not increase it by more than two barley-corns at a time.
Having divided the navel-field into two parts, one should place the pericarp in the middle;
outside, one should fashion eight petals with two lines.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one fist in size is prescribed for fifty oblations;
for a hundred oblations, it should be three spans (trimātra); and for a thousand oblations, it should be one cubit (hastamātra).
In the *Yāmala*: "For ten thousand [offerings], it is made two cubits; for a hundred thousand, four cubits.
For a hundred thousand oblations, it is four cubits; for ten million, six cubits."
It should be eight cubits for a *koṭi-homa*, and likewise ten cubits.
Alternatively, one should have it made in a single hand according to the sequence up to one hundred thousand,
increasing by one hand for every ten hundred thousand.
In all the Agamas, there is no sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) larger than ten cubits;
likewise, in both the Vedas and the Tantras, there is no sacrifice greater than the Koṭihoma.
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*, it is recorded that for ten lakṣas [of oblations], the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is six cubits, and for ten million (*koṭi*) oblations, it is eight cubits;

indeed, a pit measuring ten cubits is also seen prescribed even for a *koṭi-homa*. Here, the apparent contradiction in the statements must be resolved into a single consistent meaning by considering the heaviness or lightness of the sacrificial materials (*havya-dravya*). For light materials, such as flowers—

In rites such as the *homa*, the pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be very small; when there is an abundance of materials, it should be large, and so forth—this is the general direction. Herein is the summary: for a pit of one cubit (*hasta*), the excavation should be fifteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) deep; therein, the girdle (*mekhalā*) should be nine finger-breadths high, by which the full measure of one cubit is attained. In the case of a twelve-finger-breadth excavation, the height [of the girdle] should be twelve finger-breadths.

By that [measurement], there is the completion of the cubit (*hasta*) with the girdle (*mekhalā*). In the case of a single girdle, the excavation is eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) deep and the girdle is six finger-breadths high; by that, the cubit is completed. In the case of twelve finger-breadths [for the height of the altar], the excavation is fifteen finger-breadths deep, and the cubit is completed by the seventeen finger-breadths of the girdles; this is according to that alternative view.
Even a single girdle (*mekhalā*) shall be seventeen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height. Alternatively, for all [types of fire-pits], the excavation shall be one cubit (*hasta*) deep;

however, for the two fist-shaped pits (*muṣṭi-kuṇḍa*), the girdles, the womb (*yoni*), and the lip (*leminī*) shall have the same dimensions as the width of the pit. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Śāradā-tantra*. Now follows the description of the directions for the womb.

The wise who know the tantras have declared the sequence for the sacrificial fire-pit (yoni) in a homa: situated in the southeast it is "standing on a bull" (dakṣasthā), while in the southwest, west, and north it is "standing in water" (jalasthā).
It is also stated by Somaśambhu:
"For the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east and extending to the south, the yoni should face north;
for the remaining ones, it should face east; and for those in the northeast and southeast, it may face either way."

Regarding the two [fires], the phrase "in the northeast" (aiśānye) is an elliptical expression meaning "the location of Vivasvat. According to this statement, the priests at the southeast pit face that [northeast], while the priests at the northwest pit face the east. Now follows the description of the results of the pits and so forth, as stated in the *Śāradā*:
A quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) brings about all accomplishments when oblations are joyfully offered;
a Yoni-shaped pit bestows sons; and one with the luster of half-moon shapes bestows auspiciousness.

A triangular pit brings about the destruction of enemies; for rites of pacification (śāntika), it should be circular; for cutting and killing (chedana-māraṇa), the pit should be hexagonal and resemble a lotus.
An eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to bestow nourishment and pacify diseases;
for Brahmins it should be square, and for queens it is desired to be circular.
For Vaiśyas, it is said to be half-moon-shaped, and for Śūdras, triangular. And in the Yāmala:
"The square [maṇḍala] is the cause of peace, prosperity, nourishment, and growth."
The Yoni-kunda bestows eloquence and is a great means for effecting attraction.
The circular [seat] bestows prosperity, and in the half-moon there should be three;
that which is called the lotus is the cause of all success and shall be the bestower of nourishment.
For Brahmins it is considered square, for kings it is circular;
for merchants it is a half-moon, and for those born as Śūdras it is triangular.
Some teachers say that for all [types of rites], the [fire-pit] is square. Now, the placement of the fire-pits (kuṇḍavāsanā).
In the *Yāmala*: "One should know the form of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to be the supreme body of primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
its head is declared to be in the east, while the left and right [sides] are in the north."

The belly is said to be the *kuṇḍa*, while the womb and the two feet are in the west. Now follows the explanation of the defects [of the directions]: from the east toward the southern *kuṇḍa*, if it is devoid of a girdle (*mekhalā*), there is indeed grief; in the northwest, there is the loss of wealth.

A *kuṇḍa* that is devoid of a neck causes the destruction of one's wife; if it is at the level of the throat, it brings about fear; if there is a fracture in the threads and so forth, and if it is lacking in its base (*nala*), it results in poverty.
If the throat is missing, there will be madness; if the letters are deficient and so forth, there is no accomplishment.
If [the planet] is stronger, there will be loss of wealth; if weaker, suffering is proclaimed.
Diseases arise, and if it is both weak and exalted, there will be loss of memory.
If the image becomes displaced, cracked, or broken, or if its marks are effaced, it shall become a mere physical form;
therefore, having learned everything from the Guru, the wise man should construct that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
And in the Vṛttaratnatantra: "Now follows the exposition of the measurements beginning with two cubits. And in the Mantramuktāvalī:
"The measurement of the cord for the corner of a pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit [is as follows]."
Starting from the corner, the thread is proclaimed to be two cubits in length.
In this manner, the wise practitioner should increase the dimensions in the other pits (kuṇḍas) in due order.
And in the *Uttaratantra*:
"In a pit measuring one cubit on all sides, there is a circular border of one finger-breadth."
One should increase it by that same measure; thus, it is declared to be two cubits.
Thus, in other *kuṇḍas*, the measurement of one cubit (*hasta*) is proclaimed.
In the *Rudrayāmala*: "The cord should be thirty-three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), or [the area] should be ten-cornered with sesame seeds."
The cord should be sixty-seven finger-breadths long and twelve sesamum seeds thick.
In a pit measuring two cubits, one should duly perform the measurement as before;
in a two-cubit pit, [the circumference] is forty-two [parts], less twelve sesame-seeds.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of four cubits, the cord is fifty-one finger-breadths;
understand that in one of five cubits, it is twelve sesamum-seeds [in length].
A thread sixty-four finger-breadths long, marked with twelve sesame seeds;
a thread sixty-seven finger-breadths long, marked with twelve sesame seeds.
Having performed the rite according to the rules in a six-cubit pit, now learn about the seven-cubit [pit]:
the cord is nine and seventy finger-breadths long, resembling twelve sesame seeds.
The cord should be eighty-eight finger-breadths long and marked with twelve *tilas*;
however, one should wrap it around the pit when the pit is eight cubits in size, or else not at all.
A cord of ninety-seven finger-breadths, made with twelve sesame seeds [as units], is indeed considered by the wise to be the cord for a three-pit (tri-kuṇḍa) altar measuring nine cubits;
it is joined with twelve sesame seeds and measures six hundred and forty finger-breadths.
O best of men, extract that [mantra] from the ritual manual of the ten-cubit sacrificial pit.
Thus it is said.

In all these cases of duality, the choice rests with the will of the gurus, as it is transformed through their oral instruction. Now, regarding the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*): it is stated in the *Bṛhadyoginītantra* that the daily and occasional fire-oblations (*homa*) are performed upon the sacrificial ground.
Or one should perform it;
one should make that [mandala] with sand, very beautiful, measuring one cubit (hasta) in extent,
and naturally square, with a height of one finger-breadth.
And in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"In the case of a concise fire-offering (*homakarma*), the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) should be one cubit (*hastamātra*). For this very reason, one should perform [the rite] on a mound;
'concise' refers to the scriptural injunction of the measure of one cubit, meaning it extends up to a thousand [oblations]. Now follows the explanation of the *śruva* ladle.
This is stated in the Yāmala:
"The sacrificial wood, one cubit in length, should be divided into thirty-six parts;
with twenty parts there shall be the pit (kuṇḍa), and with eight of those parts there shall be the altar (vedi)."
The neck is measured at one part; the mouth is measured at seven parts;
and the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts.
The opening should be equal in size to the throat;
one should fashion the mouth-path with a measurement of the little finger for the purpose of extracting clarified butter.
The pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned in the center of the altar with one part;
one should fashion a surrounding enclosure (avaṭa) outside of it with one part.
Of that [mandala], one should fashion the moat with three parts outside the enclosure wall,
and with a single part on all sides, one should arrange the petals.
The girdle (mekhalā) and the sacrificial altar (mukhavedī) are each half a part in measurement;
at the base and tip of the column (kuṃdra), there are two pots (kuṃbha), each three times nine (twenty-seven) finger-breadths in sequence.
With six parts on the back portion of the altar, it should take the form of a tortoise.
One who belongs to the Pātri-gotra should write the syllable *haṃ* or *si*,
with the mark of a *śruca* on the back part of its face.
The meaning is that it is prescribed in the *Yāmala* as "sacrificial wood. And in the *Śāradā*:
Having taken śrīparṇī, siṃśikā, and a milky tree [and other ingredients], one should divide them again into thirty-six portions, each measuring one cubit in length.
The meaning is "thus the altar" (vedī) or "the altar-platform" (vedikā).

It is better that the altar-platform (vedikā) be fashioned as a balance-beam (tulā) with both [parts]. Since there is no distinction, it should be two units (dvittāra) in width and [the same] in length; the neck (kaṇṭha), however, is between the two [sides], being one unit (ekāṃśa) in width and one unit in length, having the dimensions and form of the neck.

The meaning is that the work is marked by its distinctness. "In seven parts" means that the tip should be made seven parts long. "The altar" (vedī) means having divided the altar into four parts, [one should proceed] on both sides with a width equal to half a part in the middle section.
Regarding the phrase "of that," etc., it refers to the depth of the depression at the edge.
The meaning of *ataṭasya* is "without a bank. There are eight petals; because the ministers have been accounted for, by elimination [these belong to others].

Regarding the tradition that "it is the mouth," that means it is the throat (*kaṇṭha*). By that, the end of the mouth is the throat. "Outside" means from the edge of the altar; having grasped two [lines] on both sides at the corner of the division of the scripture, one should draw them out.
Regarding the term *gaṇḍī* and so forth: at the upper and lower portions of the two *kumbhas*, this [structure] is joined by the Lord with a measurement equal to two *aṃśas*.
One *gaṇḍī* is located at the base of the *kumbha*, and the other is at the tip of the *kumbha*. For this very reason, the author of the *Ratnāvalī* states:
"The two *gaṇḍīs* are situated on both sides by means of two *aṃśas*. This has been stated by Somaśambhu: "At the base and at the tip..."
The knob of the handle (*daṇḍa*) should have a ringing sound. Now, the description of the *śruva* ladle according to the *Kuloḍḍīśa*:

The construction of the *śruva* should be made with twenty-four parts; its length is thirty-two [parts], and its circumference is four. It should have a hollow at the tip for holding the oblation, and it is distinguished by two types of handles.
One should bury it in the place of the kila as I shall describe for the deer;
at the root and tip of the staff, there should be a knob adorned with a heron's feather.

The *śruva* is endowed with the characteristics prescribed in the *tantra* for Vedic rites. Its handle (*daṇḍa*)—meaning its length—is twenty-four parts of a thirty-six-part hand; that is to say, it measures twenty-four finger-breadths. Regarding its circumference or thickness: one *karṣa* consists of eighty *raktikas*, and this is the desired weight for gold and other materials used in its construction.

Thus, in the description by Damin, "geṇḍūyā" means [the handle]. By that, the meaning is: there is a single *gaṇḍī* at the base of the staff (*daṇḍa*), and then a *kaṅkaṇa* at the tip of the blade; hence, the author of the *Ratnāvalī* [states this].
The meaning is that the two *gaṇḍī* [sections] are covered on both sides by two parts (*aṃśa*). Now follows the description of the substitute for the portion, as stated in the *Yāmala*:
"The oblation is offered with two middle leaves of the *palāśa* tree."
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā* it is also stated: "O Sage, one should make the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles from the wood of the *palāśa* tree, with holes [at their tips].

For a concise *homa* rite, one should use leaves of the *aśvattha* tree. Here, "concise" means [performed on] a thousand spikes (*sahasravedhi*). Therefore, in the case of inability, where the *homa* is performed upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), in the absence of the *sruk* and *sruva*, [one may use other materials].

Regarding the "substitute" (pratinidhi): now follows the description of the mandala, as stated in the *Śāradā*: "In a square divided into four compartments, provided with colored threads, one should likewise [draw] four lines from each corner toward the center of the four compartments."
One should drop [the lines] so that there may be fish-shaped figures in the middle;
the meaning of this is: in a square with four corners provided with diagonal threads (karṇasūtra).

In the four squares joined by diagonal lines, one should likewise drop diagonal threads through those situated at the corners, so that fish-shaped figures arise in each center; this is the description of the square.
The practitioner should draw two lines extending east-west and two extending north-south.
One should drop four equal lines through the middle of them.
The meaning of this is as follows:
two [lines] on the eastern and western sides, totaling four lines;
as before, one should drop the diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) in the corner squares.

The phrase "in the corners of the squares" (*koṣṭhakoṇeṣu*) is to be construed with the word following it [by transposition]. Thus, there shall be "fish-figures" (*matsya*) in the corners; one should drop threads upon them. The meaning is that one should drop threads in the corners in such a way that fish-figures are formed in the corners. Then, those fish-figures arise; upon them, the threads run from east to west and from south to north. By that, furthermore—

Furthermore, by combining four squares, there are eight squares; thus, the meaning is that they amount to one hundred and fifty-six. As long as the practitioner [has] two hundred and fifty-six squares, he should cast them down into the diagrams according to that very same procedure. By that—
The meaning is that there are seventeen lines running from south to north and seventeen lines running from east to west.
In the center of the thirty-six squares, one should draw a lotus with excellent characteristics;
outside, the pedestal (pīṭha) shall consist of one row, and the pathway (vīthikā) shall consist of two rows.

"Thirty-six" means that when five squares are laid out in each of the four directions, thirty-six remaining squares are left; this is the indication and detailed description of the lotus. Likewise for the pedestal (pīṭha) and likewise for the pathway (vīthikā). From the remaining [squares] at the tips of the door-ornaments (dvāraśobhā) and the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā), [one proceeds].
One should visualize this; even for these, the indication is in the tone.
Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, the practitioner should draw a lotus, the wise one having set aside a twelfth part of the lotus-grid on the outside.
One should divide that center into three circles with equal proportions:
the first shall be the place for the pericarp (karṇikā), and the second for the filaments (keśara).
The third [feature] there is that the tips of the petals are formed by a portion of the pearls. This is the meaning of these [verses].

Where there is a lotus divided twelvefold, having set aside one part, one should again divide the remaining central portion into six parts; then, having fixed a single peg upon the central line and tied a thread to it, one should rotate it three times in succession and draw three circles by means of those three divisions.

"Ājyam" means the outer circle. O wise ones, having placed [the compass] at the center, one should mark the outer circle's intermediate space by measuring with the radius; then, using that same measurement as the length for the second circle from the outer one, one should draw half-moons on all sides at the tips of the arrows, [dividing] the middle circle into eight directions.
One should contemplate. Having written down their junctions and configurations, one should drop the lines there; this is the meaning.

In some places, the reading is "sūtrasthānī" (the place of the lines); according to that view, it is an adjective of *sūtrāṇi* (the lines), meaning the lines are to be dropped at the junctions. And whatever is the measurement of the tips of the petals, that measurement [should be applied].
The circle is completed. Then, with a thread of that same measurement, the wise one should draw [lines] from both ends of the circle using the outer hand;
then, having left aside the space for the tips of the petals, which consists of twelve parts, he should draw the circle with that measurement as its width, extending evenly to the tips of the petals.

The meaning is that one should rotate it. "The interval between those" refers to the interval between the circles. "Lakṣmī" means at the end of three [circles]. "In the middle of that" means in the middle of the lotus—the thread that delineates the petals of the lotus. Having drawn two lines from both sides, starting from the left, one should draw them by moving the hand outward, keeping the hand on the outside. The remainder [of the procedure] is as before, starting from the east.

One draws [the lotus] facing west on the right, facing north behind it, and facing east on the left; that is the meaning of "descending" [into the center]. One should arrange the petals in pairs at the bases of the petals. This is declared by the knowers of the *tantras* to be the common lotus. At the bases of the petals is the second...

The meaning is that one should mark the half-moon situated in the middle of the enclosure. One should sweep away three squares for the purpose of the pedestal (pīṭha). The wise man should arrange the [remaining] squares belonging to the pedestal. One should sweep away the squares situated in the path (vīthī) according to the division of the rows. Regarding the phrase "the squares" and so forth, it refers to the single square located at the corner.

On both sides of that, there are two squares; by this, one should erase three squares in each corner for the sake of the pedestal legs—this is the meaning. The remaining squares situated in the four directions are the "squares" (pada) referred to here;
having erased the squares situated within the two powers (śakti), the path (vīthī) should be prepared in the cardinal directions—this is the meaning.

Then, one should construct the doors within the four compartments. On both sides of the door, there are two parts known as *śobhā*, formed by three and one squares respectively. "Two, four," etc., means two squares above and four below.
Regarding the phrase "by squares" and so forth: there are three squares above and one square below on both sides of the door.
The meaning is "on both sides of each door.
Next, there should be ornaments with one and three squares;
the four corners should be formed by the remaining eight squares.
One should color that captivating maṇḍala with five colors:
yellow from turmeric powder and white derived from rice.
Red is safflower powder; black is produced from burnt *palāśa* leaves;
and dark grey is produced from the leaves of the *vilva* group; thus the five colors have been described.
The boundary lines, one finger in height and width, should be white and auspicious;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are reddish-orange.
The petals should be white in color and their joints dark;
the practitioner of mantra should conquer the filaments with yellow pigment, or else the pericarp itself may be yellow.
The filaments (kesaras) should be yellow in color, and the petals (dalas), beginning with the outermost, should be reddish;
the joints (sandhis) should be black in color, or alternatively, yellow or white.
One should color the interiors of the pedestals with reddish-pink light from the feet;
its limbs are white, as are those in the four walkways.
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves and flowers,
variegated with various colors and captivating to the sight of all.
The doors are described as white in color and radiant with splendor;
the secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) should be yellow in color, and the corners (koṇas) black.
Three lines should be drawn on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence;
this is known as the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is common to all [rites].
"Sīma" means the boundary of the door, the path, the pedestal, and the lotus;
or alternatively,
it means the joints of all [these], which are conceptual constructions of desire.

According to the Amarakośa, the words *kṛṣṇa* (black), *nīla* (blue), and *asita* (dark) are synonyms for *śyāma* (dark-colored). Thus, it is white and black; [it is] black, blue, asita, and śyāma—so it is seen in the Amarakośa.
Nevertheless, the word *śyāma* (dark) does not mean "burnt"; rather, it refers to the leaf-powder (*patra-rajaḥ*).
[The statement] "yellow is turmeric powder" and so forth is because it conveys the specific capacity (*śakti*) [of the term]. Therefore, the meaning is:
"with five colors" means with five substances such as turmeric powder and the like. [The phrase] "situated on the pedestal" (*pīṭhagatām*) and so forth is [to be understood] externally.

The meaning is that these are the corner positions (*koṇasthānāni*) of the lotus-field situated within the row. "The feet" (*pādāḥ*) means those positions formed by clearing away three squares at each corner. "The limbs" (*gātrāṇi*) and so forth means the limbs of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), which are the positions located in the middle of the two feet. "Common" (*sādhāraṇam*) means it belongs to all deities.

Furthermore, regarding the initiation for the Higher Knowledge (*ūrdhvavidyā*), the mandala has already been described. Now follows the detailed exposition of the *Sarvatobhadra* [mandala] for minor rites.
As it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "Having made the ground square, the wise one should draw lines from the directions twelve times; therein, one hundred squares are seen."
The first [mandala] consists of forty-four [squares], and the latter is a lotus of thirty-six. Its meaning is as follows:

one should divide the square ground twelvefold from east to west and from south to north. In the center of the square, there is a line running east-west and ten lines running north-south; then, on both sides of these, [the divisions are made].
Twelve squares are obtained. When twelve is multiplied by twelve, one hundred and forty-four squares are obtained.
One should arrange the pedestal with these squares in rows; there are no paths here.
Just as there was previously no secondary ornament for the beauty of the gateway.
The knower of the tantra should form the corners of the squares with the remaining lines;
he should perform the rest as before, or else draw the mandala in this manner.
"It does not exist" means that it is absent due to the lack of constituent parts (*koṣṭha*). "As before" means as in the *Sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala.

"The remainder" means the remainder of what has been stated. By this, the construction of the lotus—five-colored and variegated—and the doors and so forth, as well as the three outer lines, [are indicated].
The meaning is "the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala. Now follows the exposition of the nine-navel [maṇḍala]:
the wise one should draw sixty-four squares within a square [grid].
With four lines, there should be a lotus in the center, and again around it.
One should make four paths with intermediate channels between them;
in those four squares, one should draw lotuses in each direction.

The wise one, having divided the four squares into sixteen parts, should wipe them with four lines to form the shape of a *svastika*. Having colored it white like the island of Śvetadvīpa, he should fill those *svastikas* with powders starting from the northeast (Śiva).
One should complete the remaining portion by the very same path previously described.

This mandala, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis), is said to have nine centers. The meaning is as follows: within a square, there are seven lines extending from east to west and seven lines extending from south to north;
when the eight points are filled, it results in four squares. "By means of the four [lines]" refers to these.

The meaning is that when three squares are cooked from all sides, four squares remain. Regarding the phrase "path" (*vīthī*) and so forth, the meaning is that one should create paths by means of the outer row. The word "in this" (*asmin*) refers to the center following the mandala. It is obtained because it exists as a surrounding measurement. [It is located] in the groups of four situated in the cardinal directions and in those situated in the intermediate directions.

The meaning is: "in the four [groups] consisting of four squares. "Located in the intermediate directions" means: situated in the four squares within the four-cornered [area]. Having drawn two threads, one from south to north and one from east to west, sixteen squares are formed when the squares at each corner are divided sixfold.
The meaning is that one should erase everything else except for the four *da* and *ā* syllables. By that, there is an abundance of fruit;

the remaining lotus arrangement is like a painting, such is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the description of the lotus in the *Śāradā*: "The five-lotus mandala is proclaimed as being devoid of this svastika. The meaning of "this" is the mandala with nine centers (*navanābha*).

The meaning is that it should not be marked with a *svastika*. One should preserve sixteen squares, leaving the corner squares as they are; the meaning is that one should also perform the previously described procedure. This fourfold mandala, which bestows all prosperity, has been taught according to the principles of all tantras for use in initiation and the worship of the deity.
Regarding "in the worship of the deity," it means generally in the worship of the deity; the sense is that this should be performed during the annual rites, such as the Durgā festival and others.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha, the ninth chapter is recorded.
Now follows the exposition of the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for mantras. In the *Uḍḍīśatantra*:

"First is birth (*janana*), then life-giving (*jīvana*), followed by striking (*tāḍana*), awakening (*vodhana*), then consecration (*abhiṣeka*), purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*), and likewise nourishment (*āpyāyana*)."
Satisfying (tarpaṇa) and concealing (gopana)—these ten are the purificatory rites for the mantra.

On a surface smeared with saffron, or alternatively with gorocanā and the like, or smeared with cow dung, one should draw a lotus. O lady of excellent vows, one may also use saffron and sandalwood paste, or even ashes; this is the purification of the Śakti with saffron.
In the Vaiṣṇava Caṇḍamantra, it is known as *caṃdana*;
in the Śaiva, it is called *bhasma*; and in the drawing of the Mātṛkā-mantras, it is used for writing.
Having fashioned the group of filaments (*keśara*), one should write them in pairs starting from the east.
Regarding the phrase "the *varga* in the filaments" (*keśare vargam*), there is a phonetic elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*, meaning "the non-*varga*" (*avargam*).
Therefore, on the eight petals, one should write the sixteen [consonants] by arranging them in pairs within the filaments; on the seven-petaled [lotus], one should write the *ka*-group (*kādivarga*).

The extraction of mantras from their syllables is traditionally held to be like extracting [gold] from a leaf of the *lakṣma* tree. Having placed the *praṇava* (oṃ) in between, the wise one should worship the letters of the mantra.

The Tantrikas say that [this] is the "living" [mantra], and because of its hundredfold function, they call it *tajjīvana*. Having written the syllables of the mantra on birch bark (*bhūrja*), one should strike each syllable one hundred times with the wind-seed-syllable (*vāyubīja*) and with sandalwood water.
Having drawn [the figure] without mantras, [one should worship] with *karavīra* flowers.
The wise one should strike that mantra-syllable with a well-known [seed] syllable for awakening,
or with the root of the *mālatī* bud.
Having written the mantra upon the image, the practitioner, according to the number of syllables in the mantra,
should perform an ablution with *aśvattha* leaves for the sake of purification.
One should dissolve the sacrifice, the illusion, and the light-mantra; by reciting the Tāra mantra, one becomes stainless, free from the three impurities.
The syllable *tāram* (Om), preceded by *śivā* (Hrīṃ) and followed by *tārā* (Tāram), with the *bindu* (the nasal dot), is considered the mantra of light (*jyoti*).
It is known as the *māyika*, the *nāma*, the *yāttha*, the *pauruṣa*, and the *karmiṇa* mind.
That which is to be avoided should be known as such; those three impurities are prohibited.
One should perform the sprinkling with water containing *kuśa* grass over each syllable of the mantra after it has been consecrated by recitation (*japa*).

Having written one hundred and eight [times] on a birch-bark leaf, it is considered that by means of that mantra, the invocation of the deity of the treasure occurs. With that very mantra, according to the prescribed rite, libation (tarpaṇa) is considered to be performed with honey in the case of Śākta mantras, and with water containing moon-plant (induvārī) in the case of Vaiṣṇava mantras.
In the Śaiva tradition, wise men recommend that the libation be performed with ghee and milk.
The syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* are joined at the beginning of the mantra and so forth;
reciting the mantra in this way seven times is declared to be "illumination" (*dīpana*).
The concealment and the disclosure of the mantra to be recited—
these initiatory rites (saṃskāras) are declared in all tantras to be the tenth, kept secret from everyone.
Having performed the vehicle (*yāna*) according to the tradition, the practitioner (*mantrin*) shall obtain his desire.
Thus [the ritual] should be performed.
Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) is prescribed as having preceded it, next is the dwelling. As for the time, it should be on the previous day, starting from the east.

Having performed the ritual of offering the bali according to the sequence of worship, and having first performed the rites beginning with the *nācyahita*, one should worship the principal deity, fully worship the five deities, and after worshipping the retinue, complete the recitation (*japa*), worship, and the *stotra-kavaca-pīṭha*; then one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsa*). As it has been said:
In the *Yāmala*: "One should worship Gaṇeśa, Savitṛ, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Śaṅkara,
and the Lord of Kamalā with the sixteen types of ritual services (*upacāras*)."
In that *kramaṇa*, at that very place, one should worship Śaṅkara in the center, Śrīpati in the northeast, Haṃsa in the southeast, the son of Pārvatī in the southwest,
and likewise worship Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, in the northwest.
But when Govinda is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast,
Gaṇanātha in the southeast, and likewise Tapana in the southwest.
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should recite the mantra of Ambikā in the northwest,
when the thousand-rayed sun is in the center, and that of the Lord of Pārvatī in the northeast.
One should worship Mekadanta in the southeast and Achyuta in the southwest;
one should worship the deities in the northwest who bestow both enjoyment and liberation.
One should worship Bhavānī in the center, Mādhava in the northeast,
Vācavaktra in the southeast, and Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest.
One should worship Pradyotana in the northwest and the Teacher (Ācārya) as well;
one should sacrifice to Heraṃba in the center and Acyuta in the northeast.
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should worship the five-faced one in the northwest, Jagadambikā in the southwest, and likewise Ghananī in the northwest.
Deities who have been removed from their own places bestow sorrow, delusion, and fear;
therefore, having offered flowers to the principal deity, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa.
If Gaṇeśa himself is liberation, one should worship there according to the sequence of the Sūrya-krama;
[one should worship] with the five-faced [deity] in the southeast and Jagadambikā in the southwest.

In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*: When Śambhu is in the middle, Hari [is on the left]; when Harabhūdevī is present, Śaṅkara [is on the right]; for her, the deities are in the positions of change within the retinue of Hara and Gaṇeśa. When the Goddess is present, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Ekadanta are the foremost; in the Lord with a protruding belly (*laṃbodara*), the serpent is the giver of great bliss through the enjoyment of Śaṅkara.
If one goes without having worshipped those [deities] individually or collectively, that man goes to hell; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, in the initiation (dīkṣā) according to the Pañcātanī [tradition], having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and worship for each of them in sequence, and on the day of initiation as well, having worshipped them in that same sequence with the root mantra... [the remainder of the sentence is illegible].

Regarding the five mantras: for one who follows the Ekāyana path, there is worship on both days of the fortnight, but no receiving of the mantras; however, this applies only to the state of a *paśu*. For the *divya* and *vīra*, only the worship of the Goddess is to be performed, because other forms of worship are prohibited. This authority should be understood further ahead. Now, [regarding] the deities of the world-protectors (*dikpāla*)...
The most excellent Guru should offer the *bali* offering. Regarding the sequence for the worship of the retinue, the mantras of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) are to be known.
And in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"One should present the *bali* to the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*), to the Mothers, and to the spirits (*bhūta*)."
The wise one [should offer] to the students and the Yoginīs during rites performed for specific desires or on occasional occasions.
By means of this mantra and ritual manual:
Come here, O man! Destroy the city! Shatter the moving and the stationary! Ward off obstacles! O Mahābhairava, O Kṣetrapāla, accept, accept the offering! Svāhā!
Those who are fierce, performers of fierce deeds, and dwellers in fierce abodes;
those Mothers of fierce form, and those who are lords of the Ganas.
Likewise, Vighnaretas and the others who dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
may they all, with joyful minds, accept this bali offering.

To those beings who dwell upon the surface of the earth, having received the bali offering duly presented, may they seek their residence elsewhere or go to destruction elsewhere; salutations to them! [The mantra for the bali is: "Oṃ, come, come, O Goddess, O Son Vaṭukanātha," and so forth. This is the bali for the Yoginīs. [The mantra for the higher spirits is: "From above the Egg of Brahmā," and so forth. Thus.
The Lord Gaṇeśa also receives an offering (bali) with his own mantra. As for the substance of the offering: in the state of the Paśu, it consists of black gram, cooked rice, and so forth;

however, for the Divya and Vīra, it is the five-fold service (pañcopacāra). Regarding the previously mentioned [mandala], one should worship Ādhāraśakti on a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square drawn on one's left side; the touching [of the mandala] is performed everywhere with the thumb and ring finger of the left hand.

This is the *bali* offering: at the end of each respective mantra, one says "kṣāṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ. Likewise: "oṃ mātṛbhyo namaḥ," "oṃ bhūtebhyaḥ," "vāṃ vaṭukāya," "yāṃ yoginībhyām," "ānandabhairavāya," and "gāṃ gaṇapataye. This is the procedure for the *bali* offering on the day of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*). In case of inability, one may perform it on that very same day.
Then, having summoned the disciple who has bathed well and performed the *sumala* rite,
the wise teacher should place the *ṛṣis* and other components, together with the limbs (*aṅgas*), upon his body.
The mantra for liberation should be given to him; he should recite it one hundred and eight times.
With that mantra, he should sprinkle the auspicious child from a conch shell, performing the consecration (abhiṣeka) with those same mantras.

With the mantras beginning with "The gods shall consecrate you," one should understand that this refers to the state of the consecration. Then, having offered flowers and other items, the child should prostrate before the guru.
Thereafter, the blessing should be bestowed by the Brahmins together with the practitioners (sādhakas).
Having fed the most excellent guru sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) on one occasion,
and having prepared a bed of darbha grass, he should cause the disciple to lie down upon it.
In a dream, those who know mantras should bind the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) of the child with a mantra;
at the time of sleep, one should recite that mantra there for the sake of protection.

Having meditated upon the sandals of the Guru, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) is thus described. As for the mantra for sleep, it is stated in the Yāmala: "Oṃ, salutations to the trident-wielder with two eyes"—this is the mantra for the human who sleeps, O Mistress of the Gods.
Homage to Jayā, the three-eyed one, the tawny-hued, the great-souled.
Salutation to the host of manifold forms, the lord of dreams;
may he declare the truth regarding all matters whatsoever within the dream state.
"O Maheśvara, by your grace, may the ritual action attain success.
Having thus prayed to the Lord with this mantra, the wise disciple should go to sleep.
Having seen auspicious or inauspicious things in a dream, one should ask a child, a teacher, a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, an island, a palace, or a river in the morning.
An elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, a fruit-bearing tree,
a mountain, a pleasant object, pure food, raw meat, wine, and spirituous liquor.
One shall attain success through all such [omens] by means of observation.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is meant that auspicious and inauspicious results are to be known through dreams and the sequence of instruction, according to the principle of the obstruction of merit as stated by others. Furthermore, those things mentioned in the Tantras are also stated in astrology; as it has been said:
In the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra]: "Listen, O virtuous one, to the signs of a favorable [deity], as well as those of a seeker;
they are fashioned by lions in dreams and at night during the attainment of siddhi."
Worship at the tips of the horns, wandering about, an audience with the king,
and the sight of elephants, women, and performances of dance and song.
O Goddess of gods, listen to the censurable acts— festivals, seeing kinsmen, and likewise touching them— and their resulting obstacles and fruits.
In a dream, seeing black-colored soldiers, being struck, being smeared with oil, [seeing] a butcher,
women with other men's wives, and likewise the limbs of a woman;
There is loss of agitation, fire, wind, recitation, and destruction of kinsmen;
even from a guru, there is the sight of disease for the wife, husband, and kinsfolk.
Faith in the worship of another mantra brings obstacles to the worship of another;
whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, the Guru, who is Brahmā, should offer it into the fire of the Lord of Light.

The procedure beginning with "astraṇa" has been declared as the rule for the *vidhivāsana* (the ritual preparation of the site). The meaning is that the *homa* (fire sacrifice) is performed with the mantra "phaṭ svāhā. In the independent *Kulavṛtti*, composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha under the title *Gurubhāva*, this is recorded as the tenth chapter.
Then, having risen at the auspicious moment [muhūrta], the Guru should perform the morning rites (*prābhātika*). If they are not performed, there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*);
just as a ritual action devoid of its fruit lacks purity, so it is here. And in the Vīra-tantra: "But having failed to perform the morning rite..."
Having meditated on the Guru within the lotus of the head, one should contemplate him being bathed by that nectar; then,
with a disciplined mind, one should worship him with mental offerings.
One should meditate upon the Root-Mantra from the base of the spine up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
resembling ten million suns and with a form drenched in nectar.
And in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having prostrated before the family-tree (*kulavṛkṣa*), which possesses the shade of the words of the perfected sages (*siddha*), the ritual application is:
'Oṃ, obeisance to the family-trees (*kulavṛkṣa*). As for the family-trees, they are described in the *Rudrayāmala*:"

Through the kick of her feet, the *daśoka* tree sheds its flowers; through the intoxication of her speech, the *kesava* tree blooms; through her touch with her hands, the *karṇikāra* tree releases its blossoms; and through her conversation, the *sindhuvāra* tree bears its fruit. By the mere sight of her, the *śatamīliṅga* tree opens its petals; by the acceptance of her touch, she intoxicates even the *duḥkhakāminī* trees; and by her constant embrace, she brings them to full bloom.

Regarding the *liṅga* and the *nābhi*: another method is found in the *Jñānārṇava*: "The ten [trees] consecrated as dyes for the internal union are the *aśvattha*, *kadaṃba*, *vilva*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and *ciñcā*. Then, within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of a six-petaled lotus, there is a swan-throne (*haṃsapīṭha*), a triangle marked with three white lines, beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*.
Having visualized the mandala characterized by three lines, five lotuses, and a hundred thousand [petals], one should meditate upon one’s own guru seated there on a swan-throne (*haṃsapīṭha*),
as it is said in the Rudrayāmala:
In the morning, one should meditate upon the Guru— two-eyed, two-armed, peaceful, with hands in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness— upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name.
The meaning is that it is preceded by the name [of the deity] and involves the worship of the Guru’s sandals (*gurupādukā*).
As for the visualization (*dhyāna*), it is as stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Resembling pure crystal, adorned with pure linen cloth..."
Anointed with fragrant unguents and peaceful, her lotus-hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
With a gentle smile, he gazes upon his own guru with compassion;
he is joined by Śakti at his left side and is adorned with white ornaments.
With his own power, he holds a beautiful body in his right hand, while she,
well-adorned and holding a blue lotus in her left, is most resplendent.
"The two lotus-eyes are overflowing with the nectar of supreme bliss. And in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Upon the thousand-petaled lotus, she who possesses the jar, the sovereign of the wheel, radiant and holding a lotus that inspires no fear, together with her own lineage..."
