[The disciple] is joined [to the lineage]. O one of serene countenance, for a moment he should remember the Guru—who embodies all the deities—upon his head; that is to say, according to his own ritual procedure preceded by the *pādukā* (the sandals), following the previously mentioned method.
And in the *Bhairava-tantra*:
Rising at dawn, one should meditate upon the thousand-petaled lotus in the head,
with filaments as red as the rising sun and joined by the orb of the moon.
The wise one should meditate upon his own guru, who resembles a mountain of silver,
seated upon a lotus, with a smiling face, and anointed with white fragrant unguents.
He is endowed with the power of the beautiful-thighed one (Vāmoru), gazing with compassion;
his lovely body is held by the left hand of the goddess Dhiyāyā.

One should meditate upon him, preceded by his name, as holding a blue lotus in his left hand, red in color, beautifully adorned with ornaments, and endowed with the bliss of primordial wisdom (jñānānanda).

"Preceded by the name" means it was explained previously. Then, one should worship [the deity] mentally with scents and other offerings using their respective *mudrās*. Thereafter, the wise person should recite the *Vāgbhava* mantra one hundred and eight times. Having offered the recitation with devotion, he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff. In this meditation, red garments and the like are indicated; [the deity is] very red.

Statements such as "stained with blood" and so forth refer to the conditioned (aupādhika) supreme reality; they establish the white color [of the unconditioned], because of the statement that the natural (sāhajika) supreme reality is "untainted by its own shadow" due to the absence of any dark hue.
The Śrīpādukā mantra is as follows, according to the *Tantrarājottara*:
Having written the syllables *haṃsauḥ*, one should divide *hasakṣamalavarayū* three times, joined with fire (*ra*).
First, [place] the long vowel *ā* at the end; then the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. At the end of "Śrīparā," place the word "pātrakaḥ.

After that, the word "sarvārādhya," and then the word "sarvordhva. At the end of the word "nātha," place "guru"; then "guru" itself, and then "guru. At the end of the words "śrīgurunātha," [place] "saha sumana valināna" with a long *repha* (ḥ).
One should write the first [syllable] joined with the Śruti (the vowel *i*), endowed with the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā; then one should write the fourth [syllable];
and then one should write the third and the second [syllables] as before.
One should write the Lord of Mantras (Maṃtrīśa) preceded by the Guru and the Praṇava;
likewise, the first and fourth *kūṭas*, and the third preceded by the Praṇava.
This venerable Lord is adorned with the forty letters of the Nāga-variety;
or else, one should extract the seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Māyā, and Lakṣmī.
The syllable *hasakhapreṃ*, as well as the one called *naṃdabhairava* (*sahasphraṃ*),
the name of the Guru, the name of the Śakti, and also the *śrīpādukā*.

In this very way, the adept should recite the great mantra ten times; however, this recitation consists of mere remembrance (*smaraṇa*). But the recitation that is an integral part of the worship (*pūjāṅga*) is that which originates from speech (*vāgbhava*), according to the previously cited statement from the *Bhairavatantra*. As it is heard in the *Bhairavatantra*:
One should perform those respective services and ritual offerings with their corresponding seed-syllables; fragrance has the earth as its essence, and the flower likewise has space as its essence.
Incense is said to consist of eight elements, and the lamp is declared to consist of many;
the food offering consists of water—these are the services for the spirits.
The mudrās for that very [rite] are described therein: the mudrās are proclaimed in sequence from the thumb to the little finger.
The application is as follows: "I offer here fragrance, whose nature is earth; flowers, whose nature is space."
I thus mentally conceive the incense as consisting of sound, the lamp as consisting of fire, and the food offering as consisting of seed-syllables.
Having worshipped and recited the mantra, one should perform a hymn of praise. As it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One, Śiva, in the form of the Guru! You who have assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfectly accomplishing the descent of knowledge."

Salutations to the one whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, who has the form of the Supreme Self, who is the rising sun for the darkness of all ignorance, and who is the embodiment of bliss; salutations to the independent one, whose form is assumed out of compassion, the very soul of Śiva.
And she is supreme among the three [Vedas] for the sake of devotees who are destined for liberation, bestowing auspiciousness upon those who are worthy.
For the sake of discernment by the discerning, for the sake of investigation by those who investigate,
and for the sake of illumination by those who lack knowledge— this has been revealed to the one whose nature is wisdom.

"I shall pay homage in front, on the sides, behind, on the flanks, above, and below; O Creator, please always provide a seat for me in the form of my own mind. Thus [ends] the salutations; they are described in that very same place:
"To him by whom the eye was opened with the applicator of the collyrium of knowledge for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance..."
Salutation to the most excellent Śrī Guru! Salutation to that Śrī Guru by whom that state has been revealed—the undivided, mandala-shaped form by which the moving and unmoving world is pervaded.
By your grace, O Lord, I am one who has accomplished all duties in every respect.
I am liberated from the great noose of Māyā and death, and I am Śiva as well.
Now, the Pādukā-stotra:
I worship the lotus at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], beautified by the opening of the hollow of the Kuṇḍalinī, which rests upon the lake of the Brahma-randhra and bestows all wonders.
I worship Him who sports with His beloved, whose ear-lobes are scratched by the lines of the marks of His fingernails, who is marked by the corners of His eyes,
and who possesses the splendor of a circular halo; within His embrace, she is like a brilliant flash of lightning.
I meditate upon that which is of the nature of consciousness, whose radiance is deep red like a rising mountain,

whose heart is the circle of the jewel-throne of Bindu and Nāda, where the Fish, the Fire, and the Flame reside above, which is the abode of their playful expansion, and which is intensely fierce with the great splendor of the all-pervading Dharma-rukmā. I contemplate it as the Supreme Reality.
I remember here the pair of lotus-feet of the two Lords,
which are the abode of auspiciousness, cool as moonbeams and the source of the nectar of bliss flowing between them;
upon which jeweled sandals are firmly placed, which have silenced the clamor of all sins, and whose toenails radiate rays of light as red as shimmering young sprouts.

*Saccandrikā* (The Moonlight of Truth). I worship the two lotus feet of the Guru situated upon my head, which shine like a lotus emerging from the lake of supreme nectar. This *Pādukāpañcakastotra* (Hymn of the Five Sandals) resides within the mouths of the five-faced [Śiva].
Attained through the sequence of the five vehicles, it is exceedingly difficult to find within the realm of phenomenal proliferation.
Thus ends the *Pādukāstotra* within the commentary on the *Kulamudrā* in the *Mahāhārakākhya-tantra*. Thereafter,
having meditated upon the Kula from the root [cakra] up to the *brahmarandhra* at the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī, one should meditate upon the eight Ācāryas.
Thus it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having meditated upon the *kula* from the root center (*mūlādhāra*) up to the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), one should remember the Guru—
Prahlādanānandanātha and Śanakānanda."
Then Kumārānandanātha, Vaśiṣṭānandanāthaka,
Krodhānanda, Śukānanda, and beyond that, Dhyānānanda.
Having worshipped the Vodhānanda-maṭha, one should meditate upon the face of Kula; the meaning is that having meditated, one should worship it.
With hearts overflowing with the joy of the essence of great rasa, with eyes rolling, their bodies merged with the Liṅga of Kula, they have pulverized all remaining darkness;
surrounded by Kula-disciples, they possess a flood of senses filled with the waters of fullness.
All of them, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, proclaim the meaning of the Kula-tantras;
thus, having bowed to the Guru of the Kula and having dismissed the Mātṛkā.
O child, one should resort to a Śākta holy site (tīrtha) that is pure, well-situated, and possesses a master; such a place is said to bring happiness to the Kula.
"This secret, most wonderful, has been proclaimed; it must be guarded against the danger of the uninitiated (*paśu*).
Having thus meditated, and having satisfied the Supreme with the *bindus*, he should dismiss them according to the sequence prescribed in that particular *tantra*.
Then, [he should satisfy] the Parāpara-guru, the Parameṣṭhi-guru, his own Guru, the lineage (*saṃtati*), their respective *ṛṣis*, and the Divine Current (*divyaugha*).

Having prostrated before the Siddhaugha and Mānavaugha, and having received [the teachings] from the Queen of the venerable supreme Guru, one should place Kuṇḍalinī together with the secret [mantra] within the vessel of nectar (mṛtadhāra). Satisfying the deities residing in each of the cakras, one should cause Kuṇḍalinī to return to the Mūlādhāra. The meditation on Kuṇḍalinī is as follows:
In the Śruti: "One should constantly meditate upon the triangle, the treasury of light, at the mūlādhāra;
one should sit upon its front line, which is situated from bottom to top."
When it stands in the center of the blue [light], shining like a streak of lightning—
yellow like the stalk of wild rice, like a string of a lute, or resembling the rays of the sun.

And in the center of that crest-lock (śikhā), she who is established at the ultimate pinnacle—she is Brahmā, she is Śiva, she is Indra, she is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self-ruler; she alone is Viṣṇu, she is Prāṇa, she is the Fire of Time, and she is the Moon. Having thus meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī, one is liberated from all sins.
"He becomes purified from the great sins (mahāpātaka); having accomplished all mantra-siddhis, he becomes Bhairava alone. Thus it is manifest, both at the first departure and at the return.
I take refuge in that woman who is like one dead, who moves within the state of the end, and whose form is bliss. And in the Nīlatantra:
"Having risen and gone to the northern Meru, one should meditate upon Ugratāriṇī."
Extending from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), it is thinner than a spider's thread.
She is the manifest embodiment of the root mantra, directly bestowing the bliss of immortality;
she is as radiant as ten million suns and as cooling as ten million moons.
He has the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning and is the lord whose crest-jewel is the bliss of desire;
his body is formed by a veil pervaded by a mass of that radiance.
One who is not endowed with all auspicious marks should not perform the rite of bathing.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"I shall proclaim the procedure for worship by which a person obtains their desires; O Goddess of gods, one should meditate at dawn after rising."
O Lord, one should worship the feet of the Śrī Guru with the mind, using perfumes and other offerings with a spirit of devotion;
thereafter, one should display the Yoni Mudrā as described in the Yāmala.
As stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"The Liṅga is conceived as facing north and situated within the Yoni;
it is joined with the Heart-knot and the Bindu, and is itself the support for all ornaments."
The other [letter] is situated within the anusvāra, and another is below the visarga;
here, the Mahāpadmavana is proclaimed as the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha).
The Kadamba is shaped like a globe; that Kāma exists there in the form of a drop (bindu), within the Brahma-randhra, in the mandala that is the support of the Suṣumnā.
The principles (tattvas) beginning with earth, as well as the five groups of mantras,
and the divine principle called Pūrṇa, situated between the two bows.
Above that is Nāma, and above Nāma is Udbhijana;
further above that, O Dear One, is Kāmarūpa, which is Śakti, the emission (visarga), like the Kula.
One should perceive the moon situated there— the *kāmarūpa* located at the *mūlādhāra*, the triangle, and the great thousand-petaled lotus adorned with red filaments—
showering down unmanifest drops.
The previously mentioned mudrā is called Guhyā, whose nature is like nectar.
I shall explain its binding so that one may attain conscious realization:
first, by means of the practice of inhalation (pūraka), one should fix the mind upon the foundational center (ādhāra).
One should contract and bind the vulva located between the anus and the penis;
one should indeed meditate upon the wandering Kāma, who has emerged and resembles a bandhūka flower.
Blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction (kālānala) and possessing a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
above that is his subtle crest-lock (śikhā), which is the supreme digit (kalā) whose nature is consciousness.
One should contemplate oneself as having become one with her,
proceeding by way of the path of Brahman toward that Linga in due order.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons,
it is nectar situated within creation, whose very form is supreme bliss.
Having drunk the divine nectar of the Kula, which is red, exceedingly cool, celestial, and raining down in torrents, one should enter the Kula once again.
Otherwise, one may again fall into confusion regarding the application of mantras;
and she is declared in this tantra, O Supreme Goddess, to be composed of vital breath (prāṇamayi).
That is called *udghāta*, for it is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
when one touches it by practicing this single [breath] day after day with resolve, [the result follows].
One is liberated from the bondage of existence through old age, death, suffering, and the like;
and that fourfold creation proceeds from her as its source.
Furthermore, everything from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) up to Śiva dissolves back into that [Yoni];
she is the supreme source (drā), and she is proclaimed to be bondage.
O Goddess, by means of this mudrā, there is nothing wherein one might not accomplish [the goal]. However, he who acts otherwise, or he who recites the mantra otherwise—
O Goddess of gods, he does not attain success; this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise.
For his mantras are severed and obstructed, and he is arrogant with the pride of mature youth.
Those who stand on the side of the enemy, who are devoid of vigor, abandoned by sentient beings,
deprived of their portions, and cut into a hundred pieces;
Endowed with this ritual procedure and directed by the preceptor, they all become perfected beings who grant liberation in no long time.
If the practitioner recites the mantra in the form of its syllables, whether auspicious or inauspicious, each of those will undoubtedly be accomplished by means of the reliance upon the Yonimudrā.
Having initiated [the disciple] according to the rule and having consecrated him according to the rule, he then becomes qualified in this tantra, O Goddess; it cannot be otherwise.

Having understood the womb (yoni) and the phallus (liṅga), as well as the internal disposition, through the placement of mudrās and maṇḍalas, and by means of sacrifice, fire-oblation, vows, and so forth, one should then manifest the mudrā.
Alternatively, to whomsoever the command of the Goddess arises in due time, to him one should tell this secret; otherwise, one shall go to hell.
Even thousands of murders of Brahmins and even the three worlds may be purified by the sin of one who protects a terrified woman through the binding of the *yonimudrā*.
Therefore, those who desire liberation must practice constantly;
from practice comes perfection, and through practice one attains liberation.
The practice of deceiving Time (Kālavañcana) bestows liberation; as stated in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"She who resembles ten million flashes of lightning, whose brilliant luster surpasses the glow of the fire of time, and who is like a mass of thousands of rays of light..."
One should meditate upon the subtle Brahman, which is endowed with light, revolving from the womb, possessing the radiance of a throbbing, crimson bandhūka flower,
and shining like ten million moons; above that,
it is radiant with the mass of light from a cluster of firefly-like streaks of lightning.
The subtle portion of pure consciousness situated within the midst of the pathways becomes unified;

then, with a steady intellect, the wise one should meditate upon his own self as motionless, like a lamp in a windless place. The wise one perceives the form of the *Haṃsa*, which is the power known as *Kuṇḍalinī*, the very essence of the world-manifestation.

One should contemplate within that [central channel] a form resembling a shimmering flash of lightning, like the whorl of a conch shell, having the shape of a slumbering serpent, and enchanting the world— a form comparable to a radiant thread. Then, having awakened her who was asleep according to the procedure taught by the Guru with the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should perform the ritual action.

With a concentrated mind, one should cause that Kuṇḍalinī— the Māyā united with that supreme energy (kalā) whose nature is consciousness— to emerge as the Kaulinī Śakti. Accompanied by the path of Brahman, she rises from the Ādhāra through her own self,
piercing the three Liṅgas and the Brahma-nāḍī, as she ascends upwards.

From the lotus-abode, one should cause the power of the Self (*ātma-śakti*) to reach the sky-lotus in the pool of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-kuṇḍa*). Having reached the place of emission (*visarga-sthāna*), which possesses a flowing stream of blood-like nectar, and having drunk the essence of the *kula-amṛta*,
one whose mind is concentrated should again enter that divine state within the center of the fish (*padmatsya*) and proceed.
Furthermore, O best of teachers, by means of the union with the *mātrā* as it is imparted from the *kula* to the *akula*, that energy (*śakti*)—
which is the life-force of the entire body— is declared by the foremost [masters] to be *prāṇa*.

That is proclaimed by the lords of sages as the *udghāta* (the upward stroke), when memory gradually cools down until it reaches the limit of the means of knowledge. One who abides in right conduct, daily devoted to meditation, faithful,
and constantly freed from all impurities, becomes liberated from the rise of sufferings, free from old age and death, endowed with virtues, and like a god.

Thus she lives long upon the earth; for her, the entire fourfold creation proceeds, and into her the whole universe dissolves, including everything from Kālāgni and Rudra down to the Avasāna. This very Seal of the Source of All (Khilayonimudrā) has been described by me; indeed, it is difficult even for the gods to obtain. There is nothing that cannot be accomplished through this bond.
There is indeed no [obstacle] for that bull among men who accomplishes it. Whether they are severed, obstructed, situated within, or pinned down;
whether they are young, old, unconscious, lowly, or excellent; whether they are burnt, fallen, or standing on the side of the enemy;
whether they are asleep, awake, or arrogant in their youth; or those who are devoid of valor or strength, and those whose limbs are mangled or bound by mantras—[none of these prevail].

Deprived [of these], all mantras become powerless when the *mudrā* is bound according to the *yoni*. By this [practice], the violation of the Guru’s bed, the drinking [of intoxicants], the killing of a twice-born, and the theft of gold—all these go to complete dissolution even if performed once, provided it is done correctly with the binding of the *mudrā*. He alone is the best of mantra-practitioners; he alone is the yogi.

Established in the state of the perfection of qualities, he alone is bound by this excellent bond; thus, being devoted to his own appropriate duties and actions, he remains so through that body for those who possess bodies, by means of that well-performed bond. O King of the Ancestors, neither old age nor death shall ever conquer him.

And fear has been explained. For by the thorough practice of that very bond which is hearing, a person attains incomparable success such as the *aṇimā* powers, as well as exalted realization; or else, through the mastery of yoga, he may attain the subduing of the vital breaths, the deception of time, those sciences, and even the supreme state.
The wise behold that which is stretched out; it is written at the tip of the six chakras. And in the Śrīkrama:
"That which is named Madhumatī, the Māyā that causes delusion—listen as I describe how she is to be meditated upon through her external and internal divisions."
One should contemplate the entire power (śakti) as having a single form through its own nature, while being manifold-formed through its own manifestation as the three worlds.
One should desire me, the loving goddess, who is the form of all mantras;
one should contemplate the beautiful goddess, whose form is all-pervasive.
O Goddess of gods, the syllable *īṃ* is a constituent part of the mantra consisting of four elements; O Goddess, the first of the three *bindus* is *va-bhra-ka*.
One should place the three points (bindus) and the pair of breasts in the region of the heart;
one should contemplate the subtle half-measure of the letter *ha* within the center of the womb.
Likewise, O Beloved, the form of Kāmakalā, the sprout of passion, should be brought within the range of one's vision:
resembling the rising sun, with the luster of vermilion, bearing two dots (bindus) upon her two breasts, the letter Śaṃ on her face,
and the flickering flame of a lamp at her private parts.
One should contemplate that [energy] from the base (ādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra) along its respective path.
O Goddess, I am Kāma, the Bindu; the Supreme Goddess resides there.

O Goddess, she consists of Śiva and Śakti; she is the supreme digit (kalā) whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa). Below that is the Parārdha, which is the supreme digit whose nature is consciousness. She too is the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti, whose essential form is Kāmakalā.
Proceeding along the path of the crest-lock, having pierced the fourteen knots and entered the supreme path, she is subtle in form and possesses her own essential nature.
That threefold creation, consisting of the forms of Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
having meditated upon it, the best of practitioners shall bring the three worlds under his control.
This, O Goddess, has been told to you: the definitive determination of the Kāmakalā.
It must indeed be guarded with effort if one desires one's own welfare.
And in the Rudrayāmala:

"Having led [the breath] to the eternal Brahman, which is the abode of liberation, by means of the Haṃsa, one should lead it to the supreme, radiant, and subtle lightning-streak at the four-petalled Mūlādhāra, which resembles a lotus fiber."
Having contemplated the unity of form together with the thirst for immortality within the abode, I should meditate upon the Supreme.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"I am indeed not other than Viṣṇu; I am Brahman alone, not a partaker of suffering.
I am of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss. Thus one should contemplate oneself.
Having recited the root mantra as much as possible and offered the recitation to the deity,
one should bow to one's own chosen deity and contemplate the entire world as being identical with that deity.
O Jāmalat, at dawn, the knower of the ritual should perform the selection (*varaṇa*) according to the rules.

Having meditated upon the mantra spoken by Śiva while on the ground in the prescribed order, [he should address] those people who are afflicted by all defects: "Oṃ, O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean and whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you."

"O Goddess, forgive the touch of my feet"; with this mantra, one should place one's foot upon the ground. Now, the practical application (*prayoga*): having first contracted the anus (*gudākuñcana*), one should recite the mantra sixteen times while raising and retaining the vital air (*vāyu*) through the differentiation of the six chakras and three *liṅgas*, using the mantra "Kulaṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ."

Having brought about the union of those two with Paramaśiva and manifested their state of aesthetic oneness (*sāmarasya*), one should fill the vessel of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍā*) with that nectar.

Then, having satiated the Root Goddess— who is identical in form with the Root Mantra and is the *Kulakuṇḍalinī*— within that nectar-water, and having first performed the libation for all the deities of the *cakras*, one should bring her back to the *mūlādhāra*.
Again, through streams of nectar, there is union with Paramaśiva; again, union with the Mūlādhāra;

again, union with Paramaśiva; again, union with the Mūlādhāra. Then, having meditated upon Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra up to Paramaśiva as an uninterrupted form, by means of the networks of its rays—

Having meditated on the entire body as pervaded by [the deity] in a state of unity, having visualized the form of the root-deity, and having recited the root-mantra, one should go outside, placing the foot upon the ground in the order of one's own descent. Thus ends the morning [rite]. [The voiding of] feces, urine, and so forth is the supreme food.
The practitioner, honoring [the tooth-stick], having performed the sprinkling with clay and water, should not use it for scraping; rather, he should have it cleaned by others.
"Kāma, Kāma," [it is said]—O Lord of all worlds, the mantra ending in *ṅe* is dear to the heart.
When a mantra is prescribed for cleaning the teeth, one shall not obtain purity through anything else.
And in the Somabhujagāvalī: "O Pārvatī, having consecrated with this mantra— *oṃ vasantaiśvarāya hūṃ*—
the tooth-stick produced from sacrificial wood or similar materials."
One should carefully abandon that which is half-burnt, situated in the *samāna* [vāyu], as well as remnants of food, feces, urine, and so forth, even if they have adhered [to the object].
The seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) is Kāmadeva; ending with the syllable *vāṅ*, it is beloved by all people.
The practitioner should clean his teeth with this mantra;
he should wash his mouth and all its parts with a handful of water using the root mantra.
Thus is the washing.
In this independent *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru,
this is the chapter numbered as Rudra (eleven).
(p. 50b) Now, regarding the ritual bath (*snāna*): it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having thus bowed to the family preceptor (*kulaguru*) and dismissed the family mother (*kulamātṛkā*),"
Having brought him to his family home, he should resort to a sacred bathing place for the purpose of purification.
Now I shall describe to you, my child, the bath that brings happiness to the lineage;
it is the ritual for the dark, red, and golden pastimes, whose forms are the very abodes of the Divine.
In that regard, the disciple who belongs to a particular lineage, perceiving himself as having that very form,
[perceives] heaven, the entire earth, the netherworld, and what arises in the sky.
Having sipped water (ācānta), with a blade of *darbha* grass from his family, he should apply the sectarian mark (*puṇḍraka*) along with that *darbha*;
the meaning is that the triangular tilaka consists of the nature of power (*śakti*).
Now, regarding the *tilaka*: in the *Tārātantra*, it is said:
"One should draw the weapon-mantra of the Goddess on the forehead with red sandalwood paste or *gopīcandana*, and then the seed-syllable of Tārā upon the heart."
One should place the *śakti* in the center and perform *prāṇāyāma*.

Here, the materials for the *tilaka* are the same for all mantras; however, the writing of the *astrabīja* and so forth is specifically for the subject of the lunar asterisms (*nakṣatra*), such as the *akula-darbha*.
In the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
"Silver should be worn on the index fingers and gold on the ring fingers;
this indeed constitutes the *arbha* [ornament], and its absence is permissible. However, this applies to the *divya* and *vīra* [classes]; in their absence, however—"
The inclusion of the word "vanya" (wild) refers to the family lineage. In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"A worthy vessel of the family, along with *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and likewise water."
Having taken [the materials], one should perform the ritual bath for the pleasure of the family deity.

At the outset, one should cast the *saṃkalpa* (the formal declaration of intent) into the water of the *kulacakra*; or else, the vessel of the *saṃkalpa* itself should be meditated upon as the *kulapātra*. This is because, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, the nature of the *kula* is established for all sacrificial substances (*yāgavastu*). Within the *saṃkalpa*, there should be the mention of the month, fortnight, lunar day (*tithi*), and so forth.

They perform [these acts], according to the maxim: "If what is stated by another is not contradictory [to one's own system]. In that regard, writing [the scriptures] and so forth are not the duty of a Kaula because they stem from the state of a *paśu* (bound soul).

For it is forbidden in the *Kulārṇava*: "One should not practice what is taught in the *paśu*-scriptures; one should practice what is taught in the *kula*-scriptures. Therefore, it is stated in the *Tantra*: "For the pleasure of the Kula-deity, one should perform the ritual bath (*snāna*)."
There is only a mention of the fruit itself. "Kulacakra" means the triangle of Śakti.
Having brought [the deity] from the place of Kula by means of the goad of the Kula-mudrā, one should invoke the Kula-tīrthas right there within that which is of the nature of Śiva.
Then the water is likewise threefold.

Having drunk it three times, one gazes three times at the body; this means [gazing] at the triangle whose nature is Śiva and whose nature is Śakti. Here, following the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one offers three handfuls of water to the head with the *kuṃbha-mudrā* or with joined palms (*añjali*) for the purpose of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Having first performed the libation (tarpaṇa) according to the consensus of the Jñānārṇava and other tantras,
the wise practitioner should then perform the rite of bathing while recollecting the root mantra;
having consecrated water with the mantra three times, he should pour it over his own head.
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) three times, one should cast [the water] away;
one should sprinkle the body three times and present the arghya offering to the Sun.

In this context, as part of the preceding single syntactical unit, at the very beginning [one should perform] the visualization (*saṃkalpa*), the drawing of the triangle wheel (*trikoṇacakra*), and the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrthāvāhana*).
As stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "When the ritual of bathing has arrived, one should offer a handful of water from the *mūrdhan* (the topknot) with the *astra-mantra*."
Then, having performed the rite three times with the Vidyā, one should sip water three times.
Furthermore, the libation (tarpaṇa) is threefold, and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the body is likewise threefold;
this is also taught in the independent [tantra].
The practitioner of mantra, reciting the root-mantra, should perform [the rite] upon the head with the mudrā known as the lotus-hand.
Having cast [the water] three times, the mantra-practitioner, the foremost of adepts, should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana).
Having mastered the knowledge of the Self and being established in the auspicious principles (*tattvas*), one should then enter the sacrificial hall.
Having formed a *campaka* triangle upon the water with the *kuśa*-mudrā, one should visualize the *kula*-darbha grass and the *kula*-tilaka mark.

Having invoked the sacred waters (tīrtha) with the *kumbha-mudrā* or with the hollowed palms (*añjali*), one should sprinkle them three times on the head while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
Then, having sipped water (*ācamana*) three times again and having offered libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the Goddess, one should wash the body three times with the root mantra.
Regarding the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, it is as described in the *Jñānārṇava*:
Then, having formed the right fist with the index finger shaped like a blade of kusha grass,
this great mudrā called the "Goad" is capable of attracting [beings] from the three worlds.

The mantra for the invocation of the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) in the *Śrīkrama* is as follows: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters! Thus is the jar-gesture (*kuṃbhamudrā*), as described in the *Guptārṇava*:
having placed the right thumb upon the [left] thumb with both hands.
The wise know that the continuous creation of the disciples is the Kumbha-mudrā.
Thus one should perform [the rites], ending with the recitation of the root mantra (mūlamantra). This concludes the bathing for the divine and the hero (divya-vīra).
Now, the bathing for the bound souls (paśu) according to the Nīlatantra: "Then, having taken earth and kuśa grass, one should go to the edge of the water."
Having bathed to remove physical impurities, one should perform the ritual bath with mantras.
One should not sip water on the road after having performed the triple exchange with the *vidyā*; by this, it is meant the *mūlavidyā*. In the *Vīratantra*:
"Having blocked the seven apertures, the wise one should then immerse himself three times;
[he should do so] with the principles of the Self (*ātmatattva*), Knowledge (*vidyātattva*), and Śiva (*śivatattva*), O foremost of practitioners."
O Dear One, having placed the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) at the end of the [mantras], one should offer with the pure [mantra] for the sake of Pārtha:

"To the Ātmatattva, Svāhā! Likewise, "To the Vidhyātattva, Svāhā! and likewise, "To the Śivatattva, Svāhā!"—this is common to all states of being. However, there is a specific [rule] for Tārā in the Mālinītantra:

The practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with mantras beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by the words "ātmatattva" and so forth, ending with "svāhā. He should touch three times the red [parts] of the nose, eyes, ears, arms, navel, head, and the top of the head; or he may simply perform a salutation to the night.
The knowledge of the Self is the hymn of Śiva, and the Praṇava is remembered as Vāgbhava.
The Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is the goddess Kūrca, which is to say "jam. In that context, the recitation of the Kūrca-bīja is considered the Aghamarṣaṇa rite.
Having taken up the earth with both hands using the root mantra, one should show it to the Sun; thereafter, it is prescribed that one should contemplate it as a cavity.
One should apply cow-dung up to the nose with the mantra at the two *ṭha* syllables;
then one should offer three handfuls of water upon the head, the heart, and the region of the navel.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), O Goddess, one should take [the breath] with the right hand within the triangle, following the sequence of a conch-shell spiral.
Having stirred that [water] in the ritual vessel, one should immerse oneself three times with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantras should offer three handfuls of water to Varuṇa.
Having risen from the water toward the west for Soma Bhānu and having put on two garments,
the practitioner of mantras should then perform the rites according to the prescribed rule.

The twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*) is indicated by the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Bathing (*snāna*) consists of the removal of impurities up until the point of immersion. Regarding the drawing of the triangle, the mantra is as stated in the *Mālinītantra*: "One should draw the triangle while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the *haṃsaka* for Savitṛ. As for the practical application: having taken earth and *kuśa* grass...
Having gone to the water's edge and performed his bath according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, he should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Then, having kneaded earth with both hands while reciting the root mantra and shown it to the Sun, he should apply it to all his limbs.
He should smear cow-dung on his two nostrils with the mantra "oṃ" and likewise on his head, heart, and navel.
Having offered a handful of water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), with the right hand held over the left,
one should recite the seed-syllable (*vīja*) of the root-mantra while addressing the Sun, chanting "haḥ hūṃ saḥ śuciḥ" and so forth, and [draw] a triangle.
Having drawn [the diagram] in the sequence of a conch-spiral, one should not stir it; therein one should immerse oneself—this is the removal of impurities according to the *Gautamīya*.
Having sipped water according to the rule, the practitioner, reciting the mantra, should lie down in a clean place.
Having joined the sacred waters (tīrthas) with water, one should recite the root mantra three times.
One should strike the ground with the tip of a *kuśa* blade seven times and collect [the dust] upon one's head.
Now, there is no application by means of the name of the lineage (*kulīna*).
Having first gone there, one should visualize the moving and non-moving world as blue through the splendor of the elephant, using the *aṅkuśa* mudrā.

Having sipped water (ācamana) with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and *kampa* leaves, and taking sesame, *kuśa*, and water in a vessel of his lineage, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Today, for the pleasure of the family deity (*kuladevī*), I shall perform the ritual bath. Having thus resolved, he should cast a triangular diagram (*trikoṇa-cakra*) into the water, invoke the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with the mantra beginning with "O Gaṅgā," and [perform the rite] with the pitcher-gesture (*kuṃbha-mudrā*) or with joined palms while reciting the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

Having cast [the water] upon the head and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should satisfy the Triple Root (trimūla) and then cast it upon the head with the root mantra. This is the Kaulika bath.
Now, regarding the Sandhyā according to the Rudrayāmala:
Having performed the Tantric bath according to the very procedure stated,
one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) after completing both the Vedic and Tantric counts.
In the *Tantrarāja*:
"The knower of mantras, having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), including the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*),
should take water in his left hand and, with the drops of water falling from it..."
Having performed the sprinkling seven times while reciting the mantras with water,
the wise one should hold the remaining water in his right hand.
Having drawn from within the body through the *iḍā* the accumulated mass of sins washed away,
one should expel that black-colored water through the right channel (*dakṣanāḍī*).
Then the mantra-practitioner, having visualized that [image] as the form of sin with his right hand,
should cast it before him onto a vajra-stone with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
In the *Kamārcanadīpikā*:
Having meditated upon the surface of the adamantine stone (*vajraśilā*) with the mantra "Prahara Phaṭ" according to the *Yāmala*,
and having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should then take water in the left hand.
Having taken [the water] with the right hand, one should then form the *saṃpuṭa* gesture; then, having consecrated it three times with the seed-syllables of Śiva, Water, Earth, and Fire,
and again seven times with the root-mantra using the *tattva-mudrā*.
One should sprinkle that water upon one's head, and place the remainder in the right hand.
The foremost of practitioners should wash away the sin residing within the body;
he should apply the tilaka with the root mantra during the three junctions of time according to the Kaulika tradition.
O beautiful goddess, this has been declared for the sake of my disciple Tilaka:
Śiva is the syllable *ha*, Vāyu is *ya*, Jala is *va*, Pṛthvī is *sa*, and Vahni is the letter *ra*.
In some places, the colors of the elements are shown in sequence.
As it is stated in the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
"O Goddess, the elements beginning with space [are assigned] in order, and furthermore, by the colors of the elements, they are threefold."
Having thus meditated, one should contemplate the form of radiant energy situated within the *saṃpuṭa*.

"Let this very *sandhyā* be performed by the Kaulikas"—by using the word "this very" (*atraiva*), it is indicated that for the Kaulikas there is no abiding in the Vedic *sandhyā*, whereas for the *paśus* (the bound souls), both types of *sandhyā* are to be practiced. The *sandhyā* is common to all states of being.
The obligatory nature of *sandhyā* is described in the *Lakṣmīkulārṇava*:
And he who is devoid of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) shall obtain the fruit of bathing in a river;
there is a specific rule regarding the Vaiṣṇavas and others in the Gautamīya [Tantra],
page 52a.
Now, I shall also describe the preliminary rites in this context:
by performing them, one attains the qualification for the worship of mantras and other such practices.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), one should then perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite;
thereafter, having worshipped the Root Deity and the retinue individually.
One should satisfy Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niṣaṇoddha, Vadāruka,
Viśvaksena, Śaileya, and Guru according to the prescribed rite.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

Having sipped water three times (*tri-ācamya*) and performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍ-aṅga-vinyāsa*), one should place water three times in the left hand with the right hand while reciting the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
Covering it with the right hand, one should consecrate that water three times with the mantra "haṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ."

Having visualized the form as fire (*tejas*), one should sprinkle it seven times on the head with the *dakṣatattva-mudrā*. Then, taking the remaining water with the right hand, one should block the left nostril with the right; drawing the water through the left nostril into the interior of the body, one should wash the entire body and draw the black-colored [impurity] out through the right nostril.
Having poured that water into his right hand, he should cast it before him onto a diamond-stone (vajra-śilā) like a blade of grass.
In the *Yāmala*: "Then, having performed the Tantric twilight rite (*sandhyā*), one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*)."
But he [saw] the divine sages and ancestors, together with their weapons and their retinues.
The wise one should offer libations to the Goddess either in water or within the home;
having fully satisfied the lineage of gurus, he should then satisfy Vaṭuka and the others.

One should satisfy the venerable Guru, Pāla, and the others, as well as the deities of the limbs and so forth; thereafter, one should perform the libation for Śeṣikā, Sundarī, Aiśyā, and the Guru-libation.
One should worship the supreme and the subordinate [deities] at the two front corners, Parameṣṭhin in the southwest, and the lineage of gurus from the northwest to the northeast.

One should perform libation (*tarpaṇa*) upon the limbs and other [deities] in their respective locations, and one should also perform libation upon the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*). Regarding the procedure for libation: having washed one's hands and visualized one’s own desired *yantra* in the water, and having meditated upon it as being pervaded by the Root Mantra along with its support (*sādhāraṇa*), [one offers libation] in the northeast with "Aiṃ Svāhā! O Śrīpati, [conjoined] with the glorious Amukī Devī, the excellent power (*suśakti*), of the venerable Amukānandanātha."

In the southeast (Agni), one should offer libations with *aiṃ svāhā* to the venerable feet of the supreme and subordinate Guru, Śrī Mahānanda Devanātha. In the southwest (Nairṛtya), [one offers] to the venerable feet of the Parameṣṭhi Guru, Śrī Mahādevī. In the northwest (Vāyavya), one should satiate the lineage of the excellent Gurus—the Ṛṣis, the teachers of the Divine Current (Divyaugha), the Human Current (Mānavaugha), and the Siddha Current (Siddhaugha)—and the [eight] Ācāryas. In all instances, [the mantra is] *aiṃ svāhā*.

Regarding the mantras of the retinue: having uttered each respective mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) by saying "I satisfy [Name] in the accusative case," followed by the word *tarpayāmi*. In this manner, one should satisfy the Goddess with the root mantra, saying "Oṃ *svāhā* Devīm tarpayāmi. Afterward, one should satisfy the Śeṣikā. There is a specific rule regarding Tripurā in the *Yāmala*: [one should do so] with the *Vāgbhava* [syllable].

Those who are to be purified by the King of Desire (Kāmarāja) should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with the nectar of the Lamp (Dīpanī) by means of that very Peak of Power (Śaktikūṭa). The specific distinction for Tārā is that she is to be satisfied with the water of purification by that same [means]. In the Mālinītantra: "Facing the northern direction, one should satisfy the Goddess alone with holy water, sesame paste, milk, and unbroken rice grains."

The meaning is "with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and so forth. At the end of the root mantra, [one says]: "I satiate Tāriṇī, the beloved of Agni. Then, with a vessel of gold, silver, or copper, the wise one, having devoutly performed the libation three times with straight blades of kuśa grass, [says] at the end of the root mantra: "Svāhā."
Then, facing the southern direction, he should take up a piece of moṭaka grass.
Having uttered, "May the ancestors be satisfied," one should perform this libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having spoken the sentence, "May the ancestors be satisfied," that is the libation for these ancestors; it is the act of satisfying them.

The meaning is that one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) using that name. This statement applies to the Paśus and Kaulas; however, in the independent (svatantra) rite of libation and so forth, one should recite: "May Brahmabhairava be satisfied. During the invocation of one's own ancestors, one should proclaim the names of the Bhairavas: "May Mother Kālikā be satisfied; may Father Bhairava be satisfied."
In this very manner, one should perform the libation according to one's capacity. Bhairava is to be described as the Self of Brahman.
Not only by mind, but also by speech, the mantra should be recited: "May Bhairava, the Father, be satisfied; may Bhairavī, the Mother, be satisfied," and so forth, as stated in the Jñānārṇava.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"One should satisfy the gods, the ancestors, and the sages with the water of the lineage (*kulavāri*).
Having meditated again upon those whose nature is the lineage, one should please the Lord of the Lineage (*kuleśa*) by leading him into the lineage."

In the Bhairavī Tantra, the nomenclature for these is as follows: in the Kaulika dharma of the Bhairavī Tantra, for those ancestors, [the offering] is made to the deity Bhairava by the performer, Bhairava;
having first uttered the mantra known as Bhairava, it should be presented.
The donor, the act of giving, and the recipient [should be understood] according to the nature of the heated liṅga.
Bhairavī is the very self of Bhairava, in whom existence is entirely dissolved;
[she is to be worshipped] during the offering of ancestral rites, at marriage, at bathing, and in the worship of the limbs.
O Goddess, when you are thus intent on such thoughts, I am pleased; of this there is no doubt.
And being satisfied by that, O Goddess, I truly gratify all the remaining worlds.
Now, the statement in the Nīlatantra:
The libation (tarpaṇa) is considered to end with "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) and conclude with "svāhā.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"Having uttered the root mantra ending in 'svāhā,' one should perform the libation with that [mantra]."
I offer my own vital essence as the root; I satisfy [you], O such-and-such goddess; obeisance!
In the *Gautamīya*, beginning with the Vaiṣṇava [tantras],
one should first utter the mantra preceded by "Śrī" and also "Kṛṣṇa"; then,
having spoken the word "tarpayāmi," one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ending with the name.
"Kṛṣṇa" is an elliptical designation; "the Supreme Deity is one's entire being. For Śrī Tripurasundarī, however, the root mantra ends with *svāhā*:
"I satiate the sandals of Śrī Tripurasundarī, *namaḥ*. This is the authoritative proof [for this] hereafter. Then:
One should offer the *arghya* oblation to the Sun. This is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "And having prepared the *arghya* three times for the divine Kula-Sun. And in the *Nandikeśvarasaṃhitā*:
"As long as the *arghya* and the offering are not presented to Bhāskara..."
Until then, one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Queen of the Gods.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"One should offer three *añjali*s of water to the Lord of Day with the mantra 'tiṣṭha';
then the wise man should mutter the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times."

The meditation on Sūrya, as described in the Śāradā-tilaka: One should meditate upon Mārtaṇḍa, who holds in his lotus-hands a golden lotus, a sprout, a beautiful khaṭvāṅga with its first joint, two lotuses, a discus, a spear, a noose, and a trident; who wears a beautiful rosary and carries a skull-cup; and who is delightful with three eyes and four faces shining like the Vedas.
We worship the crown made of jewels called Bhairava, radiant with necklaces;
having recollected the god Bhairava, known as Mārtaṇḍa,
the lord of Umā, the practitioner of mantra should [worship] with the root mantra or with the mantra of the Sun.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā from the ocean of delusion,
that mantra of the Sun is proclaimed [to be worshipped] with red flowers, barley, and so forth.
Having offered the arghya water ending with Mārtaṇḍabhairava, conjoined with the Śakti of Light, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.

The meaning is that the *mūlamantra* is the *gāyatrī*; this is because of the simplicity [of the procedure] according to the independent statements previously cited, and also because it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Dear One, the practitioner should [worship] either with the root mantra or with the Sūrya mantra;
[the seed-syllable] consisting of the Śiva-bīja situated in fire (Ra) and adorned with the left eye (Ū).
One should then write the word *haṃsa* joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
O Goddess, with this mantra one should present the *arghya* offering to the Sun.
The substances for the *arghya* offering are described in the *Vīratantra*.
Having placed eighty *modaka* sweets, *vakula* flowers, *kuśa* grass, and other items into a copper vessel with a handle, one should present the *arghya* offering.

Thus ends the supreme Kaulika [practice]. For the *paśus*, however, there is the injunction beginning with "with water, with the *añjali* of water," and so forth. As for the formal statement: "This *arghya*: *hrīṃ haṃsaḥ*, to Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava, conjoined with the Power of Light (*prakāśa-śakti*), *svāhā*.
The insertion of the mantra is by virtue of its being an *arghya*. Then, having meditated upon the Root Goddess in her own mandala...
As before, one should take the *arghya* offering and present it.
This is stated in the *Svatantra*:
"Having offered the *arghya*, one should then meditate upon the Goddess within the orb of the sun."
As before, one should offer the prepared arghya three times.
With the root mantra of Gāyatrī, ending with "namas" and followed by "vahnivallabhā"—this is for Tārā. In the Vīra-tantra:
at the end of the root mantra, [one says] "udyadādityavartinyai," and immediately after that...
At the end of "Śivacaitanya," the mantra is "mayai svāhā."
In the Nīlatantra: "One should extract the word 'Idyadādityamaṇḍalavartinyai' (to her who dwells within the solar disc), followed by 'śivacaitanyamayai svāhā'; this is remembered as that mantra."

Thus, when there is a conflict between two mantras, one's own preference or the instruction of the Guru is the refuge. However, for Sūndarī, the offering of water (arghya) to the Sun must be performed; [the mantra] is located in the head, throat, mouth, ears, eyes, and nose.
One should place the fifteen syllables of the Great Goddess upon the heart, the belly, the region of the back, the navel, the stomach, the anus, the feet, and the ankles.
One should contemplate the complete Vidyā within the *brahmarandhra*, possessing a reddish luster;
as it flows forth as nectar, one should meditate upon the sixteen-syllable mantra, which bestows great good fortune.
One should again cause the Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī to revolve on the left side of the body,
and one should place the Ripujihvāgrahā mudrā at the base of the foot.
Having cast the *yonimudrā* into the mouth during the state of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) and having offered praise,
the wise one should rotate the ring finger all around the region of the head.
One should cast it into the aperture of Brahma (the crown of the head) by means of the "jewel-knot" (maṇibandha);
then, the wise should place the sixteen-syllable mantra upon the forehead while recollecting it.
The *Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī* and other [mudrās] are as described in the *Kulārṇava*:
having placed the left hand in a fist and brought it to the region of the ear,
the knower of the tantra should wander about, making the index finger his refuge.
The Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī mudrā is indicated at the time of nyāsa;
with the fist formed by the inner thumb, one restrains this entire world.
The *Ripujihvāgraha-mudrā* was indicated by her at that time;

therefore, according to the *Jñānārṇava*, this rite is to be performed twice during the twilight [sandhyā], both in the ritual action and in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). This is the essence of the *Surasa*.
In the *Śrīkrama* and other [texts], specifically during the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*),
it is said in the *Śrīkrama*: "One should meditate on the three worlds as red while recollecting the *Śrīvidyā* in one's mind."
The syllable Oṃ is the seed-mantra born of speech (vāgbhava), and the syllable Ā is the king of desire (kāmarāja).
The syllable *sāṃ*, joined with *tāṃtakā* (the letter *ta*) and others, combined with a single vowel,
is prescribed for the purification of the hands by Tripurā Parameśānī.
In the triangular *mūlādhāra*, there is the syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*), the color of lightning;
from that arises [the goddess] who is lightning-colored and holds two arms.
She holds a book and a rosary, possesses three eyes, and has the form of a young girl;
she rests upon something, is yellow in color, and is thinner than a lotus fiber.
One should join that [seed-syllable], whose nature ends with the Vāgbhava, to the Supreme Śakti—
[the Śakti] who resembles pure crystal and is like cow’s milk or silver.
Resembling a kadamba bud, she is situated in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
holding the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, a rosary, a noose, and a scripture.
Having uttered the Vāgbhava syllable, one should worship the sandals of Tripurā Parameśvarī with the words "I worship the sandals," and thus offer the Arghya three times.
After the offering of water (arghya) to the Sun, one should meditate on Gāyatrī as follows; in the Uḍḍīśatantra:
"One should remember her as resembling the rising sun, holding a book and a rosary."
One should meditate upon the excellent Brāhmī, who is clad in a black antelope skin, within the starry expanse of the supreme eye.
Thus at dawn: one should meditate upon the Goddess, dark-complexioned, four-armed, with hands resplendent with the conch and discus,
seated in the midst of the solar orb, holding a mace and a lotus, and resting upon the seat of the Sun.
At midday, one should meditate on her as Vaiṣṇavī;
at evening, one should remember the goddess Gāyatrī as the Bestower of Boons—
white, holding a white [lotus], and seated upon the bull.
Meditating upon the Goddess— who has three eyes, bestows boons, and holds a noose, a trident, and a human skull-cup, and who stands in the center of the solar disc— one should practice her worship.

The knower of reality should then recite three times the Śrīkrama mantra: "O Goddess Tripurā, may we know [thee] (vidmahe), O Mistress of Vāgbhava (pada), then 'we meditate upon' (dhīmahi)," followed by the awakening of the principles (tattva-prabodha) and so forth, according to the procedure beginning with inhalation (pūraka).
The midday ritual: Within the filament at the center of the heart-lotus is the solar orb, which is the second Kāmarāja, resembling the color of the rising sun.
Arising from that, she is red in color, four-armed, and three-eyed;
she holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and is exalted in her youth.

Alternatively, having brought her who is radiant as the dawn and whose nature is that of Kāmarāja into the thousand-petaled lotus, one should meditate upon her, possessing a splendor equal to the sun.
Four-armed, greatly radiant, three-eyed, and wearing excellent garments,
she holds in her left hand a book consisting of the knowledge of Śiva and embodying the Praṇava.
The Supreme Goddess, whose right eye is like the rising sun and who possesses a splendor equal to the moon, holds the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness with her right and left hands.
Having meditated thus, raising the hands with palms joined, one should remember the word *Tripurā* and the sandals of *Kāmeśvarī*, and then offer the *arghya* three times.
Having extracted Kāmarāja, [one should recite]: "We know the noble Tripurā;
we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; may She who is Kinna impel us."
Having recited the Gāyatrī three times according to one's capacity, one should then place the Śakti-bīja;
at evening, however, the Śakti-bīja is placed within the white lunar maṇḍala.
O Lord, [he visualizes] her who arises from that, white in color, wearing a crown of matted hair,
three-eyed, two-armed, with quivering fangs, and auspicious in appearance.
Alternatively, one should meditate upon her in the form of Śakti, seated upon a conch,
a lotus, and the earth, with two hands in the right.

Having invoked the Sovereign of the Gods into the sky of supreme bliss— she who holds an excellent rosary of seeds or a lotus, as well as a book and the gesture of fearlessness— [one should worship her].
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śakti, which arises from that [mantra] and possesses a luster equal to a ruby, one should visualize the Great Goddess, who possesses a luster equal to a ruby.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śakti [Hrīṃ], one should offer the threefold arghya with the mantra: "I worship the sandals of Tripurā Amṛteśvarī."
The wise one should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra, which has the nature of the seed-syllable of Śakti:
"We know the Goddess Tripurā; we meditate upon our own Śakti."
There, having extracted the supreme *sarvabīja* from the left half of *pracodayāt*, which possesses a radiance like a ruby; (p. 54a) [one should worship].
Having invoked the Sovereign of the Gods (Sureśvarī) into the sky as supreme bliss,
[he beheld] the Great Goddess born from her, possessing a luster like that of a ruby.
Holding a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow, possessing three eyes—
having uttered the fourth seed-syllable, [one should worship] Mahātripurasundarī.
Saying "I worship the sandals," one should offer the *arghya* three times;
the wise man should mutter the *Gāyatrī* mantra, which has the form of the fourth seed-syllable, ending with the words "Tripurasundarī vidmahe" immediately thereafter.
"Kāmeśvarī dhīmahi" and "tatra kinne pracodayāt"—
this refers to the sixteenth [syllable], which is the seed-syllable of all and the fourth seed-syllable.
And in the Mālinītantra it is said:
"This triple twilight worship and salutation at midnight should likewise be performed by the best of practitioners even during the 'Great Night' (mahārātra)."
The two muhūrtas that follow midnight are known as Mahārātrika; by performing [the rite] there, one brings about destruction.

Then, having meditated on the Vidyā in his heart, the yogi, with mind withdrawn from external objects, should recite it one hundred and eight times; thereafter, he should enter the sacrificial ground.

That which is declared in the *Mālinītantra* is common to all; however, one who is unable [to perform the full practice] should worship only the five twilight-periods (*saṃdhyā-vāra*). But the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite applies everywhere. Furthermore, regarding Sundarī, because of the threefold nature of the *kūṭas*, one should worship her in her complete form for two periods. Now, the *gāyatrī* of Dakṣiṇakālī is as follows:
In the Kumārītantra: "The word *kālikāyai* is declared; immediately after that, one should say *vidmahe*;
then one should say *śmaśānavāsinīṃ dhīmahi* ending with the dative case (*ṅe*)."
Having uttered that "tanno ghore padaṃ," one should recite "pracodayāt.
By this mantra of grace, millions of great sins [are destroyed].
They go to immediate destruction for the practitioner; it is not otherwise.
Indeed, by the slaying of Rāvaṇa, Rāmacandra was liberated.
The god Candra was liberated from [the curse] by abducting his guru’s wife, and Brahmā likewise by abducting his own daughter; of this there is no doubt.
Parśurāma was purified from the murder of his mother by the grace of [Viśvāmitra],
and likewise Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Dattātreya were purified from the drinking of liquor.
Thus, O beautiful goddess, this great *mahāvidyā* is to be protected. Now, as for the *tārāgāyatrī*, it is as follows, according to the *Tārārṇava*:
"Hūṃ, O Blessed One with the single braid (*ekajaṭe*), we know (*vidmahe*)"—this is the next word.
We meditate upon the one with formidable fangs; may that Tārā inspire us.
Now, as for the Bhairavī Gāyatrī, it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should perform the recitation of the supreme-syllable Gāyatrī according to one's capacity."

Having recited the root-vidyā, [one says] "vāgīśvarī ca vidmahe"; having recited the second seed-syllable, "kāmeśvarī ca dhīmahī"; and having recited the third seed-syllable, "tannaḥ śaktiḥ pracodayāt. This is the Gāyatrī of the Three Śaktis, as stated in the Jñānārṇava: "One should perform the recitation according to one's capacity," and in the Bhairavatantra: "To Vairocanī, we offer our knowledge... (vairocanyai vidmahe).
And "ca chinnamastake yad dhīmahi"; having uttered "tanno devī padam," one should conclude with "pracodayāt. This Gāyatrī of Chinnamastā bestows all desires.

Now, the Gāyatrī of Durgā is as follows, according to the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "We know the Great Goddess; we meditate upon Durgā, O Beloved; may that Goddess inspire our intellects. There is no application of this [mantra] as an alternative to the previously mentioned one, based on one's own desire.
In the Gautamīya:
Thus have these mantras been taught to you for the attainment of the fruit of the mantras at the time of twilight.
If one should fail to do so out of delusion, one would not obtain the fruit of initiation.
One should meditate upon the Lord and recite the mantra in the evening, morning, and at midday;
if the twilight prayer has been omitted, one should recite the Gāyatrī a hundred times.

This recitation, which is a limb of the *saṃdhyā* ritual, has inference as its basis; thus, the meaning is that one should meditate on the Sun. Having recited the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times, the Kaula practitioner should dismiss the deity from his heart using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
As for the lotus [position], it is described in the *Mālinītantra*.
Having worshipped, the wise one should mutter the Gāyatrī, the supreme syllable;
then, O Supreme Goddess, placing his left foot upon [the other] foot.
The meaning is: having placed the right foot upon the left foot;
then, sitting down, one should mutter [the mantra] three times while laughing with arms raised upward.

The word "again" (punar) refers to the recitation performed at the time of bathing. The Haṃsa-mantra, however, is to be understood from the *Śrīpātrasthānaprastāra*. Then, by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should dismiss [the deity] from the solar orb into the heart. Thus, having completed the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) along with its limbs and all its constituent elements, one should proceed to the place of worship. This is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Having risen and put on two garments of the family,
and having performed the tilaka of the family form with the family [substance], [he worships] Campakuleśvara.
By lineage, he is a flower of the family; by his power, he is the ornament of the family; he is the kula-vesture for those of noble birth.

He is pure, bright, and a wearer of excellent garments—red silk and the like, or white silk and the like, as stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "He is pure, brilliant, and wears the sacred thread (*yajñopavītaka*). Furthermore, regarding specific desires, it is said in the *Svatantra*:
One seeking liberation should wear white garments; one seeking enjoyment, yellow clothing;
for the rite of killing, black cloth; and for subjugation, red—these should always be worn.

In this context, because "graha" (planet) is specifically mentioned as the subject, there is no mention of others; for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should wear a tiger skin, and for the rite of paralysis (*staṃbhana*), tree bark.
Then the practitioner of mantra should put these on and enter the sacrificial ground (*yāgabhūmi*) as prescribed by me.
In the *Yāmala*: "Having bathed, the best of practitioners should mutter the *hṛdaya-mantra* with passion;
the yogi should remain vigilant day and night, and then enter the sacrificial ground."
O Maheśvarī, having placed the conch in water and gone to the door,
one should wash one's hands and feet on a path that is well-swept.
Thus ends the auspicious twelfth chapter in the independent *Kulavṛtti*, composed out of devotion to the Guru by the venerable Pūrṇānandanātha.
Having washed one's hands, one should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) according to the independent [tradition].
Then, having performed the ācamana, one should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya).
Now, regarding the purification of water, it is stated in the Uttaratantra:
The practitioner, looking at the water situated within the jar, should touch it with the *nārasiṃha* mantra using the *devatīrtha*. He should then take hold of it.
Then, holding [the vessel] with his left hand while it remains at his left side,
he should touch the water while consecrating it with this *mūlamantra*.
Through ignorance of which [truth], the association with wine and other such things occurs here;
whereas through knowledge, there may be a different perception, as if it were water in a vessel.
O God, by bathing in a reservoir of water, the sins of one who has touched a corpse and other such defilements are indeed destroyed through the worship of the Divine.
The secret [substance] is water, because it resides within the jar;
it is the son of Prajāpati, the end of the vowels, vomited forth, and consecrated with its own essence-mantra.
The mantra accompanied by the half-moon (candra) and the bindu is that of Nṛsiṃha.
That which ends with Prajāpati (the letter *ka*) is [the mantra] ending in the final vowel (*au*) and the letter *ra*, joined with the two vowels; this is the syllable *oṃ*.
Having spoken thus, the entire sequence of phonemes (*svaratvaṃ vai*) is indeed called the garland of grammar (*vyākaraṇamāla*).
One should know the foundational mantra for the accomplishment of one's goals to be the first letter of one's own name, joined with a bindu and the crescent moon.

*Am*, the first syllable of *āsana*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the digit (*kalā*), is the primordial [syllable]. This is the general purification; however, there is a specific purification for that particular [object]. As for the ritual application: having brought water by means of a jar or similar vessel, [one should use] the mantra *srauṃ*.

Having touched [the water] with the *devatīrtha* and having gazed at it within the vessel with his eyes, he should take the water-vessel situated on his left side with his left hand. With the mantra beginning "yaṃ spṛśet," as stated in the *Uttaratantra*, he should touch it.
Having thus sipped water (*ācānta*) and attained purity, he becomes well-bathed for the worship of the deity.
Standing outside, one should perform the ritual of worship with the mantra of knowledge, mentally [placing] her within the space between four arms.
Having performed the extraction [of the mantra] while staying at home, and having bowed his head to the Guru,
he should mentally bow to his chosen deity as well as to the guardians of the directions.

"Guru" means the supreme teacher (*paramaguru*). However, it remains that the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) must first be performed. Nevertheless, even here, according to the scriptural injunction, whatever sin has been accumulated—whether on that day or on another day, O dear one—is not tainted by [the omission of] expiation; for one who remembers the purification with a mindful intellect, that sin is removed.
One should recite these two verses:
"O Goddess, my mind has entered your feet; it has been trampled underfoot by me.
O Thread, ward off my sin! Hūṃ Phaṭ! By means of this, he [is protected].
The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—
these are the witnesses here to my actions, both auspicious and inauspicious.
Then again, with the syllables "hūṃ phaṭ," having emanated his own wrath toward the sides, the head, and likewise below, he should gaze and then bow down.
When the act of purifying one's sins has been performed in this manner from the very beginning,
whatever further sin may arise will remain far away.
In the past, that place of worship returns to its own [original] state;
furthermore, one's sin will become very slight and shall go to destruction.
For one who has abandoned sin through worship, their desired wish shall be fulfilled in an instant;
as for the past, that very same [desire] becomes firm in a previous birth.
It produces the expansion of enjoyments.
For one whose body is enveloped by sin, there is the destruction of enjoyment;
that sin remains far away during worship, but returns to the self again during [the performance of] one's livelihood.
The meaning is that one goes to a solitary dwelling made on that day or another day.
For example, regarding the placement of the general *argha*, it is stated in the Muṇḍīśa:
"One should arrange the general *argha* on the left side at the eastern gate."
The wise one should fashion a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and the earth;
having worshipped Śakti below, he should place the vessel with its stand upon it.
Having purified it with the Astra-mantra, one should worship it with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
then, having invoked the Tīrtha, one should cast it [into the vessel] while offering scents and other articles with the Praṇava.

Displaying the *dhenumudrā*, one should indeed recite the *praṇava* ten times. By the term "with the *dhenumudrā*," it indicates the ritual acts consisting of the *amṛtīkaraṇa*, the *avaguṇṭhana*, the three *tāla* slaps, the snapping of fingers (*choṭikā*), and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).
Because they share a single caravan [of purpose],
one should not worship this [deity] with water of common value on the left side; thus it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*.
Having sprinkled water three times on the left side of the door, one should perform the worship of the door [deities]:
Vighna, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, located above the lintel.
Then, in the southern direction, at the constellation Vighna, on both sides of those two [gateways],
one should worship the Weapon (Astra) at each door in sequence with equal flowers and water from the Gaṅgā and Yamunā upon the sacrificial ground (ihalyā).
In this context, the second obstacle-word is the word *vaṭuka*.
In the *Kumārītantra*:
"One should worship Gaṇeśa preceded by the seed-syllable *gāṃ*, and likewise Vaṭuka preceded by the syllable *vāṃ*."
First Kṣamā and the others, then the Kṣetrapāla, and thereafter Yāmā and the others, as well as the Yoginīs.
They are proclaimed as being above, to the left, to the right, and below.

Now follows the procedure for the general *argha* offering: having drawn one's own mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and four [squares] on the left of oneself, and having worshipped it with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the support-base (*ādhāraśakti*)," one should [place] the vessel together with its base while reciting "Phaṭ."

Having established [the vessel] with "Namaḥ," filling it one-third full with water while reciting "Gaṅge ca" and so forth, one should invoke the holy waters (tīrtha) from within the solar orb using the *kuśa* mudrā. Then, saying "Oṃ," one should offer scents and flowers; saying "Avaṃ," one should transform them into nectar using the *dhenu* mudrā; saying "Drūṃ," one should veil them; and saying "Phaṭ," one should perform three upward claps of the hands (*talatraya*).

One should perform the binding of the ten directions with finger-snaps; then, one should recite "Oṃ" ten times. Having sprinkled the area designated for the Guru and the ritual implements with that water, one should worship the deities of the doorway as follows: according to the practice there, "Salutation to Gaṇeśa on the upper branch," and "Salutation to Vaṭuka on the left branch."
On the right door-jamb: *kṣāṃ* to Kṣetrapāla; below, *yāṃ* to the Yoginīs.
On both sides of Gaṇeśa: to Śrī-Sarasvatī. On the side of the courtyard: to Gaṅgā. On the side of the field:
to Yamunā. At the threshold: *astrāya phaṭ*. Thus, on the right jamb, above the gateway.

"On the left and on the right" refers to the practitioner; therefore, there is no contradiction between the two tantras. Thus, these are the general gatekeepers, while the specific details are to be understood from the tantra. Then follows the expulsion of obstacles. As it is said in the *Svatantra*:
"All the various types of obstacles situated on the earth and in the sky [should be expelled] with auspicious unhusked rice mixed with white mustard seeds and sesame."
And having driven away [the obstructors], one should sit down to eat.
And in the *Yāmala*:
"The practitioner should perform the expulsion of spirits with this mantra."
In whatever place one performs worship of the gods, spirits do not approach from afar.
While the beings remain there in the mandala of the food offering,
the greedy deities always linger and do not accept it.

"May those beings who dwell upon the earth depart; may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. In the *Śāradā*: "Touching slightly with his left [foot], the Guru should step over the threshold of the doorway; he should not contract his limbs, and he should enter with his right foot."

Regarding the mantra for entering the house, it is stated in the *Uttaratantra*: "With the mantra *oṃ meṣaphaṭ*, one should then enter the altar (*vedī*). Regarding the word "altar": in the case where there is no house, one should construct an altar and perform worship there; that is the location of the altar.
In the case of a house, the entry is into the interior of the house. This applies both to daily worship and to initiation (*dīkṣā*), as previously stated.
It is clearly stated in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra:
"The practitioner should properly perform the worship of the gateway with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
having performed the worship of the bronze bell, [he should do so] in the south-western direction."

Thus it is stated in the Kumārī-tantra: "One should worship Vāstvīśa and Brahmā in the south-western direction. This applies even to the daily worship (nityapūjā). In the Śāradā[-tilaka]: "With the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water for the arghya..."

One should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the following rule stated in the *Tantrarāja*: Cow-dung should be placed in urine [in the proportion of] one and a half palas;

milk should be one prastha; curd should be half the measure of the milk; and one should provide clarified butter (ājya) at half the measure of the curd. One should employ these with their respective mantras using the five products of the cow. The word "their own" (*svaiḥ*) refers to the individual mantras.

This refers to the Vedic ritual procedure. For example, as stated in the *Saṃhitā*: having taken cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with "gandhad-vārā," milk with "pṛthivyai," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," and water with "idam āpaḥ"; and having taken ghee with "tejo 'si"—thus is the *pañcagavya* (the five products of the cow) described.

Alternatively, equal portions of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed; having collected them with the root mantra, one should purify [the substance] with that very same mantra. This concerns the domain of the divine heroes (divyavīra).
In the Śāradā-tantra: "Then one should perform the purification of the crossroads through inspection and other rites;
inspection with the root mantra and sprinkling with the [mantra of] arrows is prescribed."
One should perform the striking with that very [mantra], and sprinkling with the armor-mantra is prescribed;
thereafter, one should fumigate with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
One should scatter the *vikirāḥ* there, having consecrated them seven times with the *kṣura-mantra*.
For the sake of success, one should offer sesame seeds (*siddhārtha*) while reciting the *nājavandana*; thereafter, *ūrdhvāṅkṣa*, *kuśa*, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
The *vikirā* have been described as the destroyers of the entire multitude of obstacles;
one should sweep them away with a handful of *darbha* grass joined with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
In the northeastern direction, one should prepare the seat for the Vardhanī vessel;
then, having caused the Brāhmaṇas to recite the Puṇyāha formula and having fed them, [one should proceed].
One should enter one of the aforementioned maṇḍalas upon the altar.

Among all the maṇḍalas mentioned, such as the Sarvatobhadra and others, this [present] maṇḍala is common to all, yet it possesses a specific distinction belonging to Sundarī. As stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "Having caused the declaration of a meritorious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having satisfied the Brāhmaṇas..."
Then, the practitioner of mantra should draw the captivating King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) upon the altar using either vermilion powder or saffron.
First, one should draw a hexagon; then, in its center, a triangle;
then a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a twelve-spoked wheel, and two sets of eight [petals].
Having drawn a twelve-spoked wheel, one should then draw an eight-petalled lotus;
outside of that, one should draw a square provided with four gates.
