Alternatively, one should draw a nine-cornered figure and then a square of four squares;
this [instruction] is indeed for the initiation [rite] according to the *Śāradā*.
For the ritual of dismissal (*mudvāsana*), the practitioner of mantra should enter facing either the east or the north.
And in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"Facing east, or facing the direction of Kubera (the north), having assumed the *baddhāsana* posture and bowed to Gaṇapati and the Guru...
Regarding that specific direction, it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
Where one might perform [other rites] facing north or facing the northeast during the day,
the wise man should always perform the worship of Śiva facing north.
In the *Phetkāriṇī*:
Having put on a clean upper garment and being pure, the practitioner, facing east,
sits upon a seat, assuming either the lotus (*padma*) or the auspicious cross-legged (*svastika*) posture.
Seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), one who is fully concentrated should perform all [the rites] facing either east or north, according to the sequence to be described.
One desiring prosperity should sit here facing west in the shape of a svastika; as stated in the Śāradā-tilaka:
"The practitioner, having assumed the lotus posture, composed and with senses subdued..."
The distinction between the directions and the seats, however, should be understood from the difference in ritual action.
Now follows the rule for the libation to the Kula-pīṭhas.
This is stated in the Matsyasūkta:
"Seated upon a soft cushion, or on other soft seats..."
Having taken recourse to these seats, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.

The wise say that one who falls from the womb within six months is called *garbhacyuta*; they know one who dies before the tonsure (*cūḍā*) and the initiation (*upanayana*) rites have been performed as *acūḍaka*.
A male who has undergone the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) but whose initiation (upanayana) has not yet been performed,
if he dies in his fifth year, they know him as "Komala."
In the Śrīkrama:

"O Dear One, listen to [the description of] the covered seat (vṛtāsana) in the absence of the hero's seat (vīrāsana). It is [the seat] of a child who has died before the age of five, prior to the tonsure ceremony (acūḍaka)."
From six months onwards, up until the seventh month,
a child who has fallen from the womb or died before reaching the eighth month of gestation is considered a miscarriage (garbhacyuta).
The wise say that this [grass] is soft when used as a seat (*viṣṭara*).
And in the *Vīratantra*:
"In the absence of a corpse, one should fashion the form of a corpse upon the seat. As for the seat, it is stated in the *Smṛti*: [as follows].
A seat for the tree [of the corpse] should be made with fifty [leaves], and a grass mat (viṣṭara) with half of that.

Herein, a corpse-seat (śavāsana) is prescribed as the primary requirement; in its absence, one should take up the skin of a man or other such materials, or alternatively, soft leaves according to the specific injunctions.
In the Matsyasūkta:
"A soft woolen blanket that has fallen in battle,
or even one obtained from a hunt, is a new seat upon which one should perform recitation."
A hero should prepare an excellent seat from the skin of women who have recently miscarried, or from the skin of those who are in their youth.
"Or it may be made from wood from a cremation ground, or yellow wood from a sacrificial tree.
Thus ends the section on the supreme animal skin. Regarding the description of the soft seat, the *Muṇḍamālā* states:
"Then, with the skin of ten animals, one should fashion a square and even [seat]."
It should be one cubit or two cubits in length, with a width of four finger-breadths.
On a pure seat, the wise one should perform the consecration and worship.
And in the *Matsyasūkta*:
"A seat made of the skin of a deer, a woolen rug, or likewise a blanket."
One should likewise prepare yellow and white garments as well as a seat.
It may be woven into a narrative, or likewise formed into a circle;
it possesses the permanence of a small amount of clay. In the Kālītantra:
"O Goddess, he who worships Kālikā without the seat of clay..."
One shall remain a denizen of hell for that duration until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.

"Kālī" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), meaning "from a noble family" (kulādarī), because it is prescribed in the *Śrīkrama* and other tantras. This, however, pertains to the divine (divya) and heroic (vīra) [practitioners]. For those who are bound (paśu), there is only a simple cloth or even a black tiger skin; on a black [skin], that is, on a black antelope skin.
In this regard, there is this specific rule:

"A renunciant (saṃnyāsī) or a celibate student (brahmacārī) may dwell upon the skin of a black antelope. [From] the Muṇḍamālā: "One who has been initiated should not enter [the assembly]; those who are indifferent (udāsīna), those who have bathed [after initiation], and celibate students [may sit there]."

"Let them enter" means "let the students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) enter. And in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "A black [blanket] grants all perfections; one made of wool brings success in knowledge and long life; a cloth-seat removes disease; one made of cow-hair increases love; silk is said to grant good fortune; and a woolen blanket grants all perfections."
In the Rudrayāmala, having drawn a triangle on the ground representing the fire-mandala,
one should worship Ādhāraśakti and there contemplate the seer (ṛṣi) and the other [limbs].
Following the worship of Ādhāraśakti, the placement upon the prescribed seat is enjoined.
O Dear One, Merupṛṣṭha is proclaimed by the sages, Sutala is said to be the meter, Kūrma is declared the three deities, and Trāsanāropaṇa is [the name], O Beloved.
The application (viniyoga) has been stated; then, having assumed a seat, one should recite:
"Oṃ! O Earth, you are supported by the worlds; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu."
"O Goddess of the Gods, having worshipped with the mantra 'By this [mantra] make the seat pure,' one should offer kuśa grass right there."
The worship of the seat (*āsana*) is performed right there:
having uttered the seed-syllable *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), preceded by the Support-Power (*Ādhāraśakti*),
one should worship the seat of Brahmā (*Brahmāsanam*) ending with "Ṅe Namah" (Ṅeṃ namo).
For half the night, the animal (paśu) is common to all; however, the divine and the hero (divya-vīrau) should not enter by any means other than the hero’s posture (vīrāsana).

"One should sit in the *vīrāsana* posture, having worshipped the seat, for it is stated in the *Kumārītantra*: 'One should resort to the seat after worshipping it. Now follows the explanation of the Lord of Devas (*Deveśa*) according to the *Unarātantra*:
'Then, [the substance] placed by both hands with the *ādhīra* mantra...'"
Having placed that [offering] and set it down, they quickly touched it with their hands.

Then, one should sit upon that excellent seat with the *ātman-mantra*. The meaning is that, having placed the seat on the ground at the time of worship, and having set it down again on the ground and touched it with the right hand, one should enter [the seat] with the *ātman-mantra*.
Any defect in the seat, such as being poorly crafted by an unskilled artisan, or any other flaw,
goes to dissolution through ignorance when the mantra-based ritual service is performed.
One should know that the syllable of one's own [name] which is first in the *soma-sāman* and is endowed with a bindu is the practitioner’s own mantra.

They know that the first letter of the name is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the mantra of the support (*ādhāra*). It is the name of the practitioner’s own support; "Somasāmi" means the half-moon (*candrārddha*), which is the support—therefore, *Āṃ*. Now, the application of the seat (*āsana*) and the supreme lord (*pareśana*) should be performed to the west or south of the altar for worship.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the general *arghya* water, one should draw a square mandala within a triangle;

having sprinkled the eastern side and others, one should worship with "Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti. Having thus worshipped and assumed their respective prescribed seats, and having placed [the deity] upon the seat, [one should know that] Meru is the *ṛṣi*, *Pṛth* is the *chandas*, and Kūrma is the deity.

The application is for the placement upon the seat (*āsanaropaṇe viniyogaḥ*). Having thus recollected the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituents], one should hold the seat and recite: "Oṃ! By you, O Earth, the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu. Support me always and make this seat pure. Then, having placed three *kuśa* grasses upon the seat, [one recites]: "Hrīṃ Ādhāraśakti..."

Saying "Salutation to the Lotus-Seated One" (*kamalāsanāya namaḥ*), one should take up the seat with both hands using the *ādhāra-mantra*, place it quickly before the book, touch it with the jewel on the right hand, and then, while reciting the *ātma-mantra*, the two divine heroes should sit in the *vīrāsana* posture, while Śambhu himself should sit in any one of the postures such as *svastika*. Having thus sat down, one should purify the ritual substances.
One should act as follows. According to the *Śāradātilaka*: "The practitioner should place the articles of worship on the right side.

The time for the placement of these articles is specifically during initiation (*dīkṣā*); however, in the case of daily worship (*nityapūjā*), it should be understood that the placement of the *śrīpātra* occurs afterwards.
As it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having ascended the *kulapīṭha*, one should perform the worship of the *kuladeva*;
'the *kulapīṭha*' means the location specified in the *puraścaraṇa-prastāra*."
Pleased by pure instructions and by dance, song, and instrumental music,
he should approach the end of the lineage and worship the station of the lineage.
Then, having cast aside the family-seat (kulāsana) and worshipped it as is pleasing,
one should thereafter assume the family-posture (kulāsana) and perform the worship of the Guru in due order.
The meaning is: preceded by prostrations to the Guru and others on the day of the *plavī*;

[one should perform] the purification of the self (*ātma-śuddhi*), the purification of the seat (*pīṭha-śuddhi*), and the purification of the deity (*deva-śuddhi*), according to their respective divisions.
Having performed the *argha* offering, the wise man should then carry out the family ritual with initiated,
noble-born, youthful women who are devoted to their families.
On the sacrificial grounds, the deities— devoted to their gurus—
have gathered various kinds of flowers and diverse fragrances.
Camphor, nutmeg, incense, and other perfumes, as well as scented silk cloths, betel leaf, and whatever materials such as incense and lamps are required, should be offered.
Having recited the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should then sprinkle the established [deity];
having placed all one's possessions on the right, one should present the water-offering (*arghya*) on the left.
In the west, one should maintain the family substances (kuladravya) of the deity;
therein, the accomplishment of the substances should be attended to according to the sequence of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).

According to the statement: "One should offer to the deities the flower arranged by the Kuladvārā, the food arranged by the Divya-vīra, the water arranged by the Meva, and the edible offering arranged by the Taduccā," the animal sacrifice (paśu) must likewise have its materials placed down through the Kuladvārā who has been initiated; other items as well should be treated in that same manner.

These [substances] are to be procured according to their respective tantras. Having thus performed the procurement of the substances, one should summon the disciple and have him choose a guru. As stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Then, having summoned the disciple and seated him on his right..."
Adorned with various ornaments and endowed with fine garments.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the disciple, with his senses subdued,
should likewise bathe for the sake of expiating committed sins and apply a golden tilaka.
Having sat down to the left of the Guru and performed the *saṃkalpa* according to the prescribed ritual,
the *saṃkalpa* is as follows:
"Today," and so forth, desiring the destruction of sins committed since birth, [I offer] this sesame-seed and gold, dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I give this to you, O Brāhmaṇa, of such-and-such a name and lineage," he should give it to the Brāhmaṇa.
The learned man, endowed with devotion, should honor the preceptor according to the prescribed rite.
With cows, land, gold, garments, and other such splendid items, as well as with noble lineages and so forth.
Adorning him with other ornaments and such as he desires according to his heart's wish,
he should worship the Guru with devotion, preceded by the gesture of joined palms.

Having circumambulated the Guru, one should offer oneself. Then, [one should say]: "O Blessed One, whose nature is the Self, O most compassionate Guru, who accomplishes the goals of human existence, please grant me the attainment of the deity of the soul, preceded by the initiation and consecration of such-and-such a mantra. O Creator of the Veda... [and so forth].

One should say, "Please grant me the mantra-initiation and consecration so that I may accomplish [the goal]. Having spoken thus, the disciple, full of humility, should remain for a long time to the right of the Guru. After performing the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites, he should carry out the ritual procedures as prescribed in the *Kalpa*.
This means at the door of the Guru. Now follows the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the form: "Today," and so forth, [specifying] the month, fortnight, and other details.

Having performed the *sumekhala* rite, I choose you, O [Name] Devatā, as my preceptor (*guru*) for the single ritual consisting of the initiations (*dīkṣā*). From this day forward, O [Name] Devatā, I choose you as the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) for the ritual of the initiation into the [Name] mantra. In this matter, the preceptors are indeed the officiating priests for the ritual of the initiation and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) into the [Name] mantra.

"I choose you as a member (*sadasya*). "Today," and so forth, "I choose you as the overseer of what has been done and what remains to be done in the rite of initiation and consecration (*dīkṣābhiṣeka*) for such-and-such a mantra.
One should say, "The three deities are initiated in the lotus" (*padme vidyādīkṣatā*). Such is the detailed procedure for the gatekeepers (*dvārapāla*) and others. Herein...

The necessity of forming a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at the time of making a vow is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "O Brahmins, whatever a man performs without a formal resolve, the fruit thereof is very small; half of his merit is lost.
Now, regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*):

during vows, sacrifices, weddings, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), worship of the gods, recitation (*japa*), and the performance of rituals, there shall be no impurity if the rite is performed; however, if it is not performed, there is impurity.
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the formal selection [of priests]; in a vow or a sacrifice, it is the formal resolve (saṃkalpa);
in a marriage and similar rites, it is the Nāndī-śrāddha; and in a śrāddha rite, it is the performance of the ritual declaration.
Regarding the invitation for a *śrāddha*, the Śruti states: "It begins from the [time of] invitation.

This applies to the animal sacrifices of the Kaulikas. Furthermore, during both birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), one should not allow the omission of ritual acts; and according to the *Mantramuktāvalī*, the recitation (*japa*) [must continue].

In the rite of worshiping the deity, initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed by people who have purified their minds; for there is no sin nor any impurity of birth (sūtaka) for those self-restrained ones. Therefore, one should accept Vijayā as it has been stated in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
O Maheśvara, having attained the state free from agitation without cause, you are liberated;
you would perform no worship for me, nor meditation, nor contemplation.
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess. In the *Vijayākalpa*:
"Between the two, [the disciple and the teacher], Consciousness is truly the most venerable deity."
Therefore, the sixty applications should be performed here in worship and other rites by the most excellent practitioners.
And a great worship (mahāpūjā) must be performed with firm resolve by those who are well-determined. In the Vīratantra it is said:
"Without bliss there is no attainment, and the deities are not satisfied."

It is not of four kinds, according to the distinction of white, yellow, red, and black flowers; rather, it is purified through the nose in sequence, as stated in the Vijayā-kalpa: "Oṃ! O Saṃvidā, born of Brahmā, daughter of Brahmā, ever sinless!
For the sake of what has been given to the Bhairavas, be forever pure. Oṃ, salutation to Brāhmī, svāhā."

One should purify with the mantra: "O Goddess, [you who are] the root-activity, the awakener of deficient understanding, the subduer of kings and subjects, the trident-bearer at the throat of enemies! Ai! Homage to Kṣatriyā, Svāhā!
Then one should purify the supreme [element]. [You who are] the giver of wealth in ignorance, the fire of knowledge, the flame of the fire of knowledge, whose form is knowledge.
They regard bliss as the oblation, joy as the clarified butter, and right knowledge as the protector. *Hrīṃ*, salutation to Vaiśyā;
*svāhā*, may she purify me, the Śūdrā.
I bow, I bow to her who bestows the path of Yoga.
O Mother, in Trailokyavijaya, be the bestower of the fruit of samādhi.
*Klīṃ*, obeisance to the Śūdrā;
*svāhā*—thus is the supreme mantra declared. Then: *Oṃ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi*, then the word *amṛtam ākarṣaya*, then the pair [of words] *siddhiṃ dehi*, then *ātmakarma*.
Then, having brought the Vṛddhaśamā [mantra], thereafter,
with the snapping of fingers preceded by three claps of the hands,
one should strike away the obstacles with divine vision and blows from the heels.
O Goddess, while reciting the mantra, one should satisfy [the deities] sevenfold in the *brahmarandhra*;
likewise, one should honor the Guru in the thousand-petalled lotus with the *śaṅkha* mudrā.
The practitioner, whose mind is intent on accomplishment, should satisfy [the deities] with devotion in three ways;
he should utter the words "Aiṃ vadavada," followed by the words "vāgvādini."
Then, with the mantra "Obeisance to you who are firm on my tip of the tongue,
obeisance to the one who brings all under control, svāhā," one should offer oblations into the mouth.

"Reciting the root mantra" means reciting the *pādukā* of the Guru. As for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), it is performed for the Supreme Guru and the Deity in this manner, while for others such as Vaṭuka and the rest, it is according to the sequence stated in the *Sandhyā* [rite]. This, however, pertains to the Divine (*divya*) and Heroic (*vīra*) [classes of practitioners].
Then one should perform the five purifications as follows, according to the *Kulārṇava*:
"The purification of oneself, the place, the mantra, the substance, and the fifth is the purification of the deity."
O Dear One, whatever ritual worship the practitioner performs for the deities— such as bathing, clothing, purification, and so forth, along with breath control (prāṇāyāma) and other practices—
it is declared that self-purification is accomplished through the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) and other nyāsas.
By means of sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other rites, [the ground] becomes as radiant as the surface of a mirror;
it is stainless, adorned with incense, lamps, and flower garlands.
The painting with five-colored powders is declared to be the purification through bathing;
the syllables of the root mantra are strung together with the letters of the Mātṛkā.

The repetition of the sequence as stated is declared to be the accomplishment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*). Having strung [the syllables] together with each individual letter of the *mātṛkā*, this constitutes the "root-strung" (*mūlagrathana*) method; it does not mean that there is a lack of authority for reciting each individual letter of the root mantra separately. In this context, prior to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), the purification of the six limbs (*ṣaṭhaśodhana*) must be performed.
Having established the Goddess upon the pedestal, the knower of mantras, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
should consecrate her with the root mantra and with water from the lamp-vessel (dīpiṇī).
The wise one should sprinkle [the materials] three times; this is called the purification of the deity. Having thus performed the fivefold purification, one should thereafter carry out the sacrifice.
That worship should be known as fruitful; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"And that which is performed by one devoid of the five purities is not truly performed."
Without the fivefold purity, worship leads to malevolent magic.

Purification of the self, purification of the place, the cleansing of the wine, then the purification of the materials, and the purification of the deity—these are proclaimed [as the five purifications]. Among these, first is the purification of the self; bathing has already been mentioned. Now, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, repeating it with seven applications of clay. As Vasiṣṭha says:

In the *Saṃhitā*: "Then, O twice-born ones, one should have a hedge of *saptacchada* trees made here; having encased the syllable *Hrīṃ* with the *oṃkāra*, O Brahmin, one should mutter this mantra seven times every day at the beginning of worship."
But by this procedure, water is consecrated for protection.
The Goddess, all living beings, and all the most excellent practitioners—
Bhairava, the god of the gods, is intensely eager for the splendor of the mantra.
They take away all splendors except for the subtle *saptacchada* [plant].

Now, regarding the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*): first, there is the salutation to the Guru and others, as stated in the *Vārāhī-tantra*: "One should first contemplate one's own Guru on the right side of the temple; Gaṇeśvara at the beginning, and the Supreme [Guru] upon the crest."
One should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) for the Guru and the deities within the heart—or, according to the meaning, in the topknot (śikhā).
This is because the terms "one's own" (sva) and "Guru" (guru) as well as "supreme Guru" (paramaguru) possess a single denotation. Likewise, it is stated in the Śāradā:
Having joined the palms in *añjali* and bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśa on the left and right sides, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
In the *Yāmala*: "On the left [is] the Guru, on the right Gaṇeśa, and in the center the Deity.
Regarding the dilemma here between saluting the Guru and the Deity, one may choose according to one's own preference; the Guru’s instruction is the refuge.

In the *Śāradā*: Having performed the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*), one should then perform three claps (*tālatraya*). Desiring the binding of the directions, one should perform the upper and lower [claps] with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
Then, one should perform protection with the fire-energy gathered by that [mantra];
in the independent [rite], it is performed with the sounds *pārṣṇighāta*, *kara*, *sphoṭa*, and faces directed upward.
One should perform three claps with sound according to the tradition,
as stated in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
Then, seated, having wiped both hands with the *praṇava* and having placed [the syllables] upon the fingers,
one should indeed assign the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in their proper order.
One should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) in all quarters with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
Having created it like a rampart of fire, the practitioner [should proceed] with the mantra; as stated in the *Kamadhenu-paddhati*:
"Then, having purified the water with the weapon-mantra preceded by the *tritārā*."
Having established the moon-disk situated within the square, one should purify this limb consisting of the elements according to the sequence of purification; and in the *Yāmala*:

Having performed the purification of the hands with scents and flowers, one should ward off the elemental spirits (*bhūtas*). The ritual for warding off the *bhūtas* begins with the cleansing of the hands and ends with the visualization of a wall of fire; prior to that [fire-visualization], there is the crushing of the flower. This is stated in the *Uttaratantra*:
The practitioner should take a flower with the Viṣṇu-mantra using the tips of his own fingers for the purpose of rubbing it during the rite of hand-purification.
One should crush the flower with both hands while reciting the *prāsāda* mantra;
one should sprinkle it with the *kāmabīja* and smell it again with the *brāhma* mantra.
Having thoroughly cleansed the directions, especially the east and the north,
with a respectful disposition, one should wipe [the vessel] with the right hand and smell it with the left hand.
And the sacred fords (tīrthas) come together at the tip of the nose and toward the hand;
therefore, O Bhairava, one should perform these rites with great effort.
The syllable *upānta* (the penultimate letter, *m*) joined with the moon (*caṃdra*, *u*), conjoined with the void (*śūnya*, *visarga*), and touched at the end by Rudra (*rudra*,
*h*), is considered this Vaiṣṇava mantra. Alternatively, it may begin with the letter *pānta* (the penultimate letter, *bh*) and likewise be joined with that same syllable *su-deva*.
The syllable preceded by fire (ra), joined with the crest (u), the tuft (m), and the bindu (m), is called Prāsāda.

The seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) should be known as either the letter *va* with the god (the vowel *u*) and the bindu, or else the first consonant and the last, followed by the penultimate and the final;
then the pair of the first and the final, followed by the consonant and the syllable Om (*praṇava*).
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Brahman, which destroys all sins.
The letter *ha* at the beginning, together with the moon—the crescent moon on the head—is colored [by it].
It is joined with the void; that is to say, it is joined with the *anusvāra*. It is touched at the end of *rudra*;
*rudra* is the letter *u*, its end is the letter *o*, and by that [is formed] the seed-syllable *laṃ*. This is the Vaiṣṇava Nārasiṃha; such is the meaning.
The letter *pāṃ* is the beginning of that [mantra]; Vāsudeva is *oṃkāra*. From that, *hau* is Śambhu’s crest-peak;
the half-moon is the *bindu*, the nasalization (*anusvāra*). By that, there is the accomplishment of the *prāsāda* seed-syllable. The *kāmabīja* is well-known.
[It is formed] by Vāsudeva, by *oṃkāra*, by the vowel *ā* joined with the *anusvāra*—that is to say, by *oṃ*. Thus, it is *oṃ klīṃ*.
Regarding the phrase "the consonant" (*vyañjana*) and so forth: the first [consonant] of the first group (*ādyavarga*), being devoid of vowel (*svaraśūnya*), is the consonant;

by that, the final letter at the end of that [group] is taken, and the one preceding it—thus [it is] *sa*. The two final letters at the end are the two *tāraka*s (the syllable *oṃ*); between those two, the subsequent consonant which is devoid of vowel is taken—thus [it is] *ta*. Following the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*), however...
The meaning is that everything precedes and follows the syllable *oṃ*. Therefore: *oṃ tatsiddhiḥ*. In the *Śāradā*:
"One should unite the self with the Supreme Self by way of the *suṣumnā* path."
Being composed, one should practice with the consciousness-mantra according to the prescribed method of yoga.
One should also contemplate the principles (tattvas) within the cause of all beings,
which are dissolved in the order of inversion within the Supreme Self in the form of seeds.
In the Yāmala: Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
having placed his hands in the mudrā of restraint (karadama) upon his own lap with the knees fully extended.
In the *mūlādhāra*, the *kulakuṇḍalinī* is the nature of the root-vidyā;
she has the form of a sleeping serpent and consists of three and a half coils.
Having meditated upon her who possesses the splendor of a stalk of wild rice (*nīvāra*), who resembles ten million flashes of lightning, and who is self-manifested and encircled by a serpent,
one should then strike with the *ahiṃsa* mantra or otherwise.
Or, O Goddess, by means of the *kūrca* seed-syllable, the Guru should firmly cause [the disciple] to flee [from worldly bonds];
having established the state of oneness between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
Having contemplated the supreme void of the earthly elements as having entered into water,
and the water as drawn away by fire, one should contemplate the form of fire.
One should meditate on the form of wind as being supported by space within the navel;
though carried by space, the wind does not dissolve into its own nature.
One who is under the sway of mind and ego should then contemplate the principle of Mahat within Prakṛti, and likewise contemplate Prakṛti within Mahat-tattva.
She is of the nature of light, the ultimate embodiment of the knowledge of Brahman;
she is Kaivalyā, she is Kaivalya, and she is the supreme Trika of all qualities.
This indeed is the supreme light, the immortal and free from disease;
it is the state beyond, situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, whose nature is emptiness.
It is empty and like a reflection, resembling the moon; it is subtle, most subtle, and supreme.

Pervading all, consisting of darkness yet known as the supreme light of emptiness, it is always composed of pure radiance, devoid of any distinction between the visible and the tangible. Having thus realized the Goddess of Reality, the practitioner—
By means of her boons, she has driven away old age. In that very place:
water, taste, and the tongue are indeed the objects of perception for the sense of taste, in their respective order.
Lustre and the eye, as well as the feet and locomotion; wind, touch, the organ of speech, the anus, and excretion are thus proclaimed.
Space and the ear are known as the stations of protection;
the mind, the ego, and the Great Principle (Mahat) are established within the roots of the principles (tattvas).
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Then, one should dry up the body with the wind through the seed-syllable of air;
with that very same [seed-syllable] of fire, one should burn the body consisting of the embryo (kalala).
Then, having washed away the defects with the flowing water of nectar,
one should bathe the body from the soles of the feet to the top of the head.
Then, one should cause those principles (tattvas), which have merged into the self, to return to their own respective places;
thereafter, one should bring the self from the heart into union with the Supreme Self.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites for the deity Haṃsa according to Manu;
one should contemplate the syllable Vayaṃ, smoke-colored, at the region of the navel.
With that very [mantra], one should purify the liṅga and the body with sixteen measures;
having performed the kumbhaka with sixty-four [measures] consisting of ritual action, one should proceed.
Then, one should exhale through the right [nostril] for thirty-two measures, or through the other;
one should contemplate the seed-syllable of fire, red in color, at the root of the genitals.
One should burn the body— the single *liṅga* of impure seats—
by means of that [fire] according to the previously mentioned sequence of yoga, specifically through the process of the right nostril.
The preceptor, likewise, should perform the counting with the sound "ma";
and having visualized the syllable "va," the seed-mantra of Varuṇa, within the small bell.
Having produced that nectar from the thousand-petaled lotus,
one should cause it to flood [the body] by performing the inhalation (pūraka) and other [breath-control techniques], down to the soles of the feet.
One should visualize the seed-syllable *laṃ* of the earth at the root of the anus;
by that very sequence of yoga, the wise one should cause it to be flooded with the mind.
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon himself as the supreme body of Śambhu, liberated from both sin and merit;
immediately thereafter, he should accomplish [the rite] by that very same previous path.
Thus, with the mantra, one should establish the living soul within the lotus of the heart.
Furthermore, the wise one should bring that goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who is drenched in supreme nectar,
as well as the five elements, back to their respective places.
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon himself as the abode of the Great Auspicious Tripurā.
According to this system, one should perform the stabilization of the location and so forth, as well as the breath-retentions (pūraka) and other practices.
And in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"I shall describe the procedure for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*); one should perform it according to the sequence of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having uttered the great seed-syllable of Vāyu situated within the six directions..."
O Maheśānī, one should indeed dry up the black-colored body by means of this [mantra].
One sees a personified sin situated in the left side of the belly, with the luster of lampblack;
it has the murder of a Brahmin for its head and the theft of gold for its two arms.
Minor offenses (upapātaka) are located in the limbs, and secondary offenses (pratyamga-pātaka) in the minor members;
drinking liquor is associated with the heart, and violating the Guru’s bed with the two hips.
One should contemplate the sinner, enraged and bearing a sword and shield, within the belly;
according to Caṇḍikā,
the sinner resembles the citadel of the city, beginningless and marked with the signs of existence.
The murder of a Brahmin constitutes its head, and the theft of gold its two arms.
Having made it dry together with the sin by that sequence,
and having armored it with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ) along with the sin, O Śivā;
One should meditate on [the deity] who causes sleep and downfall, with red beard and eyes,
holding a sword and shield at his side, and black in color on the left.
In that very same [text]:
"O Supreme Goddess, one should dry the body with that seed-syllable;
having made it withered together with its sin by means of that sequence."
O Śivā, having incinerated [the self] along with the sin by means of the fire-seed (vahnivīja),
one should subsequently flood that which was accompanied by sin with the water of the [Gāyatrī] mantra.

After performing the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, one should subsequently bestow life and install it [within the image]. As stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "The *liṅga* should be fashioned as residing in the heart, the consciousness that is the witness of all."
The wise know that [the breath] should be expelled through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) by means of the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having encased [the deity] with that very [mantra], one should don it upon the head;
thus the deity, both external and internal, becomes endowed with consciousness.
Stable in the center of the navel-mandala by means of the seed-syllable in the form of fire, one should burn [everything]; then that heap of ashes becomes the very form of ash.
One should meditate on the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, located in the center or situated in the heart;
it is white, shaped like a half-moon, and marked with two lotuses and a foot.
Then, with the Navakāra mantra, one should bathe the sweet-formed [deity];
having placed the earthly seed-syllable, one should meditate upon the golden mandala.
Having divided [the self] into two by means of the syllable Om (praṇava), one should then meditate upon the Self there as having the form of consciousness and the form of the deity of the mantra.
Thus is another opinion stated in the Uḍḍīśa:
"One should cause the goddess Kuṇḍalinī to enter from the Ādhāra; she is exceedingly subtle, coiled like a sleeping serpent, and endowed with three and a half loops."
Then the practitioner, using the *kūrca* seed-syllable, should firmly drive away that [obstacle], which resembles ten million flashes of lightning and is coiled around the self-manifested *liṅga*.
Together with the five elements, by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal,
one should [lead] that Goddess through the path of Brahma along with the mind and the individual soul (jīvātman).
In the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, within the full orb of the moon,
resides the Supreme Self in the form of a drop (bindu) inside the triangle situated therein.
Having joined [the breath] with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, one should then purify the reality (tattva) together with its sins by means of fire,
following the sequence of prāṇāyāma.
Afterwards, being composed, he should burn that very [impurity] with the *kumbhaka* breath;
then, with the nectar of the water-seed (*vaṃ*), he should perform the immersion of those ashes.
Then, by means of the sequential practice of exhalation (recaka) and the seed-syllable of the earth (bhū-bīja),
one should make the body very firm and perform the remainder as previously described.
Thus ends the section for those who are unable [to perform the full rite].

Even without the preliminary filling [of the vessel] and so forth, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is performed in that very same place. Alternatively, one may perform the purification of the *kuṇḍalinī* together with the five elements and the rest.
Having united [the individual self] with the Supreme Self, one should contemplate the identity of the two;
through the yoga of meditation, one should mentally contemplate "I am He" (Haṃsa So'ham).

Thus ends this lamp of valor; according to the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however, it is supreme. In the Yāmala: "Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) or even the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one possesses the authority for the nyāsa of the weapons without having performed [the former]."

The five elements within this body are exactly the same as those [elements] that are specifically portions of Brahman. There should always be supreme purification by means of the *mātṛkās*, beginning with the vowel *a*. For it is indeed through the conceit of being a living soul (*jīva*) and the web of defects therein [that impurity arises].
Just as Brahmā remained established in his own creative activity, so too did the gods remain established in their own;
and thus those defects, namely the identification with the body, were completely dispelled.
It should be understood that for them, purity consists in the thorough knowledge of the self, recognizing one's own nature as Brahman, and the complete relinquishment of egoism.
Now, the exposition of *prāṇāyāma*. In the *Yāmala*:
"One should perform three *prāṇāyāmas* with the root mantra or with the *praṇava*;
or else, one should perform the *prāṇasavam* of Śrīvidyā."
Having meditated upon the Supreme Lakṣmī in the form of consciousness at the Mūlādhāra,
one who is composed should, by the utterance of the syllable *Hūṃ*, raise her upward.
One should draw in the breath with sixteen mātrās using the *mṛḍayā* [technique],
perform the *kuṃbhaka* (retention) with sixty-four, and the *virecana* (exhalation) with half of that.
Holding the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb together in a hollowed cup,
while excluding the index and middle fingers— that is to be known as *prāṇāyāma*.
In this manner, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) in successive order;
the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the foremost winds within the body, and their restraint is [the practice].
"Breath control (prāṇāyāma) is declared by the wise to be the destroyer of sins," as stated in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The knower of mantras should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) with either the root mantra or the *praṇava*,
while uttering the *praṇava* in a single tone.
Having filled the abdomen with the left [nostril] and remaining there as long as possible, one performs breath-restraints through death; this is the "filling" (pūraka) that fills the body.
Having covered all the limbs, one should exhale breath devoid of sound;
having filled [the body], one should remain like a jar—this is the *kumbhaka* breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
The knower of mantras should likewise release the breath through one [nostril] while closing the other;
the liberation through the yoga of exhalation consists of expelling the air through the external [nostril].
This is declared to be *recaka* (exhalation), and it is undoubtedly *prāṇāyāma*.
Then, with twelve *mātrās*, *pūraka* (inhalation) is always performed.
Therefore, the wise practitioner performs exhalation (recaka) with double the measure;
thus, each of the three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consists of a triad.
And in the *Svatantra*: "O Dear One, with thirty-four (34) measures— sixteen (16), two (2), two (2), and six (6)—
having omitted the *praṇava*, [one should practice] inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and retention (*kuṃbhaka*)."
And in the Tripurāsāra:
"He respectfully filled his own brother’s mouth with the gusts of wind from the path of the moon.

Free from the constraints of modification and free from the constraints of the body, with the fluctuations of his mind offered at the root of the fire of time (Kālāgni), he should then hold the vital air (māruta) within the city [of the body] for sixty equal measures (mātrās). When it is filled, he should exhale it slowly through the bright opening [of the nostril]; when that is completed, he should restrain it for half that duration. After this, he should perform the reverse [process].

Furthermore, the wise have stated that it is the opposite of that. Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should practice excellent self-restraint. Now follows the explanation of the measures (*mātrā*) from the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra*.
Having circumambulated the knee neither too quickly nor too slowly,
the snapping of the fingers is proclaimed as the measure (mātrā).
In the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*, it is proclaimed that "the duration of the utterance of the syllable Oṃ is one *mātrā*. In the *Kriyāsāra*:
"From the base of the little finger to its tip, and from the base of the ring finger to its tip..."
The wise know that *mātrā* to be divided into sixteen phonemes (*varṇa*).

By means of the vowels beginning with *a*, *ā*, and so forth—thus [there are] 6,432; this is the meaning. The number of *mātrās* is established according to the division of the capable and the incapable within the dual nature of the *mātrā*. In the *Tripurāsāra*, it is stated that the purification of the mind and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) occurs through *prāṇāyāma* independently. This *prāṇāyāma* destroys all evil; such is the description of its results.
The detailed exposition is found in the *Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya*.

Regarding this breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) according to the sequence of the elements. In this regard, it should be understood from the respective tantras that there is a distinction: in some cases breath control precedes the purification of the elements, while in others the purification of the elements follows.
Now, is there not a sequence? [Is it] the practice of *mātrā*, the practice of *pūraka* and so forth, or the practice of the left nostril and so forth?

True; one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through these—whether by the practice of *mātrā*, the practice of *pūraka* and so forth, or the practice of the nostrils and so forth.
This sequence remains exactly as follows: at the time of *pūraka*, [one performs] *śeṣa*; at the time of *kuṃbhaka*, *dāha*; and at the time of *recaka*, [the remaining stage].

At this time, the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is performed; according to that system, there is no [need for] cremation. Since the body has been reduced to ashes, there is the immersion [of the remains]. Thus, as previously stated, for one who is unable [to perform the cremation], one should first contemplate oneself in the form of the Goddess and then perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), as follows:
In the *Śāradā*:
"The mantra consists of three syllables beginning with *pāśa* and ending with *ātman*; then the word *padam*, followed by *amuṣya padam*.
Then, in sequence: *prāṇa iha prāṇāḥ*, and likewise *jīva iha sthitaḥ*."
May all the senses of this person become [unified], and may his state be that of the Supreme;
may speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath likewise [attain that state]. Having returned here from there, may he remain happily for a long time, rising upward.
"This Prāṇa is proclaimed as Manu, the bestower of life upon all beings.
Thus is the general mantra for the installation of Prāṇa (Prāṇapratiṣṭhā) on a movable seat.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"Then one should meditate upon oneself as the form of the Goddess within a lotus at the moment;
then, having placed the life-force (*jīva*) by means of the three-syllable mantra beginning with *prāṇa*."
Then, joined with the mantra of the two bases (dvāṇa), one should utter the word "of the thief" (muṣyāḥ padaṃ).
After that, one should say "prāṇāḥ," and immediately thereafter, "iha prāṇaḥ."
The life-force of such-and-such a person is here; then [the mantra] "the station of such-and-such";
then "all the senses of such-and-such," followed by speech, mind, and sight.
"O ear and nose, having come here from your own abodes, stay for a long time in happiness within the fire"; this is declared to be the Prāṇa-mantra.
And as it is stated in the Jñānārṇava regarding Tripurā:
"O Supreme Goddess, having uttered the function of the mouth (the letter *ma*), one should extract the *haṃsa* in reverse;
this is considered the three-syllabled Vidyā."

The phrase beginning with "amuṣyā" (of such-and-such) and so forth is to be inferred. Here, in place of the word *amuṣyā*, one should take the name of the deity to be accomplished through the construction of the case-ending. As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇī Saṃhitā: "Whatever form the word *adaḥ* (that) takes..."

In whatever place [the deity] is seen, one should place the ritual procedure (vidhāna) of that form in that very place. Regarding the placement of the fingers (javanyāsa), as it is in the *Yāmalatantra*: one should make the index and middle fingers level and rest them comfortably at the base;
having made the little finger straight, one should place the ring finger upon it.
This is the lelihāna mudrā, proclaimed for the placement of life-force (jīvanyāsa).
Then one should worship oneself as follows. In the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"O Sage, one should worship [the deity] with the ritual services even without the food offering (*naivedya*). In the *Uttara-tantra*:
"The practitioner should perform the 'tortoise-hand' gesture (*pāṇi-kacchapikā*) with the Kūrma-mantra."
There, one should worship one's own body with a consecrated flower.
By worshipping with that flower, one's own divinity arises.
The second is the Vaiṣṇava seed-syllable (bīja) conjoined with the bindu.
The sixth vowel, followed by the letter *paricara*, is proclaimed to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Kūrma;
the second is that of Vaiṣṇavī according to the Tantras, while the others are easy to understand.

The mudrās are to be understood from the exposition on meditation (*dhyānaprastāra*). Now follows the ritual procedure for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhiprayoga*): after prostrating before the venerable Guru and others, one should take perfume and flowers with the fingertips using the *kūrca* seed-syllable, rub them with the palm using the *prād* [seed-syllable], wipe both the backs of the hands with the *kāma* seed-syllable, and likewise smell them with the *brahma* mantra.
With the left hand in the *prasāda* gesture, one should cast [the water] in the northeastern direction. Then,

having wiped both hands with either the *praṇava* or the *astra-mantra*, and having performed the finger-assignment (*nyāsa*) of the *ūrdhva-mantras* upon the fingers, one should strike the ground three times with the heels,
perform the triple *tāla* sound with the *astra-mantra*, and effect the binding of the ten directions (*digbandhana*) with snapping sounds (*choṭikā*).

Having enveloped oneself with the water of the general *argha* offering, having visualized the form of the fire, and having placed both hands palms-upward upon one's own body, one should visualize the six-petaled lotuses of the *mūlādhāra*, *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūra*, *anāhata*, *viśuddha*, and *ājñā* chakras,
as well as the thousand-petaled lotus, and visualize them becoming fully blossomed by means of the syllable *Hūṃ* or the *praṇava* (*Oṃ*).

Having first contracted the anus, through the union of wind and fire, one should awaken the *kulakuṇḍalinī* as consciousness; then, by means of the mantra "Haṃsa," one should establish that [consciousness] together with the individual soul (*jīvātman*) upon the Supreme Reality (*paramatattva*).
From the *mūlādhāra* and other centers, [one should withdraw] the five elements beginning with earth, along with the twenty-four principles.
Having meditated on the dissolution [of the universe] into Kuṇḍalinī, and having meditated on the dissolution into Kuṇḍalinī,

and having merged Kuṇḍalinī with Paramaśiva, and having contemplated the entire universe as void, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of air, *yam*, smoke-colored, in the left nostril, and recite it sixteen times through the left nostril.

Having filled [the breath] with air for sixty-four *mātrās* and having retained it (*kumbhaka*) in both channels, one should dry up the wind along with the *puruṣa* by means of the wind emerging from the wind-seed-syllable situated within the circular mandala marked by six dots located in the heart; then, one should exhale the wind through the right [nostril] for thirty-two *mātrās*. Thereafter, [one should contemplate] "raṃ."

Muttering the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), one should fill [the breath] with the wind through the nostril of the right-hand seat for sixty-four *mātrās*. Having visualized the syllables as divided by the *bhakta*, one fills the wind through the right nostril and performs *kumbhaka* (retention). Then, by means of that fire located within the triangular mandala adorned with a *svastika* at the navel, together with the sin, [one expels it] through the wind from that fire-seed-syllable.
While the body is being cremated, one should cause it to be gathered together with ashes;
with the left [hand], one should scatter them.
Then, having visualized the white seed-syllable *vaṃ* of Varuṇa, one should fill [the body] with air through the left nostril and perform breath-retention (*kumbhaka*).

Having meditated upon the mantra of Varuṇa for one *ghaṭikā*, one should flood the *mātṛkā*—which has been burnt in its own form—with the nectar arising therefrom, and then exhale through the right nostril. Thereafter, the seed-syllable of Earth...

Having visualized [the dissolution] at the base of the anus, one should visualize a new body; according to the view of some, one should also perform this for the sake of stabilization. Then, having established the five elements together with the five *tatvas* in their respective locations, and having placed the *kuṇḍalinī*, stirred by nectar, within the *kulakuṇḍas*, one [should worship] one's own Goddess.

Having visualized the form as the self, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) as follows: forming the *lelihānā* mudrā and placing it at the heart, one recites: *Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Haṃsaḥ*. "The vital breaths of the beloved deity are here; the vital breaths are here. O life-force, remain! All the senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and breath—having come here, may they abide in happiness."

"May you remain for a long time, svāhā! Having thus stabilized the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and having meditated upon "I am she, I am she," one should offer a flower with the *kūrma-mudrā* while reciting "oṃ āḥ klūm. Then, even without an offering of food (*naivedya*), one should worship with perfumes and other offerings and perform the ritual placements (*nyāsas*) as follows:
In the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*:
One should remember the sage, the meter, and the deity at the head, face, and heart; then, having performed the recitation, one should worship oneself after having adorned it.
The meaning is that one should perform the placement [of mantras] while recollecting [the deity].
The meaning is that after performing the placement of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, one should become adorned and then perform worship. This is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*.
The knower of mantras should assign the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas),
and the deity of the mantra to his own head, face, and heart, respectively.
In the *Svatantra*: "One should perform the *ṛṣinyāsa* at the region of the head, the *chandas* upon the lotus of the mouth,
the deity at the heart, and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) at the secret place."
And having placed the *śakti* upon the feet, one should place the *kīlaka* on all the limbs.
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"Having remembered the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), and the deity (*devatā*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*)."
In the Gautamīya: "He who, having known Maheśvara directly through his face, accomplishes the vow of asceticism with a purified soul— he is declared to be his *ṛṣi*."
Because of its weightiness, its placement is proclaimed to be on the head;
because it conceals all the principles of mantra, it is called *chandas*.
Because it flows and because it is a foot, the Veda is said to reside in the mouth;
likewise, it is so called because it causes all living beings to speak and because it impels them.
Then, one should place the deity residing in the center of the heart-lotus. From the Dakṣiṇāmūrti [form],
the great mantras emerge like sparks from a great fire.
O Dear One, the letters of the Mātṛkā emerged from the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable];
for this very reason, that alone is called its Vāgbhava seed-syllable.
From whichever seed-syllable the letters of the Mātṛkā that constitute the beginning of a mantra are produced, from that very one they arise.
The mantra for that is "vūjatvaṃ. She who flashes forth as the supreme form, the Mother of the Universe (Viśvamātṛkā), the Goddess of Gods, pierces the three worlds with great delusion;
therefore, O Goddess, she is called the Stake (Kīlaka) and is proud of her auspicious fortune.

Protecting the seeds from causing delusion in the world, she is called the power (śakti) that brings about the dissolution of the universe. This concludes the explanation of the seed-syllables (bīja).
One who knows the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity (devatā) shall partake in the fruit of the mantra.
There is a loss of power for those mantras whose application is not understood.
In all ritual depositions (*nyāsa*), because of the connection with the word *namaḥ*, the application must indeed end in the dative case;
thus, one says "obeisance to the *ṛṣi*" (*ṛṣaye namaḥ*) and so forth. However, some do not perform the deposition of the *ṛṣis* and the others at all.
They perform that which was previously intended; such knowledge of the application (viniyoga) is indeed the ritual placement (nyāsa).
That [application] is verbal; therefore, it is the expression of the application itself. Thus, after these placements, it is stated in the Śāradā-tantra:
"Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule with the root mantra," and so forth.
One should perform the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās immediately after the nyāsa of the mantras.
One should assign the [mantras] to the thumbs and other fingers along with their respective seed-syllables (jāti);
having assigned the weapon-mantra (astra) to the two palms, one should perform the three-fold clapping of the hands (tāla) and so forth.
Then, one should bind the directions with snaps of the fingers using that very [mantra].
In the *Phatkāriṇī Tantra*:
"The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), and the ritual placement of the body (*dehanyāsa*); thus it is threefold."
Through the qualities differentiated by the divisions of creation, maintenance, and destruction, he first performs the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa),
then the placement on the body (dehanyāsa) in the middle,
and the third is the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa); such is the certainty of the scripture.
Having encapsulated the syllable Oṃ, one should perform the pervasive placement with the mantra.
Thus ends the placement upon the body (*dehanyāsa*).
In this regard, according to the *Śāradā-mata*:
after the placement of the sages (*ṛṣinyāsa*) comes breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), after that the placement of the mother-letters (*mātṛkānyāsa*), and immediately following that—
First the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, then the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) [nyāsa] on the hands, and after that the other nyāsas; such is the sequence in initiation (*dīkṣā*).

According to the *Phetkāriṇīmata*, the sequence for daily worship (*nityapūjā*) is as follows: first the *ṛṣi-nyāsa*, then the nyāsas of the hands and limbs, and then the *mantra-nyāsa*. The *mantra-nyāsa* consists of the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) nyāsa performed with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) upon the limbs.

The meaning of the *Śāradā* [Tantra] is that [the assignment of mantras] is generally performed on the thumb and other fingers with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) together with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), or with the seed-mantras alone, or with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) itself. Now, regarding the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the hand-assignment (*karanyāsa*), the *Phetkāriṇī* [Tantra] states: "Beginning from the thumb of the right hand..."
Likewise, from the little finger to the end [of the hand] is the placement of origination and conjunction; its reversal is the placement of dissolution.
Beginning from the base of the middle fingers of both hands up to the tips of the index fingers is the placement known as "Stability," which brings great prosperity.
Now, regarding the emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal within the body:
in that very context,
it is held that emanation occurs from the head down to the feet.
From the feet to the head, there would be the destruction of one's own self.
The approach to the abdomen and the subsequent stationing from the heart [are performed] according to the *Phetkāriṇī*.
Having first [placed them] on the hand starting from the elbow down to the little finger, one should then perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) in due order upon all the limbs.

And "in sequence" means the root [mantra], because no other [mantra] is heard. Here, this is the sequence: first the placement of the Ṛṣi and so forth, then the bodily placement (dehanyāsa) starting from the elbow, then the hand-placement (karanyāsa) and the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), and after that the other placements. Thus it is in the daily worship (nityapūjā).
Regarding the mantras for the hand and limb placements, they proceed in order up to the back of the palm. Now, regarding the limb-placement (aṅganyāsa), [it is stated] in the *Śāradā*:
The authority for such descriptions of the locations is found in the *Tantrarāja*:

"After the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) comes the name Tripurasundarī; thus, [the mantras] ending in *namaḥ* should be placed simultaneously with the thumb and the other fingers, externally from the base of the fingers to the back of the palms, in due order."
Having thus recited the six-limbed mantras, one should apply them to the six limbs.
One should worship the mantra-manu there for one who possesses the five limbs;
for one whose mantra lacks limbs, one should mentally provide those limbs by means of the mantra itself.
The placement of the limbs [of the mantra] is performed by repeating the words and syllables. As it is stated in the *Svatantra*:

"In mantras for which the limbs are not specified, one should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the hands (*karanyāsa*) either by taking a sixth part of the words or of the syllables, or by means of the root-mantra itself in its entirety."
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:

"On the forehead, at the crown, in the place of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), on the arms, on the sides, in the directions, and on the two eyes— this shall be the sequential placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*) of the mantras."
The wise know that the eight weapon-mantras and the limb-mantras are prescribed for the Śaiva and Śākta traditions;
likewise, those ending with the *netra* (eye) mantra are stated for the Vaiṣṇava ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) and worship.

Now follows the exposition of the *jātis*. One should utter "Namaḥ" at the heart; two [syllables] at the head with "Vaṣaṭ"; at the crest, "Hūm" is remembered for the armor (*kavaca*); then "Vauṣaṭ" for the eyes; and likewise "Phaṭ" is said for the weapon (*astra*). This is the meaning. In the *Candrikā*, regarding the sequence beginning with "Namaḥ," there are six *jātis*.
One should sequentially apply these [mantras] to the six limbs. Now, regarding the mudrās, the *Phetkāriṇī* states:
"The four fingers, excluding the thumb, [are placed] at the heart and the head."
At the crest [of the head], the fist is formed by the thumb acting as the stalk due to the state of being overwhelmed.
One should perform the binding of armor (*kavaca-bandhana*) on both hands up to the navel using all the fingers;
with the index finger, one performs the rite for the three eyes (*trinetra*); and with the palms of both hands, the rite for the weapon (*astra*).
Or else, one should indeed strike the directions with the fingers of both hands;
using the tips of the thumb and forefinger, one should [strike] the directions starting from the east in sequence.
The knower of mantras should place [the mudrā] on the head with the middle and ring fingers;
having placed the crest-lock (śikhā) with the thumb, he should place the armor (kavaca) with all the fingers.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place [the mantras] at the heart, the vital breaths, the eyes, the directions, and the elephants;
then, O Dear One, one should place the weapon-mantra with the index and middle fingers.

And in the Jñānārṇava, regarding the number three, two, one, eleven, nine, three, and two, which arises from the mountain (seven): here, in the absence of duality, the Guru is the remembrance of the Guru. Now follows the Mātṛkā-nyāsa according to the Jñānārṇava.
Then, one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā through the yoga of the six-limbed sequence.
Brahmā is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and Gāyatrī is its meter (chandas).
The deity is the Mother Goddess; the seed-syllable is the collection of consonants. O Goddess, the powers are the gods; one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa).
The *va* group is between *aṃ* and *āṃ*; the *ka* group is between *iṃ* and *īṃ*;
the *ṭha* group is between *uṃ* and *ūṃ*; and the *ta* group is between *e* and *aiṃ*.
Oṃ Oṃ! One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the *pa*-group in the middle, joined with the nasal bindu.
The *śa*-group and *ṣa*-group, ending with the anusvāra and visarga, are the indicators of that [latter].
Thus are the mantras for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*); the remainder is as before.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"The sage is Brahmā by association, and the deity is Gāyatrī."
The consonants are the deities, the seeds are the powers, and the vowels are their energies.
The stake (kīlaka) should be known as appropriate; one should install it according to the stated sequence.
Then, the practitioner should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Mātṛkā.
Of the vowels,

the neuter ones, the fire-letters (vowels with *r*), and those with the *bindu*, one should place the five groups of consonants along with the *bindu* respectively within the intervals between each pair.

One should place the groups beginning with *ya* (the semi-vowels) within the intervals between the remaining consonants—excluding the neuter vowels (*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*). Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), there is a distinction in the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the Mātṛkā according to the divisions of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); this distinction applies to both meditation and the ritual placement as follows:
One should place the *Śāradātilaka* [mantra] endowed with the *sarga* (visarga) upon one's own heart, having meditated on the Goddess according to the rule; then,
one should place the *vidyāntikā* (the end of the knowledge-mantra) along with the two final letters by means of the path of maintenance (*sthiti*).
Having reversed these [syllables] and refined them in reverse order, one should meditate thereon in sequence upon the fifty letters.
[One should visualize her] whose middle region is divided by fifty letters, who bestows happiness, whose crown is radiant, adorned with a full circle of jewels,
possessing high breasts, and holding a mudrā, a rosary, a jar of wine and other offerings, and the Vidyā.

One should take refuge in the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā), who possesses three eyes, radiant splendor, and holds a lotus and a rosary in her hands. Thus [ends the description] of the Sṛṣṭimātṛkā in the Śāradātantra,
page 63b.

One should place the other six [limbs], beginning with the thumb, starting from the east; one should meditate upon Varṇeśvarī, accompanied by her beloved, possessing the luster of vermilion, wearing a girdle, and holding a young [deer], three eyes, a rosary, a thread, and a deer-skin, while the Goddess Kāminī stands at her side. One should also [meditate upon] Nābhā.

"One should meditate on [her] holding a book and a rosary of letters in her lotus-like hands"— thus it is said regarding the Sṛṣṭimātṛkā. Regarding the Saṃhāramātṛkā, it is stated in the Śāradā-tantra:
One should perform the previously mentioned nyāsas, including those of the ṛṣis and so forth;
the auspicious Goddess Vāgvallabhā is to be meditated upon within the lotus composed of phonemes.

I bow to the Mistress of the Letters (Varṇeśvarī), who is never-failing, golden-hued, holding a raised chisel and a manuscript in her hands, possessing three eyes, wearing the crescent moon upon her head, ruddy in color, clothed in a lotus, and bending under the weight of her breasts. Now follows the final Mātṛkā.
In the *Jñānārṇava*: One should place the sixteen vowels upon the eight-petaled lotus at the throat;
one should place the twelve vowels, beginning with 'ka', upon the twelve-petaled heart-lotus.
Then, one should assign the letters beginning with *U* to the ten-petalled lotus at the navel;
and one should assign the six letters beginning with *Va* to the six-petalled lotus situated in the middle of the *liṅga*.
O Dear One, one should place the four vowels on the support (ādhāra), and having placed [the consonants] beginning with 'da' on the four-petalled [lotus],
one should assign 'ha' and 'kṣa' to the two-petalled lotus situated between the eyebrows.
Other types [of nyāsa] should be understood from the section on the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
Now, regarding the locations for nyāsa in the Śrīkrama:
[the forehead], the face, the circle [of the head], the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, and the two cheeks.
On the teeth of camels, on the mouth of a goat, and on the tips of the joints of bamboo;
Then, on both sides, at the back, at the navel, in the abdomen, in the region of the heart,
and in the portion of the shoulder-blade, one should place [the syllables] extending upward from the heart, followed by the pair of hands and feet.

"By means of the pervasion of the stomach and the mouth, one should perform this placement (nyāsa) for the Embodied One (Rūpiṇī). 'By means of pervasion' means that, together with the heart, there is contact at the beginning of the pair of hands and so forth, ending with the mouth; such is the meaning according to the *Svatantra*."
Likewise, [one should worship] at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), the two downward-facing mouths, the two eyes, the two ears,
the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two lips, and the hair.
One should place sixteen [syllables] on the two heads and faces of the pair of *chaṃ* syllables;
one should then place them in sequence upon the joints of the arms and shoulders, and upon the pair of excellent sides.
Then one should place [the elements] on the back, the navel, and the two [shoulders], as well as on the abdomen;
skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituent elements (dhātavaḥ).
The supreme *prāṇa* and *jīva* are situated within the letters beginning with *ya*;
thus, O Mistress of the Gods, they have been fully described in this sequence.

Having likewise deposited [the mantra] at the root of the heart and the navel, one should deposit it in the throat; having praised it, one should deposit it in the locations beginning with the mouth, starting from the root of the hand at the location of the mouth and so forth, and likewise in both hands and feet, as well as in the belly and face— one should thus deposit the Rūpiṇī [mantra].

Thus, the demonstration of the locations of the phonemes according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is as follows: during emanation, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the forehead and other locations with "aṃ namaḥ" and so forth; during maintenance (*sthiti*), one should perform the placement starting from the ankles and other locations in the sequence beginning with "traṃ namaḥ";
and during reabsorption (*saṃhṛti*), one should perform the placement starting from the mouth and other locations in the sequence beginning with "kṣaṃ namaḥ".
Now, regarding the mudrās, as stated in the Jñānoḍḍīśa:
"One should place the ring finger and the middle finger upon the circle of the face at the forehead."
The index, middle, ring, and little fingers are placed at the two eyes.
One should place the thumbs on the two ears, the little fingers and thumbs on the two nostrils, the three middle fingers on the two cheeks, and the middle fingers on the upper and lower lips.

Having placed [the fingers] on the ring finger and the little finger, [one places] the middle finger on the head; with the mouth, the ring finger and the middle finger [are placed] on the hands, feet, and sides.
One should place the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger on the back [of the hand];
all of them, together with the thumb, one should place upon the navel region and the belly.
One should strike the entire palm upon the heart, the two shoulders, and the chest;
likewise, one should strike the palms upon the heart, the forearms, the sides, and the mouth.
These Mother-mantra mudrās have thus been proclaimed in their proper sequence;
for him who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing them, that placement shall be fruitless.
Regarding the specific details of the ritual placement (nyāsa), it is proclaimed in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"The placement of the fifty syllables is described in due order;
[the mantra] begins with 'Oṃ', ends with 'Namaḥ', and consists of the word 'Tārā' devoid of the nasal bindu."
That *visarga* bestows sons; that same [seed-mantra] beginning with *māyā*, *lakṣmī*, and the *vīja* grants devotion, or alternatively, it may begin with the *vāgbhava*.

The three stars (tritārā) and the primordial Ghorā are to be placed by the best of practitioners. Its meaning is as follows: it is enclosed by the syllable *oṃ*, or the word "or" (*vā*) here indicates a conjunction;

thus, among the four types [of mantras] beginning with the one with the *bindu*, there is the enclosure by *oṃ*, while the application of the word *namaḥ* is common to all placements (*nyāsa*). "With the *bindu*" means joined with the *bindu* alone, while "devoid of the *bindu*" means without the *bindu*.
The *bindu* is the void (*śūnya*). The *visarjanīya* (the letter *h*) is the *mātrā* of existence (*sati*). The *sotaya* is that which is joined with both the *bindu* and the *visarga*.
These are the four types. The mention of other results refers to the excellence of the fruits of *bījayoga*. Thus it is said in the *Tantrasāra*:
The Mātṛkās are said to be fourfold: the pure, those joined with the Bindu, those with the Visarga, and those with both; hear now as the secret is told.

The solitary *vidhākarī* bestows splendor; the one with the *visarga* bestows devotion; that which possesses the *bindu* bestows wealth. And in the *Mālinītantra*: "Pure [the letter A], joined with the *bindu*, accompanied by the *visarga*, combined with the *kṛt-lekhā* (the letter Ā), likewise enclosed by the *bālā*, and adorned with the supreme *śrīvidyā*; this is the ascent and descent."
He who knows the *nyāsa* consisting of the *Haṃsa* performs the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire world.

In this system, his *mātṛkā* consists of seven types; furthermore, there is a general *nyāsa* with *mudrās*. One may perform the *nyāsas* mentally, or with flowers, or with *namaskāra*, or indeed with the thumb and ring finger.
One should place the syllable VĀṂ on the vital points along with the Ṛk.

In this very manner, one should perform other ritual placements (*nyāsa*); the meaning is that one should perform the placements—both those mentioned and those not mentioned—along with the mudrās that have been described, according to these methods. As it is said in the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*:
"The placement known as 'origination' (*utpatti*) is for those residing in the first stage of life."
For householders, the placement of stability is known as "withdrawal" (saṃhāra).
And in the *Kramadīpikā*: "They say that among the prescribed nyāsas on the lines of the *mudrā*, the one ending in withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is for those who have renounced the world;

for householders, it ends in maintenance (*sthiti*); and for those in the [other] stages of life (*varṇin*), it ends in emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Some teachers say that for the householder there is liberation through detachment (*vairāgya-mukti*), while for the forest-dweller there is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and maintenance (*sthiti*) for the one born of the innate nature (*sahaja*)."

The creation [of duties] is for the sake of students of knowledge. However, by their very nature, those such as celibates (*brahmacarya*) have authority over creation and the other stages in due order. The meaning is that when they are seekers of fruits, there is no restrictive rule (*niyama*). As for the fruit, it is described in the *Kulamūlāvatāra*: "From creation comes a son, flowers, and so forth; from maintenance comes the protection of that."

The destruction of defects occurs through reabsorption; therefore, one should perform these three. Now follows the *pīṭhanyāsa* (placement of the seats), preceded by the various *nyāsas* prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpas*). As it is stated in the *Sāradātantra*: "One should perform the various *nyāsas* according to the procedure prescribed in their respective ritual manuals."
(p. 64b) Now, the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa). [As stated] in the Śāradātilaka:

The wise preceptor should mentally construct the seat within his own body through the principles beginning with Dharma, proceeding in order from the pair of shoulders to the pair of knees by way of circumambulation.
One should likewise arrange Dharma-knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty in due order;
one should place Adharma and the others at the mouth, the sides, and the side of the navel.
Dharma and the others are established as the feet, while others are the limbs of the pedestal;
upon the heart of Ananta is this lotus, containing the sun, moon, and fire.
O wise one, one should assign each of their own respective arts preceded by the first letter [of the alphabet];
likewise, the supreme guru [should assign] the three qualities, such as sattva and the rest, in this very manner here.
Having properly established the inner self as bliss and that very same supreme self as the self of knowledge,
one should then install the unsurpassed seat.
Thus, one should worship the beloved deity upon the seat consisting of the body; this is the general rule for all. In the Kumārī-tantra:

"Then one should perform the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭha-nyāsa), beginning with the Support Power (ādhāra-śakti), followed by Primordial Matter (prakṛti), the Tortoise (kamaṭha), Śeṣa, and likewise the Earth."
The nectar-ocean, the island of jewels, the wish-fulfilling gem, and likewise the house;
the cremation ground, the Pārijāta tree, and at its base, the jeweled altar.
The best of practitioners should place the pedestal upon that upper mandala,
[and arrange] the sages, gods, Śivas, and corpses with severed heads in the four directions.
O Maheśvarī, one should contemplate dharma and adharma upon the four limbs of the body;
likewise, the heart-lotus, the sun, and the moon.
Likewise, having placed Vaiśvānara, as well as the qualities of sattva,
rajas, and tamas, and the Self itself, within the filaments of the heart-lotus, one should establish the powers there.
Will, knowledge, and action—these indeed are Kāminī, the bestower of desires;
the beloved Ānandā resides in the pericarp, while Manonmanī is in the [central channel].
Having first uttered the Vāgbhava [bīja], then [the word] "to Parā," then "to Aparā," and then "to the one who possesses two forms," thereafter "hasau" is said to be spoken.
"Sadāśiva-mahāpreta-ṅentaṃ padmāsanaṃ tataḥ | namaḥ"— this indeed is the mantra declared for the ritual placement of the seat (pīṭhanyāsa).
"In this way, one should contemplate the beloved deity within the body consisting of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Thus [it is stated] regarding Kālikā in the Rudrayāmala.
Then one should perform the deposition of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) according to their successive distinctions:
first, one should deposit Maṇḍūka, and then Rudra in the form of Kālāgni.
The foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), likewise Ananta, Varāha, the Earth,
the Ocean of Nectar, Maṇidvīpa, and Mount Anandhara.
One should worship the Golden Mountain on the Jewel Island, the Nandana grove,
the garden consisting of various trees, as well as the Kalpa garden,
the Mandāra garden, and the Pārijāta garden.
The Kadamba forest grove, as well as the jeweled rampart,
and likewise the Puṣparāga, Padmarāga, Gomedha, and Vajra [gems].
Vaiḍūrya, indranīla, pearl, emerald, and likewise coral—
these nine are known as the jewel-enclosures.
Then there was the Māṇikya-maṇḍapa, the Sahasrastambha-maṇḍapa, the Amṛtavāpī, and likewise the Kāmavāpī and the Ānandasāpikā.
The maiden [constructed] Vimarṣavāpikā, Tapoddāraka,
