Candrikoddāraka, Mahāśṛṅgāra, and Parikhā as well.
Then one should worship the Kalpavṛkṣa tree at the Mahāpadmāṭaṃvī;
thereafter, the Cintāmaṇi house with its altar-platform constructed of jewels.
Then, one should worship the eastern door, which consists of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya);
thereafter, [one should worship] each respective tradition in the southern, western, and northern [directions].
One should worship your lion-throne and white parasol with earth;
one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya from the fire.
One should worship these unprecedented [deities] in the directions, starting from the east and proceeding in order;
then, however, the inner self and the supreme knowledge-self in their respective sequence.
Then, one should visualize a lotus situated in the center of the wheel, with many petals,
its stalk above and its calyx below, and the moonlight which has the nature of reality (tattva).
One should worship the mandala of the moon and sun, as well as the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; and likewise Jñāna, Māyā, Kalā, and Vidyā.
Furthermore, within the square [of the mandala], there are the names and so forth, as well as the seed-syllables of the letters;
and [the lords] Īśa, Agni, Nirṛti, Marut, Indrīśa, and Uḍḍīśanātha.
Likewise, the seat Jālandhara and the seat Pūrṇagiri—
the practitioner of mantra should worship them with desire, worshipping in this sequence.
In due order, beginning from the east, [he should worship] Vāsana on the plank,
as well as Pṛthivīpati and Brāhmaṇa, the lord of the earth.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu as the intellect of splendor, Rudra as the intellect of wind, and likewise Īśvara on the eight petals, one should then worship the Pīṭha-śaktis in their proper order.
Mohinī, Kṣobhiṇī, Vaśinī, Staṃbhinī,
Ākarṣiṇī, Drāviṇī, Hlādinī, and likewise Kledinī.
Having pronounced the word *pada* in the middle, one should utter the word *viyat*;
then, having said "to the lord" (*adhipataye*), one should join it with *parakraye*.
Then one should worship the seat with the mantra "To Sadāśiva, to the Great Preta, to the Lotus Throne," or else with the supreme mantra.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of the preta and the great station of Sadāśiva,
[the mantra] "preta padmāsanāya" is then proclaimed as the mantra of the preta.
Then, according to the sequence of nyāsa, upon that [seat] is the mṛḍāsana;
above that, the practitioner of mantra should worship with a cushion made of flowers and wool.

One should likewise worship Kāmeśvarī and Kāma, as well as the Śrīmūrti. Here, according to the *Śāradā-mata*, the placement (*nyāsa*) of dharma and the other [virtues] is prescribed for the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*), while according to another system, the placement of Ādhāraśakti and the others is prescribed for the worship itself.

Now, in whichever ritual manual (*kalpa*) the *mātṛkā* and *śrīkaṇṭha* assignments (*nyāsa*) are not mentioned, they are not to be performed in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*). However, they must be performed during initiation (*dīkṣā*), because they are prescribed in general for initiation according to the *Sāmānya-tantra*. As for the *śrīkaṇṭha*, it should be performed in whichever ritual manual it exists; where it does not exist, it is not to be performed. Now...

The time for the Śrīkaṇṭhādi-nyāsa is after the Mātṛkā-nyāsa. As it is stated in the *Svatantra*: "First is the Mātṛkā-nyāsa; afterwards, the Śrīkaṇṭha [nyāsa] is taught. Thus, in the *Svatantra*: "One should install the Śrīkaṇṭhas and others in the places of the Mātṛkās in due order."
O Pūrṇodarī, remain together with the letters of the Mātṛkā;
[the lords are] Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara.
Adhīśa, Śobhā, Ārambhu, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, Ugra, Ghaṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara.
Akrūra, Mahāsena, and the sixteen forms of the Svaras;
thereafter Krodhīśa, Candreśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama.
Then some say there are Rudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, Caturānana, Aja, Īśa,
Sarva, Someśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka.
Then Arddhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Cāṣāḍa, Daṇḍin, Spuradri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, and Śikhin.
Chāgalāṇḍeśa, Dvirāṇḍeśa, Saṃvaha, Kālavān, Anila, Bhujaṅgīśa, Pinākīśa, Khaḍgīśa, and Vyomakeśvara.
Śvetabhṛṅgin, Īśana, Kuliśa, Śiva, and Saṃvartaka are remembered;
these Rudras are known to be red in color and to hold tridents and skull-bowls.
Pūrṇodarī shall be there, followed by Virajā and Śalmalī;
after that come Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā.
Sudīrghamukhī and Gomukhī, likewise Dīrghajihvā,
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and Vikṛtamukhī as well.
Then Jvālāmukhī is to be known, as well as Khecarī and Mañjarī;
after that, Ulkāmukhī,
then Suśrīmukhī, Vidyāmukhī— these are the principal powers of the gods— and Mahākālī, Sarasvatī, and Sarvasiddhi.
Endowed with these, Gaurī— the foremost in the three worlds— attains supreme mantra-siddhi;
she is likewise considered to be Ātmaśakti, Bhūtamātā, and Laṃbodarī.
Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, Khecarī, Mañjarī, Rūpiṇī, Vīriṇī, and then Kākodaryā and Pūtanā are to be known.
There may be Kālī and Yoginī, as well as Śaṅkhinī;
she is Kālarātri, Kubjinī, Kaṃpardinī, and Vajriṇī;
and Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, and likewise Rohiṇī.
Vāruṇī and Vāyavī, followed by Rakṣovidāriṇī;
likewise Sahajālakṣmī and Vyāpinī, all endowed with Māyā.
These [goddesses], seated upon the seats that are the lap of Rudra, possess bodies as red as vermilion;
their forms are adorned with red lotuses, skull-cups, and other [ornaments].
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Ardhāṅga, Bhārabhūti, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, and Hara.
Miṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta,
Anugraha, Akrūra, and Mahāsena— these are the sixteen forms of the vowels.
Then there were Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, Śivottama,
Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, and Caturānana.
Ajeśa, Sarvalomeśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka; Arddhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Āṣāḍha, and Daṇḍin.
Likewise Meṣa, Lohita, and Śikhin; Chavya, Laṇḍa, and Dviraṇḍa; and Mahākāla and Vālin;
as well as Bhujaṅgīśa, Pinākīśa, Khaḍgīśvara, and Vaktra.
Śvetabhṛgvīśa, Nakulī, Śivā, and likewise Saṃvartaka—
these Rudras were born from the [five] colors and possessed of old age in due order.
With bodies embraced by their beloveds and tridents and skull-bowls in their hands,
Pūrṇodarī is said to come first, followed by Vijayā and Śalmalī.
The Lolākṣī, the Vartulākṣī, and after that the Dīrghaghoṇā;
then the Sudīrghamukhī and the Gomukhī as the ninth;
and the Dīrghajihvikā.
Kuṇḍodā and Ūrdhvakeśī, then Vikṛtamukhī as well; Khecarī and Mañjarī, and likewise Rūpiṇī.
Jvālāmukhī, as well as Ulkā and others, Mukhā, Śrīmukhī, Vidyāmukhī, and Surotpannā— these are the powers (śaktis) of the gods.
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī, as well as Sarvasiddhi;
Gaurī, Trailokyavidyā, and likewise Maṃtrātmaśakti.
Bhūtammatā, Laṃvodarī, Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, Kodarī, Pūtanā, Bhadrakālī, and Yoginī.
Śaṅkhinī, Garjinī, Kālarātri, Kapardinī, Karṣiṇī, Mahāvajrā, Jayā, and Svamukheśvarī.
Revatī, Mādhavī, Vāruṇī, and Vāyavī; Raktā, Avidāriṇī, Sahajā, Lakṣmī, and likewise Vyāpinī.
And Māyā—thus are proclaimed the Śiva-śaktis beginning with Ka;
they rest upon the lap of Rudra, shining with the splendor of goats, their forms exceedingly beautiful.
O Lord whose eyes are like red lotuses, shining with both hands; Śāradātilaka, Śrīkaṇṭha,
Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara.
Arghāśa, Bhārabhūti, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, Hara,
Phiṇḍauśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara.
Akrūra, Mahāsena, and the sixteen forms of the Svara-mantras;
then Krodheśa, Caṇḍīśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama.
Then there were Ekarudra, Kūrmaka, Ekanetra, Andha, Caturānana, Ajeśa, Sarvasomeśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka.
Ardhanārīśvara, Ekānta, Cāṣa, Hṛdaṇḍin, Spuraṇḍi,
Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, and Śikhin.
Chagaleśa, Ḍāṅkeśa, Viraṇḍeśa, Mahākāleśa, Vālinī, Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, and those known as Khaḍgīśa and Vakreśa.
Śvetabhṛṅgī, Īśana, Kulī, Śiva, and Saṃvartaka—
these are the Rudras, smiling, with slightly reddened eyes, and holding tridents and skull-cups.
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and Śālmalī follow after that; Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā are proclaimed [as the next].
Sudīrghasvāsā, Gomukhī, and likewise Dīrghajihvā;
Kuṇḍodarī, Ūrdhvakeśī, and then Vikṛtamukhī as well.
Then Jvālāmukhī is to be known, followed by Ulkāmukhī;
Suśrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī are the foremost divine powers (suraśaktis).
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī, endowed with all perfections;
Gaurī, who is the knowledge of the three worlds, and thereafter the power of mantra.
Ātmaśakti, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Laṃvodarī are considered [the powers]; furthermore, Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, Khecarī, and Mañjarī.
Then there are Rūpiṇī and Vīreṇī, followed by Kākodaryā and Pūtanā;
there should be Bhadrakālī, and likewise the two Yoginīs, Śaṅkhinī and Garjinī.
And Kālarātri with Kubjinī, and Vajrā with Kapardinī;
Jayā with Sumukheśvarī, as well as Revatī and Mādhavī.
Rāruṇī is proclaimed as Rāyavī, followed by Rakṣo and Vidariṇī;
thereafter Sahajā, Lakṣmī, and Vyāpinī are accompanied by me.
These goddesses reside upon the seats that are the limbs of Rudra; their bodies are as red as vermilion, and their lotus-like hands are adorned with a red lotus and a skull-cup.

Here too, the sequence of emanation and so forth is to be inferred, because it is contained within the *mātṛkā*. The meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) together with whichever *mātṛkā* has been prescribed for that [deity]. And thus it is said in the *Tripurāsāra*: "Afterwards, [one should place] either the *mātṛkā* alone upon the body..."

"Whether they should be placed [on the body] or accompanied by the power of Rudra (rudraśakti)—this is the sequence for initiation (dīkṣā) regarding these various nyāsas; however, for daily worship (nityapūjā), it is as stated in the Kalpa. In the Kulaprakāśa, the wise declare that recitation (japa) performed without nyāsa is demonic and fruitless.
Having become one with that through the ritual placement (nyāsa), and having become a deity, one should recite the mantra.
He who constantly performs the ritual placements according to the path taught in his own tradition [attains this].
One attains the state of the deity and mantra-siddhi arises;
without performing the various nyāsas, one who has realized the true nature of the self may recite the mantra.
One would be overwhelmed by all [such] efforts, just as a deer or a beast is by tigers.
Here, "recitation" (*japa*) is an elliptical expression that includes "worship" (*pūjā*) as well. [The mantra] is entirely within the heart.
Or else, at the time of dawn, during the rite of oblation consisting of worship.
Or even at the time of recitation, their application is distinct for each.

"At the time of worship, the best of practitioners should perform [the ritual] in its entirety. Having thus performed the *nyāsas*, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*; this is the power of the self (*ātmaśakti*). [This is from] the work composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha.

In the *Kulavṛtti*, the independent work [composed by] Guru Bhāva, this is the thirteenth chapter. Now, regarding the inner sacrifice (*antaryāga*), as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Dear One, having thus performed the placement upon the body and being composed and equanimous, one should perform the procedure for the inner sacrifice, which is directly identical with Brahman."
O Dear One, at the Mūlādhāra, one should meditate upon the Root-Vidyā, which possesses the splendor of ten million obstacles,
resembles ten million suns, and has the radiance of ten million moons.
O fair-faced one, by the descent of the upward-pointing power (ūrdhvakā-śakti),
one should become attached through the firmness of the root power (mūla-śakti) and through awakening in the central channel.

O Supreme Bliss, for the sake of the ultimate blissful state, [I bow] to the Supreme One. Now, O Lord of the Upper Realm (Ūrdhveśa), by the descent of power (śakti) into the Supreme Śiva within one's own state, through the innate union with Kuṇḍalinī,
and by means of the mantra born from both— meaning the Haṃsa-mantra— the description is given in reverse order.

Because of its purity. Regarding "mūla" and so forth: it means that because the triangle situated at the *mūlādhāra* is exceedingly firm, it is like a breast (*kucāna*). "The central seed" refers to the *kāmbīja*, which is the seed-syllable of Kāma; by that, it is "placed before," meaning it is placed in front of Kuṇḍalinī. As for "Kāmarāja," it is indeed [the seed] of Tripurā; the son is the *kūrca* seed-syllable.

"Even more clearly [stated] thus: 'Having performed the worship of the noble ones (āryajana), one should perform the external sacrifice (bāhyayāga),' so says Bhairavī in the *Prastāva*. Furthermore, in the *Sundarī-prastāva*, in that very same place:
'Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great sacrifice and the movement (cāra).'"
Extremely subtle, it enters from the base up to the aperture of Brahma.
She who consists of the splendor of millions of lightning flashes, possessing a mass of light like that of the rising sun,
and who effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe— having divided her [form].
O Goddess, just as one who has ceased eating becomes motionless,
so too does the mind become motionless through the power of Śiva and Śakti; in an instant, it becomes an abode for the mass of bliss.
Therein, concentration arises, manifested by two types of perception.
One is known by the name Sura, and another is known by the name Asura;
yet he who possesses self-known power becomes even greater than Śiva.
Indeed, through the reality of Śiva, there arises that which is called non-cognitive [samādhi];
yet, by means of self-known differentiation, it becomes intense and most intense.
But the variety of non-cognitive [samādhi] is likewise characterized by intoxication and delusion,
and is permeated by laughter, weeping, horripilation, lightning-like flashes, perspiration, and so forth.
O Goddess, characterized by a concentration more intense than the most intense,
with eyes devoid of blinking, [the mind] is established upon the objective point situated before one.
O Goddess, a progressively deeper and more subtle meditative absorption (samādhi) is observed through the Śāmbhava and Vaidika [methods], whereby one becomes continuously blissful.
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), a person may then perform the external worship. This internal sacrifice is supreme.
Now, I shall describe the subtle internal sacrifice which bestows both visible and invisible fruits.
By means of which the lords among men are always born as yogis,
one of vast intellect should perform meditation upon the Guru, just as was done before.
The meaning is as follows: "as before" refers to that which was previously established as part of the external worship according to the morning sequence;
this has already been stated above. Thus ends the morning [rite]. Thereafter, the wise one should perform the bath for the sake of the bliss of consciousness (*saṃvidānanda*).
And bathe in the pure sacred ford of Puṣkara, which is kindled by the fire of the heart.
Or one may bathe at the Viṇdu-tīrtha; then rebirth is no longer found. In this body, which is the Śiva-tīrtha, the Iḍā and Suṣumnā flow, filled with the water of knowledge.

Then the wise one should perform his bath; he who burns away his afflictions with knowledge, who always bathes with the waters of the Vedas—for what need has he of the waters of the Gaṅgā or of Puṣkara? The true purpose is residence at the Puṣkara-tīrtha within the heart.
Having mentally visualized that water, one should perform the immersion. According to the different traditions, this occurs at the Bindu-tīrtha.
O Consort of Paramaśiva, who resides in the triangle within the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*) in the form of the *bindu*, and who has emerged as nectar from the sixteen digits (*kalās*);
[the phrase] "in the path of Iḍā" also implies Piṅgalā because they always accompany one another;

the meaning is that [one should bathe] in the triple-confluence (*triveṇī*) situated in the nectar-water of Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā—or one may do so here [at this point]. This is the bath (*snāna*). Now...

Regarding *saṃdhyā*, the *Yāmala* states: "The union of Śiva and Śakti which occurs at a particular time—that is *saṃdhyā* for those established in the Kula; it is dissolved by those who abide in *samādhi*."

Now, the Supreme Śiva resides in the thousand-petalled lotus (*sahasrāra*), while the individual power (*jīva-śakti*) is said to abide at the base of the energy (*śakti-mūla*). Having perfected that which exists as *kuṇḍalinī* through ritual sacrifice according to the established doctrine and the method taught by the Guru, one should meditate upon the secret of the union through the performance of the rite, bringing [the soul] to the Supreme Śiva. As for the mantra of union, it is as follows: *antaḥ*.

"Wherever the union of Śiva and Śakti, which is Light, arises, there this mantra 'Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ', ending with the two seats (Dvithaṃtika), [is to be employed]. Thus is the twilight ritual (sandhyā). Now, the libation (tarpaṇa): In the Rudrayāmala—[one] should satisfy [the deity] with that divine nectar which is stirred up by the friction of the surfaces of the Moon and the Sun."
The Supreme Deity (Paradevatā). Now, by the term "moon, sun, and fire," the power Kuṇḍalinī is meant, because she consists of the triad of lights. "Union" (saṃghaṭṭa) means connection;

through that union of Paramaśiva and Kuṇḍalinī, one should satisfy the nature of the Supreme Deity with the supreme nectar (parāmṛta) that flows from their conjunction. This is the explanation of the libation (tarpaṇa).

Just as Svacchanda Bhairava is in the Brahma-randhra, so too is the supreme lunar [element] in the lower portion; having worshipped with the essence of the digits (kalā), one should satisfy Khecarī with that. Then, in the portion starting from the Brahma-randhra, in the triangle situated within the thousand-petalled lotus (sahasrāra) moon, the vessel is the digit, the essence of the digits.

The sixteenth digit is the stream, the shower, the falling rain; having filled [the channels] with that supreme nectar, one should satisfy the Khecarī Kuṇḍalinī. Now, as for the ritual placements (nyāsas): first, the Mātṛkā-nyāsas, as described in the Rudrayāmala:
[one places them] in the Ādhāra, the Liṅga, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, the forehead, the two petals, and the sixteen-spoked [lotus].

On the two petals, the ten petals, the twelve half-petals, or the four [petals], at the end, at the beginning, and in the middle; together with *ḍa-pha*, *ka-tha*, and *sa* in the region of the throat; and the vowels, *ha* and *kṣa*, in the middle of the staff—this indeed is for the wise one whose intellect is pure, for the sake of attaining perfection in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). The naming according to the number of words and syllables follows the sequence of ascent and descent from the *ādhāra*.

Having meditated on the sequence of cakras beginning from the throat-cakra up to the ājñā-cakra, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon their respective petals in order, starting from the east and so forth, with the syllables "aṃ namaḥ" and so on. The specific detail is as stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"In the thousand-petaled [cakra], resembling a jewel and adorned with all colors..."
In the three-lined [yantra] that is not preceded by the letter 'a' and is adorned with the syllables 'ha' and 'la', it shines forth.
In the center of that, one should meditate with a concentrated mind upon the supreme point (parabindu), which consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; this is the final placement (nyāsa).
The wise one should meditate upon the Mātṛkā, whose nature is consciousness, from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should satisfy her with streams of nectar flowing from the drops and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having uttered each syllable individually from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*,
ending with "namas," this is proclaimed as the internal ritual placement (*vinyāsa*).

The meaning of these [terms] is as follows: within the pure syllable situated in the thousand-spoked [lotus], one should visualize the three groups of sixteen—beginning with the first sixteen and so forth—in a clockwise sequence starting from the front corner of the triangle. Having focused on "laṃ kṣaṃ," one should contemplate the supreme bindu (parabindu) in its center. Alternatively, [it begins] from the *mūlādhāra*...

Having meditated upon the Kuṇḍalinī at the point of the supreme bindu within the Brahma-randhra and having satiated her with nectar, one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) by proceeding upwards from the letter *a* to *kṣa*, starting from the Mūlādhāra and ending at the supreme bindu, in the sequence beginning with "aṃ namaḥ" and so forth;
this is the tradition according to these three methods. This concludes the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Now, the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). As stated in the *Gautamīya*: "That which is being worshipped, which has the heart as its object, and which consists of consciousness, is placed thereafter by means of the Heart-mantra with total devotion."
The object of worship (artha) is that which is being worshipped; it is the heart’s object, the one to be sought by the heart. That is the Self, the Puruṣa.

Because the world—which is other than the Self, distinct from it, and of an illusory nature—is withdrawn into the Self through the state of being centered upon it, one should meditate upon that essential form of the world with the *hṛn-mantra*, namely the mantra "Namaḥ."

The preceptor performs the "feeding on objects" (*viṣayāhāra*) within the Heart-limb—the Self whose nature is consciousness (*cidātman*), which is of the form of pure awareness (*saṃvidrūpa*) and exalted by qualities such as omniscience and the rest—by means of the Head-mantra (*śiro-mantra*).

The meaning [of the qualities] is: omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), power (*śakti*), beginningless awakening (*anādivodha*), autonomy (*svatantratā*), eternality (*nityatā*), and non-deficiency (*aluptatā*). By these qualities, even though unstated, [the mantra refers to] the Self whose nature is knowledge; thus, with the Head-mantra, [one says] *svāhā*.

By means of the mantra, one should perform the withdrawal (pratyāhāra)—that is, the offering—of the objects of the ten external senses, such as sight and the rest, as well as the objects of the internal sense, the mind; this is done with the Śikhā-mantra. Through the firm contemplation that the nature of consciousness resides within the crest (śikhā), the crest of one's own body is thus established by the Śikhā-mantra.

The Guide [says]: "Artha" is the heart-form, the non-difference of the worlds from Brahman; "Śiras" is the head-form, the collective withdrawal (saṃpratyāhāra) into the three. In the Consciousness-possessor (cidvān) characterized by these two forms, one should perform the act of delighting one's own body with the mantra "Vaṣaṭ"—this is the subsidiary limb (śākhāṅga). [This applies] to the King of Mantras, whose body consists of mantras.

By means of the *tejas* [mantra], through the *brahma-mantra*, the concealment (*saṃvṛti*) [is performed] for three days. Regarding the body whose nature consists of the grasped mantras and which has the form of limbs such as hands and feet— when that [body] is being grasped by the mantra, it is concealed elsewhere by the mantra with the mantra "asyami" (I am).
It is performed daily; one who is not to be killed [is protected]. By remembering that, the injury to those who are not to be killed—such as those holding weapons in hand—is not to be taken away.

And the offering of the oblation (*bali*) is supreme; one should avoid injury everywhere. But the *bali* itself is indeed subject to injury. There is no injury to a living being in the abode [of the deity] without cause, nor is there any other breaking of armor when a sword or similar weapon falls.
Just as there is no object for one who is enveloped by the armor [of non-violence], so too there is no violence for one covered by the armor of *ahiṃsā*. This is the "armor limb" (*kavacāṅga*).

That which bestows supreme knowledge, the nature of consciousness, the splendor consisting of the heart and so forth within the conscious self—this is designated as the "eye" (*netra*). The meaning is that it consists of the heart and the head; this is the "eye limb" (*netrāṅga*).

That which is the internal form and so forth of the practitioner, produced without me, is considered born of ignorance; in the *mata-raṇa*, it is the weapon (*astra*) through the application of the mantra-sound in the tantra, its neuter gender being established by the rule [of grammar]. Thus is the weapon-limb (*astrāṅga*).

Thus is the six-limbed [practice]. Now, as for the meditation, according to the *Udayākara-paddhati*: "The mantra, which is the principle of light situated within the cavity between two powers and joined with two *malakṣas*, is declared to be the supreme abode. The meaning is as follows: the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the mental form imagined by the internal self (*adhyātmika*), while by that same term the material form (*adhibhautika*) is also expressed.

The form composed of the five elements—these two forms would destroy the practitioner. Why? Because it is the mantra born of ignorance; ignorance is the Kuṇḍalinī power. When that is known, how does it become so? It is the supreme, transcendent light; that very [light] is the subduer of the wicked. One should employ the pure self in the Kula and Akula. The meaning is "power" (śakti).

There are two triangles, two thousand-spoked wheels (*sahasrāra*), one triangle situated at the *mūlādhāra*, and another situated between these two; within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) there are two unmanifest (*alakṣa*) self-arisen lingas (*svayaṃbhū-liṅga*) residing in Paramaśiva, because they abide as their respective prior and posterior substrates. [This is] Kuṇḍalinī.

Through union with Paramaśiva, one should contemplate the principle of light (*jyotis-tattva*) as consisting of that [light], as well as the entire world of moving and non-moving beings. By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*), when the *kuṇḍalinī* is joined, the meaning is that the internal macrocosm (*antara-brahmāṇḍa*) comes into being.
It is situated between two triangles (*śṛṅgāṭa*) and encased within two powers (*śakti*).
This constant meditation on the battlefield is indeed the true meditation for yogis.

The meaning is as follows: there are two *śṛṅgāṭas* (triangular nodes) and two triangles because of their *śṛṅgāṭaka* shape; there are two powers (*śakti*), namely the upward-moving power and the downward-flowing power of liberation, which is the *kuṇḍalinī* power. One should meditate upon that which resides between these two, the *samara*, which is Brahman, the nature of the bliss of Śiva and Śakti. This alone is the meditation of the Yoginīs.

But it is with form (*sākāra*), because it illuminates conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Having made the abode of the great void—that which resides in the rays, that which resides at the tip [of the nose], and that which is situated between the moon and the sun—the King of Yogins remains full.
By the word "rays" (*kiraṇa*), the light-beams (*mayūkha*) are meant; those light-beams which exist in the *mūlādhāra* and other centers.
The watches [of time] are the years. The cosmic egg situated therein is situated at the tip of Kuṇḍalinī as a portion of her power;
the sun and moon belong to it, and the cosmic egg, joined with those two, is dissolved in the Great Void—the void above all—and remains full within every limiting adjunct (upādhi).

When [the elements] have dissolved, because there is an absence of division, the full [state] itself remains as the fullness of the hands; the remaining measures are thus. In the void state of the Visalamba, that light which arises—meditating constantly upon that as the womb is indeed the meditation of yogis.
Because of the absence of the body and so forth, Māyā is rendered supportless; therein, that light is the absence of even the slightest perception.

Because its nature is luminosity, it is the light that is the very essence of Brahman. It arises; it remains as the residue when everything else is negated, for it alone is what remains after that negation. Therefore, in the *Bhāgavata*: "That which remains after negation is the remainder.
Scripture (*śruti*) also understands [the Self] through the exclusion of what it is not. One should practice this method regarding the Self.

One should perform repeated reflection. For the yogi, that alone is meditation (*dhyāna*). These types of meditation are to be understood according to the distinction between the capable and the incapable; such is meditation. Now, regarding worship (*pūjā*) in the *Bhairava-tantra*:
"By worshipping with objects as flowers, one becomes identical with That in that very moment. The movement of consciousness (*cid-vṛtti*) shall take on the form of Brahman."

The meaning of the word *ullasati* (it shines/manifests) is that it serves as a purifier of the words; the meaning is that it becomes [so]. The eleven sense organs are themselves the flowers in the form of their objects; the worship (*pūjā*) consists precisely in the cultivation of the realization that these are identical with the Self.
As it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha:
"Whether it be happiness or suffering, whatever falls into the stream of existence, one should make it all consist of the Self; thus says the supreme teacher Ātmārca."
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, it is said: "The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), identification with that [deity], and the realization 'I am He'—one should worship with such a state of being.
In the *Bhairavatantra*: "Free from illusion, free from egoism, likewise free from passion and free from pride..."
Then, one who is free from delusion, pride, and arrogance, and who possesses non-hatred and vision, becomes devoted.
The wise know that non-avarice is a flower born of freedom from impurity;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower.
Compassion is a flower, forgiveness is a flower, and wisdom is the fifth flower;
with these eight flowers, one should worship the Supreme Deity.
The explanation of the flowers of the objects [of worship] is in two and a half verses.
Now, regarding the recitation (*japa*):
in the *Mātṛkā-arṇava*:
The fifty-fold garland has been declared; the thread consists of Śakti and the nature of Śiva.
Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is strung upon it, extending to the end of the Kalās, with Meru as its central support.

The meaning is as follows: Kuṇḍalinī performs the threading—that is, the stringing together—of the fifty-syllable thread-complex, which consists of the five limbs and is of the nature of Śiva, using the channel Citriṇī itself as the thread; from her alone arises the production of all the syllables.

The production of phonemes occurs in sequence from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣ*. The "weaving of the gods" (*devagrathana*) consists of the *kalās* within the phonemes; at the end of the phonemes are the *kalās*, for the *kalās* are indeed the generators of the *kalās*. Alternatively, by the term *kalā*, the *mātṛkā* is meant, because the *mātṛkā* has the nature of *prakṛti*. This is the summary. The detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Varṇamālā*.
The *prastāra* (arrangement) is to be known. Thus ends the recitation (*japa*). Now follows the fire-oblation (*homa*). In the *Yāmala*:
"In the fire whose form is consciousness at the navel, with the ladle of the mind, one should offer the oblation."
I perpetually offer the functions of the senses into the fire kindled by wisdom.
Having placed this mantra of the Supreme Goddess within the root mantra,

[its] meaning is as follows: at the navel, in the forefront of the form of consciousness, are the four squares of the nature of the Self (ātman), the Inner Self (antarātman), the Supreme Self (paramātman), and the Self of Knowledge (jñānātman).

That which resides in the *kuṇḍa* (the sacrificial pit) as the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), which is perceived by the self, and which extends the consciousness of the gods and the fire—that very thing is the sense-organ (*indriya*) whose function is the object of experience; it is for that purpose that one offers the oblation (*havis*) with the oblation. The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is according to the Tantric system: one should offer with this [mantra] beginning with the root [syllable]. This is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*: "The intermediate self..."

The Supreme Self is proclaimed as the Knower-Self (Jñātman). O fair-faced one, its form is the square fire-pit of consciousness (cit-kuṇḍa), beautiful with the girdle of bliss, adorned with the three circles of the bindu, and possessing the form of the yoni of the half-measure.
Therein, the river of the All-Knowing One, consisting of the bliss of Brahman and eternal supreme I-consciousness, flows forth.
O Goddess, one should offer the intense oblation of the phenomenal world into the fire of consciousness—
the imperishable syllable, radiant in form, which is known as Sound and consists of the Mātṛkā.
The syllable, which is the state of being twice-born, arises as the soundless Brahman;
having performed what was to be done and offered the oblation here in this world, one attains the auspicious state, O beloved.

O Goddess of supreme lordship, O lady of pure countenance, one should offer into the fire the mental constructs and conceptualizations, as well as merit and demerit, using the two mantras as the oblation.
Having meditated upon the Root-Vidyā in the form of Brahman immediately thereafter,
the preceptor should subsequently recite it at its conclusion for the sake of attaining Brahman.

With the ladle of the mind, I perpetually offer the oblations of merit and demerit into the fire of the Self, which is kindled by those very offerings, along the path of the *suṣumnā* and through the functions of the senses.

The meaning is that the self, as previously described, is the fire; it blazes with the two oblations of merit and demerit, and by merit and demerit alone does the state of being a living being persist. The rest is easy to understand.
O Goddess, with that [mantra] one should offer oblations with "svāhā" to the entire world, both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala).
O Goddess, this internal fire-sacrifice mantra is the transformation of all māyā.
With the hands of light and space, and with the ladle of the state beyond mind (*unmanī*), I offer into the fire the fuel of merit and demerit, filled with the oil of their fruits.
The mantra born from the fire-born [Agni] has been told to you at the end of the Vidyā. Its meaning is as follows: Brahmā and Rudra are one;

that which is light is the nature of consciousness, and space is the state of being devoid of parts. Grasping and holding these two by means of the hands—which are the essential natures of both—one becomes "unmanned" (unmanā) through the state of Unmanā, wherein the mind is like a bird [in flight].

The state of Unmanī has already been explained at length; it is understood as having the nature of light. The emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of all worlds, in the form of space, is precisely that Unmanī, because of the absence of objective referents (*viṣaya*).

In this manner, both the portion of merit (*dharmakalā*) and the portion of demerit (*adharmakalā*)—these two are "oil," namely clarified butter (*ghṛta*); it is filled with that, and [the result] is born from that.

Because the world arises from these two principles (Dharma and Adharma), I offer them into the fire of consciousness; by means of the contemplation of the identity of the self [with the Divine], there arises the experience of the state of distinction characterized by the absence of objects. Having thus offered this triad, one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as described in the *Yāmalatantra*: "Into that which incessantly obstructs [the senses] while they are increasing, the adversary of the darkness of *māyā*..."

In some wondrously radiant fire of consciousness, which is the ground of all manifestation, I offer the entire universe as an oblation until it reaches the state of nectar; within the inner mind, this offering is made continuously in a fire that is devoid of cessation, lacking fuel yet swelling with the illusion of growth, and acting as the enemy of darkness— that fire of knowledge.

The meaning is that the previously mentioned oblation is offered into the fire of consciousness (*caitanya*). In a certain indescribable void (*śūnya*)—a ground of rays of wondrous manifestation, possessing names other than [the usual]—there are "wondrous rays" (*adbhutāmarīci*); according to the *Śruti*, these are the rays of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which is the form of the world. This is the place of its origin, distinguished from the ordinary fire by these specific attributes.
"I offer the universe into that fire as ordained; I cultivate the realization that everything is composed of Me.
Through this detailed exposition of the universe beginning with the earth, the practitioner's state of being *sac-cid-ānanda* (Existence-Consciousness-Bliss) is realized.
Thus, the internal sacrifice of the gross level is described in the *Yāmala*.
Now I shall describe internal sacrifice (antaryajana), which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
The Supreme Brahman is one, subtle, eternal, and beyond the senses.
When the portion of the wife has passed and through the very act of procreation,
there arises the subtle interval of cyclic existence, which is the supreme form of the Buddha.
Then the worlds would be within that, and the egg would split into two;
both of them were filled with water, and beneath that was the imperishable One.
The practitioner of mantra should worship at its tail the one whose form is Kālāgnirudra,
and right there, the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), who is the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti).
One should worship the Tortoise, who is mounted upon a row of tortoises and bears another tortoise upon his head;
one should worship Ananta, who has the luster of a blue sapphire and resembles a white jasmine flower.
The best of practitioners should worship the white deity in the form of Varāha seated upon a tortoise, situated upon his head.
She who sustains the earth, which was being led away by him, held it at its end;
she had blue lotuses in her hands and was adorned with necklaces and armlets.
One should worship the earth, rich in treasures and girdled by the oceans,
which is divine, surrounded by red waters, and resembles pure lac-dye.
In the center, one should worship the ocean and the island resembling coral,
strewn with the nine gems and frequented by the eight supernatural powers.
One should worship Uḍḍiyāna between the Śakti and the Nāḍikā;
likewise, Jālandhara in the mouth and Kāmarūpaka in the anus.
Pūrṇagiri is in the center of the heart, at the Śrīhṛd above the palate;
on that mountain is the Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha, which the wise one should then worship.
The practitioner of mantras should worship a Kalpa-garden all around with fragrant sandalwood;
in the midst of it, he should place a Kalpa-tree that fulfills all desires.
The supreme tree consists of all beings and consists of all things; it is manifested through the earth, the imperishable, and the three [Vedas],
and it unfolds as all the scriptures.
The three worlds were covered with leaves having eyes of water;
it was radiant with syllables the color of fire, resembling coral sprouts.
The supreme abode of all beings, possessing the color of the Maruts, illuminating its splendor with shimmering flowers, and bending under the weight of its fruits in the sky.
He sprinkles the Supreme Goddess with the nectars of the highest immortality,
[a form] fashioned by the Vedas, Agamas, and other scriptures, possessing lofty and captivating majesty.
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate at its base the enchanting Pārijāta tree, which consists of Śiva and Śakti and from whose shade the three worlds are reflected.
One should visualize kadamba, nāga, punnāga, campaka, and other such trees;
at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), there is a jeweled ground with sand that has the luster of gold.
In the center is a wish-fulfilling jewel palace, infinite in extent and of the nature of light,
resembling the rising sun and pervading the entire circle of the universe.
It was a hundred yojanas in extent, beautifully adorned with various jewels,
provided with four gates, and embellished with golden ramparts.
Resplendent with the craftsmanship of jewels, joined with a circle of cowries, adorned with auspicious archways fashioned from the nine gems,
and embellished by rows of banners hanging from golden staffs at their peaks.
Therefore, it is endowed with the nine jewels situated in the central corner.
Adorned with great rubies, lapis lazuli, and jeweled chowries, enriched by canopies of pearl necklaces, and graced with golden jars.
Adorned with mandāraka flowers and embellished with fragrant blossoms,
it shone with conchs, bells, and various ritual substances from Kambudvīpa.
It was filled with bees intoxicated by honey and graced by the humming of bees;
it was adorned with fruit-bearing *kāśa* grass clinging to its walls and served as a destroyer of my pride.
That space was gazed upon by hosts of gods led by Indra;
above the pavilion stood a canopy fashioned from gold and jewels.
In the center of that [mandala] is a jewel-mandala of blazing form,
like a jeweled altar situated in the middle of the Nandana grove.
In the center of that, one should contemplate a red lion-throne, adorned with four corners and endowed with various jewels, situated within its interior.
In its center is a great wheel filled with nectar;
in the middle of that, one should meditate upon a throbbing three-peaked [mountain] consisting of light.
One should perform protection with the Astra-mantra and with the Dhenu-mudrā at that very spot;
then, having formed the Yoni-mudrā, [one should protect] both externally and internally.
Having contracted the root [channel] and likewise the supreme Brahma-sutra,
one should contemplate the circle of nectar, which has the form of a flickering lamp-flame.
The streams of nectar flow back again to the root-lotus;
and thus one should perform this sevenfold process, remembering the supreme Goddess who consists of Brahman through the yoga of meditation and the root-mantra.
Having filled [the breath] by means of pūraka and having retained it by means of kumbhaka,
one should worship that beautiful lady who is served by hosts of yoginīs.
I bow to the glorious Tripurasundarī, who flows forth from the lotus within the divine limbs, is united with the nectar of immortality, and is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Then he should meditate upon the door-keepers, each armed with a spear at every gate;
and in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus, he should contemplate the supreme Sundarī.
The Bhairavānanda-linga is situated within that [cavity] in the form of a yoni;
having then brought about their unification, the wise one should cause the nectar to flow forth.
Through the union of tongue and mouth, the wise one should drink the nectar of the extracted essence; having brought the beautiful woman into his heart, the wise one should worship her.

In this very [rite], there is no invocation (āvāhana), nor the heart-mantra, nor the mental worship (mānasārcana). One should prepare three vessels for the water for the feet (pādya) and likewise three vessels for the respectful offering (argha).
One should have sixteen cups made for the six types of mouth-washing water, three cups for honey,
and one cup for enjoyment, arranged upon the sixteen petals.
I bow to the thousand-petaled lotus, held aloft by the neck of the water-vessel,
containing the supreme nectar-water, well-perfumed with the flowers of meditative visualization.
One should fill the golden vessel according to the prescribed ritual;
the most excellent substance is offered through mental services.
The practitioner should diligently worship the Supreme Goddess with self-born flowers, or those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, or even with the flowers of his own inner disposition (*bhāva*).
One should offer an ocean of nectar, a mountain of meat, and a heap of fish;
having prepared a mandala to one's left, one should lead the Goddess of the Gods there.
Having performed the ritual anointing according to the rules with clarified butter, the wise one was [anointed] by thousands of divine maidens with fragrant, celestial oil,
as well as by thousands of Naga maidens, Kinnaras, and hosts of Apsarases.
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk, and curd from cows as well.

With coconut water, sugarcane juice, and cool water; with the seven types of earth, with pearls, and with whatever else is cooling; with pure cold and warm waters, as well as with waters containing gems and the waters of all medicinal herbs—with these, one who is supremely composed should perform the rite using the *sahasraśīrṣā* mantra.
One should perform the ceremonial bath of the Goddess with the eight auspicious jars and with erotic adornments.

One should clothe the body with a garment of fine silk (*dukūla*) dyed with saffron by means of its luster; likewise, one should perform the grooming of the hair with a comb and the ritual washing according to the rules.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead and vermilion in the parting of the hair;
likewise, one should wear red flowers, red garlands, and red ornaments.
Likewise, anointing with two unguents—such as perfumes, sandalwood, and musk—should be performed;
having offered the auspicious jeweled sandals marked by coral staffs.
Having brought [the deity] into the center of the yantra, one should pay homage with a concentrated mind:
"With a concentrated mind, I salute the venerable Tripurasundarī."
Having again offered water for the feet and other articles, one should worship the Supreme Goddess, who generates all auspiciousness and whose very nature is that of all the gods.
One should offer the goddess of fragrance (Gandhadevī) at the tip of the nose through the essence of smell;
having worshipped her with the flowers of meditative state (bhāvapuṣpa), one should offer the incense of the vital breath (samīraṇa).
One should offer the supreme splendor, the lamp, the food offering (naivedya), and so forth;
then, having offered the earth, one should perform the mental worship of the Lord through the essence of the wind.
The solar disc as a mirror, the full moon as a parasol,
a lotus with its stalk and girdle, and a brilliant necklace of joy.
Various kinds of beautiful flowers produced throughout the seven continents [are offered] from the base of the root up to the aperture of Brahmā by means of the root-wind within the Suṣumṇā.
One should offer an immeasurable bell consisting of the sound of the unstruck (anāhata);
having performed salutation with lamps, one should give [the offering] and cause it to be restrained.
Having raised the wind from the base through the *suṣumnā* with the sixteen-syllable mantra,
one should fix it at the tip of the nose, free from blinking or opening the eyes.
Having brought [the breath] to the center of the brows, one should not touch the teeth with the teeth;
the sword of knowledge does not touch the upper lip with the lower lip, nor the palate with the tongue.
If one is capable, one should perform the *lakṣa* [breath-retention] externally, free from the blinking and opening of the eyes;
this is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, which brings delight to Bhairava.
The right hand joined in a fist with the index finger at the nose is the *vismaya* mudrā;
it is the sign of wonder, causing one to be overcome by amazement.
Forming a fist with the right hand while excluding the thumb is the *nāda-mudrā*.
The union of the index finger and the thumb is proclaimed by the Śaivas as the *bindu-mudrā*.
When that [mudrā] is joined with the Jñānamudrā,
facing toward it and well-bound at the region of the heart, it is called Yogamudrā.
Then, having performed the *yonimudrā*, if that very [mudrā] should become internalized,
the wind perceived therein becomes intoxicated; this is the cause of liberation— this is that supreme liberation.
Possessing the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
her own will is the self-arisen Bhairava of supreme bliss.
The power of the vital breath (vāyu-śakti), situated in the bulb (kanda), moves toward the gateway of the Suṣumṇā.
Thinner than the awn of a wild grain, entering even more subtly,
she resembles ten million flashes of lightning and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
She who effects the creation, sustenance, and destruction of the entire world without exception, resides within the heart; she is intent upon bursting open the knots and bolts of the door.
Between the two nostrils, she should form a triangle;
having entered it, she sports intensely with the person day and night.
When one is of steady mind and always meditates, then life becomes stable;
therein arises concentration (samādhi), manifested through these two perceptions.
One who knows the name himself becomes one whose name is well-known;
indeed, by means of the reality of Śiva, he becomes one whose very consciousness is self-evident.
Having personally realized the perception of wisdom through the signs of concentration and the absorption of Śambhu, may one become eternally blissful.
Having mentally offered the water known as supreme nectar, produced from the union of those two, there is no further rebirth.
Likewise, Sundarī became delighted by that knowledge consisting of bliss;
having placed a flower at the edge, she led Maheśvarī there.
With dramas of the mind and mountains arising from the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra),
therefore, she is Mother Kāmeśvarī and he is Father Kāmeśvara.
Oneness of mind is the great worship; having performed this supreme internal sacrifice, one attains perfection and is not bound by the cycle of rebirth.
Thus concludes the sacrifice at the site (sthalāntaryāga). Now follows the description of the previously mentioned sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa), as stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the all-knowing one, having meditated upon the fire-pit known as the square through [inner] knowledge, should understand that the self is indeed square."
The number of the *ātman* and the *veda* must indeed be known by the best of practitioners;
through the mere knowledge of these, rebirth no longer exists.
It does not abide in a partial position toward common beings; O Parameśānī, O fair-faced one, that Self exists in all creatures in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa).
O Goddess, the vital breath is indeed the wind; it resides in the heart, not in the body.
Pervading the entire body, you move through both the mobile and the immobile;
you should be known as the very form of the *haṃsa*, with inhalations and exhalations as your days.
The individual soul would not belong to that [Self] alone; rather, it exists everywhere. Therefore, the state of the Self is great.
I have thus declared the knowledge of the Self; now hear, O beloved, concerning the second.
Listen now to the great term "antarātman" (the inner self). O Lord of Gods, by the word "antaḥ" (inner), a secret and subtle meaning is expressed.
When the Supreme Self has expanded, pervading everything by way of its own essential nature,
it is through that internal presence that the imperishable [Self] rejoices here.
Because it pervades everything, it is called the inner self (antarātman);
that very self is indeed the Haṃsa, which becomes accessible through yoga.
O beautiful lady, he has the Vedas and Agamas as his wings;
he possesses the pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, and his three eyes are the three *bindus*.
O lotus-eyed one, when this Supreme Swan abides everywhere, then all beings are born in succession.
O fair-faced Goddess of the gods, space, wind, fire, water, and earth— of this pentad, O Mistress of the Gods, the mind is said to be the first.

In the midst of the lotus of phenomenal existence— which is filled with the mud of space and has ignorance as its stalk, and which is adorned by the wings of beings and their opposites— there is the arrow known as nescience.
Through the creative power (*sṛṣṭi*) of this Maheśa, his abode becomes composed of *māyā*.
O Great Goddess, when he himself becomes free from phenomenal proliferation (*niḥprapañca*), [then that abode likewise becomes so].
The Haṃsa, whose form is that of withdrawal, then reveals itself;
it exists as a bird and as a fish, yet that "I" is established as the Self.
Know, O blessed one, that the Supreme Self indeed knows these three as presented;
He is called the Knower-Self (Jñānātman), who directly assumes the form of the Witness.
By which all this is known through equanimity, O fair-faced one,
just as the moon and sun are seen within the body, in water, and in milk.
There is no distinction for him [the enlightened one] based on differences such as water and milk;
O Daughter of the Mountain, just as there is no difference between mud and sandalwood when smeared upon the body.
"Then, O auspicious lady, the Knower of the Self is proclaimed as the witness of all. Thus ends the description of the fire-pit of the self (*ātma-kuṇḍa*).
Among these, if each preceding one is impossible, there is authority for each subsequent one.
This should be understood as the constant internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).

Then, one should perform the purification of the place, the mantras, and the ritual substances according to the method previously described. Thus concludes the section common to all states of being, from the *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru.
In the independent [tantra], this is the fourteenth chapter.
In the *Śāradā*:
"Thus, one should contemplate the chosen deity upon the seat consisting of the body;
having displayed the mudrās according to the rule, one should perform the ritual installation of the arghya."
Therein, first, the sequence of the animal state (*paśubhāva*) is described according to the maxim of "the needle and the mat" (*śūcīkaṭhahaṃ nyāya*). [As stated] by Śāradā:
"Having sprinkled [the victim] with water from a conch placed on the left side of the fire-mandala..."
The wise man should establish the common fire with the *svadhā* formulas.
One should fill it with water, fragrant flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rite. And in the *Yāmala*:
"Water is said to possess ten qualities; scented water is unsurpassed."
From milk comes curd, and from that, O Dakṣa, clarified butter (ghṛta) is produced in a hundredfold measure.
One should meditate on ghee as having a hundredfold potency, the weapon (hetih) as the cause of the body, and the Goddess as the supreme source.

One should contemplate the fire-pot (ādhāra), the fire (pāvaka), the conch (śaṅkha), the sun (sūrya), the water, and the moon (sudhākara); one should then sequentially contemplate the digits (kalās) of fire, sun, and moon within these [elements].

The knower of mantras, having touched [the image], should recite the root mantra and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon its limbs; having worshipped it thoroughly with the heart mantra, the preceptor, perceiving the deity with the intellect of the deity, should offer the shadow-mantra and flowers according to the rule, protect it with the weapon mantra, and veil it with the armor mantra.
Having covered [the vessel] with the *dhenumudrā*, one should awaken it with the *tatsumudrā*;
then, taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel in the right hand, one should awaken it with water.
Having taken up a small amount of the long [water], one should pour it into the *prokṣaṇī* water;
the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* vessels should be placed to the north of the *argha*.
The Guru should sprinkle himself, the sacrificial materials,
and the mandala with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, using [the appropriate] mantra in the proper sequence.

Having thus performed the installation of the *argha*, one should worship Dharma and the other [principles] according to the sequence of placement (*nyāsa*). Now follows the sequence for the divine and heroic states (*divya-vīra-bhāva*). In the *Kulārṇava*:
"The conch, the *argha* water, the vessel for worship, the offering (*bali*), and the five vessels."
Sudakṣiṇā should be established at the end of the day and worshipped with a seat.
Having performed the worship with the root-mantra purified [by the breath], O Mistress of the Kula,
the knower of the ritual procedure should place therein fish and meat in the measure of a māṣa.
If libations are offered using impure, stale, or leftover substances, or with foul-smelling or scentless materials held in the hands or a vessel, the rite becomes fruitless.
O Maheśānī, through substances such as the most delicious and intoxicating drinks that resemble nectar, and which are captivating to the mind, the act of libation becomes fruitful.
Unconsecrated liquor brings about quarrels, disease, suffering,
and sin; consecrated liquor destroys disease, suffering, calamity, and sin.
It increases longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, dharma, and learning;
therefore, having purified the family substance according to the rules, one should offer it.
Otherwise, O Beloved, the giver goes to hell without a doubt;
one should recite [the mantra] without the preliminary perfuming of the substances, and one should not even think [of it otherwise].
For those great fools who remember [only one], there is suffering at every step;
for there is no mantra without liquor, nor liquor without mantra.
"How can worship be performed given their mutual exclusion?"—
having understood the resolution of that doubt from the lotus-like mouth of the Guru.

Without the *āsava* there is no authority [to perform rites] with the root-mantra; without the mantra there is no authority with the *āsava*; and without the purification-mantra there is no authority with the *āsava*. Thus is the removal of doubt. Purification consists of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), mantra, and mudrā.
The substance suitable for satiation is that which has been purified by the four through sexual union.
In the *Udayākara-paddhati*:
"Without the unrefined [wine], even the refined is Bhairava himself;
this auspicious procedure for the worship of the wheel brings about all accomplishments."
The unrefined animal sacrifice is a cause for impaired limbs;
the refined [sacrifice] generates accomplishment and is purified by rites of atonement and the like.
The throbbing [of the fingers] of those who have committed offenses against their mother destroys great sins;
through the recitation of the *Saṃskṛta-pāṇa*, there is longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, and knowledge.
The eightfold sovereignty and the power of moving through the sky result from the falling [of the seed] according to the prescribed rule.
In the *Kulāmṛtasaṃhitā*:
"One should drink the unrefined substance and engage in sexual intercourse by force."
One who eats a fish killed by his own dear [relative] shall go to the Bhairava hell.
Thus, the impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from hearing such censures is recorded.
In that very same [text]:
"One should collect the *kula* substances for the sake of the deity according to the scriptures."
O Maheśvarī, by your grace, one obtains everything desired.
If one is unable to perform the rite in one's own home, one may take [the materials] from a consecrated person;
by seeing, smelling, or touching them, the substance becomes purified through life itself.
The effect is considered to depend on light; otherwise, there would be no conjunction.
Life is proclaimed as arising from the conjunction with the vital air known as *jīvana*.
One should worship Kuṇḍalinī at the Mūlādhāra with the aforementioned meditation;
through the yoga of the nose, her drinking occurs when [the practice] is performed.
The purification of substances is proclaimed to be fourfold;
that substance must be fit for contact [with the mouth], otherwise it would be fruitless.
In the *Tattvānandataraṅgiṇī*:
"All [the attendants], such as those in amorous attire, were resplendent in youthful dress;
their foreheads were marked with vermilion, and their mouths were filled with betel."
Her lotus-eyes were rolling from the intoxication of the fragrance of the supreme nectar;
she was accomplished in the arts on her left side and proud of her fresh youth.
Devoted to her guru and husband, skillful, initiated, with tremulous eyes,
adorned with all ornaments, possessing a beautiful nose and a lovely smile.
She who triumphs over the nectar of immortality, resplendent with the two jars of her breasts,
whose nature is the love of the practitioner, and who is devoid of pity and shame.

Having established this messenger (dūtī) within the heart of the seeker’s desire, this [practice] pertains to the sphere of the initiated Śakti; however, for the uninitiated, it should be understood as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of the Kula. (p.
Having drawn a hexagon within its own [mandala] on the left, surrounded by a full moon and a city of earth (bhūpura),
the wise one should gaze upon it with water for general purposes.
In that very place, O Hero, one should worship the fire with its constituent parts (kalās).
There, one should place a pitcher purified by the weapon-mantra, made either of gold, silver, bell-metal, or even clay,
provided it is not made of iron.
One should smear with red sandalwood paste that which is covered with a garland of *śuma* flowers; as stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
"In the midst of a bed of flowers, crowded with a perimeter of blossoms..."
In a place filled with various sounds, one should prepare a mechanical device using family property.
Having written [the mantra], one should worship it, preceded by the placement of a conch and a water-pot (ghaṭa).
To one's left, draw a six-cornered (ṣaṭkoṇa) *vaṭu* [diagram], with the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmaraṃdhra*) in its center.
Having written [the names] there, one should place a conch shell made of gold,
silver, copper, or even clay, provided it is not made of iron.
O Lord, one should place [the deity] within the pitcher, which is well-scented with fragrance, by means of a digit (kalā).
And in the *Svatantra*:
"Having brought that divine cause and placed it within the pitcher..."
It is wound with red thread and adorned with a red garland.
O Maheśānī, on the left side, one should devoutly establish a square mandala there with the intellect of the Goddess, O fair-faced one.

In the *Svatantra*, it is said: "Upon the support (ādhāra), within the kalās and the substances, are the orbs of Fire, Sun, and Moon. Then, by means of the thread, a hexagon is formed; in its center is the Brahma-randhra."
At the end of that, one should draw a circle, and outside of that, two square enclosures (bhūpuras).
There, having placed the support, one should worship the fire-maṇḍala;
the practitioner of mantra should worship the sun-maṇḍala with its constituent parts (kalās).
The meaning is that one should worship. In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*:
"The practitioner of mantra should place [the vessel] upon the foundation (ādhāra), whether it be made of gold or silver."
Alternatively, one should consecrate a jar made of bell-metal or clay with the mantra while it is filled with rice.
A golden vessel is said to bestow enjoyment; a silver one is remembered as providing delight;
a bell-metal one brings peace, and an earthen one shall grant nourishment.
Having wrapped that jar with a red cloth and a red garland,
the practitioner should meditate upon it as having the very form of his chosen deity.
Since this pitcher was fashioned by Viśvakarman from taking a portion from each of the gods, it is therefore called *kalaśa*.
But according to Pādapadmācārya: he who serves the *kalās* (arts/energies) is called *Kalasa*. By this, there is a twofold form: *kala* and *sakala-sattva*.
Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the ornaments of the venerable hands (*śrīhastābharaṇanyāsa*), as stated in the *Yāmala* according to one's capacity:
"If, having performed the ritual placement of the ornaments of the venerable hands, one should touch [the disciple]..."
That goddess may become angry from the touch of the hand of one who has visited a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Uttering the root mantra at the end of the syllable *vāṅmāyā* (AIM),
one should likewise [place it] upon the lower left hand of the illustrious Tripurasundarī.
Having uttered "ṅeṃ yutaṃ ca amṛtam" (ṅeṃ yutaṃ ca amṛtam), [one says] "namo vai pūrṇahastāya.
Having extracted everything as before, one should also [recite] "vāmordhvahasta" (the left raised hand).
Then, having performed the act of giving for the sake of the recipient,
he should bind everything as before, including the right hand.
One should place [the mudrā] on the hand with the mantra ending in "namas" while saying "varadāne karāya";
having raised everything as before, one should likewise form the "chest-upward-hand" [mudrā].
One should place [the mudrā] on the hand with the mantra ending in "namaḥ": *varābhayakarāyai namaḥ*.

As for the ritual application (*prayoga*): *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mūlaṃ śrītripurasundaryāvadho-hastapi aṣṭeta pūrṇahastāya namaḥ*. Thus one should place it on both of one's own hands. The mention of "Sundarī" is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for one's own chosen deity.
The meaning is "of the deity. Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the wise one should touch [the vessel];

however, if he is the one who fetched [the substance], he should do so at the very time of the preliminary offering (*āvāraṇa*); but if someone else fetched it, then at the time of the filling (*āpūraṇa*).

Reciting the root mantra "Tat-tva-vam-da-taraṅgi," the practitioner should worship the digits of the moon and perform salutation with the five mudrās, perceiving them as one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva).
In the Śaktiyāmala: One should prostrate with devotion to the form of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) five times, using the [appropriate] mudrā.
The wise one, having turned his hands downward, should place them upon the ground;
in the form of straight lines, this is the *śaralākārā* mudrā.
One should apply this mudrā, which destroys all sins, to those who have entered [the path].
One should join the two hands facing each other in the form of a hollowed cup (*puṭa*).
Into the base of the little fingers of that very same mudrā, one should insert the two thumbs; this is declared to be the *puṭāñjali* [mudrā].
Then one should perform the *yonimudrā*, and subsequently join [the deities] in sequence within the two [seals]. The *vāṇamantra* is as follows, according to the *Jñānārṇava*:
Having drawn two vertical lines situated within the fire [triangle] in sequence,
[one should draw] that which is situated on the ground by means of a circular mouth.
O fair-faced one, the fourth [syllable] begins with the vowel and the bindu, and has the form of sound (nāda).
One should draw the letter PHĀṂ joined with Śakra (the vowel *i*) and adorned with the left ear (*u*),
along with the Yoga-mudrā and the syllables beginning with *madvatī*, using red sandalwood, vermilion, and saffron mixed together;
one should then draw a triangle within a circle upon the ground next to the water-pot.
With this mantra, one should offer a bali-oblation filled with cooked rice and other offerings.
Having performed the purification and endowment with the left hand,
one should then perform the fivefold process (*pañcīkaraṇa*) upon the substances offered to oneself.
One should perform the veiling with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*),
the visualization (*darśana*),
and the fivefold process (*pañcīkaraṇa*) as prescribed.
Having recited the mantra "toreṇadamukaśaravījam," one should worship with the mental conception of the deity.

Having recited the Vāmadeva mantra, complete with its seed-syllable (*tāra*) and the *amṛta* syllable, along with the *netra* (eye) mantra, the practitioner, being composed, should worship Vāmadeva while offering flowers into the jar.
One should join the left eye with the word *vāhinī* and with the great illusion (*mahāmāyā*) at the place called Kuśa.
At the end, [having placed] the supreme mistress (*paramasvāminī*) with the right hand, one should recite the mantra ten times:
the seed-syllables of Speech (*vāk*), Illusion (*māyā*), and Lakṣmī (*kamalā*), followed by the word "Nandeśvarī" ending in the dative case (*ṅe*).
And we know [thee], O Sudhā; may we meditate upon thee...
[may it] impel us.
And at the place called Ānamna, which bestows happiness upon all beings,
one should recite this mantra three times, O Hero, as the cause for [attaining] this form.
One should perform the consecration three times with the *haṃsapādī* mantra;
one should consecrate it with the mantras for liberation from the curses of Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and Śukla.
The Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, and the six long vowels combined; followed by "sudhā" and "kṛṣṇapadasyānte," and then "pāpaṃ mocaya tatparam."
One should cause the couple to hear the nectar (the mantra *amṛta*), with the wife of fire (*svāhā*) at its end;
by reciting the mantra ten times, one shall be liberated from Kṛṣṇa’s curse.
One should extract the Praṇava ending with the syllable of Varuṇa (va), differentiated by the six long vowels,
followed by the words "vimocitāyai" at the end of the verse concerning the curse of Śukra.
One should release the curse of Śukra by reciting "Obeisance to Sudhādevī.
According to the Tattvānanda-taraṅgiṇī-mata,
the practitioner of mantras should release the curse of Kavya with the same single mantra.
In the Kumārītantra: "Listen to something else, O Goddess of gods, regarding how no fault arises in rites such as the *pāṇigrahaṇa* (taking of the hand), O Goddess; hear those mantras, my dear."
The mantra beginning with "ekameva" and so forth has already been written above.
Having uttered "ekam eva" three times, it is endowed with the three [vowels] bindu and the three long [vowels].
The seed-mantra preceded by *māyā* (hrīṃ) and *lakṣmī* (śrīṃ), adorned with the form of a dagger (*churikā*),
followed by the word for "modification" (*vikāra*) and the name of the substance, ending with "Hara Hara."
The two *ṭha*s are called "the knife" (*churikā*); by reciting them three times, one is freed from faults. "One-eyed" refers to the letter *cha*. And in the *Śaktiyāmala*:
"The fish, fire, and wind [letters], adorned with the dot (*bindu*), are the two 'one-eyed' ones."
It is pervaded by long vowels and is beautiful as the "knife-edge" (chūrikāra).
Thereafter, having extracted the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā) from that substance which consists of the *vikāra* (the letter 'e'),
one should recite the mantra three times.
In that regard, having uttered the venerable Vāgbhava in sequence, likewise [the words] "O you who arise from death" (mṛtodbhave),
"O showerer of nectar" (amṛtavarṣiṇi) at the end, and then the word "Great Radiance" (mahāprakāśa):
When [the breath] is released, one should say to the wife of Fire: "O you who destroy through recitation.
Now, the meditation on Tiraṃkariṇī is as follows, according to one's capacity, in the Yāmala:
The supreme practitioner should meditate upon the Great Vidyā, the Dispeller [of obstacles],
as the Blessed Lady who proceeds ahead mounted upon a dark blue horse, her eyes obscured by a veil of sleep consisting of a mass of blue rays, and bearing a sword as her weapon.
May she protect her devotees! One should extract the goddess Kāmeśvarī, who is the embodiment of modesty (*lajjā*) and speech (*vāṇī*), consisting of the syllables *glaiṃ*.
Then, from the word *tiraḥ*, one should extract *utkariṇī*; from *sa kāla* [comes] *janā*; then *ragrodinī*; and *sakalapaśuvrāta jalā*.
From the words *manaḥ*, *cakṣuḥ*, *pada*, *śrotra*, *jihvā*, and *ghrāṇa*, and from the word *śabda*, and from the word *tiraḥ*, one should likewise extract *kariṇī*.

One should extract the two *kurus*, the two *ṭhas* joined with the *sarga* (visarga), and the fire (*ra*) and the beloved (*kā*), in this sequence. In another method, there is the pair of *śaktis* in the *yamala*;
at the end of the pair of *māyā* and *lakṣmī*, one says "namo bhagavati."
At the end of the word "Māheśvarī," [one should say] "sarvapaśujana" as well.
Insert *manaṃś-cakṣus-tiraskarī* and the pair of *ṭha*s twice.

In this matter of the duality of mantras, the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the refuge. Then, one should purify the *kāraṇa* vessel with the mantra according to its measure; the mantra is that of the Śruti.
Oṃ! Pāvamāna is supreme bliss, Pāvamāna is the supreme essence;
Pāvamāna is supreme knowledge—with that, I purify you.
Having dried [the body] with the seed-syllable VāM, the practitioner of mantra should then burn it with fire;
thereafter, he should visualize the sun, the solar disc, above.
Recalling Varuṇa with the solar mantra while [visualizing him] above the head,
one should then contemplate the new moon falling from him as a continuous stream.
Ākāśa is conjoined with Kula; Manu is like a fragment of the moon at the time of creation;
he brings great bliss, is praised by heroes, and is Varuṇā-manu.
Then, reciting the seed-syllable *saum* ending with *hāṃ*, together with the nasal bindu and the visarjanīya, which consists of nectar,
he should fill the vessel with the mudrā of the cow (dhenumudrā) while muttering [the mantra].
One should worship Amṛtā seven times under the name of Kūrma;
having uttered Māyā, who is dear to Viṣṇu, as "aṃ āṃ iṃ" according to her form, O Mortal one.
At the end of the word *amṛtodbhava*, one should say *amṛtavarṣiṇi*;
then *amṛta* and *śrāvaya* in the dual, followed by the *pāśa* (the letter *pha*) and the long *śruti* (the vowel *ī*).
Having uttered "seṃdukhaṃḍau" as Bhṛgu, and then [uttering] "mṛte'mṛteśvarīṃ," one should extract "ṅeṃ namostāṃ" and recite the Amṛta mantra.
Then, having rendered it immortal, one should perfume it with camphor and other substances;
with the mantra of the principle of Vidyā, one should display the Yonimudrā.
Having meditated upon Ānandabhairava and likewise upon Ānandabhairavī, one should worship them in the Kāraṇa [mandala], O Goddess; hear the mantra according to the sequence.
Now, regarding meditation in the Śaktiyāmala:
In the midst of that, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate [the deity] who bestows the bliss of knowledge,
resembling ten million suns and as cooling as ten million moons.
The god has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes;
he stands in the midst of an ocean of nectar, seated upon a lotus on the foundation of Brahmā.
Mounted upon a bull, blue-throated, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, resounding with the ringing of a bell and a ḍamaru drum.
The god holds a noose and a goad, and bears a mace and a club;
he carries a sword, a shield, a paṭṭiśa, a mallet, a trident, and a spear.

The foremost of practitioners should meditate upon the Lord of the gods, who is red in hue and holds a shield and a severed head, while his hands display the gestures of granting boons and protection.
And one should meditate upon the goddess Sudhā, whose splendor is equal to ten million moons,
white as snow, kunda flowers, and the moon, possessing five faces and three eyes.
Endowed with eighteen arms, intent on bestowing all bliss,
smiling, large-eyed, and six-faced, she belongs to the God of gods.
Thus is the meditation. The mantra is as follows, according to the *Tattvānanda*:
"Akula conjoined with Kula, Saṃvarta, Vāla, Bhū, Jala, Tejas, Samīraṇa, and Śrotra, joined with the long vowel and the half-moon."
One should extract Ānandabhairava ending with *ṅeṃ* and joined with the crest-syllable (*śikhā*).
Its first [syllable] is reversed, while the left eye is in the ear.
This Ānandabhairavī is the foot and the eye of the goddess Sudhā;
meditating upon the Goddess who consists of all beings within the root triangle.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Self, Śiva, within the Suṣumṇā by way of the Brahma-path, using the mantra that will be mentioned, O Hero.
One should join the nectar arising from that into the vessel by means of one's own abode;
the living soul, consisting of Śiva and Śakti, [is joined] in due order through the mouth.
Then the mantra-practitioner should meditate upon her as the beloved of Fire (Svāhā), possessing the splendor of the sun;
this is the mantra of unification for all yogins who know yoga.
The Amṛta mantra is as follows, according to the Kulāmṛta: "Vaṃ Phaṭ," joined with the long vowel [Ā], ending with "namo varuṇāya.
This is declared to be the Amṛta mantra, which effects the purification of substances.
One should contemplate the substance as nectar; one should recite the nectar-essence mantra joined with the long *vaṃ* and ending with *namaḥ* to Varuṇa.
Then, having taken up the jar, one should recite the root mantra eight times.
In the *Svatantra*, it is said:
"O Dear One, having visualized [the deity], one should contemplate the substance as resembling divine lac."
In the three rows beginning with 'a', 'ka', and so on, the first is adorned with the letter 'ha'.
As before, [one performs] the union of Śiva and Śakti within the yoni-mudrā;
then follows the thread of the jar (ghaṭasūtra).
While the Kṣīroda, the best of oceans, was being churned,
the goddess Surā was produced there, assuming a golden form.
Having a form resembling cow urine, with froth arising from death,
one should visualize the Goddess with eighteen arms and rolling eyes.
The staff (daṇḍikā) may be the color of refined gold, or it may be four-colored;
it may also be the color of cow’s urine or milk, or another auspicious black color.
The slayer of animals is eternally [the giver] of liquor, which is extremely difficult for the gods to obtain;
that liquor is the goddess Dravī, and he who enjoys it is Śiva himself.
He who is Yogaṃdha is himself Brahmā; he who is Rasa is Janārdana;
in the form of desire he is the god Manmatha, and in the midst of the waters he is Bhairava.
The foam of the Gaṅgā is here; salutations! The seven oceans are present directly within this jar, for the protection of the gods and for the destruction of the Daityas.
By means of this "pot-thread" (ghaṭasūtra), the purification of the substance is accomplished;
one should worship it with perfumes and flowers, and thereafter apply the "passion-fire" (kāmāgni).
In this manner, during the fire-oblation, the sacrifice, and the drinking, one should purify the substance;
without performing the purification, one should not effect the preparation of the substance.
A person who has consumed [it] out of delusion or ignorance must perform penance;
however, in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, it is stated that this occurs after the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭasthāpana).
One should complete [the ritual] according to the distinctions of cause, substance, brahmins, and so forth;
therein, having first inscribed the yantra arising from the six families.
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times therein;
then, displaying the dhenumudrā, one should contemplate that [mantra] as nectar.
This is one [tradition] due to differences in the oral transmission (saṃpradāya).
