One should scatter curd, unbroken rice, fragrance, flowers, and vermilion on the outside.
One should designate four jars at the four corners of the altar, each containing water, sprouts, and a conch shell, with unhusked rice poured over them.
In the case of the Sarvatobhadra and other [mandalas], as well as in the Sundaṛī-pakṣa,
one should place a very beautiful nine-jar [arrangement]; however, in the case of the Śeṣamaṇḍala-pakṣa,
one should deposit the nine-yoni [arrangement] filled with gold, gems, and other [substances].
Thus it is common to all entities. In the *Śāradā*:
"Having fashioned a form with the root mantra, one should project its shadow upon this [altar] from the wish-fulfilling trees."
The meaning is: of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpaśākhin) cultivated by the mind.
By this, the purification of the deity is indicated.
This sequence applies specifically to initiation (*dīkṣā*); however, one should incorporate it into the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).

Thus, having first performed the common sixfold offering (*ṣaḍargha*), the installation (*sthāpanā*), and the fourfold purification (*catuḥśuddhi*) for all states of being, one should perform the *pīyūṣayāga*, fashion the form (*mūrti*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), and complete the remainder. This is the purification of the deity (*devaśuddhi*). Now, in the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*), there is mounting (*vāhana*) and worship (*pūjā*); however, in the divine (*divya*) and heroic (*vīra*) states, [it is otherwise].

Having performed the offerings of *validāna* by accepting the drops (*bindu*) of the essence of libation (*tarpaṇa-tattva*), one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*). As for the measure of the libation, it is stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "Upon seeing the vessel of the *arghya*, the hosts of *yoginīs* will indeed gather."
All the Bhairavas dance; the hosts of Mothers dance;
and all the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy;
having divided the vessel of the *arghya* offering into three parts, one part is given to the Guru.
Having offered one [portion] to the *kulāya*, the offering to the deities (*devatārpaṇa*) is performed with special distinction.
And in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Having worshipped the circle (*āvṛtti*), the lineage of gurus (*gurupaṅkti*), and Vaṭuka and the others..."
Likewise, a sower who drinks [the water] in vain shall go to the Raurava hell.
"Not having worshipped" means not having satisfied [the deity]. And in the *Kalpasūkta*: "The wise woman [should place] the sandals of the Guru upon her own head. And in the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"Ānandabhairava on the head, and likewise Ānandabhairavī."

Or, O Goddess, one may satisfy [the deities] within the heart by means of the previously mentioned Vidyā; separately, one should satisfy the Guru, and there, within that heart, one should also satisfy the Goddess. This concludes the determination of the deities to be satisfied. Now, the sequence: the lineage of Gurus, Vaṭuka, Yoginīs, Kṣetrapālas, Gaṇeśa, all Bhūtas, Ānandabhairava and Bhairavī, the Root Goddess, and the enclosures.
The Deity: Now, regarding the *tarpaṇa* mudrā in the *Svatantra*:
O Pārvatī, by joining the thumb and ring finger of the left hand, one should offer libations to the goddess Kālikā, together with her weapons and her retinue.

In this context, "kālika" (the time-bound) is an illustration; for libation (*tarpaṇa*) is common [to all]. Thus, it is said in the *Uḍḍīśa*: "Having taken up the purification, the wise one should thereafter perform libation three times with the mudrā.
The mudrā formed by the union of the ring finger and the thumb is known as the Kaulikī."
The thumb is the goddess Bhairavī, and the ring finger is considered Caṇḍikā;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should always offer libations with these two with great care.
[In the Tatvānanda:]

Then, having undertaken purification, the leader of the *kula* should satisfy [the deity] with the two mudrās known as *tattva*, through the union of the left and right [channels]. Or else, O Goddess, while recollecting the sandals (*pādukā*) of the venerable Guru, one should satisfy [him] with the left [mudrā].
Having performed that three times according to his desire with the nectar situated in the vessel,
the knower of mantras, as Ānandabhairava, [should worship] the venerable Mahādevī in the heart with the root mantra, while holding the nectar of the Śrīpātra over his head.

With devotion, one should satisfy that [deity] together with the multitude of rays by means of substances contained in the *vīrapātra*. Then, one should satisfy the Goddess of the *pīṭha* with substances contained in the *śaktipātra*, and satisfy the retinue with the offerings (*dūṣya*) contained in the *vīrapātra*. [The *śaktipātra*...]
With substances placed [on the vessel], one should satisfy the Mistress of the Kula; while meditating on one's own deity, one should offer the drink in the Hero’s Vessel (*vīrapātra*).
Then, with substances situated in the Hero’s Vessel, one should satisfy the Bhairavas;
and with substances situated in the Hero’s Vessel, one should likewise contemplate the Guardians of the Directions.
The vessel for worship should be understood as that used for the worship of the Yoginīs;
with the nectar from the vessel of the bali offering, one should not satisfy Vaṭuka and the others.
Thus concludes the procedure for the nine vessels.
In the ritual option of seven vessels, there is likewise the vessel for the *bali* offering and the vessel for the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Thus, in the absence of that [specific] vessel, it should be done with the vessel for enjoyment (bhogapātra) alone; so it is said.
In the Kulārṇava it is said: "One should offer libations according to the path taught in the scriptures with drops [of wine],
drawn out silently with the thumb and ring finger, using the nails."
O leader of the lineage, having performed the ritual pouring of the liquid from the vessel according to the rules,
and having offered the libation once, one should recite the root mantra and the *pādukā* mantra.
Having recollected the internal power, one should satisfy the deity of the body;
O Goddess, the thumb is considered Bhairava and the ring finger is considered Caṇḍikā.
Now, the optional libation (tarpaṇa) as follows:
one should perform the libation for the rite of subjugation (vaśyakarma) using the thumb and ring finger;
for malevolent rites (abhicārika), one should perform the libation by joining the forefinger and thumb.
O Dear One, for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana), one should offer libations using the union of the little finger and the thumb;
having thus offered libations according to the rule with the substances of the Kula, O Goddess of the Gods.
O Goddess, one should worship the lineage of gurus accompanied by the deities;
having meditated upon the three lineages in their proper sequence with undistracted mind, one should perform the worship correctly.
In that very place is Dhyānā;

she holds the *cinmudrā* with her two hands and a skull-cup filled with honey; she resembles molten gold, is adorned with red flowers and ointments, possesses a body full of compassion, has reddish eyes, and is endowed with curly hair.
Victorious is the lineage of gurus through the streams of Siddhas, O wise one!
Having thus worshipped with incense, lamps, and food offerings,
as well as wine accompanied by the Goddess and various kinds of edibles;
One should offer fruits such as the kadamba and betel leaf as well. This is the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Now, regarding the purification of the principles (*tattvaśuddhi*): Tattvānanda states that one should worship the Supreme Goddess even without the purification of the principles;
however, the worship should be known as fruitless, resulting in the loss of accomplishment at every step.
In this state of heroism (vīrabhāva), having become one whose nature is bliss, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
having attained [this state] without cause, one should never recite [mantras], nor should one ever fail to recite them.
Even in bliss, there is no falling away, and the deities are never satiated;
when the practitioner experiences agitation, agitation arises within me.
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess until the purification of the flesh— characterized by the scent of the sacrificial meat— is complete.

"O Dear One, one should not worship the Goddess, nor recite mantras, nor meditate [upon Her] until then"— by such statements, for one who is enjoined that worship must be performed as a preliminary limb, there is the "time of bliss" (ānanda-samaya) and the "time of the purification of reality" (tattva-śuddhi-samaya). If he has not yet engaged in the daily worship (nitya-pūjā), then at that time—

The purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi) must be performed afterwards. However, in the state of the divine (divya-bhāva), since it is established as being the state of bliss (ānanda-avasthā) within the purification of the principles, its very nature is bliss and not [the result] of drinking. As it is said in the Kulārṇava: "The triad of principles is the commencement of the essence."
In the *Tattvānanda*:
"Then, one should purify the hands with the root-mantra using the *tīrtha* of one's own vessel;
having drawn a circular central wheel upon the right hand."
On the ground to the east, south, and north of the mouth [of the pit], the best of preceptors should place a purification [mark] made of beans or sesamum, measuring the size of a bean or a mung-bean.

With the left hand, one should hold Menā with the deer-gesture (*mṛgamudrā*). As for the deer-gesture, it is described in the *Yāmala*: having joined the ring finger and the thumb, one should place them at the tip of the middle finger.
One should form the beauty of the remaining fingers; this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā*.

Now, regarding the principles (tattva) and so forth, it is said in the *Śāradā*: "In this system, primordial nature (prakṛti), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), the objects of knowledge (jñāna), and the sense organs (indriya)."
The organs of action, the subtle elements, and the five gross elements are the teachers.
In this [system], there are twenty-four pure principles (tattvas) within the category of Rāga;
these are known as Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, and Vidyā.

O Puruṣa, these seven principles—both pure and impure—are called the Śaiva tattvas: Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva; ||| Rāgaḥ puruṣa etāni śuddhāśuddhāni sapta ca | tattvāni śaivāny ucyante śivaḥ śaktiḥ sadāśivaḥ ||
The Lord, together with Vidyā, [is placed] upon the five *dūra*s on the head;
this is written according to the sequence of the *Śāradā-tantra* because it follows the sequence of the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*).

This very sequence is the one for the purification of the principles; however, the sequence of *Sāradā* is for the purpose of purification below, and that occurs at the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*).
It should be stated: as for the authoritative source, it is in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Dear One, O Kuleśvarī, by means of the twenty-four principles beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with earth, and by means of the *vāgbhava* syllable which is pure in its true nature."
One should purify the gross body by means of the nature of the Self as it is joined [with the subtle body].
The knower of mantras [should worship] with the seven principles— beginning with Māyā, Puruṣa, and Kalā— which are both pure and impure, and with the non-dual mantras of touch and Kāmarāja.

With a disciplined mind and through the act of creation, one should contemplate and purify the subtle body by means of the five pervasive principles (tattvas), beginning with Śiva and ending with Vidyā, which are all pure.
O Dear One, one should purify the supreme body by means of the supreme Śivatatva,
or by means of the Mālinī with its thirty-six principles, using the *bālā* [mantra].
With that mudrā, one should purify the *jīva* by means of the reality of all things (*sarvatattva*).
One should give the triple purification; he is the Guru who removes the third impurity.
Reciting "I purify," the disciple receives the handful of water offered by the Guru.
Bowing with devotion and proper conduct, the disciple, remaining silent and moving slowly, should touch his limbs and body with both hands while reciting the entire *Sarvatattva* mantra.
One should contemplate the pure body, from the head down to the soles of the feet;
the gross [body] is the principle of the self (ātmatattva), while the subtle is within the sphere of knowledge (vidyā).
The ultimate limit is the Śiva-tattva; thus it is contained within the three principles.
Having thus understood these three principles through knowledge from the Guru, one should take refuge [in them].
"It is said that one becomes liberated even while living. Thus spoke Bhuvaneśa. Meditating upon Viṣṇu, Śakti, Vastu, and Maṃ with the Bindu, he said: "The fourth element beyond that is his own Self."
O beloved of Agni, I purify the gross body through its true nature.
"O Goddess, with this mantra one should collect [the substance] situated directly in front," so it is said in the *Somadhūtajagāvalī*.
This refers to the taking [of the substance] in a handful (*culūkagrahaṇa*). According to another view, it refers to the taking of the purity (*śuddhi*) located within the mandala.
At the time of taking the *prasāda*, this must also be performed by the disciples; this will be explained in the section on the ritual procedure for the *cakra*. Now, the Vedic [method]:

Another method: For example—*Oṃ prāṇāpāna-vyānodāna-samānā me śudhyantāṃ virajāni padmā bhūyāsaṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ pṛthivy-apa-tejo-vāyv-ākāśā ime śudhyantāṃ jyotir aham ityādi*. *Oṃ prakṛti-ahaṃkāra-buddhi-manas-śrotrāṇi...*

May [they] be purified. "I am light," and so forth. *Oṃ*, may my skin, eyes, taste, smell, and speech be purified; *viraja* (free from passion), and so forth. *Oṃ*, may my hands, feet, smell, touch, sound, and space be purified; *viraja*, and so forth. *Oṃ*, [may] touch... space be purified.

"May [the elements] be purified; O Virajā," and so forth. "Oṃ, may my air, fire, water, earth, and self be purified; O Virajā," and so forth. Having thus rubbed the hand seven times, having wiped the palm, and having drawn a triangle on the right hand, one should place the *kalās* facing the triangle in the right, left, and middle [sections].
Having performed a similar purification, joining the left thumb, ring finger, and middle finger together, one should recite: *hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ ātmatattvena sthūladehaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*.

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hūṃ Klīṃ: by means of the principle of Vidyā, I purify the subtle body, Svāhā! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Sauḥ: by means of the principle of Śiva, I purify the supreme body, Svāhā! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ:
by means of that mudrā, I purify the soul which is its support, Svāhā! Then, having purified the hand with the Astra-mantra...

"One should wipe [the body] from the head down to the feet with the two hands held separately. Regarding this point as well, where there is a division of opinion, the established tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the refuge. Now, the acceptance of the *bindu* (the drop). As it is said in the *Tattvānanda*:
"The Goddess, residing in the root-knot (*mūlakanda*), moving through the center of the *suṣumnā*..."
Having brought the vessel to completion, the practitioner should become absorbed in that.
One should accept the initiated disciples with the *tattvamudrā* while reciting "ārdrā" and so forth.
In the *Kalpasūtra*: "Oṃ, the moist one blazes."
"I am light; the light blazes. I am Brahman; I am He. I alone offer myself;
Svāhā!"—this is the meaning of invoking the Self into the Kuṇḍalinī. "Purification" refers to Śiva.

According to this view, it is done with a single Ṛg-verse. However, according to another school of thought, one should perform the three offerings to the Sun with the Astra-mantra itself, as follows: *Oṃ ca me*... [and so forth].
I shall speak of Brahman as directly perceived;
I shall declare the truth, I shall speak the reality. May he protect me, may he protect the speaker.
Whatever word I shall speak, whether it be immortal or composed of meters, may Indra touch that with wisdom, for from the meters the immortals have arisen.
"May Viśuva protect [me]. These are the two mantras. In this matter as well, the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the refuge. Now, regarding the offering of the *bali*: in the *Kulārṇava* it is said:
"O Kuleśvarī, as long as one does not offer [it] to Vaṭuka, [the rite] is not truly performed."
All the deities are satisfied by the mere recollection and worship [of this].

One should worship Vaṭuka and the others with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and meat offerings, according to the specific rules for their respective mantras; thus one shall attain divine delight. By the word "and others" (ādi), the Yoginīs and so forth are intended.
O Goddess of the Gods, whatever collection of substances has been brought for the purpose of worship and enjoyment, let it be given with devotion to the Kṣatriyas.
How can one worship on the sacred fields (kṣetra) without first giving to the lords of the kṣatra?
How is the ritual of worship performed when one gives only after having begged from Vaṭuka?
How can one worship [her] without first offering [oblations] to Gaṇeśa and the Yoginīs? If one should worship Tripurā without the offering of the bali, [it is fruitless].
At the conclusion of the worship, everything becomes fruitless and obstacles arise at every step. As stated in the Kulārṇava:
"O Dear One, [this applies] in the northeast, the southeast, and likewise in the southwest."
O Goddess, in the northwest, there is a sequence of four mandalas.
O Goddess, one should draw a triangle within the void surrounding the Śrīcakra;
O Daughter of the Mountain, having first worshipped Vaṭuka and the others here with mantras.
In the *Yāmala*: "A wise man should construct mandalas in the northeast, the southeast, the southwest, and the northwest; or else, he may construct them in the four cardinal directions."
In the *Kulārṇava*, it is stated that [the worship] is performed with the fourfold power;
or else, one should indeed draw the mandala on the left side,
and right here one should perform the offering of the bali for the sake of accomplishing all aims.
And in the *Kulāmṛta*: "The practitioner, having accepted [the offering], with his knee on the left side,
should gradually fashion a triangle, a circle, the orb of the earth, and an eightfold [mandala]."
One should draw either a triangle, a hexagon, or a square.

In this manner, four circles (valayas) are established. According to another opinion, there are five circles; in case of inability, one should perform only the five-pervading mandala (pañcavyāpakamaṇḍala). Thus it is stated in the *Tattvānanda*.
Then, beneath the lion throne, in the four directions starting from the east— namely the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest— or alternatively, in those same corners.
Having drawn four mandalas consisting of triangles and circles,
one should further construct on the left side a wheel resembling a fortified city (bhūpura).
Alternatively, O Goddess, one who is capable should offer the fivefold oblation to the left;
if incapable, one should collect a single bali for all beings.
In the *Yāmalatantra*, regarding the power of the mandala-worship:
"The seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbhava*), Mahāmāyā, and 'Kavaca for the Mandala'—this mantra, ending with the Heart [syllable], is proclaimed; the wise one should worship the mandalas."
The practitioner of mantra should cast Vāṇī into the mouth of the pervasive maṇḍala;
with "Namaḥ," he should worship the pervasive maṇḍala on the left.
Now, the worship of Vaṭuka and others in the maṇḍala. In the *Śaktiyāmala*:

"One should always worship Vaṭuka at the beginning, having meditated upon him with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings—[him] whose staff is dripping with nectar, who holds a fierce fragment of a skull, and whose mighty staff-like arms are exceedingly fierce."
Fierce, with cheeks adorned by a pair of glorious earrings, the lordly blue youth Vaṭuka, wearing a garland of great serpents— the practitioner,
having meditated upon him preceded by the seed-syllable Oṃkāra, should worship him.
Half-filled with water and joined with a red flower.
By joining the index finger with the thumb, or even the little finger with the thumb,
the practitioner should then cause [the offering] to be given by means of the two thumbs of the left hand.

In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Come, come, O Goddess! [O you] at the end of the word 'putra' (son) and at the end of 'vaṭuka' (the youth), O Lord! O you who shine with a mass of tawny matted locks, O three-eyed one!"
And Jvālāmukha at the very end; with the name of the obstacle [deity] and the word for "lying down" (śayana),
accompanied by all ritual offerings (upacāra) and the dual form of the word,
joined with the wife of fire (svāhā)— this is declared to be the mantra of Vaṭuka.
In the Śaktiyāmala: "Then, having meditated upon the Yoginī, one should worship her in the left mandala.
The Yoginīs take any form at will, are endowed with all qualities, and are intoxicated by the beauty of molten gold."
The lords of the gods— whose necks are adorned with garlands of skeletons, who wear red garments as upper cloths, who hold a trident, a noose, a skull-cup, and a goad,
who are perfectly proportioned and exceedingly serene,

and who bestow the desired fruits upon their devotees and practitioners— the wise one, having meditated upon them and worshipped them with incense and other offerings, [should recite] the syllable *Oṃ*.
Having uttered the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should then worship the Yoginī. The mantra is found in the *Jñānārṇava*:

Whether she resides above the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, in the netherworld (*pātāla*), in fire, or in water;
or wherever she may be situated, whether in a sacred field (*kṣetra*), a seat (*pīṭha*), a secondary seat (*upapīṭha*), or other auspicious places—[there I worship her].
O Vīrendra, when the Goddess is pleased by incense, lamps, and other offerings, and you are seated upon her throne, perform the auspicious rite of bali.
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable *Yām*, followed by *yoginībhyaḥ svāhā*. After the end of all mantras, one should inscribe the word *yoginī*.
Having written the armor (kavaca) and the weapon (astra), one should write the wife of fire (vahnijāyā) again.
O Goddess, by means of this mantra, there shall be an offering for the Yoginīs;
[it is performed] with the right thumb and ring finger, or else with the little finger and the thumb.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *KṢĀṂ*, one should worship Kṣetrapāla:

"I [worship] the illustrious Lord of the Field (*Śrīkṣetranāyaka*), whose hands are adorned with a staff, a skull-bowl, a sword, a trident, and a raised staff; who is as radiant as a mass of dark collyrium, and who is gracious."
I take refuge.
Then, having formed the left fist, make the index finger straight like an arrow.
Or, with the thumb and forefinger, this is considered the mantra for Kṣetrapāla.
As for the mantra, it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"O Dear One, one should write the letter *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels;
or one may write the words 'sthāna', 'kṣetrapāla', followed by 'dhūpa', 'dīpa', and so forth."
Having written "sahitaṃ vālim," one should then write "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa";
O beautiful one, this is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, conjoined with the wife of Vahni (the letter *ra*).
In the Śaktiyāmala: One should worship Gaṇeśāna within the maṇḍala while maintaining this very meditation:
[him] with an elephant’s face, holding in his four hands the noose, the goad, the nectar, and the skull-cup, and adorned with various ornaments.
I perpetually bow down to the glorious Gaṇeśvara, who has a blue body, for whom there is constant celebration, and who is the cause of the destruction of all obstacles.
A wise person, having contracted the fingers of the right hand, should perform a prostration like a staff.
Having placed the middle finger between [the thumb and forefinger], this is considered the offering (bali) to Gaṇeśa.
The mantra is found in the Jñānārṇava:
having extracted the three syllables *gāṃ*, *gīṃ*, and *gūṃ*, one should then write *gaṇapataye* ending in the dative (*ṅe*),
followed by *varadaṃ te*, *varadāya te*, and *sarvajanam āveśaya*.
Having uttered "meva śaṃcānaya," one should take the offering (bali) with two steps;
the mantra for the offering to Gaṇeśa, joined with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), should thus present the bali.

Having meditated upon the universal being (sarvabhūtaka), the practitioner of mantras should offer an oblation (bali) to all beings; within the circle of the gods, he should place the common oblation.
The mantra for that very purpose is as follows:

one should write the word "vartulam" (circle), then "bhuvaneśānīm" (the Mistress of the World), then the phrase "sarvavighnapadam" (the state of all obstacles), then "hṛdam" (the heart), then "tyaśca" (and [the syllable] ty), then "sarvabhūtebhyo hūṃ phaṭ svāhā". One should write these words.
With this sixteen-syllable mantra, the best of practitioners should offer [the oblation] to the sun and to all beings with the mudrā known as Tatva.
The *vali* (offering) is declared to be fivefold, which always provides protection for all;
there is a specific procedure regarding the offering of *vali* with mantras such as those of Vaṭuka and others in the *Kulārṇava*.
O Mistress of the Family, listen as I shall proclaim the Vaṭu-mantra,
by which, when worshipped with this mantra, all calamities are utterly destroyed.
Then the three *tāras*, followed by "Devī," "Putra," and "Vaṭuka," and then "Nāthasya," [addressed to] Kapila, whose mass of matted hair is blazing and tawny.
Then the word "Trinetra," followed by the word "Jvālāmukha," [and then] "Accept this worship and offering"—O Beloved of Fire! [Thus ends the mantra.]
Thus Vaṭuka has been described with forty-four syllables;
when satisfied by the offering of bali, Vaṭuka bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
One should always write "Śāntiṃ kalā tu me," followed by the three *tāra*s (oṃs), and then the word "sarvāyoginībhyaḥ."
After that, [the offering] for all beings, and then for that which dwells at the beginning of all beings;
then the word for the Ḍākinīs, and after that for the Śākinīs.
One should say "trailokyati" and "imā vāsinībhyaḥ";
the mantra of the Yoginī is "pūjāṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa yugaṃ svāhā."
O Mistress of the Kula, this has been declared in fifty-one syllables:
she who is Viyoginī, Raudrā, Saumyā, Ghoratarā, and Parā.
May Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Vyomacārī be ever pleased with me;
one should utter "Tāra" three times for all beings and for oneself as well.
Afterwards, "bhūtapatibhyaḥ hūṃ phaṭ" is said; this consists of seventeen syllables.
The spirits (bhūtas) are of various forms, dwelling in the divine realms, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
Those residing in the depths of Pātāla, purified by Śiva-yoga,
as well as the seven beginning with Dhruva and those beginning with Indra who dwell in heaven;
"O you whose minds are joyful, be satisfied by taking this *bali* offering; then utter the three *tāras* twice, followed by the word for 'Goddess'."
Then [one should say] "putrātha vaṭunāthāya," followed by "paścāducchiṣṭhahāriṇe.
After that, one should utter the word "hūṃ" twice, and then the term "kṣatrapāla."
Afterwards, destroy all obstacles and calamities, and again, the pair;
accompanied by all ritual offerings, one should utter the offering of flesh and the bali.
This mantra of Kṣetrapāla, ending with two Ṭha-s (Ṭhaṭha) and consisting of a pair of syllables (Gṛ), is considered to be sixty-four syllables long; it bestows all spiritual perfections.
And he who dwells in this field, the servant of the field-protector—
may he, pleased by this offering of bali, always grant me protection.
O Goddess, one should utter the three *tāra*s, the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda,
and then the pair *hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ*, followed by *bhairavādhiṣṭhitāya*.
After Akṣobhyānaṃdataḥ, he spoke the word *dhama* again for the sake of the desired accomplishment; then the word *padam*, followed by *varada* and the two syllables *ṭha*.
After that, the word *kṣetrapāla*, and then the word *mahāśāstra*.
After the term "mother" and "son," there should follow the term "son of good family."
Then, for the attainment of the state of a son, [one should worship] the Lord of this Place;
then, the Lord of this Place, and then the Lord of this Region.
After that, the word *meghanāda*; then the word *pracaṇḍogra*;
after *bhīma*, the word *kapālī*; and then the word *bhīṣaṇa*.
O Lord of all obstacles, one should say this for the offering and the bali:
"Accept! Make a pair! Grind the guru into a powder, O pair!"
One should utter *jvala-yugmam* (the pair of *jvala*) and *prajvala-yugmam* (the pair of *prajvala*) to overcome all obstacles; then one should utter *kṣāṃ*, *kṣīṃ*, and thereafter *kṣūm*.
"Kṣetrapālāya vauṣaṭ hūṃ phaṭ tyūtta"—this is the hundred-syllable mantra. With one or the other of these two, one should offer two *bali* offerings to Kṣetrapāla.
Afterwards, one should utter the two *tāra*s (oṃ oṃ) and then [the name] "Amuka Kṣetrapāla."
This worship and offering for the Lord of the Kings of Kings follows from this point onward.
The pair of oblations ending with *dviṭha* is said to consist of twenty-eight;
by this offering of the *bali*, one is accompanied by the host of young students (*vaṭu*).
O God, Lord of the Kings of Kings, be gracious to me at all times!
O Goddess, there is the offering to Vaṭuka in the west and the offering to the Yoginīs in the north.
O Mistress of the Kula, one should first offer the bali-oblation to the spirits in the east, to the Guardian of the Field in the south,
and worship the Lord of the Kings of Kings in the center.
One should offer the bali-offering to Vaṭuka with the thumb and the ring finger;
the bali-offering to the Yoginīs is made with the index, middle, ring, and thumb fingers.
O beloved, the bali offering for Abhūta is made with all the fingers;
however, the bali offering for Kṣetrapāla is prescribed to be made with the thumb and the index finger.

According to the view that the *vali* (sacrificial offering) for Rājarājeśvara is placed between the thumb and the middle finger, the location for the *vali* is distinct [from the central deity], because the *vali* is prescribed for Rājarājeśvara in the center. Thus, there is a traditional practice (*saṃpradāya*) following two methods: in the former system, the worship of the central deity is performed while the *vali* is offered in the four directions; in the latter, the *vali* is placed between the thumb and middle finger. This is the established path.
In this *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his guru, this chapter, titled "Pātāla," concludes with the offering of the *bali*. One should worship the deities of the water.
This has been stated in the *Śāradā*:
The practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should invoke and worship the deities of the mantra within that [image].
The phrase "within that" means within the form fashioned for the purpose of purifying the deity; "having invoked" is the intended meaning.
Having recited the root mantra, the wise one, drawing forth the light from its own place through the path of the suṣumnā, brings it out through the aperture of the brahmarandhra.
Having gathered the Mātṛkā residing in one place and the consciousness within the collection of flowers,
the wise one should, having joined them through the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra), invoke [the deity] by means of the form (mūrti).

In this context, the invocation (*āvāhana*) is preceded by meditation (*dhyāna*) alone. As for that meditation, it should be understood according to each respective ritual manual (*kalpa*). Regarding the method therein, the *Kālikā Purāṇa* states:
"With the index finger of the left hand [joined] with the little finger of the right..."
Likewise, one should place the left thumb upon the right index finger.
One should raise the right thumb and place the fingers of the left hand, starting from the right,
upon the back of the right hand.
Then, with the *pitṛtīrtha* of the left hand— that is, the middle and ring fingers—
one should likewise turn them downward on the right hand.
One should make the palm level like the back of a tortoise with the right hand;
such a "tortoise-hand" bestows all accomplishments.
Thus is the general rule.
For Tripurā, however, it is specifically three-fold; that [procedure] is written in her ritual manual (*kalpa*) in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"One should close both eyes and perform [the rite] near the heart."
The wise should keep the body, head, and neck perfectly straight and motionless.
The practitioner of mantra should commence meditation, which destroys all sins.
As stated in the Kālītantra: "Then, [one should meditate upon] the supreme digit (kalā) flashing within the lotus of the heart."
Having invoked [the deity] into the center of the yantra, one should duly perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa).
In the Kumārī Tantra:
Then, O Maheśvarī, having led [the consciousness] from within the heart-lotus— vibrating and having the form of lightning— along the path of the suṣumnā to the abode of Śiva;
O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion and accompanied by your retinue,
while I worship you, one should then indeed bring [the deity] into the reality of the heart by means of the mantra.
O Goddess, the knower of mantras should [perform this] through the nose with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yaṃ).
And with the mantra "Deveśi," the wise one should invoke the Bindu.
In the Kulārṇava:

O Supreme Goddess, who dwells within the remembrance of me, overflowing with supreme bliss; O Sovereign of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by Your retinue, protect me in this shoreless cycle of worldly existence!
"Remain perfectly steadfast for as long as I shall worship you."
Having invoked the Goddess with this mantra, one whose mind is focused on no other should worship her,
displaying the meditative posture (dhyāna-mudrā) and offering water for honor (arghya), fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth.
For the benefit of practitioners, the conceptualization of forms was devised for Brahman, who is composed of consciousness, immeasurable, devoid of qualities, and the embodied soul.
The Brahmasra is established on a linga, a sacrificial mound (sthandila), an image, or in the first of the recitations;
it is proclaimed as being tenfold when located in a mandala, on a wooden board, on the head, or in the heart.
According to the Gautamīya Tantra:
"The daily worship of Hari should be performed at Śālagrāma, on a gem, in a yantra, in an image, or on an altar; it should not be done solely upon the bare ground."
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "Hope is indeed the heart-cakra of Viṣṇu, born from his field;
it is the yantra and the image in its place, and the constant worship of Hari."

In this regard, for whomever the Śālagrāma discus is indeed the supreme Viṣṇu, for that person alone is there worship [of it]; all others are concordant [with this], being nothing other than yantras. Thus it is said in the Yāmala:
One should worship the Goddess as residing in the *liṅga*, and likewise in a book;
one should worship Mahāmāyā on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), in sandals, and in images.
Or one may worship it painted on a trident, or even situated in water;
[one should worship] a sword measuring fifty finger-breadths, as well as a trident with three prongs.
Among these, the preeminence of the yantra alone is as stated in the Kulārṇava:
"For those who do not know that the deity, whose form is mantra, is pervaded by the yantra..."
O Śāmbhavī, all that has been performed, such as worship and other rites, becomes futile;
for the deity is of the nature of the mantra, and it is the mantra that I have proclaimed.
When that Goddess is worshipped in the yantra, she becomes instantly propitious,
because it restrains all suffering arising from defects such as desire and anger.
That which they call the "machine" (yantra), in that the God truly finds delight,
just as the soul delights in the body and a lamp in its oil, O beloved.
The yantra is likewise proclaimed for all the gods;
therefore, having written the yantra, one should then meditate upon Śiva along with his protective enclosure (āvṛti).
Having first learned this from the mouth of the Guru, O Dear One, one should perform the worship according to the prescribed rite;
for he who performs the worship on a single pedestal without separate [offerings] or without the yantra [is at fault].
O Kuleśānī, even by abandoning the relationship of limb and whole, one incurs the curse of the deity;
on a single pedestal, each of one's own yantras must be kept separately.
One should worship the Goddess, accompanied by her retinue, according to the prescribed rules for the principles (tattva).
Having invoked the primary deity, one should worship another deity.
A practitioner whose mind is fickle incurs a curse from both [the deity and the mantra].
O Dear One, having understood such characteristics from the guru and the scriptures...
One should worship correctly according to the prescribed rite; thus the deity becomes well-pleased.
With the sixteen modes of service, one worships Śiva together with his limbs and his retinue.

One should worship with the root mantra using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings. As stated in the *Kulārṇava*: "O Goddess of the gods, in these places they worship the supreme Śiva."
Having rendered the formless into something possessing form, men become devoted solely to the ritualistic section of the Veda.
Just as the milk of cows flows from the openings of their udders through all their limbs,
so does the omnipresent Lord shine within images and other such forms.
Due to the beauty of the image, especially during worship,
and through the faith of the practitioner, the deity attains presence.
The ghee residing within the bodies of cows does not provide them nourishment;
rather, it is that which is given as their own performed action that nourishes them once again.

By its own term, "ghee" (sarpiḥ) is expressed; its function is that which produces it. Through the churning of its functions and so forth, he who has fashioned the ghee—if he intends to give it—performs the nourishing of cows; such is the meaning.
In this way, the Supreme Lord, residing within all bodies, is like ghee.
And without worship, O Goddess, it does not bestow fruit upon men.
Having made his life-breaths and his sense organs fruitful, one should install and worship the deity; otherwise, it shall be fruitless.
Whatever action one performs apart from the prescribed rules (niyama),
not even the slightest fruit thereof is accomplished for him due to the fault of violating the proper sequence.
Deficient or excessive rituals never bear fruit;
indeed, even minor rites, when performed according to the prescribed rules, do yield results.
The ritual action performed according to that injunction— such as recitation, fire-oblation, and worship—
shall bring delight to the deity and bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

This, however, follows as a secondary point. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): Having united the Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra with Paramaśiva, one should, while remaining in the state of the nectar-licker (*amṛtalolī*), draw forth the Mātṛkā residing there through the left nostril by means of the wind-seed syllable (*vāyu-bīja*).
Then, having assumed a conceptual form and established her within the Brahma-randhra, one should perform the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth.
As stated in the *Śāradā*:
"After performing the stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), the bringing near (*sannidhāna*), and the complete restriction (*sannirodhana*),
one should subsequently perform the ritual of total identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and likewise the veiling (*guṇṭhana*)."

Having made the *amṛta* (nectar) the instrument, one who is composed should perform the supreme transformation (*paramīkṛta*) by means of the *sumudrās*. One should perform these in sequence. Regarding their *mudrās*, as it is said in the *Jñānārṇava*: Īśvara said:
O sinless one, I shall now describe the mudrās for establishing, placing nearby, invoking, and so forth.
One should lower the raised añjali; this becomes the *āvāhanī* (invoking) mudrā. When this same gesture is reversed, it is considered the *sthāpanī* (establishing) mudrā.
The two hands joined together in a double-fist is the mudrā of Sannidhāpanī;
with the thumbs placed inside the fists, it is the mudrā of Sannirodhanī.
When the two index fingers of this very same mudrā are held straight,
it is the Avaguṇṭhana mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
O Goddess, the most excellent practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs of the Goddess using the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra).
This is the sakalīkaraṇa; thereafter follows this Vāmamudrā.
Having crossed the two hands behind, with the index fingers and the pair of middle fingers [joined],
one forms the Vyāptirūpiṇī mudrā.

Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making the deity manifest) as if it were included within the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of installing the vital breath), one should then perform that [mudrā] according to the *Kulārṇava*.
Because of the scriptural statement: "The *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantras and mudrās [are performed] according to the previously mentioned method; the *bhūtaśuddhi* has been described in the *Prastāra*.
O Dear One, having joined the two hands together like an *ārātrika* lamp..."
This mudrā is called "making supreme," and after that [comes the next].
Having crossed the two hands behind [the back], the pair of index fingers and middle fingers,
as well as the pair of little fingers and ring fingers, are joined together with one another.
O Dear One, this is declared to be the Dhenu-mudrā for the purpose of making [the offering] nectar-like (amṛtīkaraṇa).

Having first displayed these common mudrās, thereafter, O Goddess of Devas, one should display the special mudrās with a spirit of devotion. As for the special mudrās, they are the mudrās of their respective weapons and others prescribed by the ritual manuals (kalpa).

That [procedure] is to be understood in the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of that *Kalpa*. Now follows the explanation of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites, as stated in the *Uḍḍīśa*: "Therefore, in the worship of the fully perfected deity, the invocation is said here to be the act of bringing [the deity] face-to-face with due reverence."

For this very reason, O All-pervading Lord, by the mere sight of the *mudrās* such as the vehicle (*vāhana*) and so forth, the wise have described the "establishment" (*niveśana*) everywhere— that is, the placement [of the deity]—
as well as the worship (*pūjā*) and that which is being worshipped, including the bestowal of grace (*anugraha*) and other rites.
The capacity of the agent for this [action] is declared to be its presence (sānnidhya).

Indeed, that presence of the All-pervading Lord which extends as far as the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is designated as "complete withdrawal" (sannirodha) when it is made radiant by men who know the mantras.
Bliss is the foundation, the reality characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
that which pervades all this here should be meditated upon as the veil (Avaguṇṭhana).
In this context, "sarvasakalaśarīre" means in the entire body with all its parts.
The purpose of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the deity] manifest in all its parts) is the inseparable connection with *saccidānanda* (existence-consciousness-bliss).
The purpose of *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) is meditation; for [otherwise], the deity would be perceived as limited and possessed of constituent parts.

Faults arise from the pervasiveness of Brahman, from its being partless, and because rites such as invocation (*āvāhana*) produce faults. Having understood this, one should contemplate the retinue outside the forms of the limbs of that body, thinking, "O Brahmin, may [the deity] become the cause of remembrance. Having done so, and having performed the *paramīkaraṇa* mudrā, one should accept [them].

One should contemplate that the limbs of the body, beginning with the hands, as well as the retinue and the external wheel, have become firmly established by completely forgetting their respective original locations. This concludes the explanation of the purpose and nature of the rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*). Now follows the consideration of the rites beginning with stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*). [The] meaning of the term:

Reflection: Having first determined the name of each respective deity's sādhana according to the guru’s instruction, one employs a verbal form ending in the fifth case (the ablative), derived either from the root *vah*, meaning "to carry," or from the root *pañca*.

In this regard, because the word "āyuṣman" (O long-lived one) is employed [in the vocative], there is only the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*), as established by the traditional teaching through the act of addressing. Therefore, having uttered twice either "āvaha" (bring hither) or "ihāgaccha" (come here), that which is situated at the beginning of the invocation-word is obtained from the prefix; for the root *vah* (to carry/bring), which has the sense of "attaining," is used here without a prefix.

If the purpose were accomplished by a single word, the auxiliary elements would be rendered useless; for it is precisely this that is correct: the instruction of the ritual action is preceded by the utterance of the words, and that [utterance] serves as the manifestor for the performers and the grasper.
The repetition occurs among people in cases of distress, fear, and so forth. This should be understood to apply likewise to the *saṃsthāpana* (concluding rites) and other such acts. Therefore...

One should perform the worship as follows. In the *Śāradā*: "Then the knower of the Tantra should perform the services beginning with 'welcome' (*svāgata*). The meaning is that the Guru, accompanied by his consort, should first perform these two—namely, the welcome and the inquiry concerning the lineage—at the very beginning of all the services. Here, "this seat" refers to the seat for the eternal Ananta; these are the constant services.
Or the libation (tarpaṇa). The authoritative measure for this is written immediately below. The ritual services (upacāra) are as stated in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra:
"The seat, the vehicle, the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and then the water for sipping (ācamana)."
Or bathing with its full ritual accessories, and all kinds of ornaments.
Incense, flowers, as well as incense smoke, lamps, and garlands; following that, unguents after the garlands, prostrations, and the dismissal.
The practitioner of mantras should perform the worship with the eighteen types of offerings:
water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping, bathing, clothing, and ornaments.
Then [one offers] perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and water for rinsing the mouth;
followed by betel nut, worship, hymns of praise, the offering of water for satisfaction (tarpaya), and prostration.
One should employ the sixteen-fold excellent ritual service for worship.
Now, the classification of the sixteen-fold service is given in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, an offering of honor,
water for sipping, the honey-mixture, another sipping of water, and then fragrance and flowers.
Incense, lamps, food offerings, bathing, sipping water for purification,
ornaments, fragrant scents, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostration.
One should employ the sixteen modes of service worthy of worship:
the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), the food offering (naivedya), and likewise the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), the sipping of water (ācamana), fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings— these are known as the eight modes of service (aṣṭopacāra).
The five-fold worship consists of various perfumes and so forth offered in abundance.
Now, regarding the sixty-four modes of service, it is stated in the Kalpasūtra:

In the Vaiṇava [tradition], one should perform the sixty-four services (*catuḥ-ṣaṣṭy-upacāra*) with the *mācāhya* [mantra]. The service mantras should be performed ending in "I prepare; obeisance" (*kalpayāmi namaḥ*), such as:

1. "I prepare the water for the feet; obeisance" (*pādyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*); 2. "I prepare the respectful offering; obeisance" (*arghyaṃ kalpayāmi namaḥ*); and so on in sequence: 3. the seat (*āsana*); 4. the lamp (*āloka*); 5. fragrant oil for the limbs (*sugandhi-tailābhyaṅga*); 6. bathing (*majjana*).

1. Entry into the pavilion; 2. Seating upon the throne in the bathing pavilion; 3. Divine bathing materials; 4. Rubbing with unguents; 5. Bathing with warm water; 6. Consecration with the waters of all sacred fords poured from golden jars;
7. Wiping with a yellow cloth; 8. Donning a lower garment of reddish-yellow silk; 9. A yellow silk upper garment.
Entering the self-maṇḍala; entering the self-pavilion and the jewel-throne; prostration;
[anointing] with camphor, saffron, musk, kastūrī, gorocana, and divine fragrances over the entire body.

16. Anointing with unguents; 17. Incensing the mass of hair with black aloe-wood; 18. Adorning with garlands of jasmine, *mālatī*, jasmine, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *śatapatra*, *pūtigaṃdhahara*, white water-lily, and preeminent *punnāga* flowers; 19. Entering the pavilion of ornaments; 20. [Wearing] golden ornaments.

Seating upon a jeweled throne in a variegated pavilion (20), the forehead and crown (21), the crescent moon (22), glorious vermilion (23), the jewel-tilaka (24), the single-strand necklace (25), the pair of ear-lobes (26),
the pair of jeweled earrings (27), the nose-ornament (28), the lac-dye on the lower lip (29), and the ornamentation of the teeth (30).
31. Golden variegated sandals; 32. A great foot-ornament; 33. A string of pearls; 34. A divine canopy; 35.

Four pairs of armlets; 36. A series of bracelets; 37. A series of finger-rings; 38. A girdle and waist-cord; 39. An ornament for auspiciousness; 40. Foot-ornaments consisting of golden gems and anklets. 42.
A toe-ring on the foot; 43 a noose in one hand, 44 a goad in another hand, 45 a sugarcane bow in yet another hand, 46 flower-arrows in another hand; 47 glorious ruby sandals;
48 well-adorned with ornaments and accompanied by deities; 49 the mounting of the great chariot (mahācakra) [by] Kāmeśvarī.
51. A couch of jewels; 52. A vessel of nectar; 53.
A betel-roll with camphor; 54. Joyful, radiant, playful laughter; 55. An auspicious night-lamp; 56. A white parasol; 57. A pair of chowries; 58. A mirror; 59. A palm-leaf fan; 60. Fragrance.
"One should not perform the sixty-four services [ending with] flowers (61), incense (62), lamp (63), and food offering (64).

Thus it is stated in the *Kuloḍḍīśa*: "Among all the services, whatever may be difficult to obtain, one should meditate upon all that mentally and offer it as a 'flower-field' [of mental visualization]. In each instance, one should offer water between the various services."

In the context of the "offering of service" (*upacāradāna*), "immediately following" (*antarā*) means "without interval. After the offering of service, there is the offering of water; however, the water intended for the act of renunciation (*tyāga*) must be contained within three vessels (*tripātra*). As stated in the *Svatantra*: "Whatever has been prepared by others [is offered] while remaining in the *argha* vessel."
The Great Goddess does not accept it to be given, even by means of hundreds of ritual procedures.

However, some maintain that after giving water for each respective offering, there is a dismissal with the water from the *arghya* vessel; this should be considered. The ritual action for the deity is always beneficial. Now follows the detailed explanation of the presentation of the services (*upacāra*):
one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the lotus-feet of the Lord with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
This has been proclaimed with water from āṃmāka, durvā, and viṣṇukrāntā.
Then, by means of one's own nature (*svadhātman*), one should place the *madhuparka* into the lotus-face [of the deity].
Now follows the explanation of the *madhuparka* according to the *Kuloḍḍīśa*.
Having prepared the madhuparka consisting of honey, sugar, clarified butter, curd, and alkali, one should offer it according to the prescribed ritual.
Honey in greater quantity than all other ingredients, curd, ghee, and sugar in equal measure,
and water more than all else— this is declared to be the *madhuparka*.
And in the *Svatantra*:
"The knower of mantras should offer water for the feet at the feet with the mantra ending in 'namas';
O Goddess of Gods, he should offer the *arghya* upon the head with the *śiras-mantra*."
One should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) into the mouth with the mantra "madhupayas svadhā";
one should offer the bath and the fragrance with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), and likewise offer flowers with the mantra "vauṣaṭ."
p.

89b) Then, saying "I offer," one should give everything, O Maheśvarī. Some recite the mantra as *svadhā* with the letter *u* in the middle (*svadhūkāra*); however, that is contrary to the *Svatantra-tantra*. [One should place] the *madhuparka* in the mouth.

The preceptor should offer water with the mantra; and in the *Jāmalam*: "With the *vāruṇa* seed-syllable, one should offer the *madhuparka* into the lotus of the mouth. By this, it is meant that [he offers it] with the *svadhā* mantra, which is the *vāruṇa* seed-syllable. With that very same mantra, he should perform the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping); by "with that very same mantra," it is meant [he uses] the *madhuparka* mantra itself.
One should cause him to bathe with fragrant waters, and having put on two garments,
one should give him a sacred thread, necklaces, and other ornaments.

Scent has already been described; it should be offered according to one's qualification, distinguished as divine (*divya*), heroic (*vīra*), or animal (*paśu*). Now follows the exposition of flowers. In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"The gods are pleased by flowers, and the gods reside within flowers."
And all the excellent flowers are always known to possess the essence of nectar.
What is the use of saying more? The flower is called *mallikā*;
the supreme light resides within the flower, and it is pleased by the flower alone.
The flower is the means for accomplishing the three goals of life (trivarga), the source of prosperity, and the vessel for heaven;
Brahmā resides in the root of the flower, while Keśava resides in its center.
Mahādeva resides at the tip of the flower, and all the gods reside upon its petals;
therefore, a person endowed with devotion should always worship the gods with flowers.
"Uktimatallikā" means an excellent statement; as it is said in the *Śāradā*:

"The two types of lotus, the two types of oleander, the two types of water-lily, the two types of *tulasī*, the two types of jasmine, the two types of *ketakī*, the white water-lily, and the *campaka* and blue lotus."
The jasmine, mandāra, punnāga, paṭalī, agastya, and campaka; the āragvadha, karṇikā, pāraṃta, and the nine varieties of mallikā.
The *dhustūra*, *sarjaka*, *bilva*, *arjuna*, and *muniputraka*,
as well as other fragrant flowers and leaves, [are offered] by the preceptors.
The wise one should accept those [flowers] that have been offered at the conclusion of the worship; as stated in the Muṇḍamālā:
"One should likewise offer flowers that are red, yellow, and white."
O beloved, [the flowers] are white, red, the javā flower, and likewise the karavīra.
Tagara, mallikā, jasmine (jātī), yūthikā, and likewise mālatī;
dhustūra, aśoka, bakula, and the white and black aparājitā.
Vakapuṣpa, bilvapatra, campaka, nāgakeśara, mallikā, giṇṭikā, kāñcī, and that which is proclaimed as red— these are [the flowers].
Arka flowers, barley, Varvara flowers, and Priyaṅgu are dear to the Earth; on the eighth lunar day, Pārvatī especially becomes pleased.
All the deities are satisfied by means of a red lotus flower.
Whether she be black or white, Kālikā shall be the bestower of boons.
Pārvatī was satisfied by *śmaśāna-īdhustura* flowers; the supreme Dhūmāvatī was satisfied by various wild flowers;
and the goddess Pārvatī was satisfied by the flower and the leaf of the *āmalaka*.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should worship with various kinds of flowers.

One should spend the remainder of the night in a cremation ground on a Saturday or Tuesday at night. In the *Matsyasūkta*: "O Mistress of the Kula, one should worship with fragrant flowers that are white or red, with bilva and maruvaka and other auspicious flowers, while avoiding *tulasī*."
Especially when mixed with *udra* flowers and *vajra* flowers.
And one should offer all flowers with a mind endowed with devotion. (From the Kālikāpurāṇa, p.
The *kokanada*, the *padma*, the barley-flower (*yava*), and the *avadhūka*—
among all varieties of flowers, the red lotus (*raktapadma*) is preeminent.
In the *Kriyāsāra*: "For the goddesses, the arka and mandāra; for Āditya, likewise the etaga;
and for Gaṇeśa and Sūrya, the red flower is exceedingly dear."
Now, regarding those that are prohibited, as stated in the *Śāradā*:
"The Guru should discard that which is soiled, touched by the ground, defiled by worms, grass, and the like,
touched by a limb [of his own], smelled, or stale."
And in the *Kriyāsāra*:
"One should not worship the Goddess with buds, nor should one offer fruit that is overripe or pierced;
even fruit that is naturally ripe should be rejected if it has been kept for too long."
One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains, nor Gaṇeśa with Tulasī;
one should not worship Caṇḍī with Dūrvā grass, nor Vināyaka without Bilva leaves.
The wise should always avoid the *unmattā*, the *markaṭapuṣpa*, and the *viṣṇukrāntā*.
In the *Gautamīya*: "One should never take red sandalwood or red flowers."
One should not worship the Son of Devakī with bilva leaves or its flowers.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with white leaves, flowers,
or fruits that have been brought after bathing, or those that are stale, or those that are black in color.
One should avoid a *vṛhatī* flower that has blossomed on its own, as well as one that has fallen to the ground by itself;
one should especially avoid a flower that lacks fragrance.
One should never worship with flowers lacking three petals;
one must avoid the kuruṇṭaka, the pāṭalī, and the śirīṣa.
Thus for Viṣṇu.
One should avoid flowers from the earth, except for the *sephālī* and the *vakula*. This is the general rule. A wise person should not offer [flowers] covered with garments to Śivā.
Likewise, buds should be discarded, except for those of the *padmaka* and *campaka*.
One should not worship Viṣṇu with dry leaves, flowers, or fruits;
nor with those brought after bathing, nor with stale offerings, nor with black-colored items, nor with those obtained by begging.
One should avoid the *vṛhatī* flower, especially one that has blossomed on its own and fallen to the ground by itself, as well as any flower that lacks fragrance.
One should never worship with flowers that have fewer than three petals;
one should strictly avoid the kumuda, the pāṭali, and the śirīṣa.
Thus, it is Viṣṇu alone [who is the recipient]. One should avoid flowers that have fallen on the ground, with the exception of those from the śephālī,
the vakula, the bilva, the khadira, and likewise the dhātrī fruit.
The Tamāla and the lotus are defiled by being cut or broken;
likewise, the Kunda, the Bhavanti, the Yūthī, the Bandhūka, and the Ketaka are defiled when offered to Śiva.
One should avoid red lotuses at the three junctions of the day, as well as both *mālatī* and *ketakī*, fried grain, white water-lilies, and the red *hayāri*.
In the *Puṣpamālā*: "The *guñjā*, *parājita*, *unmatta*, along with *varāhakrāntā* and this *āmratika* flower—
these are forbidden in the worship of the Sun."
The sunflower, tagara, kaṭikāraka,
mandāra, arka, dhattūra, śālmalī, kāñcana, and juna are prohibited and prescribed [according to the occasion].
The flower of the *vaibhītaka* tree is prohibited for the worship of Viṣṇu; likewise, the *śirīṣa* and the *śakrapuṇḍraka* are both forbidden and yet prescribed [for other purposes].
Regarding the distinction between what is prohibited and what is prescribed: in the absence of these [specified flowers], this is prescribed; when those prescribed are available, this is prohibited.
In the worship of Narasiṃha, the two types of *ketakī* are prohibited. Apart from those mentioned, red flowers are not recommended, nor are those originating from trees that are white or thorny.
Of Viṣṇu: [Flowers] that are odorless, stale, from the Kokaṭa region, or infested by insects are to be avoided; however, those honored by all the gods are acceptable everywhere.
[These include: śirīṣa, bandhūka, vibhītaka, madantikā, ketakī, and puṇḍraka.

O Śivā, the flower of the kunda tree is highly praised; it should be red like the karañja, sājāṃdra, or mahīruha flowers. It should be washed in water within [the vessel] and offered by oneself, even if it has withered on the ground or is slightly fallen. All these flowers are suitable for the ritual worship of all the gods and serve many purposes; however, O Goddess Durgā, the mandāra and arka flowers are not [recommended] for your worship.
The *droṇa* flower is not recommended for the worship of Kamalā (Lakṣmī);
nor indeed is Lakṣmī worshipped with lotuses, nor Śambhu with conch-water.

They recite that a flower requested [from someone] is fruitless, and one purchased for a price is likewise without merit. Even when prescribed [for an offering], they say that an oily substance (satyājya) is impure. "Paryuṣita" means prepared on the previous day; this refers to anything other than *tulasī* and similar [sacred substances]. As the *Smṛti* states:
For tulasī, agastya, and bilva, there is no such thing as being stale;
even for vaka, it does not become stale until six months have passed.
Withheld is stale flower; withheld is stagnant water.
Not withheld is the water of the Ganges; not withheld is a leaf of Tulasī.
"Worship devoid of Tulasī shall not yield the fruit of worship.
And in the Kālītantra:
"Not even with various offerings, oblations, or charming flowers..."
With auspicious Apāmārga leaves and Bhṛṅga flowers, excluding Tulasī.

They should always be worshipped and fed by men for the swift attainment of results—this refers to the *divya* and *vīra* states when [the worship] is devoid of *tulasī*. As for that which is stated in the *Kolāvalī*: "Worship devoid of *tulasī* is not true worship and shall yield no fruit"—this pertains to the *paśu* state.
Even therein, there is a specific distinction: for Bhairavī, Sundarī, Kālā, Brahmā, Vighna (Gaṇeśa), and Vivasvat, worship devoid of *tulasī* [is permissible].

That worship would become fruitless. For this very reason, there is a statement in the *Yāmala*: "The beautiful goddess becomes enraged by the mere scent of *tulasī*. Here, even the offering of prohibited items is heard of. In the *Kriyāsāra*, it is stated: "She is always to be worshipped with all flowers, both those prescribed and those not prescribed."
Devotion to all the gods must be practiced; in this matter, the yoga of devotion is the cause.
Worship of the Goddess is always auspicious, whether performed with water-born or land-born offerings.
Whether by means of prescribed or prohibited [substances], with a mind endowed with devotion. Now follows the exposition of giving (*dāna*).
In the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
"Whether it be a flower or a leaf, everything is most excellent when offered face-down."
That which causes suffering has been fully explained; likewise, the means of its appeasement as it arises has been taught.
A fruit facing downwards is most excellent; in the rite of offering handfuls of flowers, it should be bent down.
As stated in the Mālinī Tantra:
"One should worship the Supreme Goddess with flowers, or in the absence of flowers, with leaves."
But for those who do not know the mantras, there are trees and shrubs [to serve as] bonds.
But if one does not obtain those [specific] substances, one should worship with their fruit;
or else with unbroken grains (akṣata) or water, and in the absence of even those, with mustard seeds.
If one does not obtain these [materials], one should perform mental worship. Now follows the description of incense (*dhūpa*). In the *Śāradā*:
"That [incense] consists of guggulu, agallochum, *śīra*, sugar, honey, and sandalwood."
O Goddess, one should fumigate the four corners with incense mixed with clarified butter.
In the Kuloḍḍīśa [Tantra]: Guggulu, śarala, dārupatra, that which originates from Malaya,
hrīvera, agaru, kuṣṭha, jaggery, and the essence of all juices.
Harītakī, nakha, lākṣā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and śailaja—
this sixteen-ingredient incense (ṣoḍaśāṅgī vidūdhūpa) is for use in rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
Alternatively, [one may offer] camphor and sandalwood together with guggulu,
as well as honey, clarified butter, jaṭāmāṃsī, śailaja, and saffron.
These ingredients should be mixed together to prepare this incense, which is dear to Pārvatī.
In case of inability, however, one should burn guggulu. According to the *Kriyāsāra*:
"Having sprinkled the incense vessel with the mantra and worshipped it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*)."
While sounding a bell consecrated with the Astra-mantra, one should burn guggulu incense.
And in the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra]:
"Then, having uttered the mantra 'Jagaddhvani mātaḥ svāhā' and having performed worship while ringing the bell, one should present incense and lamps."

In the *Svatantra*: "Then one should offer incense and ring the bell as musical accompaniment. Regarding the two-fold mantra for the bell here, there is an option according to one's preference. Now follows the explanation of the lamp, as stated in the *Śāradā*:
"With a wick containing camphor, or with clarified butter, or even with water..."
Having placed them there, one should display lamps that are fragrant and burn steadily.
In the Uḍḍīśa: "The first lamp is with ghee; those produced from sesame oil, mustard oil, oil from fruits, castor oil, or that arising from lotuses."
The seven radiant [flames] are proclaimed as Dadhida, Ambuja, and the others;
the wick should be made of lotus fiber or else of darbha grass.
Wicks for the purpose of lamps are always remembered as being of five kinds: those made from *śāla* wood, those from *badarī*, those from *phalaka*, and those originating from *uṣa*.
A lamp-vessel made of bell-metal, copper, iron, clay,
or coconut-shell, or even one produced from grass or grain, is recommended.
In this manner, one should prepare a lamp, which is the cause for the beautification of the eyes;
however, until the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should arrange the lamp with its flame facing downwards.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "It should not produce a roaring sound, it should be well-kindled, situated far from anything that obstructs it,
devoid of the sound of flames, smokeless, and not too short."
On the right, the lamp-constellation is the lamp that increases prosperity;
it is placed upon its own circular cloth in a vessel that is beautiful to behold.
One should diligently offer a lamp at the peak of the Sūśrāya-vikṣaka,
using a wick containing camphor and either clarified butter or sesame oil.
If a lamp is obtained that gives off heat when its wick is dipped to four finger-breadths, it is not known as a true lamp; rather, it is remembered as an increase in sin.
A lamp should be placed on a tree, but never on the ground;
all [the gods] are Sahas and Sumati, yet these two do not tolerate this.
One should avoid kicking the lamp and likewise causing it heat;
one should offer salutations to the lamp and provide ghee and other oils as fuel for it.
Having mixed these together with oil, one who wears them goes to hell;
whether they be made from lotus fibers or from darbha grass.
Whether made of *śāla* wood, or from the *vadarī*, or even produced from the shell of a fruit—
five or ten types of wicks are prescribed for the purpose of lighting lamps.
It should be made of cotton, produced from threads, or of silk derived from fruit;
it may be made of *śāla* grass, cotton, or even worn-out, soiled cloth.
One should never give away a lamp that has been used for the purpose of a wick,
nor should one ever extinguish a lamp prepared for the sake of the gods.
One who steals a lamp shall become blind, and one who extinguishes it shall become deaf.
Now, there are six types of collyrium: *añjana*, *sauvīra*, *yāmuna*, *nakhya*, *māyūra*, and *śrīkara*; as well as *darvikā* and *meghalīlā*.
Having ground them, one should cast these [substances] upon a whetstone or into fire.
O son, one should offer [these] to all the gods and goddesses as well;
the five types of collyrium, such as *sauvīra* and others, should be offered ground into the form of a paste (*prastara*), and he speaks of the collyrium for the ladle (*darvikā*).
When fire has been cast into copper or other vessels containing ghee, oil, and so forth, whatever collyrium (añjana) is produced therein is called *darvikā*;
one should prepare this *vidhavā-añjana*, which is unsurpassed for the Great Goddess (*Mahādevī*).
The practitioner should not apply eye-salve in an earthen vessel.
Now, the description of the food offering (naivedya). In the *Śāradā*:
"The practitioner of mantras should present the ten-fold pure, delicious milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar, combined with plantains and ghee."
In the Matsyasūkta:
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), combined with sugar and jaggery;
one should present cow’s products such as honey and milk in the mouth, as well as other offerings.
The knower of mantras should diligently offer śāla fish, pāṭhīna fish, and the most excellent meat of the iguana, along with food mixed with honey.

One should repeatedly offer to the Goddess as an oblation (naivedya) that which is prepared independently— such as food cooked in a vessel, cooked in oil, cooked in ghee, or mixed with milk-rice (pāyasa)— and whatever is pleasing to the mind.
In the Kumārī-kalpa: betel leaf with camphor, coconut with sugar,
milk-rice, ghee, and likewise ginger with jaggery.
He [offered] rice, sesame seeds, curd, sour gruel, sugar,
as well as citron, jackfruit, and the āmrātaka fruit.
O Goddess, [offer] plantain, timiḍī, and the excellent śrīphala fruit;
food mixed with honey, the flesh of birds, and that of the boar; as well as karañja, vakula, tāla, and kharjūra.
And other fragrant and delicious fruits; as stated in the Muṇḍamālā:
"The Śāla fish, the Pāṭhīna, the Sa-kula, the Iṅgaja, the Madgura, and the Elviṣa."
One should offer buffalo meat,
as well as the meat of birds, boar, and various kinds of game;
likewise, black goat, "great meat" (mahāmāṃsa), iguana, and deer.
Water-born fish meat, the most excellent gaṇḍakī fish,
various side dishes, milks, and many other condiments.
In the Kulāmṛta-saṃhitā:
"With a mind full of supreme bliss, one should offer sweet substances;
one should satisfy [the deities] with sweet, nectar-like substances mixed with honey."
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with nectar and nectar-like substances;
thereafter, one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) with cow’s milk in the consecrated fire.
The vessels, such as those made of copper, should be washed with the Astra-mantra;
then, rice grains produced from the Śāli variety should be consecrated with the Mūla-mantra.
Having cast [the oblation] with fifteen [verses] that have been produced, while recollecting the weapon-mantra,
one should cover the face of the vessel and wash it with the *śruva* ladle.
Facing east, the eminent practitioner should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra;
then, having visualized it, he should offer the sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) there with the tip of the sruk-ladle.
The Guru should consecrate that vessel with the root mantra and protect it with the armor mantra (kavaca),
having drawn the mandala with kusha grass according to the ritual rules using the weapon mantra (astra-mantra).
Having divided that [offering] into three portions, one should assign one part to the deity;
another he should offer into the fire, and the other, the most excellent portion, [he should consume].

Thus has the *caruka* been described, as well as its procedure for the *ārātrikā* rite. Here, it should be understood that all things contrary to the Vedas, those belonging to the animal state (*paśubhāva*), the fire-rituals (*agnika*), and those pertaining to the Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, and other [sects] which are opposed [to this path], are surpassed by the divine and heroic (*divyavīra*) states. Now follows the description of the vessel for the food offering (*naivedya*). In the *Rudrajāmala*:
Furthermore, the book may be placed in vessels made of precious gems, or likewise in those of gold,
silver, copper, or even upon a lotus leaf.

A wise person should prepare the food offering (naivedya) either on a plate made of sacrificial wood or, in the absence of all such materials, on a vessel of stone provided it has not been handled by hand. Having placed it in a suitable arghya-vessel, one should present it. Now, the placement for the water for the feet (pādya) and the other offerings is as previously described.
The procedure for perfumes and other offerings is now stated. As it is said in the Rudrayāmala:
"One should present perfume, flowers, and ornaments in the area directly in front [of the deity]."
One should fashion the head of the deity, equal [in size] and adorned with flowers.
Thus, according to the statement of Śāradā mentioned in that context: "Or [the incense] facing forward is for the purpose of concealment. However, the incense and the fire should be on the left;
the lamp should be given on the right, in front, but not on the left."
The food offering (naivedya) should be placed to the right, to the left, or in front, but never behind.
One should not place the incense on the ground; it should be set upon a seat or held in the hand.
The mantra-practitioner should display a ghee lamp on the right and its source on his own left,
as well as a most beautiful garland of lamps.

The ritual procedure for the *ārātrika* (luminous waving) is written in the *Sundarī-prastāra*. Now follows the description of the food offering (*naivedya*) and the giving of gifts (*dāna*). In the *Yāmala*:
"One should draw a mandala either to the south, in front, or to the left."
One should indicate the triangle, the circle of the earth, and the sphere of the earth, and one should destroy the power.
Having placed the food offering (naivedya) there, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the Astra-mantra;
then, having offered a flower, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should recite the mantra seven times.
Having recited the verses beginning with "hemapātre gatā," the supreme practitioner should then offer a mouthful of water and other offerings, and display the five mudrās.
Regarding "a mouthful (*culluka*) and so forth":

one should offer [the water] at the beginning and at the end with the two mantras, "Thou art the under-layer of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and "Thou art the covering of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*).
The under-layer (*upastaraṇa*) is offered at the end of the mantra of presentation. This occurs immediately after the display of the five mudrās.

Regarding the term *āpadhāna*: then, having offered this *naivedya* to such-and-such deity by pouring water from the *argha* vessel [with the words], "I offer this *naivedya* to such-and-such deity," one should give a mouthful of water (*jalagaṇḍūṣa*) and so forth.
As it is said in the *Tattvānandataraṅgiṇī*:
Having taken pure substance well-perfumed by whom,
the mantra-practitioner, with his right hand and the mudrā called grāsa, [should take] the pure [substance].
The practitioner should always offer [the oblation] to Mahādevī within the circle of the nectar of the face, or he should place it on her left side facing her.
In this very manner, having taken up the vow, one should offer what is appropriate;
then, endowed with the mudrās, one should present it and pay homage with a concentrated mind.
O Supreme Goddess, pure, identical with the essence of all things, and overflowing with the bliss of supreme savor; protect me in this boundless cycle of worldly existence.
Then, the wise one should offer to the Goddess, in due order, foods to be chewed, sucked, and so forth;
having offered according to the rule, he should display the *prāṇa-mudrā*.
The *prāṇa-mudrā* is proclaimed [to be formed] by joining the thumbs with the little fingers;
those of the *apāna* are proclaimed [to be formed] by the thumbs, middle fingers, and index fingers.
The deer-seal (mṛgamudrā) belongs to the vyāna-vāyu; from that, it becomes the [seal] of Rudraṇī. It is joined with the little finger and all [the other fingers] in an equal manner.
Displaying the five mudrās, one should meditate upon them as being like the five vital winds;
one should form the left thumb and fingers so that they are open and resemble a cluster of petals.
The wise who are knowers of the tantras have declared this to be the *grāsamudrā*;
it is called "offering" (*nivedana*), and such an offering (*naivedya*) is unsurpassed.
In the *Yāmala*: "One should offer all the ritual implements and so forth with the root mantra;
if one is unable, one should give them mentally, so that this rite is not omitted."
One should offer a handful of water according to the rule and display the five mudrās;
having offered another handful of water again, one should present excellent betel.
Combined with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and other ingredients,
it is honored with portions of *tāla* leaves, camphor, and betel nut.
And according to the *Kramadīpikā*:
"One should display the village-mudrā with the left hand, resembling a blue lotus,
and with the right hand, one should display the breaths and so forth."
One should touch the little fingers with the little fingers, and the thumbs with the tips [of the fingers]; this is the first mudrā.
Likewise, the index fingers may be joined with the ring fingers, or the middle fingers with the ring fingers, or the ring fingers with the index fingers.
The middle finger should be that [fourth], and those [other fingers] are the little fingers; they are established as the *padī* (feet) in the principles (*tattva*s).

These are the *mudrā*s of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* etc.), released by their own mantras. Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna are released in sequence through the fourth [state]. These are the mental states (*manas*) of non-awakening, awakening, pierced, ignited, blackened, and burnt. Herein—
