The rinsing of the mouth with water and so forth has been described previously. The first sipping of water is performed with the mantra: *amṛtopastaraṇam asi*. The second is performed with: *amṛtapidhānam asi*. Thereafter, one should display the *grāha-mudrā*.
Reciting *oṃ prāṇāya svāhā* and so forth, one should display the *prāṇa-mudrā* and the others. Now, [the procedure continues].

Praise of the Naivedya (Food Offering). In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "Even one who speaks with devotion, 'May I offer the naivedya,' shall attain the state of a Kāmāvatāra and rejoice here in my world. This [offering], however, is common to both divine and heroic [deities].

But as for the animal [victim], it is contrary to the Vedas; therefore, having abandoned that, one should offer other naivedya. Now follows the ritual of the renunciation of the offerings (*upacāra-utsarga*).

"In the *Svatantra*, [it is said]: 'O Goddess, one should offer the services with the two mudrās of Kaulinī. This was explained in the context of the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, the procedure for offering the services (*upacāra-arpaṇa-prayoga*): as stated in the *Mālinītantra*: 'One should employ "namas" at the beginning of all the services, ending with the case-ending. Here, "namas" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); therefore, wherever..."

Having uttered the mantra beginning with "yaṃtro vihitaḥ samaḥ svāhā" and so forth—consisting of the name of the offering in the nominative case followed by the word "namaḥ" at the end—one should offer the utterance. Thus, it becomes "etad pādyaṃ namaḥ," "arghyaṃ svāhā," and so on. According to the *Kalpasūtra*, the word "kalpayāmi" is stated before "namaḥ. Next, [one should perform] the ritual gesture (*mudrā*) for the offering.
As stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"One should extend the hands in the *dhauta* [position] and apply them to the region of the heart;
the fingers should be relaxed, and the two thumbs should be placed in their proper order in the middle."
The lotus mudrā is prescribed for the arrangement of the seats of the deities;
the meaning is that one should say, "May this seat be spread."
The fingers should be known as slightly bent, supporting the joined thumb;
the little finger and the index finger of both hands should be curved and their tips brought together.

One should form the middle and ring fingers; this is the *āsana-mudrā*. The meaning is that in rituals such as the sixty-four offerings (*catuḥṣaṣṭhy-upacāra*), where the offering of a seat occurs, this is the mudrā used therein.
The right hand has its fingers slightly bent, with the thumb tucked into the hollow of the wrist.
In the *svastika* posture, the middle fingers form the *mudrā*, with the other fingers resting at the base.
These two should be employed by the wise one during ritual service and in the act of beholding;
when those two hands are extended, they are proclaimed as the *pādya* mudrā.
The two hands marked with the *svasti* [auspicious] gesture are proclaimed as the *mudrā* of the *arghya*;
[in this gesture], the index finger is at the base of the thumb, and the little finger is below the right [hand].
The three middle fingers extended are proclaimed as the mudrās on the left;
when the ring finger and thumb are joined, the other three are likewise proclaimed.
The mudrā of the madhuparka, as described by those learned in the tantras,
consists of the fingers released from the fist, with the tips of the thumbs facing downward.
The middle finger and the thumb joined together, with the other three fingers extended—
this is declared to be the *vastra* [mudrā], which increases the merit of the gift of clothing.
The little finger and the thumb joined together— these three [positions] are proclaimed as mudrās. This is called the *yajñopavīta* mudrā by the most excellent knowers of the tantras.

The *madhuparka* is known as the *samuttānā*; the one that forms the ornaments is considered the *mudrālaṃkārakāriṇī*. That which is released by the index finger is celebrated as the *svastigaṃdha-mudrā*.
The middle finger raised with the thumb joined by the index finger, facing downwards,
is declared to be the Puṣpa-mudrā (Flower Mudrā), which increases the merit of offering flowers.
The thumb and index finger joined, with the other three fingers contracted—
this is the mudrā for offering incense, which brings satisfaction to the gods.
The *uttānāpauṣpikī* mudrā is celebrated as the *dīpa-mudrā* (lamp mudrā) if it is formed by joining the five fingers tightly together and raising them with the palms facing downward.
This mudrā, formed by joining the three [fingers] together, is proclaimed as that for the food offering (naivedya).
One should rotate the two hands with their palms joined and the fingers raised.
One should display the mudrā known as *sphoṭikā* for the act of prostration; alternatively, one may display these mudrās in sequence for the offerings of fragrance and so forth.
The mudrā formed by joining the little finger and the thumb is proclaimed as the Gandhamudrā;
for the flower, it is joined with the index finger, and for the incense, with the forefinger.
The middle finger is proclaimed for the lamp, and the forefinger for the food offering (naivedya); through the joining of these other fingers, the five mudrās are proclaimed.
Whatever rite is performed with the *mudrā*, that alone shall become fruitful.
Now, regarding the offering of perfumes and so forth: the *grahaṇa-mudrā*. In the *Sāṃbhava-saṃhitā*:
"O Pārvatī, [it is formed] with the middle and ring fingers and the tip of the thumb."
And the preceptor should offer pure fragrance with the root mantra.
With the thumb and forefinger, one should offer flowers upon the wheel;
O Goddess, as with the scent, so should the wise one present incense.
The preceptor, using the middle and ring fingers, [should place it] upon the middle joint.
O Goddess of gods, having grasped the lamp with the tip of the thumb, one should present it.
Having performed the lifting three times through the root-yoga of the Gāyatrī,
O Goddess, one should present the food offering with that Sāṃkhya-mudrā.
Having offered water for sipping with the root mantra, one should present betel-leaf;

the meaning is that these two constitute the "limb-offering" (*aṅga-naivedya*). Thus, having worshipped the Root Goddess according to the prescribed rites, one should satisfy her. This is stated in the *Somabhujagāvalī*:

Then, the wise practitioner should offer libations three times with the root mantra. "Then" means immediately after the worship. Thereafter, one should worship the retinue. As it is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*: "One should worship the enclosures, beginning with the limbs (*aṅga*) and ending with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). In the *Rudrayāmala*: "Now, one should worship according to the procedure declared in the ritual manual."
The supreme practitioner, having invoked the Supreme Goddess within the shade of this wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru),
together with the moon and the rows of serpents,
and having received the command of the Great Goddess, should worship her retinue.
The first [mantra] is with six limbs, while the second is with the teachers of the Kalpa.
The third [layer] consists of the attendants, the fourth of the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the fifth is said to consist of their weapons; such is the general sequence.

Specifically, however, that [procedure] should be understood according to each respective kalpa. Regarding the six-limbed deities (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*): by the term "six limbs," the heart, head, and so forth are designated as the six limbs;
the deities presiding over these are the *ṣaḍaṅgadevatās*. Their names are as follows, according to the *Mālinītantra*: "Now, omniscience, contentment, primordial awakening..."
Svatantratā, Anyā, Nityā, Asyāsyā, Dū, and Luptaśakti—
these indeed are proclaimed by name as the deities of the six limbs.
The principal female forms are white like frost, crystal, dark, black, blue, and reddish-brown; they hold the gestures of granting boons and dispelling fear.
As for the location, it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
"One should worship the Heart-mantra and the others, beginning from the southeast corner among the hair-tufts."
In this manner, the deities of the limbs should first be meditated upon in their respective directions.

Regarding the passage beginning with *tuṣāra* and so forth: in the *Jñānārṇava*, it says, "The worship of the limbs is performed in the directions starting from the northeast (Īśāna), through the southeast (Agni), the northwest (Vāyu), and the center.
In the *Somabhujagāvalī*, it says, "Having worshipped the Heart in the southeast (Agniyā), one should worship Śiva in the northeast (Maishānyā)."
The Śikhā should be worshipped in the southwest, and one should sacrifice to the Kavaca in the northwest.

Having worshipped the Eye (Netra) in front, one should then worship the Weapon (Śastra) in the directions. According to the *Mālinī*: "The [deities] beginning with Fire (Agni) are to be worshipped in front, or else sequentially upon their respective limbs.
Now, as for the ritual application (*prayoga*): the mantras are to be known from their respective *kalpas*. *Hrīṃ*, obeisance to the power of the command of all.

And so forth. According to the *Kalpasūtra* tradition: *Aiṃ*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Heart-Śakti of the Omniscient Śrī Mahātripurasundarī. Likewise: *Nitya*, I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the Head-Śakti; *Anādi*, the Crest-Śakti; *Nityā*, the Eye-Śakti; and *Aluptā*, the Weapon-Śakti. *Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Thus: *Śiraḥ-śakti-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Śikhā-śakti-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Netra-śakti-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*; *Astra-śrīśakti-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*.
*Śrīpādukā*. Thus is the mention of the locations, beginning with the heart. In this matter, the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the refuge.

However, the mention of the sandals (*pādukā*) pertains specifically to *Śrīvidyā*; the authoritative evidence for this should be written from the respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*). Now follows the description of the Guru, as stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Lord of Gods, in all cases, the giver of the mantra is first and foremost the supreme Guru."
She is herself manifest in form within all mantras and tantras;
thereafter, she appears in the form of the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), and then as the lineage of one’s own gurus.
Therefore, those who possess devotion to me, and especially my devotees, are like the rays of the moon.

O Goddess, the Lineage Masters of the Directions (dikaugha-guravas) and likewise the Lineage Masters of the Siddhas (siddhaugha-guravas) are the source of all mantras and bestowers of accomplishment everywhere.

"I shall describe the multitudes of human [lineages] here before you in brief"—thus by way of summary. The divine lineages (*divyaugha*) and so forth are to be understood as specific [categories] within their respective systems. However, for those for whom the divine lineages and so forth do not bring joy, it is stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "Or rather, among all Śākta [traditions]..."
The gurus are indicated by all [the scriptures]. In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "O Lord, listen, or else, being composed;
by him [it is said that] Prahlāda, Ānandanātha, and others have been described in the sequence of morning rites. Furthermore, in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
In whichever mantras whatever groups of sages are recorded, they should all be worshipped at the beginning and end; this has been stated by me in brief.
Out of ignorance, one may worship the triad of gurus by their names;
or one may worship the tetrad, but beyond that, no further restriction should be made.
The Guru, the Paraguru, the Parāparaguru,
and the Parameṣṭhiguru— these are the Gurus described by her.
The word "guru" is the predicate that governs the term "catuṣṭayam";
therefore, the meaning is that one should worship either the fourfold [set] or the Guru.
The meaning is "the Supreme Guru" (*paraguru*) because he is the very essence of the reckoning of the triad of gurus; the meaning is "the Highest Guru" (*paramaguru*).

This is because of the previously cited statement: "O Mistress of the Gods, everywhere at the beginning is the giver of the mantra, and thereafter is the Guru," and so forth, since the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) therein refers to salutation, libation, and worship. Furthermore, this [group] is a triad.

The seer is one. As for the determination of the place and the mantra, because they are common [to all], they are already established in the *Saṃhitā*; however, the specific details of each *vidyā* should be understood from their respective *kalpas*. As for the ritual application (*prayoga*), while reciting the mantra of the venerable Guru’s sandals ending with *svāhā*, one should say: "I worship the sandals of Śrī Amukānandanātha, obeisance," and so forth.

Regarding the specific [vidyās]: the particularity should be understood as pertaining to each respective *kalpa*. The retinue consists of the excellent host of deities situated in the corners, petals, and so forth.
These [mantras] are to be known for each respective ritual procedure (*kalpa*). Now follows the exposition of the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*). In the *Śāradā*:

"At the end, one should conquer the World-Guardians, accompanied by their primary and secondary attendants, endowed with the *heti* and their respective classes, in the directions starting from the east in due order."

"Accompanied by their root retinues" (mūlapāriṣadānvitān) means that at the end of the names of the chosen deities, one should worship them with mantras joined by the word *pārṣada*. By this, it is established that [the mantra] for the Goddess is "to the retinue of the Goddess" (*devī-pārṣadāya*). The phrase "those arisen from the excellence of their species" (*jātyādhiyotpetān*) contains the word *heti*, which is expressive of a weapon; by this, [the mantra] for the Vajra-handed one is "to the Vajra-handed one" (*vajrahastāya*). By the word *jāti* (species), [classes such as] *suratva* (godhood) and so forth are meant.

It is said: "The lord of the gods" refers to those who are the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Regarding them, there are two types of expressions: those proceeding from the perspective of their birth (*jāti*) and those proceeding from the perspective of their sovereignty (*adhipatitva*). The meaning is that they are addressed with mantras and worship according to these [two] modes.
By this, the form *surādhipataye* is established. And in the *Tūrṇāyāga*: having uttered the word *indrāya*, [one says] *surādhipataye*.

After "to him with his vehicle" (*sa-vāhanāya*), one should then utter "to him with his retinue" (*sa-parivārāya*). At the end of the word *namaḥ*, one should likewise extract the vehicle and other attributes for the others. Here, the intent of the ritual manual (*prayoga-mantra*) is not in the sequence; the addition of "to him with his vehicle" (*sa-vāhanāya*) is established as being [implied]. And in the *Kalpasūtra*: *Laṃ indrāya vajrahastāya rakṣādhipataye*.

Salutation to Airāvata, who has an elephant as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Rāvaṇi, the lord of the power of the *śakti*, who has a goat as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Vāyu (Vāṃ), who holds a banner in his hand, the lord of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others, who has a *ruru* deer as his vehicle, together with his retinue; salutation to Soma (Saṃ), who holds a conch in his hand, the lord of the stars.

Salutation to Aśvavāhana (the horse-vehicled one), together with his retinue. Haṃ! Salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, the lord of knowledge, who has a bull as his vehicle, together with his retinue. Oṃ! Salutation to Brahmā, who holds a lotus in his hand, the lord of the heavenly world, who has a swan as his vehicle, together with his retinue. To Śrī Viṣṇu, who holds a discus in his hand...

Homage to the Lord of Nāgas, who has Garuḍa as his vehicle, together with his retinue! Homage to Brahmā, the Puruṣa, the Lord of Vāstu and the rest! Thus one should worship the eleven guardians of the directions. By these words, the ritual application is accomplished through a single unified utterance. Lāṃ! To Indra, together with the goddesses and their attendants.

"Obeisance to the Lord of the Gods, who holds a vajra in his hand, whose vehicle is Airāvata, and who is accompanied by his retinue. This sequence applies everywhere. Regarding the worship of Brahmā as the Lord of the Site (Vāstvādhipati), there is a difference of opinion as to whether there are ten or eleven guardians of the directions (dikpālas).
Here, the worship of Soma is prescribed in place of the worship of Kuvera; this is likewise stated in the *Śāradā-tantra*, as follows:
One should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, and the Lord of Serpents (Pannagādhīśa) in the directions starting from the east;

in the center, one should worship Pitāmaha (Brahmā). However, in the treasury and other such places, there is the worship of Kuvera. According to Amara and also in the Tripurāsāra: "Kuvera is the lord of the directions starting from the east in sequence. [He is] equal in color to a mass of gold.
Only the position of the Lord of Wealth (Dhanapati) is written here. Regarding the occasion of abandoning the *arimaṃtra*, the worship of both [the Guru and the deity] was mentioned, as in:
"May Kuvera and the Lord of Stars (Tārakādhīśa) understand that we two are not enemies.
Thus, according to the tradition, one should perform the worship of whichever one is known by the Guru; this is the general direction.
Now, regarding the description of their vehicles,
it is stated in the *Caṃdrikā*: "Airāvata, as well as Goṣa, Mahiṣa, the one known as Preta, and the two named Makara, and Mṛta."
Afterwards, the horse, the bull, the tortoise, and the swan— these, the wise know, are the vehicles of the [four] gods in sequence. Now, their meditation (dhyāna) is described in the Śāradātilaka:
Yellow, red, white, smoky-grey, pure white, and both smoky-grey and white; fair-complexioned and ruddy—these are proclaimed in order according to their colors.
And in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"She who bears upon her head the *priyaṅgu* flower, which is the body of the sky, adorned with a crest-jewel shining like a gem,
whose form is mounted by the best of elephants, and who possesses a thousand lotus-eyes that surpass the sun."

One should worship here in the eastern part of the altar with flowers, jewels, and other offerings. Then, one should worship Agni, who resembles a blooming flower, seated upon a goat, holding a sharp spear in his hand, wearing a crown made of gems, adorned with fragrant substances, holding excellent flowers, and wearing radiant earrings. Thereafter, one should worship [the deity] Nīla on the southern side.
One should worship the Lord of the Ancestors (Pitṛnātha), who is heroic, whose hand holds a staff, whose eyes are red like the sun, whose body is covered with matted locks,
and who is resplendent in his attire; he has a fierce appearance, possesses large and formidable tusks,
wields a well-sharpened sword dripping with water, and has a stainless body— [one should worship him] with trembling hair and horripilation.
Thereafter, one should duly behold the Lord with eyes as red as the *palāśa* flower and adorned with various ornaments;
he who possesses the splendor of an autumnal cloud, the moon, and the three-eyed [Śiva], who is seated upon a crocodile (*makara*), and who wears radiant attire;
one should worship him on one’s own head—he whose pair of cheeks is adorned by a circle of jewels, who holds a noose in his hand, and who is the bestower of boons.
Listen to the description of the Lord of the Maruts (Indra), who wields the thunderbolt, is pure, whose banner is the elephant, and whose luster is like smoke-colored clouds;

one should worship him in his own quarter according to the rite with flowers and other offerings, adorned with necklaces of jewels. Then, in the southeast, one should worship the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), whose color is like a mass of gold, seated upon a bull, and surrounded by all the Yakṣas.

With treasures; one should worship him who holds a mace in his hand, whose complexion is tawny, with a pair of lotus-like hands, with beautiful flowers, perfumes, and incense. He should always be worshipped in his own direction for as long as an eon. In the north-eastern direction, one should worship Hara, whose mass of matted hair is adorned with the crescent moon, who has three eyes, and whose body is red like vermilion.

The practitioner should always worship Śūla, who holds a skull in his four arms, who inspires fear in the wicked, who displays the mudrā known as Yoga, whose body is smeared with ashes, who is mounted upon a bull, and who is worshipped with perfumes and other offerings. The mantra for these is from the *Tripurāsāra*: "Obeisance to the head, etc., ending with the ocean (the letter *sa*); obeisance to the head, to the sandalwood."
The bow: the subtle one joined with the eastern face, preceded by the eastern [vowel], is proclaimed as the mantra of the world-protector (Lokapāla).
From the head (the letter *a*), followed by the anusvāra (*m*), situated in the ocean—the fourth position—is the seed-syllable of Īśa (*aiṃ*) together with its own anusvāra;
thus is the extraction of the Vāgbhava-bīja. From the head, situated in fire (the letter *r*).
The anusvāra is the letter *ga* situated in the third position; the letter *śa* ends in *va*, as in *mukavaka*; from that comes *ṣa*.

From the conjunction of the letters *ka* and *va* comes *kṣa*. *Sūkṣma* (subtle) is preceded by the vowel *ā* (as in *ākāramukha*), followed by the anusvāra; joined with those two, it becomes *aikṣāṃ*. Here too, there is an option (*icchā-vikalpa*) regarding the vowel *ī*; these are its weapons (*astrāṇi*).
As follows: they know the weapons in sequence to be the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus.
[Their colors are] white and red, white and sky-colored, lightning-red, and measured as white and black.
Kuruviṇda, parailābha, vaghnī, and others are thus proclaimed.
The place for the independent [deities] is in a square; the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons are outside of that. (p.
As for the mantra:

the first letter of one's own name is mentioned in the *Vimalatantra*: "The seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the first letter of one's own name is proclaimed [to be used] when a [specific] mantra is not obtained. Here, in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), where there is no worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), it is used in that case; and in initiation (*dīkṣā*).

It must certainly be performed in initiation because of the general injunction; however, in the daily worship, it need not be performed where it is not prescribed—such is the rule. Thus, because it is the supreme worship (parārcana), one should again worship the Root Goddess with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. This is stated in the *Svacchanda-tantra*:
Having again performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), meditated, and visualized [the deity],
one should satisfy [the deity] as before and worship again with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings.
Now, the explanation of the words of worship (*pūjāvākya*).

For example: having taken the water for the feet (*pādya*) from the vessel for the feet into another vessel with the *tattvamudrā*, one should offer it to the two feet while reciting the mantra as prescribed in one’s own ritual manual (*svakalpa*), saying: "This is the water for the feet; obeisance to the venerable [Name] Goddess. Thus one should give it.
Having offered the *argha* water with the *amṛta-mudrā*, one should release it and, having displayed the *pādya* mudrā, recite the offering mantra (*nivedana-mantra*).
The offering mantras are those declared in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*.
Combined with fragrant flowers and endowed with scented water.
"O Goddess of gods, accept the water for the feet (*pādya*) for the sake of accomplishing all purposes.
Having thus accepted the *arghya*, one should offer this *arghya* mantra, saying "Svāhā to [Name] Devī," and placing it upon the head;
then, having offered the nectar from the *arghya* vessel and displayed the *utsṛjya-mudrā*, one should recite the offering mantra (*nivedana-mantra*).
O Sovereign of the Gods, accept this *arghya*— blended with *durvā* grass and rice grains, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood— for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.

Having offered this water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) into [her] mouth with the words, "O Goddess [Name], likewise," and having displayed the mudrā: "O Śrī Tripurasundarī, please accept this water for sipping, which is joined with well-perfumed waters and purified by fine silken cloths."

When worshipping another deity, one should utter the name of that other [deity]. "This bathing water, joined with fragrant water, scented with camphor and other perfumes—O Goddess of the gods, accept this bathing water for my success; *namas* to such-and-such a Goddess. Having thus offered one *madhuparka* into the mouth and displayed the mudrā:
"Please accept this honey-mixture (madhuparka), which is mixed with curd, clarified butter, and honey, delicious and most enchanting, for the attainment of dharma, kama, and artha. Then,
one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) as prescribed for the ācamana rite.

Saying "This is the scent," and having applied [the substance] to all the limbs with the tips of the thumbs and the middle and ring fingers by cutting it directly in front [of the deity], one should display the mudrā. [Then recite:
"With moon, sandalwood, musk, gorocanā, agallochum, and saffron..."
I prepare this consecrated food, fragrant with divine scents, for you who dwell in the sky.

Having offered this flower with the *puṣpamudrā*—the gesture of joined palms—saying "This flower, *vauṣaṭ*," and having displayed the mudrā, [one says]: "I respectfully offer this fragrant, blossoming flower, variegated, stainless, beautiful, and scented with perfumed waters. Having placed the incense (*dhūpa*) either to the left or directly in front, saying "This is the incense, *namaḥ*," one offers the *arghya*.
Having sprinkled with water, while ringing the bell— which has been worshipped with the mantra *oṃ gajadhvani maṃtramāna svāhā*—
with the left hand, and waving it three times before the Goddess with the incense-bearing mudrā [while reciting]:
"Born from the sap of the lord of trees, fragrant and most enchanting..."
May this incense, worthy of being smelled by all the gods, be accepted.
Alternatively, one should fumigate with incenses preceded by the root mantra,
using the finest fragrance produced from the combination of fragrant substances and musk.
"I shall now manifest the divine incense upon the camphor-seat. Thus, he offers the incense, either on the right or the left side of the face, by means of a wick soaked in ghee.

Having established [the deity], offered water for the *arghya*, displayed the mudrās, and sounding the bell with the left hand, one should take up the lamp with the right hand using the lamp-holding mudrā; having circled it three times above the head, [one recites]:
"This great lamp is brilliantly radiant, dispelling darkness on all sides; this lamp is the light of both the external and the internal."
"May it be accepted! Or rather, I now present this lamp, which bestows a divine vision, burning continuously with a wick soaked in clarified butter.
Having prepared a mandala to the right, left, and in front, [I offer] the food offering (naivedya) with the nectar from the Śrīpātra."
Having sprinkled [the area] and worshipped the *ādhāra-śakti*, having placed the vessel as described and filled it with offerings,

having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra* and recited the *amṛta-mantra* according to one's ability, one should offer the *naivedya* by pouring water while reciting the mantra: "I offer this *naivedya* to [Name] Devī," and then display the *mudrās*.
O Supreme Goddess, please accept this beautiful, well-prepared supreme food (paramānna), endowed with five or six flavors, served in a golden vessel.

One should offer everything else as "I present," placing it in the appropriate location according to what is available. One should offer ornaments after considering which part of the body each is suitable for; this too should be understood. Having thus worshipped up to the offering of food (naivedya), one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa). As stated in the Śāradā-tantra: "Having worshipped in this manner according to the rules up to the end of the food offering, then..."

The Guru: Having established the sacrificial fire on the altar to the south and having consecrated it according to the rules, the learned one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite. The Vaiśvadeva is so called because the word *viśva* is a pronoun [encompassing all]; thus it pertains to all the gods. This is from the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānanda out of devotion to his Guru.
The eighteenth chapter is thus remembered.
Now follows the Tantric Kuśaṇḍikā.
Since the two types of oblations (homa) depend upon ritual purification (saṃskāra), there follows an exposition of those purifications.
As it is stated in the Kuloḍḍīśa:
"First, one should perform eighteen purifications of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)."
The wise practitioner should perform the inspection with the root mantra and sprinkle [the object] with the eight-syllable mantra.
Striking with that very [blade] of darbha grass is considered the sprinkling by Brahmā;
what is called *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) is the scattering of water from an upturned hand.
That same scattering of water is called *abhyukṣaṇa* when performed horizontally; likewise, the Smṛti states:
"Sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is declared to be done with the palm of the hand turned upwards."

Sprinkling [water] across [the site] is prescribed; digging, the removal of earth, filling with sand while reciting the Śara-mantra, leveling with the Hṛdaya-mantra and the Astra-mantra for water, and digging—
this refers to the digging of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) on that day, or [filling] what was previously dug.

The traditionalists maintain that these [rites] up to the pit (kuṇḍa) should be mentally visualized. Some say that purification applies only to the pit already constructed, because even by mere inspection the constructed pit becomes pure, as it exists in its essential form. We, however, hold that from inspection through to excavation, both the pit and the ground are purified.

First, following that, in a location consecrated by the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) occurs through the very act of preparing the pit. This is because an unpurified location is unfit. Therefore, the sequence is as follows: digging has the function of production (*utpādakatā*) with respect to the four [purificatory rites] as its prior limb (*pūrvāṅga*), while it has the function of removal (*aparakatā*) with respect to the void. Filling refers to small pits and the like.

Leveling for the purpose of filling [the gaps] means moving the clay with the hands and so forth to eliminate depressions and elevations. Smoothing is performed by pounding with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and the weapon-mantra (*heti*).

Sprinkling is for the sake of softening the thick clay; kneading is the beating of the clay for the sake of making it firm; then one should perform sweeping with the *chūma* mantra, followed by smearing.
Sweeping is for the purpose of strengthening the surface against red lac and earth, while the smearing is done with cow-dung water.
One should not even conceive of those [elements] as being parts of the moon, sun, and fire;
one should perform the "three-thread" rite and worship with that mantra.
"Som" and so forth refers to the thirty-eight digits (*kalā*) of the three fires; the meditation on their non-difference (*abhedabhāvanā*) is performed by that very path.

The "making into three threads" (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*) is the threefold wrapping with a thread consisting of the three qualities (*guṇa*). This is the opinion of Bhadra. However, some, having drawn a triangle, worship therein. The mantra for the cleansing (*mārjana*) and other rites is the *kūrca* [mantra]; this has been stated.

Somaśambhu [states]: "The sweeping, the smearing, the fashioning of the form of the digits (kalās), the drawing of the three lines, and the worship with the *varman* [mantra] and the *hṛdaya* [mantra]. And in the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Pounding [the powder] is performed with the *kuṭṭana* mantra; sprinkling is performed with the *varma* mantra;
thereafter follows the application (*kalpana*) in the form of an ointment (*vilepana*).

"Subsequently, the making of the three threads (trisūtrīkaraṇa) is held to be performed with the heart-mantra and the auspicious Īśa-mantras. Thus, according to the view of some, *vajrīkaraṇa* consists of bringing the form of the fourfold path into the eyes, the non-piercing of the eyes, the making into a vajra, and the contemplation of firmness, performed with the Vajrī-mantra, the heart-mantra, and the auspicious Īśa-mantras.

The display of the Vajra-mudrā: Regarding the renunciant (saṃnyāsī), however, it is said that one should make three lines in the middle of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), each measuring a span (prādeśa) in length, using thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass consecrated with the Astra-mantra. These *darbha* blades are to be placed with their tips pointing eastward, northward, and directed upward and downward.
Within the center of the *kuṇḍa*, one should fashion a four-way junction (*catuṣpatha*) consisting of equal divisions.

In the middle of that four-way junction, one should visualize the *Āvasathya* fire in the east, the *Satya* fire in the west, the *Āhavanīya* fire in the south, the *Anvāhārya* fire [in the north], and the *Gārhapatya* fire in the northeast. This has been stated in the *Uḍḍīśatantra*: "The *Āvasathya* is in the central portion."

One who knows the mantras should contemplate Truth in the east, the Āhavanīya fire in the west, the Anvāhārya fire from the southern region, and the Gārhapatya fire as the portion. Regarding the term *akṣapāṭala*, the word *akṣa* refers to the sense organs (*indriya*); thus, it means the destruction of the senses, because the root *paṭ* has the meaning of "going" or "perishing."

Some say that the sense organs (indriyas) are those which remain steady. Others, however, state that the "akṣapāṭa" is a sacred site (tīrtha) twelve finger-breadths in length, consecrated with the root mantra for the purpose of spreading out a seat (viṣṭara).
According to the traditionalists, however, it is called "akṣapāṭana" because it is the place where the demon (rākṣasa) was crushed (pāṭana) before the eyes (akṣa) [of the Lord].

The meaning is that as long as the piercing of the right [eye] has not been performed—that is, until one brings about the realization of the emptiness of the protector (rakṣa) within that sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). According to the *Śāradā-tantra*, however, the piercing of the right [eye] is performed with the *nāganata* mudrā; in case of a conflict between mantras, there is an option according to one's preference. If this is impossible, it is done by means of the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
One should purify them. As it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "Alternatively, one should consecrate those [materials] with the four [substances], beginning with *vākṣaṇa*.

Thus, there are eighteen fourfold consecrations (*catuḥ-saṃskāra*). In the absence of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the oblation (*homa*) is performed on a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*). Or rather, the best of practitioners should perform the oblation on a leveled mound, cutting [the grass] with the thumb and middle finger.
The mandala for the wind element is square, measuring one cubit, and smeared with iron filings. One should purify and prepare the site by means of the four rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
Thus it is stated in the Nīlatantra.
Furthermore, the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared by means of the Īkṣaṇa mantra,
as follows:

Regarding the inspection of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) and the consecration of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍasaṃskṛti*) performed with the root mantra, the traditionalists (*sāṃpradāyikāḥ*) maintain that by the term "inspection" (*vīkṣaṇa*), the eighteen consecrations beginning with inspection are implied; this is because they function within a single context and for the sake of brevity in the syntactical unity of the statement. However, some hold that there are either eighteen or four [consecrations], depending on whether one is capable or incapable [of performing them all].

Alternatively, there is a single consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the mention of the consecrated site. They say that because it is established on the feet, these are the consecrations (*saṃskṛtayaḥ*). In the case of nine fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), first in the teacher’s pit; in the case of four pits, first in the square one;
in the case of a single pit, in that very same one. Having thus consecrated [the site], the placement of the ritual materials (*dravyāsādana*) follows.

One should perform those acts of purification using vessels made of gold and other precious materials, or vessels fashioned from copper and the like; these include the *praṇītā*, the *prokṣaṇī*, the fire-support (*vahnyādhāra*), the *śruk* and *sruva* ladles, the primary pot, the *caru* cooking-pot, a handful of *darbha* grass without a central core, a *prādeśa*-length bundle of ten *kuśa* leaves, and a set of six consisting of eight *darbha* blades.

A tuft of hair (*juṭikā*) fashioned from three or five blades of *kuśa* grass tied with a *brahmagranthi* knot; two *kuśa* leaves with a knot, each measuring one span (*prādeśa*), to serve as the three enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); clarified butter; the sacrificial materials for the oblation as prescribed in the ritual manual;
the articles of worship such as perfumes and so forth; and a vessel of water together with *kuśa* grass for the food offering (*bali*). These are the items to be set out.
In the autumnal [rite], one should draw three lines each with the heart-mantra, oriented toward the east, north, and upward.
The deities for the lines facing east are remembered as Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara;
for the lines facing north, they are Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu.
Alternatively, one should draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon there;
having sprinkled everything with the *tāra* mantra, one should then worship the *yogapīṭha*.

In that regard, for the purpose of worshiping the deities of the lines, one should worship three deities at each of the three [points] in that sequence, with "Oṃ, obeisance to Mukunda," and so forth. Now, as for the word "atha" (then) or "vā" (or): here the word "vā" indicates an option;
thus, according to the *Laghudīpikā*, one may draw either the two [triangles] separately or both together in a single triangle, representing the Śakti.

They say: "In that regard, according to the line-drawing method (*rekhā-pakṣa*), there is no triangle at all; how then can there be a triangle in both methods? Furthermore, the state of being in both [methods] is required for the *yogapīṭha* mandala. If one is capable, one should draw the lines and worship the deities; if one is incapable, one should neither draw them nor worship them. In the *Kuloḍḍīśa* and other such texts, it is indeed both.
Regarding the drawing: the wise one should draw three lines extending from west to east;
each should be known to be a span (prādeśa) in length, released in the form of the lords of the directions.
From the heart [of the mandala] with the mantra, [he should draw] from south to north.
Likewise, one should draw three lines representing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
there, one should place the pen by joining the index finger and the thumb.
Having extracted the best among them, one should sprinkle it with the *praṇava*;
and the *yogapīṭha* [should be prepared] with vermilion, camphor, or saffron.
Alternatively, one should grind it with turmeric in the midst of a meditation vessel;
having drawn a triangle within a hexagon, complete with a city and its gates, one should cast young flowers into its center.
And in the Jñānārṇava:
"In this regard, O Dear One, the drawing [of the mandala] is performed there; from the western side of the three lines, one should subsequently draw three lines ending toward the east."
O Goddess, having then [prepared] the tip of that reed, one should draw the lines there;
then, having performed the sprinkling, one should [draw] with vermilion.
Then, O Goddess, with saffron, or with camphor powder,
or with the powder of indrāyaṇī, or with parched grain, O beloved;
One should draw a triangle and a hexagon, as well as an eight-petaled lotus;
one should then draw a square mandala distinguished by four gates.
O fair-faced one, having cast a flower in the center of Tripureśī,
from that [flower]— whether for the sake of [attaining] the goal or for the sake of [the ritual] itself— the word "vā" (or) is used.

This is clarified by the statement "then beyond that" (*tataḥ param*) in the *Jñānārṇava*; the meaning is "beyond the drawing of the lines. Otherwise, there would be an absence of a mandala for the worship of Vahni (Fire), since the worship of Mukunda and others is prescribed within the lines. Furthermore, this avoids the contradiction regarding the specific application (*viniyoga*). "Śakti" means the seed-syllable of Māyā; [it is] Kāmeśī.
As for the seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), it is stated in the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"One should worship the seat there according to its successive divisions;
one should worship Maṇḍūka there, as well as Ādhāra, Kūrma, and Śūkara."
One should worship the Earth, the bulb, the stalk, the pericarp of the lotus, and the filaments; and one should also worship Dharma and its opposites in the cardinal directions.
One should worship the eight Śaktis on the eight petals in order, starting from the east:
Mohinī, Kṣobhinī, Vaśinī, and likewise Jambhinī.
Ākarṣiṇī, Drāviṇī, and Vahlādinī; likewise, Klinnā is the eighth; in the center of all is Sundarī; in the [Kāmeśvarī] division are Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara; the other triad is Vāgīśvarī;
and the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhapūjā) is as described in the Śāradā.
On the seat (pīṭha) uttered by the Mātṛkās, the wise one should worship Vāgīśī.

Right there, one should worship the Mātṛkā-pīṭha and the Ādhāraśakti-pīṭha intensely. Medhā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Vidyā, Śrī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, and Buddhi—these are proclaimed as the first [forms] of you, O Vidyeśvarī.
The nine powers:
one should provide a seat with a lotus of syllables (varṇābja) and fashion the form (mūrti) by means of the root mantra (mūla).
"Hsau" is the seed-syllable (bīja) for the red lotuses; it is stated that in all cases, this refers to the seed-syllable situated in the center of the Mātṛkā-pīṭha.
The application of the verse beginning with "pīṭhavījai vāme medau vasanāṃ tu karṇikam" and ending with "tārāpūrṇa" is as follows:
*Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara, the Yoga-pīṭha. *Hyau*, salutation to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgeśvara, the Yoga-pīṭha. [This is] the Mūrti [section] in the Kuloḍḍīśa.
Having meditated upon Kāmeśvarī, who is exceedingly mature and resembles a blue lotus,
together with Kāmeśvara, one should worship her with water for the feet and other offerings.

One should worship Kāmeśī and Kāmeśa from the center using the seed-syllable of Śakti; this refers to Bālā. The mantra of Vāgīśvara, however, consists of ten syllables beginning with *vada vada*. The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows:
*sauḥ kāmeśvarīṃ klīṃ kāmeśvarī pāpū vada* etc. [10], followed by *namaḥ vāgīśvarībhyām*.

Thus they accept this as a summary. However, the followers of the Viḍa school accept in detail whatever is stated in their respective Kalpas. In the Uḍḍīśa: "Whether born in the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), or from the sun-crystal (sūryakānta), or from the ocean, or even produced from the earth—[the substance] cast into a vessel of gold and so forth. In the Gautamīya:

If one who is unqualified for the sacrificial rite—having obtained what he desires by chance—should take fire from a stone, or from a forest, or from the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya), or from a serpent’s lair, or from a forest-dweller; or if he is a greedy Brāhmaṇa without sacred fires, he would obtain half the fruit. If he is a greedy Kṣatriya, he would obtain a fourth part of the fruit.
The consumer of oblations (Agni) would grant [the fruit]; however, for a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, the rite of homa becomes fruitless.

One should collect that which is joined with fire. In the Uḍḍīśa: "Therefore, having taken a little from that, the practitioner [should take] the fourfold purification and thereafter the secret [mantra] within the seed-syllable of fire."
Having performed the binding of the ten directions, one should display the *dhenumudrā*;
then, having offered the *kūrca*, the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and so forth, one should completely abandon the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) in the southwest.
The meaning is: "by means of the mantra joined with the *kurca*, the weapon (*astra*), and so forth. In the *Laghudīpikā*:

"Having taken up the fire with the *astra* [mantra] and having established the wheel with the *kavaca* [mantra], one should [place] the portion of the opening toward the southwest by that same [mantra]."

One should cast [the fire] forth; that is to say, having placed gold and so forth in a vessel located in the fire-place, according to the *Śāradā*: "Having brought fire produced from sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) or from the first-born of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one should discard the flesh-eating (*kravyād*) fire with the vessel. And in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Or [from] the cremation ground... [and so on].

Fire is called *vahniruc*. One should not omit anything from the name of that [fire] which devours raw flesh (*kravyāda*), starting from the end up to the *hūṃ phaṭ* at the conclusion of the oblation.
And in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should not omit the staff (*daṇḍa*) from the beginning of the encapsulated mantra (*saṃpuṭa*) until the end of *hūṃ phaṭ*."
O Goddess praised by heroes, the portion for the flesh-eaters and the Rākṣasas is in the corner.

It was said by Gaṇeśvara that with the root mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should cause the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) to abandon [the victim]. With the root mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should cause the flesh-eaters to depart.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: from the aforementioned place, having taken [the substance] in a vessel of gold or the like with the mantra *phaṭ* and covered it with a copper vessel, one should bring it and, from the casket, cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) toward the direction of Rākṣasa with the blazing staff [of fire] using the mantra *hṛmūlaṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Here, in no case...

According to the Tantric view, after performing the fire-consecration (*vahnisaṃskāra*), one should discard the "flesh-eating" portion (*kravyādāṃśa*) somewhere; however, the discarding of the flesh-eating portion may occur either before or after the consecration, as there is here an option based on one's own preference. For this very reason, it is established even in the Veda by such passages as "the flesh-eating portion," and so forth. In the *Uḍḍīśa*, it is stated: "Thereafter, one should kindle the fire."
And having kindled the fire of knowledge, one should, by the power of recollection, transfer a portion of the terrestrial [element] to the Vaiṣṭiva and Agni fires;
then, by means of the seed-syllable of fire, one should establish consciousness within that fire.
Shining in every direction according to the principle of light passing from one lamp to another.

Then, one who knows the mantra should worship with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) by way of the universal path (*viśvamārga*). In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Having invoked Kāmeśvarī, who is joined with the nectar of desire, into the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and having worshipped her, one should bring the fire into her womb."
Thus, regarding that very point, he states the commentary on the Sūtra: "For the sake of accomplishment, one should gaze with the Netra-mantra of the Root-Vidyā;
having worshipped it with the Astra-mantra, one should then rotate it three times clockwise around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) while it remains within the *sampuṭa*."

Having established [the deity] within the center of the *kuṇḍa*, one should worship the pure [deity] with the mantra, having written the *kāmabīja* and the fire (*vahni*) within its womb according to the form.
[One should contemplate] the central channel (*vahannāḍī*) situated in the middle of the navel-center, proceeding in due order through its two cavities.
Having unified the fire of knowledge with the external fire, one should worship them as one.

Having recited the previous ritual procedure, one should also utter "Āḥ Sohaṃ. Then, having recited the fire-mantra and the consciousness-mantra, one should join them with the heart-mantra ending in the dative case.
With this mantra, one should meditate upon Kāmeśvarī within the womb.
In the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra]: "Having placed the knees on the ground, [one should recite] the *kūrca* seed-syllable and the fire [syllable]."
With "caitanyaṃ ṅeṃ namoṃ," one should awaken the pure [deity] by means of this.
With the thought that it is the seed of Śiva, one should cast the fire into her womb,
facing oneself, upon the previously described sacrificial altar.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), one should worship the form of Fire;
having uttered the Bālā mantra, one should write "Āṃ So'haṃ."
Having uttered the fire-consciousness (vahni-caitanya) ending in the dative case (ṅe), which is remembered as the heart-mantra (hṛn-mantra),
one should meditate upon the fire within the womb of Kāmeśvarī by means of this mantra.
The preceptor should consecrate that [disciple] with the Śāradā-mantra through rites such as gazing,
while recollecting the fire of the sun (saura-tejas) within the fire of the moon (vaṃdava), which is free from pride, for the sake of the disciple's prosperity.
Then the practitioner of mantra should join the consciousness with the seed-syllable of fire within the supreme [state];
it is consecrated by the Tāra-mantra and rendered immortal by the Dhenu-mudrā.
Having empowered it with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with its own mantra,
the practitioner, having worshipped it, should circumambulate it three times above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the fire while reciting the mantra,
he should face the fire and, with his knees touching the ground, recite the mantra.
With the thought that she is the seed of Śiva, one should place him within the womb of the Goddess;
thereafter, one should perform the water for rinsing the mouth for both the God and the Goddess.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
having cast away the flesh-eating [spirits], it is gazed upon with the root mantra;

sprinkled with water while reciting the Astra mantra; struck with Kuśa grass or similar items while reciting the Astra mantra; and [finally consecrated] with "Hūṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of the fire."
Thus, having sprinkled the ground with the syllable *Bhūḥ* using the right hand, having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā* with the syllable *Vam*, and having veiled the ground [with the syllable *Bhūḥ*],

one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) by means of three claps (*tāla*) and finger-snaps (*choṭikā*) with the syllable *Phaṭ*. Then, having transferred the fire of consciousness residing in the *ṣaṇḍa* at the navel to the ground via the breath through the nostrils with the syllable *Bhūḥ*, [one recites] *Klīṃ Vahni*.

Having worshipped the fire with "mūrtayena maḥ," one should raise the fire with the right hand while reciting "vahni-caitanyāya namaḥ. Then, with "aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ āṃ so'haṃ vahni-caitanyāya namaḥ," one should cast the seed (vīrya) awakened within Kāmeśvarī's womb. This is the general procedure according to the Tripurā tradition; furthermore, as stated by Śāradā:

The sequence is as follows: having discarded the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda), having established the fourfold fire, and having meditated on the non-proud unification of the earthly and fiery elements, one should join consciousness to the fire with the breath and the syllable *vaṃ*; then, consecrating it with *oṃ*, transforming it into nectar with the *dhenumudrā* and the syllable *raṃ*, veiling it with the earth element, and [protecting it] with *phaṭ*.
Having performed the binding of the image with three claps of the palms (*tāla*) and a snap of the fingers (*choṭikā*), and having worshipped it with "Oṃ, obeisance to Agni" (*vahnaye namaḥ*),
he should take [the fire] with his right hand, circumambulate it three times clockwise, bring it facing toward himself, and,
perceiving it as the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*) with the mantra "Oṃ," [place it] within the mandala prepared in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for Vāgīśvarī.
One should place [the offering] in the womb [of the fire]. Then, one should give water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) to the God and the Goddess.
In the *Śāradā-tantra*: "The preceptor, having uttered the mantra 'Kṛṣṇa-agni-vit-piṅgala-hana-daha-paca-yugma' followed by 'Sarvajña-jñāpaya-svāhā', [should perform the rite]. This is the mantra.
This was previously stated in the Uḍḍīśa: First, with the *vyāhṛtis*, and afterwards the fire-mantra (*vahnimantra*) in a circle;
reciting "O Citpiṅgala, slay, slay" in two ways, the wise one should lead the fire to its wings [the coals] with the mantra "Omniscient One, make known, svāhā," using dry wood and so forth.
Having made the two hands equal in measure, with the fingers extended,
and having joined the two middle fingers, one should place the two thumbs in between them.
The supreme practitioner should display this Jvālinī mudrā:
having made both hands steady with the fingers extended according to the intent of the mantra in the *Kriyāsāra*,
one should join the pair of little fingers and thumbs and insert them within.
This mudrā, known as Saptajihvā, is dear to Vaiśvānara.

Thus ends the chapter on the desire for the two-fold division of mudrās. In the Uḍḍīśa: "I praise the blazing fire, the Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in all directions."
Having thus performed the ritual attendance upon the fire according to the ordinance of Manu, the wise one [should proceed].

The same applies to Śāradā. In the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra]: "A sacrificial fuel-stick (samidh) one span long, combined with clarified butter from a slaughterhouse, [should be offered] silently into the fire."
Having sprinkled [the water], one should place the deities upon the tongue. One should assign Śāradā to one's own body with mantras;
the tongue is for the Fire-eater (Agni), the lotus-sign (liṅga) is for the Lotus-born (Brahmā), and the head-mantras are for the nose and eyes everywhere.
The fire-syllables (va), conjoined with the Lord of Speech (sa), beginning with 'sa' and ending with 'ya', are the Viṣṇus.
The mantras of the tongues of fire have been fully described by the teachers;
these tongues are said to be of three kinds in ritual acts, according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas).
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhāmatā,
Bahurūpā, and Tiriktā are [employed] in the sacrificial rites.
The first is Padmarāgā, the second is Suvarṇā, and the third is Bhadralohitā;
after Lohitā comes Śvetā, then Dhūminī, and finally Caravālikā.
The rājasa [form] is prescribed by means of rajas for rites performed with desire;
one should mentally place the smoke-colored [form], consisting of many sparks of the universal-formed fire, into the fire.
Lohitā, Ākarālī, Kālī, and Tāmasī are said to be these [seven]. When these seven were prepared for cruel deeds by their respective ministers,
they spoke with their own names as the tongue of that one of auspicious seed was being churned.
The immortals, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Piśācas,
and Rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the seven tongues of fire.

"Vahni," and so forth. *Vahni* is the letter *ra*; *ira* is *vāyu*, which is *ya*. *Argāśa* is the long vowel *ā*. Joined with these, beginning with *sa* and ending with *ya*, along with the *bindus*, [the forms are] joined with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*. Thus, *strīṃ*, *ṣṭrīṃ*, *śrīṃ*, *vyūṃ*, *nyūṃ*, *śrāṃ*, *yprāṃ*—these are the seven seed-syllables (*bīja*). At the end of each individual seed-syllable is the name of each individual tongue.
That which was spoken in the *Jñānārṇava* should be employed: "One should worship the names [of the tongues] in sequence, ending with the King (Rājan).
In the tradition of Uḍḍīśa, the installation (*nyāsa*) is of the deities of the tongues; in the tradition of Śāradā and others, it is the installation of the tongues.
Some, however, maintain there are twelve. According to the view of some, the installation is of the tongues whose respective deities have been identified.

In my view, because it is heard that "one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in both cases," there is syntactic unity due to parsimony; thus, there is only one *nyāsa*. Regarding the practice of using the name of a single deity for all the tongues—that is, for all the deities' mouths—it is as follows: first, for the immortal deities, "Obeisance to Hiraṇyā"; second, for the ancestral deities, "Obeisance to Gaganā."
Obeisance to the Gandharva deity Raktā; obeisance to the Vyaṅgākṣa deity Suprabhā; obeisance to the Nāga deity Tryaṃ; obeisance to the Piśāca deity Bahurūpā;
HŪṂ, obeisance to the Rākṣasa deity Pratiraktā. These are the sattvika deities for the daily tantric homa.

"Śrūṃ, obeisance to the immortal deity Kāyā Padmarāgā," and so forth; this is the well-established *homa* for the seventy *tāntrika* rites of desire (*kāmyakarma*). "Sprūṃ, obeisance to the immortal deity Kāyā Viśvamartyā," and so forth;

this is the *homa* prescribed by the learned *tāntrikas* for the rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*) and killing (*māraṇa*). One should then assign the mantra of the limbs (*aṅga-mantra*) of the fire according to the *Śāradā*.

The six-limbed mantra of the Fire-god, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, is declared to consist of the following names in sequence, each joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*): *Tanū*, *Ukta*, *Varṇanā*, *Sahasrārcis*, *Svasti*, *Pūrṇatuṣṭi*, *Puruṣa*, *Dhūmavyāpī*, *Saptajihva*, and *Dhanurdhara*. One should apply these as the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the body of Agni, which is the ocean of knowledge.
One should assign the limbs of the thousand-rayed fire: *Svastipūrṇatuṣṭiṣṭapuruṣa*, as well as *Dhūmavyāpin* and *Saptajihva*; these six, ending in the dative case, are declared for the six limbs.

One should apply [the mantras] to the lotus-eyed one. As for the ritual application (*prayoga*): "To the Thousand-rayed One, *namaḥ* at the heart. This means that by the stated path, one should apply them to the heart and other limbs with their respective mudrās. "Well-being to the Full One, *svāhā* at the head; arise, O Puruṣa, *vaṣaṭ* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*); to the Smoke-pervading One, *hūṃ* at the armor (*kavaca*); to the Seven-tongued One, at the three eyes."

"Vauṣaṭ to the wielder of the bow; Phaṭ to the weapon. Even according to the opinion of Śāradā and others, because of the mention of *vaṣat*, these [mantras] alone are to be recited. According to the statement in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The seer (ṛṣi) of this is Bhṛgu, the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, the deity (devatā) is Agni, the seed-syllable (bīja) is *vīṃ*, and the power (śakti) is *svāhā*; one should assign the seer and the others as before. Thus, [one should perform] the assignment of the seer and so forth to the hands.

The six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga), the tongue-form (jihvāmūrti) nyāsa, and the pervasive (vyāpaka) nyāsa should be performed in sequence; next is the hand-nyāsa (karanyāsa). The form-nyāsa (mūrtinyāsa), however, will be written later. The pervasive nyāsa as well [is performed] later with the root mantra, according to what will be stated subsequently. This is explained in accordance with the statement from the *Śāradā Tantra*: "By that which has been spoken, not by that which has not been spoken," following the path already described.
First is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣis and so forth; subsequently is the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), as stated in the section on *nyāsa*.

"The locations of the threads" refers to those well-known [locations]. "Endowed with a thousand" [refers to the repetitions]. Thus ends the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). In the *Uḍḍīśatantra*:
"Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) in sequence, preceded by the Praṇava."
Everywhere, one should offer the oblation together with Agni Jātavedas.
One should install Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, and Aśvodara; then Vaiśvānara, Kaumāra, and Tējasa immediately thereafter.
One should place the Viśvamukha and Devamukha mantras in these locations:
on the head, in the portion of the wife, and likewise on the sides and the hips.
One should then place his left foot on the ground at its side; thus it is stated in the Śāradā-tantra:
"Then, for the sake of Agni, those who are the forms of fire [should offer] what begins with 'ya' and ends with 'na'; Om, salutation to Agni Jātavedas."

Such is the application [of the ritual] according to the *Jñānārṇava*. According to the view of the *Uḍḍīśa* and other texts, one should first perform only the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*); thereafter, the placement of the tongue (*jihvānyāsa*) and subsequently the placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*). In this matter, the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is the refuge. Even therein, these must be performed in sequence: the [placement of the] seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, the six limbs on the hands, and the placements of the tongue, the forms, and the pervasive [placement].
Prāṇāyāma is highly praised. In the *Kriyāsāra*, Bhṛgu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and [the deity] is the presiding divinity.

The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) are "vaṃ" and "svāhā. One should perform the placement of the seer and the other factors (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*) as before; that is to say, according to the sequence stated in the chapter on initiation (*dīkṣāpaṭala*).
The placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the tongue and the placement of the forms (*mūrtinyāsa*) have already been demonstrated previously.

The pervading [deity] is [worshipped] with the root mantra; the extraction of the mantras is according to the recitation. In the *Śāradā*: "Having prepared the seat in the southeast, one should fashion the form with the root mantra. The seat is the pedestal (*pīṭha*). As it is said in the *Vahni-paṭala* of the *Śāradā*: "One should worship the pedestal within its own mandala as consisting of the power of the mind."

Yellow, white, reddish, black, smoky, intense, spark-emitting, radiant, and dark—these are said to be the rows of flames of the fire. One should offer the seat with one's own seed-syllable and fashion the form with the root-mantra. "With one's own seed-syllable" means with the syllable *vaṃ*. [The mantra for the seat is: *Raṃ, namaḥ to the Yogapīṭha which is the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala).* The seat.
It is accomplished by means of the root-mantra *oṃ vaiśvānara*, which refers to that which will be described hereafter.

As for the visualization (*dhyāna*), it is as stated in the *Śāradā-tantra*: "One should meditate on the desired Śakti holding a noose, a goad, and gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her long arms."

One should meditate upon the Fire-god, who possesses six limbs, is adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, and has three eyes; his head is bound with matted locks, he is the essence of the sacrificial oblation, has three eyes, a reddish luster, a bound crown, and is resplendent with many beautiful, pure, and stainless ornaments, standing in a posture of majesty, and holding a supreme spear.
[One should meditate on] the one who bestows well-being and fearlessness, who is pure, who holds a javā-flower firmly with his long arms, who is adorned with golden ornaments,
seated upon a lotus, three-eyed, holding a lotus in his hand,
whose body is garlanded by a stream of fire, and who, having consumed the three cities, possesses seven hands, three feet, and two heads.
He has four tusks, three folds on his belly,
is joined with a yellow [garland], possesses eight eyes, and has four ears; he is Agni seated upon a red lotus,
white, with one foot hanging down, and has mounted the lordly bull with his face turned toward the west.

Facing forward, he should rise up with four right arms and also three left arms; holding a spear, a vajra, and a *śruk* and *śruva* ladle with the right hands, and a javelin, a palm-leaf fan, a vessel filled with ghee, and a heated golden-colored bowl with the left hands, he should eternally maintain his tongue.
In the extensive ritual service:
[one should visualize the deity] resembling the bandhūka flower, with the luster of well-refined gold,
seated upon a lotus for the sake of the patron, and adorned with two faces.
The god consisting of the seven meters is seated upon a celestial chariot;
he has three waters, three lotus feet, and is the destroyer of the offerings to gods and ancestors.
The four-horned [Veda] is resplendent with the offices of Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ;
it consists of the Pañcarātra, Pāśupata, Kāpila, and Mahāmatam.
This [face], with six tawny eyes, represents the Buddhist and Vedic traditions;
it has four ears for the meaning of the Vedas and the sound of the scriptures.
That wicked man was not bound with matted hair, nor was he swift as ten million suns;
he was adorned with golden ornaments and wore golden earrings.
Seated upon a swastika posture in the center of a red lotus,
his third right hand rests against his back.
He is always honored for his sound and shines with his own splendor;
he holds a spear, a thunderbolt, and a *śruk* and *śruva* ladle in his four right arms.
Holding a trident, a palm-leaf fan, and a golden vessel for the dead with his three left arms, and clad in red garments.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Dakṣānanā, Suprabhā, Atiriktā, Bahurūpā, and Jihvikā reside in the face of Dakṣa.
These are the attachments; all these are established in him through passion.
With all these tongues, his split-open mouth is filled.

Thus, having meditated in sequence and visualized the form of the Fire-god, one should perform the strewing (*paristaraṇa*). In the *Kuloḍḍīśa*, it is said: "Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body, one should carry out the strewing with self-respect. Having sprinkled [water] over the central girdle, [one should lay the grass] with the tips pointing north in the eastern region, and then from the east toward the south with the tips pointing east."

On the western side of the northern [line], one should spread [the grass] with the tips pointing east, and likewise on the north, having first placed the roots at the beginning; thus one should encircle it three times. Upon that, the practitioner should [place the items] with the *śivoṃḍāyaspṛdha* mantra. As stated in the *Śāradā*:
"One should spread [the grass] around the middle girdle with *darbha* blades containing [seeds]."

And in the *Tripurāsāra*: "Then, one of sharp intellect should properly strew [the grass] with tips pointing eastward and tips pointing northward; there should be a single girdle (*mekhalā*) at the base of the wall, below the girdle."
One should spread [the grass] over the two girdles; that is, over the second girdle. However, in the case of the second girdle, one should place it over the middle girdle.
One should arrange the blades facing outward at the corners of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). One should arrange them.

The most excellent preceptor should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the *Śāradā* [fire], excluding the eastern one. Kātyāyana states that he should enclose the fire with enclosing sticks made of *ārdra*, *ku*, or other trees, measuring one cubit (*bāhumātra*). These may be made of *palāśa*, *vaikaṅkata*, *kāśmarya*, or *bilva*; if these are unavailable, they may be made of *khadira* or *udumbara*. The girdle (*mekhalā*) is likewise made of these same materials. It is not to be worn for a year.
In the *Śāradā-tilaka*: "Having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, the forms of Brahmā and the others [are to be placed] upon them.

The phrase "Brahmā and the others" means Brahmā, Vaivasvata (Yama), and Indra; this is because they are present in the worship of the primary lines, whereas the word "others" (*ādi*) is used in connection with those not already present. Therefore...

The explanation regarding Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara is refuted. To Caṇḍā, ending with the dative suffix (ṅe), [is] "Oṃ Lohitāyai Kṛṣṇāyai Namaḥ. In the south-west corner (Nirṛti), this is the mantra. Yūṃ, joined with the Self, to Varṇā, Śvetā, and at its end, "Suprabhāyai Namaḥ"—this is the mantra in the western corner with the *mlūṃ* mantra.
To Padmavarṇā, the red one; immediately after that, "Obeisance to Dhūminī"—this is the mantra for the one born in the northwestern corner.
Then, at the end of the word "caṃdrakoṭi," [follow] "varṇāyai. Immediately after that—
Then one should utter the mantra "Vahurūpā," followed by the dative case ending "-ai" and the word "Bhaumasatatī."

One should worship [the deities] situated in the south and north in sequence in the middle; that is to say, one should worship the tongue situated in the south and north in the center of the hexagon. One should meditate and worship Rati in the middle with this mantra: *Gandha-vairma*.
"O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, carry [the oblation] from the place behind;
O red-mouthed one, accomplish all rites at the end of the word 'pada'.
This mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā), is declared to be the beloved of Pāvaka."

In the Jñānārṇava: "Thus, at the end [of the invocation], one should worship Vahni properly with the mantra: 'O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here; O you who are called Lohita, accomplish all rites,' followed by the wife of Vahni (Svāhā). There are seven tongues."
Having thus worshipped him, O lotus-eyed one, one should contemplate a hexagon within his mouth and worship the seven tongues there—
Vahni (Fire), Vāyu (Wind), adorned with the left ear [the letter *u*], and [conjoined] with Nāda and Bindu.
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should join the tongues to the region of the heart by means of this;
indeed, there are seven tongues, beginning with Sarā and ending with Yakā.
Then, in the tongue-mantra *prajārājñī*, one should worship the seven tongues (*jihvā*) joined with the lords of the *gaṇas* in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Everywhere, beginning with *susvarī* and ending with *vāmīkarā*, the speech (*vāk*) will be produced for the sake of the phonemes (*varṇa*). After that follows *sarayū*.
Then, in the northeast corner, one should offer salutation with "Oṃ Padmarāgadvīpāya Hiraṇyāyai Namaḥ" upon the word "Vaiḍūrya."
"Salutation to Varṇā, Suvarṇā, and Kanakā"—this is the mantra.
In the northeast (Indrakoṇa), one should recite the mantra "Śrīṃ" along with the words "prodyadāditya."
There, ending with the word "varṇāyai," then "lohitāyai," and after that "raktāyai namaḥ" in the corner, beginning with the seed-syllable "yūṃ."
At the end of the word *indranīla*, [it is said] in the *Uḍḍīśa*:

"Having worshipped the fire (*agni*) at its mouth, the best of practitioners should worship the latent impression (*vāsanā*) in its opening, starting from the northeast (*īśa*) corner, proceeding through the other corners, and finally in the center."

One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) by means of the path provided with filaments (keśara). One should discern the forms and the syllable *hūṃ* upon the eight petals, starting from the lords of the directions (digīśvaras), along with the [eight] moist [energies] (*ārdra*) together with the principles (*tattva*). And in the Śāradā-tantra:
In the center and in all six corners, one should worship the tongues, radiant with flames;
on the filaments, one should worship the deities according to the sequence of the petals.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the Śakti who bears the form of the adept within the Daṇḍas;
thereafter, he should worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in the directions according to their described characteristics.

Furthermore, in the Uḍḍīśa, the best of practitioners, having meditated upon Vaiśvānara, should worship him; he should sprinkle the vessels with arghya water for the sake of purification. Here, according to the Jñānārṇava, the placement of the ritual substances occurs after the worship of the six-cornered maṇḍala. According to the Śāradātilaka system, it occurs after the worship of the Fire-god along with his retinue.
In the Jñānārṇava:
"Then, O fair-faced one, having divided curd, *darbha* grass, and *durvā* grass into three parts, one should perform the purification (*paritrīkaraṇa*) of the vessels, beginning with the *śṛṅga*."
One should place the cooking pot, which serves as the vessel for the *caru*, according to the distinction of pairs;
thereafter, one should again set forth the pair consisting of the *praṇītā* and the *prokṣaṇī*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place them in pairs with their faces turned downwards;
then, taking the water contained in the *argha* vessel, one should worship the *prokṣaṇī*.

The meaning is that, having taken the *praṇītā* water from the vessel, one should set down the *prokṣaṇī*. Having performed the purification (*utpavana*) three times, one should sprinkle all those vessels with that water and perform the rite of consecration (*pavitrīkaraṇa*).
Then, having turned them upward, one should consecrate them with the *vālā* [mantra];
however, in the case of Śrīvidyā, it is with the *vālā*, whereas for others, it is with the root mantra (*mūla*).
And in the *Tripurāsāra*:

"Then, having spread on the left side *darbha* grasses made from three types of hair, with their tips pointing toward the cardinal directions, the wise man should place upon them pairs of leaves, or otherwise all those that are triple-folded."

Vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay are highly recommended for rites such as *śāntika* (pacification) and others, just as they are in other ritual acts. Furthermore, vessels fashioned from the *seluka* tree, the *druma* tree, or the *sibhruruha* tree are exceedingly recommended for acts such as *vidveṣaṇa* (enmity), *uccāṭana* (expulsion), *sādana* (subjugation), and *māraṇa* (killing). These vessels have also been described; among them, the vessel [is as follows]:

Having thus filled the ritual vessels (*tīrtha*) with water, one should carefully sprinkle the womb (*garbha*) of the altar from above with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*. Then, having placed the collection of materials on the left side facing [the practitioner], one should consecrate them with the *Vālā* mantra according to the *Uḍḍīśa*. One should pour water and flowers into the pair of *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels, and [place] the *sruva* ladle.

Having turned [the ladle] face-downward, one should perform the cleansing with the arrow. Having taken up the *śruci* in the autumn season, and subsequently taking both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the hands while they are face-downward, the preceptor (*deśika*) should heat them three times in the fire. Taking blades of *darbha* grass, he should purify their tips, middles, and roots respectively, in due order.

"Successively" means that one should take hold of the tip with the tip of the *darbha*, the middle with the middle of the *darbha*, and the root with the root of the *darbha*. Having held them with the left hand and heated them again over the fire with the right hand,
the practitioner should cast the *darbhas* into the fire and place those other *kuśas* to his own right side.

One should sprinkle the collection of ghee-pots with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*. Having poured the consecrated ghee—purified by rites such as *vīkṣaṇa*—into that [pot], one should pour it back from another vessel that has been purified, because the purpose is the same; having restrained it, one should cast the *vāyavya-aṅga* mantras into them. This...

The heating [of the ladle] has been prescribed by the teachers who know the Tantras. Having drawn it out from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and placed it in the north-eastern corner of the pit, one should place the vessel containing the clarified butter (ghṛta) upon them. This is the meaning.
Having kindled a pair of Darbha blades and cast them into the clarified butter, one should then throw them into the fire.
This purification is performed with the mantra of the Guru’s heart.
"Having kindled" means having formed a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
[One should perform the rite] with a pair of blazing *darbha* blades, or by another path [of ritual procedure].
One should cast the embryo into the fire, as it is declared in the Abhidyota.
With a blazing, flaming, and excellent guru-mantra—
that is, with a *kūrca* [brush]— the Guru, having shown the *darbha* grasses while reciting the *astra-mantra*, sprinkled the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
One should deposit [the mantra] in Jātavedas; by that, this is remembered as [the procedure for] gambling.
Having taken clarified butter and the embers, one should combine them in the fire and touch water.

The meaning is that one should bring the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī), intended for heating, before oneself; having cast the embers into the fire, one should touch water. With a pair of blazing *darbha* blades, as stated in the *Uḍḍīśa*: "One should cast the *darbha* embers into the fire, and he [should offer] the consecrated hair-tip of clarified butter."
One should properly diffuse incense that completely fills the sacrificial pit and the pavilion;
one should arrange rows of lamps upon all the tiers of the altar.
He should cast away the scrapings from the rim and the knots of the thread.
According to this view, the purification by blowing (*utpavana*) and the immersion in clarified butter (*ghṛtasaṃplava*) do not exist; thus it is stated in the *Śāradā*.

Holding two blades of *darbha* grass, each measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length, with the thumb and the little finger, one should pour clarified butter over them while reciting the *astra-mantra*; this is the purification (*utpavana*) of the ghee.

Holding two blades of *darbha* grass with their roots and tips joined together between the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands, and supporting them on both sides with the right hand turned upward, one should divide the ghee toward the fire so that it falls through the middle of the *darbha* blades.
In the same way, one should sprinkle the face of the child with ghee using two blades of kuśa grass while reciting the heart-mantra; thus, the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are declared.
