The distinction is that "ud" (upward) is like the act of purifying [the fire], being directed toward the fire there, whereas here it is directed toward oneself.

Thus, having performed the six purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one should purify [the offering] with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). According to the Śruti, one should offer with the first root mantra recited; in the case of Śrīvidyā, there is consecration with the *bālā* mantra, while elsewhere it is with the root mantra—this is the meaning.
And in the Śāradā:
"Having placed a knot the size of a span along with a pair of *darbha* blades within the clarified butter,
one should divide it into two parts and contemplate them as the eastern and western wings."

The meaning is that these refer to the bright fortnights (the waxing moon). Having meditated upon the *nāḍī* Mīḍā in the left part, Piṅgalā in the right, and Suṣumnā in the middle, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule. Taking clarified butter from the right side with the *śruva* ladle, the Guru, with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya-mantra*), should offer it as an oblation into the fire, specifically into the southern eye.
Taking that [offering] from the left, one should offer it into the fire on the left with the mantra "Svāhā to Soma," employing the heart-mantra.
Taking the clarified butter from the center, one whose eye is on the forehead of the fire should offer it into the fire with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni and Soma," while contemplating the heart-self.
Then, using the heart-mantra and the *śruva* ladle, one should take the clarified butter from the southern portion.
One should offer oblations into his mouth with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭikṛt, svāhā!"
One should perform the *saṃpāta* (the pouring together of remnants) in the portion of the clarified butter (*ājya*) by offering oblations in sequence with the words *heti*, *dā*, and *svāhā*.

Having performed the *homa* with the portion of the clarified butter using the word *svāhā*, one should then place the remainder of the *saṃpāta* in its portion for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) at the end of the portion with the word *hā*. One should deposit the residue with the *śruva* ladle.
The meaning is "held in the hand. As it was stated by Somaśambhu: "The practitioner, having taken the clarified butter from the vessel with the *śruva* ladle in three successive portions...
With the mantra *svāhā*, one should cast the remaining clarified butter (ājya) into the fire portion with *hūṃ* in due order. As stated in the Śāradā-tilaka:
"The Guru should perform the opening of the eyes and faces of the Fire [deity] with the *tārā* and *vyāhṛti* mantras;
he should then offer oblations again with clarified butter."
Now, regarding the holding of the *śruva* ladle, it is stated in the *Nāradīya*:
"The sacrificer indeed suffers loss from the sight of the base of the *śruva* ladle;
therefore, one should conceal the base of the *śruva* at the time of the oblation."
It is said that [the ladle] causes disease at the tip, is known to cause grief in the middle, and is said to cause loss at the base; how then can one hold the *śruva*?
Having trimmed it to four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) at the tip and leaving two fist-lengths (dvimuṣṭika),
one should hold it at its center with the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā).
In the *Homasāra*: Having left six finger-breadths from the root, or indeed four finger-breadths,
one should cover the root on the forearm and wear it with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
Now, regarding the *vyāhṛtis*, it is stated in the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"One should not offer four oblations to the Goddess, nor to Tārā, nor to half [of them]. [The *vyāhṛtis* are:
*bhūḥ agnaye pṛthivyai ca mahate* and *vagnivallabhā*."
The *śruva* [is used] for the two feet; likewise, for the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*), it is by sound. For the divine one, "vahni" is prescribed as the limit of the wife.
Svar, Āditya, and Candramas end in *ṅ*; after that, there is no *kṣap*.
To them, Svāhā; and at the end of the feet, the words Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ.
Having recited "Agnīāditya-candramobhyo nakṣatrebhyaḥ" together with the dative case endings,
one should then utter the word "agnīāditya" followed by the [nominative] case ending.
These great Mahāvyāhṛtis have indeed been given by me to the fields of Candramasena and to all the deities in their entirety.
And in the Śāradā [Tantra]:
"The best of preceptors should offer oblations into the fire three times with the mantra;
he should then perform the rites of the fire, beginning with the formation of the womb (garbha) and the nostrils (ghoṇā), in due order."
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having thus worshipped Agni, O Goddess of Gods, one should take a blade of darbha grass born from the womb of Kāmeśī and tie it with the root mantra in the fourth case-ending."
One should perform the oblation.
Having thus performed the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), as well as the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) and so forth,
the root mantra is the fire mantra, beginning with "vaiśvānara" and so on.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
"With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the Praṇava,
one performs the Garbhādhāna, Puṃsavana, and Sīmantonnayana, as well as the rite for the infinite seed-stock."
Likewise, there is the auxiliary rite for the [Karma-]sacrifice;
thereafter, the recitation of mantras and the consumption of food are prescribed.
Then follow the tonsure ceremony (caula), the initiation (upanayana), the Mahānāmnī verses, and the Great Vow (mahāvrata).

The Mahānāmnī, the sacrifice to the chosen deity, the names of the fires, the Mahāvrata, the Samāvartana, as well as the Upaniṣad and the ritual bath (snāna)—these end with the letter 'p'; death occurs at the letters 'ṣ', 't', 'h', and 'k'.
Those rites ending with marriage are prescribed for cruel acts;
those ending with killing are declared for the fire-rituals by the knowers of the Agamas and Vedas.
The *upanidhana* is found in the *Vedāvastra*. In the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"O Agni, you shall perform this placement of the *darbha* grasses," in due order;
having first sprinkled [the site] with the *praṇava*, one should utter the form of the drying fire.

Having thus offered seven oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), as well as the *kṣapana* and the *saṃhota*, together with the *samit* and *kṣemaka* in the group of seven, and including [the others] to make eight according to the statement of Śārdā, in this sequence [one performs] the *puṃsavana* and likewise the *sīmantonnayana*.
Then, having completed the birth-rite (jātakarma) and for the purpose of removing impurities,
[he should offer] a fuel-stick (samidh) one span long, with its root and tip smeared with clarified butter.
One should offer with "Oṃ, svāhā to Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśī.
In the case of the Ūrdhvavidyā, [one offers] "svāhā to Kāmeśvara and so forth, and to Vāgīśvara and Vāṇīpurī, which are common [to all]."
Thus, the practitioner should unite the parents of the fire within his own body. These [rites] occur immediately after the *jātakarman*.
However, according to the *Śāradā-mata*, the consecration (*seka*) and dismissal (*visarjana*) of the fire occur after all the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*). Such is the tradition.
The establishment of distinctions: one should perform the naming of the fire by means of the name of the chosen deity. And in the *Tūrṇayāga*:
having offered eight initial oblations, one should perform the rite of naming;
the preceptor should designate [the fire] with the root mantra, saying, "You are such-and-such."
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantras of the tongue, limbs, and forms in their proper sequence;
one should likewise perform the oblation for the fire with the mantra of its six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
And in the *Śāradā*:
"One should offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*), drenched with ghee at both root and tip,
to the tongues, limbs, and forms of the Fire-god in sequence, according to the prescribed rite and with their respective mantras."

The most skilled knower of the ritual procedure should offer one oblation for each of the forms (*mūrti*) in sequence during the worship of the many forms that are supreme over all. Having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle while standing, he should offer it into the fire with the mantra: "O you who are equal to the gods, may you be established."

With his mind fixed on the teacher’s instruction, he should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of success. The meaning is that one should utter the word *vauṣaṭ* at the end of the fire-mantra, beginning with "Oṃ Vaiśvānara... and so forth, followed by the word *svāhā* and then the word *vauṣaṭ*.
Some say that in place of *svāhā*, one should utter the dative form of the name. Thus ends the fourth [chapter].

By this, its optional nature [is established]. In the *Uḍḍīśatantra*: "One should first offer ten oblations at the site with the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati, using the *vṛtta* meter, and indeed with the *samaṣṭha* [mantra].
And in the *Śāradātilaka*:
One should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara;
that which is common to all the gods is known as my Nāgamukha.
The mantra is as stated in the Uḍḍīśa:

first the Praṇava (Oṃ), then Śrīṃ, Mahāmāyā (Hrīṃ), Smaraṃ (Klīṃ), and Glauṃ; then again the five-syllabled [seed-mantra] joined with the Bindu (Auṃ), followed by Gaṇapataye ending in the dative case (Ṅeṃ).
At the end of "vara," one should write "varadam," and at the end of all [the syllables], one should write "janam.
Then "mervaśamānaya svāhā" consists of twenty leaves and ends with "gajāntaka."
In this regard, there are ten oblations for all the mantras.
The following is the established procedure:
first, one oblation is offered to Gaṇapati with the seed-syllable; then, five oblations are offered with the five seed-syllables joined with the preceding one.

Thus, there are five [offerings], and six offerings with the entire mantra; these together amount to ten offerings. According to another opinion, there are fourteen offerings. In that regard, the following is the arrangement: "The seeds, O Gaṇapati" is one word (pada), and "bring all people under my control" is one word.
Having combined the four words, there are ten types of oblations; subsequently, there are four oblations with the complete root mantra— thus,
there are fourteen oblations here as well, according to the established tradition.
The king of mantras, accompanied by a network of rays, [is placed] within the mouth of the fire.
Having meditated upon her, the practitioner of mantra should worship the illustrious Tripurasundarī;
"Sundarī" is an epithet used for Śāradā as well. (From the Śāradā-tantra).
Then, having worshipped the pedestal,
one should worship the deity who bestows desired boons in the form of fire within the sacrificial fire.
The mantra-practitioner should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter into its mouth with the root mantra; this is indeed the unification of the faces.
Contemplating the identity of the fire, the deity,
and the mantra, one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
The conjunction of the channels has been taught by those who know the scriptures;
one should offer oblations to the limbs in the sequence of their names.
The supreme preceptor should correctly offer each individual oblation with clarified butter for the principal limbs;
that same [offering] is the primary [rite] for those retinues whose limbs consist of the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga).
It is indicated that there is no fire-oblation for the deities of the gates. In this manner, when the other sacrificial pits have been consecrated according to the rule,
the preceptor, composed and facing eastward, should place the tip of the Veda-grass in the eastern and subsequent directions.
And in the Uḍḍīśa:
"Then one should offer a single oblation for each of the deities of the enclosures;
having then made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the optional homa."

Having uttered [the name] ending in *svāhā*, while saying "to such-and-such deity, this," one should offer oblations into the blazing fire; one should perform this around the entire prescribed number. Now, regarding the authority for the *homa* [as stated] in the *Vārāhītantra*:
The tongue has authority in the tantric rite of homa;
even a Śūdra may perform the homa rite if he possesses desire.

Having omitted the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), [the mantra] ends with "namo namaḥ" at the conclusion of the heart [mantra]. Now, regarding the tongues of the fire: performing oblations in the eastern tongue of the fire ten times bestows success.
One should perform rites for pacification under the shade of a tree, and rites for immobilization in the western direction.

For expulsion (*uccāṭana*), [the mudrā] is on the tongue; for killing (*māraṇa*), it is on the forehead. Now, the *mudrās* are likewise there: three *mudrās* are prescribed for the fire-oblation (*homa*): the deer (*mṛgī*), the swan (*haṃsī*), and the musk-deer (*kastūrī*).
The musk is that which causes the hand to contract, joined with the little finger like a female swan.
Excluding the little finger and the index finger, there are three mudrās;
among them, the beautiful Haṃsī is proclaimed for use in sacrificial rites and pacificatory ceremonies.
In rites of sorcery (*ābhicārika*), musk is prescribed;
[the mantras] should end with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, or *hūṃ phaṭ*.

"Vidveṣaṃ...ṇe"—this is the determination of the mantra. The practitioner, while performing the recitation (*japa*) and the clarified-butter oblation (*ājyahoma*), should remain standing; among those remaining, the mantra-knower should offer the oblation.

There is mental anguish and loss of wealth at the head; where there is wood, there is the ear, and where there is smoke, the six-limbed fire blazes—there the tongue is proclaimed to be. It resembles gold, vermilion, the rising sun, saffron, and honey; it is like the golden semen.
It is proclaimed as auspicious. The fire, which destroys its own nature, blazes with flames resembling a split water-vessel, a serpent, a *caṃpaka*, a *punnāga*, a *pāṭalī*, and a *yūthikā* flower;
it is like *pameṃdaka*, *kahlāra*, clarified butter, and *guggulu*.
The sacred grass possesses a beautiful fragrance and bestows all forms of prosperity.
The crest of the peacock, characterized by its clockwise whorls and possessing a luster of patience,
bestows auspiciousness upon the sacrificer, and especially so upon Rāhu.
Smoke that is white like a jasmine flower is said to be auspicious for fire; however, smoke that has turned black in color will bring destruction to the sacrificer.
It should be similar [to the jasmine].
O Fire, a sound resembling one's own voice brings about the destruction of all.
If the sacrificial fire emits a foul odor, it will bring about suffering;
if its flame is broken, circular, or black, it portends death upon the exhaustion of one's wealth.
But it causes the decline of various castes and of cattle after a long time.

"In such cases as these, for the sake of expiation, the preceptor should offer oblations with the root mantra twenty-five times. Thus are the remedies for inauspicious signs, according to the *Śāradā*.
Then, having caused the composed disciple— who had first bathed and ended [the rite] with "svadhā"—
to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he brought him near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having beheld her with divine vision, the Guru, having united that consciousness from the lotus of her heart into his own self, should perform the purification of the paths (adhva-viśodhana).
In the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"Having taken that consciousness residing in the heart, which has the form of a shimmering star, one should establish it in one's own heart by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*."
And in the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra] as well.
Having beheld the most divine within the divine, one should then contemplate the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) in sequence upon the soles of the feet, the heart, the forehead, and the crown of the head.

In the Jñānārṇava: O Supreme Goddess, once the pure disciple— adorned with all ornaments, dress, and the like— has been seated there upon his own purified seat to the left, [the teacher should proceed].

One should contemplate the Śrīcakra, which is the form of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva), upon its head; that is to say, upon the head of the Śrīcakra itself. Regarding the two-fold tradition concerning the locus for contemplating the six paths, it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
It has been stated that, according to the Rudrādhā-tattva, there is a triad consisting of the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan),
and another triad consisting of the paths of phonemes (varṇādhvan), words (padādhvan), and mantras (mantrādhvan).
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti and the rest, are proclaimed as the path of kalās (kalādhvan).
The path of principles (tattvādhvan) is divided in many ways according to the different Śaiva Āgamas.
They know that there are thirty-six principles in total: thirty-two belong to Viṣṇu, while twenty-four principles are known as belonging to Prakṛti through Maitra.
Thus have been stated the seventeen principles belonging to the three-fold nature;
at the end are the Śaiva principles: Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva.
The Lord, together with Vidyā, and the five purities— Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, and Vidyā— are indeed remembered as the sixfold Muni.
Passion is the Puruṣa; these seven— pure and impure— are Nature (prakṛti), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya),
the organs of action (karmendriya), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the five gross elements (bhūta), and the teachers (deśika).
Bring these twenty-four pure substances for the Rāga ritual.
Here, the classification of the principles (tattvas) according to the Śaivas is also demonstrated:
the individual soul (jīva), vital breath (prāṇa), intellect (dhī), mind (citta), and then the organs of knowledge and action.
The five elements are his limbs, the heart-lotus is non-dual splendor, and Vāsudeva is his serpent;
these are the principles (tattvas) of Śārṅgin.
The wise know the five elements, the subtle essences, the sense organs, as well as the mind, ego, intellect, and primordial matter (pradhāna) to be the "friends" (mitrāṇi).

From that [arise] the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti; then, from the essence of the bindu and kalā, they know [the sequence as] Nāda, Śakti, Sadāśiva, and Prakṛti. After that is Ātman and Vidyā as the head (śiras), and then again Vidyā itself as the head.
And omniscience, as well as the principles (tattvas), are declared to belong to that which consists of the three steps.
The wise call him "dūrita" because he has driven away the worlds from the world;
they call him "varṇādha" because he bestows colors upon the waters, and the sages call him "ādīkṣāṭa."
The supreme guru should purify these paths in succession: the path of phonemes, the assembly of phonemes, the path of words, the path of mantras, and the masses of mantras.

Then, touching him according to the rule with the *kūrca* grass-bundle, the Guru should perform oblations in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) using sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*). He should purify each of the paths individually, saying: "O Ācārya, purify the path of the elements (*bhūta-adhvan*), the path of the breath (*prāṇa-adhvan*), and the path of the worlds (*bhuvana-adhvan*)."
One should lead those [deities] into discipline by offering eight oblations in sequence beginning with Tārā;
one should generate them, merged into the head of the head, by way of emanation.

Having visualized those [deities] dissolved up to the head in that respective order within the head-mantra (*śiraḥ-śira-mantra*) which is to be grasped, one should again visualize them as arisen by that very same sequence. As stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
For those of the Śūdra and Śaṅkara castes, purification of the path is not prescribed;
one should effect their release from the side by means of offering water for the feet and other such acts.
Beholding the divine illustration, the best of instructors, having become that very consciousness abiding in the self, should again employ the disciple by means of enumeration.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the ladle using the root mantra,
the preceptor then dismisses the deity, along with the limbs and the retinue, into the water-pot (kumbha).
Having gathered there from the *Yāmala* the well-known hymn to the deity with perfumes and other offerings,
the preceptor, having become [one with] the *tāra* and the *vyāhṛti*s, [should proceed] with the root mantra.
Having performed twenty-five oblations with clarified butter and milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by the *vyāhṛti* mantras, one should worship again with perfumes and other offerings.
Having performed that union, one should dismiss the fire from the image upon the pedestal;
then, having become [established] again by means of the vyāhṛtis, [one should perform the worship] of the tongues and other parts of the Fire-god.
Having offered each oblation one by one and sprinkled water over himself,
he should first join the fire with the enclosing sticks and the surrounding grass mats.

The mantra-practitioner should perform these [offerings] in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), but he should not burn them in the daily rite (*nitya*). As in the passage beginning "the full offering" (*pūrṇā*): in the *Uḍḍīśatantra*, it says, "Then the mantra-practitioner should worship a maiden (*kumārī*) and a married woman (*suvāsinī*)."
Having performed the oblation of the goddess with the vyāhṛtis, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
And in the *tūrṇāyāga*:
having first filled the *śruva* ladle and placed a flower at its tip,
one should rise with the *śruva* held over *darbha* grass and perform the covering.
Holding [the vessel] with joined palms (añjali) while reciting the mantra from beginning to end,
one should offer a stream of oblations in the form of Yama, preceded by shouts of victory.
One should offer eight oblations in sequence with the *mantra* beginning with "ātmāpanena" during the *tūrṇayāga*.
Having first filled the *śruva* ladle [with ghee], one should then fill the *śruc* ladle with it once more.
Having made the fourfold opening, the knower of mantras should perform the oblation with the *śruva* ladle according to the rule.
Having placed the root of the two straight desires upon the fire-knowledge,
one should utter the root ending in *nāda*, preceded by the left foot.
O noble one, holding a vessel filled with fruits and flowers,
the practitioner of mantras should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the thought that it is supreme nectar.
The mantra is as stated in the Uḍḍīśa:
having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by the root mantra, one should say "from this time forward" (itaḥ pūrvam) and then recite "prāṇabuddhi... and so forth.
"May all this indeed be offered into the fire as Brahman;
and may my entire *praṇava* be the deity to be accomplished."
Having sprinkled [the fire] with water, the wise one should worship the fire with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the mantra for self-surrender: "Oṃ Tāṃ Samarpitaṃ Tāraṃ Tat Sadā Ātmārpaṇam."
Having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, the preceptor should offer one oblation each for the tongue and other parts of the fire, using their respective mantras.
O Vahni, O you of great power, bestower of all success!
In this other task and in this encounter, act with due reverence.
Having thus entreated the fire with this, one should dismiss it with the words, "Forgive me.
In the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), one should not remove the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); however, in the case of regular rites (*nitya*), one should burn them.

Thus, this *homonyubjapāṇi* (the hand gesture of pouring oblations) must be performed. It is stated in the *Tripurāratnasāra*: "If the offering of the sacrificial oblation (*havi*) into the fire is performed with variegated hands, the donor receives no fruit of merit, and the officiant shall go to hell."
And in the Bhairava Tantra: "The oblation offered with an upward gaze and a laugh into the mouth of Vaiśvānara leads to the destruction of the priest's eyesight, and the sacrificer perishes."
And it should also be performed in silence, as stated by Manu:
"If one performs the bath while facing the west, one would take away the splendor from Agni."
Yama is for one who is eating; therefore, one should not speak during those three [periods]. The number of oblations for the *śruva* ladle is as follows:
in the *Trailokyamohana Tantra*, it says:
"Either a hundred thousand, or ten thousand, or a thousand, or even a hundred."
Out of respect for the importance of the tasks at hand, the minister should perform the respective homa offerings.
In the *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru, this is the nineteenth chapter.
Now, the rites following the fire-oblation (*homa*). In the *Śāradā*:
"The preceptor should bind the eyes of the disciple with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having taken the hand of the disciple, the donor [preceptor] should indeed lead him to the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*)."
Having again filled a handful of flowers for him according to the ritual,
one should cast them into the pitcher for the pleasure of the deity while reciting the root mantra.
Having placed a handful of flowers in his hand while reciting the root mantra,
the practitioner of mantras should dissolve the digits for the sake of pleasing the deity.
If the falling of the flower occurs in the north-west, it brings destruction to one's own nature;
in such inauspicious cases, the preceptor should offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra.
In the *Śāradā*:
"O Lord, having removed the blindfold from the disciple seated upon the sacrificial seat,
the preceptor, having again consecrated him through the sequence of the sons of Brahmā (the *brahmasaṃskāras*), should rise."
Then, one should perform the various other nyāsas prescribed for that particular kalpa upon the body of the child.
Immediately thereafter, as stated in the Śāradā-tantra:
"One should then scatter the remaining sacrificial oblation (havis) as a bali offering."
[One should offer] to the attendants of the deity [an offering] accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, having lifted it up and purified the ground once more,
one should worship with the five offerings and display the parasol and fly-whisks.
One should offer betel-leaf mixed with all the camphor;
"with the remainder" means with the *caru* that remains after the *homa*.

Having purified the area all around and the ground on all sides with cow-dung water, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) to Candrikā— that which was consumed by her— one should further purify a small portion of the space.
Viṣṇu is remembered as Viśākṣena, and the splendor of the fire is Caṇḍa.
Śeṣikā belongs to Śakti, and Caṇḍeśa belongs to Śaṅkara.
"O Gaṇapati, you whose belly is pendulous, [accept] the leavings," thus [is the mantra for] the first portion of the food offering (*naivedya*).

One should set aside the remainder, which consists of the leavings, for oneself and for the practitioner. According to the *Gautamīya*, the food offering should be placed upon the head with eyes closed; "of Hari" is an elliptical expression (an *upalakṣaṇa*) [applying to all deities].

The meaning is that this applies to all [mantras] in the same way. Having worshipped [the deity] together with the *āvṛtti*, one who is single-minded should offer that recitation (*japa*) to the deity for the sake of attaining all prosperity, while reciting the root mantra.
In the *Kāmeśvarī Tantra*, regarding daily worship (*nityapūjā*),
one should recite the mantra a thousand times while remaining self-controlled,
or twenty-one times; one should not perform less than that.
Then, in the autumn [rite], the Guru should scatter [the materials] in the eastern direction previously prepared,
consisting of gold, garments, and so forth, together with a water-pot filled with water.
One should worship the deity of the weapon (Astradevatā), who is established upon a pillar, seated upon a lion, bearing a sword and a shield,
possessing a formidable form, and facing west.
Having taken [the deity] and worshipped him on a movable seat, the Guru should protect it with water associated with the names of the world-protectors (lokapālas). Then,
having circumambulated [the area] clockwise, he should cause [the disciple] to hear the command of the Vedas.
Having recited the weapon-mantra, one should install it as before.

Having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings, one should command the weapon (*astra*) there while seated on a firm seat: "Protect! and so forth; thus Indra protects the eastern direction, and likewise in the eight directions.
Now follows the exposition of the secret of recitation (*japa-rahasya*). Regarding that, first is the exposition of the bridge (*setu*), as stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.
The *praṇava* is the bridge for mantras; that bridge is remembered as the *praṇava*.
That which is not marked by it at the beginning and at the end falls apart.
Just as water flows down a downward path when there is no dam,
even so the mantra of sacrificers leaks away in an instant if it is without a dam.
Therefore, in all mantras, those of the twice-born classes [should] perform the rite of recitation (japa), having established a boundary on both sides with four syllables.
For Śūdras, there is indeed one bridge, or two bridges according to their desire;
however, all twice-born ones (dvijātis) are declared to have three bridges.
In the Īśvarītantra, by the use of the plural "dvijātanyaḥ," both the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are included:
"For a householder, the Praṇava is at the very beginning and within all [mantras];
for one who has lost it at the beginning and end, it serves for the increase of knowledge."
One should recite the mantra beginning with the Praṇava, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
As stated in the Vārāhī Tantra:
"For householders, [the mantra] should begin with the Praṇava; without that, it becomes void and fruitless."
Of those two, one should prescribe the first for ascetics dwelling in the forest.

This is their meaning: for all mantras and for the *praṇava*, the *praṇava* is the bridge (*setu*). At the beginning, that which is performed by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows away as fruit when it is not restrained; this is the meaning. Furthermore, it extends beyond [the bridge] according to one's qualification (*adhikāra*), and therein also [occurs] misfortune (*vipad*).

This is technical terminology. As stated in the Vārāhī Tantra: "Whether there are many Śūdras or even just one, according to one's wish—at the beginning or at the end—the Brāhmaṇas and others [should be seated]; however, there is a specific distinction therein:
for twice-born householders it is at the very beginning, while for forest-dwellers and others it is at the end; but in that case, for Śūdras it is always [at the end]."
This is the specific rule for householders. Here, the term *praṇava* is technical. As stated in the Vārāhītantra:

"Speech, desire, power, and *praṇavas*—these are called *praṇava-mantras*. Thus, in such tantras, one should employ the *praṇava* at the beginning and the end; likewise, one should employ the *āvāhana* (invocation) at the end of the *āvāhana*, and the *nāmārcana* (worship by name) at the end of the name.

At the end of "smarānte" and at the end of "smarovarya," there is the Viśrama mantra ending in "phaṭ. Whatever constitutes the bridge (setu) within that mantra, or whatever stands at the beginning of the mantra, by its very nature, that alone is the bridge there; it is not [necessarily] the "nāda" and so forth. The statement "ending in 'catvayaṃ'" and so on was mentioned as an incidental point. One should apply the Vaiṣṇava Praṇava and the Śiva-Śakti Praṇava.
One should employ [the seed-syllables] accordingly:
one should place the Śakti-bīja at the Lord of Kāma (Kāmadeva), and then the Ramā-bīja;
for Sūrya, the Vāgbhava-bīja, and for the others, one should employ the Praṇava.
The specific rule for Vaiṣṇava Śūdras is as follows:

For the twice-born, the Praṇava is the bridge (setu), and at its end is the six-syllabled mantra; by joining these with the anusvāra during recitation, it is called the bridge for Śūdras. This is likewise stated in the Jñānārṇava and the Kālikā Purāṇa.
Thereafter, he should commence the recitation (japa) following his previous devotion;
then, taking the weapon-mantra in his hand, he should meditate upon Śivā with his mind.
Having meditated on the gurus upon his head, just as the lineage of teachers (vaṇīdika) exists,
and having visualized the mantra as being of dark-blue color and golden in nature, he should perform the rite.
One should place Mahāmāyā in the heart, oneself at the feet of the Guru,
and thereafter the wheel of command (ājñācakra) of the Guru, the mantra, and oneself.
Having meditated on the oneness of the Goddess and your own single form, one should cause it to descend through the six chakras.
Having diligently meditated for a moment upon Mahāmāyā within the six chakras as well,
one should cause her to descend by means of the root mantra up to the sixteenth chakra.
The practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess, who resides in the sixteen primary cakras and bestows bliss upon the aspirant, and then perform the rite of recitation.
The end of the channels above the eyebrows is said to be the location of the triple-path at the conclusion of those [channels]; it is hexagonal and four finger-breadths in extent.
The white-colored [center] is called the Ājñā-cakra by means of the limbs of yoga;
at the throat, there exists an encircling of three channels for human beings.
The six-spoked [lotus] of four finger-breadths, consisting of Suṣumnā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā,
is declared to be this six-cakra situated in the middle of the throat, which is white.
At the heart, the three channels become one;
that location is the sixteen-spoked [cakra], measuring seven finger-breadths in extent.
The first sixteen wheels, joined with their respective seats, belong to those who know yoga;
they pertain to meditations, mantras, contemplations, and recitations.
Since it is the primordial heart, it is therefore called "Ādi" (the First).

Now, regarding the duties at the time of recitation (*japa*), the *Vimalā-tantra* states: Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, contemplation on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of recitation.

Abstention from speaking of other subjects during the time of recitation (*japa*) is prescribed; the conduct (*ācāra*) mentioned in the *Tantras* is the meaning of the mantra (*mantrārtha*). This should be understood according to each respective ritual manual (*kalpa*). Absence of haste, not moving the tongue or lips, and not manifesting physical discomfort—these are the causes for attaining the fruit of recitation. Such is the meaning of the mantra. And the meaning of the mantra is not mere consciousness (*caitanya*).

Even for one who recites [the mantra] a hundred million times, joined with the imperishable and the non-imperishable, while holding the *yekanīmudrā*, success (*siddhi*) will indeed come to him. Now, regarding recitation (*japa*):

in the *Yoginītantra*, it is said that loud recitation is declared the lowest, whispered recitation is remembered as the middling, and mental recitation is the highest, O Goddess; thus the threefold recitation has been described.
An illness that is too short is a cause of disease, while one that is too long leads to the exhaustion of vitality;
therefore, one should recite [the mantra] joined with both the syllables and the non-syllables, like a string of pearls.
Whatever hymn one might remember with the mind, or whatever mantra one might mutter with the voice—
both shall find them fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel.

In the *Yāmala*, the greatness of vocal recitation alone is proclaimed for one who knows how to perform *japa*; therefore, whispered recitation is a hundred times more effective, and mental recitation is a thousand times more so.

For those seeking spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), mental recitation is prescribed; for those desiring nourishment (puṣṭi), whispered recitation; and for the purpose of killing (māraṇa), vocal recitation is said to be most excellent.
One should recite the mantra aloud; this is proclaimed as *vācika* (vocal). That which may be audible to some is proclaimed as *upāṃśu* (whispered).
Then, having recollected it with the intellect, one should recite the sequence of syllables consisting of mantras, vowels, and words; that is known as mental victory (mānasajaya).
Now, regarding the mantra-sūtaka: at the beginning, there is birth-sūtaka according to the *Yāmala*, and upon death, there is death-sūtaka.
A mantra that is joined with both types of sūtaka does not attain success, O Supreme Goddess, even after the seed-syllable of Brahmā has been placed at the beginning and end of the mantra.
One should recite the mantra seven times for liberation from the two types of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
Thus one should recite at the beginning of the *japa*.
Now, the offering of the *japa* (according to the *Yāmala*):
"O Goddess, you who guard the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us; may success be mine through your grace while you remain present.
O Queen of Gods, with this mantra, preceded by the offering of water (arghya),"
One should offer the fruit of the recitation, in the form of light, into the left hand.

Having first performed the recitation in this manner, one should offer the recitation into the hand of the Goddess— specifically her left hand— with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and water with *kuśa* grass.
In the Gautamīya [Tantra]:

Having first performed the recitation in this manner, one should offer the form of radiant energy (tejorūpa) with the right hand, using *kuśa* grass, flowers, and water for the respectful offering (*argha*).
Having thus contemplated that fruit, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
at the beginning and at the end of recitation (japa), there should be a triad [of breath controls].

"Dakṣiṇa" refers to the male deity; the breath-control (prāṇāyāma), however, is common [to all]. Now, regarding the ritual services (upacāra) in the *Yāmala*: "At the conclusion of the recitation, while offering the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the bell, one should recite from one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*) with composure, according to the sequence."
In the Vārāhī-tantra:
Having taken up the bell, one should then utter this mantra.
One should offer all the various oblations with great effort, O wise one, as described in the *Prapañcasāra*. One should cause a bell consisting of all musical instruments to be sounded;
in the absence of [other] instruments, one should offer a bell marked with Garuḍa and consecrated by Viṣṇu.
At the conclusion of worship, and especially at the time of bathing,
one should not touch [the vessel] with the left hand, nor should one ever place it upon the ground.
If one should ring the bell during the midst of worship out of negligence,
the merit accumulated over a year is lost at that very moment.
At the time of worshiping Viṣṇu, one should always cause the *ṛṃḍi* mantra to be imparted;
through hearing that essence, there shall always be the burning away of the inner ego and the attainment of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
One should not play the *dhūrvara* in a temple of Śiva, the *śaṅkhaka* in a temple of the Sun, nor the *śavādya* or the sweet-sounding instruments in a temple of Durgā.
One should worship the bell in the house of Viriñci and Lakṣmī in the house.
With the left hand, one should offer incense and lamps, while the other objects are for the other [hand]. Now follows the commentary on the recitation of this hymn, according to the Vārāhī:
"In the recitations of the hymns, chapters, and so forth, there shall be stability within the chapter. Thus ends the chapter.
If the arrangement of the chapters is not complete, one should request the beginning of the chapter again;
having first beheld that presiding deity and having prostrated before the Lord.
Then the Praṇava should be chanted, or one should recite a hymn or the Saṃhitā;
having placed the Praṇava at the end, the Primeval Puruṣa spoke thus.
It should be understood that it must be recited everywhere; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
It should be recited with effort by one who is pure and whose mind is focused.
One should not recite the hymn with a distracted mind;
rather, the wise person should place the book upon its support and perform the recitation.
Because it was taken away from its original place of installation, its fruit shall be meager;
furthermore, that which is written by one who is not a Brāhmaṇa shall be fruitless.
One should not consider this hymn to have been composed by oneself, nor even by another;
for in the Kali age, it is not recommended that one recite what has been spoken by a mere mortal.

The meaning is that one should recite the hymn while contemplating it as the limbs of the deity; having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and so forth, the wise practitioner should recite the hymn.
Wherever [the procedure] is not explicitly seen in the hymn, one should perform the placement of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om);
wherever the seer and other details are not heard, there the *praṇava* should be applied.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in the prescribed locations according to the sequence "Oṃ Nama It. Among those [texts], the *Bhīṣmaparvan* is considered the most excellent for sacrifice in the Kali age;
likewise, the *Padmapurāṇa* and the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*.
The liberation of Gajendra, the hymn of Vāmi’s compassion,
the Nārasiṃha hymn, and likewise the hymn to Śrī Rāma-Śaṅkara.
Likewise, the Saptashati of the Goddess as declared in the Markandeya Purana,
and her thousand names from the Skanda Purana.

The *Ślokāṣṭaka*, the *Nīlakaṇṭha*, the *Sahasranāma* of Śiva, likewise the *Daṇḍaka-stotra*, the six-line hymn (*Ṣaṭpadī*) of Tārā, the hymn called *Prasāda* of Tripurā, the royal hymn (*Stavarāja*) of Sūrya,
the *Rucistava* of Paitra, and the *Indrākṣī-stava*.
And in the Vaiṣṇava [Purāṇa], a hymn to Mahālakṣmī was spoken by Indra.
Furthermore, whatever other forms are mentioned there in the ancient texts were cursed by Rāma, known as Bhārgava, for a specific reason.
If those [mantras] are to be recited, one should first utter the seed-syllable (bīja) for each respective deity;
for each one, [the mantra should be repeated] a thousand times.
Having first recited the initial hymn, one should then recite that [specific] hymn;
having fixed the number for the intended recitation of the hymn, the wise person should perform the japa.
In the recitation of mantras, there should be neither deficiency nor excess in the counting;
in the fire sacrifice and the recitation, one should subsequently recite eighteen times for each count.
Having obtained an auspicious sound while reciting the *saṃhitā* for the sake of praise, one should conclude;
for from an inauspicious sound comes an inauspicious result, whereas from an auspicious one, one obtains an auspicious fruit.
One should cease only upon reaching the end of a chapter, never in the middle;
however, if one has ceased in the middle, one should recite the chapters again from the beginning.
This is the established rule in the Purāṇas and other texts: one should recite the hymn starting from the beginning.
If, for some reason, it becomes necessary to perform the recitation of the hymn [in its entirety], [this is the procedure].
Likewise, half of what was to be recited and that which remained from the study session should be meditated upon;
one may recite it on another day, for there is no fault in doing so on that day.
And in the Matsya-sūkta:
"O Goddess, as long as the chapter is not completed, one should never stop; one should recite the *anukramaṇī* and avoid shaking the head or other such gestures."
Thus, even in the recitation of the armor (*kavaca*), there is the word "mā" and so forth. Now, the explanation of prostration (*praṇāma*). This is stated in the *Nīlatantra*:

"Then, having indeed placed a flower upon the head, one should prostrate with the eight limbs. And in the *Yoginītantra*: "The gods are always pleased by physical prostrations; through prostration, one obtains [the fruit]."

O Mahāmati, for the sake of attaining all success in every respect regarding the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), bowing alone is praised. Through bowing one conquers the worlds; through bowing one’s own heaven increases. By bowing before the Great Goddess, one obtains progeny after crossing over the river of worldly existence. Therefore, the *Vāmakeśvara* [Tantra] states that bowing to the Great Goddess and circumambulating her is the measure of true honor.
It is taught that [salutation] is of two kinds: vocal and physical.
Among these three types of salutation, the physical is considered the most excellent.
Praise is performed by means of either Puranic or Vedic mantras.
This salutation would always be considered mediocre and merely verbal,
which is that salutation composed by oneself in both prose and verse.
When performed with devotion, it is remembered as the most excellent verbal [veneration];
likewise, when the hands are joined together and offered, it is done in that same manner.
O Lord, touching the ground with both knees and the head is called *śodham*;
touching it with the forehead is *mukham*, and with the nose is *vasukam*.
Touching the earth with the crown of the head (brahmarandhra), the two ears, and [the other limbs] in succession—
this is proclaimed by the learned as the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra).

Furthermore, in that very same [text]: "With the two arms, the two sides, the two shoulders, the chest, and with the mind and speech—this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*). When ten [limbs] are mentioned, the five-limbed prostration is [also taught].
In that same [text]: With the two arms, the two knees, the head, speech, and the intellect—this is the five-limbed [prostration]."
And it is proclaimed by the learned in the *Gandharva Tantra*:
"The triangular, the hexagonal, the half-moon, the circumambulatory (*pradakṣiṇa*),
the staff, the eight-limbed, and the *muṃmuṃgra*— these are the sevenfold characteristics of the *tilaka*."
In the worship of the Dīkṣāmākhya [deity], the northeast or the north is recommended;
likewise, for rice and other offerings, a handful from every direction is prescribed for all.
If one who faces east performs the ritual, one should first establish the arrangement of the triangle and so forth;
then, having moved to the western Āchāmbhavī [position], one should likewise indicate the arrangement.
When one performs the practice of accomplishment and the worship of the deity facing north, then one should go to the south or the northwest and take up one's position there.
Having gone from the south to the northwestern direction, and from there to the northeastern direction,
and likewise having gone to the southern direction, one should perform salutations in the shape of a triangle.
The one called Trikoṇā is Namaskārā, who bestows joy upon Tripurā;
having gone from the south to the northwest, and likewise from the northwest to the northeast.
From there,
having gone to the south and entered the southeast from that point,
one should go to the Rākṣasī in the southeast, and after that, to the northern direction.
Beyond that, one should rotate toward the southeast; this triangular enclosure becomes a six-pointed star, which is a salutation that bestows pleasure upon both Śiva and Durgā.
Having gone from the south to the northwest, or alternatively from that point back toward the southeast, one performs a self-prostration; this is proclaimed as the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra) gesture.
Having performed a single circumambulation, one who accomplishes the circular form offers a salutation;
this is declared by the twice-born to be "pradakṣiṇa."
Having left one's own seat and place and gone behind [the teacher], one should perform a salutation;
and having performed a circumambulation, one who is disciplined should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
This is called *daṇḍa* by the gods; it brings joy to all the deities.
As before, one should prostrate upon the ground like a staff with the heart.
O Lord, the touching of the face with the chin,
the nose, the jaw, the aperture of Brahma, and the two ears, in successive order, is what is called *prameri*.
Then, having performed three circumambulations clockwise in a circular form, the practitioner is said by the wise to have performed the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra).
That salutation whose contact reaches the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is called "Ugra" by the hosts of gods; it grants satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
Just as the ocean is among rivers, as the Brahmin is among bipeds,
as the Ganges is among rivers, and as the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) is among the gods—
even so is he saluted with intense prostrations among all forms of homage.
By performing prostrations with the *trikoṇa* and other gestures out of sincere devotion,
the devotee who practices the deity will, before long, become fourfold in merit.

Salutation is a great sacrifice that always bestows joy; I consider it to be the foremost among all salutations to the primordial deities. O supreme practitioner, this salutation constantly grants pleasure to Hari and brings delight to Mahāmāyā.
This is the supreme method of salutation.
Now, the sequence for circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa): it is stated in the Vārāhī Tantra:
"In this manner, one should offer seven circumambulations to the Goddess, eight to Vasu, and three to Vināyaka."
One should offer four [prostrations] to Keśava and half a circumambulation to Śiva.
At the beginning of worship and recitation, at the end of worship, and likewise at the very conclusion,
one who knows the rules for the eight-limbed prostration should perform the threefold salutation according to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Having offered [oblations] with one of these, he should dismiss the deity of the heart;
according to the prescribed rule and ritual procedure, he should dismiss the deity of the heart.
The dismissal (*visarjana*) consists of the ritual procedure for the wheel (*cakravidhi*) and the procedure for the departure (*prasthāvidhi*), which should be understood as follows:
having placed a water-pot (*gargarī*) together with its spout in a location within the northeast,
one should wrap it— once the recitation is complete— with a pair of linen cloths.
Into the midst of that, the practitioner should place the three pungents (trikaṭu) as well as the three fruits (triphalā).
Ashes, dūrvā grass, and earth, as well as camphor, gorocana,
sandalwood, saffron, and likewise the king of discs (cakrarāja).
Protect [the cow] with the Astra-mantra and show her the vulva;
[visualize] the Great Goddess seated upon a lion, bearing a sword and a shield.
One should worship the weapon deity (Astradevatā) of terrible form on the western face;
above that, the knower of mantras should recite the root mantra ten times.

In the *Śāradā*, the place for the water-jar (*gargarī*) is on the hand of the arm. According to the *Uḍḍīśa-mata*, after the dismissal of the Goddess, one should place the water-jar for the purpose of bathing;
having drawn a mandala to one's left, one should establish the disciple there, as the mandala is described in the *Śāradā*: [The description of the mandala follows in the *Śāradā*.]
One should first cause the disciple to sit upon another layer of *darbha* grass in the northeastern quarter of the mandala, with those seeking liberation facing north.
One should present the disciples there facing east for the sake of their enjoyment,
according to the *Maṇḍala* as described in the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"Then one should draw a lotus on the left and inscribe the Lord within the filaments."
Then, one should write the groups of consonants beginning with 'ra' and so forth in pairs, following the sequential order.
In the midst of that, upon the pericarp, the Guru should cause the disciple to stand;
having covered the disciple's face with the Astra-mantra, he should rise up with the gargari-vessel.

One should bathe with water containing the roots of *jāṃṭha*, *nāla*, and *muktā*, as well as *vālaka*. Having duly extracted the *kuṃbha* [pitcher], one should place the musical notes (*svara*) in their proper sequence upon its mouth.

The meaning is that, with a mind focused on the sequence of protection, [the mantra] placed in the mouth of the jar should be recited in reverse order over the head of the mother and within the interior of the child.
Then, the knower of mantras, using that very sprout, should sprinkle the pure water from the jar three times with the root mantra.

"Mantrajñaḥ" means one who knows the mantras of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Likewise, [this is stated] regarding other consecrations in the *Nārāyaṇīya*. According to the *Uḍḍīśa-mata*, first is the station of the *gargarī* (the large water-pot), and then follows the jar-consecration (*kumbhābhiṣeka*). However, according to the *Śāradā*, O Brahmin, the Guru is Śiva, together with the five [substances] beginning with water and the foot-washing (*pādya*).
Having extracted the sacrificial pit according to the ritual injunctions and having placed the celestial trees at its opening,
one should place the auspicious Mātṛkās upon the head and mentally recite them.
The knower of the Self should sprinkle [the disciple] with water consecrated by the root mantra;
then, having taken up the worshipped vessel and lifted the pitcher with the *astra* mantra.
The teacher should immediately sprinkle it with the well-prepared waters for protection;
then, with the remaining water, he should cause the disciple to perform the ritual sipping (ācamana).
In this view, even Maya is incapable of providing protection. In this matter, the traditional practice (*sampradāya*) is the refuge:

having thoroughly cleansed the body with pure [water], one should seat that disciple on one's own left side. As for the mantra for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), it is as stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: Oṃ...
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you;
may Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the omnipresent Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, grant you victory.
The Lord Ākhaṇḍala, Yama, Nirṛti,
Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and likewise Śiva;
May these guardians of the quarters, together with Brahmā, protect you always:
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kriyā, and Mati.
May Vṛddhi, Lajjāvatī, Śānti, Nidrā, and Bhāvanā—
along with the honored Rāhu and Ketu— consecrate you.
The serpents,
the ṛṣis, the munis, the cows, and the mothers of the gods; the wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the hosts of apsarases.
Missiles, all weapons, kings, vehicles,
ornaments, jewels, and whatever are the divisions of time.
"May the rivers, oceans, mountains, clouds,
and lakes consecrate you for the attainment of all desires and goals.
Having spoken thus, he should position the disciple, cover the face of the disciple with a cloth, and take up the water-pitcher while reciting "phaṭ."
Having bathed the child with water from the mouth of the vessel using the root mantra, and having lifted the pitcher, the one performing the installation,
while reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, places it upon the head of the child; then,
having consecrated him with the root mantra and the consecration mantras of the reverse *mātṛkā*, he removes the water with a cloth and dries [the child] with that same cloth.

Having clothed [the disciple] in a garment, one should cause him to sit upon a pure seat on one's own left side; placing flowers and fruit in his hand, one should insert that hand into the *brahmarandhra*.
Then, having performed the service (*sevā*), the Guru should speak word by word;
thereafter, he should impart to the disciple the knowledge of the six chakras (*ṣaṭcakra*).
He should then perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Ṛṣis and so forth, as well as the Mātṛkā, upon the body of the disciple.
One should reveal the white section spoken by Śiva into the ear of the disciple;

this means the Kaivalya Upaniṣad. If the disciple is superior in vital strength (*prāṇa*), then subsequently, in the course of time, one should recite the *Vālā-mantra* three times into the right ear. Having performed the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) with the *Tattva-mantra*, [one should proceed].

"According to the injunction"—the meaning is "as before. The best of gurus should give a mouthful of water (*gaṇḍūṣa*) into the hand of the disciple once, according to the rite, and likewise recite the entire *astra-mantra* for both of us.
Then, the most excellent disciple, knowing the [proper] disposition, should receive it along with the *ahaṃ* [mantra]. This is called the "giving of the mouthful of water" (*gaṇḍūṣadāna*).
If a doubt arises in the disciple, his success will be nowhere; the Śrīvidyā turns its face away from him.
Therefore, as stated in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā: "Having placed one's hand upon the head of that [disciple], one should mutter the mantra a hundred times;
thereafter, one should give the mantra preceded by the [consecrated] water."
But for us two, this [teaching] would not be fruitful; therefore, you should proclaim it to others.

The meaning is that one who possesses knowledge of the *yadīnā* (the "if-not" principle), devotion to the Guru, and is distinguished by the previously mentioned qualifications—he alone is superior even to [one's own] life-force (*prāṇa*). Thus, this consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is common to the Śākta, Śaiva, and other traditions. Regarding the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*), it is achieved through the people themselves;

in the divine-virile (*divyavīra*) state, it is through the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) of conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), while in the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) state, it is through the primary [means], as has already been stated before.
It has been explained in the Uḍḍīśa:
"Then, having written the vidyā upon the ground, one should worship it with flowers and other offerings."
And having placed his right hand, which bestows enjoyment, upon the head of the disciple.
The disciple should reveal the vidyā to me; by reciting it, the best of practitioners [attains success].
If there is great affection for the giver of life, that [affection] belongs to the giver of the disciple.
Then, by the mere act of utterance, one should whisper the supreme Śrīvidyā— the form of Brahman, O Indra, which bestows liberation— into the right ear.

This, however, is the supreme *Śrīvidyā-ṣoḍaśī*. In the *Uḍḍīśa* concerning liberation and knowledge, the Guru, having diligently performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of that [disciple], should whisper the mantra into the right ear, honoring the disciple as one who is alone. With a full mind, he should do so three times. The word "right" (*dakṣa*) refers to the twice-born; for a woman, it is the other [ear].
For Śūdras, however, the Yoginī [mantra] should be uttered three times with a single pronunciation into the right ear.
Such is the rule for the twice-born; for women and Śūdras, it is from the left.
One should reveal the divisions of the sages (ṛṣi), meters (chandas), and deities (devatā).
The disciple, perceiving the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, should recite it a hundred times while remaining unafraid;

he should dwell nearby for three days. Otherwise, there is no doubt that he will fall into the power of the *saṃcāraṇī* (the wandering female spirits). Then, quickly, as if by the power of the mantra, the guru reveals the disciple's [inner] state. Thereafter, O beloved of the guru, he should touch some limb of the disciple.
Then, O dear one, the most excellent gurus, having taken the letters of the Mātṛkā,
should fashion a name for him consisting of two, three, or even four syllables, ending with the word "Ānandanātha."
Then, having circumambulated the Guru three times, the disciple,
performing an eight-limbed prostration, should offer himself.
It is poured out to the south-west.
This compassionate initiation (dīkṣā), which bestows all prosperity, has thus been described.
Now, the distinction between initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (abhiṣeka) is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
O Goddess, initiation (dīkṣā), which bestows liberation, is proclaimed to be sevenfold, consisting of action, substance, art, touch, speech, sight, and mental [initiation].
The one known as Samaya, the one known as Viśeṣa, the Sādhaka by the command of Pūtaka; the Sādhaka known as Pūta, he is the Ācārya known as Nirvāṇa.
If the qualities are to be cultivated, one should perform [the practice] joined with action, knowledge, faith, and so forth;
O Goddess of Gods, for the sake of purifying the body, one should follow the previously mentioned procedure.
The meaning is that she should be joined with a man of noble birth and a sacrificial animal;
the meaning is that one should commence the worship preceded by the five purifications.
The detailed classification, however, is in the section on the Full Initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*). Regarding the initiation by means of the phonemes (*varṇadīkṣā*), it is said to be threefold:

O Goddess, [it may be performed] with forty syllables, or with fifty phonemes, or with sixty-three scripts; or with the forty-three [phonemes] of the *bhūtalipi*; or with the rosary beginning with the letter 'A'; or with the sixty-three scripts. [This is] the phoneme...
From the fifty-one syllables consisting of ten [groups] and eleven syllables, the Kālikā-syllables are to be mentioned in the context of the expansion (prastāva).
One should withdraw the sixty-three syllables by means of the two *haṃsa*s through the attraction of the disciple’s body into another [body].
Having joined that consciousness in the Supreme Self, the Guru should cast it [therein].
Therefore, having mastered the phonemes, one should initiate the disciple according to the prescribed rule.
And one should unite that consciousness with the ritual procedure of the path of emanation;
thus the state of divinity, consisting of supreme bliss, arises in the child.

This initiation consisting of the [five] elements (varṇa), which is dear and removes the bonds (pāśa), has been declared; O Dear One, it should be known as threefold and performed according to the rule. Nivṛtti is situated starting from the soles of the feet up to the knees;
Pratiṣṭhā stands from the knees up to the navel, O Dear One; and [Vidyā] reaches from the navel up to the throat.
Likewise, O Dear One, the Vidyā-śānti [kalā] extends from the throat up to the forehead, and from there up to the head;
it should be known as the Śāntyatītā-kalā, and thus the pervasion of the kalās is described.
In the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, the Guru,
abiding in union according to the rule, [transfers the consciousness] from one station to another station correctly, up to the crown of the head.
Or with thirty-eight, or even fifty parts (kalās),
one should perform the aforementioned nyāsa in due order, according to the paths of emanation and reabsorption.
O Goddess, having learned this from the mouth of the Guru, one should pierce the disciple with the *sāra* [essence];
then the state of the deity arises, as does the union of the Yoginīs and the Vīras.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, the initiation of *kalā* is radiant and removes the bonds of the bound soul (*paśu*); it is known as the third, following the *jñāna*-initiation.
O Goddess, initiation is traditionally said to be threefold, being free from physical exertion and the like;
just as a bird gradually nourishes its young with its two wings.

O Dear One, such has been described as the initiation by touch (*sparśa-dīkṣā*) and the instruction by sight (*darśana-dīkṣā*); O Dear One, such has been described as the instruction by the glance (*dṛg-īkṣā-upadeśa*). Just as a fish does not nourish its offspring through mere looking, so too is the instruction by the glance; just as one nourishes one's own children through the mere act of meditation (*dhyāna*), so it is here.

The instruction on the initiation by piercing (*vedhadīkṣā*) is likewise a procedure for one who is equal [to the teacher]; according to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), it is fit for the grace of the disciple. Where there is a falling of power, there perfection (*siddhi*) arises. "Power" means capacity; the meaning is that it resides in service.
Having visualized Śivapura in one's hand, one should recite the Mūla-aṅga-mālinī;
when the Guru touches the body of the disciple, this becomes the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).

Having concentrated the mind on the reality of consciousness and augmented by the supreme reality, the mantra-practitioner should utter the mantras joined together; he is called a "eloquent one" (vāgmin).
Closing his eyes and meditating upon the supreme reality with a blossomed intellect, the Guru should clearly perceive the disciple; that, O beloved, is the initiation by sight (dṛgdīkṣā).
By the mere sight, the speech, or even the touch of the Guru, one attains the world, the reality, the parts, and the phonemes and words for the sake of liberation.
Knowledge arises immediately; that is remembered as the Śāmbhavī initiation.
Mental initiation is said to be twofold: the ordinary and the more intense. O Dear One, having understood the sixfold nature of the mind, the disciple should burn it away.
O Ambikā, I bow to you who are the universe for the sake of the Kalpa, the reality, the phonemes, the words, and the mantra;
[I bow to you] at the places beginning with the navel, the heart, the throat, the palate, and the head.
The wise practitioner should perform the piercing (*vedha*) according to the path instructed by the Guru.

Having contemplated the dissolution of the former state into the subsequent one, and having visualized the entire path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) as dissolved into Brahman, he should meditate upon the disciple as being of that very same nature; this is the meaning.

O Kuleśvarī, among those [methods] mentioned here, the examination (*vīkṣā*) is declared to be the most excellent; O Goddess, it is superior even to the other deities. Furthermore, when the disciple is properly constricted by the power of *smṛti* (mindfulness), he then becomes one whose bonds are severed. Through the two—knowledge and the absence of knowledge—the afflicted one attains a state of intensity and greater intensity, becoming liberated from external activities upon the ground.
At that very moment he falls; having attained a divine state from consciousness, O Śāmbhavī, he knows everything.
Whatever exists at the time of piercing is experienced by him of his own accord.
Once awakened, however, O Īśvarī, he does not utter a word, nor does he experience much suffering.
Śiva himself, the knower of piercing, does not undergo rebirth;
this is the most intense initiation that removes the bondage of worldly existence.
O Mistress of the Kula, this initiation bestows the state of Śiva; O Sovereign of the Kula, it is the intoxication that grants liberation.
Sleep, fainting, and piercing—these are proclaimed as the six stages;
O Kuleśvarī, these six qualities are observed in the lamp at the time of piercing.
Wherever one who has been pierced by the piercing [of consciousness] may abide, he is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
O Dear One, the Śrī Guru who performs the initiation of piercing is difficult to find in this world.
Such a disciple is also difficult to find; he is obtained again through yoga.
One should not give [this teaching] to just anyone—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.

Now follows the initiation for the Kaulikas: having worshipped the Kula-circle with Kula-substances according to the prescribed rite, O Goddess, one should show it to the disciple; this is known as the Kaulika initiation. With the Siddha-substance, the Pūrṇapātra, and the substance endowed with nectar, one should consecrate the beloved disciple.
This is declared as the rite known as *gaṇḍūṣā*, which is the supreme general Kaulika practice for the Kaulikas of the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*).

Initiation therein occurs precisely there. He is born when [the vessel] is joined with blue liquor and worshipped; then, at the conclusion of the full [rite], one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) in a new jar. Furthermore, the external [consecration] is described again.

Having first prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and having established the conch and the water-pot (kalaśa), one should perform the consecration of the navel according to the previously mentioned sequence. Both [the conch and the pot] are to be taken; however, O Goddess, the fish is said to be the pendant (laṃvikā), and the discus is said to be the stalk (nala). One should then sprinkle the disciple with the fivefold nectar that is full.

Thus, between both [the nostrils], one should visualize the *laṃvikā* (the uvula) as flowing with nectar, and the six chakras—possessing the previously mentioned characteristics and marked by the five mudrās—as filled with nectar. Having thus satisfied Kuṇḍalinī, one should consecrate the disciple; this is the meaning. This, then, is the consecration for the attainment of siddhis (*siddhābhiṣeka*).
O Pārvatī, this is the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* (full consecration) known as the *ādhārya*, meaning it is the day of the full consecration for the *ācārya*.

Indeed, this is the detailed exposition of the *kriyāvatī*. In that very [text]: "Acceptance, the staff, the wooden staff, the handful of flowers, the command, the conch, the piercing (*vedha*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the command of the *guṇa*—they know [these] to be the eightfold [consecration]."

“Eightfold” means consisting of eight parts (*aṣṭāṅgaka*). “The one called the commitment” (*samayākhya*) refers to the vow that [the teacher] must give; “the one called the rule” (*viṣeyākhya*) refers to the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*).

From the tooth-stick (*daṃtakāṣṭha*) up to the purification of the deity, the practitioner performs the offering of handfuls of flowers; the worshiper performs the consecration with the conch (*śaṅkhābhiṣeka*); the awakener performs the piercing (*vedha*), namely the piercing by power (*śaktivedha*); the consecration known as "Full" (*pūrṇa*) is the bestowal of the noble mantra (*āryā-mantra-dāna*). By extending this, there is the equality of the disciple with the deities of the mantra and so forth, which is *nirvāṇa*.

The designation "bestowing the state of Nirvāṇa" means that *ājñā* (command) is the transition to *ājñā*. It is taught that there are five stages: the initiate (*samayin*) by means of the tooth-stick; the practitioner (*sādhaka*) by means of the handful of flowers; the son (*putra*) by means of the conch-consecration; the awakener (*vodhaka*) by means of the name of the Creator (*vedhas*); and the teacher (*ācārya*) by means of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).
When the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* is to be performed, the disciple is initiated by the Guru through five rites;

thus there are five stages. Indeed, by the rite ending with the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), one becomes a *samayin*; by the rite ending with the handful of flowers (*kusumāñjali*), one becomes a *sādhaka*; and by the peaceful consecration (*śāntābhiṣeka*), one becomes a *putra*.
The meaning is "the savior from hell. By virtue of power (*śakti*), one becomes a revealer of Brahman in the obstruction of wealth;

this means that through the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) and the union with the five full jars, one becomes an *ācārya*. The meaning of the name *ācārya* is "one who leads [others] by example" (*ācāra-nayana*).
Those who are solely devoted to the conduct of their lineage, who are devoted to their gurus, firm in their vows,
and purified by the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), are liberated in this very birth.
O Mistress of the Kula, those who die deprived of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) obtain once again a supreme birth through their Guru, who is the very form of Śiva.
"Purified by the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) which bestows union with Śiva,
they attain that respective liberation"— thus spoke Antarī.
Therefore, the knower of the *sādhana* who possesses the *snāya* is superior to the fettered (*paśu*).
It must have been stated previously that when those fettered ones who worship other *snāyas* remember the former [state], they become *kaulikās* in a future birth and attain liberation.
If a Kaulika who has received only the inferior *pūrṇābhiṣeka* dies,
he becomes a *piśāca* until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the world.

The meaning is that the *sādhaka* is a *kaulika* belonging to the *Urdhvāmnāya*. According to the *Kulārṇava-mata*, the *Urdhvāmnāya* alone possesses the nature of the *Kula* tradition; the *Pūrṇābhiṣeka* is its preeminence;
and those who confer this initiation are the most eminent. In that very [tradition], the venerable teacher (*śrīcaraṇa*) is one who knows the reality and the meaning of the root mantra.
"The deity shall be devoted to the guru, and one shall become a Kaulika through the initiation of the river," and so forth, according to such statements.
Furthermore, initiation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as external and internal.
The initiation of action (kriyādīkṣā) shall be that known as the piercing of the arms (bāhvāvedha), which brings about peace.
Thus ends the supreme *Urdhvāmnāya*.
"Purity within comes from the three bodies (*tanūtraya*), while external purity comes through initiation (*dīkṣā*)," this is the general rule regarding the daily ritual (*caitya*).

For one who is unable to perform initiation, there is a distinction between the capable and the incapable; [the purification] may be performed by means of the *gaṇḍūṣa* (mouthful of water) and *arghya* (offering water), following the procedure of the *Kriyāvatī* and other [rites].

Even a Cāṇḍāla is liberated through the instruction on the *vāsakṣāma* [the purification of the dwelling]; without these two, O Mistress of the Kula, a Kaulika is not liberated at all. This refers to the common Kaulika practice. For those who worship the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*), this has already been stated. Indeed, these initiations (*dīkṣā*) establish different objectives when there is an equilibrium of karma (*karmasāmya*). This is the intentional application (*abhisaṃdhāna*).

The meaning is this: although the ritual action (*karma*) is the same for both the teacher who instructs through effort (*kṛdyatnādeśika*) and the most excellent disciple (*uttamaśiṣya*), O Karmashambhu, external purification (*bāhyaśuddhi*) and mental purification (*manaḥśuddhi*) are presented as distinct because they possess different purposes and different procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
O Kuleśvarī, just as poison neutralizes its power when it encounters a mantra,
so too does one sever the bonds of the bound soul (paśu-pāśa) through initiation and the vision of the mantra.

Having his karma burnt by the fire of initiation (dīkṣā), his bonds severed by Māyā, and having reached the ultimate pinnacle of the supreme tradition, he becomes Śiva once his [impurities] are worn away. The Śūdra-status of a Śūdra and the Brāhmaṇa-status of a Brāhmaṇa both vanish.
In one who is perfected through the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā-saṃskāra), distinctions of caste do not exist.
One who perceives a Śiva-liṅga as a mere stone incurs sin;
likewise, by remembering its former state [as a stone], even one who has been initiated incurs that same sin.
But having first granted his assent and preceded by the worship of the wheel, one should initiate the disciple; otherwise, he would become devoid of parts (niṣkala).
In the *Śāradā*:
"Then, having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) of him [the disciple], the knower of the Self,
having risen by means of the [mantra] step, and having caused the disciple to put on two garments..."
Having sipped water and become restrained in speech, the best of teachers should sit in the presence of the guru;
he should then transfer his own deity into the disciple.
Offering worship with perfumes, flowers, and other articles, and mentally presenting the food offering,
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before the Guru, who is the very essence of the deity.
One should place his pair of lotus feet upon one’s own head;
one should offer everything—body, wealth, and life—to him.
From that time forward, with undivided mind, he should do what is pleasing to the Guru;
he should give the sacrificial fee to the officiating priest, being full of affection toward me as well.
Thereafter, one should gratify the Brahmins with pure foods and excellent sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). And in the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"Then, having worshipped the sandals of the Guru, one should give the sacrificial fee."
Or one may give all one's possessions, or half of them, or even a fourth part.
Regarding the rule for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Then,
for the sake of purifying his own self, the Guru should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times."
The learned preceptor, having conquered his senses, should recite [the mantra] one thousand times;
the meaning is that if he is capable of a hundred thousand recitations (lakṣa-japa), he should recite one thousand.
If a preceptor, even when joined with mantras, should observe a fast out of delusion or even unintentionally, the ritual act remains valid; it does not become otherwise.

O Lord, if a practitioner of mantra, having performed the initiation, should then observe a fast, the deity will always be enraged; having cast a curse upon him, the deity shall depart for his own city.

This initiation involving ritual action has been described as bestowing all prosperity. Now, for one who is incapable due to the absence of materials or the absence of a sacrificial pit and pavilion, there is the consecration [of the mind]. As it is said in the Jñānārṇava: "One should contemplate the Śrīcakra in the form of heat (uṣma) as his liberation."
But in its absence, O beautiful one, having filled a great conch with water,
one should invoke the Kalās into it, worship the Goddess, and recite the consecration mantra.
And in the Uḍḍīśa:
"Alternatively, the practitioner, having filled a conch vessel with water,
should worship therein the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon."
One should perform the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjana) in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Sura, Vāyu, and the center;
having worshipped with the Astra-mantra, one should recite the root mantra ten times.

The conch-vessel (*śaṅkhapātra*) is indeed a substitute for the water-pot (*kumbha*); thus, at the very time of the installation of the water-pot, the conch-vessel is installed. Now follows the explanation of the statement of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) from the *Jñānārṇava*:
