"One should look at that with the [divine] sight; having seen it with the sight, there is a union. This is the Command (*ājñā*).
One should perform the transition until immobility occurs; that immobility is the state of Śambhu, which is Māyā, free from both the void and the non-void. (p.
O Supreme Goddess, the void is the reality consisting of Śiva, which is the Puruṣa;
O Supreme Goddess, that which is non-void is indeed Śakti, the speech, which is Prakṛti.

When there is an excess of *śakti* and the *rajas* is thickened due to the union of Śiva and Śakti, that state is to be known as the dream state (*svapnāvasthā*); thereafter, the yoga is characterized by an excess of *sattva*.
O Dear One, that which is known as the "awakening of power" (śaktijāgrat) is the state of immobility in Śiva;
O Knower of Mantras, it is described and written here as "deep sleep" (suṣupti).
The three qualities have been described: O Dear One, the waking state consists of the quality of sattva;
the deep sleep state consists of the quality of tamas, which is the form of Śiva, immovable and tranquil.
O beautiful one, know that the class of objects transcends the qualities (guṇa) due to the preeminence of Śiva;
for when there is the union of Śiva and Śakti, it is the preeminence of Śiva that occurs.
Then one should attain that samādhi which cuts through all bonds;
for, O Goddess of gods, it arises from the sixteen-fold knowledge of the Self.

Absorbed in the seed-syllable of Śrīvidyā, one should cause [the power] to manifest within the body of the disciple. Birth, waking, and obstruction—these are the digits (kalās) of the waking state (jāgrat), characterized by mental activity. Death, forgetfulness, fainting, and sleep—these are the digits of deep sleep (suṣupti). Longing, fatigue, anxiety regarding sense-objects, and the recollection of one's own mantra—these...
The state of dreaming; neither-object-nor-subject (naivārtha-naivāsūkṣmatva) is the state of meditative absorption (samādhi). These are the states of the Sun (Sūrya);

one should establish these sixteen digits (kalās) within the body of the disciple. Thus, regarding the Śrīvidyā Ṣoḍaśī, this introduction to the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra) will become manifest as the subject matter of the Ṣoḍaśī itself.
By that [process], the sixteen-syllable Vidyā of Mahātripurasundarī is established;
at the conclusion of its oblation, it is called the "Unmanī" state, which abides as the root.
The bird of the mind, whose knowledge is Brahman, is delayed by the eye of craving;
it is ever restless due to its two wings of conceptualization and discursive thought.
Bound by delusion, stinginess, and desires, and intoxicated by anger, egoism, and pride,
he was thick with attachments and possessed of the two states of "what is to be done" and "what is not to be done."
O Goddess of the gods, when the eightfold cycle of saṃsāra is shaken off by the wind of wisdom,
and when the flower of desire has blossomed, one becomes free from sins and other afflictions.
O beautiful woman, it is situated upon that gross tree composed of branches, which is filled with leaves and endowed with the fruits of sin and merit, and is known as the "Joyful."
O beloved of the illustrious Guru, having seized that bird with the noose of knowledge, [the yogi] constantly [binds] the playful bird with side-long glances.
O Dear One, when both sides have been decisively severed by him, he then becomes *tunmanī* and, through certainty, turns upward.
Free from all conceptual constructions, she becomes the tenth digit (*kalā*); indeed, she is named *unmanī*, the cutter of the bonds of worldly existence.
When she is united with *unmanī*, she is like camphor, a lamp, not a [mere] light, nor again the moon.
Therefore, the Great Sovereign (Maheśānī) should perform the transition by means of her vision;
thereafter, one should indeed join the practitioner with the reality through such statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi).
O fair-eyed one, having joined the vowels beginning with 'a' along the side,
that which arises from the hand of the illustrious Guru appears as if it were a touch within a touch.
O you who are served by the gods, all these elements, beginning with earth, through touch, attain the state of gold; having become so, they all become distinguished when fashioned into ornaments.
But the touch of the hand, O Goddess of gods, indeed destroys the state of iron— even that which is defiled by the phenomenal world— and brings about the state of gold.
Having placed the first fruit in the hand, one should cast that hand into the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
Therefore, you are indeed Brahman; such is the meaning of the statement arising from that hand.
Although this region is difficult to traverse, it is reached by touching the *brahmarandhra*.
Within the thousand-petaled lotus of the *brahmarandhra*, the Guru is white as camphor.
O Supreme Goddess, he who is the illuminator of all places remains eternally awake, bestowing boons and fearlessness, possessing the form of Brahmā, and forever sinless.
One should awaken the consciousness of the six chakras for the disciple:
the support, golden in color and beautifully adorned with four petals.
And the center between the genitals and the anus, shining with a luster like molten gold, know that to be Svādhiṣṭhāna, accompanied by Gaṇeśa; beyond that is the next.
O beloved, it resembles an indragopa insect, adorned with the syllables of Brahmā that shine like glowing coral and possess radiant colors at their tips.
Indeed, the third [wheel] is blue in color, consisting of ten spokes at Maṇipūra,
possessing the brilliance of a mass of lightning, and adorned with the letters from 'ḍa' to 'pha'.
O Pārvatī, O fair-eyed one, listen to the fourth [mantra] of Gadādhara, which is profound like Hari; it pierces through the ten vowels by means of the consonants beginning with 'ka'.
O beloved, O Goddess of gods, the Viśuddha-cakra is joined with Śiva along with sparks, radiance, and other qualities; it is smoke-colored and consists of the Kalās.
O Supreme Goddess, know that it is adorned with the vowels resembling jewels and is presided over by the individual soul (jīvātman). Immediately thereafter—
O Great Goddess, the Ājñā-cakra has a luster equal to ten million flashes of lightning;
it consists of two petals and is adorned with the two white syllables Ha and Kṣa.
Indeed, the seventh [state] consists of the non-hearing of the nature and other attributes of the Supreme Self;
because there is no sound (nāda) without that [hearing], it is therefore called Brahman.
O Goddess of gods, Nāda alone is the cause of the syllables of the body;
Nāda arises from the conjunction with the vital breath when it is joined with Kuṇḍalinī.
O Supreme Goddess, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, through his emanation upon the petals of the six cakras, he realized the nature of the fifty letters.
Having attained the state of the unmanifest through the sequence of accents such as the udātta and others,
the true guru, having thus bestowed that which is endowed with all [these qualities] upon the disciple, [should proceed].
Then the disciple should perform worship of the true guru for his own protection,
offering beautiful jewel ornaments and the like, as well as garments.
Immediately thereafter, the Guru, having taken hold of the disciple's arms,
should then whisper [the mantra] into his right ear.
One should then cause the Vidyā residing on the five lion-thrones to emerge;
thereafter follows the supreme secret, Mahātripurasundarī.
O beloved, one should reveal this mantra, which consists of the Supreme Brahman, into the right ear;
it generates all auspiciousness and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent vows, I shall not reveal the Śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables, which is the throbbing digit of the bliss of Brahman, as if it were my very life-force.
O lady of excellent vows, this sixteen-syllable mantra is indeed hidden within the Vedas, Shastras, Puranas, and even the Yamalas; one should remember it as if it were a treasure trove.
By the phrase "one should reveal the limbs," the instruction regarding the *aṅga-mantras* is indicated. As it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇī*:
"From instruction, the *aṅga-mantra* and likewise the *bali-mantra* must be known by the wise; for success is attained through the acquisition of the *aṅga-mantra*."
Thus ends the general [section]. This is the concise exposition of initiation (*dīkṣā*). In the *Uḍḍīśa*:
"Now I shall proclaim the initiation that bestows success, in its abbreviated form."
Whenever there is the desire, then initiation [should be performed] in accordance with the command of the Guru.
There is no requirement for a lunar day, nor for vows, fire-offerings, ritual bathing, or the practice of recitation;
rather, the sole cause for initiation is the spontaneous desire of the true Guru.

That very moment is the auspicious conjunction (*lagna*), that very day is the good day; that is the strength of the stars (*tārabala*) and that is the strength of the moon (*candravala*). That alone is the strength of knowledge (*vidyābala*) and that is the strength of the deities (*devabala*), as well as the true strength derived from the presiding deity. Alternatively, the mere recitation of the mantra at an eclipse, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), in a field of accomplishment (*siddhikṣetra*), or in a temple of Śiva—that is called "instruction" (*upadeśa*).
In the *Tārākalpa*, however, there is a specific rule in the *Nīlatantra*:
one should perform one hundred and eight fire-oblations (*homa*) using leaves of the *vi* tree.
Or alternatively, one should perform eighteen or even twenty-eight oblations.

One should offer milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, sweetmeats, parched grain flour, and sugar; as for the sacrificial offering (bali), one should present a goat, which is the most excellent among offerings of iguanas.
One should diligently offer oblations of *raṃbhā* flowers and *śālamatsya*; then one should present cow's milk along with rice cooked in milk (*śālyanna*) mixed with honey and clarified butter.
Thereafter, one should offer coconut water along with its shell;
then one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar, together with sweetmeats (modaka) and other such items.
One should give silk garments and likewise golden ornaments;
having duly performed the ritual sequence, the worship, and the fire-oblation (*homa*), the knower of mantras should whisper that knowledge into the right ear of the disciple.
One should satisfy one's own guru with cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth;
one should give one's entire possession as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and should also give milch-cows.
One should grant land that provides a livelihood, which shall follow one's sons and grandsons,
together with a moon situated within a coconut.

therefore, one who desires success should never perform that [rite] in one's own country.
O Maheśvara, one should strive for the destruction of desire so that,
having encountered the rod of karma, one may attain equality with Śiva.
That body was encircled seven times by the thread of the wheel;
it was made into a noose by the Self-Existent One for the protection of all ascetics.
O highly fortunate one, you have been manifested; a fierce binding is being performed.
Thus, O three-eyed one, the auspicious body is encircled seven times.
Having attained the waking state, one should then recite the mantra for sleep;
this occurs through the sequence of the waking state according to the divisions beginning with the Āgneya.
The withdrawal [mantra] is the *praṇava* (OM) encased by the *svapnavodhinī* [mantra] three times;
this is declared to be the *sāpamantra*, which bestows happiness upon all living beings.
Having thus recited [the mantra] three times, the deity Maheśādhika alone,
if his lineage possesses that yoga and is characterized by a crest and a mind eager for passion—
Therefore, wise men should never perform actions that involve such inducements;
listen to my words regarding the excellent portions, and listen to the causal reasoning concerning the two killers.
O Maheśvara, having accomplished this task, your own activity must be performed by the best of practitioners; once their own work is completed, they must neither speak of nor perform the root-yoga.
She was the wife of a hero, the daughter of a hero, and the foremost among the courtesans of heroes.
Practitioners should not perform the extraction [of the vital essence] until mental stability has first been attained;
for if agitation of the mind arises therein, whatever fruit results from the root-yoga will be lost.
That fruit arises, O God, truly, truly, and not otherwise;
for the wife of a hero is supreme, being Maheśvarī herself.
Her daughter was Tripurātanā, the foremost of the Kula-vidyās; her daughter-in-law was Tvaritāveśānī, the awakener of all mantras.
O Goddess, by means of right conduct toward the wife of a hero and even toward the Guru,
one shall become an achiever of all goals through the power of Viṣṇu alone.
O Goddess, if by the force of fortune the wife of a hero is obtained, [then success follows].
Having brought their fruit to maturity, why then do they not achieve success upon this earth?
O Mahādeva, I shall describe the fruit that wards off disease, which is honored by all the gods; it must never be disclosed.
The family deities, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,

provoked by [the sight of] the offering, come for the sake of the ripening of the fruit; therefore, one should reflect with diligence upon the rite of dismissal (visarjana) and the remaining drink which consists of one's own portion.
One should make the family well-disciplined according to the specific ritual injunctions for each occasion;
O Mother, the duty of devotion to one's husband is the true dharma, a dharma not found even among the three twice-born classes.
The husband is the constant bestower of happiness; the husband alone is the supreme refuge;
the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman; the husband is the lord who is dearer than life itself.
The glorious Lord consists of all sacred fords; He is the Lord who embodies all the gods;
and the Great Guru, the Lord himself, is indeed composed of all the Vedas.
Having arrived, she should sit at his side; she should remain there, gazing at his face.
When her husband is honored, she is skillful and joyful upon seeing him.
One should give a reply with increasing loftiness and speak thus during the performance of the ritual;
for that woman who, having abandoned him who embodies all the gods, goes to another man [is lost].
She will certainly be born as a female jackal, a greedy one, and then as a sow;
but I, O protector of the earth, have spent three nights there like a son.
O Īśvarī, when the wearer of form (the deity) goes anywhere accompanied by you,
one should offer water upon his body while reciting the root mantra;
if he does not emerge from there, they indeed command the essence (rasa).
In this manner, women of noble family should be trained through instruction;
they must be protected according to the prescribed method, and not merely by verbal description as previously mentioned.

O Bhairava, a great worship of the Yoginīs and the Vaṭukas should be performed on the day of the moon for the purpose of destroying obstacles, according to the conjunction of the Kula-day, the asterism, and the yoga.
Having written the desired root-mantra at the base of the tree of their pride during the remaining time, one is thereafter no longer smeared by obstacles.
O Goddess, when the application of the Kāpī-mantra is performed by the wife of a hero at the base of the root according to the rite, whatever fruit falls at that time should be discarded.
O best of the lineage, when there is delight in that form,
Bhairava, Vaṭuka, and the others assume that very same form for the sake of that family.
O Lord, having sown the seed therein, they protect the fruit by means of wise words and phrases, once they have understood the arising of the fruit.
O Lord of Devas, free from despondency, just as the eternal one has made it known;
having understood the knowledge of the fruit, O Lord, there is indeed a state beyond the fifth.
In the midst of the lunar mansion during the seventh or eighth month,
having placed the hand upon the soles of the feet, one should [recite] the Vidyā known as Pādukā through the yoga of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Indeed, Rūpadeva will fall from the tree himself eight thousand times;
thus, whatever fruit falls is created by the gods. It falls ownerless, having been abandoned at the end of its conjunction.
Having understood this fruit of the liṅga, one should bring it and then wash it.

Having abandoned the portion of defects and having bowed to the fruit-bearing tree, one should cast away that portion of defects; the meaning is that it is the *nāḍī* (channel) together with the mind.
In the great forest of Tāmrapāta, one should perform the ripening of the fruit;
having prepared a hundred thousand [offerings] and so forth in this manner, they should be combined with the three pungent spices.
Having recognized that it has been prepared and mixed with various fragrant substances, the wise one should then perform the *āghora* oblation in the midst of men after it has been consecrated.

The Aghora [mantra] is stated in the *Homasāra*: "Having rendered [the offering] nectar-like by means of the Dhenu-mudrā, one should perform the oblation unobserved. Having performed these two in this manner, one should then consume the remainder of the sacrifice.
As soon as that has been consumed, the state of being long-lived will indeed be attained."
The primary [form] is Madhumatī, which resides in his hand and bestows enjoyment.
O Maheśvara, the supreme practitioner, possessing a divine nature, becomes equal to Śakra among mortals; by performing what is pleasing to you, he shall grant me liberation.
For practitioners who possess knowledge of the *kula*, there is no fault in the ripening of the fruit;
indeed, they proceed in close proximity for the sake of the maturation of that very fruit.
"Understand that the delusion regarding the realization of the Vedas and Āgamas arises solely from the failure to grasp their true meaning.
For the sake of causing this fruit to fall, the one who desires the fruit creates obstacles at every step everywhere, due to his own inherent contraction.
Likewise, the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) certainly moves about as an obstacle;
for if, by the turn of fate, there should ever be a lack of fruit on that tree.
The practitioner likewise should maintain the divine conception here without conceptualization;
whether by speech or by body, he should not be bound by anything that lacks the essential core.
Then the deity of the fruit-bearing tree destroys the command of Smara;
however, O Radiant One, if the family-tree (kulavṛkṣa) is propitiated for the sake of the practitioner, [the goal is achieved].
Family worship does not belong to one as long as no transformation has occurred;
therefore, one must diligently avoid speaking of one's own family.
There is no one on this earth capable of providing such a specific qualification for this [task], being as it is in a region so extremely remote, devoid even of the mention of a name or color.
If he were to create an obstacle to what is auspicious or to the accomplishment of the goal,
then having attained the twofold fruit, if one reaches the further shore, [it would be in vain].
O Lord of Gods, there is a fruit [of this], and he is certainly tormented by sin.
The primary Madhumatī Tantra is born therein; there is no doubt about this.
O God, listen as I describe the fruit of the Madhumatī.
From his mouth there arises a mass of streams bearing nectar;
he is omniscient through all the scriptures, a sovereign lord, and a leader of the gods.
With the sun and moon as his limit, he enjoys abundant happiness on earth;
after remaining in the intermediate state for a long time, he shall attain liberation at the end.
O Mahādeva, there Fortune shall always remain perfectly stable;
one must certainly recite the mantra for awakening from sleep at the foot of a tree.
It should be applied with effort, for obstacles may arise;
O God, this divine state which brings happiness has been described to you.
It must not be given to just anyone; O Mahādeva, it should be guarded with effort even from animals. O Bhairava, listen as the nature of the hero (vīrabhāva) is described.
Having become free from dualities in mind, with a heart that is a subtle body of art,
he is indeed always liberated, the most excellent one, gracious at night, the very cause;
having taken up his own lineage, he himself assumes the form of Bhairava.
And the Kula is the form of Bhairavī;
having performed the placement upon its limbs according to the rules, one should likewise perform the entire placement consisting of the nine wombs.
In the midst of a bed of flowers, crowded with a perimeter of blossoms,
and filled with various fragrances, one should place the yantra using the kula-substance.
Having written [the mantra], one should worship the conch after first performing the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭa).
To the left of oneself, there is a circle with a hexagon; in its center is the aperture of Brahmā (brahmaraṃdhra).

Having written [the mantra] upon a vessel made of gold, silver, or even iron or diamond, one should place that vessel— scented with fragrant perfumes— within the *tattva-kumbha* (the vessel of reality) according to the prescribed portion, O Lord; one should then fill it with the causal substances (*hetu-dravya*) according to the distinctions of the Brahmins and other castes.
Having first drawn the *tara* yantra and meditated upon whichever desired deity originates from one's own *kula*, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times there.
Having assumed the dhenu-mudrā, one should contemplate that [nectar] as nectar;
by the sight of it, the hosts of yoginīs dance within the vessel of the arghya.
All the Bhairavas dance; the hosts of Mothers dance;
and all the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent upon their joy.
Listen to the *argha*: having divided it into three parts, one portion is for the Guru.
Having thus given the *kulāya*, and having satisfied the deities with one [portion],
he drinks the *kularasa* while adorned with various divine ornaments.
If he meets the Guru in person, he should then dismiss him into water;
having become one whose form is bliss, he should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Having worshipped the mantra there according to the procedure prescribed for each respective kalpa,
and having performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), one should then unite [the disciple] with the Akula.
Therefore, O excellent one, by drinking that, nectar is enjoyed by me;
and through the tasting of its essence, it has become perfectly sweet.
O Lord, the attainment of that fruit consists of ascending the peaks of Mount Sumeru;
by the mere embrace of the creeper-liṅga, the body becomes washed with nectar.
When the root-yoga has been performed there, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, taking the sacrificial substance purified by austerity, one should perform the libation.
Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) and proceeding clockwise around the deity,
one should then propitiate Him by bowing and praising with the hymn prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa).
Thus is the sequence for the worship of the seed-syllables (bīja).
This is the clan of heroes (vīrakula), O God, beautiful and most enchanting;
in whatever region this exists, O Bhairava, that clan is indeed a clan of heroes.
There shall be no fear of pestilence there, nor any fear of the king and so forth;
it shall always be most auspicious there, increasing wealth and sons.
O Mahādeva, there Fortune shall always remain firmly established;
this is the mantra for awakening from dreams, [to be recited] in a forest at the foot of a tree.
It should be applied with diligence so that no obstacle arises;
it is not suitable for another hero to grasp, even by the gods themselves.
Joined with the Yoginīs, one is not tainted by sin,
even when traveling to a temple, a sacred ford, or a cremation ground.
There, the fruit of worship for an entire fortnight is obtained in seven days;
when the fourteenth day arrives within that fortnight, the fruit of worship for that whole fortnight shall be attained.

If one worships there with a sense of movement [thinking], "There is no doubt that he is merely a beast," or being intent on the thought, "The god is not superior to another," [one does not attain the fruit].
When the practitioner experiences agitation, agitation arises within me;
therefore, with effort, the wise hero should remain united with enjoyment.
O Maheśvara, by means of enjoyment one attains liberation, and by means of enjoyment one increases the lineage;
having encountered this without cause, one becomes possessed of agitation.
One should not perform worship for me, nor meditation, nor contemplation;
therefore, the wise and excellent hero should strive to be endowed with enjoyments.
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
there is no deviation from the Krama, no fault of the Krama, and no corruption by the fault of improper conduct.
Whatever one speaks, sleeps, does,
or worships— the wise person should perform all that while meditating upon it as having the form of the Kula.
Alone in a secluded place— in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank— he should wander joyfully, free from attachment.
For heroes, every time for recitation is indeed praised;
it should be performed at any sacred seat (pīṭha) and in any country—of this there is no doubt.
If one is devoted to the supreme substance of the Kula during the state of existence,
then, by this procedure, the gratification of the Kula must be performed.
"O twice-born one, he is called a *vipra* because he is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

This has already been explained at length previously, based on such statements as "In the *Sautrāmaṇī* [sacrifice]... and so forth, which declare that even a Brāhmaṇa possesses primary eligibility (*mukhyādhikāritva*).
Furthermore, within the interior of the flower is the captivating seat of the Kula;
that indeed is the face of all the gods, consisting of the essence of Mahākāla.
"O Goddess, among those flowers, which one always possesses a man? [The answer is:
The horse-enemy (the lotus) and the oleander. Taking a small flower from among them, [one should place] a four-petaled [lotus] in the midst of the flowers."
Having offered the Aparājitā flower, which possesses the fragrance of red saffron, there to the one whose nature is Śiva,
he performed a supreme offering with flowers that are themselves of the nature of Śiva, characterized by the eight [qualities].
One should unite [the self] with the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti), contemplating their oneness with a focused mind;
having reflected for a moment upon that very state, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.

"Having recited [the mantra] and performed the austerity, that very substance which is the portion of knowledge is to be known as most difficult to obtain; this substance is to be known as superior to nectar and exceedingly rare. Thus ends the substitute for the *kulapuṣpa*.
O Bhairava, where there is the *aparājitā* flower and the *japā* flower—
Wherever the leaves of the red and white karavīra remain, [there one should stay].
The Goddess shall dwell eternally within that yantra; by offering me even a single hibiscus flower, leaf, cloth, or fruit, my worship is accomplished.
"Sin such as the killing of a Brahmin is certainly destroyed in an instant.
Such is the fruit for Aparā and the others.
Furthermore, regarding the majesty of Aparā, I, Maheśvara, am not red.
Thus, the greatness of flowers has been mentioned incidentally; in reality, it is general. For the practice of *vīrasādhana* must be performed by heroic men (*vīrapuruṣa*);
it may also be performed by the divine (*divya*), but not by the bound (*paśu*) or the vulgar (*pāmara*).
It is certain that even the work of a commoner is better than that of a beast;
for whatever convention or mantra-attainment was previously declared by me [is not for the latter].
The hero of great power should prepare collyrium, pills, and so forth.
Thus, there is a distinction between the divine [practice] and the heroic; that distinction is now described.
He is peaceful, disciplined, sweet, and endowed with modesty;
he is divine, like a god, generally heroic, and high-minded.
Thus is the distinction between the divine hero (divyavīra) and the other. That which is to be described hereafter is common to both:
"Whether adorned with divine ornaments or anointed with sandalwood paste..."
O Kulabhairava, you are both hidden from the cowherdesses and yet manifest.
With his limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, adorned with a red loincloth,
and clothed in red garments— whether he be a Vaiṣṇava or even a non-Vaiṣṇava.
Whether unadorned with matted locks or adorned with ornaments, may he, the Lord of the Family,
always remain joyful and contented in both dishonor and worship.

Whether one is intent on censuring other gods or even worshipping them— this refers to those devoted to other deities. One who is free from such [devotion] stands established in the Kulākula doctrine.
Endowed with his own true nature, he should move about upon the earth like a god.

The meaning is that the *puraścaryā* must be performed at the end of one's own lineage during the night, and not otherwise; for success will not be attained. Regarding these two as well, there is a prior service (*pūrvassevā*) which serves as the authority for performing the *puraścaraṇa*, as shall be stated.
O God, for a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas, there is no Vedic consecration (*śrutisaṃskriyā*).
Without devotion to Viṣṇu, there is no true devotion, just as there is no power without it.

Devotion to Viṣṇu, however, is ninefold; as stated in the Bhāgavata, it produces the characteristics of devotion, and even the longed-for blessings mentioned in the worship of other deities are not obtained [through it].
Therefore, devotion to Viṣṇu is superior to the devotion to all other deities.
The meaning is: wherever a person's horripilation and so forth are observed upon hearing a particular Vedic passage.
Just as liberation without the knowledge of Śakti leads only to ridicule,
so too there is no way to have authority over the Tantra without a Guru.
Just as a woman deprived of her husband is excluded from all ritual duties,
so too a divine lineage devoid of a hero is not a means for my accomplishment.
O follower of the Kaula path, one who lacks devotion has no authority; therefore, become devoted to the inner state. How can he whose family is undisciplined be a worshiper of me?
Therefore, one should act with such effort that [the disciple] becomes endowed with discipline;
for by the power of the Lord of the Family, authority over states of being arises from state to state in no other way.
Through that, the practitioner becomes a Kaulika by means of the purification of existence.
The Goddess said:
I shall explain the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva); listen with a concentrated mind, my child.
Having received the knowledge of the animal according to the rule, one should be intent upon that state.
First, for the sake of preliminary service, one who is self-restrained shall attain accomplishment;
he should not consume fish, nor should he even mentally recall a woman.
There shall be no greed for wealth from others, nor shall there be any mental attachment to enjoyments,
whether on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, and in a beautiful, sacred field,
one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual] and should diligently abandon all crookedness.
The deity, white in color, should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed.
There should be worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day, and one should perform the recitation (japa) at the three junctions of the day.
At night, one should never touch the yantra or the rosary;
one should not recite the mantra with devotion [at that time], but should remain silent in all ritual acts.
On the occasion of a festival day, the best of practitioners should never approach a woman;
having personally brought flowers, incense, and water, he should perform worship.
One should avoid sexual intercourse, its preliminary dalliance, and its social gatherings; and one should not approach even one's own wife with passion except during her fertile period.
One who has faith in hearing the Purāṇas and is devoted to the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas should not eat at night, O Supreme Lord; nor should the wise man consume betel leaf.

Whatever qualities or defects one encounters, one should diligently practice [to overcome] them all. Therefore, O Bhairava, by touching and remembering a lineage (tva-kula), as well as the cause and the substance, one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) after repeating [the mantra] three times.
One who is devoted to the Goddess should not wear red garments.
One should perform the ritual practices for as many kalpas as are mentioned in the Viṣṇukalpa;
however, such a person has the qualification for worship, but never for the office of a guru.
In worship—that is, in Kaula worship—there is a connection in both cases;
however, there is no entitlement for the former regarding the coming and going within the place of worship.
Previously, however, one should perform the rite outside of one's own country according to all the Kaula traditions;
one should not practice the Kula vision merely by staying in one's native land.
O Lord, even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are easily endured;
however, merely seeing you first—I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
The previous state of being an animal was my own nature; O Lord of all gods, although I am not truly an animal due to my omnipresence, O Master,
nevertheless, doubt arises within me at every step.
Better to abandon one's family; better to bring harm upon one's own kin; better indeed to face reproach from one's own family; better to suffer the ruin of one's own lineage.
Bowing down before the body with speech is better than bringing ruin upon one's own family.

One should not, however, form an association with those who were previously connected to me; for such a person is the leader of a family most burdened by sin, and there is no doubt that this brings great infamy upon one’s own lineage. The other [type] is divided.
This is the meaning.
Therefore, even great sin arises from association with animals;
under no circumstances whatsoever should one's inner state (*bhāva*) ever be revealed there.
That state (bhāva) and that manifestation (vibhāva) are established as two-fold in the bound soul (paśu);
that state exists through the nature of the bound soul because of its manifestation of the three worlds.
O Lord, the state of a hero arises, and from that, a god is born;
from a god a hero is born, and a hero gives birth to a god.
A distinction exists between the divine hero and [the ordinary being], yet it is said that there is similarity;
however, since emotion (bhāva) is a property of the mind, how could it be expressed through words?
Therefore, existence (bhāva) should not be described; only a mere direction has been illustrated.

"Mere direction" means a mere indication, a mere pointing out by way of that method. Thus, one who is liberated through initiation and consecration, contemplating [the self] as Brahman, and being liberated from those respective activities, is a divine hero (divyavīra).
The meaning is that it possesses the excellence of being a divine designation. The meaning is that because Brahman is of the nature of pure consciousness, it cannot be described [in ordinary terms].
Just as sweetness is perceived as the taste of molasses, O Lord, so too is the state of being (bhāva) and its manifestation (vibhāva) contemplated by the mind;
indeed, the one great state of being alone is contemplated by the mind.
Since the one and only great reality assumes manifoldness.
The Lord assumes multiplicity through the differentiation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); the meaning is that this occurs through the differentiation of the powers of the adjuncts.
The Lord, who is a mass of intense bliss, assumes the form of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is that one's own chosen deity is non-different from Brahman. That very Self, who is of the nature of rasa, is the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara;
He is to be heard, meditated upon, and indeed contemplated.
O Lord of Gods, the Lord is to be directly perceived through various means in the Āgamas;
He is to be heard from the words of the Vedas, and His thoughts are to be contemplated through reflection and other such practices.
One should meditate upon this by means of logical arguments taught by the Guru;
then, that very Self of all becomes manifest in an instant.
O Lord of Gods, when that supreme deity, the Supreme Lord, is directly perceived,
even the divine state dissolves there through various dispositions.
By "states" (bhāvaiḥ) is meant modes of conduct (bhāvācāraiḥ). A state is a state differentiated by the distinctions of this or that conduct; it is the very nature of the self (ātmasvarūpa).
The meaning is that, having dissolved the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the divine heroes, one becomes merged in the full Brahman which is devoid of adjuncts.
He provides an illustration:
"Just as the various kinds of food consumed become a single essence within the cow."
Through the yoga of superimposition upon milk and other substances, it assumes diversity in an instant.
From grass is born the divine juice; from that comes a superior juice. From that it takes away, and from that arises the emergence of the essence.

That which is born from grass, that which is from *parūṣaka* fruit, milk, and even from the sacrificial oblation (*havya*)—all these, through their various forms such as *laḍḍuka* cakes and so forth, belong to the class of the sweet. That which is the most sweet and so on is the very same cause; in that regard, its effect is not found [as something separate]. Therefore, taste is the cause. That very thing is itself, it is praised, it is the immutable (*avyaya*). It exists both as the effect and as the cause.

The meaning is that the essence of grass is not known. Furthermore, it is observed that neither the effect nor the cause of Mahādeva is perceived even by the mind. As it has been stated, milk and other substances are likewise not perceived by the eye as being the essence of grass; this is the meaning.
In the very same way, this self, though one and the same, is born and dies within various bodies and wombs; having been born, it is perceived as distinct due to the difference in time.

He is born; he is dead; he is bound; he is liberated; he is present before us; he is the person. He is woman; he is neuter; for he is indeed he; he is the wise one; he alone is the face. Here, the two uses of *tat* (he) are for the purpose of repetition (*vīpsā*). The Lord assumes manifoldness through various superimpositions (*adhyāsa*) which are always equal to Himself. Superimposition is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). He is the Self, truly one and the same.
The eternal one is of the nature of *rasa*. *Rasa* is perpetual bliss.
He is both unmanifest and manifest; he is certainly known through *prakṛti*.
Therefore, he is known through union with *prakṛti*, and never otherwise.

It is attained through devotion to the *prakṛti* and not otherwise; it is not obtained by devotion to anything else. Therefore, devotion alone is the cause—this is the meaning. Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"Just as a jar is not perceived without its connection to the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*)."
The other, even though existing, does not undergo differentiation.

The meaning is as follows: even though [the jar] is being distinguished from and distinct from another object such as a cloth, it nevertheless appears to the observer as having the nature of "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) within the scope of the cognition of difference; this is just like that. However, this [nature of jar-ness] is not known to reside in both the jar and the cloth through their mutual absolute non-existence (parasparātyantābhāva). That very [nature] is jar-ness.
The cognition of difference does not arise regarding the co-occurrence of the two [properties] clothhood and whiteness within a single substratum.
119a) Without me, it never proceeds as being endowed with a person.
Neither through union with a male, nor by means of [other] knowledges, nor through sacred revelation, nor through the lineage of gurus.
For this person is known by nature, and by nature the person is dissolved;
everything is presided over by nature, and the entire world is colored by nature.
By its very nature it undergoes differentiation; by its very nature it may undergo differentiation.
The meaning is that differentiation belongs to Brahman, which is itself undifferentiated;
this is known through Māyā alone as its material cause (prakṛti).

The superior [state] is through knowledge; when the inferior [state] exists as a ritual procedure, Brahman is known. When the mind is presided over by Me, it is dissolved. It becomes unarable, colored, and established in duality. That temporal duality is the bondage of *prakṛti*. But *prakṛti* is not a real entity, nor is it the true reality of the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). There are two negatives.

This is for the sake of repetition. O Maheśvara, having understood the true nature of the reality known as the "pair" (the two), and having understood the state of the two—Prakṛti and Puruṣa—one should become a knower of Brahman; such is the meaning. When that is known, this person himself becomes wise and [realizes] his own true nature.
Unchanging and the god of all, he alone exists throughout the worlds;
the Lord of Gods, the self-born Self, becomes manifest by himself.
The genitive case is used here because there is non-difference [between the means and the goal].
When the eternal Brahman is known in its manifold aspects through the means of approach,
nevertheless, through the application of *prakṛti*, it quickly attains direct perception.
But those who rely on their own vessels within a family, having boarded a ship and crossed over various lands and the ocean, emerge after a long time.

O Lord, just as one reaches the opposite shore by boarding a boat in an instant, so too does one attain Brahman through devotion to Viṣṇu; and even in the absence of that devotion, O Lord, [one attains it].
If there is no difference in kind (*vaijātya*), then how can Brahman be the cause?
Therefore, those [entities] which have emerged from another must indeed attain the status of being the cause.

These causes do not directly constitute the entity itself; rather, the causal status of an object is apprehended through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Through devotion to Viṣṇu, Brahman is attained, and likewise, it is attained through devotion to Śakti. In that regard, if there is no absence of the effect when there is an absence of the cause, then how can it be considered a cause? [In this case,] the flower...

Or rather, it is a cause but not a direct one; just as traveling by one's own land is a cause for reaching the other side of a boat, but devotion to Viṣṇu and so forth is the direct cause for a person’s realization, whereas the direct realization itself is of a different nature. Thus, the female state is to be known as *prakṛti*, while the male state is considered *puruṣa*. [This is] consciousness (*jñapti*).
"Let Bhairava, the Lord, be known through the differentiation of the knowable; let Prakṛti be known as cognition (jñapti) and the Person (puruṣa) as knowledge (jñāna).

Thus, by means of this differentiation, both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are to be known—this is the meaning. Just as light is the manifestor in the perception of a jar, the eye and other [senses] are not anything additional to that."

It is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). In the case of the connection with objects such as light, the causality of the eyes and other [senses] is exhausted by the mere cognition of the object. Therefore, for the cognition of "pot-ness" and so forth within that [subsequent] cognition, [the preceding cognition] is the cause; for others, it is an indirect cause (*paraṃparā-kāraṇatva*).
Furthermore, the state of being a jar (ghaṭatva) is indeed the cause of its differentiation;
it is not so for individual instances, even though other [phonemes] have attained the status of manifesters (vyañjana).
In the case of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) regarding an object, the eyes and other sense organs are the cause; however, "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is not the cause in that same way.
Similarly, in the case of qualified knowledge (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*), the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-jñāna*) is the cause, but non-conceptual knowledge is not.

Likewise, others such as the devotees of Viṣṇu consider the indirect cause (*vyañjanatā*) to be the mediate cause (*paraṃparā-kāraṇatva*), while [the direct cause] is immediate perception (*sākṣātkāraṇa*).
That, however, is both *prakṛti* and *bhairava*; the meaning is that it is indeed *prakṛti*.
[He] in whose mind the divine state (*divyabhāva*) or the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*) is established—p. 119b).
That very Self, liberated while living, wanders the earth for the sake of experiencing [the fruits of past karma].
That very Self, in the form of the Goddess, is conceived as Bhairava;
for among the three states (bhāva), two states are firmly established therein.
O Mahādeva, these two, the essence of the Kula, should not be spoken by the best of the Kula.
In this independent *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion for the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha, the twenty-first chapter [is concluded].
Now, one who has received initiation from a true guru for his benefit should describe the *puraścaraṇa* for the sake of accomplishing occasional (*naimittika*) or optional (*kāmya*) rites.
Regarding that purpose, here is the exposition of *puraścaraṇa*: "Having bowed to the pair of lotus feet of the venerable Guru, who is compassionate toward those who prostrate before him..."
Pūrṇānanda composes this *Puraścaraṇanirṇaya* (The Determination of Preliminary Rites),
because he has heard of the transgression [of failing to perform them] as taught in the final chapter on the Knowledge of Reality (*Tattvavidyā*).
As it is said in the *Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā*:
"O Mārkaṇḍeya, when the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is perfected, [the mantra] indeed bestows its fruit;
what then is the use of daily fire-oblations, what use of recitations, and what use of elaborate mantra-depositions?"
Regarding secret mantras, if their nature is to be restored, the *pradhāna* (the primary element) is said to be the *jīva* (life-force) of the mantras;
for just as a living being deprived of its life-force is incapable of performing any action.
Likewise, it is proclaimed that even a mantra devoid of preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) is effective.
And in the Yāmala it is said:
"Just as a living being devoid of vitality is incapable of performing any action,
so too is a mantra proclaimed to be when it is devoid of *puraścaraṇa*."
Therefore, at the outset, the wise person should perform that himself or have the Guru perform it.
Regarding the *puraścaraṇa* in the *Yoginītantras*, it is stated: "In the absence of a Guru, [one should approach] a Brahmin who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings."
One should employ this affectionate friend, who is endowed with various virtues, as well as a wife possessed of good qualities and accompanied by sons, in [the practice of] this scripture.
If one lacks the capacity, one should have it performed by a Guru; in his absence, by a Brāhmaṇa; and in his absence, by a woman.

As for its characteristics, that [practice] consists of the preliminary rites (*pūrvavidhi*) followed by the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra for the specified number of times as the preparatory service (*puracaraṇa*). The fire-oblations (*homa*) and other rites are its ancillaries (*aṅga*). [The text continues with: *lakṣa*... [lacuna].

One should recite the mantra the required number of times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), being pure during the day; according to this statement, the word *puraścaraṇa* has its power specifically in the act of recitation (*japa*). As for the separate mention of the subsidiary practice (*upāsana*) in the *Saura-puraścaraṇa-mata*, that refers merely to the ritual action itself and does not establish the power [of the mantra], because of the scriptural statement: "Success comes from recitation alone."

But where no number is heard [in the scripture], one should recite according to the number indicated by the wording of the mantra. This is stated in the *Yāmala*: "Or one may recite a hundred thousand times per syllable for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*. Even when a number is explicitly heard, there is an increase in that number according to the difference between the ages (*yugas*). As stated in the *Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā*:
However, for those [mantras] whose number is not specifically prescribed in the Tantra,
in all such cases the number of mantras increases by four in successive order.
The number stated for the Kṛta age remains as it is; in Tretā it becomes double;
in Dvāpara it is said to be triple; and in Kali, the number is fourfold.

Success in the worship of the Vidyās is attained within a single lifetime; furthermore, there is no need for the exertion of service over the course of the Yugas. As it is stated in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*: "By that [Vidyā], success is achieved; here there is no exertion of service over the Yugas. Also, in the *Ekavīrākalpa*:
"And [the practice] devoid of emotional states (*bhāva*) is for those who are base and of small minds; it is fourfold [in its requirements]."

Japa is prescribed for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*); it shall not be otherwise. This means that in the Kali Yuga, the *vidyās* of accomplishment will be taught hereafter. Now, regarding the selection of a place, it is stated in the *Yāmala*: "A sacred field, the bank of a river, a cave, or a mountain peak."
O Girijā, sacred sites, confluences of rivers,
purifying groves, secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, and riverbanks— these are the places for you.
A grove of Tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of bulls,
the root of an Aśvattha or Āmalakī tree, or else the midst of water.
The abode of the deities, the shore of the ocean, one's own home,
the presence of spiritual teachers, and likewise a place of one-pointed concentration of the mind.
The Pretabhūḥ and other such [sites], as revealed in their respective Kalpas,
are located at a solitary liṅga, in a cremation ground, in a secluded place, or at a crossroads.

"In mountain caves, on mountain slopes, in deserted temples, at the root of a *vilva* tree, on a riverbank, at a shrine (*caitya*), at the base of a hollow, or at the root of an *aśvattha* tree—this indeed is her worship.
Thus it is stated in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: "In a solitary *liṅga*, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads—one who stays there..."

The yogi should accomplish the Vidyā of the Sovereign of the Three Worlds. Regarding the "Single Liṅga," as stated in the *Matsyasūkta*: "That place within a distance of five *krośas* where no other liṅga is seen is called 'Single Liṅga'; therein, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is unsurpassed. Furthermore, in the *Vīratantra*, it is said: "In a temple of the gods, in a place devoid of deities, in a secluded spot, or in a lovely dwelling..."

If a dull-witted person recites [the mantra] in an empty house or a cremation ground, or if one of pure and stainless intellect, always endowed with devotion, recites it in Kaliṅga, by a pond, on the banks of the Gaṅgā, or on a mountain, he becomes the Lord of the World, the Master of all beings,
and a knower of the meaning of all scriptures; at the end of his body, he becomes a preeminent yogi who attains the state of supreme bliss.
In the *Brahmanirvāṇa*: "At the end [of life]"; and in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"Upon a corpse, or on a head, or in water up to the neck;
on a battlefield, in a womb, on dry land, or in a solitary forest."
In whatever place, or wherever the mind may find its absorption—
according to the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"Worship performed in Vārāṇasī bestows the fruit of perfection."
Therefore, it is said that [the merit] is fourfold in the presence of Puruṣottama.
It is said to be twice as great even than that in Dvāravatī specifically;
it is said to be a hundred times greater than that in the Gaṅgā, which is equal to it [in merit].
In Āryāvarta, Madhyadeśa, and likewise in Brahmāvarta;
in the Vindhya mountains, at Prayāga, and in Gahvara, it is said to be fruit-bestowing.
Beyond that, it is said to be fourfold at Lauhiya and at the Kuṇḍaka river;
it is equal to that at Kāmarūpa, and everywhere in both water and on land.
Just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent of all, and Lakṣmī is likewise the most supreme of all,
so too is the worship of the Goddess highly praised in the ancient city of Kāmarūpa.
There exists another field of the Goddess, Kāmarūpa, which is peerless; elsewhere the Goddess is rare, but in Kāmarūpa she is in every house.
Then it is said that [the merit] at the head of Nīlakaṇṭha is a hundredfold;
even greater than that, it is said to be twofold at the Herukeśvara Liṅga.
Thereafter, Kāmākhyā in the Yonimaṇḍala is said to be a hundred times more [meritorious];
whoever has performed worship to Mahāmāyā at Kāmākhyā, he has attained this.
If he obtains desires in another world, they take on an auspicious form;
there is nothing equal to him, and for him, no further duty remains.
Recitation performed at home is said to be of equal merit; in a cow-pen it becomes a hundredfold;
likewise, in a sacred forest or a beautiful grove, it is said to be a thousandfold.
Ten thousandfold is said for a mountain, ten millionfold for a river,
a hundred millionfold for a temple, and infinitefold in the presence of the Guru who is greater than the Infinite.

In this regard, one should understand that the divine Purāṇas which contradict the Vedas, as well as others characterized by the three states of being (*bhāva-traya*), are likewise [intended] for the worship of Śiva and the other deities. Now follows the rule regarding time (*kāla-niyama*). In the Vārāhī-tantra (p.
One should commence the *puraścaraṇa* during the waxing moon (*śuklapakṣa*), on an auspicious day favorable to the movement of the planets, provided that Lord Hari has not yet fallen asleep.

The time for *puraścaraṇa* is precisely the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*). A specific rule is that one must avoid the period when Hari lies down to sleep. Now, the rules regarding food: this has been stated in the *Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā*: "For those who are devoted to the Vedas from the beginning, who are pure, prosperous, and virtuous..."
For those born into noble families and of high birth, alms are recommended;
or they may eat sacrificial food (haviṣya), or vegetables, or even barley-gruel.
"Milk, roots, or fruit— whatever is available there" means from among those items specified.
"White, various, wintry rice, and one's own provisions."
That which has been placed by a non-Śūdra into a vessel, and then thoroughly stirred and lifted out.
The meaning is that, having been compiled from various sources, it has been extracted here in this different location.
Curd, milk, cow’s ghee, sugarcane juice (excluding molasses),
coconut, plantain, and *lānī*— these are likewise [forbidden] for one who has committed a sin.

The mango, the *mānalaka*, and up to the breadfruit (*panasa*), as well as the *harītakī*—because these are specifically mentioned [in this context], among all fruits, these are to be eaten. "In season" (*ārta*) means produced in their respective seasons; this qualifies the fruits, meaning that one should avoid those produced out of season.

Alternatively, there may be milk alone for the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) and for sustenance. Now, the external [prohibitions]: it has been stated by that same [author]: "Alkali, fermented gruel, meat, *grañjana*, a bronze vessel, black beans (*māṣa*) and the like, animal flesh, and even forest products—these are substances [to be avoided] on the discus."
One should avoid betel-leaf, eating twice a day, and the intoxication of improper conversation—
improper conversation meaning vulgar speech.
One should perform recitations, fire-offerings, and other rites with wealth acquired through righteous means.
Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment at all; everything would become fruitless.

The meaning is that wealth acquired by unjust means must be avoided. When one who is ill-favored in appearance and of low status accumulates a store of merit, there is no doubt that half of the fruit belongs to the person for whom he acts and half belongs to the doer himself.
Therefore, with every effort, a wise person should avoid another's food;
the tongue is scorched by another's food, and the hands are ruined by accepting gifts from various sources.
O fair-faced one, how can there be success for one whose mind is consumed by the wives of others?
[Furthermore, there is failure] from conversing with women, enemies, those who have fallen from their vows, outcasts, and inauspicious persons.
One should avoid false speech and crooked words;
one should not speak even the truth during the performance of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like.
One should avoid singing, instrumental music, and the like, as well as the sight of them constantly; likewise, one should avoid oil massage, the application of unguents, and the wearing of flowers.
One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it.
One should never touch women who have not bathed, nor Śūdra barbers, nor a twice-born man [who has not bathed].
A twice-born performing the *puraścaraṇa* should avoid bathing in water that has been stepped over by others, food not offered to the deity,
and he should not commit violence against living beings.
Indeed, there is no object whatsoever that cannot be abandoned for the sake of the kingdom, provided it is possible;

yet, when it is impossible, one should accept [wealth] from a source purified by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), other than from a relative, through domestic recitation (*japa*). In that regard, O lady of Anga, if one is unable to maintain purity day after day, one should not accept even alms from one's mother if they exceed the limit of passion.
There would be no loss of merit even after a hundred such eons. And in the *Yāmala*:
"One should avoid crookedness, shaving, oil massage, eating food that has not been offered, unpremeditated actions, and such things as body rubbing."
The best of practitioners should avoid betel nut, bronze vessels, eating during the day, and other such things as these.
p.
121a) Other [substances] are not prescribed for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth, such as eating [offerings].
Now follows the rule regarding what should and should not be done (*kṛtyākṛtyavidhi*).
One who is engaged solely in the practice of mantra should worship the deity at the three junctions of the day;
for the sake of accomplishment, one should recite the chosen mantra alone, either once or many times.
Then, after muttering [mantras] and drinking [the consecrated water], one should perform the mental bath and eat;
and one should bathe with either the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure water alone.

If one is able, there should be a bath with pure water; if unable, a bath with two or three handfuls [of water]. For one who does not bathe, there is no fruit [from the rite], nor for one who does not offer libations to the ancestors.
Having made the deity present and having steadied the heart,
and having bowed to the supreme lords and gurus, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind—
slowly and clearly, neither too fast nor too slow.
One should perform the recitation day by day neither deficient nor excessive;
this is declared to be the rule for uninterrupted practice, and one should not let a single day pass by.
Through the gradual passing of days,
success and awakening arise for one whose mind is well-composed and free from other thoughts, until midday.
One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one whose hair is loose or covers the neck,
one whose hands are unpurified, one who is impure, or one who is prattling— such a person should never recite the mantra.
In this regard, there is no fruit for one who has not bathed, nor for one whose hands are covered, nor even for one whose head is covered;
nor for one whose mind is distracted, nor for one whose mind is agitated, nor for one who is angry, deluded, or possessed by an earth-demon (bhūta);
nor for one who is naked, lying down, or walking, or for these very reasons.
They do not perform their recitation even while standing on a street, nor in a place devoid of a dwelling.
One should not speak with sandals on, nor with feet covered, nor while seated on a seat;
one should not speak with feet extended, nor while sitting in a squatting posture.

One whose mind is distorted by contempt for those who are lepers, afflicted with skin diseases, or deficient in limbs will not attain the perfection of mantras; therefore, one should be devoted to diligent effort.
She should not mutter the mantra alone, nor should she do so even with her kinsmen;
for she becomes fallen at the mere sight of the terrifying outcastes who rush toward her.
One should abandon the recitation upon feeling hunger, when moving in the wind, or when yawning;
having stood up and sipped water (ācamana), one should perform the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) once those [distractions] have occurred.
Alternatively, it refers to the sight of the sun and so forth;
for one who is free from the suspicion of feces, urine, blood,
and the like performs rituals such as recitation and worship, and shall always remain pure in every respect.
Upon seeing a cat, a cock, a crane, a dog, a Śūdra, a monkey, or a donkey, one should recite the *Sana* mantra; upon touching them, bathing is prescribed.
This, however, refers to general recitation (*japa*) and not merely to the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
One should always remain in a single village and go to pay homage to the Guru;
for the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, therefore one should worship him first.
One should constantly perform obligatory and occasional rites, associate with the virtuous,
always wear clean clothes, and sleep upon a pure bed.
Every day, one should wash the bed alone, fearless and pure.
Now, regarding the acquisition of ground,
it is said in the *Yāmala*:

Having gone to the aforementioned sacred field, one should perform the ritual acquisition of the ground (bhūmiparigraha) for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of such-and-such a mantra.
"May this ground be accepted; may this mantra be successful.
Having thus performed the formal acceptance of the ground, he establishes its boundaries on all sides.
The fourteen [verses] are exceedingly significant.
In rivers, mountains, trees, and the like, measurement is absent;
however, in the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), there is a measure of four *tulas* (handfuls), though in some cases a specific measure exists.
A place measuring one *krośa* from me, not crowded, and chosen according to my own wish—
either within a city, at its gate, or at a distance of one *krośa* or two *krośas* from it.
One should traverse that extent of ground for the purpose of dwelling for a day and night,
using stakes made from milky trees and consecrated with the sword-mantra.
One should dig [the stakes] in the ten directions and worship them there;
when the field has been thus secured with stakes, the practitioner of mantras remains unharmed by obstacles.

Then, one should worship the guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla) and others there according to the prescribed rite; having offered oblations (bali) to the lords of the directions, one should thereafter take refuge in the field.
At the proper times,
having observed the tortoise-wheel and the face, one should look upon the hut for cold and heat,
which is four-cubit high, square, and likewise possesses a beautiful altar-platform.
The meaning is that each direction is four cubits in measure;
it is beautifully adorned with moon-like splendor and the like, and decorated with archways and chariots.
Having constructed a secluded place, smeared with plaster, and enclosed by a wall,
one should then observe a single meal on an auspicious day.
Having bathed at dawn, the best of practitioners, being self-restrained, should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times for the sake of destroying known sins.
Thus is the indication of the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*.
One should propitiate the obstructing spirits (*vighnas*) with devotion through food, clothing, and other offerings;
and having honored one’s own guru abundantly with many garments and riches.

Non-existence has been explained above; the command of the *pada* follows thereafter. Whether this is done once or as part of the initiation (*dīkṣā*), that day is declared [as the time for worship]. Even the gods are worshipped following the *saṃkalpa*. In the view where recitation (*japa*) is not an ancillary (*aṅga*) of the worship, in that view, the recitation occurs after the *saṃkalpa*. Having sipped water (*ācamya*) and performed the preliminary rites (*dikyatīnatva*), then—

One should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). The meaning is that on the following day, having performed the daily obligatory rites and bowed down, one should make the resolve: "Desiring success in this mantra, I shall perform *japa* of this many repetitions; thereafter, I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite," while facing either east or north. Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): taking three blades of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water, [one says] "Oṃ tat sat."
In the month of [name], in the bright fortnight, on the lunar day of [name], desiring the accomplishment of the mantra [name],
I shall perform the *puraścaraṇa*. Herein, worship is to be performed three times daily, as well as constant recitation (*japa*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*).
The fire sacrifice (homodyāga) and the ritual enjoyment (bhukti) are declared to be puraścaraṇa.
Thus, according to the *Jñānārṇava*, the term *puraścaraṇa* refers to the preliminary practice (*purascarana*) for the worship of the five [deities] and so forth;

even in that system, this is the very same resolve (*saṃkalpa*). However, some include the mention of fire-oblations (*homa*) and other rites, while others desire it to be a separate ritual manual (*kalpa*). That is not so; for it is said: "By omitting even a single limb [of the rite], the practitioner of mantra shall not attain the desired goal."

Since no greater fruit is heard of from the words of the *Jñānārṇava* than this, and because it would be improper to apply a separate ritual procedure (*ullekha*) without first ascertaining [the source],
one should then recite [the mantra] and perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) every day with one-tenth of that number.
Alternatively, indeed, when the count has been completed, one should perform the fire-oblation.
One should perform libation (tarpaṇa) into the mouth of the deity with a tenth part of the oblation (homa);
and with a tenth part of that libation, one should perform sprinkling (mārjana) upon the crown of one’s own head.
The rite of feeding Brahmins should be performed with a tenth part of the *mārjana* (sprinkling).

According to this view, worship (*pūjana*) is a single auxiliary limb [of the ritual]: after the *saṃkalpa*, there is worship, and then the recitation (*japa*). According to the view where worship is not an auxiliary limb, in that system, the recitation follows immediately after the *saṃkalpa*.
Then, with water containing kusha grass and unbroken rice grains, one should proceed with the formal resolve (saṃkalpa):
"O you of sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon!"
"O Bhairava, salutations to you; you ought to grant me permission.
Having thus obtained his permission, he should purify the place for his recitation (japa).
p.
122a) One should perform the installation of the seats through gazing and other [ritual acts].
Having established the general *argha* offering and so forth, according to the sequence of one's own respective ritual manual (*kalpa*).
Having placed four full water-jars in the corners of the pedestal, beginning with the southeast, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī within them.
The best of practitioners should duly worship Durgā or the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrādhipa),
and thereafter perform the worship of the deity according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa.

Then one should perform the recitation (*japa*). Now, if they are unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites, they should perform a recitation according to the rule of doubling the number and so forth.
As it is said in the *Kulārṇava*:
"Whatever limb [of the rite] may be omitted, one should perform a recitation twice that number."
One should perform it three, four, or five times, O beloved of the practitioner.
And in the *Kulaprakāśa*:

"If one is unable to perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) and other rites, that [merit] is doubled; for Brahmins, the recitation (*japa*) is doubled. For the other castes (*varṇas*), however, it is declared to be threefold and so forth. Thus it is stated in the *Candrikā*.

In the event of inability to perform the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform recitation (japa); the number of recitations should be fourfold, sixfold, or eightfold, according to the respective order of the twice-born (dvijāti).
The recitation (japa) that is prescribed here for the twice-born should be understood as applying to the wives of the twice-born as well. For Śūdras, it is said to be double;

however, some authorities state otherwise. O Four-eyed One, in the event of an inability to perform the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform the entire mantra-recitation four times the number [of oblations].
— *Muṇḍamālā Tantra*.
O beautiful one, if one is unable to perform worship and other rites due to a lack of materials,
the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is accomplished through mere recitation alone.
The doctrine of non-attachment is established as the bestower of the three worlds;
therefore, having abandoned that [other path], perfection shall come through recitation alone.
O Goddess, when the Brahmins have been fed with other four kinds of articles endowed with the six flavors, everything indeed becomes fruitful.
O Kuleśvarī, by means of the worship of the five limbs of the mantra, all mantras indeed become perfected through my grace once that mantra has been correctly accomplished.

Now, the mantras for the fire-oblations and other rites: Having performed the mantra-recitation as prescribed for the *puraścaraṇa*, the practitioner of mantras should then offer oblations into the fire ten times the number of recitations, according to the stated rule.
Having given [the oblation], one should mutter the mantra ending in "svāhā" while reciting it in its fourth part;
then, with a tenth part of the *homa*, one should satisfy [the deities] with water ending in "svāhā."
Performing the *tarpaṇa* by reciting the mantra ending with "Namaḥ" ten times for each part,
one should sprinkle the head with water using the *kuṃbhākṣa* mudrā.
Having thus performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) with effort for the Candrikā-mantra, the best of practitioners should,

at its conclusion, perform a grand worship, feed the Brahmins, and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to his guru, as well as to the guru’s son. Having honored his own guru with many garments and ornaments, [he should proceed].

Having honored the poor and the helpless with the best of consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), success will indeed arise from a tenth part of the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Now, the specific ritual procedure (*kalpa*): as it is stated in the *Svatantra*:
"Being pure, one should perform a hundred thousand [recitations] by day; being pure, one should perform a full hundred thousand by day."
Then, O Dear One, one should perform the fire-oblation with sacrificial offerings at a tenth part of the number of recitations.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall satisfy [the deities] with water from a sacred bathing place, or with milk, or with ghee,
or with honey mixed with sugar, by means of which [they are gratified].

Then, with devotion, one should feed the Goddess with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) equal to one-tenth of the libation (tarpaṇa), which itself is one-tenth of the water-offerings made during the elevation of the consecration.

One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins who know the Kālī-mantras, and to the preceptor. The feeding of Brahmins with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) should be understood as applicable to all deities as well. One should honor those who know their respective mantras; however, if those who know only the mantra of the Goddess (Devī) alone are unavailable, one should give to ordinary Brahmins.
Regarding Tārā, however, there is this distinction:
eating sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) at night and being pure during the day, one should recite [the mantra] exactly one hundred thousand times.
Through the destruction of that [defilement] and through steady mental recitation, one attains perfection.
One should avoid [other] Viṣṇu-mantras and prepare an offering of tulasī leaves;
one should avoid mālatī flowers and avoid worshiping other deities.

One should perform the washing of the hands and the *saura* [oblation] at that time. Even if, during the time of worship, one might perform the washing of the hands and other such acts for the sake of the deities by chance, there is nonetheless a prohibition regarding these practices of the *vidyopāsanas* because they belong to the state of a *paśu*. Likewise, one should place the flower of the goddesses in the vessel.

One should know that the separate offering of food (*naivedya*) and fruit-water is indeed for the Lord alone; this is the meaning of the worship of the retinue of gods and goddesses. In the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the five-shrine system (*pañcāyatana*), these deities also become the limbs (*aṅga*) [of the principal deity].
This is because of the scriptural statement: "Having abandoned even the state of being limb and possessor of limbs, one should avoid the worship of others. This also applies here.

The worship of another mantra and faith in another mantra are common to all; likewise, the prohibition against worshipping another mantra is for the purpose of indicating that there is a greater sin in doing so. Now, the recitation of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) times of the *vidyā* is generally the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). This is because of the statement in the *Śāradā Tantra*: "For the power of Bhairavī, a true *lakṣa* [is required] by one who has conquered the senses."
In the *Jñānārṇava* and other texts, when the state of being the supreme peak (*kūṭaparatva*) is present, the definition of the collective [mantra] is that its recitation (*japa*) alone is *Sundarī*;

this is the very same explanation in the *Sundarī-prakaraṇa*. The number of recitations for the other goddesses should be understood from their respective chapters (*paṭala*). Such is the general rule; however, there is a specific distinction regarding *Sundarī*.
Now I shall describe the marvelous method of accomplishment through the various types of *kūṭas*:
the heroic [substances] such as semen and the bestowers of boons, adorned with sulfur and musk.
Adorned with ornaments of pearls and wearing a pure garland, the excellent one who delights in celibacy should worship [the deity] whose body is white through his own middle [self],
using white flowers;
the food offering (naivedya) should consist of milk-rice (pāyasa) filled with ghee, as well as ten thousand fruits.
Having offered a vessel filled with medicinal sweets (modakas) and various cakes and foods,
the practitioner should show it to the Goddess Vāgīśvarī.
Having formed a pure intention in his mind, or one that is common to all, he should recite the Vidyā known as Vāgbhava,
consisting of the syllables of Vāgbhava, while clearly remembering the Goddess Vāgīśī.
White as camphor, radiant, adorned with brilliant ornaments,
her hands resplendent with a rosary of pure pearls and stainless gems.
She holds a book, a boon-granting gesture, a lotus, and bestows fearlessness; her breasts are heavy with the weight of the *Mahābhārata*, she is radiant, and her form is beautiful yet inspires awe.
Proceeding by way of the path of Brahman through the sequence of the piercing of the *liṅgas*,
[one perceives] the supreme, divine nectar situated at the point of emission, resembling a stream of milk.
Having drunk the nectar of the Kula, one should enter the Kula once again;
having gone to Vakula once more, one should establish it at the end of the twelve.
In the thousand-petaled great lotus is the Vāgbhava syllable, like the full moon;
then, having pierced the Brahma-knot with the flow of the seventy-eight vowels and consonants, [one proceeds].
The knower of mantras, having filled the tongue with the water residing in the Mātṛkā, should cause the Laṃvikā to enter the root of reality by way of the Brahma-path.
From its root up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), one should contemplate that tongue as the form of the Vāgbhavī seed-syllable, which bestows grace, like the flame of a lamp.
Having raised [the breath] from the foundation (ādhāra) through the hands, the feet, and likewise through the three channels, one should lead the Vāgbhava [syllable] to the twelfth [center].
Having brought [the breath] to the twelve supports, one should pierce that knot;
then, having brought it to the tip of the tongue, one should contemplate the state of the lamp.
Having recited this one hundred thousand times, one becomes a destroyer of all sins;
moreover, O Mahākūṭa, one certainly becomes a master of speech.
He shall indeed become utterly mute, like a stone, if he is unable to paralyze the speech of those beings who are present in the debate.
A true wise man, whose splendor has been eclipsed by the dullness arising from the swelling of his own pride,
becomes a minister who composes great treatises through logic, having understood the meaning of words and sentences, and being adorned with the essence of reality.
One whose intellect is unimpeded in the scriptures shall become victorious and a lord of speech;
one should write this upon the tongue of a child within three days.
With honey, or with *ūrvā* grass, or with a rod of gold,
one should [apply] the nectar of the Vāgbhava-kūṭa, which bestows the state of Lord of Speech.
He alone is truly wise and illustrious, and certainly not a fool;
this is the Vāgbhava-kūṭa which resides upon the head of the child.
