If a wise person places his hand [upon the image] and recites one hundred and eight verses,
he too will certainly become like Vākpati, the Lord of Speech, in every respect.
This essential practice of the Vāgbhava [bīja] has been declared:
one who is beautiful with red ornaments and anointed with red perfumes and unguents.
Properly clothed in red garments, one should worship Madhyā from the Lotus Grove with red flowers and with saffron and other substances according to the ritual rules.
Then, in the center, [one should contemplate] the form of Kāmakalā, the sprout of passion,
resembling the rising sun and possessing the radiance of a flickering lamp-flame.
Proceeding along the path of Brahman as far as the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra),
she falls like a stream of nectar, resembling the juice of red lac.
Adorned with ornaments and possessing a luster like that of a *vaṃdhūka* flower,
she holds a staff and a water-pot, while her radiant hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate upon her who is the very form of Kāmarāja, as ruddy as the rays of the rising sun, within the Kula-pīṭha; then agitation arises in an instant.
The meaning is "for those who are capable. [One should meditate on her] with a luster like vermilion in the center of the heart;

she is the captivator of the minds of women, especially so. From the region of her head, raining down a stream of gems, through this practice, she brings the world under control. Through this application, she performs the oblation that subdues the entire world.
Now I shall explain: by means of the Vidarbha-union, one should form the eyebrows, the mind, and the breasts;
having fashioned the casket of Kandarpa, the best of practitioners should then cause it to be placed within the interior of the city, known as Makaradhvaja.
Having fashioned a hundred fish on a beautiful birch leaf with yellow pigment (rocanā),
agallochum (guru), musk (kastūrī), camphor (karpūra), saffron (kuṅkuma), and other substances;

One should cause the gold, situated in the center, to represent the established vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*). The practitioner (*sādhaka*), being desirous, should diligently accomplish the root-mantra, which consists of five hundred and ten [syllables], and the thousand-fold solar [mantra]. The wise one should strive to achieve this.
Alternatively, [one may place it] in the center of the navel, in the heart, or on the circle of the face.
He who contemplates in his mind [the mantra] that counteracts the ruby [passion], subdues the king of desire, and deludes [the senses], shall indeed attain sovereign power.
One should contemplate a flame of light extending from below up to the navel;
from there, it extends up to the crown of the head, possessing a radiance equal to a ruby.
Clad in red garments, staying in a house of lac-dyed wood,
seated upon a red throne, and adorned with red garlands.
Supreme bliss residing in the heart, having assumed the form of Tripurī—
one should thus meditate upon the seed-syllable of Kāma, beautiful in its manifested body.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice of the Śakti-bīja;
one should contemplate the Supreme [Śakti] within the body from the beginning of creation until its dissolution.
She was raining down streams of nectar, removing all poison,
possessing a golden luster, speaking with a radiance like a mass of lightning.
She holds a full lotus with a throbbing digit of the moon, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
and the gesture of knowledge, being the very embodiment of nectar itself.
Having meditated upon the poison situated within the body of the serpent,
the practitioner of mantras should extract it from the end of the twelve [finger-breadths]— the supreme delight of the world.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the Śakti-kūṭa,
beginning with *ka* and ending with *tālu*, from the Ādhāra to the Brahma-randhra, and from there back down to the Ādhāra.
Then, from the center, one should contemplate the seed-syllable of Śakti, possessing a radiance like lightning and fire, appearing as pure ruby, situated between the eyebrows.
And from that [heart] up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is the fourth [state], ruby-colored;
extending to the base of the thousand arms, it possesses a luster equal to a ruby.
Therefore, one should contemplate the Kula-śakti as extending to the Brahma-randhra;
such a practitioner of mantra becomes equal to Vainateya (Garuḍa) in neutralizing a thousand loads of poison.
It destroys thousands of *bhūtas* and *pretas*; of this there is no doubt.
It certainly destroys all types of quartan fevers (*caturthaka-jvara*) and others as well.
When that Mahātripurasundarī, complete with the [nine] peaks,
is meditated upon by the practitioner, she swiftly brings the three worlds under her control.
[The mantra] consisting of three [syllables],
possessing a ruby at its tail, brings about the success of the practitioner through meditation.
The sovereign powers of *aṇimā* and the other qualities, as well as good fortune, are produced;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should remember Manu, and he shall become dear to the Yoginīs.
The Great Wheel is his in the realm of desire; through it, he shall become happy.
By means of mantra and meditation, the practitioner will undoubtedly possess sons.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the bound souls (*pāśava-kalpa*). In this regard, this very procedure applies to the bound souls; however, for the crooked ones (*kuṭīla*), the authority is that "the bound souls are enemies" regarding liquor. Now follows the ritual procedure for the heroes (*vīra-kalpa*). Here too, in case of conflict, that which is stated in the *pāśava-kalpa* should be adopted. Now, in the *Vīra-tantra*: at the time of commencement, one must certainly personally smear the ground with mud. [If] the rite is deficient...
And cakes endowed with various flavors, milk mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar— these [are offered] in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Furthermore, at the time of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), having worshipped the supreme parched grains (*parāmāṣāṃ*).
The initiated ones [should be honored] with garments, flowers, and the like, and with foods consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa).
At the time of its preparation, it is certainly intended for one’s own cooked food;
indeed, sugar-candy powder is a multi-faceted elixir (rasāyana).
The coconut, the orange, the *sudarśaka*,
the *śivāka*, the citron, and the excellent pomegranate fruit;
likewise, fruits of various flavors and ointments of various fragrances.
Sandalwood, musk, śrīkhaṇḍa, fresh sprouts,
ṭaṅgaṇa, and lodhra— both those born in water and those born on land.
Having brought [the deity], who has manifested in various forms and is adorned with various ornaments,
into an empty house, one should purify [him] with arghya water.
Having performed the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should lead the mantras toward [the object]. As for the fifth power in the Tantra:
"The Naṭī, the Kāpālinī, the Śauṇḍī, the Rajakī, and the Nāpitāṅganā."
A daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a daughter of a Śūdra, and likewise a daughter of a cowherd.
p.
124a) Eight excellent women of all castes who are skilled and pure [are required]. And in the *Uttaratantra*:
"The actress, the *kāpālinī*, the courtesan, the *pukasī*, and the daughter of a barber."
A washerwoman, a deceitful woman, a follower of the Cārvāka school, a Śaiva woman, and a newlywed woman.
Neither chalk nor a water-clock is like a cowherd’s daughter;
indeed, all noble women are especially difficult to consume with fire.
Devoted to the guru and devoted to Śiva, free from compassion and devoid of pity,
primarily intent on concealment, she bestows all accomplishments upon the young woman.
Thus, one should begin the worship, properly arranged upon a cushion of flowers as is appropriate. As stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"If the worship of the Kula is not performed, the Kula alone turns its back."
When another woman becomes the guru of her own son, [that is a violation].
In the Vīratantra: "A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and one from a Śūdra family who is an ornament to her lineage;
a courtesan, the daughter of a barber, a washerwoman, and likewise a Yoginī."
Indeed, all these excellent women are specifically ten thousand times superior in every respect. And in the *Kulārṇava*:
"The Caṇḍālī, the Karmakārī, the Mātaṅgī, the Prakusī, the Svapacī, the Svaṭhakī, and the Kaivarttī—these are the women of the universe."
The meaning is that the eighth power consists of all the classes of women (*uṣit*).
This group of eight cognitions is proclaimed as the "Aṣṭaka of Akula."
The chamberlain, the vintner, the one who lives by weapons,
the prostitute, the female singer, the washerwoman, the artisan, and the female owl as the eighth.
Those who are fully engaged in mantra and tantra, who observe the conduct of the samaya,
whether they are virgins or established in their vows, likewise bear the yoga-mudrās.
At the time of worship, she who has obtained a son is to be worshipped by the wise as the Sahaja;
according to the stated caste, she may belong to any of the four varnas and proceed to the Kula.
She is beautiful, youthful, peaceful, compliant, and possesses a pure smile;
she is free from suspicion, endowed with devotion, and capable of applying the profound scriptures.
Then, she who was suitable, virtuous, with a gentle smile, speaking kindly,
devoted to her gurus and deities, pure-minded, and possessing the splendor of a Kaulika woman—

This Śakti, named Sulakṣaṇā, is charming, possesses excellent conduct, knows the distinctions [of all things], and is ever eager to propitiate the deities. She is the very embodiment of the sky and of progeny.
She is wicked, harsh, contemptible, yet adorned by her lineage;
she is of evil conduct, dependent on others, fearful, deformed, and lazy.
One who is sleepy, very powerful, dull-witted, deficient in limbs, afflicted by disease,
foul-smelling, hasty, foolish, aged, intoxicated, or a keeper of secrets [is not to be approached].
Pining for bad reasoning, contemptible, greedy, shameless, fond of quarreling,
with deformed limbs, wicked, tawny, and having a distorted face— such is Piṅgalā.

One should avoid such a Śakti who is joined with [worldly] mantras in the sacrifice. As for the sequence: having consecrated the eight Śaktis in order, having placed the vessel for the *arghya* offering and so forth as before, having sprinkled them with the *arghya* water, and having rendered them nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā* while reciting "vaṃ."
One should cause liquor, meat, fish, and chewed food to be offered;
then, O beloved, one should gratify the Guru with devotion by means of gold and other gifts.
In these two eons, mantras certainly do not succeed for one who has drunk liquor,
eaten meat, or gone to a woman in her menses.

Whoever should mutter [the mantra of] the goddess Dakṣiṇā, for him there shall be suffering at every step. Here, "Dakṣiṇā" is an elliptical designation (upalakṣaṇa) meaning "the goddess of any family."

Because it has been stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* and other general treatises, as well as in the *Nīlatantra*: "The practitioner of mantra, intent upon acting according to his own will, [should act so] for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
One should always recite the *Rahasyamālā* one hundred thousand times. Also, in the *Kulārṇava*:
"At night, naked, with hair disheveled, or even during sexual union, one should diligently perform this according to reality on a festival day for the sake of attaining perfection."
The procedure for all twice-born castes is prescribed here for the daytime;
however, for all others, including Śūdras, it is desired at night and yields great fruit.
Whatever desire one may long for, that one obtains perpetually;
this refers to those of the twice-born who are characterized by conceptualization (*vikalpita*). "Of the *śūdras*" means those who are free from conceptualization (*nirvikalpita*).
And in the *Kālikā-śruti*: "Then indeed, Kālikā Manupāñjapī, being pure in soul, [attained] knowledge..."

For one who has not been described as possessing dispassion (*vairāgya*), initiation into the *Śāmbhava* [state] occurs by its very nature. In the *Śākta* [traditions], one should practice celibacy during the day;

at night, while naked, one whose mind is incapable of sexual union should perform the observances of recitation, worship, and so forth, acting to please women, offering libations with fragrant substances, and worshipping with those very same things. At all times, one should perceive oneself as the form of Kālī.

One should meditate [upon this]. He who is devoted to his own nature becomes the protector of all; he transcends the slaughter of all beings. Through the fivefold mode (pañcamakāra), one attains everything: knowledge, cattle, wealth, grain, all living beings, and poetic genius—and none other. Just as liberation exists for the sake of sacrifice and for the sake of dharma, so too does all that has been and all that is to be.
Whatever is seen or unseen, whether stationary or moving—all that is known as the *preta* in the *Kālikā-tantras*. By realizing this, even a human being becomes one who possesses his own true nature;
he understands all scriptures, he dwells in all happiness, he becomes a renouncer of everything, and he becomes dispassionate.
He becomes a student of all the Vedas; he becomes a reciter of all mantras; he becomes a knower of all scriptures;
he becomes a performer of all rites; he becomes a friend to us both. Thus said the Blessed Lord Śiva:
"With a mind free from conceptual construction, one accomplishes everything. Then, having performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) according to this procedure—

And one should perform the preliminary practices (*prayoga*) and so forth. Now follows the alternative procedure for the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa-anukalpa*) for those who follow the Śākta tradition, which is bound by fetters (*pāśavaka*).
As it is stated in the *Kālīkulasarvasva*: "O Goddess, for those who are incapable [of the standard rite], the preparatory rite is now being declared. Lord Śiva said:
O Goddess, the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) to be performed in a cremation ground has been described as difficult to accomplish;
alternatively, the preliminary practice is now stated in another manner.
On a Tuesday or a Saturday, one should take a human skull filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and especially mixed with sandalwood paste and other substances.
Having deposited [the image] on the ground at a depth of half a cubit for some specific reason,
if then, on that very day, a person [recites it] a thousand times during the night...
The practitioner of mantra should recite it alone; he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree.
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is now described.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
beginning at sunrise until the next sunrise,
by reciting [the mantra] during that interval, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all accomplishments.
And according to the *Muṇḍamālā*: "O Great Goddess, having performed the recitation from sunrise until the next sunrise, the *puraścaryā* is thereby accomplished."
Also in the Kālitantra:
"Alternatively, another method of *puraścaraṇa* is described:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, from the moment of immersion until liberation [from the shadow]."
Having recited the Saṃkāmantra as many times as possible, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites;
a time other than the moment of a solar eclipse is recommended for this.
In that regard, whatever action is performed there shall have infinite fruit;
"to that extent" means that the fire-oblation (homa) should be one-tenth of the number of recitations (japa).
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, being pure and having fasted beforehand,
one should stand waist-deep in the water of a river flowing to the ocean.
Alternatively, standing in pure water in a clean place, being composed and with a one-pointed mind, one should perform the recitation from the beginning up to the point of liberation.

Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites ten times the number [of recitations] out of devotion; at its conclusion, one should perform a great worship and feed the Brahmins.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the mantra, one should satisfy and worship the Guru.
And in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Alternatively, there is another method for the procedure of *puraścaraṇa*."
And having bathed during an eclipse of the moon or sun, with a restrained mind.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the moment of contact until liberation;
having seen [the deity] and bathed, one should perform the recitation with a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) until liberation.
If a person, out of hostility toward the deities, should abandon the recitation [of mantras],
he becomes an offender against the gods and casts his ancestors down to the seventh hell.

Thus, because the performance of the *śrāddha* is mandatory at the time of the eclipse, one who exerts himself with a concentrated mind should recite the mantra from the moment of contact until its release. Otherwise, since the *śrāddha* is obligatory, it would be impossible even to begin the recitation; therefore, [the claim that it is] "not to be performed" is a futile statement. Regarding the subject matter of the recitation, there is no such rule as "at the beginning of the full moon," etc. [as previously stated].

It may be that the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) belongs only to one whose father is living; however, even for one whose father is deceased, [the rite] is performed because of the understanding that it must be honored through the performance of the *śrāddha*. Once the commencement of the recitation (*japa*) has been made by him, the duty of performing it is fully understood; therefore, the recitation must not be abandoned. By abandoning it, sin arises from the non-performance of the *śrāddha*.
Evil that has arisen perishes in this way; and thus the Smṛti says: "Even while not performing a meritorious act, one sinks into the mud like a cow.
In the Muṇḍamālā it is said:
"Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the [next] eighth day of the dark fortnight..."
When it has been recited one thousand times, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is considered complete.
Having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, during the great festival ending on the ninth day,
worship should be performed especially on the night of the eighth and ninth days.

On the tenth day, one should perform the breaking of the fast with fish, meat, and other such foods. Devoted to a state of devotion, one should daily recite the six thousand [mantras] that are dear [to the deity]. Furthermore: beginning from the fourteenth day until the next fourteenth day...
O Maheśānī, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired to consist of that many recitations (japa).
Indeed, mantras become perfected through mere recitation alone,
even without fire-offerings, gifts, or especially the worship of sacred seats (pīṭhas).
The Yonipīṭha, the Mahāpīṭha, and likewise the supreme Kāmarūpa—
any one of these two should be worshipped by one who is devoted to the melting of Rudra’s body.
"Recited that many times" means six thousand times every day;
this is because of the instruction regarding the first kalpa immediately following.
Also in the Kālītantra:
"In the autumn season, specifically from the fourth to the ninth [day],
having worshipped with devotion at night, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times."
One should recite [the mantra] alone in a secluded place, in a dwelling devoid of darkness;
from the eighth day until the ninth, one should be intent upon fasting.
One must never cause the path of the Guru to be transgressed;
otherwise, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired to be performed in another manner.
On the eighth day, at the time of accomplishment, the mantra-practitioner should enter the house of the one hundred and eight creepers and then worship them correctly according to the ritual rules.
Having adopted the previously mentioned ritual procedure, one should perform the worship and other rites;
being solely of the form of desire, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.

Having diligently gathered the root of the leaves of these [plants] that have grown there, the accomplishment of the mantra becomes real through the sight and worship of the creeper. Having gathered the "vermillion of reality" (tattvasindūra) of those powers by means of the root of the leaves— such as the leaves of the *śrīphala* tree— and having placed it upon one's own head, one shall become [divine] to that extent.
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
having written the mantra itself upon a creeper-house drawn in the family style (kulākṛṣṭa).
Having worshipped [the mantra], performed its consecration, and offered it to her,
and furthermore, having recited the mantra while being intent on the state of the deity;

Having dismissed her and paid obeisance, and having himself recited [the mantra] with self-restraint, he should offer an oblation to women in the morning; then the perfection of the mantra will occur without a doubt.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
having brought the Guru and established him there, one performs the worship of the Lord as if he were a deity.
One should satisfy one's own guru with garments, ornaments, decorations, and so forth;
likewise, one should especially satisfy his son, his daughter, or even his wife.
One shall become a lord of accomplishments (*siddhīśvara*).
Or else, as in the passage beginning with "atha vā" and so forth:
having meditated upon the lotus feet of the Guru in the thousand-petaled wheel (*sahasrāra*) according to the prescribed rule.
By reciting [the mantra] while maintaining the state of the deity alone, one shall become supreme in accomplishment.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to one's means;
by the mere permission of the guru, even a flawed mantra becomes effective.
Even for the gods, there is no authority in this scripture if they bypass the Guru;
and if the application of these mantras and tantras is performed [in such a manner], [it will be fruitless].
O Goddess, without the mouth of the Guru, the loss of accomplishment arises;
one should not show this mantra even to a disciple.

Otherwise, one will certainly go to the abode of the King of the Pretas. Now, regarding the explanation of mantra-siddhi beyond the [mere] performance of prostrations: in the *Tantrasāra*, it is said that one should recite the mantra for one month after having smeared oneself with [the ashes of] a corpse.
Gradually, step by step, his mantra shall become perfected after [reciting it] a thousand times.
In the Nīlatantra: "Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme among the supreme, the perfection of the Guru."
One who has mastered the secret mantra, however, achieves success even without the preliminary rites and other such practices.
Hidden within millions of scriptures, it has now been made manifest;
knowing this, the one who possesses special knowledge should conceal it out of love for me.
The seed-mantra of Ugrāprabhā consists of these two unprecedented syllables: *Śiva* (Ha), *Śikhin* (Va), *Śitabhānu* (Sa), followed by the fifth vowel (*Ū*) and the final vowel (*Au*).

Having meditated for even a moment upon this well-concealed [mantra] within the circle, one becomes a Lord of the Moment (*Kṣaṇapati*), with his gaze fixed on the vowels during the day. Its meaning is: *Śiva* is *Ha*; *Śikhin* is *Va*; *Śita* is...

*Bhānu* (the letter *u*) and the digit of the moon (*caṃdrakalā*, the letter *m*), which is the final of the fifth vowel (*ukāra*), together with *u*— thus *kū* is established. Having meditated for even a moment upon this pair, which is unprecedented and obtained from time immemorial, within the orb of the suns— the most radiant among the gods— for one who possesses fierce splendor (*ugraprabhāya*) or for the one who delights in the forest (*vanahargāyāḥ*).

It destroys or eliminates the evil that obstructs the accomplishment of mantras (*mantra-siddhi*) when wrongly perceived; thus one becomes most excellent. This is the external meaning. As for the hidden meaning: it refers to the thousand-petaled lotus within the mandalas of the suns and moons, specifically in the center of the moon. One should meditate upon her form as being of this nature.

Having contemplated the union (*sāmarasya*) of Kuṇḍalinī and Paramaśiva, one should contemplate the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) as having dissolved into the midst of nectar; then, having caused [the deity] to drink the nectar, one should meditate.
He is victorious; through debate he confounds the kings of speech who claim knowledge of the three cities (*tripura-jñāna*);

for a long time he has captivated the hearts of lovely women. He composes poetry never before seen even by the kings of poets, possessing a sweetness that is to be abandoned even by those who have attained perfection—how much more so by the mere assemblies of accomplished ones! This is the fruit of his former practice: [the beauty of] a noble maiden.

Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra—leaves of the entire Veda—into its own source (svayoni), [the practitioner], whose inner self has been purified by residing in the preceptor’s family, who knows the ritual procedure, and who is skilled in encapsulating [the syllables] with the *manu* (seed-syllable), should accomplish [the rite] with a concentrated mind, having removed all defects such as those arising from sleep or exhaustion. The meaning of this is as follows: in the *kulavadhū-mudrā*...

The letters of their respective independent systems, analyzed according to the distinction between vowels and consonants; the mantras whose Vedic and Āgamic origins were not grasped; those previously mentioned as "asleep" (*supta*);
those whose internal organs have not been awakened within the teacher’s lineage (*gurukula*); and likewise, those who are crooked toward their teacher.

The instruction is as follows: one who knows the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) should be intent on the accomplishment (*sādhana*). One who knows the required ritual procedure should write the mantra in a clear manner upon a cloth (*paṭṭa*). With a mind focused on the *pāhimā* and other verses, one should accomplish [the goal]. Having encased each of these three seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should place one's own respective mantra within the mudrā at the *mūlādhāra*, distinguishing between the outer and the inner.

The meaning is that for one who recites the mantra after having drawn a triangle or meditated upon it, success (siddhi) occurs. Having sat down, having focused on the path of the Kula and the honeyed [essence] within his own ground, he— being free from mental distress— should satisfy [the deities] with water from sacred sites (tīrtha), with blood, excellent flowers, bulbs, garlands, and ointments, together with a young woman.
"Veśas-tad-dhi-pādhyā-matesaḥ. This is its meaning: "Tad-dhi" means "O Goddess, by Your intellect it is known";

"aya daivī" means "this is known by the Omniscient One. Having established the state of *sāmarasya* (equilibrium) through the distinction between the external and internal, one should thus satisfy the bearer of the *veśas* with the waters of the sacred fords (*tīrtha*). This is the concluded meaning; [he] performs the service with all the ritual depositions (*nyāsa*).

Having worshipped the womb with your renowned retinue of attendants from former times, he—himself possessing limbs of pleasing form and devoid of shame—approached you, who are born of a most pure lineage and are the agitator of the Yoginīs. The meaning of this is:
O Goddess, [he approached] you, who are born of your own pure lineage and are devoid of shame; in the internal sense, [he approached] Kuṇḍalinī.

Because it is seen that the power which is external and whose nature is identical to that [deity] is indeed Mahādevī, she attends upon You as such; she performs worship with a multitude of retinues—that is, with clusters of rays—preceded by the placement (*nyāsa*) of all the ritual procedures (*vidhi*). By this, the general preparation of the *argha* vessel and so forth is indicated.

Having fashioned the limbs according to the prescriptions of the Tantras by means of ornaments and so forth, one should worship Kulakuṇḍalinī—who is the form of the Root-Vidyā encased within these two seed-syllables—by means of the method for binding the Yonimudrā.
Alternatively, on the external level, one should worship her by means of the ritual of the Dūtī-yāga; at that time, she becomes the agitator of the Yoginīs.

The meaning is that one becomes a master of perfected mantra (*siddhamantra*). The "beast" (*paśu*) is the wheel of the Brahmin lineage (*viprakulacakra*); the Lord of the Gods, the celestial tree, having fallen by a curse, is the Lord of the Kula (*kulapati*), the Lord of the Kula (*kulanātha*). Having joined those two, one should join that which is to be sought, encased within the *manu*, on the outside. The meaning of this is: the "beast" is the arrow (*iṣu*).

This is because there is no authority for [the practice] based on the power of heroes (*śūra*). Alternatively, by the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that one is the enemy of living beings (*paśu*), one attains the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and abides in the state of Brahman. "The wheel of the lineage" (*kulacakra*) refers to the *mūlādhāra*, the central channel (*madhyaśaṅkha*), meaning the channel situated between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
On the path of the family and the path of Brahmā, one is of noble birth. That refers to the two seeds previously mentioned. Being of what nature?
It should be sought as that which envelops the Manus; one should join it both externally and internally. This is one's own respective mantra.

Having formed it into a fold, one should contemplate Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is that very [fold], from the root (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). One should also contemplate her externally. O Mother, who indeed knows the nature of your powers? Even one of evil intellect, whose mind is fixed upon you, should repeatedly draw that auspicious [power] three times—[he who is] free from fear, dispute, and the web of doubts.

O Lord, he who has his body covered by vast clouds of dust from the surface of the earth beneath his feet, and whose path is honored by the gods—he, that wise one, becomes the sovereign of the city of liberation. One should write the mantra within the triangle at the *mūlādhāra*, enclosed between two seed-syllables (*vīja*) at the end of each of its three sides; [then] on the outer side—

He who should draw [the mandala] with saffron and other substances— everything else being merely descriptive and not specified as a fruit— the meaning is "by nine," that is, by the family dharmas worthy of worshiping the deity. One who is wise, possessing the knowledge of reality, and who performs the improper conduct of the *paśus* (the bound souls) by serving and worshiping [in this way], becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), meaning he becomes a partaker of supreme liberation.

Having extracted the seed-syllable (*bīja*) from the "shaking of the intoxication of Madana" (the god of love), and having placed that hard seed-syllable within the *Śakti* (the tongue) and the *Lokadhātrī* (the earth-element), if one recites it while attaining internal absorption (*antarbhāva*), then immediately those who have gone to the beautiful city [of the Siddhas], though ignorant, shall worship one as a perfected being (*siddha*). The meaning of this is as follows: *Madana* refers to Kāmadeva; this is the seed-syllable of his very form.

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used here despite the lack of distinction [between the two], as is Vedic usage (*chāndasī*). The seed-syllable *śakti* (Hrīṃ) is the "hard seed" (*kaṭhinabīja*), and the earth (*bhūḥ*) is the "earth-seed" (*pṛthvībīja*). If one recites this seed-syllable—which is not the world-sustainer (*lokadhātrī*) but rather *māyā*—along with the "toothless" (*dantabhīna*) state of worship, or in the form of *kuṇḍalinī*, then it becomes fruitful. As for the practice of enclosing (*puṭita*) and so forth, the first two seed-syllables are: *śiva* (Ha), *bhṛgu* (Sa), *mada* (Ra), and *pṛthvī* (La).
Endowed with power, well-perfected, born from the respective domains of Hari, Hara, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā), he is the supreme knower of rasa,

the agitator of passionate women, the intoxicant of Śiva, Hara, and Bhṛgu, the lord of the earth, whose power is the seed-syllable of Māyā, produced from the respective glories of Viṣṇu and the others; [he is] the creation and maintenance.
The knower of the supreme essence [should employ] the seal that effects dissolution; as for the practice of encapsulation through the division of external and internal,
one should first place the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) below the hard *bhṛgu* (the letter *ṛ*),
and having joined it with the "agitation" (*kṣobhaṇa*) which destroys the fear of the worlds at its tip, if one recites it while meditating upon her as being enraged, she is instantly subdued.

Vījasimha: The agitator within the families of noble maidens, the very essence of passion for amorous women; having applied the seed-syllable of power (śakti-bīja), he is the form of Smarahara-Hari, the embodiment of desire, and the lord of wealth (Kuvera). Through the service of the vast lineage of the lotus-eyed women of the enemy clan, his own heat is diminished at the end [of their union]. Madanaka.
O Madana, here the seed-syllable of Śakti is *krīṃ*; all else is as previously described, being enclosed within the *ayoma* [mantra].

If one worships the root of greed along with its foundation—the Śiva-Bhṛgu and Bhṛgu-muni—and if one seeks the root of dharma belonging to the gurus, then even the Lord of Treasures (Kubera), though not a yogi, would become destitute. If [one acts thus], even the Destroyer (Śiva) would be reduced to insignificance.
Therefore, this [is] the master of the auspicious; this is the auspicious day. Bhṛgu is that [source], and Bhṛgu has its root in greed.

With the seed-syllable Hrīṃ, together with the armor (varma), the root of the gurus exists through the sequence of contemplation (bhāvakrama). If one possesses that fruit, yet is of a base mind, then it is not to be invoked, like a deer that does not avoid the hunter's snare.
One should exclude the single [organ], the nose;
one should avoid the nose alone. That which is sought after as its sign is the pair belonging to Bhavānī.
When no one among all the excellent men was found capable of composing a mantra that would cause an unshakeable state of self-restraint, the King— having abandoned his own nose (the organ of smell)—
marked it with the crescent moon, which is the sign of the life-breath (prāṇa). Therefore, the genitive case is used here in the sense of "selection" (*nirdhāraṇa*) from among all the excellent men.

Everything else is as before. [The seed-syllable] *analān* (fire), excluding the letter *dha*, with *caṃdra* (moon) and *asamanayana* (the eye of the Uneven One), is the liberated seed of that Bhavānī. Maheśa is capable of describing even the second celestial chariot (*vimāna*). What is the use here of thousands of births, O Janman? Even the letter *ra* of the word *dharma* begins with *ra*.

"Varjanī laghu" means "one who has uneven eyes" (three eyes), and "iti laghu" means "one who is free from pride"—these two qualities belong to Maheśa alone, the speaker of this fruit; even Brahmā is unable to describe it with a thousand births.
O Mother, whoever among those born here worships this best of mantras for the sake of auspiciousness, [it arises] from the lotus feet of you, the Mother.

Out of devotion, he abandons his priceless body somewhere at some time; indeed, at some point, he may obtain the perfect fruit from the mouth of a guru, or from a child, or even from a beast, or from that which is written—even if it be poorly understood—suddenly and unexpectedly. O enemy of the essence of passion, remember the practices for liberation.

The meaning is: having seen this entire majesty of that very [Lord] as described in the Tantras, and having extracted it by the power of one's intellect from the enjoyments of all auspiciousness dissolved in the supreme state on the further shore; and having obtained it unexpectedly—without regard for prior or subsequent order—from some source whatsoever, on the further shore of the city of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva).

Because it is inaccessible even to Māheśapura, and because it is beyond Brahmapurī and thus inaccessible even to Brahmā; such is the supreme state (*paramapada*), and the meaning is that he is dissolved (*līna*) therein.

If one were to place the *kālikā* (the letter *i*) and the *bandhu-bīja* (the letter *u*) in the division of the city of fire (*analapura*, the letter *r*), and if one were to add the letters of the teeth (*daṃtavarṇān*, the letter *d*) joined with the directions (*digyuta*, the letter *10* or *ka*).

The seed-syllable of the eyes joined with the head [Ū], followed by the fierce seed-syllable accompanied by a protruding fang [R]; the meaning is that the seed-syllable which is in the region of the city of fire [E] is tripled. By that, the seed-syllable of Kālī is formed;
then the letter *ka*, from the dental letter *u* [the eighth letter before *u*], the vowel *a* arises, and thus it becomes *kā*.
From the extraction of the seed-syllable *bhūḥ* (bha) joined with the two eyes (*naya*), the syllable situated before it is the seed-mantra named *Kālī*;

this is joined with that name here. If one recites the fierce seed-mantra of the formidable fangs—that is, the *kūrca* mantra—in its entirety, which is the most secret of secrets, what power of affliction could possibly exist here in the three worlds?

If that person who delights in consciousness and bliss, who is solitary and free from worldly attachment, should resort to me— whether he follows the previously recited path entirely without fault, or another supreme path that is inverted and contrary in form— he is a human being on this earth who is truly curious; he is a human being who honors people, yet he is a human being who is curious by his own will.

A human being; yet, in the ultimate sense, he is a god. Now, the mantra: *śivāmukhī* etc., *harakuṃ 2*, *manetyādika e īla hrīṃ*, *śivetyādityādiha sakalaṃ hrīṃ*, *śivetyādityādiḥha sakala hrīṃ*, *mṛgumadetyādi sakalaka hrīṃ*.

With the mantra of Vanadurgā, beginning with *madanamadalatā* etc., [the seed syllable] *hrīṃ*; with *śivabhṛgvī* etc., *hasa hrlīṃ*; with *varaṇe t pāvaṃkāṃ* and *analaśirasi* etc., *ghriṃ 2*; and with *anala* etc., *trīṃ 3*; and *kāli lūṃ*.

There is no other means for the accomplishment of mantra than this. In the *Kulārṇava*: "Through the power of the instruction and by the grace of the venerable Guru, as well as through devotion to the majesty of the mantra, the accomplishment of mantra arises.
This mantra, received from a Guru who possesses accomplished mantras, shall become possessed of success."
O Kuleśānī, because of the practice performed in previous births, this mantra bestows swift accomplishment;
it has come down through the lineage of succession, preceded by initiation.
Whatever mantra is obtained through nyāsa becomes perfected without a doubt;
O Mistress of the Kula, one should recite the mantra with the *bhūtalipi* as its enclosure (*saṃpuṭa*).
Gradually, by reciting it a thousand times, his mantra becomes perfected;
he should then recite the mantra encapsulated within the letters of the Mātṛkā, arranged in a mandala.
Whether recited in direct or reverse order, his mantra becomes perfected;
by the mere recitation of the Mātṛkā, crores upon crores of mantras are accomplished.
There is no doubt that you have arisen as the sun; all this originates from you.
Through your wealth, you are the cause of the multitude of millions of mantras and the source of the Kula.
A single mantra obtained through the grace of the guru shall grant all accomplishments;
whereas a mantra heard by chance, or even through deception or force, [is ineffective].
Or one should recite that [mantra] written on a leaf; it brings about no harm. In the Gautamīya:
"If success does not arise when a mantra has been properly performed, one should not perform it again; thereafter, it will certainly become effective."
If, despite being performed again and again, the mantra does not yield success,
then the seven expedients spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed therein.
Now, by way of digression, there is the *lipi* (script). As it is stated in the *Śāradā*:
"I shall now describe the *bhūtalipi*, which is extremely difficult to obtain even for the *guhyakas*;
having acquired it, Śambhu caused the sages to attain all their desires."
The five short vowels are the junction-letters; they are also the sky, the water-bearers, the final, the initial, the second, the fourth, and likewise the middle.
In sequence,
the letters of the five groups of consonants, along with the vowels and the letter *kṣa*, together with the *u* and *duṃbhi* (the nasal bindu),
constitute what is called the *bhūtalipi* script, consisting of forty-two letters.

The meaning is as follows: the five short vowels *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ*; the diphthongs *e, ai, o, au*; the nasal *aṃ*; the sky (*vyoman*), fire (*agni*), and the upholder of the waters (*jalaṃdhara*); and the consonants *ha, ya, ra, va, la*.
At the end [of these] is *aṃ*. Then, in sequence: the second, the fourth, and likewise the middle [vowels]; the directions; and *ka*.

The letters *kha, ga, gha, ja, ḍa, ḍha, dha, dh*, the banner (*dhvaja*), *ṇa, ṭa, jha, ca, ḍa, na, ta, tha, ṭa, dha, da, ma, pa, pha, bha, ṣa*—and so forth; *śa, ṣa, sa* in direct order (*anuloma*), and *sa, ṣa, śa*;
*ra, bha, pha, pa, ma, da, dha, tha, ta, na, ḍa, ḍha, ḍha, ṭa, ṇa, ja, jha, cha, ca, ña, ga, gha, kha, ka, ṅaṃ, la, va, ra, ya, ha, a, aṃ, u, ai, e, ḷ, ṝ, u, ī, a*.
Having encapsulated all the mantras with this, one should recite them; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected. Now, as spoken by the seven Śaṅkaras in the Kuloḍḍīśa:
"If one does not find perfection among all these beings in this manner..."
In that matter, the seven expedients spoken by Śaṅkara should be employed.
One should perform retention, awakening, subjugation, drinking, drying, piercing, and ending with burning in due order; therein one will certainly become accomplished.
The "drāvaṇa" (liquefying) occurs through the seed-syllable *vāraṇa*, and the "mathana" (churning) occurs through the application of passion (*kāmayoga*).
That mantra is the mantra which, having been written with white camphor and saffron— [p.
One should write the mantra mixed with usīra and sandalwood;
that writing should be placed in the center of eight portions of milk and honey.
Through filling, recitation, and fire-offerings, [the deity] becomes melted and bestows success;
if he is not melted and does not grant success, one should cause him to give wealth.
One should recite that [mantra] encapsulated by the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī;
thus it becomes perfected, otherwise one must certainly practice this.
Having smeared sandalwood, kuṣṭha, turmeric, beeswax, and śrīkhaṇḍa,
one should inscribe the mantra upon these upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf.
Once perfected, it should be worn around the neck; otherwise, it will cause suffering.
Without wearing it, one should indeed recite the supreme mantra four times in conjunction with the steps.
And likewise, one should meditate upon the deity in the form of a human being;
having written the Vidyā with the milk of the sun, one should step over it with the foot.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) day after day with such a mantra;
then, one who is afflicted and overcome by shame shall become perfected, and thereafter, one should nourish [the deity].
One should join the three seed-syllables (vālayā) at the beginning, middle, and end of it;
having written the vidyā with cow’s milk and honey, one should hold the two nooses.
If this [mantra] becomes nourished and perfected, it will succeed; otherwise, one should perform the rite of withering.
Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra should interlace the vidyā with the two seed-syllables of Vāyu.
This knowledge should be held by one who has mastered it, having written it with the ashes of a hero;
even if one is emaciated, there is no failure in the accomplishment of the *grahaṇī* vessel through this seed-syllable.
In this regard, for the rite of incineration, one should join each individual syllable of the mantra with the seed-syllable at its beginning and end, both below and above.
Having written the mantra with the oil of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, one should wear it around the neck; thereafter, the mantra will grant success as proclaimed by Śaṅkara.
Having thus performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), the wise one should worship the Guru;
the intelligent one should reveal the Guru [to others], but should carefully conceal the mantra.
One should not show one's rosary or ritual hand-gesture even to one's guru,
nor to the mantra, nor to the deity of that mantra, nor to the guru who bestowed the mantra.
Devotion should always be practiced toward these three, for that is the primary means;
indeed, the mantra is to be known as the deity, and the deity is of the nature of the mantra.
One who desires the supreme state should not create a division between the two;
for when a mantra is correctly perfected, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished.

Now, the greatness of recitation (*japa*) through various measures such as one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) is described for the purpose of destroying those specific obstacles to the accomplishment of [one's goals] that arise from sins. It is stated in that very same work: "He who performs the recitation exactly one hundred thousand times is liberated from great sins."
By means of two hundred thousand [recitations], one shall destroy the sins committed even over seven lifetimes, including the primary great transgressions (mahāpātaka); of this there is no doubt.
Then, having recited it one hundred thousand times, one whose body is composed of the yantra-mantra shall destroy even ten million great sins; of this there is no doubt.
By reciting it four hundred thousand times, one becomes a great lord of yogis;
by five hundred thousand times, one possesses jewels and such like Kuvera—of this there is no doubt.
By merely reciting [the mantra] six hundred thousand times, one becomes supreme in the Great Vidyā;
by reciting it seven hundred thousand times, the practitioner of mantras attains union with the Khecarī.
O Goddess, by reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times, the practitioner will certainly become worthy of worship;
that supreme adept becomes a leader of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.
Kings and women, especially, come under his control;
one should recite the Tripurasundarī mantra nine hundred thousand times.
The form of Rudra is himself the creator and the destroyer; he is directly so, there is no doubt. "Sundarī" is an indicative term (upalakṣaṇa) meaning all the goddesses.
In the penis, it has the form of a lamp flame; in the lower lip, the luster of gold;
situated at the navel, it has the appearance of the solar disc; and in the heart, it is seated upon a crest of light.
Above that, at the throat, is the syllable *Laṃ*, resembling the sun and the flame of a lamp;
and between the eyebrows is the syllable *Vikaṃ*, resembling the orb of the moon, shining with the luster of jewels.
In the ninth [stage], one should pierce the universal splendor and those nine lakhs [of syllables] by means of the mantra, sequentially piercing the Kuṇḍalinī through the nine stations.
Having drunk the nectar situated at the point of emission (visarga), one should again enter the foundation;
thus, one should remember the mantra located in its respective places in due order.
Even one of meager fortune will certainly attain success; there is no doubt in this matter.
Or else, at Dharapadma, there is a Liṅga facing westward.
Staying there, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times,
adorned with camphor powder according to the sequence of family tradition,
remaining composed wherever one may be.
Then this vidyā becomes the subjugator of the three worlds.
However, in this case, only one who has performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) is authorized, because it is a ritual application (prayoga). And in the Jñānārṇava:
"I shall now declare the expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin."
The mind-wheel is [visualized] with red flowers, endowed with all its rays of light.
By following the sequence of family tradition alone, adorned with camphor and saffron,
ten million great sins are certainly destroyed within a single month.
All [deeds] performed in previous births come together here in an instant;
may Lakṣmī, the granter of all desires, remain firm in his house.
The knower of mantras should worship Śivā with javā flowers in every respect;
[this destroys] even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed in previous births.
One shall destroy [all obstacles] here, of this there is no doubt; the man becomes wealthy.
One should worship Śivā daily with fragrant flowers as well.
Having been liberated from a great sin (mahāpātaka), the practitioner, whose soul is freed, is instantly released from that evil;
[he should perform this] with śamī wood, sprouts of dūrvā grass, and leaves of the aśvattha tree.
Flesh certainly destroys the impurity created over seven lifetimes;
tell me how one should worship as before with fresh ketakī flowers.
Minor sins are destroyed here by its mere sight; of this there is no doubt. Unparalleled and most wonderful good fortune arises for him.
By worshipping with lotuses, one shall destroy all sins;
if one worships the All-pervading One, the sins committed throughout all lifetimes are destroyed.
The three worlds are to be brought under control, and all sins are certainly removed;
one is fully worshipped with bilva leaves along with aquatic flowers.
Then, removing [the flowers] in every way, he became possessed of great abundance:
jasmine, *mālatī*, *pātī*, *kunda*, and *śatapatra* flowers.
One should worship for the duration of one month with pure white lotuses;
by following this sequence in the Kulācāra, even a hundred sins born of a hundred lifetimes are purified.
It destroys [the sin] born of killing a Brahmin and other such acts; there is no doubt in this matter.
Liberation is surely in his hand; by his word, he is equal to Brahma on earth.
Or, with Agastya flowers, Navamallikā, Java, or red lotuses,
one should worship according to the previous procedure for one month with a serene mind.
The practitioner of mantra shall destroy all sins and become equal to Kāmadeva himself;
[he should worship] with Campaka, Pāṭala, Vakula, and Nāgakeśara flowers.
If the practitioner worships with white water-lilies and *sindhuvāra* flowers,
incomparable good fortune shall indeed be his within a single month.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter as recorded in the independent *Kulavṛtti*, composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha.
Thus, for one who has performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), there is the undertaking of occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) rituals.
Among those rituals, because they serve to bestow excellence, there is the worship of the *kula*.
Whatever may be threefold in that [rite], that is the fruit resulting from the worship of the lineage (kula).
One who chooses such a maiden—this is first the exposition on the worship of the maiden in that form. Now, the worship of the maiden (*kumārī-pūjā*). As it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"I shall describe, without doubt, the auspicious worship of the maiden."
By the mere worship of her, the worship of the three worlds is accomplished.
O Lord, I am indeed Sukumārī, established as the threefold form:
the supreme (Parā), the lower (Aparā), and the third, which is both supreme and lower (Parāparā).
At that time, when the gods, asuras, and mahoragas were [in conflict],
you became a young maiden for the sake of the three worlds.
The primordial one who effects creation is indeed directly perceptible, and she is threefold;
she has become Umā, the digit (kalā) whose form is creation within the ocean of existence.
One year old is Sandhyā; two years old is Trisarasvatī;
three years old is the triple-formed [Goddess]; and four years old is Kālikā.
Subhagā is five years old, and Umā is six years old;
Abhimālinī herself is seven, while Kubjikā is eight years old.
With nine [years] she is Kālasaṃkarṣī, with ten she is Aparājitā;
at eleven she is Rudrāṇī, and at twelve years she is Bhairavī.
In the thirteenth [chapter], Mahālakṣmī is the mistress of the seat (pīṭhanāyikā) with fourteen [syllables];
in the fifteenth, Kṣetrajñā with fifteen; and in the sixteenth, Aṃvikā is held [to be the mistress] with sixteen.
In some places, the reading is *carcikā*.
In this manner, one should worship in sequence until the flower appears;
one should worship from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the full moon (*pūrṇā*), according to the divisions of the waxing phase.
On all the great festival days, and especially on the Pavitraka day,
O Goddess of gods, one should worship the Kumārīs on the Mahānavamī.
During these times, the worship is especially abundant.
A devoted person should worship maidens and the sixteen-year-old [Goddess];
indeed, by worshipping with devotion, one shall possess all prosperity.
O Bhairava, one should worship each one of the *kulavidyās*, or even just one;

the meaning is that the worshiper of the *kulavidyās* may worship even a single one. This is for one who is incapable [of more]. If one is capable, one should worship them in increasing numbers, up to the sixteen; for him who undertakes more, there is a distinction in the fruit.

Thus there is an abundance of fruit. In this manner, one should worship Caitanya through union with the *praṇava*. "Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ"—these indeed are the *praṇavas* and the *ahnauḥ*; thus shall be the seed-syllable (*vīja*) of Caitanya. When joined with the two seed-syllables of *nata*, it may be performed by one, two, three, seven, eight, or nine times, O Goddess of Gods, according to the eternal sequence.
One should worship according to the prescribed rite; when worshipped, O dear one, they destroy obstacles and most formidable enemies.
Diseases, all portents of misfortune, and evil omens—of this there is no doubt—are destroyed.
Planets, yakṣas, bhūtas, vetālas, and serpents go to their destruction.
Or else, O Mistress of the Kula, there are the Guhyakas, Pretas, Yoginīs, and Guhyadākinīs; the Great Illusion is difficult to behold, and death falls [upon those who do].
Indeed, through the worship of Kumārī alone, neither death consisting of bad dreams nor any other great fears have power over him.
The supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as subterranean treasures, magical pills, and collyrium, are attained;
through the worship of the maiden, one becomes a manifest divine vetāla.
Water should be offered with the syllable *aiṃ*; the washing of the feet with the syllables *hrīṃ*;
the *arghya* offering should be given with the syllable *śrīṃ*; and sandalwood paste with the seed-syllable of the fourth [tūrya].
With the *kūrca* seed-syllable, one should offer flowers; in the sixth [position], one should cause incense to be offered. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hlīṃ kulanāyike hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

Aiṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hlīṃ, to the head of Kulakumārikā, svāhā! Aiṃ hriṃ śrīṃ hūṃ āṃ hlūṃ, to the crest-lock (śikhā) of Kulakumārikā, vauṣaṭ! Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hlaiṃ, to the armor (kavaca) of Kulavāgīśvarī, hūṃ! Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hlauṃ, to Kulakumārikā...
*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes. Having worshipped with *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hlaḥ kulavāgīśvarī astrāya phaṭ*, [one says]: *oṃ siddha pūrvavaktrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ japāya uttaravaktrāya namaḥ*;
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kubjike paścimavaktrāya namaḥ*; *aiṃ kālidakṣavaktrāya namaḥ*.
Through the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, one attains agitation once more, and the eight qualities reside in the seed-syllable;
through the Śrīyā seed-syllable, one becomes the Lord of Fortune (Śrīnātha), and through the Hūṃ seed-syllable, there is the destruction of women.
By means of the seed-syllable Bhairava, one attains the state of immortality and reaches the abode of the gods;
for I am indeed the Kumārikā, O Lord, and you are eternally the Kumārika.
Or one may worship either one hundred and eight or even a single girl;
when she is worshipped by the worshipper, the Veda, being purified, burns away [her] sins.
The maiden is the yoginī manifest; the maiden is all the deities.
She alone is the immortal form of Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ; thus the maiden is well-worshipped.
Asuras, wicked nāgas, and even those who are evil planets—
[all these] one should worship with a single maiden.
Likewise, from Kālāgni up to Śiva, as well as Gaurī and the others, along with bhūtas, vetālas, gandharvas, and ḍākinīs.
The Yakṣas and Rākṣasas,

though terrifying, are not able even to look upon all the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar; nor can they behold the earth and all other elements, including the entire cosmic egg with its mobile and immobile beings.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva,
as well as the Bharuḍas and all the Ṛṣis— [they honor] he who worships a maiden.
From Kālāgni up to Śiva, as well as joined with Gaurī and the others,
there are the seven continents, the oceans, and the fourteen worlds.
One should feed a maiden who is a virgin according to the prescribed rite, as well as Bhairavī;
likewise, one should offer water for the feet, the arghya offering, incense, saffron, and auspicious unguents.
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion, one should offer [the food] to young maidens;
one should perform three circumambulations and then proceed toward the auspicious eastern direction.
Afterwards, she should be given silver, gold, and pearls;
by marrying the girl himself, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed.
Even the killing of a cow or the slaying of a woman—every such sin—is utterly destroyed;
and his mother, father, and brothers likewise always [attain liberation].
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishment, everyone should perform the ritual of taking up the *kalpa*;
through that, there shall be enjoyment and liberation, as well as good fortune and all forms of prosperity.
The three-eyed Lord Hara dwells eternally in the world of Rudra;
and the fruit that comes from sixty thousand crores of horse-sacrifices [is attained there].
A mortal who marries off a daughter shall obtain this fruit;
gems, bell-metal, and gold should be given as a gift—thus indeed is Maheśvara.
Having rescued each family one by one, even though they have gone to the heavenly world,
those inhabitants of heaven enjoy their pleasures for as long as the earth endures.
The gift of a daughter is a great gift, the most excellent among all gifts;
misfortune is swiftly destroyed, and good fortune increases.
At the king’s gate he shall receive honor, and the royal fortune shall dwell with him of its own accord;
moreover, he should diligently worship all the Kumārīs.
O Bhairava, he who worships a maiden born of great fortune attains liberation at that very moment; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
And in the Jñānārṇava, the Lord said:
"All rites such as the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed without feeding the maiden."
And through worship, it shall become fruitful and possess its full reward.
O Goddess, by worshipping a maiden, one obtains the fruit of ten million worships;
the fruit of a flower offered to a maiden is equal to that of [offering] the entire earth.
By whomsoever a maiden is fed, by him the three worlds are satisfied;
the water given to a maiden is equal to the ocean.
O lady with eyes like those of a beautiful fish, the age [of the girl] should be equal to the Kulavelā; girls from one year up to sixteen years of age are auspicious for worship.
If they are married according to the prescribed rites, they grant progressively higher accomplishments;
however, O Goddess of Gods, those who are married while still children are indeed *kumārikās*.

If a girl becomes married at eight years of age, then she is to be known as a *kumārī* (virgin) from the second year onwards until the end of the eighth year; in that period, she is one who bestows the fruit of mantras—according to the statement: "She is to be known as a *kumārī* as long as menstruation has not occurred."
"O virtuous one, abandon doubt regarding the statement that [the rite] is supreme when performed by a *suvāsinī* who is not yet mature. O Goddess,
the meal for the *kumārīs* should be provided by the *kumārīs* themselves."
One should worship Śrīvidyā with that very same mantra without disclosing it to others;
therefore, she is called "the youthful" up until the age of sixteen.

In that regard, the statement beginning with "If there is manifestation of being (*bhāva*), that being is considered supreme" indicates the excellence of the fruit. Following that is the exposition of the *bhāva* of the young woman (*yuvatī*). This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala, in the Tārā-kalpa:
O Mother Goddess, salutations to you, the bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees;
I worship at your lotus feet—grant me your compassion.
By what means may devotees attain prosperity in this world and liberation in the next? Please tell me that method.
The Goddess said:
Listen, my son, I shall tell you that supreme secret reality,
by the mere remembrance of which one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
If that practitioner fails to perform the practice, death will occur;
yet for the practitioner who is devoid of recitation and fire-offerings, it bestows accomplishment.
O Omniscient One, I shall become your guide toward the awakening to reality;
this is the truth, the truth, and again the truth—this is my certainty, free from doubt.
Neither a woman, nor Viṣṇu, nor even Śaṅkara is a giver equal [to a wife];
women are life, women are gods, and women alone are indeed the ornament.
One should always speak to a woman without [her] being alone; otherwise, she will not be pleased. One should not enumerate the faults of women, but should manifest only their virtues.
One should not strike even one who is intent on a hundred offenses with a flower;
for even the impure becomes pure when touched by the hand of a messenger.
In ancestral rites, at a wedding, in giving gifts, and likewise in the worship of the gods,
one should first honor a woman and then commence the ritual act.

If one does not attain poverty despite [offering] perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as garments and other charming foods and edibles, then that knowledge is indeed the mantra for worshipping the cow.
Just as the daily *śrāddha* performed at the time of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-vaṃdana*) gratifies the ancestors,
even so is the worship of women, which bestows supreme bliss.

When a woman is hungry, I am always her hunger; when she is distressed, I am her distress; and when she is one who bestows a curse, I am that curse. You must bring about the sacrifice for the excellence of mother and father, or else you must abandon me, your own beloved wife, as a boon to Śambhu.
Or rather, what is the use of various kinds of recitations? Śiva is the one who acts for the pleasure of women and brings about the destruction of women and kings; of this there is no doubt.
For a man, devotion to the Durgā-mantra increases progeny; for a woman, it likewise increases her lineage. However, if she is internally agitated, it destroys her wealth and her primary status.
Pride is in vain, worship is in vain, recitation is in vain, and praise is in vain;
that sacrificial offering along with its fees is in vain if it does not bring pleasure to his wife.
Better that one’s life be lost than that one should take what is not given, whether it be water or anything else;
thus, one should sacrifice one’s very life rather than commit an act with another’s wife.
Generally, for one who subsists on stones, the mantra for drinking [liquor] is the Gaṅgākṣayodbhavā;
it should be recited three times by a man who is impotent, provided he is devoted to his mother and father.
If you were to become his companion, I would surely take away all of his growth, strength, fame, beauty, longevity, wealth, sons,
and youth; therefore, a woman of modesty should be honored with every effort.
Whatever one stands upon in this world, that very thing is indeed obtained.
In the end, one attains the fourfold liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Vaṃsa, I have thus told you of the practice of the Śakti-mantra.
Mantras do not succeed through disparagement even in hundreds of kalpas;
nor does Śambhu reside in the physical elements, nor is Rāhu eternal.

A woman is capable of honoring one who performs what is pleasing; thus, the lineage of the initiated is praised. Now, the power of the Śruti regarding the purification of the body is described. As it is said in the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
From association with those who have not been initiated into the Kula, the loss of spiritual accomplishment arises;
this is also the case if one listens to their talk or visits their dwellings.
"How should that person of noble birth worship the Supreme Goddess? Also, in the *Śrīkrama*:
"The practitioner, having been thoroughly purified, [should worship] among women, in the midst [of the assembly]."
There would be a loss of what has been accomplished, and Candrikā becomes angry.

Therefore, having performed the purification of the Śakti, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and other rites as prescribed. However, in the context of worship (*pūjā*), it is only the initiated Śakti who is fit for installation (*sthāpanā*). For there is this scriptural statement: "One who undergoes initiation into the six *kula* families [without being a Śakti] is indeed a sinner. Consequently, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the offering of the *māyā*-seed syllable are for the sake of mere sexual enjoyment; such is the initiation of the Śakti.

It is written at the beginning: now follows the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). That has been stated in the *Kaulatantra*: "O Maheśānī, when there is a desire for another consecration, one becomes pure through the utterance of the mantra; likewise, O Kanyakā, [one is purified] at the time of sexual union and at the time of initiation."
Even by force, one should strive to bring about the attainment of one's purpose.
Or with wine, semen, or even water, according to the mantra;
and whatever woman who is devoid of matted locks and the topknot [is approached], that is the *sāṃbhavī* mudrā.
First, having uttered the *vāsāḥ*, one should utter "to Tripurā";
then, having uttered the word "namaḥ," one should thereafter speak this mantra: "śaktim."
"O Dear One, O Sovereign of the Gods, at the end of the word *pavitrī*, say *kuru mama śaktiṃ kuru*; having uttered the wife of Vahni (*svāhā*), this is the purification mantra."
O Goddess, by means of this mantra one should always consecrate women;
thus, he shall ever find delight and attain all perfections.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one shall attain supreme liberation.
Also elsewhere:
Having brought a beautiful maiden who is devoid of shame or modesty—
whether she be his own wife or another's, initiated, and in the full bloom of youth—
The worshiper should always perform the worship after placing [the deity] on the left side;
he should then perform the entire network of nyāsa according to the procedure prescribed in his own ritual manual (kalpa).
Then, while approaching a woman, one should recite the *vidyā* Bhuvanatāriṇī. As stated in the *Kaulatantra*:
"A dancer, a female ascetic, a courtesan, a washerwoman, and the wife of a barber..."
A Brāhmaṇī, a Śūdra maiden, and likewise a cowherd’s daughter.
The daughter of a garland-maker is proclaimed as the "new maiden" (navakanyā);
having brought any one of these [maidens] there, into the circle of her womb—

Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then engage in sexual union; for it is heard in the Śruti that the mind is the oblation of dharma and adharma offered into the blazing fire of the self.
"By means of the path of Suṣumnā, I constantly offer my bee-like mental functions; Svāhā!
This great mantra, ending with 'Svāhā', is proclaimed for the commencement [of the practice].
Then, while approaching his wife, he should mutter [this] to the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds."
Supporting the Unmanifest (Unmanī) with the hands of Light and Space,
I offer into the fire the essence of merit and demerit, filled with the oil of attachment.
This great mantra, ending with "svāhā," is prescribed for the sacrifice of the good rite (sukrati).
Then, having meditated upon the one consisting of Brahman, one should release [the offering] into the mouth of the Kuṇḍalinī.

Now, another secret: O Gandharva, if one constantly gazes upon the Earth when she is in her menses for a thousand times, then, by the power of one's own spiritual realization (*svasiddhānta*), he shall strike her and enter the surface of the earth. *Hrīṃ*.
"Sleeping constantly for three days" is the meaning. "The earth is in her season" means [one should approach] from the feet of the venerable Guru alone.

Likewise, having placed his hand upon a mountain, being fearless and steady-minded, he attains poetic composition and goes to immortality; these are two verses. Furthermore, in the *Nīlatantra*: "Having seen a lotus as well as a reflection..."
Having gazed upon the broken person, the peak, the chowrie,
the solar disc, the sesame flower, the lotus,
and the triple thread, one should recite [the mantra] hundreds of times with a sense of devotion toward the Guru.
Happiness, serenity, eloquent speech, beautiful eyes, a pleasant smile, beautiful hair, a good rebirth, fragrance, sweet scent, and indeed happiness itself.
And listen with respect, O Pārvatī, to what he obtains according to the respective order:
having meditated upon the Mahācīnakrama and having worshipped the Goddess there.
One should worship that [deity] in sequence with the *bhava* flower out of a spirit of devotion;
he shall become the family deity (*kuladeva*), pure and established in the family lineage (*kulakrama*).
Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the prescribed rite within the great lotus at the root of the Tree of Brahman,
one should worship her in the grove of the Mother-letters (mātṛkā) with the essence of that stream of nectar.
He shall become the best of practitioners and dear to the Mothers;
encircled by the Mahācīna-krama-latā, he is the most excellent of adepts.
If one recites the mantra at night, that very [mantra] becomes a wish-fulfilling creeper;
provided it is encircled by creepers according to the number of lunar days in their proper sequence.
Then success shall be attained through the recitation of a thousand [mantras] on the new moon day;
however, if it is seen to be doubled on the eighth or the fourteenth day, [success is even more certain].
At that very moment, there is great accomplishment, difficult even for the gods to attain,
having written the seed-syllable of the Mahācīna-krama with saffron.
Having drawn a circle with its sides to be accomplished, one should contemplate it by means of the staff-like and circular movements;
there the woman afflicted by desire goes, where she may find that tree.

"Bīja" means the single syllable of Kālī, because it is liberated from [the constraints of] its own independence (*svatantra*). Having formed the *piṇḍa* according to the sequence of Mahācīna, as stated:
131b) "And having formed the *piṇḍa* according to the sequence of Mahācīna..."
O Goddess, he whose name is uttered when [the food] is taken shall meet death after a long time.
Having worshipped the Goddess a thousand times with *bilva* leaves and the marrow of the *mahācīna-kramalatā* plant in a cremation ground, the most excellent practitioner [attains success].
Then one attains sovereignty, provided she does not flee;
and whatever fruit results from the encircling of the Mahācīna-krama creeper, [that too is obtained].
Even for him, the lords of the lineages (gotras) are worthy of sixteen-fold honor;
the creeper-like [plant] yields a fruit exceeding that of Indra himself upon entering the house.
Such a one is always like a god, difficult even for the most excellent of practitioners to find.
O Goddess, who indeed is seen as the sixth of the speech-sounds?
Through the manifestation of this, O Goddess, death occurs; it is not otherwise.
Whether it be this ritual procedure, or this mantra,
I shall take away everything belonging to him, together with the hosts of great elements.
And you, who bring about their destruction, are accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs.
Now follows the worship of the seven seats (pīṭhas) as practiced by their devotees in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi.
Then, having brought the Goddess, the best of practitioners should first place her pervasively upon the crown of his head.
Having inscribed the previously mentioned mantra, one should complete it according to the lineage path (kulavartman).
First, one should worship the Goddess of the Seat with perfumes and flowers.
Then, having recited the mantra of the highly fortunate goddess Mūla together with her attendants one hundred thousand times, one should thereafter enter the Uḍḍīśa [mantra].
Having worshipped that seat known as the Yoni-mudrā, one should then perform recitation;
there, with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra of one's chosen deity one hundred thousand times.
Then, having gone to Kāmarūpa, one should worship Kātyāyanī there;
after reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should first worship Kāmākhyā during the night.
Then, having gone to Jālandhara, one should first worship Pūrṇeśī;
there too, being composed, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times.
Then, having gone to Pūrṇagiri, one should worship Caṇḍī;
thereafter, O child, she becomes Kāmarūpā, and one should first worship the one named Kāmā.
And at its edge, having chanted and worshipped the goddess Umā and one's chosen deity,
one should chant seven hundred thousand times at night, concentrated on the seven seats.
When the number is complete, he should ask again, "O Goddess of the best of families, as you please. If she is thus made to wonder, [he should inquire] regarding her own name, lineage, and birth.
"I am indeed your chosen deity; choose an excellent boon.
Then, having bowed to the Goddess of Devas, one should hear of one's own spiritual accomplishment.
If that goddess does not act according to what was previously stated,
then one should be devoted to the service of the conduct of the clan appropriate for the lunar mansion.
Then, one should worship Mahiṣamardinī on all the sacred seats (pīṭhas);
thereafter she becomes pleased, O beloved of the gods and the people of the clan.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one shall become a master of supernatural powers (*siddhīśvara*).
Thus, "Devīkūṭa" means the pair of feet; "Uḍḍiyāna" means the pair of thighs; "Kāmarūpa" means the womb; "Jālandhara" means the pair of shanks; and "Pūrṇaśaila" refers to the head.

This is the meaning. "Within Kāmarūpa" means within the center of the *yoni*. "Then at the edge" means at the anus. Thus ends the optional worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*). Furthermore, in the Kālītantra:
"Now I shall describe the procedure for optional rites (*kāmyavidhi*), by which one becomes omnipresent everywhere."
The practitioner shall accomplish the siddhi that is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The practitioner of steady mind who, having seen a flowering *kulāgāra*, recites [the mantra] ten thousand times, attains success.
Only by keeping it secret shall one become a treasury of knowledge;
[this applies to] words refined and vernacular, as well as Vedic and worldly.
They all come under the control of the practitioner, and not otherwise;
or else, Muktakeśa himself is considered to be the consumer of the oblation.
By reciting this very [mantra] ten thousand times, O wise one, this same fruit shall arise.
Thus, regarding the state of being a *paśu* (bound soul): "The practitioner who beholds a supreme woman naked [attains] ten million [fold merit]."
If one should recite it, he himself will immediately become beloved by the Vidyā.
Merely by the sight of him, the days of those who have reached the edge of despair become bright;
eloquence consisting of both prose and verse arises in his assembly,
and all the wise bow to him with joy, uttering his name.
Or else, due to familiarity with his speech, he becomes dull-witted;
or again, a man may eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) while his hair is disheveled.
He who recites it ten thousand times is considered a substitute;
this is the rule for the wise man who desires wealth or seeks power through intoxication.
A man who desires to become equal to Bṛhaspati should,
as a knower of reality, recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times after addressing the source (yoni).
If this [practitioner] engages in sexual intercourse with any of the celestial creepers (kalpalatas), he must recite the mantra for the pacification of that great sin (mahāpātaka).

If there is no contact with the creeper, then having diligently removed even the marrow [of the transgression], he should recite the mantra; thus she herself becomes a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā).
Even the fruit that results from being entwined by the great Chinese creeper (*mahācīnakramalatā*) does not equal even a sixteenth part of those sixteen digits.
A creeper that bears more fruit than arrows and enters the house [indicates success]; this is also stated in the *Siddhasārasvata*:
"If a creeper enters the house, one should carefully remove it from contact [with the body] and then recite the mantra."

For the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, there is a specific instruction in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: having observed the state of the menstrual flow (*rajas*), one should worship one's chosen deity at its source during the great night, performing worship for three days.
O God, one obtains the family of the hundred-thousand seats; of this there is no doubt.
O Bhairava, one also attains the siddhi of the vetāla, the siddhi of the sandals, and the siddhi of the sword.
The most excellent practitioner should accomplish the collyrium, the forehead mark, and the protection;
he should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight thousand times—this is the meaning.
From its arising,
the Kula is declared to be Śakti; that which consists of her worship and so forth is to be known as Kulācāra, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
In the *Devīyāmala*:
"O Goddess of the gods, that which was previously mentioned cannot be accomplished without a woman.
This region near women is superior even to Kāmarūpa."
The illustrious Goddess said:
Not by hundreds of thousands of *puraścaraṇa* repetitions, nor even by tens of millions of fire-oblations (*homa*),
nor by millions of *koṭi-homas*, nor by sacrificial fees, nor by extensive ritual worship.
