One does not attain the accomplishment of mantras without the presence of a woman;
for there is no interval between the exhaustion of a woman and the attainment of the goal.
O Śiva, the Śākta [devotees] desire to abandon Vārāṇasī, Kāmarūpa,
Jālandhara, or even other sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Sometimes she appeared as a woman, or even in the presence of women;
she had manifested in female form, exceedingly haughty and full of pride.
That [power] of mine should be known as hers; the remaining power, however, belongs to the Lord (Īśvara).
Whether she be a girl, intoxicated by youth, or likewise an old woman or beautiful, [she is that power].
Or, having paid homage to Kubjikā, who is exceedingly fierce, one should meditate upon her;
for women are to be worshipped by practitioners, even when they are engaged in any state whatsoever.
The root of all accomplishments is the woman who possesses every form and abundant goodness;
she is to be worshipped directly or even through the mind, simply by the sight of her.
Sometimes, indeed, women should be conversed with through skillful means, for women are like the gods; women are their very life-breath, and women alone are their ornament.
One should always remain in the company of women; otherwise, one may even become estranged from one's own wife.
Virtuous men should never, under any circumstances, despise women who are not to be known [as unchaste].
Even if one has personally witnessed their faults, one should never speak ill of women— whether they be one's own kin or the wives of others— not even once, nor ever at any time.
Censure of me, hatred toward me, injury to me, and my destruction;
likewise, censure of the Guru, hatred toward the Guru, and injury to the Guru.
The practitioner should rather perform his duty; he should never consort with a woman. He would rather not perform worship, and he would rather abandon the ritual offering (bali).
One may completely renounce family customs, family property, and family livelihood;
nevertheless, one should never direct the mind toward censuring women.
What is the use of saying much more? A man should abandon anger; nevertheless, he must never engage in reviling women or the like.
Having attained this body not in vain through the gift of pleasure given by the practitioner, she— being beloved by him who is now pleased— obtains the eternal state.

Now follows the determination of the duties of the messenger (dūtī). In the Pañcamī Tantra: "One should worship the supreme Pañcamī with flowers produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, with the *svayambhū* flower, and with flowers that bloom at all times."
Without the nectar of the hero-substance (vīradravya-amṛta), nor with that [ordinary] auspicious [nectar],
one should not worship the Supreme Goddess during the heating of the power (śakti).
One who worships with devotion and self-restraint shall find that the mantra becomes perfected for him; the Goddess shall become manifest to him—of this there is no doubt.
She is the form of worldly existence, yet she is composed of pure consciousness, formless, and the bringer of bliss.
She is the womb within all beings, worthy of worship, and the embodiment of yoga.
She is the eternal one whose form is the foundation, the bestower of intelligence, the giver of perfection, and the auspicious one;
she is the womb of men, the womb of women, and the granter of desires for all living beings.
She is the abode of all, whose nature is dissolution;
in her womb, it is said, the entire world still exists even today.
In that city where one dies and from which one is born again,
resides the Yoni, endowed with the three powers and consisting of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
In union, however, she is the fourth; when fully realized, she is the fifth, the Supreme.
Therefore, one should recite the Vidya that bestows divine bliss within the womb.
One should meditate upon the supreme beloved as united with him in the form of the *liṅga*;
she resides within the *liṅga*, has the nature of the *liṅga*, and dwells within the three *liṅgas*.
The beloved woman, moving through the womb by her own power,
dwells within the center of all lingas and resides in the Great Linga.
She is the very nature of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, and she is bound to the *bhaga-liṅga*.
She is the embodiment of desire, established in Rāma, and consists of the essence of the powers of desire and non-desire.
The beloved one is the heart; she resides there in the form of the breasts. She who grants desires and assumes any form at will should be worshipped with diligent effort.

Success shall come to men through practice; Sundarī herself will become manifest before their very eyes by means of flowers produced from a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka*, as well as with self-arisen (*svayambhū*) flowers.
One should describe the rosary as being made of yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma),
as well as camphor, agallochum (aguru), musk (kastūrī), and sandalwood (caṃdana).
Placing the rosary before him, he should perform the consecration according to the rules,
having repeatedly brought together a pure [rosary] marked with those specific substances.
Having purified the waters, one should then cast sindūra and bone [into them];
thereafter, a person should worship the deities upon a clean cloth or painted canvas.
Having recited the Viśuddhamāyā mantra, one shall obtain all desires;
having brought forth a divine maiden, a woman in the full bloom of youth.
He initiated her, who was of beautiful smiles, whose heart was filled with the bliss of his own arts, and who was devoid of pity and shame, by means of the root mantra.
Then, having partaken of various flavors and drinks until satisfied,
one should worship with garments, ornaments, flowers, and according to one's capacity.
Just as one should diligently protect a flower when it appears in its proper season,
so too should one carefully take hold of that which is a self-arisen flower.
The supreme practitioner obtains the divine self-arisen flower, which is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds; indeed, he shall accomplish on earth that which is otherwise unattainable.
If one should personally worship with that very flower,
having recited the *divyasvapnāvatī* mantra, the swift summoning [of the deity] will occur.
The deities, the planets, the nāgas, the rākṣasas, and those who are dānavas—
all these, as well as all women, become eternally subject to the king.
The best of practitioners, having performed worship daily with self-arisen flowers and having recited [the mantra], should place that divine garland upon the yoni at the point of union.
Performing worship of the Guru, the rites of attraction and the expulsion of obstacles;
listening to secrets, kissing the breasts, sitting upon the lap, and kissing the cheeks.

The purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is known as the preliminary stage; in the absence of that, they know the senses [to be the means]. Prāṇāyāma is declared to be the equalization of the breaths through the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Mutual gazing is taught as the function of meditation;
likewise are the scratching with nails and teeth, and the warming by incense and lamps.
The four special fragrances and the mudrās are proclaimed with affection;
[the five acts are] worship, going, praise, the emission of semen, and dismissal.
In the Devīyāmala: "Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you the secret according to its true meaning:
it is the truth that without union with a woman, a mantra does not attain success."
Indeed, attachment alone should be practiced, and sexual intercourse should not;
a woman who is firmly resolved upon the true state of being should always be honored.
Therefore, why should sexual union not be performed by my practitioners?
For she whose nature is my own being is indeed myself, whose very essence is mine.
"O Lord, how can she be won over by anyone else? For one becomes like the other through such a disposition;
he who has attained my own state is the one authorized for sexual union with her."
Similarity [of nature] occurs when there is firm knowledge. "Having me as his sole supreme goal," he sometimes assumes the state of a father, sometimes the state of a son;
sometimes he assumes the state of a teacher, and sometimes the state of a disciple.
He who possesses such constant and unwavering knowledge regarding women is truly Viṣṇu, Śiva himself, and a true yogin in all his actions.
For I am indeed the sustainer of the worlds, the mother, and the cause of birth;
for her who has attained my state, I alone am the certain refuge.
Sexual intercourse must never be performed by that person who lacks authority;
if a wise man performs it, whether out of delusion or through arrogance toward his teacher, [he incurs sin].
Whether he be a hero or even the Sun himself,
one who fails to honor the wife of his guru, the wife of a Brahmin, or the wife of his father shall go to hell.
Whatever merit there may be in sexual union, that same amount becomes ten millionfold [in its opposite];
this is the meaning of "sin.
For a woman who has fallen under the influence of illusion (māyā) is indeed composed of everything.
But I, filled with rage, shall destroy him, O Lord.
"His head shall be severed, as if one were to strike off his own;
even though struck by me, that evil-souled one shall fall into a great hell."

Or even if he should live for a long time, he faces a most miserable state of wretchedness; that sinner suffers from constant affliction by disease. At times there arises the torment of six-fold fever, at times a burning heat in the limbs, and at times a crushing pain in the body.
At times there may be itching, and at other times ringworm.
Loss of sight, deafness, lameness, and likewise hunchback;

other various diseases as well arise for the sinner. Furthermore, the destruction of the eyes, or likewise the cutting off of the ears, the cutting off of the feet, the cutting off of the arms, and even the cutting off of the head occurs.
Affliction from the king, affliction from bandits, and affliction from fire arise;
his family dies in great suffering—of this there is no doubt.
Even while making such prayers, he did not obtain even a handful of food;
subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and water.
The sinner who performs penance devoid of the fruit of austerity will be reborn;
for him, the ten-fold obstacles and the burdens from the officiating priests shall arise.
There will be constant strife within one's own family and perpetual injury to that family;
hatred will be instigated by friends, and one will boast of great power against enemies.
O Lord, even one who nourishes him, a kinsman, a friend, or a servant, may become poison for him; likewise, even a medicinal herb may become like the Hālāhala venom.
Wholesome, beneficial, and well-spoken words never find favor;
yet some speech that is harmful may emerge from the mouth as food from the mouth.
The mantras and weapons spoken by a woman become quite the opposite;
likewise, friends, servants, and attendants do not remain obedient to one who follows her words.
Even a householder who occupies only a single portion [of the house] will certainly be afflicted by the planet;
otherwise, mantras that have attained accomplishment would have their powers stolen away.
These faults which have been described do not arise from women or wine;
rather, they arise again from one who lacks authority, yet acts as if he were authorized.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of gods, what kind of person would be qualified for the worship of you?
And how does one who performs the ritual practice become qualified?
O Sovereign of the Universe, as this doubt regarding Mahālaya increases,
I desire to hear about that very matter and the means for its eradication.
O Goddess, by your grace, you ought to tell me that very thing.
Listen, O God, I shall proclaim the supreme secret, more secret than the secret.
This has been concealed in all the tantras and should not be given to just anyone.
I alone am the supreme knowledge; I alone am the supreme goal.
I alone am the supreme meditation; I alone am the supreme revelation. One should not perceive anything else whatsoever as a reality higher than me, the All.
I alone am the entire world that has been born, and I am Maheśvara;
O Śiva, a woman who is permeated by my being shall become just like me.
Then every person indeed becomes Sadāśiva through such cultivation;
thus, one distinguished by this knowledge shall be an authority, O Maheśvara.
For he indeed consists of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
[he is present] in the mother’s womb of the child being born, who possesses a fine phallus.
For just as *dadhikāra* never arises from contact [with other substances], so too,
having abandoned the mother's womb, one perceives every kind of womb.
Recognized as the best of practitioners, he sports upon the earth like Śiva. He whose mind is thus fit for authority shall always be an authority, as declared in the Vāgādi-sahaya.
Having attained my state, she is of my own nature and possesses great power.
Even in the case of a woman who has undergone transformation, it is indeed that very same [nature]. Thus,
he whose intellect is firm is undoubtedly qualified.
Having abandoned the womb of a mother and investigating all wombs,
that best of practitioners of the sciences sports upon the earth like Śiva.
If, however, another primary [task] arises at that time, one must strive diligently to set aside the former for as long as that new task requires.
For the sake of destroying the state of desire, I shall not have association with women;
that is my goal above all undertakings, O Goddess.
My birth is equal in caste to theirs, and the entire circle of the world is full [of them].
Having stabilized the deity through meditative cultivations, one should be intent upon that meditation.

One should contemplate the nature of the mantra, its phonemes, and so forth, with a restrained mind. As stated in the Devī-jāmala: "The practice of the hundred-thousand-fold lore (lakṣavidyā) should always be performed by a maiden alone;
it should never be performed by a householder or a married woman."

From such statements as these, it follows that those words which set forth injunctions (*vidhi*) are intent upon the qualification (*adhikāra*), while those words which do not set forth injunctions are intent upon the qualified person (*adhikārin*); this is the general direction. Now, because the necessity of the purification of the *kula* (*kulasaṃskāra*) has been indicated by such [passages] as, "If one who is uninitiated associates with a *kula*, the attainment of perfection (*siddhi*) does not arise," a detailed exposition is provided. As it has been said:
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Having brought his own beloved wife, who is virtuous and renowned for her own glory,
and having obtained a tree devoted to the lineage (*kulabhakta*), he should initiate her with the lineage-initiation (*kuladīkṣā*)."
The Guru, accompanied by Rakṣa, was happy; his eyes were rolling with the nectar of supreme bliss, his mouth was full with betel, and he gazed upon that noble and virtuous woman.
O daughter, let the teacher write upon his forehead-plate the wheel of power (śakticakra) with three enclosures, and then write the Kāmakalā.
In the center of that, one should place [the deity] consecrated with darbha grass and colored with kāmarañjana,
having invoked the Goddess there, meditated upon her, and worshipped her.
Then that young girl, having joined her palms together, should whisper the root mantra three times into the left ear of the assembly of sages.
Today she beholds her state as a mother, devoted to the worship and honor of her family;
having taken up one who knows her own lineage, she is freed from shame and sloth.
Having attained equipoise through the method as instructed,
and having received this permission for the hymn of praise, prostrate yourself upon the ground like a staff.
Save me, O Lord, you who follow the noble lineage, the lotus-like leader of the lotuses;
O you whose wealth is glory, place the shade of your lotus feet upon my head.
Having given the sacrificial fee to the preceptor, with eyes reddened by betel-leaf,
she should bring her own family to the highest state and perform whatever was seen [in the vision].
If one's family [tradition] does not permit the worship of the limbs and so forth,
then, having meditated upon the Guru at the crown of the head, [one should proceed] with the nectar-essence of the Kula.
Having gratified the lineage and meditated upon it, one should recite the mantra with an undisturbed mind.
Thus ends the initiation of power (śaktidīkṣā).
In the *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha, this is the twenty-third chapter, [concerning] the Maṭala yantra.

Now, regarding the sacrifice to the messenger (dūtīyāga), it is said in the Kulārṇava: The Lord said: "O Goddess, O you who are worshipped by the gods, I shall explain the occasional rite (naimittika) by which one becomes absorbed in Brahman; O Mistress of the Gods, this is for the changeless one and not for anyone else."
Completely freed from all doubt, the omniscient and supreme practitioner,
having performed the ritual of the sacrifice with the messenger (dūtī), becomes a sky-walker (khecara), O Dear One.

In the *argha* vessel, [one should visualize] Fire, Sun, and Moon; within the Moon, which consists of nectar, Śiva is present. Having scattered flowers, one should know that in the center there is the nectar of the Moon, which is always composed of various substances. By this, as stated in the *Kalpa*...
The section on worship includes the general preparation of the *argha* offering and so forth, as well as the presentation of the *bali* as indicated by the ritual manual;
following that is the seating and worship of the supreme messenger (*paradūtī*). Her couch (*mañcaka*) is made of gold, silver, or other materials, and is adorned with jewels.
One should place there a mattress made of pure linen.
Having scattered flowers in the center, as well as camphor powder—
here "rajāṃsi" (dusts/powders) is the intended meaning, though the use of "rajasas" is a Tantric usage.
O Goddess, there, upon the mountain,
one should first worship Maṇḍūka, Pṛṣa, and Rudra joined with Kālāgni, each situated one above the other.
The foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), likewise Ananta, Varāha, the Earth, the stalk (Kanda), the pericarp (Tāla), and the petals of the lotus (Padma).
Having worshipped the filaments, one should then worship the pericarp;
and having thoroughly honored the couch, [one should worship] there at its four legs.
One should worship these unprecedented [deities]— Dharmajñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya— in their respective order at the foot-stalks of the lotuses.
Having worshipped the five internal deities— Ātmā, Antarātmā, Paramātmā, and Jñānātmā— in successive order, one should then worship the three qualities (guṇas).
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the messenger (dūtī), who possesses her own auspicious characteristics, is beautiful, endowed with all marks,
adorned with the *hā-hā* ornaments, and as fortunate as the autumnal moon,
by means of the five objects of desire and even the five arrows.

One should worship Vaṭuka and the others in the four directions for the sake of attaining success; one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās upon one's own body, accompanied by the arrows of Kāma. One should contemplate a triangle above the head and perform your worship there in due order.
In the center of that triangle, at the place called Bāla, one should fully worship Kāmeśī.
And Gaṇeśa, the presiding lord of the Kula, as well as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī.
Having worshipped Vasanta in the triangles, O beloved of Madana,
one should thereafter worship Kalādhara on her breasts and in her mouth.
O beautiful one, one should worship all the digits (kalās) of both Kāma and Soma, beginning from the right foot up to the head, and from the left head down to the feet.
Now, as for the sequence in the ritual: by that [method], one should worship the digits of Kāma from the right head down to the feet, and the digits of Soma from the left head down to the feet.
These are Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti, and Manoramā.
O beloved, you are Manoharā (the heart-stealing), Manoramā (the delightful), Madanonmādinī (the intoxicant of passion),
Mohinī (the deluder), Dīpanī (the illuminator), Śodhinī (the purifier), and Vaśaṅkarī (the subduer).
Vaṃcanī, the goddess Bhagā, and the sixteen-fold Priyadarśanā;
these, conjoined with the sixteen vowels, one should worship as the arts of Kāma.
Puṣpārasā, Sumanārati, Prīti, Jayā,
Dhṛti, Ṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, Śailajā, and Jāmbūmālinī.
Aṅgiras, Śaśinī, Chāyā, Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalī,
as well as Tṛcchāmṛtā— these are the sixteen gentle digits (kalās).
As before, one should join the Śrīvidyā there through the sequential yoga.

Having worshipped the two wheels—which bestow all siddhis, consist of universal bliss, and take the form of the triangle and the bindu—one should then worship the Śrīvidyā Tripurasundarī. Even by means of the power of worshipping the complete wheel, the two wheels [are attained].

Worship is mandatory. Even a practitioner of another vidyā should worship his own respective cakra. If he is incapable, he should worship the root goddess along with her weapons, her vehicle, and her retinue, using water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings.
For one who is capable, incense and the rest [should be offered] to that liṅga immediately thereafter.
And [one should worship] Tārā, Bhuvaneśānī, and Mahātripurasundarī.
"O Goddess, this Vidyā, ending with the ten syllables, is proclaimed as 'Salutation to Śiva' (namaḥ śivāya). With this Vidyā, one should worship the auspicious Liṅga of Śiva."
One should worship that Puruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and the consecrated Vāmeśa;
likewise, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Siddhi.
Having fully worshipped Śāntyatītā, one should worship the six-limbed enclosure (ṣaḍaṅgāvaraṇa);
having uttered the entire Vidyā, one should worship Nandikeśa.
O Goddess, having offered [the oblation] between the testicles with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other items,
and having presented flowers, incense, and so forth, one whose senses and mind are conquered—
One should bind the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī mudrā and display the yoni; or else, O Goddess, [one should worship] the Goddess with the Kṣobhiṇī or the mudrā known as Gajatuṇḍa.
One should utter the garland of bhagas while reciting the seed-syllable of Drāviṇī;
O lady of excellent hips, when he is unperturbed, the supreme semen flows forth.
Uttering the seed-syllable *drāviṇī* while forming the mudrā known as *gajatuṇḍa*, the practitioner, remaining undisturbed,
should insert his *liṅga* into the yoginī’s *bhaga* and proceed in such a manner that her arousal (*kṣobha*) occurs; this is the meaning.
O Lord, there is no doubt that passion itself is directly composed of passion;
the sound of "sīt" is the form of the mantra, and speech shall become hymn of praise.
Nail-scratches, tooth-marks, and various other such acts—
as well as massaging, singing, praising, striking, and seizing— constitute [the forms of worship].
Embracing, kissing, musk, sandalwood paste, rubbing, and so forth;
churning, satisfying, piercing, the descent of semen, and emission.
O beloved Pārvatī, having purified the seed-nectar— which consists of Śiva and Śakti and is the supreme Brahman— with the family substance (kuladravya), one should pour it out.
Having abandoned the notion that the vessel for the *arghya* offering is made of clay, being free from conceptual construction and ever sinless,
one who has worshipped the Śrī Cakra becomes identical with the Supreme Brahman.
Thus has been told this knowledge, the essence, the delightful one, O fair-faced lady;
yet that man who harbors doubt regarding it becomes a partaker of sin.
A mantra practitioner who is overcome by doubt becomes one who violates the Guru’s bed;
therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, one should always remain free from conceptual construction.
And in the *Uttaratantra*:
"When the night has arrived during the *māyāyoga*, the man who has gone to the *kulageha* shall be fragrant with the scent of incense."
Smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with the ornaments of a cowherd,
wearing red garments and reddened by lac-dye, he remained within his home.
Clad in red garlands and gratified by red flowers,
one should worship the Mistress of the Kula with the conventions of the fivefold process (pañcīkaraṇa).
One who has attained the state of non-duality, who is endowed with virtue and good fortune,
whether she is always attended by others or has come to a secret rendezvous.
Or else, at that very moment, she was seized by Madana, who afflicted her;
she was smeared with red ointment, crimsoned, and adorned with the sun.
One should employ a female messenger who is adorned with fragrant flowers, beautified by all ornaments, perfumed with excellent incense, and well-attired.
One should worship her in such a state upon a cushion of flowers,
disregarding whether she has defective limbs, deformed limbs, or external conceptualizations.
The best of practitioners should avoid a woman who is aged, sinful, cruel, excessively greedy, or whose mind is devoid of devotion.
The characteristics of the presence and absence of power (*śakti*) have been explained in the *Kaulapuraścaraṇa*; this, however, is a summary.

Having properly brought together the *kula* and immediately after performed the ritual of anointing (*udvartana*), one should prepare a place adorned with pure silk garments and the like, and beautified with unguents.
Having adorned [the deity] who is free from fear, and having offered a welcome and a seat,
he should place [the deity] upon the middle of a cotton mattress with fragrant flowers.
On one's own couch, strewn with yellow pigment (rocanā), frankincense, camphor, musk, saffron, and other such substances, one should worship the Mistress of the Kula.
Having performed the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and thereafter the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma),
one should then perform the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa) and also place them upon the body of the Kula.
One should worship the couch in the center, with Maṇḍūka in front;
Rudra at the tip of the corner, Śakti on the support, and Ananta immediately after the tortoise.
One should offer the Boar, the Earth, the bulbous root, the lotus stalk, the filaments, as well as the petals, the pericarp, and the mandala.
One should worship virtue, dispassion, sovereignty, knowledge, ignorance,
as well as lack of dispassion, lack of sovereignty, and even vice.
One should worship the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Knowledge-Self;
having offered scents, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth, one should likewise offer incense right there.
Having established the Kula upon that [liṅga] and performed the ritual worship,
one should then worship the five desires within it and subsequently practice them.
Aim aim Kāmarāja, Klīm Kandarpa Ulūm Manmatha, Strīm Makaraketu, and Saḥ Manobhava.
Having worshipped with flowers combined with fragrance, beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with *Namaḥ*,
the leader of the lineage should perform worship in the four directions.

In this regard, according to the *Jñānārṇava-mata*, desires are indeed to be abandoned in other rites; however, this [practice] pertains specifically to the *dūtī-yāga*. Even in the *Jñānārṇava-mata*, this sequence consists precisely of desires, because it prescribes them as specific attributes within the *dūtī-yāga*: "Vaṭuka, Bhairava, Durgā, and Kṣetrapālaka."
In the *Kulāmṛtasaṃhitā*, having uttered the Vāgbhava, the Kāmarāja, and the Strīvīja (which consists of the syllables *hasaklema*),
one should pronounce the Ādhāraśakti;
then, having uttered the Śrīpādukā, one should subsequently say "I worship" (*pūjaya*) or "bow down" (*vada*).
With this mantra, O fair-faced one, one should offer a very beautiful cloth upon a bed,
having drawn a triangle there with vermilion and other substances.
In the Uttaratantra: Having carefully drawn a triangular yantra upon his head,
one should then worship Vālā in the center, seated upon a great corpse-throne.
He should meditate on Maunī Gaṇeśa at the tips of the hair, Kulādhyakṣa on the forehead,
Durgā on the eyebrows, Lakṣmī on the tongue, and Sarasvatī on the tongue as well.
One should worship Madana residing in the two breasts;
Sudhākara in the mouth; and the seed-syllable *glūṃ* on the back, as subsequently declared.
Residing in the right portion, with her blessings extending as far as the feet,
she is the worshipful Kāmakalā, especially for the sake of the practitioner.
Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Bhūmi, Kānti,
Manoramā, Vimalā, Mālinī, Ghoṇā, and Madanonmādinī are likewise considered [to be present].
Mohinī, Dīpanī, Śodhanī, and likewise Śāṅkarī, as well as Vañjulī—
these belong to the Madana family and are resplendent with their respective vowels.
Then the digits of the moon (Candrakalās) are to be worshipped from the head down to the feet:
Pūṣā, Valā, Sumanā, Rati, Prīti, and Dhṛti.
R̥ddhi, Saumyā, Amarīci, as well as Aśumālinī, Madirā, Śaśinī, Chāyā, and Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā— these are their [names].
Tuṣṭi and Mṛtā as well—these digits of the moon (Candrakalās) are to be worshipped;
they should be worshipped with the vowels for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
In the *Lalitāvyāptidīpikā*:
"Within her vulva reside three principal channels;
one channel is lunar, while the other channel is solar."
The other should be known as Āgneyī; the practitioner should worship them both.
The lunar goddess (Cāndrī) causes water to flow, and the fortunate one (Bhāginī) causes flowers to fall.
The seed-syllable flows forth from the fire; one should indeed render the yellow ones fruitless.
One whose face is well-pleased should worship with mantras joined by the *vāgbhava* and other syllables.
Also in the *Uttaratantra*:
"One should worship in the house of Madana, which has been smeared with red sandalwood paste."
Having uttered the Bhagamālā mantra, and likewise the three Tārās thereafter;
The Bhagamālā mantra is as follows, according to the Jñānārṇava:
one should write the Vāgbhava syllable followed by the word "bhaga," then "bhugo bhaganicāli," then "bhagodari," then "bhagānte," and finally "bhagamāle bhagāvahe."

One should write *liṅkha*, *tābha*, *godarī*, at the end of *bhaga*; one should write *bhagamāle* and *bhagāvahe*. Then [one writes] *bhaga* in the secret place (*guhya*), at the edge of *bhaga*, and at the edge of the womb (*yoni*).
Then, at the very end of all, one writes *nipāntāni* and *bhagavaśaṃkari*.
Then, having drawn the form of the vulva (*bhaga*), with wide lotus-like eyes,
one should write "Nityaklinne" at the edge of the vulva and "Svakṣye Sarvacāli" [therein].
One should write: "O Bhagā, bring me great fortune," saying "Vatā" (O Goddess).
Then: "Retas, suretas, bhaga, klinne, klinne, dravet."
O Mistress of the *bhaga*, moisten and dissolve all sentient beings!
O Infallible One, in the piercing of the *bhaga*, agitate and cause all to be agitated!
O Bhageśvarī, one should address sentient beings with the Vāgbhava syllable *mlūṃ*, followed by *yam* and so forth:
*maiṃ mlūṃ moṃ mlūṃ cāaṃ kinne*, and after that...

And [he said], "O Blessed One, bring all [these] here," and [he uttered] the seed-syllable of the woman (*strīvīja*), which is the syllable *hrīm*, consisting of the power of the final limit (*antavalema*).
Having written [the mantra of] Bhuvaneśī, this Nityā Bhagamālinī has been described here incidentally; she is the lore that brings all the worlds under one's control.
Having worshipped the wheel of vows with perfumes, flowers, and likewise unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as incense, lamps, and various food offerings, the practitioner of the lineage [should proceed].
Having performed the rite up to the embrace, one should personally remove that which remains as the leavings;
then one should worship one's own head with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, for it is infinite.
Then the root mantra: *aiṃ krīṃ*.
After that, one should worship Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and also Vāmadeva and Īśvara.

In this context, "tatpuruṣa" is an illustration; for the six limbs were indeed assigned [to the mantra]. As it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "The preceptor should perform the six limbs of the mantra with six syllables;
he should assign the five forms beginning with the first syllable of the mantra in their proper order."
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and Vidyā follow immediately after that.
Then Śānti and Śāntyatītā; immediately after that, having recited the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) and all the vidyās, one should worship the triangle.
In the *Kulāmṛtasaṃhitā*:
"In this [tradition], there is no invocation (*āvāhana*) nor even the placement of the vital breaths (*jīvanyāsa*) and so forth;
here, one should worship the chosen goddess with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) alone."
Thus it is said in the Uttaratantra:
"The Goddess Avadhūteśvarī, Kāmākhyā, Samayā,
Vajreśvarī, Kālikā, and likewise Ādivārāhī."
There the practitioner should worship Mahācaṇḍeśvarī Tārā;
then, having obtained her permission and offered excellent betel leaf, he should proceed.
And having deposited Śiva there with the mudrā called Gajatuṇḍa—
the Gajatuṇḍa mudrā is as described in the Jñānārṇava:
one should join the thumb, ring finger, and middle finger in the form of a vulva (yoni).
O Goddess, she who has the form of an elephant's trunk causes moistening for women.
Now, regarding the application of the time of commencement, there is another statement showing its nature as a mantra. For example:
"At whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti arises, at that very moment the mantra consisting of the pair—dharma, adharma, and so forth—is to be grasped."
Then, with an undistracted mind, one should worship [the deity] one hundred and eight times, or one thousand and eight times. Likewise, it is stated in the *Uttaratantra*:
"One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, free from agitation."
Or even one hundred and eight times, remaining unperturbed and with a steady mind.

At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer that [recitation] to the deity of that recitation; immediately thereafter, for a long time, one should worship her as she is agitated within the mouth of the god of love (Manobhava).
Then, having taken the essence of the "Galaccaṃdra" (the moon of the skull) from that [liṅga], which is the *kuṇḍagolaka*,
one should join it with sandalwood and so forth at the end of the mantra for the installation of the *argha* offering.
And in the Jñānārṇava: "In the union of Śiva and Śakti alone—of this there is no doubt. And in the Jñānārṇava:
"Embracing, kissing, the massaging of the breasts, as well as gazing, touching, the arousal of one's own [sexual] transformation, and the friction of the linga."
One should perform the entry and stabilization and worship with nine flowers.
Also, in the Rudrayāmala:
"From union, bliss arises; supreme bliss does not last for even a moment."
A man should diligently take up the rare nectar of the lineage.
With that divine nectar, one should satisfy the supreme Tripurā;
her presence shines forth instantly, and being pleased, she bestows accomplishment.
One should perform the libation for all the deities with the nectars,
and likewise perform the libation for all the gurus and practitioners.
Indeed, all become satisfied by that divine nectar;
at whatever time the practitioner performs [the rite], it is accomplished at that very moment.
Also in the *Samayācāra*: "The wise one, having taken the nectar of the *kula*, should then cast it into the womb. For one who is incapable, [the practice] is in brief:
the throwing into the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is the rite; that has been stated in the *Kulāmṛtasaṃhitā*:
"Having brought a beautiful woman who is initiated and endowed with youth..."
Whether it be his own wife or another's wife, she is devoid of both shame and modesty.
Seated facing the east at midnight,
he gave her betel-leaf accompanied by the appropriate ritual formulae and performed the ritual depositions (nyāsa).

Then, with her nails, she should draw the *sīmantam* (parting line) on his chest; thereafter, in the temple of the Mind-born God, they should perform the unrestrained sport of Mātaṅga, striking each other’s feet, ankles,
and hips with their thumbs.
Having uttered "syaguruṣtauṃ," the practitioner should then recite "ktemātmakaṃ";
thereafter, having uttered "llūṃ plāṃ vaḥ," the practitioner [should proceed] with this mantra.
Having displayed the *yonimudrā*, remaining silent, one should contemplate agitation;
then one should utter the *vāgbhava*, the *kāmarāja*, and the *vadhūbīja*.
Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā*,
the practitioner indeed utters the *vāgbhava* mantra and thereafter should speak *lleṃ klaiṃ llūṃ*.
One should intentionally cause the agitation of that Māyā, who is composed of the syllables *kṣa-mā-g-lau-t-mā*.
Then, by means of the root mantra, one should cast her into the womb through the fivefold process.
This is the Vidyā named Satalī, which effects the total loss of consciousness in others.

One should offer three handfuls of flowers, or otherwise, one should contemplate the arousal [of the seed-syllables]. Then one should utter [the mantra] at the throat with *vāk* and *māyā*, but not in the mind.
One should utter *retoṣum* and *paradvaṃdvam*, then say *aiṃ* and *llūṃ*;
having addressed *kāmastri*, one should then utter *māyā*.
The other [mantra] is known to consist of twenty syllables, with two vowels and no consonants;
one should write this vidyā upon its head and practice sexual union.
I constantly offer the sense-activities as oblations into the fire of the Self with the ladle of knowledge, using dharma and adharma as the clarified butter, along the path of Suṣumṇā; Svāhā!
By means of this mantra, "Gudūmāgajavaktra," the practitioner should regard himself as Śiva and the Goddess as his own form, Śakti.
Having meditated upon the essential nature of the power of the deity, the practitioner should enter the *liṅga* into the *yoni*; he should repeatedly utter the mantra *pratighātam*.
In the case of *japa* ending with "svāhā," the wise man should not relinquish his own vital energy (*vīrya*).
With pure mantras and medicinal herbs, one should never perform the churning of the womb (*yoni-pramathana*).

Furthermore, while it is being churned, the supreme mantra will arise; one should diligently grasp that auspicious substance born from the *kuṇḍa*. Now, regarding the pure mantra-herb, it is stated thus in the *Kuloḍḍīśa*: "The word *māyāgaccha*, [followed by] *śakrastambhanakāriṇi* and *catvaraṃ*."
With this [mantra], one should collect the root of the *jāti* plant at a heap of charcoal.
O Lord of practitioners, having retained this, one should perform the immobilization of semen;
likewise, O Goddess, that which is produced from the cow is emitted and enjoyed.
One who is of noble birth, initiated, devoted, husbandless, discerning, capable, and of suitable form— one should bring her here with a spirit free from deceit.
She was beautiful, radiant, yet distressed, with full and elevated breasts;
appearing sixteen years of age, she was always longing for love.
Having performed the nyāsa and other rites according to the previously mentioned sequence,
the best of practitioners should diligently grasp the *tattva* for the purpose of worship.
Thus, this flower produced from the *goḷa* plant causes delight to the deity;
indeed, he who worships with this shall obtain all his desires.
O Self-Existent One, you shall explain for the sake of worship, O supreme practitioner,
[the rite] after having brought a divine woman who is intoxicated and in the full bloom of youth.
Having initiated her with the root mantra, she was one with a beautiful nose and a lovely smile;
through the maiden Sarvānandā, she became free from both pity and shame.

O Goddess, one should cause a beautiful woman— one who is devoted to her guru, modest in her own attire, and intent on the worship of the deity— to perform the ritual arrangement as previously described.
In her temple of pride, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
having oneself become unperturbed, the practitioner should worship the fifth [syllable].
The woman in her season who acts according to her own will is the Śakti; she is the Great Goddess Maheśvarī herself. Her very flower must be beheld with diligent effort.
The householder should always worship with garments, ornaments, and flowers according to his capacity; he should diligently keep secret from others what flowers were used and at what time.
One should perform the worship with self-manifested flowers through diligent effort; one should worship with a pair of self-manifested flowers along with unbroken grains of rice.
Having recited the Vidyā Svapnāvatī, one quickly effects summoning and other rites;
[this applies to] the deities, the great nāgas, the rākṣasas, and those who are dānavas.
Kings and all women shall always remain under one's control [by wearing] even a garland of skulls.
O Goddess, the Svayambhū flower is known to be of three kinds.
For one who has not reached sixteen years of age, she is the most excellent, bestowing all accomplishments.
By force, she increases the enjoyment of the middle [channel];
another, by the power of the union with *rajas*, bestows the lowest [state].
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
"Listen, O child, to the supreme and most auspicious majesty of the kula-substance,
by partaking of which the great triple state is attained through the Kula-deity."
O Goddess, the lunar day of the new moon (amāvāsyā) resides in the center as Suṣumnā;
she indeed rains down nectar upon the surface of the earth for three days.
O Goddess, if one should recite the vidyā, it sprinkles that family;
indeed, it becomes effective there even from the very first utterance.
Therefore, with every effort, examine the lineage and perform the recitation;
for by that vision, O Goddess, the nectar that has flowed forth is fully grasped.
One should accomplish every practice for the sake of attaining the family tradition (*kulācāra*).
And that power (*śakti*) which is devoid of Śiva rains [grace] twice at the very beginning of the year.
That very substance is the supreme substance known as *svayaṃbhūkusuma*;
the *svayaṃbhūkusuma* substance is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
O Lord, sometimes the fragrance-seed is not found, or perhaps it is;
if it is found, it is auspicious, resembling lac-dye in color.
Having prepared a pill from musk and saffron, the practitioner should conceal it;
having inscribed the seed-syllable of the yantra, he should worship it if he is a seeker of success.
By this method of unbroken yoga, one should attain the honeyed success;
for those corrupted by the defects of sleep and so forth, the mantra-sciences have been proclaimed.
They become awakened through that application until she returns;
then one should perform the application of the vidyās, mantras, and so forth.
Thus awakened, it is never like that [ordinary state];
among these three, the self-arisen flower is indeed great.
Also in the Śrīkrama:
"Having added musk, saffron, sandalwood, agallochum, and various other fragrant substances there, one should mix them together and perform worship."
By means of this performed yoga, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
she who performs the worship daily with self-arisen flowers [attains success].
O Goddess, for women, the primary accomplishment that bestows sweetness arises.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru, this is the [numbered] chapter.
Now follows the exposition of conduct from the Kālītantra.
Now I shall proclaim the conduct by the practice of which one attains immortality;
devoted to the welfare of all beings, one should be intent upon the conduct of the observance.
One who has renounced impermanent actions and is intent upon the performance of prescribed duties,
being devoted to the propitiation of the mantra with a disposition toward Śiva.
One who offers all ritual actions to another deity,
who has faith in the worship of one mantra while performing the propitiation of another mantra;
A wise man should always avoid censuring a hero, seizing his property, showing anger toward women, and striking them.
One whose mind is striving in yoga should contemplate the entire world as consisting of women;
likewise, one should contemplate what is to be chewed, sucked, licked, eaten, consumed, the home, and happiness [as such].
With a disciplined mind, one should meditate upon the form of every young woman;
having beheld a young woman born of a noble family, one should pay her homage according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune the vision of the Kula arises,
then at that very moment one should perform the mental worship there.

The meaning is "of those goddesses beginning with Bhaga. As for the goddesses beginning with Bhaga, it is stated in the *Gandharvatantra*: "Bhaginī, Bhagajihvā, Bhagāsyā, Bhagamālinī, Bhagadattā, Bhagākṣī, Bhagakarnā, and Bhagāvara."
Having worshipped her who has a vulva-like nose and vulva-like breasts with fragrant substances and other offerings, as well as with mental worship, one should likewise honor the Guru,
whether she be a young girl, one intoxicated with youth, or an aged woman, provided she is beautiful.
Or, having paid homage to those who are contemptible or greatly wicked, one should meditate upon their blows,
their censure, their deceit, and likewise their unpleasantness.
Under no circumstances should one act otherwise, for it creates an obstacle to accomplishment. One must never harbor hatred toward women; indeed, the worship of women is especially important.
Having placed a large conch shell at the place of recitation, one should perform the recitation while facing upward;
and while approaching, touching, or beholding a woman—especially one of noble birth and auspicious appearance.
Just as one might chew betel and wear garlands while eating some small food at any time, so too,
having today eaten all kinds of foods with devotion, one should perform the recitation while chewing the betel.
Thus, there is no restriction regarding knowledge here, nor any restriction concerning abiding and so forth;
there is no restriction on the time for recitation, nor even regarding worship and offerings.
In this practice for the accomplishment of the Great Mantra, a rule of personal choice has been stated:
this recitation is mental. As it is said in the *Yāmala*:
"Whether pure or impure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping."
A wise person who knows the essence of each mantra should practice it in this manner.
There is no fault in reciting [the mantra] mentally, at all times and in all places.
By constant recitation, the deity becomes pleased with one who is thus engaged.
Being pleased, they shall grant desires free from obstacles and eternal liberation;
likewise, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and all terrifying grahas [shall be subdued].
Terrified on all sides by fear, they do not approach the reciter,
[avoiding] his clothes, seat, bathing water, house, touch, and even his water.
One should not concern oneself with the purification of food; rather, one should practice a mind free from conceptual construction.
If one desires fragrance, one should worship with red flowers and with the *kula* [lineage].
O fair-browed one, there is no unrighteousness in using auspicious flowers such as bilva and maruvaka, provided they are devoid of *tulasī*; rather, great merit shall accrue.
"Acting according to one's own will as described here, one should conduct oneself with a mind that has seen [the truth];
thus the glorious lord of the enclosure (āvāravara), intent upon recitation, worship, and so forth."
The Protector of the principles of the Kula dissolves into the Supreme Principle;
he is the risen creative power, consisting of bliss, and the liberator from saṃsāra.
The practitioner shall become a master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (*aṇimā*). Now, following the conduct of the *Kulīnas*, it is said in the *Kaulatantra*:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the conduct of the *Kulīnas* as it is."
If you have delusion regarding living beings, you ought to feel revulsion toward blood and semen.
Whether it be a delusion regarding purity or a suspicion of sin concerning sexual intercourse, such a fallen person may worship the Goddess; how then could there be a mantra for Caṇḍī?
The patient will surely become miserable and shall go to the Raurava hell;
for when the Goddess is without mantra, effort is obtained only through force.
One should recite that Karṇamantra with one's own body as its essential form;
then she, being of the nature of Śakti, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The meaning is that it is the seed-syllable *māyā*. The Kaulika is indeed the lord of that woman who is foremost among those on earth— such as Rambhā, Śacī, or Umā— who may reside either on the earth or in the netherworld (*pātāla*).
Even in that regard, O beloved, hear the rule concerning that Lord:
the Guru is Śiva himself in person, while the wife is his consort.
One should avoid worldly conduct there through mind and deed;
devoted to his very feet, having attained liberation, one shall go to the supreme state.
The wife of the preceptor, his daughter, and likewise the "mantra-daughter"—sexual union with her is excellent; however, [union with] the property of a Brahmin is [avoided] by means of the mind.
And the wife of the Kaulika, O Dear One, is the Goddess herself;
by merely covering her, the Kaulika would become a denizen of hell.
When a sacrifice must be performed with a female messenger (*dūtī*) who is other than the mother, sister, or daughter-in-law,
the most excellent knowers of mantras should carry out the ritual separation (*vihāra*).
In the investigation of another location, the curse of the Goddess arises;
one should avoid from afar that power which is devoid of Śiva.
O Goddess of gods, by the utterance of the mantra following the interval of the consecration (abhiṣeka), one who performs this with the fifth [vow] is liberated from all sins.
By means of the first reality alone, the practitioner becomes Bhairava;
by means of the second, the worshiper attains the nature of Brahman.
By the third reality alone, one attains the state of Mahābhairava;
by the fourth reality, however, one becomes a poet, the sole leader worthy of worship.
O Goddess of the gods, by the fifth [stage], the yogi becomes equal to me and attains the highest state beyond all accomplishments.
Thus, O Goddess, this which is extremely difficult to conceal has been told with great effort;
it must not be given to a *paśu*, O Goddess, nor to one intent upon reviling the *kula*.
Also in the Kulārṇava:
"Having gone to the house of one who follows the Kula conduct, one should with devotion request the nectar of knowledge for the purification of sins; in its absence, one should drink water."
Whatever honey-vessel has been given by the family preceptor with devotion, one should receive it after performing the ritual salutation (maskṛti);
otherwise, one shall go to hell.
A wise person should not let time pass in vain through gambling, games, and the like; rather,
one should spend it in the worship of deities, sacrifices, hymns of praise, and so forth, as well as in the compassionate instructions of the guru, discourses, hymns, and the study of the Āgamas.
One should pass the time without hesitation and not speak of the faults of others, whether in their presence or in their absence; one should bow to the guru in their very presence.
One should avoid performing separate worship before the Guru and avoid [teaching] non-duality;
one should avoid initiation, exposition, and authority in the presence of the Guru.
One should never step over the bed, seat, stool, sandals, or drinking vessel of the guru, nor his bath-water, nor his shadow.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
therefore, one should consider him as even greater than a father.
Gazed upon by the Guru, the disciple should rise and leave his seat;
one should not, even in thought, revile the Guru who is of the Guhyakula lineage as if he were a mere deity.
A wise man should always avoid censuring heroes and noble women;
for those who are Śākta within, Śaiva without, and Vaiṣṇava toward their wife.
Kaulas, assuming various disguises, wander upon the surface of the earth.
And in the Liṅgāgama:
"Beheld by the Guru, the disciple should rise and leave his seat."
One should not transgress whatever has been spoken by the Guru, whether it be true or false.
He who engages in violent sexual intercourse, falsely in the presence of his guru, goes to a terrible hell; thus it was spoken by Bhairava.
One should not allow the omission of ritual acts on the days of Saṃkrānti, the ninth, the full moon, the eighth, the fourteenth, the eleventh, or during the Vyatīpāta yoga.
Any action performed devoid of reality, as well as the act of recitation, is fruitless;
Śāmbhavī becomes enraged with them, and the sin of killing a Brahmin accrues day after day.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "Solitary and free from attachment, one should wander with joy in a desolate region, a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest, in an empty house, or on a riverbank."
For heroes, every time for recitation is indeed praised;
it should be performed in any place and on any sacred seat—of this there is no doubt.
It is stated elsewhere that in that very city at the end of one's own lineage, the practice (caryā) must be performed at night and not otherwise;
just as for a twice-born man devoid of Vedic knowledge there can be no refinement through the Vedas,
and just as devotion to the gods cannot prevail without devotion to Viṣṇu.
Just as liberation without Śākta knowledge leads only to ridicule,
so too there can never be any qualification for the Tantra without a Guru.
Just as a woman deprived of her husband is excluded from all ritual duties,
so too is a divine hero or my practitioner [excluded] without his lineage.
O follower of the Kaula path, one who is undisciplined is not authorized; therefore, one should be devoted to effort.
How can he whose family is undisciplined perform my worship?
Therefore, one should act with such effort that he becomes endowed with discipline. And in the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
"O dear one, when a devotee of Viṣṇu is initiated by a Śakti who is devoted to the Supreme..."
I shall destroy his sons, wife, and wealth; of this there is no doubt.
If a disciple of the lineage kills his family deity, a brahmin, or a Vaiṣṇava preceptor, he certainly becomes fallen from his status.
Just as fire becomes radiant by the mere placing of an oblation,
O child, so do I become radiant from the mouth of the Kula deity.
Having received the vidyā of the sacrificial animal (paśu), if one should be intent upon worship, then,
having gazed upon its face, one should gaze upon the face of the Kula.
O Mahādeva, whatever action whatsoever is performed by men born of noble lineage according to the teachings of the Paśupatas, that very act leads only to malevolent magic (abhicāra).
If the knowledge is obtained from a deity through an animal sacrifice by people of noble family,
one should again seek the Kaulika knowledge from a twice-born man after making a request.
O Mother, having churned up my well-performed karma through ignorance according to the Kulakaulika system, forgive that sin; O Goddess Hari, have mercy.
Having thus obtained [it], the best of practitioners should perform the initiation again.
In the Vārāhītantra:
"One should not revile a Brāhmaṇa, nor should one censure a young woman."
And [one should honor] the Lord of the Seat (Pīṭheśvara), the youthful woman, the mother, the father, and the guru.
One should not step over the eighth day [of the lunar fortnight], nor should one step over a sacred thread;
one should not step over the shadow of the guru, and especially not that of the guru’s wife.
If slander or even censure of the guru should arise,
one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
If one censures the Guru of the Kula and Akula, whether through thought or word, even if it be something else spoken in that very context, my curse falls upon him;
this applies even to a mere mention of this scripture or the sight of this book.
Even at the cost of one's life, one must never speak ill of the leader of the flock;
having made the face of the Sun [as a witness] and looked upon it, the Lord of the Clan (Kulanāyaka) should be remembered.
Conversing with animals, sharing their beds, sitting together with them, and even associating with them— these alone are the [faults] of a high-born and noble-souled man in this world.
But for the destruction of these [defilements], there is no casting down; heaps of merit are not effective, nor are sacred fords, nor the Gaṅgā, nor even Kāśī.
By the mere recitation of this Great Vidyā, the four mortal sins and even [the sin of] association with such sinners are destroyed; they never again come to fruition.
If, through ignorance, a beast is born from contact [with a human] by chance,
then one should exert effort for twelve years for the sake of performing a vow.
Staying near a woman of noble birth, he considers her family alone as his ultimate refuge;
eating her leftovers, he even causes harm to the subjects and to her husband as well.
At the conclusion of that, having worshipped her and gratified her with jewels,
and having become pure once more, one should receive the vidyā again and attain purification.

If one becomes incapable of observing the vow, the practitioner of the lineage, for the sake of destroying the sins of those in his family, should give gold to his kin so as to bring satisfaction to the family.
Having attained union through knowledge, the practitioner does not indeed fail to achieve perfection;
even upon reaching the state of the five elements, he takes recourse in a womb such as that of a speaker of the scriptures.
One who is joined with various afflictions falls into the hells;
one should not initiate such a person, nor should one perform the ritual of showing him the [mandala] image.
In this regard, one should diligently avoid discussing my scriptures;
likewise, one should avoid the worship found in the scriptures of the bound (paśu) through action, mind, or speech.
Those who commit great sins must be abandoned; they are indeed defilers of their lineage.

Whether in a lifeless piece of wood, a clod of earth, a pebble, or even in a blade of grass, I am present there in everything that is thought of; yet for a beast, there is no mantra-body. It is only when presided over by consciousness that pleasure and pain are fashioned; it is in that very state [that they arise].
There is no such restraint as that spoken of in the *Nabho-vākya*. Therefore, she who is tranquil must be protected by those of noble lineage for the sake of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
It is stated elsewhere in that same work:
"In initiation, in the worship of the *Kula*, in the status of a disciple, or in the case of a guru..."
In that [state], shame is the supreme lineage; though it is eternal, it is also eternally censured.
By casting a downward glance, his vidyā indeed becomes face-down;
by closing one's eyes, the vidyā dies, and by weeping, one will certainly cause death.
Like one collapsing to the side, afflicted by disease and poverty,
she becomes driven toward ruin by looking in the four directions.
O Goddess, if such a family should somehow reveal itself.
Then, having requested the family preceptor, one should cause the initiation to be performed;
O Goddess, when there is an instructor, then others are indeed auspicious.
O Goddess, when she is for the sake of worship, then she is the Mother; of this there is no doubt.
In every respect, the root is not seen apart from the father and the son.
O Bhairava, if one pronounces "pāpa" (sin) when it is actually "tat kṛte kṛte," both [the teacher and the disciple] go to hell;
even if another who knows the scriptures performs the animal sacrifice at Cuṃvuka.
One must not speak, one must not act, and one must not utter anything at all;
if one acts thus toward the guru, O disciple, he will fall under my curse.
And in the Śivāgama:
"If the Lord of the Cakra should drink the remains of the Śakti without reflection,
he will certainly go to a terrible hell upon falling into the path of Kutala."
Therefore, having investigated with effort, the wise one should drink the remnant of the *śakti*;
the hero should cause bliss to arise and drink the reality without delusion.
Śakti is Śiva, and Śiva is Śakti; Śakti is Brahmā and Janārdana;
Śakti is Indra, the Sun, and Śakti is the Moon and the planets—this is certain.
He who does not know that the entire universe is of the nature of Śakti is a denizen of hell. Also, in the Vīra-tantra:
"Bathing and so forth are mental purification; mental recitation is the most excellent."
In this regard, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding mental recitation (*mānasajāpa*). As it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"Whether pure or impure, whether walking, standing, or even sleeping..."
The wise person, taking refuge solely in mantra, should practice it with the mind alone.
There is no fault in mental recitation at all times and in all places;
by such recitation, the deity, being constantly praised, becomes pleased.
Furthermore, when pleased, he bestows enjoyment and eternal liberation;
as do the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and all terrifying grahas.
All beings, terrified by fear, approach the reciter [of mantras]. As stated in the Vīratantra:
"The mental worship is divine; so too are the mental libations and other rites."
Every moment is indeed auspicious; nowhere is there anything inauspicious.
O Goddess, there is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the dead of night;
in every way, O Goddess, one may perform worship whether bathed or having already eaten.
At midnight, in a pure place, one should cause an offering (bali) to be given with the mantra; this day and night is truly declared to be auspicious.
O Goddess praised by heroes, the great worship (mahāpūjā) must be performed specifically during the great night;
on that day, O lady of excellent vows, it must be performed in every way according to my teaching.
One should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day and employ the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) consisting of one hundred thousand recitations.

Regarding this, the statement from the *Svatantra-tantra*—"In that regard, worship during the day alone [is required], O Goddess praised by the heroes, as in the case of a bound soul (*paśu*)"—should be understood as referring to the subject of the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Here, the word "alone" (*mātra*) serves to exclude worship during the day within the context of the preliminary rite. Between the two types of preliminary rites...

One in the state of *paśu* (the bound soul) should perform worship only by day; the word "only" (*eva*) here excludes worship by day in the *kulapuraścaraṇa* (Kula preliminary practice), because that specific *puraścaraṇa* is so regulated. However, elsewhere there is no distinction between the states of *divya* (the divine) and *vīra* (the hero); for them, worship may be performed at night, during the day, or even at the two twilights.

The meaning is that one should perform [these rites]. As for the statement: "Whatever worship of the *bali* offerings and so forth is always performed at night, one attains the merit of that specific constellation through the grace of the Kālī-vidyā," that refers to occasional (*naimittika*) rites; for it is said: "O gods, one should perform the worship of the Vidyā at night as an occasional rite."
p.
140a) "The determination regarding both [types of] ritual action is that they are optional (*kāmya*). This is the statement from the *Kulārṇava*.
That refers to the obligatory daily worship (*nityapūjā*) on an occasional day (*naimittikadina*). Having performed the daily worship during the day, one performs the occasional worship.

The meaning is that one should perform [the rite] at night. Regarding the passage beginning with "na viśeṣa" (no specific [time]), this is to be understood as a promise for the daily worship on days other than those occasional ones. Also, in the *Chinnamastā-kalpa*: "There is no fault in using a perfected mantra; there is no impurity, no restrictive rule, nor any lack of ritual completeness; there is no [restriction of] night, nor twilight, nor bathing."
One should always worship the Goddess, especially through sexual union;
however, one must not look at a naked woman, nor one who is insane, nor one whose breasts are exposed.
"One should not look at a man during the day nor a woman during the night, nor indeed at her private parts"—
this statement from the *Kulārṇava* refers specifically to the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Kula tradition. Although, according to the contradictions found in various Tantras,
looking at those who have fallen [from their vows] or those who are insane always produces sin, nevertheless, in the case of the *puraścaraṇa*, it is more [severe].
Regarding the phrase "producing sin," it is also stated in the *Rudrayāmala*, in the section on Bhairavī:

"O Goddess, through conversation with a *paśu*, the accomplishment of mantras (*mantrasiddhi*) does not occur. O Goddess, that *paśu* is of two kinds; one who has not received initiation (*adīkṣita*) is a *paśu*."
Even one who has been initiated becomes a beast of various kinds by censuring the Kula conduct;
yet, through contact with those consecrated by the *saṃbhāva* [initiation] during the arrival at Goloka, he is purified.
O Maheśānī, they do not succeed; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Those who are full of conceptual doubts do not succeed, even if they were to grant worldly boons.
Therefore, having abandoned these, success shall come from recitation alone:
[namely,] the killing of a hero, drinking in vain, and the service of a hero’s mother.
O Maheśvarī, they say that for Kaulikas, [the failure to do so] constitutes a great sin (mahāpātaka), whether it occurs through greed, intentionally, or even unintentionally. As for the man who—
A practitioner devoted to the *liṅga* shall go to the Raurava hell;
one should indeed honor a person of noble birth with a woman of noble birth.
When those who know the Kula are pleased, the presence of Kālikā occurs;
oh, how fortunate is she in this world who understands the vision of the Kula!
Even among them, if any man should worship the family deity,
yet worship Kālikā while being devoid of the family tradition (kulācāra), [he is not truly successful].
One who partakes of this shall undoubtedly attain heaven and liberation;
or else, other sovereignty, strength, nourishment, and great fame.

From the worship of the feet of Kālī, there is poetry, as well as enjoyment and liberation. In this context, "Kālī" is an elliptical expression for the worship of the *kula*; such is the meaning. As stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"The sandals of the venerable Guru, the *mudrā*, the root-mantra, and the excellent sandals..."
O Goddess of the Gods, one should not speak of this to anyone other than a disciple.

O Dear One, O Sovereign of the Guru’s Family, the lineage transmission, the tradition, the mantras, the conduct, and so forth—all this becomes fruitful [only] when based on the venerable scripture; otherwise it is not so. Whatever has come down through the lineage and whatever book exists, O Dear One, that which relies upon the Śrī-Śāstra is like a deity.
One should always worship with devotion and must not cast it into the house of a paśu.
O Pārvatī, one who desires the welfare of his family should study the Kula scriptures, but should avoid the scriptures of the Paśus as if they were a rival deity.
Firm, steadfast, attained, and rendered perfect through silence— these are the five or seven powers (śaktis) that have come under his control according to his will.
Having brought [them], one should worship the Guru and the wives of that Guru;
the Kula-yoginīs always reside within the Kula-trees.
One should not eat from its leaves, especially from the leaves of the *arka* tree;
one should not sleep under sacred trees (*kulavṛkṣa*), nor should one perform [religious rites] beneath them.
Now, the Śivāvali. As it is stated in the Kālītantra:
"O Dear One, the general procedure for the Dakṣiṇā [initiation] is now being told;
by performing which according to the rules, great calamities flee away."
And the Śivāvali should be offered after worshipping for the sake of all accomplishments,
during a great portent, a most terrible calamity, a great fault, or a great danger.
In times of great calamity, in a great war, amidst the confusion of a great conflict,
when entering into great poverty, and when great suffering is manifested;
In the great teacher, in the great forest, and likewise in the great auspiciousness;
in the battle against terrible sorcery, it is the destroyer of terrible calamities.
For deceptive warfare and the like in battle, for warding off treacherous enemies,
for the pacification of fear from kings and others, and for the quelling of a king’s wrath.
He who does not offer an oblation to you, Śivā, for the sake of attaining auspiciousness,
would feel no shame in failing to worship the family deity of the most sinful.

Now follows the method for the Śivāvali. As it is stated in the Kulacūḍāmaṇi: "At the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, or even in a cremation ground, the practitioner should offer an oblation consisting primarily of meat at the time of twilight."
When it was said, "Kālikālī," that goddess in the form of Śiva,
appearing in the form of a beast, arrived together with her hosts of attendants.
If, after eating, it raises its face toward the northeast and cries out with a beautiful voice, that alone is auspicious for it; there is no other favorable sign nor any fault.
One must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā with the gift of food;
likewise, one should perform the daily śrāddha, the twilight rites (saṃdhyā), the application of sandalwood paste, and the libations to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
Likewise, for those who constantly serve the Vakula tree in the worship of the Kula,
he who does not worship the goddess Śivā in her animal form in a secluded place [is at fault].
By the power of Śiva, all of that— his recitations, worship, ritual procedures, and whatever meritorious deeds he has performed— is certainly destroyed instantly.
Having taken the curse and assuming its power, Śivā weeps in solitude;
for there, Kulabhairava is enjoyed by a single Śivā.
In that very place, O Bhairava, the supreme delight of all goddesses is exceedingly difficult to attain; it consists of the power of animals, the power of humans, and the power of birds.
Since a well-honored person can transform a flawed action into one endowed with merit,
one should therefore exert every effort to ensure that no great error is committed again.
When one encounters fear from kings and the like, or fear arising from traveling to another country and so forth,
one should offer the bali-oblation after reflecting upon one's auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
Accept it, O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O Śivā, whose form is the fire of time!
Reveal the manifestation of the fruits of good and evil; accept this offering for you.
Having uttered this, O Dear One, the bali offering should be given by one born of a noble family;
for if it is not consumed, O God, then no auspiciousness will arise.
If there were any merit for him, it would have been exhausted entirely;
knowing this, O Mahādeva, one should perform rites for peace and well-being.
O lady of virtuous vows, this family tradition has been told to you by me with the ritual fee;
it must not be given to anyone if one desires one's own spiritual success.
The formal declaration (nidāna) must indeed be made, but not in the presence of people;
likewise, it should be performed neither in the presence of the maternal grandfather when granting success, nor in the presence of the father.
Or else, one should not even cause [the image] to be seen by birds, insects, and the like;
nor should it be placed in the realm of Pātāla, or among the Gandharvas, even if they are well-restrained.

Indeed, one should not perform the flower of the family (kulapuṣpa), the substance of the family (kuladravya), the worship of the family (kulapūjā), or the recitation of the family-mantra (kulījapa) in a pavilion or in the presence [of others].
One should always reveal the Guru, the head of the family, the lineage-rosary, the lineage and non-lineage, the lineage-circle, the lineage, and the meditation on all that is to be given.
From disclosure comes the loss of accomplishment; from disclosure come bondage and the like;
from disclosure comes the betrayal of mantras; from disclosure comes the destruction of one's life.
O Goddess of the Gods, if anyone should enter here at the times of worship, there will be the attainment of death through exposure, never through concealment.
One should indeed display the Vaiṣṇava mudrā, perform the Viṣṇu-nyāsa, recite hymns, and so forth; if there is concealment despite being manifest, that manifestation is not a fault.
If manifestation were to occur through concealment, then there would be no secrecy as it is prescribed;
at some point there might be a loss of the constituent parts, yet there is never any manifestation [of the whole].
One should never perform worship nor reveal [the practice] at any time. Now, regarding the conduct of the *samaya*: it is said in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"Listen, my son, to my secret concerning the origin of the conduct of the *samaya*."
Deprived of which, they do not attain success even throughout thousands of millions of births.
A man who follows the family scriptures and the traditions of his lineage,
who is noble-minded, and who is everywhere devoted to the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava.
One should be patient with the censures of others and always intent on doing good;
whether on a mountain, in a forest, in a secluded place, or in an empty pavilion.
If the lunar day (tithi) of Devī or another deity falls on the middle of a crossroads,
one should meditate for a moment, recite the mantra, and then proceed as one pleases.
Having beheld the vulture, one should bow to Mahākālī without blinking;
likewise, having beheld Kṣemaṃkarī, Jaṃbukī, and Yamadūtikā, one should bow.
O descendant of the Kuru lineage, O you who are like a crow on the earth, O black cat, O slender-waisted one,
O large-mouthed one, O you with disheveled hair, O lover of wrinkles!
O beloved of Śaṅkara, one who follows the family tradition should offer salutations before eating;
and upon seeing a jackal or a Gaṇa, one should proceed by circumambulating it.
By bowing with this mantra, the practitioner shall obtain happiness:
"O you of terrible fangs, hollow-eyed one, you who resound with such a cry!"
Beholding her who is the very essence of Tripura, whose form is the consciousness of the self, who utters most terrible roars, and who is clad in red garments and adorned with red flowers.
One should prostrate like a staff upon the ground with this mantra for both of them:
"O Tripura, O daughter of the Aśvins, you who resemble the bandhūka flower!"
O lady of excellent complexion, salutations to you who have arisen from the dawning of fortune;
[you who see] a king or a prince dressed in black garments and adorned with flowers.
Having seen the elephant, the lord, the chariot, the weapons, the shields, the heroic men, and the buffalo who is the family deity, [she became] Mahiṣamardinī.
Having prostrated before Jayadurgā, he is not smeared by obstacles:
"O Victorious Goddess, Mother of the World, Primordial One of the Three Cities, O Triple Deity!"
O Goddess, granter of boons to your devotees, O slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations to you!
[Having seen] a vessel of honey, fish, meat, and a beautiful woman...
And having seen the goddess Bhairavī and prostrated before her,
he reflected upon the mantra for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the prosperity of the Kula practice.
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
I bow to you, the boon-granter, who is drenched by streams of blood.
O Goddess who removes all obstacles, salutations to you, O beloved of Hari!
O Goddess, if they do not perform [this] even upon seeing these [images], [the following occurs].

If one prioritizes the mantra of power (śakti-mantra), its accomplishment does not arise; nor do the rites of killing, driving away, or harming these [enemies], nor the worship of the Guru and so forth.
If one who is evil-souled performs [this], how could he be my devotee?
These [beings] have arisen from Pradhāna and are hostile to their own families.
And likewise for all the ḍākinīs—listen to this, O Bhairava:
if a ḍākinī who has attained siddhi through union should commit violence, [the following occurs].
Alternatively, for those who are devoted to me— especially for the Yoginīs,
the Vaṭukas, and the Bhairavas— no success arises for him.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha,
this is the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now follows the sequence of Nīla. There are two types of funeral pyres: that which has the form of a cross (dvicitā) and that which has its own natural form (svarūpa).

Because it is easy to understand, the description of the former is given first. Among those, first is the characteristic of the Vetāla-pyre: for a Gandharva, an unprepared (asaṃskṛta) pyre at the head of the cemetery should be taken, but not one joined with ritual preparations (saṃskāra).
And even if it has been washed, if one should cause it to be made again, there is an accumulation [of sin].

"O Lord, there may be swift accomplishment through the Mahānīla-krama alone; yet it has been merely indicated in the Vīra-tantra and not fully revealed. O Mahādeva, please explain it, so that it may become the bestower of all siddhis."
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, it directly bestows all accomplishments, is saluted by all the gods,
removes all diseases, and destroys all sins.
O future one, [you shall be the mother] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, as well as of all the world-protectors (dikpālas),
the Bhairavas, the Gandharvas, and the Yogins.
O Goddess, this great garland bestows the respective accomplishments of all;
O Goddess, there is nothing else that grants accomplishment apart from the practice of the heroes (vīrasādhana).
He possessed great strength, great wisdom, and great courage; he was pure, possessed waters of great clarity, and was devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
O Great Goddess, for their sake I shall describe the sādhana of Nīla;
[it should be practiced] on the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights.
One should especially accomplish harmful rites with this [mantra] during the dark fortnight;
specifically on a Tuesday coinciding with the Maitra nakṣatra and occurring under the Agneya yoga.
Within half that distance, one should properly arrange the articles of worship and the sacrificial offering (bali),
consisting of meat with its bones, molasses, a goat, liquor, flour-cakes, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
