Having brought various fruits and sacrificial offerings (naivedya) prepared according to the specific prescriptions of their respective tantras to the cremation ground, accompanied by friends bearing weapons in their hands;
The practitioner himself, endowed with equal virtues and free from fear,
having taken either a corpse or [the remains] to a funeral pyre, proceeds according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed and put on protective garments, the practitioner, intent on meditation upon the deity,
should stand there in the four directions if they are afraid.
And that which is curved to the left is proclaimed as Bhairava;
he is adorned with garments, ornaments, and decorations, and faces the east.
One should perform the sprinkling on the sacrificial grounds with the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra (astra),
after meditating upon the dust of the Guru’s feet, and then upon Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka.
The Yoginīs and the Mātṛkās preceded her with their left feet;
and whatever gods and Rākṣasas were stationed there, they were half-terrifying.
Piśācas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and hosts of Gandharvas; Yoginīs, Mothers, Bhūtas, and all the women who move through the sky.
The Rākṣasas there became granters of success to me;
having bowed with this mantra, one should scatter three handfuls of flowers.
One should diligently worship Bhairava, Kālabhairava, and Mahākāla— the lords of the cremation grounds— in the four directions beginning with the east.
The knower of mantras should subsequently present the bali offering with water for the feet and other items;
thereafter follows the seed-syllable of sound (Śabdbīja), and after that, the Lord of the Cremation Ground (Śmaśānādhipa).
O Sāmin, accept this offering (bali) with this mantra; thereafter,
[recite] the pair of words "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa," followed by "vighnanivāraṇam."
"Grant me success, O radiant one, joined with the syllable *bhām* and accompanied by *svāhā*;
this is declared to be the first offering (*bali*) with the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*."
After *māyā* (hrīṃ) and following *bhairava*, then the word *bhayānaka*;
having first extracted the mantra, one should offer the *bali* oblation in the south.
One should extract the syllable *hūṃ* from Mahākāla as before;
for Kāla-deva in the west, one should assign it preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ).

At the end of the word [of the deity's name], at the end of the word "kāla," and then after "bhairava," one should likewise offer the oblation (bali) as before, saying "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (śmaśānādhipa).
Then, in the midst of the funeral pyre, one should offer the unsurpassed bali-oblation, saying:
"O Kālarātri! O Mahārātri! O Kālikā of terrible sound!"
"O Mother, accept this offering (bali) and grant me supreme accomplishment.
Having offered the bali to Kālikā, one should cause it to be given to Bhūtanātha."
At the end of the word "śabda" and at the end of "bhūtanātha," one should say "śmaśānādhipa";
with this mantra beginning with "praṇama," one should cause the supreme bali offering to be given.
One should place *hūṃ* and *mataṃ* everywhere, and at the end of the *nātha*, the word *adhipa*.
Having placed these within the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), one should extract them as before.
O beautiful one, having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra beginning with Tārā and the fifth middle [mantra],
and having performed the thorough sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa), one should then place the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
One should place the mantra upon a seat made of birch bark or a banyan leaf;
having spread that seat, one should then likewise place a cloth or a mat upon it.
O Goddess of the gods, one should arrange the directions with the Vīrārdana;
O Goddess, [one should place] the two Kūrca-bījas, then Māyā, and after that [the following].
Having joined Kālikā, Ghoradaṃṣṭrā, Pracaṇḍā,
and Caṇḍanāyikā with the word "dāraya" (tear asunder), one should then utter the pair "hana hana" (slay, slay).
One should again sever the great obstacle, the corpse-body, twice;
at the end of *dviṭha*, at the end of *varma* and *śastra*, and again at the end of *dviṭha*—this is considered the mantra.
One should cast a clod of earth consecrated with this mantra in the ten directions;
in their midst, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles.
O Goddess of gods, if through negligence the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear,
he will not be overcome if protected by pillars and his circle of friends.
Having placed a lamp there, using a wick made from *nirguṇḍī*, white cloth, and the hair of a serpent, one should worship the weapon (*astra*) therein.
When that great lamp is overcome by obstacles,
one should bury the family lamp below it with the Astra-mantra.
Then, according to the specific ritual procedure for each, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth in due order;
thereafter, one should install and worship either the Śrīvidyā or the Tārikī mantra.
Being intent on mantra and meditation, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
if it consists of a single syllable, one should then recite it ten thousand times.
For a mantra of two syllables, there are eight thousand repetitions; for one syllable, half of that (four thousand);
and beyond that, O Gajantaka, the knower of mantras [should perform] one thousand repetitions.

Or, beginning at night, he should perform it until its conclusion. Now, as for the Tārakanyāsa: the practitioner should perform the Ṣoḍhī-nyāsa, which consists of the six-syllabled Tāra (Om) encapsulated by the Mātṛkā, with that [Tāra] itself encapsulated by the Tāra in the place of the Mātrās.
One who has offered all their limbs in service becomes another Śiva in person.

The *mātṛkā* [system], consisting of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth, should be understood according to the distinctions among those qualified for it; however, the sixfold [system] is well-known in the *Svatantra*. In the *Matsyasūkta*, it is said: "Then, one should conquer the deity before oneself with the five offerings.
After closing one's eyes, one should meditate upon the Goddess and recite the mantra;
if there is unbearable fear, one should bind the eyes with a cloth over the ears.
If nothing at all is perceived until the end of the night,
one should offer arghya with the Jayadurgā mantra and likewise scatter mustard seeds.

Now, the mantra for the recitation (japa) of Durgā is as follows: Tāra (Oṃ), followed by the pair "Durge," then "Rakṣi," then "Ḍhānta" (ḍhaṃ), with "Locana" (netra, i.e., the letter *i*) within it, ending with "Dviṭha" (svāhā).

If one is not disturbed therein, then what is not obtained?
[One attains] the Goddess assuming the form of a woman, and the Man assuming the form of a brahmin.
Upon the utterance of the words "Take the boon" at the end of the third repetition, one shall receive the offering;
whether by a virtuous person or an unvirtuous one, she grants the boon if she is pleased.
Then, for that lord of heroes, what on earth would not be accomplished?
For one who is sinless and of noble birth, [the rite] is consecrated.
The supreme goddess is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and free from evil; there is no doubt that she appears face-to-face, whether in the refined (saṃskṛta) or the unrefined (asaṃskṛta).
She herself is that Goddess, there is no doubt; he himself is that Lord Bhairava.
Otherwise, his form would indeed be merely a body constructed of illusion.
One should not request a boon there, nor should one say anything at all;
for she [the Fire] would speak a refined narrative, while the Fire itself remains thus unmanifest.
If not, one should oneself grasp a superior, untroubled worldly statement;
or else, some intense light red like fire.
Even sound arises correctly, or even immortality may be attained;
having reflected upon this, it should be grasped—thus has the direction been proclaimed.
But men of unrefined intellect, driven by various divine mandates, must certainly fear that; there is no recourse against it anywhere.
The Bhairavas and Vaṭukas, who are devoted to the Kula scriptures,
have assumed crooked forms as Kṛtyās through their attachment to this scripture.
Having become a son, he may steal one's knowledge; having become a woman, she may delude one.
Therefore, whether it be that or the other, one should exert effort in investigation.
If the truth is established, one may abandon the recitation and other rites once the boon has been obtained;
having realized the fruit has arisen, one should then release the packet.
In the Kulāmṛtasaṃhitā:
Having washed and bathed [the deity], one should release it from its bonds and place it on its seat;
having cleansed the wheel of the feet, one should cast the materials of worship into the water.
One should cast the corpse into water or into a pit and perform an ablution;
then, having gone to one's own home, one should offer a bali-oblation on the following day.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, it is stated: "O Agni, for those whose sacrifice is performed with the fire established for the sacrificer, accept this food, this offering (bali), as proclaimed by me.
Furthermore, O elephant among men, for those who have requested pigs,
one should provide them with well-nourished ones made of flour.
On the following day, having performed the daily rites, one should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
there, one should feed twenty-five Brāhmaṇas.
A person who has fallen away from the five [virtues] should perform [this rite] for ten days;
then, having bathed and eaten, he should dwell in an excellent place.
If it were not edible, then one would fall into poverty;
and if one should become impoverished, then the Goddess becomes enraged.
It is prescribed that [the fast] lasts for three nights, six nights, or nine nights; this is known as the *godhūma* [vow].
Furthermore, when no specific measure is mentioned for herbs, one should take the equivalent amount of leaves, roots, and so forth.
"Leaves and roots are to be taken for that purpose; this is the opinion of those who know the Tantras.
Thus it is stated in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā:
"For those [mantras] for which no specific number has been mentioned by the wise regarding recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa)..."

"The number of thousands for these [mantras] is stated for japa and homa. Regarding this, the scope of the written statements is determined by the division of subject matter among the learned (śiṣṭas). The statement from the Kālītantra attributed to Vaiśampāyana is intended for practical application (prayoga), whereas the statement from the Vārāhītantra prescribes one hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa).

The statement from the Vārāhī Tantra, "the puraścaraṇa and the mere application," means that the puraścaraṇa is for rites to be accomplished through small efforts; this is the extracted meaning. Alternatively:
saffron, aguru, musk, rocanā, camphor, and sandalwood...
Camphor, ruby, saffron, and yellow sandalwood.
Having accomplished it once in one place, one should then accomplish it individually;
then, by means of the *tilaka* mantra, one should bring forth the colored powder from the bamboo tube.
O Hero, one should personally draw blood from the tip of the tongue into the sky;
having formed a pill with that very [blood], one should then recite the mantra of Kālī there.
Having applied a tilaka on his forehead, the practitioner himself becomes free from all fear before Nīlā, Nīlapatākā, Lalajjihvā, and Karālikā.
On the conjunction of the Mahā-aṣṭamī with the Navamī— meaning when the junction occurs before [the end of the eighth day]—
one should cast corpses of goats, buffaloes, and rams in the four directions.
These should be headless trunks and heaps of severed heads, adorned with lamps and other offerings.
Then, having spread out his lute between them, he assumed the form of a Gandharva.
Having made one's mouth red with betel-leaf filling and having anointed one's eyes with collyrium,
and having recited the mantra for nasal drops (nāvana), one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).

O Goddess, O Pārvatī, the seed-syllable (bīja) for each individual substance as well as for the substances combined together consists of the letter *vi* joined with *ya*, ending with *na*, and adorned with the moon (*caṃdra*).
The knower of mantras should recite the root mantra three hundred times plus one;
[visualizing] Cāmuṇḍā of terrible roar, seizing blood upon the tip of her tongue.
Having severed the offering, O Giver of Boons, [offer] blood upon the surface of the sky;
O Kālikāli, Pracaṇḍogrā, then [recite] the weapon-mantra and then the armor-mantra.
This Kālikā has been fully described out of a desire for the welfare of heroes;
thereafter, O Goddess, the two kūrcas of Līlā have been told to you.
O Goddess, [the mantra consists of] *viyat* joined with *bhṛgu*, then *valamiṃdra*,
*ravīrati* joined with the crescent moon (*caṃdrakhaṇḍa*), and then the word *nīla*.
The mantra *hūṃ phaṭ* should be at the beginning for the banner; this is considered the *kūrca* mantra.
This great vidyā is well-guarded, which is used for the practice of Nīla.
Victory to you, O Śrīdharaṇīdevī! On this excellent site of Varaṇa, what is this that you have made blue, which serves as a blue means for the sacrifice?
O beloved, Ugracaṇḍā is declared to be the supreme Mahāvidyā;
she is called Lalajjihvā in the Nīlasādhana.
That great language of knowledge which is proclaimed as leading the practitioners,
when joined with the son of the Earth (Mars), bestows auspiciousness upon Śaurāṣṭra.
In the month of Bhādrapada, during the Puṣkara conjunction, on that [day], the most excellent of heroes brought Viṣṇukrāntā and sowed it in his beloved lands.
Having established her there on that day at the market for the deceased,
one should cause a single fish spread out there to be given for its price.
And with that water, as before, one should sprinkle the corpse;
then, by means of the path of the navel and the mouth, the prepared Vijayā [should be introduced] into its belly.
Having cast [the offering] there into the mouth, with eyes anointed by collyrium, one should apply a tilaka with the previously mentioned substance; then, having risen, one should mutter the mantra.
There, the Lord Bhairava himself indeed resides, marked by the syllable Guḍa.
Then, having become free from fear upon seeing him, the hero should recite the mantra.
O Goddess, if by the power of destiny molasses is not obtained there,
then Bhairava himself shall become Vīreśvara.
O Goddess of gods, having brought the fish, one should cast it into the cremation ground of the ancestors;
then, by reciting [the mantra] a hundred times, union with the deities occurs.
Therefore, O noble lady, by worshipping Mahādeva and Mahādevī with this [mudrā],
and having applied that ash-mark (bhasmatilaka), one shall oneself become Vīreśvara.
At night, in the marketplace of the dead, Unmattā and Nandabhairavā [are present],
naked, pure, adorned with ashes, and with disheveled hair.
Bearing a skull-bowl and holding a sword in his hand, a man should recite the Mātṛkā;
then the Great Goddess stands before him, bestowing all accomplishments.
Whether it be a ḍākinī, a yoginī, or any other female spirit,
by bringing her there as well and worshipping her, one shall become a master of all siddhis.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha,
this is the twenty-eighth chapter. Now follows the exposition on the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) for specific desires (*kāmya*).
By offering oblations of honey mixed with *mālatī*, *mallikā*, and *jātī* flowers,
together with clarified butter, one attains the status of Vāgīśvara.
Even for one who is mute, deluded, or formless, there is no other way;
by offering oblations of *karavīra* flowers along with *javā* flowers and clarified butter, the world is brought under control.
Indeed, all those remaining women become her female servants;
[he should worship] with honey-smeared, red-colored karavīra flowers and guggulu resin.
Having offered one hundred thousand oblations, one shall bring twenty rulers of the earth under control;
with Karavīra flowers smeared with honey, one shall bring the entire earth, along with its constituent parts, under subjection.
For seven nights, one who is wise should offer oblations with clarified butter,
using *pāṭala*, *kudaka*, *śatapatra*, and *jāti* flowers.
Whether by worshipping or by offering oblations with *mālatī*, *navamallī*, *mallikā*, *padma*, and *kiṃśuka* flowers— either individually or combined in various ways.
One attains all good fortune and becomes a wise poet through intellect and right conduct;
a homa performed correctly with red lotuses bestows perfect prosperity.
By means of red lotuses, the world is brought under control, and even kings become submissive in an instant;
by means of blue lotuses, even great enemies come under one's power—there is no other way.
By offering white lotuses, one certainly attains prosperity and eloquence;
O Goddess, by offering white water-lilies, there shall be good fortune and wealth.
Great good fortune arises from the fruits and flowers of the *vakula* tree,
especially when mixed with camphor, saffron, and musk.
Through oblations of jujube fruits (*badara*) performed by the practitioner, victory shall be attained;
through oblations of *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, supreme and radiant prosperity is brought forth.
The practitioner of mantra attains greatness and can paralyze this entire world by offering oblations of sandalwood,
agallochum, camphor, and guggulu.
Furthermore, O Lord of Nagas, he shall bring even the celestial damsels under his control;
all the worlds will undoubtedly come under his sway.
A hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) results in sovereignty for one oppressed by the burden of poverty;
the offering of three palas of honey brings about the destruction of difficulties.
With *mahāpala*, one will certainly destroy the army of an enemy;
by performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) at a crossroads at night, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*).
By means of goat's meat smeared with blood,
mixed with the three sweets, and offered at night in a fire sacrifice according to the procedure taught by the Guru.
One should bring Mahārāṣṭra and Mahādvandva under control by making milk, honey, curd, and ghee the sacrificial oblation and performing the fire sacrifice.
Longevity, strength, health, and prosperity arise for men;
by performing oblations with honey mixed with milk, one shall destroy death.
A wise person should offer eight hundred oblations of honey mixed with milk;
O Indra among kings, by means of honey, clarified butter, and guggulu, one shall surely bring others under one's control.
By means of hair-roots, madhuka, milk, and parched rice, the most excellent practitioner shall indeed become a destroyer of diseases, a destroyer of time, and a destroyer of death.
One hundred and eight oblations of ghee and durvā grass bring about good health;
even a mere offering of sesame seeds accomplishes all undertakings.
Having offered white oblations, the knower of mantras should perform the rite of paralyzing the enemy;
and by the homa of guggulu, he shall ward off all suffering.
Even those who are under the control of enemies are quickly brought under one's power by an oblation of sandalwood;
likewise, men and women are brought under control by an oblation of red sandalwood.
By the oblation of camphor, the subjugation of the speech of men is achieved;
indeed, by the offering of musk, the practitioner becomes all-subduing.
By an oblation of sesame and rice, all [calamities] are pacified;
by an oblation of sugar and molasses, one shall accomplish all undertakings.

By performing oblations of ghee and milk-rice mixed with white sesame seeds, the practitioner brings the three worlds under his control; indeed, through grains, there shall be an increase in prosperity.
Through the use of ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga-dhūpa), incomparable good fortune shall arise;
by offering a full pomegranate (pūrṇa-dāḍima) in the fire-sacrifice, one may bring great houses under one's control.
O Maheśvara, one may bring others under control by offering oblations of ripe jujube fruits (*pūrṇavadarahoma*).
By offering oblations of ripe *mātulaṅga* fruits, one certainly obtains ten cows from a Kṣatriya.
Indeed, by offering oblations of *nāgaraṅga* fruits, Vaiśyas become submissive.
Indeed, by means of the Kuṣmāṇḍa fire-offering, even Śūdras become submissive.
Through the offering of one hundred thousand *kadalī* fruits, one attains kingship; through one hundred thousand offerings of *drākṣā* fruits, one attains success, of which there is no doubt.
The ten [directions] will indeed become submissive, there is no doubt;
by offering one hundred thousand oblations of date fruits, even kings [become subject].
She becomes submissive and the number [of days] reaches twenty; of this there is no doubt.
Through oblations of coconut fruits, prosperity arises after some time.
By means of one hundred thousand [recitations], the knower of mantras certainly becomes equal to a king;
by means of one hundred thousand oblations of ripe fruits, the knower of mantras [attains the same].

One may bring the earth bounded by the four oceans under one's control with *jaṃbū* fruits; women are brought under control by *striyo-vaśya* [preparations], and daughters of the gods by *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruits.
Through oblations of *śrīphala* fruits, flowers, or leaves, one obtains prosperity (*lakṣmī*);
through pieces of sugarcane, one attains happiness, and by its power, even a princess becomes submissive.
Now, there is no fixed measure of substances. In the Rudrayāmala:
"The wise man should offer flowers in their entirety; he may also offer tamāla, lotus, kusuṃbha, or bāṇa flowers, offering as much as he desires."
There are one hundred sesame seeds, one hundred grains of black mustard,
one hundred royal creations (rājāsṛṣṭi), and likewise one karṣa measure of ghee for each man.
Likewise, half a mouthful of milk-rice, as well as thick gruel, pumpkin, and citron; p. 147a) likewise, citron.
The fruit is certainly auspicious when cut into various pleasing pieces;
however, the plantain fruit is auspicious only when cut into four pieces, provided it is not cut into smaller fragments.
One should offer jackfruit from within its fruit-pulp and mangoes mixed with honey;
and sugar-cane pieces at the joints, which are a cause for the satisfaction of the mind.
There should be a complete drākṣāphala, as well as nāgaraṅga, kharjūra, guggulu,
and half a karṣa of kuṅkuma;
likewise, camphor, musk, and ghṛṣṭana should each be equal in measure to a guñjā.
Agaru, candana, and likewise kramuka—these together form a [fragrant] mixture.
Having made all objects dear to the mind into oblations for the fire,
and having offered these oblations dear to the mind, the wise man should shake off everything else.
One should place a measure of curd-cream and flattened rice (pṛthuka),
as well as jaggery weighing one karṣa and half a pala.
Half a mouthful is known as the measure of the sacrificial oblation (caru); one leaf is prescribed [as a measure];
a citron (mātuluṅga) is divided into four pieces, and a jackfruit (panasa) is made into ten.
The wise know that coconuts should be split into eight pieces;
a wood-apple fruit should be cut in two, and a wood-apple should likewise be split in two.
Other fruits, pieces of sugar-cane, and śaṭha should be placed below;
there should be a handful of rice, and red and other kinds of barley as well.
Rice is used for that [quantity], half of that for śāli rice, and sesame for a single measure;
however, when no specific sacrificial substance is mentioned, it is declared to be either parched grain (lāja) or clarified butter (ājya).
In the Vārāhī Tantra: "For the homa, the flesh of the best of boars (buddhāgramāṃsa) with its hair should be used in half a mātrā;
likewise, [the flesh of] the haṃsa, the bilva, the vadara, and the pūga."
Having understood the measure of the old and the new to be equal,
one should likewise regard the measure of the twice-born and the embryo-born as identical.
The measurement of the tiger's bow is equal to that of the lizard and the *dhātukī*;
this is declared for the raw [bow], while the cooked one is said to be of human measure.
One should avoid from afar the meat of inferior women and animals;
one should not offer meat as an oblation by day, nor even mentally at the two twilights.
One should perform the oblation during the Brāhma-muhūrta or at the junctions of the lunar phases;
there should be one thousand recitations, and double that number at midnight.
The merit is threefold during the *brāhmī* muhūrta and fourfold during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*);
it is a hundredfold on the conjunction of the lunar phases (*parva*) and a hundred-and-one times greater at the junction of lunar days (*tithi*).
One should employ meat in rites performed for specific desires (kāmya) and at the conclusion of preparatory rituals (puraścaraṇa);
one may also perform it a hundredfold at a sacrificial pit (yoni-avaṭa) or upon a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila).

Now, the explanation of the directions beginning with the East, as stated in the *Mānasollāsa*: "The knowers of the Vedas declare that very place where the sun rises in the sky to be the East (*prācī*); likewise, [the direction] behind the worshipper is the West (*pratīcī*)."

Those who know the true scriptures declare that this [direction] is indeed for worship. Furthermore: "The space between the deity and the practitioner is called the eastern direction; moreover, because of the relationship between the one worshipped and the worshipper, it is specifically designated as the east."
And in the *Tripurāsāra*:
"The eastern portion is indicated as being in front of the sacrificer; the left side is [known as] the southern by those who know the Āgamas;
the right side should be known as the northern portion, and the middle is the western by the wise."
The direction has been explained. "Savya" means "left. And in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"The space between the one being worshipped and the worshipper is designated as 'prātik' by the wise; that is considered the south, and the north is considered the north."
It should be known that in every instance of worship, the final [verse] is what is asked;
however, if the practitioner, whose face is like Indra's, should worship the beautiful lady, [he should do so with this].

"The Goddess is in the west, likewise in the east and the north; she is before the city of Tripura"—this statement from the *Kulārṇava* should be understood as referring to the measure of Tripurā alone.
There is no evidence for the conception of [the Śrīcakra] as being solely for the Mother of the Goddesses. Thus it is stated in the Jñānārṇava:
"In this way, O Goddess, one should contemplate the Śrīcakra, which is pure by its very nature;
provided that, O Goddess, one raises up the Cakra facing the northern direction."
Then, O Goddess, the northern direction becomes the east for Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
Then the northwest becomes the southeast, and the northeast becomes the southwest.
When that [line] is facing south, the mantra-practitioner should then extract the wheel;
when it is facing east, that same line is then in the south-east corner, which is the fire-quarter.
Now follows the exposition of the family-day (kulavāra) and so forth.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:

"On the day of the lunar mansion of one's own family, on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight of one's own family, and especially on the fourteenth day, the worship of the Yoginīs is performed there; therein, the worship of the Kula is paramount."
Just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on the *citithi*, bestows one's desires, so too Śakti, when worshipped on the *kulatithi*, is the giver of boons.
It is stated in the Yāmala: "The Sun, the Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are considered Kula;
Mars and [Saturn] joined with them are called Kulākhyas; whereas Wednesday is Kulākula."
The second, tenth, and sixth lunar days are declared to be *kulākula*; all odd-numbered days are *akula*, and the remaining lunar days are *kula*.
Vāruṇī, Drā, Abhijit, and Mūla are declared to be Kulākula;
the Kulas are presided over by [the deities], while the remaining ones are non-Kulas.
On the lunar day, the weekday, and the asterism, victory belongs eternally to the practitioner of recitation who abides in the *akula*,
as well as to that which is called *kula*, the *sāman*, and indeed the *kulākula*.

Thus, having understood the day of the week and other such factors, one should perform [the rite] for the practitioner. Now follows the exposition on the praise of those of noble lineage (*kulīna*). As it is said in the *Kālītantra*:
"One should not despise a person of noble lineage; one should worship him who knows the *kula*."
When the kula-knowers are pleased, the presence of Kālikā shall manifest.
Ah! One knows the sight of the lineage as the source of merit and delight in this world;
among them, whoever should worship the family deity (kuladevī).
If a man devoid of family tradition should worship Kālikā, he shall not partake in heaven or liberation; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Longevity, health, sovereignty, strength, nourishment, great fame,
poetic talent, enjoyment, and liberation are attained through the worship of the feet of Kālikā.

Having beheld the Māheśvara [liṅga] in the Somabhujagāvalī, one should worship it according to the prescribed rules; one should offer the five tattvas according to one's means. Then the Goddess will be pleased and shall grant all desires.
Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment at all; the Yoginī becomes enraged toward one who, though having reached the further shore of the Vedas, treats the entire earth with such contempt.
Whatever fruit one obtains by knowing this, that same fruit is obtained from the worship of the Kaula;
it is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices or hundreds of recitations of mantras.
The fruit that one obtains by performing a sacrifice is obtained from the worship of the Kaulika.
The fruit that one obtains by giving gold equal in weight to Mount Meru to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas— that same fruit is obtained from the worship of the Kaulika.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by constructing ponds, wells, and the like,
that fruit is multiplied a hundred thousandfold by worshipping the Kaulikas.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving tawny cows and elephants, that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by worshipping the Kaulikas.
He who reviles the Kaulika devoted to the Kula scriptures goes to a terrible hell; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Now follows the expiation for weavers.
That is stated in the Liṅgāgama:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most excellent expiation."
And the procedure for its purification was indeed spoken by Bhairava.
A disciple who abandons his guru will certainly become liable for penance;
however, by reciting the mantra of the Śrīpādukā one hundred thousand times, he is purified from that sin.
In that case, a disciple who has abandoned [the practice] should not associate with them at all;
being purified by offerings and libations, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

This should be understood as the abandonment of the guru; however, a disciple of the Kula tradition must never abandon the guru. This authority was previously stated in the *Cārapaṭala* and written down according to the sequence taught in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* and the *Rudrayāmala*.
Just as a bee, out of greed for nectar, moves from flower to flower,
so too a disciple, longing for knowledge, should go from teacher to greater teacher.
Some maintain that "from mantra to another mantra" is an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*).
One should abandon a doubtful mantra that is devoid of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the enemy or the target, and take up another supreme mantra;
or else, having abandoned the [doubtful] mantra, one should undertake the practice of a great mantra (*mahāmantra*).
It is stated in that very same work: "A mantra that is incomplete, devoid of its seed-syllable (bīja), doubtful, or likewise unaccomplished—
by such a mantra, the preceptor becomes a slayer of Brahman."
Then, having suddenly recognized him, one should abandon that mantra and the teacher of the gods;
O fair-faced one, even a learned teacher should be abandoned once his essence has been understood.
Even one who possesses little knowledge is worthy of worship if he knows the *kulākula*;
he who sleeps or sits down in the same place together with the Guru [is likewise honored].
Having disregarded the word of his guru and caused his own words to prevail, he goes to a terrible hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
O Guru, those Kaulikas whose minds fall into the ocean of hell, and who consume the food of many kinds of animals; [may their minds not fall].
The Goddess becomes angry with them; therefore, one should not allow contact with them.
One should recite the *lopām* mantra three hundred thousand times, or even just one hundred thousand times.
If one performs the fire sacrifice (*homa*) for half the duration of the poison, one will certainly become free from sin;
yet the Kaulika who approaches a *paśu* woman will forcibly dwell within the power of that *paśu*.
And in the midst of a gathering, one should not intentionally allow contact with him,
even if the hero who is a devotee of Maheśvara drinks from the same vessel.
If the drink becomes the leavings of a dog, that Kaulika must perform expiation by means of a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī and three days of fasting.
Having thoroughly purified the mind, one should give the gold to the Guru;
O Goddess of Gods, having given the cakra, one should perform worship without libations.
Four things perish for him— life, knowledge, fame, and strength—
who acts as an Ācārya after the manifestation [of the deity] without having undergone consecration; he shall go to the Raurava hell after passing through hundreds of millions of wombs.
If one abandons the form of the Mother and instead takes up the form of a woman as a Śakti,
he goes to a terrible hell for hundreds of millions of births.
Having recited three hundred thousand times the *parā* mantra, and one hundred thousand times the *ajapā*,
and then five hundred thousand times the *tūryabīja*, purification is then produced.
The mantra-mother, the daughter, the sister, and the noble wife of the family—
the Kaulika should truly worship these nine in the proper manner.
If one takes up the Śrīpātra and then causes the Cakra to rise, that becomes the drinking of a beast (paśu); for this, an expiation must be performed.
Sexual intercourse with the mother of a mantra requires an expiation ending in death. As it is stated in another mantra:
"Whether out of passion or by one's own will, he who approaches the mother of a mantra should recite the mantra ten hundred thousand times and shall not consume snow."

If one approaches a mantra-daughter, a woman of noble family (*kulāṅganā*), or a sister, purification consists of reciting the root mantra. This is stated in that very same source: "By means of a hundred thousand recitations, one becomes purified from sporting with a mantra-practitioner’s daughter, a sister, or a woman of noble family."
The Kaulika says further in another Tantra:
"On a festival day, having failed to worship the Goddess of the Gods, the Guru, and the Fire according to one's ability,
and having failed to offer the bali-oblation there, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times."
One should not eat leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, food, drink, or medicinal herbs,
nor anything intended for consumption, without first offering it.
One should not eat without having first offered [the food]; such a man becomes liable for expiation.
By reciting the mantra of the Goddess one hundred and eight times, he shall become purified by the mantra and excellent.
Having killed a boneless creature, or having killed ten animals, or having killed birds, one should recite the *tri-rekodaśaka* mantra over all of them.
[This applies to killing] a donkey, a cat, a mongoose, a rat, a man, or a horse.
And having killed all wild animals, such as elephants and others, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times.

One should recite it eight thousand times; those who know the Veda declare this for the killing of a member of the Kṣatriya caste, as well as for approaching a heroic woman's bed and likewise for drinking liquor in vain.

By approaching the daughter of one's guru who has been purified by mantras, one becomes a Kaulika. This, however, should be understood as referring to the case of ignorance; for in the case of knowledge, purification occurs through one hundred thousand recitations. Thus it is stated in the Yāmala:
Having committed the act of a hero— drinking alcohol in vain and sporting with the wife of the guru—
the practitioner of mantra should sport with the daughter of mantra at the hero’s hamlet and recite the mantra ten million times.

Now follows the exposition of the duties for the rainy season. In the *Tantrarāja*, it is said: "I shall describe the offering of the *damanaka* flower for the benefit of practitioners, by which the worship performed throughout the year will certainly become complete."
Formerly, due to the obstruction of Śiva’s asceticism by Madana, he was reduced to ashes;
at that time, his wife Rati and Prīti were filled with grief.
From the water produced from those eyes, the creeper of passion (Madana) shall arise;
and your fragrance and great beauty shall indeed be unsurpassed.
With my heart thus satisfied, O beloved, she was offered by me for the sake of pleasure and delight;
therefore, Madana was manifested.
And for that mantra-practitioner who worships Madana throughout the course of a year,
his worship of Madana for the entire year shall be accomplished.
Thus was the boon granted to him by the high-souled Śaṅkara;
therefore, the worship of Madana should be performed by the best of practitioners.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra, one should perform the offering of the *damanaka* flower;
having gone into the presence of the *damanaka* on the twelfth day together with the practitioners (*sādhakas*).
Then, one should consecrate the four kalpalatās with the mantra:
"Oṃ! Born from the grace of Śiva, be present here!"
By the command of Śiva, you must be brought here for the sake of Śiva’s work;
having worshipped Kārma, Rati, and the others, you may then return home.
Having gone again on the thirteenth day and consecrated it with the Astra-mantra before him,
one should cut off and bring back that which is departing by means of the Drātri and other mantras.
Then, having consecrated it nine times with the Ādhāra-vidyā mantra,
one should divide it within the vessel and arrange the nine yonis.

Having worshipped [the syllables] ending with the names [of the deities], starting from the center and proceeding clockwise from the east, using *haṃ*, *saṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, *maṃ*, *laṃ*, *vaṃ*, *raṃ*, and *yūṃ*— as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should also fashion the intoxicant (madana) together with the root-mantra, conjoined with the wind (vāyu)."
One should perform the subduing [of obstacles] in nine ways, and thereafter, one should worship.
O beautiful one, by that seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara,
which is unattached, [one should worship] with the seed-syllable of Ānandeśvara nine times together with the bindu.

One should worship the ninefold *damana* in sequence with the previously mentioned *aghora-vidyā*. Having thus worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*) situated in the southern direction, one should then worship the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).
The form of the Aghora-vidyā is indeed the cutter away of great sins;
in "Aghore" is Vāgbhava, and in "Vaghore" is Bhuvaneśvarī.

From all sides, for the sake of all and everything, [and] thus for the most terrible of the terrible; one should write the pair of seed-syllables of the Goddess for those forms of Rudra: "Obeisance to you! (namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ).
O beloved, this vidyā is said to consist of thirty-three syllables;
one should perform protection with the Astra-mantra, and thereafter with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should brandish the trident mudrā (triśūlamudrā) over the *damana* [flowers].
As for the trident mudrā, it is described in the *Vāmakeśvara*:
"Having joined the little finger with the thumb, the remaining three fingers [are extended]."
Extending [the fingers] forward—this is proclaimed to be the mudrā of the trident.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra, one should perform the planting of Madana;
one should uproot it with the Astra-mantra and smear it with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
On the first day, one should apply sandalwood paste rubbed with ghee and the like,
and cause an excellent anointing (adhivāsana) to be performed.
Or, for the sake of success in a year-long worship,
one may perform the immediate consecration (adhivāsana) at dawn on the fourteenth day, following the daily ritual worship.
Then, having fashioned a nine-cornered [mandala] with vermilion mixed with great quantities [of other substances],
one should place excellent water-pots (kalaśas) filled with gold, gems, and so forth.
Or, having prepared a beautiful mandala adorned with saffron and other pigments to the right, the supreme preceptor should place a single water-pot there.
Having drawn an Aśoka tree, one should draw a triangular mandala;
in its center, one should worship Kāma, youthful and of reddish luster.
O Dear One, [he] wears red garments and red ornaments;
on his left and right are Rati and Prīti, who are most beautiful; he holds the five arrows and the bow.
For the sake of attaining perfection, one should worship Kāma together with Vasanta,
using the Vāgbhava, Bhuvaneśī, and Śrī mantras, along with the essence of Kāma.
Having drawn this Rudra-colored Vidyā upon a surface equal [in size] to the heart,
one should utter the seed-syllable of Kāma and then extract the syllable consisting of the letter Pha.
O fair-faced one, "Ratye" (for pleasure) is the eight-syllable Vidyā;
I shall state "Prītim" (pleasure) in the place of the vow, for this is the eight-syllable Prīti-mantra.
Delighting in the fair and dark [consorts], adorned with jewels and gems,
holding a lotus and betel leaf in his hands, and clothed in red garments.
Having meditated on the destroyer of Kāma at the left and right [sides], adorned with ornaments of knowledge and resplendent with garlands of flowers.
Thereafter, one should worship Vasanta situated in the midst of a Kadamba forest,
who is fair in complexion and holds in his left hand a lotus and a jar filled with nectar.
Having worshipped Kāma along with his limbs, who holds a collection of various flowers in his right hand, one should then present incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Kāma, when worshipped with *damanaka* flowers, shall accomplish all undertakings;
having thus properly worshipped him, one should then worship Tripurasundarī.
The wise practitioner should properly worship the sequence and honor the young maiden;
having worshipped the resident woman, he should then worship the assembly of Yoginīs.
In this context, "Tripurasundarī" is an illustration; the meaning is that one should follow the sequence of one's own respective *vidyā*.

After honoring the Brahmins and various followers of philosophical systems (*darśana*), one should subsequently honor the Guru with jewels and other ornaments following the oblation (*havana*) performed as part of that rite.
O Goddess, having worshipped with a thousand loads of gold and enchanting divine garments, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
O Goddess, born of the mountain, by this rite one should perform the installation of Madana; for him, the annual worship shall be fruitful.
On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with golden flowers,
or else with camphor, musk, sandalwood, and cool water.
And on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Goddess with plantain, jackfruit, and mango fruits, as before, for the sake of attaining all perfections.
Now, the installation of the *pavitra* (sacred thread).
That is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"In the month of Vaiśākha, on the full moon day (*rūpā*), I shall describe the installation of the *pavitra* for the benefit of practitioners."
Worship performed for even a single year clearly becomes fruitful;
therefore, the Pavitraka worship must indeed be performed for the sake of attaining accomplishment.
O Goddess of the Suras, beginning from the sun in Gemini until its entry into Libra,
one should perform the most delightful great worship of the sacred threads (pavitra).
Worship of these two Yakṣas should take place on the fourteenth or eighth day;
or one should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) on the ninth or the fourteenth day.
Or on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Śivā with sacred threads (pavitra). And in the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra]: "With threads made of gold, silver, copper, or those produced from silk cloth..."
[He should worship] with those produced from the sacrificial thread and those arising from lotus stalks.
One should prepare the purificatory thread (*pavitra*) for all the Śaktis using auspicious Darbha grass that is soft, fresh, and ninefold-twisted, measuring sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Alternatively, it should be nine finger-breadths long, provided with knots and so forth numbering that same amount;
for the purpose of *homa*, having made one hundred and one knots, one should worship them in sequence with those [offerings].
And in the Jñānārṇava:
"One should have fine threads made of gold, silver, and copper;
or it may be produced from silk thread, according to what is available."
One should prepare the purifier (pavitra) from the fibers of the *drākṣā* vine, from the bark of the lotus, or from the stalks of *darbha* grass.
One should worship Praṇava, Candramas, Vahni, Brahmā, Go, Guha, Aravi,
Sarvākhya, and Sarvadeva within the nine threads.
Then, having consecrated it with the Śiromantra and subsequently with the Trāṇamantra,
the preceptor should then wash it while reciting the Śastramantra.
Having veiled the eyes with the Netra-mantra and bound [the thread] with the Kavaca-mantra,
one should worship it with yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kuṅkuma), and red sandalwood.
One should cause a most beautiful and variegated design to be made with musk, yellow orpiment, camphor, lotus-essence, red ochre, and other such substances.
Having sprinkled them with the root mantra, one should place the entire collection of sacred threads in the northeast corner,
having worshipped them with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
O Goddess of the gods, having performed [the rites] during the day in the east,
[one should proceed] with one hundred and eight threads fashioned from nine strands.
The best purifier is indeed [the first]; half of that is remembered as the middling;
half of that would be the smallest—thus it is declared to be threefold, O beloved.
Having fashioned a purifier for the root powers (mūlaśaktis) measuring ninety-six finger-breadths and provided with five arrow-lengths (pañcaśara), one should offer it in three parts.
O observer of excellent vows, at the time of the formal acceptance (adhivāsana), having spread out barley grains there,
the preceptor should cast a flower upon them after four nights have passed.
These purifiers are indeed purifying, fashioned from the collection of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
prepared with the stainless Pañcarātra rites, and endowed with all medicinal herbs.

Then, O lady of excellent vows, having properly covered [the deity] with a pair of new garments, [one should proceed] with the four seats, and so forth. Regarding the "seats," these are the seat-mantras;
the seats are: the Seat of the Ocean of Nectar (Amṛtārṇavāsana), the Lotus Seat (Potāmbujāsana), the Self Seat (Ātmāsana), and the Wheel Seat (Cakrāsana). Their mantras are as follows:

In the *Maṃtrakhadga*, the introduction to *Sundarī* should be understood as follows: "Purified" means sprinkled with the collection of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). "Adorned" means joined with the five jewels (*pañcaratna*) and with jewels accompanied by all medicinal herbs. By these two [qualities], the purified [threads] are released upon the worshipped barley grains.
The meaning is "one should establish. Thus ends the ritual of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Having installed the Goddess’s pitcher (kumbha) with full oblations, water-sprinklings, and so forth,
one should invoke the Goddess into the pitcher and worship her with the root mantra (mūlamantra).

Then, having worshipped the *krama*, one should begin the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārpaṇa*). "Having worshipped the *krama*" means having performed the worship together with its ancillaries (*sāṅga-pūjā*).
Of Śrīvidyā;
the purificatory threads [are offered] with the name of the Guru, and the preceptor [is honored].
One should give the purificatory thread to the Guru, and immediately after that, to all [the others].
The pride of being the Guru, Śakti, Vīra, disciple, or pavitrī.
Starting from the shoulder-blade, the wise one should perform the rite of purification (pavitra) for the group of rays numbering [as many as] that,
and for the three kinds of gurus.

Just as one should perform the rite of the sacred thread-offering (pavitrāropaṇa) on the lunar days (tithis) and the permanent deities (nityagaṇas), so too should one worship the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśī) for the sake of the ninefold assembly (navaka) situated within the wheel.

Thus, regarding the subject matter of the Śrī [Tantra] from the perspective of other sciences: the meaning is that worship should be offered in sequence, giving each of those very things to the retinues.
And always, O Goddess of Gods, the rays are yours, each preceded by the former.
Having worshipped the *pavitraka*, one should then proceed to the water-jar (*kalaśa*).
Immediately thereafter, one should wear pure garments and ornaments of clear luster, as well as a collection of various jewels and a sacred cord made of the finest silk.

Then, my dear, having completed the fire-oblation (homa), one should worship with the purifier (pavitra). "One should worship" means that one should perform the oblation. Furthermore, there is the worship of the maiden (kumārī) and then the group of women living in one's own household.
The yoginīs and the yogins, as well as the various hosts of brahmins.
O Supreme Goddess, he who desires his own success should indeed perform worship on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna for the pacification of all sins.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with vermilion, kuṣṭha, and other such substances, with various types of sandalwood, with fruits, and with blue and red lotuses.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the Goddess with ketaka flowers, accompanied by an extensive display of great opulence.
Having observed the specific worship of the horse on the first lunar day (pratipad),
the best of practitioners should worship the Goddess beginning from that day until the full moon.
With *japā* flowers, *parājitā*, *droṇa*, and *karavīra* flowers, as well as with lotuses, *saugandhika*, and *kahlāra* lilies, along with garments, ornaments, and mirrors;
With pure vermilion, stainless sandalwood and other such substances,
with various kinds of fruits and materials, and with various types of elixirs.
Having performed worship, one should recite the vidyā; one should offer oblations every day, either a hundred or a thousand times, for the sake of pleasing Tripurā.
O King, by that means the vidyā shall become perfected;
perform it in the forest on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, beneath a coconut tree, O moon-faced one.
One should worship me with blameless meat, flour-cakes, and bread according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa,
or with sugar or jaggery.
One should worship with the perfections of the earth and offer cow’s milk;
and on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, one should likewise offer white sesame seeds along with the northern [offerings].
One should worship with perfumes, food offerings, incense, flowers, and so forth;
and on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship with campaka flowers made of gold and silver.
One should worship with flowers fragrant as the mango tree for the attainment of one's desires;
likewise, worship should be performed on the equinoxes, solstices, the new moon days, and the anniversaries of the Yugas.
One should perform the specific rites for each of those [deities] as prescribed in their respective scriptures;
thus, one should diligently perform the duties pertaining to the twelve months.
Year after year, the knower of mantras should perform this; otherwise, he shall become a partaker of sin.
The goddess Śrī Tripurā will become enraged and he shall become food for the Yoginīs.
The term "Tripura" is an illustration; the meaning is that it is supreme among all vidyās.
In the independent *Kulavṛtti* composed out of devotion to the Guru by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha,
this is the twenty-seventh chapter.

"Whatever is recited [of a mantra] beyond the count of one hundred thousand would all become fruitless"—thus it is said. Since the *Muṇḍamālā-tantra* establishes that a rosary (*mālā*) is the means for the practice of recitation (*japa*), the description of the rosary is now provided.
Among these, first is the rosary of the hand (*karamālā*). As it is stated in the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*:
One who joins the tips of the index and middle fingers together is indeed a doer of evil;
the three joints of the ring finger should be extended, while the little finger has three joints.
The three joints of the middle finger [are used] at the root-joint of the index finger;
and in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "Performing the recitation with the fingers, one should perform the recitation using the fingers together with the thumb."
Without the thumb, that ritual act performed will be fruitless.
Beginning from the middle of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction,
one should recite over the ten joints up to the base of the index finger.
Regarding the difference of opinion:
the middle finger, the three [fingers], the ring finger, and the root [finger] are to be grasped;
having made the joint equal to the ring finger the Meru here, one should not overstep it.
If one joins the tip of the index finger with the middle finger,
his four things— longevity, knowledge, fame, and strength— will certainly perish.
Thus, from the syllable-garland consisting of nine joints, within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra),
one proceeds by turning clockwise starting from the root of the ring finger (anāmā).
One should recite on the middle finger at the eight excellent joints down to its base;
likewise, starting from the base of the ring finger and ending at the base of the little finger.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) on the eight joints from the tip of the index finger to its base.
Regarding the number for further recitation according to the divisions of Śākta and Śaiva, it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*:
"A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand (*ayuta*), and likewise a hundred thousand (*niyuta*)."
And likewise, he who performs the majapya and the mānaka [rites] one hundred thousand times or ten million times;
Likewise, one should recite [the mantra] eight times on each finger-joint of the image;
or alternatively, according to another method, with the eight seed-syllables or the eight groups of consonants.

Regarding the *karamālā* (hand-garland) for recitation: it is the measurement of the hand used for reciting the seed-syllable (*bīja*). Regarding the *akṣamālā* (rosary) for recitation, it consists of eight or six joints;
this is because the *karamālā* is subject to the breaking or joining of the fingers. This is also stated in the *Haṃsapārameśvarī*:
"The two joints of the ring finger are to be rotated in succession."
One should bring together one [finger] from the middle mountain and the index finger.
The Śaktimālā has been fully described; it is the illuminator of all mantras.
Regarding the male deity, as in the Caṇḍrikā: the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger are considered the fourth [group];
these three fingers should have three joints each, while the middle finger has one joint and two joints [respectively].
One should avoid [these] at the time of recitation for the middle [vowels].
One should understand it exactly thus: "It has been defiled by Brahmā himself.
Therefore, there is no contradiction among the statements.
And in the *Yāmala*: "One should pay homage to the Meru of the Śākta [tradition] and perform circumambulation of the Meru of the Śaiva [tradition].
One should perform the daily recitation (*japa*) at the sprout, but not for the sake of obstructing [the attainment of] desired fruits."

"One should perform the method for optional rites (*kāmya*) with the hand-garland (*karamālā*) in the absence of [another] garland, O fair-faced one"—from this statement in the *Muṇḍamālā*, daily recitation (*nityajapa*) is performed with the hand-garland; however, optional recitation is not performed with the hand when a [proper] garland is available. It is stated in that very same text that it may even be done with the hand in the absence of a garland.
The fruit that is said to result from reciting with all types of rosaries is obtained by reciting on the finger joints;
that fruit is increased a hundred-thousandfold when reciting on the finger joints.
Therefore, the joints of the fingers are suitable for the purpose of recitation.
On page 151a),
it is heard that the measurement of the rosary for the purpose of recitation, for daily recitation, and for all purposes is prescribed for the sake of regular practice.

However, it is heard in scripture that [the recitation] is for the sake of occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) purposes. As for that which is called the *Sahasranāmastotra*, O Goddess of Gods, by means of which all rites such as recitation (*japa*) are performed with the great conch—that is intended for optional purposes.

This is because both the finger-garland (*karamālā*) and the rosary of letters (*varṇamālā*) are employed for daily (*nitya*) recitation; [it is said: "by the finger-garland and by the rosary of letters..."

The *Śaktiyāmala* states regarding the *japa*: "In the daily recitation (*nityajāpa*), the *mātṛkā* sequence of phonemes is the 'hand-bearer' (*karabhāk*). This is because of the simplicity of interpreting it as a single coherent statement. Having first performed one hundred and eight recitations, one should employ the neuter [seed-syllable]. Now, the procedure for *japa*: it is stated in that very same text, "One should not separate the fingers even slightly."

One should contract [the fingers] like a balance-beam. If the fingers are separated, the recitation flows away to the leftovers. Whatever is recited on the tips of the fingers, whatever is recited by skipping the *meru*, and whatever is recited at the previous joints—all that becomes fruitless.
If one should apply the recitation while transgressing the rules of the sequence out of negligence, the *rākṣasas* will certainly seize it.
The wise one should count [the beads] in this manner; this is the *karamālā* (finger rosary). Now, the *varṇamālā* (syllable rosary). As it is stated in the *Viśuddheśvaratantra*:
"O Pārvatī, listen to the supreme method of the rosary according to its true nature, by the mere knowledge of which mantras are perfected in that very instant."
Through the forward and reverse order, and by the division of the mantra into four parts;
a syllable separated by a mantra, and a mantra separated by a syllable.
One should fashion a rosary made of colored beads, which illuminates all mantras;
one must never transgress the Meru-form, which is the ultimate reality.
Just as Meru and Śiva are for all, so too is Hari;
therefore, one should perform action day and night with a steady body.

"O Goddess," [this is] a locative case used for selection. "O Sovereign of the Gods, this supreme secret has been told to you by me; it must be kept even more hidden by you and must not be disclosed to anyone at all."
And in the Rudrayāmala:
"The wise man, having first quickly uttered that *viṃdu* (the nasal bindu), should thereafter recite the mantra.
Having fashioned it as Mount Kṣamera, he should recite it and must not overstep the navel."
And in the Śrīkrama:
"The garland of letters is proclaimed to begin with the letter 'A' and end with the letter 'Kṣa'.
Having uttered that letter together with the bindu, the wise man should thereafter recite the mantra."
One should perform the *meru* with the letter *kṣa* in both forward and reverse order.
And in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*:
"The garland [of letters] consists of the phonemes of the *mātṛkā*, including *kṣa* and *meru*, arranged in successive order."
In the rite of internal worship, he [should use] the seed-syllables (viṃdu) together with the eight groups of consonants.
The lips are proclaimed to be like the *ādi-kumuda* flower. Also, in the Nāradīya Tantra:
"Having meditated upon the sequence from the letter 'a' to 'kṣa' joined with the bindu, the garland of letters is declared to be both in direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order."
Having uttered the bindu and the phoneme, the wise one should subsequently recite the mantra;
having swallowed the Kṣameruka until the end of the kalpa, he should recite it and must not overstep the navel.
In the *Sūracaraṇacaṃdrikā*:
"With the letters of the Mātṛkā arranged in direct and reverse order, joined with the *bindu*,
along with the eight groups [of consonants] beginning with *ka* and *ma*, and the garland of syllables through the process of realization (*jñapti*)."

If each individual object is consecrated by the recitation of the *puṃ-mantra*, it bestows success upon the practitioner. When these become mature, they grant results even more extensively; this is stated at length. Even the mantras of enemies become [beneficial] for men, so what need is there to mention other mantras? In the *Muṇḍamālā*, the Goddess said: "And the rosary (*akṣamālā*) has been described."
It has not been revealed with effort. Tell me also, what is the name and what is the fruit of this *akṣamālā*?
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of the Gods, the rosary (akṣamālā) indeed becomes manifold through the differentiation of its parts;
listen to that as it is being described by me in full detail.
O Supreme Goddess, the garland of letters is arranged in both direct and reverse order; it begins with 'A' and ends with 'La', and likewise begins with 'Na' and ends with 'Ka' in sequence.
One should not mentally cross over the letter *kṣa*, which has the form of Mount Meru;
for a rosary that is devoid of Meru, or one that is crossed by Meru, is defective.
If it is faithless and unilluminated, that garland becomes fruitless;
it is variegated, possesses the luster of twenty fibers, and resides within the interior of the Brahma-nāḍī.
Woven together by her, she is to be meditated upon as the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
having first recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, they declare the initial syllable to be *klīṃ*.
The pair of *ṛ* and *ḷ* is declared to be neuter;
these are also the divisions of the kalās of the consonant classes in their respective order.
The eight groups [of consonants] are as follows: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and ṣa;
this is stated in the Rudrayāmala.
Alternatively, one may place the vowels beginning with 'a' in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra].
Furthermore, having understood the syllable within the garland [of mantras], one shall become a possessor of accomplishment;
with a restrained mind, one should contemplate it according to the path taught by the Guru.
One should meditate on the vowels with their bindus in the pure sixteen-petalled [lotus];
in the heart, one should meditate on the consonants from *ka* to *ṭha* with their bindus in the twelve [petals].
One should meditate upon the letters beginning with *ma* and ending with *ṇi*, starting from *pūra* and ending with *kā*, on the ten petals at the navel;
or one should contemplate those beginning with *va* and ending with *la* on the six petals at the end of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
In the Mūlādhāra, which has four petals, one should remember the directions ending with the intermediate points along with the bindus;
in the Ājñā-cakra, one should remember the syllables "haṃ haṃ"—this is declared to be the garland of letters.
The sound arising from the withdrawal of these phonemes is called *tamas*;
it is also designated as *anāhata* (the unstruck) by those who discourse on Brahman.
One should perform the external recitation with the syllable *m* (the color of the moon), while the mental recitation is performed with the syllable *i*.
Having thus uttered these syllables together, one does not become subject to the [limitations of] numerical counting.
From the throat down to the center of the earth, there are fifty [letters] in sequential order;
and by reversing that very sequence, the full one hundred are produced.
In meditation, however, one should contemplate the syllables of the mantra being recited within the mind;
consisting of light and endowed with the abode [of Brahman], the mind dissolves by that very means.
With a restrained mind, one should recite [the mantra] in this manner, counting by the hundreds up to a hundred thousand; thus, it is held that accomplishment (siddhi) becomes stable here.
The groups beginning with the vowels, the consonants, and those beginning with *ya*, *sa*, and *ṣa* are likewise eightfold.
First, by multiplying that by eight and eight (sixty-four), it becomes one hundred and eight.
Within the Suṣumnā is the Citrā channel; therein resides the Śakti in the form of sound, which, in the form of a thread, is white and binds together the phonemes.
The mantra known as Ajapa is said to consist of the nature of inhalation and exhalation;
since it must be crossed over as if by Mount Meru, one should indeed recite it there.
Just as the determination of recitation for this garland of phonemes will be explained:
it is strung upon the thread of Śakti and adorned with the Haṃsa-Meru.
"Beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa,' she whose form consists of the letters of the alphabet"—
thus is the garland of letters. As for the garland made of jewels, it is as described in the *Muṇḍamālā*:

Because it encompasses the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', it is celebrated as the "Garland of Dakṣa"; the rosary for recitation is proclaimed to consist of strings of beads numbering according to those syllables.
Through crystal beads, there shall be the attainment of liberation; through lotus seeds, many sons;
through *jīvaputra* beads, the granting of wealth; and through those that have crossed over evil, the overcoming of all obstacles.
O Śivā, a rosary of pure crystal bestows great prosperity;
however, for the rite of Dhūmāvatī, a rosary made of *dhustūra* from a cremation ground is prescribed.
But a garland of human finger-bones, strung according to the previous method,
bestows all accomplishments and grants liberation, O woman of excellent complexion.
O Dear One, the sevenfold [mantra] beginning with *nā* has been taught; the remainder as well must always be guarded with effort, like a mother’s paramour, O Beloved.
One should likewise recite "parvabhiḥ";
the same applies to the breaking of joints as well as to the stringing.
A garland strung with pearls bestows the fruit of all sovereignty.
And [ornaments] made of gems, pearls, and corals, as well as those produced from gold and silver.
A garland knotted with *akuśa* grass grants the fruit of the destruction of all [karmas];
O Dear One, a garland strung with *nāḍī* fibers bestows great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*).
The number is as follows:
that which consists of thirty bestows the fruit of sovereignty; that of twenty-five bestows liberation;
and that consisting of fourteen bestows liberation while increasing worldly enjoyment.
O Goddess, consisting of fifteen [syllables], she is considered for killing, driving away, paralyzing, deluding,
subjugating, awakening, and for the purpose of collyrium and eye-salve.
The sandals for the purpose of attaining siddhi are proclaimed to be one hundred in number;
they should be made one hundred and eight, or else they grant all desires.
In the *Yāmala*: "Now, a rosary made of pearls bestows the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*);
likewise, a rosary fashioned from crystal grants the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*)."
A garland of rudrākṣa beads bestows liberation and grants all prosperity;
a coral garland is for subjugation and accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
A rosary of putrajīva beads bestows the attainment of Lakṣmī;
by means of a rosary of lotus seeds, one becomes Lakṣmī herself, possessed of great fame.
A garland of red sandalwood brings subjugation and bestows good fortune;
a garland fashioned from gold and silver grants all desires.
Fashioned from garlands of conch shells, it produces a stream of fame;
for by means of these garlands fashioned by all [these materials], liberation is attained by men.
One should fashion a garland for liberation with twenty-five arrows;
for nourishment with twenty-seven, and for the rite of liberation with thirty.
In rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), a rosary of fifty beads with three sets of six and five knots is used;
that rosary of fifty beads is auspicious for all ritual actions.
A garland of one hundred and four beads bestows the fruits of all desired rites;
likewise, with one hundred and eight beads, there shall be attainment of all perfections and the granting of liberation.
There is a great fault in exceeding [the prescribed number], yet the practitioner does not achieve success. As stated in the *Caṇḍrikā*:
"With rudrākṣas, those called śaṅkha, padma, putrajīvaka, and pearls..."
And with crystals, precious gems, gold, silver, and coral.
With all the previously mentioned *kuśa* grasses, with the joints [of the staff], and with the letters of the Mother-syllables (*mātṛkā*),
one should perform the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) even while making the sounds of donkeys and men.

A garland of *tulasī* is recommended for the worship of Viṣṇu; for Gaṇeśvara, one made of elephant tusks; for the recitation of the *Tripurā* mantra, *indrākṣa* beads are praised; and for [the worship of] Raktacaṇḍa, red sandalwood.
A rosary made of great conch shells bestows abundant good fortune, vast prosperity, the attainment of one's desires,
direct perception [of the deity], spiritual accomplishment, as well as peace and nourishment.
A rosary fashioned from Rudrākṣa beads, strung upon a sapphire of the Nīlasārasvata variety, bestows all desires;
likewise, a rosary fashioned from conch shells certainly grants fame.
Rosaries made of lotus seeds bestow nourishment and fortune, as well as the destruction of enemies;
those made of putrajīva grant sons, sovereignty, wealth, and prosperity.
A garland fashioned from pearls brings abundant fortune and splendor;
it grants the direct realization of mantras, as well as the accomplishments (siddhis) of pacification and enrichment.
Likewise, a crystal rosary bestows liberation; a ruby rosary brings eloquence, and similarly, one of emerald brings abundant wealth.
A golden garland on a silver thread grants all desires;
when worn during the Sārasvata [rite], it brings about the acquisition of even greater wealth.
A rosary fashioned from these joints— beginning with *rudrākṣa* and ending with *kuśa* grass, which destroys evil—
is for the auspicious success of men.
For rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*), a rosary of teeth has been proclaimed by the ancient authorities;
it consists of thirty-two teeth and is strung together with a human sinew.
A rosary that destroys all sins is fashioned by stringing together various garlands;
the prayer-bead necklace should be made from the lower teeth of a *preta*.
In the rite of causing hatred, it should be performed with fibers produced from the body of the person against whom the act is directed;
the meaning is that one should tie it together with the hair of the target using fibers from his own head.
The finger-joint (*aṅguli*) is innumerable, yet it is declared to be one; ten times a hundred *padmajīvas* is a thousand *saṃkhyas*.
A necklace of ten thousand strings made of coral and precious gems is prescribed;
one made of crystal is declared by the gods to be [worth] a hundred thousand, and one made of pearls is said to be [worth] a lakh.
With lotus seeds, ten lakhs [of recitations] are required; with silver beads, it is said to be ten million (one koṭi);
with gold, it is ten times that, and likewise, with all [precious materials], it is a hundredfold.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred times, or half of that, for the sake of common success;
by fifty plus four more, the accomplishment of desired rites shall occur.
It is said that with one hundred and eight [recitations] made into a garland, all perfections (siddhi) are attained;
one seeking liberation should recite twenty-five, and one desiring wealth should recite thirty.
In the rites of creation and so forth, there are twenty-five [beads], while in the malevolent rite of *abhicāra*, there are ten;
even with rosaries of white lotus seeds, the same result is attained.
The *Śaktiyāmala*, the *Kuśamālā*, the *Raudrākṣī*, the *Śvetapadmākṣamālā*,
and likewise the *Akṣamālā*— these are remembered as yielding infinite fruit when used for recitation (*japa*) that is common to all purposes; thus they have been proclaimed by me.

However, regarding the daily recitation (*nityajapa*), which is common to all, optional, or occasional, one who desires success (*siddhi*) is enjoined [to offer this] according to the previously cited statement. This is the specific detail concerning the *arghya* offering.
Success is spontaneously achieved through the rosary known as Mahāśaṅkha; protection is provided by that garland,
and likewise, when the fierce Tārā and Sarasvatī are recited with it, they shall bestow liberation.
Likewise, [it is said] in the *Nīlasarasvatī*: "The garland of bones from the forehead of a celestial being," and in the *Tārārṇava*:
"If one is unable [to use those], one should perform the recitation with a crystal rosary, even if it is made of large conch shells."
And in the Kālītantra:
"With a rosary made of teeth, with the upper incisor as the *meru*,
[this] is always difficult to obtain on earth for the worship of Kālikā."
In the Yoginītantra:
"Or [one may use] red sandalwood, *narāṣṭi*, or the fruit of the *dhātrī* according to the prescribed rite;
or water produced from *bilva* wood in the middle..."
One should employ the beads produced from the *amalaka* fruit according to the [prescribed] times:
the first rosary consists of one hundred and eight seeds, the second half of that, and the third consists of twenty-five. Thus ends the daily recitation (*nityajapa*).
Having first made the seed-syllable (bīja), one should then make the womb-syllable (yoni);
O Dear One, one should recite the Śakti-mantra together with knots made of Rudrākṣa beads.
He falls into an evil state of existence, and his recitation becomes fruitless;
one should employ Viṣṇu in all [mantras] using knots of kusha grass and other such beads.
A conch shell made of coral or silver is recommended for Tripurā;
this is stated in the Vārāhī Tantra.
A rosary (akṣamālikā) should be made with golden strings and Guñjā seeds.
One should take a rosary made of living beings, or one fashioned from crystal or conch shell.
One should not make [rosaries] from coral at all; one should avoid the *putrajīva* fruit;
and finally, [rosaries may be made] from lotus seeds, *rudrākṣa*, and *indrākṣa*.
Thus [is concluded] the section concerning Tripurā. Now follows the detailed exposition of the *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration).
In the Kubjikātantra: "First, one should worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments;
then, together with friends, one should have a pure garland made from materials of various forms."
At the beginning, not at the time of separation and so forth, one should take a rosary (*mālā*) consisting of beads (*varṇa*) of equal number,
arranged according to their proper sequence, just as previously described;
it should indeed be free from doubt, stainless, and devoid of any breakage.
Just as a skillful garland-maker would create a suitable and well-strung garland.
And in the Muṇḍamālā:
"Having performed his daily rites, being pure and a knower of mantras regarding the pure half-months,
he should diligently collect the [required] substances at the proper time and according to what is available."
They are of uniform appearance, neither too thick nor too thin,
free from the infestation of insects and the like, and neither worn out nor brand new.

In the case of Kubjikā, one should perform the purification with *taṃ-stu-nā-ye-na-yā* and immerse it in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three days; furthermore, on the fourth day, one who is self-restrained should wash the thread in water.
And in the *Muṇḍamālā*:

"Having washed those [seeds] individually with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the meaning is that those seeds are to be immersed in *pañcagavya* for three days; this constitutes the pair of immersion and washing."

The distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable is thus established. Therefore, O best of the twice-born, having folded three times a sacred thread made by a virtuous woman—free from knots and consisting of three strands—or even a piece of cloth; |||

And in the *Yāmala*: "For the rites of pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and malevolent magic (*abhicārika*), the wise man should prepare a thread that is white, red, or black, or else a silk thread (*paṭṭasūtra*)."
A Vaiṣṇava rosary is made of cotton threads or even of silk threads;
a Śaiva rosary is proclaimed to be made of wool or of bark fibers.
And in the *Yāmala*:
"If a man recites a mantra with rosaries that have not been consecrated,
all of that shall be fruitless, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged."
That [garland], fashioned by a beloved woman, is considered to grant swift success;
it should be made with three threads wound upwards and then wound downwards.
One should perform the pacification of obstacles using the Sūtra composed by Puṇyastrī;
then, reciting the Mūlāstra Sūtra, one should wash the seed-syllable.
Taking each individual jewel, one should designate a Brahma-knot.
And in the Yoginītantra it is said:
"O Daughter of Śaṅkara, one should string them with a thread of earth or with silk thread."
It is considered highly praised, well-spoken, white, and a bestower of liberation.
Having made it threefold and provided with a *brahmagranthi* at the top,
[one should wear it] with twenty-one threads thus tripled; for one who is not a householder, this applies to all mantras, as well as for the attainment of desires and liberation on the right side.
In the Kubjikātantra: "One should string together threads of uniform color with the heart-mantra;
then one should apply either the Brahma-knot or the Nāga-noose."
Then, having protected himself with the Kavaca mantra and being intent on the meditation of the deity,
he should thereafter [place] Mount Meru, complete in all its parts and endowed with two threads.
