The supreme practitioner should string them together using the *tāra* (oṃ) mantra and bind them;
as stated in the *Vārāhītantra*:
"With silk threads and cords, one should first string the rosary."
Through red [spots], one attains liberation; through white ones, the practice of yoga and other means.
Through yellow [offerings] desired by people, there arises black disease and the like; and according to the *Muṇḍamālā*:
"The nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree are arranged in the form of a lotus."
One should place there a thread, a gem, and fragrant substances that have been washed within [the vessel].
One should not wash the ritual seat with water from a cremation ground;
rather, it should be washed with pure water, blood, musk, and saffron.
Having thus deposited the Śakti, the Mātṛkā, and likewise the Sūtra and the mantras,
one should worship them and offer oblations of clarified butter with a spirit of devotion.
If one is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should perform double the number of recitations (japa).
Taking each bead one by one, one should designate it as a Brahma-knot (brahmagraṃthi).
One should join mouth to mouth and tail to tail;
this is for the *phava* [mudrā] during the recitation (*japa*).
It should be made like a cow’s tail, or it may take the form of a serpent.
She should conceive that single sense-faculty of her own kind as being Mount Meru.
In the Śāmbhava Saṃhitā:
Furthermore, the Sūta, the Sūtra, and Vītihotra constitute a triad;
these are declared to be Day and Night. Therefore, this is the auspicious triad of fires (tejas-trayī).
In the *Yāmala*: "Then, having well-bathed it, one should place the garland in a golden vessel,
or alternatively, one should arrange it upon nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree in the shape of a lotus."
From the *Muṇḍamālā Tantra*, the procedure for the worship of the *aśvattha* leaf and its stringing is as follows:
according to the *Yāmala* and other systems, following the stringing, there is the placement and worship of the *aśvattha* leaf.
Having fasted previously and being pure, one should perform the worship with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
"One who has fasted" refers to the sacrificial animal, as in the Vīrāgama.

A garland of red thread is always pleasing to the Goddess. That Vaiṣṇava garland should be made by one who knows the mantras, using Viṣṇu’s mantra with effort during the daytime while observing a fast.
One should fashion the Śāktī-mālā at night after eating according to the prescribed rule,
especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth lunar days.
O Goddess of the gods, one should indeed perform [the rite] for Śiva on the thirteenth day;
and in the Vārāhītantra it is said:
"One should not make [the thread] devoid of knots, for it becomes defective through [excessive] tail-to-tail joining."
And in the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Gāṇeśa, and Śrīkara [tantras] as well.
Furthermore, one should perform [the rite] upon the touch of the seed-syllable; regarding this, there is no doubt.
Now listen to those goddesses who reside in the knots and those goddesses who are dissolved within the knots:
they are the Indrākṣās produced by Kālikā, according to their sixfold division.
And one should likewise join it with Vārāhī, who dwells on the Tītalā mountain.
One should install the Mātṛkā letters, interspersed [with the seed-syllables], both in direct and reverse order;
then, one should sprinkle the rosary with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) after it has been consecrated with the Śiva-mantra.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"One should make it provided with a Brahma-knot, positioned as prescribed;
or else, it may be without a knot, provided with a strong cord."
By revolving three times through the middle from the region of the upper end, a clockwise-turning knot is formed; this is known as the Śabdagranthi (Sound-knot).
One who protects oneself in this manner and performs the supreme recitation (japa) is liberated from untimely death and the effects of the Kali age; of this there is no doubt.
In the case of Kubjikā: having thus accomplished [the visualization], O Goddess of Gods, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Having fashioned a maṇḍala upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), according to the sequence of the rules for yoga.
Having worshipped the chosen deity according to the rules and in the proper sequence,
one should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and then recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.

One should perform oblations with a tenth part [of the recitation] of whatever is dear to whichever deity. As stated in the *Muṇḍamālā*: "Having thus performed the procedure for the rosary of recitation, one should then carry out the consecration."
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with fresh water.
Oṃ, I shall proclaim [the mantra] for Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! O Bhava, O Bhava, O primordial Bhava, favor me; salutations indeed to Bhavodbhava!
One should grind [the substances] with sandalwood, agallochum, fragrance, and so forth, using the Vāmadeva [mantra].

Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Jyeṣṭha; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Manomanas.
One should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra and smear it with the Puruṣa mantra: *Oṃ aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyo ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ | sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyo namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ*.

Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt. One should consecrate each [part] one hundred times with this very fifth mantra: "Īśāna is the lord of all sciences, the lord of all beings, the sovereign of Brahman, the sovereign of Brahman; may Śiva be ever auspicious. As for Meru:

Then, one should consecrate [the materials] with the fifth mantra alone. For the Sadyojāta and other mantras, there is a recitation of one hundred repetitions each; for the Meru-mantra, there is only a single recitation. This is stated in the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā.
One should consecrate each [of the others] once with the fifth mantra;
likewise, one should consecrate Meru itself only once with the mantra.
Having consecrated the garland, one should place it upon his own life-breaths as a weapon;
having worshipped the Guru with effort, one should receive it with a spirit of devotion.
The ritual procedure for another mantra is stated in the *Kubjikā-tantra*:
"Then the wise practitioner should place the rosary in the center of the mandala."
Then, having assigned the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should thereafter assign the root-mantra (mūlamantra).
Having performed the placement of those limbs, one should contemplate the deity therein; having attained a state of non-difference, one should then form the rosary as being of that same nature.
Then the best of practitioners should offer the bali-oblation according to the rule;
having thus performed the consecration of the rosary for his chosen deity.

The practitioner of mantra should worship the preceptor and the artisan according to the prescribed rule. As stated in the *Yāmala*: "Having bathed [the image] well with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water..."
The practitioner should place the seed-syllable upon that great throne of the hungry ghosts.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess there along with her retinue of attendants,
one should duly kindle the fire and offer oblations of ghee according to one's capacity.
If one is engaged in the rite of fire-oblation (homa) and becomes distracted, one should perform double the recitation;
having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer it to the Goddess.
Then, having himself recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over the hand of the disciple,
he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to his means.
One should personally perform the consecration of the rosary that was previously in the possession of the Guru.
Regarding the ritual to be performed immediately after receiving the rosary,
it is stated in the *Kubjikātantra*:
Then, having taken the rosary from the hand of the guru, one should consecrate it with this mantra:
"O rosary, you who always grant pleasure to all the gods, [grant it] to me."
"O auspicious one, O blessed one, may there always be welfare, glory, and valor for me.
Having thus addressed the auspicious [flower] and held it, one should then conceal it within the weapon-mantra (astra) and the rest.
Thus, having prepared the rosary, the wise one should perform recitation using the Mātṛkā.
From the various divisions of the Mātṛkā mantra, all mantras were born.
Then, the recitation of independent mantras should be performed with that garland;
as stated in the Muṇḍamālā:
"One who is impure should not touch it, nor should one cause it to fall from the hand."
One should not touch the rosary with the index finger; having worshipped it, one should keep it concealed.

One should not show [this] even to one's guru. For eating as well as for attracting, the wise man should recite with the middle finger; for the highest rite, he should recite between the thumb and the ring finger.
For the rites of killing and expulsion, the recitation is performed with the joining of the index finger and the thumb;
for the rite of killing, one should recite with the joining of the little finger and the thumb.
Having worshipped this rosary during the time of recitation, one should keep it concealed;
the recitation rosary must be protected, for the recitation rosary is most auspicious.
The wise one should reveal himself to the guru, but never his mantra;
nor should he show his rosary or his mudrās even to the guru.
Bhūtas, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas carry away success from that which is manifest; therefore, always keep it secret.
When the thread has worn out, one should string another thread and recite [the mantra] over it;
if it falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
First, having washed [the vessel] with the touch and sight of a perfected one (siddha) as prescribed in the *Yoginītantra*:
"When it has been fried in the hand and the sound has been made, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times."
And in the *Yāmala*:
"Having first worshipped the rosary, one should recite [the mantra], and likewise at the end of the recitation;
one should offer the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], Bhuvaneśānī, and the rosary (akṣamālā) along with the [deity] Śrī."
Having recited the heart-mantra, the best of practitioners should perform worship:
"Oṃ, Mālā, Mālā, Mahāmālā, you whose nature is all powers!"
"The fourfold aims of life are entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success. Then, having consecrated it with this mantra, one should take the rosary in the right hand.

The mantra of Māyā Siddheśvarī, ending in the vocative case (ṅe) and concluding with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), is remembered as this seven-syllabled mantra for use during eclipses and at the conclusion of recitation.
Having brought [the thread] to the *hā* region, one should not touch it with the left hand;
O Dear One, touching with the left hand is prohibited in the composition of the Mahāyāna.
Having placed [the rosary] in the middle part of the middle finger, being composed, one should not touch the garland with the index finger; rather, one should move it with the tip of the thumb.
One should not cross over Meru or any of the individual [mountains];
one should move the rosary beads, resting on the thumb, with the tip of the middle finger.
One should perform the recitation with the thumb and the ring finger for the highest rites;
for the rites of inciting hatred and eradication, the recitation is performed by joining the index finger and the thumb.
In the rite of killing, one should perform the recitation by joining the little finger with the thumb;
at the conclusion of the recitation, having placed the rosary upon the head, one should worship it with this [mantra].
O Tyamālā, you who grant delight to all the gods and bestow auspiciousness upon me;
O blessed one, bring me well-being, fame, and valor at all times.
In the Yoginītantra:
"O Śaṅkarī, one should recite [the mantra] starting from the base (mūla), having covered oneself with a cloth;
for the performance of rites for specific desires, one should cover oneself with a pair of upper garments."
One should never touch the garland with the left hand;
O beloved, contact with the left hand [is forbidden] regarding the garland that has been strung.
If [the tooth] is touched by a deity or broken within a year, one should perform the consecration immediately; one should place it in a copper vessel with water.
Joined with the letter of space (ha) and fire (ra), adorned with the left eye (ī),
and surmounted by the syllables of sound (nāda), the drop (bindu), and the digit (kalā), it is conjoined with the heart-mantra for the sake of accomplishment.
This five-syllabled mantra is proclaimed for the rosary;
one should employ it during its acquisition, its installation, and its worship.
At the end of the recitation (*japa*), one should recite a hymn of praise over his head at the conclusion of the mantra.
As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"If [the flower] falls from the hand, there will be an obstacle; if it is severed, death shall occur."
At the beginning of the recitation (japa) and other rites, one should carefully worship the rosary and sprinkle it with water; having placed it within the mandala,
either held in the left hand or otherwise,
and having worshipped it, one should then take the rosary in the right hand.
Then, having excluded the index finger, [one should place them] in the middle portion of the middle finger.
Having placed the rosary upon the ring finger joined with the little finger in a state of humility, one should then hold it with the tip of the thumb.
Taking each individual seed-syllable, Bhairava should perform the recitation (*japa*).
Holding the rosary with his right hand upon his heart, he should meditate on the Goddess and recite the mantra at every repetition; he should do so slowly, moving his lips.

O Bhairava, one should not touch the seed-syllable of the garland or the portions of the worship with one another; rather, it should be performed with the tip of the thumb as employed during the preliminary recitation.
If one first moves the seed-finger (the ring finger) and then touches the other fingers with the thumb, that recitation indeed becomes fruitless for him.
Holding the rosary with the right hand close to the heart, one should perform the recitation while meditating on the Goddess; one should not touch it with the left hand.
Having recited [the mantra] over the rosary, one should place it upon the head in a high position. As stated in the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā*:
"One should perform the mental recitation (*japa*) of that very same [mantra] by which the consecrated rosary was established."
Those who bear the marks [of initiation] should not constantly perform the recitation of other mantras.
Now, regarding the consecration of the great garland (*mahāmālā*) in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Taking each individual gem, one should designate a Brahma-knot;
one should place them separated by the *mātṛkā* [syllables], in both direct and reverse order."
By that, one is born endowed with all virtues and becomes a possessor of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Here, there is a state of being a sentence within a sentence (*vākya*);
some say it is "muṇḍamāyukta mathuhyam. Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): first, [one should choose] an artisan...

One should cause a garland to be made after honoring it with garments, perfumes, and ointments. First, it should be thick, then increasingly dense, compact, free from breaks, and devoid of defects. It should be fashioned appropriately, uniform throughout, neither too thick nor too thin, ungnawed by insects or other creatures, and not decayed; such is the fruit [of the garland] one should have made.

In the case of the seed-syllable (*bījapakṣa*), one should bring [the materials] there; the distinction is that the worship of the artisan (*śilpin*) takes place there. Likewise, having performed the daily rites on the day specified, one should throw the aforementioned tantric measure into the *pañcagavya* for three days—or if unable, in a single day. Having washed it with the *pañcāga-astra* mantra, [one should wash] the cremation ground with scented water.

Having washed the horse with water mixed with *saṃbandha* [fragrant substances] and purified water according to one's capacity and availability, and having established it in its proper place, one should arrange eight leaves in the eight directions so that they form the shape of a lotus;
then, having placed one leaf in the center, one should place the thread and the garland there, [reciting]: *oṃ hrīṃ*.

Saying "Aṃ 5 Namaḥ," one should place [the thread] upon the garland and the cord; having worshipped the Root Goddess there according to the ritual rules and recited the mantra one thousand and eight times, one should perform the consecration in the refined [fire]. Then, having knotted the thread with the mantra "Gauṃ" and "Namaḥ," one should apply the Brahma-knot or the Naga-noose with the mantra "Lūm. Thereafter—

Having combined the two sūtras, one should face Mount Meru with the mantra *oṃ* and draw it forward as before. However, according to another mantra: having washed the rosaries according to the rules, having strung them according to the rules, and having placed them in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and rinsed them, one should place them upon leaves of the *aśvattha* tree in the shape of a lotus. Now, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is as follows:

Having washed the rosary with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting *oṃ sadyojātaṃ* and so forth; having rubbed it with sandalwood, agallochum, incense, and other substances while reciting *oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ* and so forth; having fumigated the rosary with incense while reciting *oṃ aghora* and so forth; having anointed it with sandalwood and other unguents while reciting *tatpuruṣa* and so forth; one should consecrate it while reciting *oṃ īśāna* and so forth.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) of each *ṛc* one hundred times. Having consecrated even Mount Meru with the mantra beginning with "Oṃ Īśāna," and having placed it in the center of the mandala, one should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) of the Goddess after assigning the *astra-mantra* and the six root-limbs (*mūla-ṣaḍaṅga*). Therein, one should meditate upon the Goddess in that form.
Having meditated upon the goat and other offerings and presented the bali, one should recite the Mātṛkā in both direct and reverse order,
then recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times, offer praise, and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru.
In the *Tad-yāmala*:
Now, the consecration of the great yantra, which bestows all accomplishments, is declared.
Having performed his bath on an auspicious day, under an auspicious lunar mansion, and at an auspicious moment.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, the practitioner, facing either the east or the north,
should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other preliminary rites, and then carry out the ritual according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa.
Then, with a mind purified by resolve, he, being composed, brought the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) which had been purified by divine mantras and recited the mantra over it there.
The knower of mantras, reciting the Praṇava, should cast gold and other substances into the jewel;
then, having extracted them, he should place them in a vessel made of gold or other materials.
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with sacred water (tīrtha), and with cool water,
preceded by the root mantra and the Sahasraśīrṣā mantra.
Having bathed [the deity] with a pure cloth, one should offer water for splendor (*tejas*) and,
having placed [the image] upon a lion-throne or similar seat, one should anoint it with saffron and other unguents.
Then one should perform the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual,
while touching the king of yantras with kuśa grass one hundred and eight times.
One should extract the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) for the King of Yantras; then one should write "vidmahe," followed by "mahāyantrāya dhīmahe" and then "tanno mahī."
That form of Rudra, which is proclaimed as the deity, should be offered;
by chanting this Gāyatrī of the Yantra, one shall attain divinity.
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity as desired, one should invoke it in sequence with the appropriate mudrā;
then, one should perform the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) and worship the chosen deity.
With the sixteen types of ritual services and extensive displays of various riches,
accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music preceded by the fivefold sounds.
Then one should recite the desired mantra one thousand and eight times;
thereafter, having prepared the fire according to the ritual manual with sacrificial oblations, one should proceed as prescribed.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations according to his pure means,
he should satisfy [the officiant] with gold, garments, and other gifts, and also bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:
"Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) purified by the seed-syllable of Śiva (the *śivabīja*),
the practitioner of mantra should then cast the wheel [of the mandala] along with the water for sprinkling (*akṣatāḥ*) while reciting the Praṇava."
Then, having lifted that cakra, one should place it upon a full leaf;
[one should perform] its bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water.
With salutation, with fragrant incense, with musk and saffron, with gold,
and with eight jars filled with water, [one should worship] the Goddess.
One should cause an excellent bath with decoction-water and conch-shell water to be performed;
having drawn up the water with a cloth, one should place it upon a golden pedestal.
Then, having performed the purification of oneself through the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*) and so forth,
one should invoke the Great Goddess here and perform the placement of the seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*).
The practitioner of mantra should always worship the deity with the sixteen services, beginning with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), as well as with fruits, betel, and food offerings.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer silk threads and the like, as well as garments and ornaments, saffron, a fly-whisk, and a bell, according to what is appropriate.
Then, for the sake of accomplishment, one should perform a thousand recitations while the lamp is burning;
having then offered the bali-oblation, one should prostrate before the King of Mandalas.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with medicinal herbs, grains, and sesame seeds;
and having brought two cows adorned with golden horns.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru and then dismiss the Goddess.
Now, the procedure for yantras that have been burnt and so forth:
O Dear One, a yantra that is burnt, cracked, or has been tampered with by a thief—
One should diligently observe a fast for one day and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, preceded by fire offerings (homa) and libations (tarpaṇa).
Having satisfied the Guru with true devotion, one should also feed the Brahmins.
One should avoid [a rosary] whose marks are occasionally missing or which is cracked;
a mortal who uses one that is damaged by fire or burnt will face death within three months.

Therefore, O Goddess, one should cast it into a great river or the ocean; otherwise, one would meet with death. Now I shall describe the procedure for the excellent installation of a deity: on a sacred site, in a place free from impurities and the like, the practitioner of mantras (mantrī) should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the preceding day, according to the ritual manual (kalpa).
Having made the formal resolve in the evening according to the rules, preceded by the ritual installation of the banyan tree.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and the others, one should fully honor the guardians of the directions;
one should worship the root deity with offerings and services according to one's capacity.
One should consecrate it with divine substances such as fragrant oils and perfumes,
preceded by the sounding of victory drums and the recitation of the mantra beginning with "caṃdra."
Having performed this consecration, self-restrained and with his senses conquered,
he should enter the prepared sacrificial ground after completing the preliminary rites at dawn.

"Adorned with a circle of suns crowded with banners and flags" means it is decorated with a circle of suns, variegated with powders of five colors, and adorned with the circles of the sun and other [deities].
It is graced with canopies, yak-tail whisks, and umbrellas, adorned with flower garlands,
and distinguished by auspicious sprouts, leaves, and lamps.
One should draw the Sarvatobhadra mandala upon the altar,
facing east and remaining silent, for the sake of accomplishing one's intended purpose through right resolve.
Having worshipped the five purities and having placed a bundle of kusha grass together with unbroken rice grains within that mandala, one should recite the mantra of the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti).
The wise one should establish the entire [deity] with the mantra ending in the *pīṭhamantra*,
according to the procedure for consecration and the ritual for the water-pot as prescribed for the time of initiation.
Then, one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), purified by the Śiva-mantra;
with that, the practitioner of mantras, while reciting the life-infusing mantra (prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā), should bathe the image thoroughly.

One should sequentially place the deities within the heart using the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), sacrificial oblation (*havis*), curd, and milk. Then, one should perform the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the installation of life-force) with the appropriate mantra. One should then rub [the image] with that [mixture], bathe it with water, and clothe it in a fine silk garment after lifting up the water.
The wise one should lead the deity near the installed pitcher;
then, having meditated upon her as described, he should invoke her in sequence with the appropriate mudrā.
With the *lelihā* mudrā, one should place the hand upon the heart of the deity;
then, one should recite the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra ten times.
Then, one should recite the Daivata-gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa, one should worship her together with her retinue.
Afterwards, one should worship the deities; having established the maṇḍala of the site upon a pedestal, it should be provided with eight petals.
Indeed, one should apply an ointment to my limbs with fragrant divine oil;
a wise person should do so in this measure, reciting the *Sahasraśīrṣā* [Puruṣasūkta].
One should bathe [the deity] with a spirit of devotion using ten thousand jars for the consecration,
filled with water scented with camphor, agallochum, musk, flowers, and sandalwood.

One should diligently sprinkle [the image] with water from various sacred fords (tīrtha), as well as with waters containing precious gems and the like, with waters containing all medicinal herbs, and with fragrant waters.
Then, having put on two pure silk garments, the practitioner, holding water in his uplifted hands,
[should sit] upon a swing made of gold.
Having brought [the deity] into the mandala with the sounds of dance and song,
one should worship with the sixteen services according to the ritual manual.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), on a consecrated altar (sthaṇḍila), or upon a purified fire, the practitioner of mantra,
having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, should then offer the oblation (caru) after sprinkling it with water.
Having heard [the instructions] according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, having offered clarified butter with the sacrificial ladle (śruva), one should also make oblations directly in front [of the deity].
Having diligently performed this twenty-five times for the sake of the deity,
one should offer the previously mentioned oblation (bali) beginning with the "carā" [formula] to the goddesses of the lunar days (tithis).
Then one should offer an oblation of clarified butter to the deities of the limbs, or likewise with sacrificial porridge (caru); thereafter, one should go near the deity.
One should offer a handful of perfumes and flowers, along with an umbrella and chowries;
then, having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should likewise recite the [principal] mantra.

Then, one should consecrate the Goddess with the sprouts contained within the water-pot while reciting the Mātṛkā-mantras. Having gone there with a voice chanting "Victory!", one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) equal in measure to the fire-oblation (homa).
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, measuring one karṣa of gold,
or else a fourth part of that, according to one's means.
Ten *guñjā* seeds constitute a *māṣa*, and half of that is said to be one *karṣa*.
Then, having taken [the fee], he should satisfy the twice-born with various gifts for his disciples.
Thus, O Lord, the installation previously described is the bestower of prosperity;
for that high-souled one who performs the installation, O Lord—
He shall dwell for thousands of years in the world of Brahmā and be honored there; or else, having fallen from that state, he rejoices for the duration of ten million kalpas.
Now I shall describe the consecration of a house, preceded by the Vāstu sacrifice,
during the highly meritorious autumn season, in a sacred field, on an auspicious day.
For the sake of purification, one should offer a temple according to the respective mantras;
having first performed all the preliminary rites, one should direct the intellect toward the Self.
Then, having made the formal resolve according to the prescribed rites, they set out in that beautiful chariot,
which was crowded with banners and flags and filled with excellent horses.
Having drawn the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is beautifully adorned with parasols, chowries, garlands, and canopies, one should place the jar situated therein.
One should worship the chosen deity with the sixteen types of offerings;
having worshipped the limbs of the deity, one should then sacrifice to the respective hosts of deities.
With great reverence, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the ten-syllable mantra; one should then present an excellent temple to Durgā.
Having uttered "Bhuvaneśī," the great seed-syllable, "Durge," and "Manum" (the mantra), and then saying "Rakṣaṇī" in sequence, one should utter "Vahnijāyā" (svāhā); this is the mantra.
Whoever should give a well-established temple with this mantra attains all sovereignty and shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.

O Goddess, on this excellent seat (pīṭha), one who has become perfected on the seventh [tithi] should accomplish the highest siddhi on the great eighth; thus one shall conquer Śivā—this is the ritual for the relinquishing of the house (gṛhotsarga).
Now follows the exposition of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*). It is stated in the *Somabhujagāvalī*:

"O wise one, the six rites of the learned consist of pacification (*śānti*), subjugation (*vaśya*), immobilization (*staṃbhana*), piercing (*vidveṣa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and likewise ending with killing (*māraṇa*)."
The pacification of diseases, malevolent spells, planetary influences, and so forth has been proclaimed;
likewise, the method for bringing all people under one's control has been declared.
The awakening of activity in all beings is declared to be *staṃbhanam* (paralysis);
the generation of hatred among those who are affectionate is considered *vidveṣaṇam* (inciting enmity).
The expulsion from one's own country and so forth is proclaimed as *uccāṭana* (driving away),
while the taking of the life-force of living beings is declared to be *māraṇa* (killing).

One should worship one's own respective deity and others in the cardinal directions, and having understood this, one should accomplish the ritual actions; [the goddesses] are Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī, in due order.
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should worship them at the beginning of the ritual. Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Agni, and Varuṇa are considered to be the directions.
Starting from sunrise, ten successive *ghaṭikās* constitute the seasons,
beginning with spring, day after day throughout the day and night.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
winter is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), while spring is for the rite of subjugation (vaśya).
The winter season is declared suitable for paralyzing, while summer is said to be excellent for inciting enmity;
the rainy season should be known as appropriate for expulsion, and autumn for the rite of killing.
In the Śasomabhujagāvalī:
"The rite for pacification (śāntika) is to be known as appropriate for autumn; likewise, the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika) for winter;
attraction (ākarṣaṇa) for spring; and incantation for causing enmity (vidveṣaṇa) is prescribed for summer."
One should perform subjugation in the summer and eradication likewise in the winter;
the practitioner always performs these [rites] during these seasons.
Midnight is the autumn season, and the forenoon is the winter;
the morning is spring, and midday is indeed the summer.
Prāvṛṣ and Parāhna are known as Pradoṣa, and Śiśira is likewise remembered [as such].
Alternatively:
Uṣā-yoga is Hemanta, and Prabhāta is Śiśira.
Spring lasts for half a watch, and summer occurs during the interval until midday.
In the fourth watch [of the night], the sun is in the signs of Leo (Siṃha) and Scorpio (Vṛścika);

during the rainy season and autumn, rites such as those for nourishment (*puṣṭika*) and others should be performed according to the conjunction of the weekday and lunar day (*tithi*) in the *Svatantra* [Tantra].
These should be employed according to the prescribed rule, which shall now be fully explained:
namely, the fifth, the second, the third, and likewise the seventh.

The sixth, fourth, and thirteenth lunar days, when conjoined with Thursday (the day of Jupiter) or Monday (the day of the Moon), are highly esteemed for rites of pacification (śāntikarma). The sixth day, when joined with Jupiter and the Moon, is likewise auspicious. The fourth and thirteenth days, when combined with these, are also honored for such purposes.
The ninth lunar day is auspicious for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika); likewise, the eighth and ninth days, as well as the tenth and eleventh, when joined with Sunday or Friday, are propitious.
For the rite of attraction, the eighth and ninth lunar days as well as the first (pratipad) are suitable;
for the rite of causing enmity, the full moon day, excluding Sundays, is prescribed.
Likewise, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and the eighth day when the stars have dimmed are auspicious lunar days for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana),
especially at the time of dusk.
The fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, as well as the new moon day,
when joined with a Saturday or a Tuesday, are auspicious for the rite of exorcism.
The fifth lunar day (pañcamī) joined with Mercury and the Moon, as well as the tenth (daśamī) and the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
should be known as the appropriate lunar days for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana).
One should perform auspicious deeds when there is the rising of auspicious planets and at an auspicious rising;
one should perform acts of violence during the Riktā and Ārka [parvan] and during the Mṛtyu-yoga.
Now follows the determination of the qualified practitioner.
As it is stated in the Nīlatantra:
"One who has mastered the mantra should perform rites for specific desires; not otherwise."
Now, regarding the signs of accomplishment in the *Svatantra*:
the effortless fulfillment of one's desires is declared to be complete success;
the acquisition of ornaments and the like from fire, as well as pearls and gold, [are also signs].
Longevity, health, long-lasting prosperity, and gratitude—
these are declared to be the perceptible accomplishments for one who possesses a perfected mantra, O lady.

O Dear One, the ritual applications must be performed with a perfected mantra; otherwise, they will not succeed. And in the *Yāmala*: "The characteristic of the effortless accomplishment of one's desires is [the perfected mantra]."
In that same way, there is the removal of deaths as well as the vision of the deities.
The application, the accomplishment of the afflictions, and the supreme characteristic of accomplishment; likewise, the entering of another's body and the going to the supreme city.
Thus, the upward ascent, the movement through the city of the moving and the unmoving,
the journey of the Khecarī, and likewise the hearing of her discourse [are attained].
One should observe the fissures in the ground, as well as the characteristics of the highest [type];
likewise, there is the taking away by death and the vision of deities.
The accomplishment of the application of effort and the supreme characteristic of that accomplishment consist of renown,
riding, ornaments, and so forth, as well as being led [by others] and the enjoyment of pure food.
This is the supreme means of subjugating kings and their queens;
it brings wonder to all people everywhere and bestows happiness.
By sight, the practitioner of mantras removes disease and likewise removes poison;
thus, through diligent effort, he attains the fourfold state of scholarship.
Dispassion, the desire for liberation, renunciation, mastery over all things,
devotion to the eightfold yoga, and the total abandonment of the desire for enjoyment.
Compassion toward all beings and the arising of qualities such as omniscience—
this attainment of such qualities is the characteristic of middling accomplishment.
Great sovereignty, wealth, and the prosperity of children, wife, and so forth—
these are declared by the Mantrin to be the inferior attainments (siddhis) arising at the first stage.
The Siddhis and the Tattvas are directly Śiva himself; there is no doubt in this matter. Now, regarding the postures (āsanas): in the Somabhujagāvalī, it says:
"The one called Padma, Svastika, Vikaṭa, and again Kukkuṭa."
The wise say that the vajra is auspicious; it is the latent impressions (vāsanās).
And in the *Svatantra*:
"For nourishing rites, the lotus posture (*padmāsana*); for pacifying rites, the *kokhastika* posture;
likewise, for attraction, the side-lying posture; and for inciting hatred and the subjugation of enemies."
The Arddhasvastika mudrā is recommended for rites such as expulsion (uccāṭana) and killing (māraṇa). Now, regarding the mudrās in the Somabhujagāvalī:
the six mudrās, beginning with Padmā and Rāgā, should be known in their proper sequence.
The *muśalā*, *śani*, and *khaḍgā* [mantras] are used in rites such as those involving *kṛtyā* and *śāka*.

Now, regarding the *bhūtodayas*: therein, for the rite of pacifying water-spirits (*jalauśānti*), [the earth element] is recommended; for subjugation (*vaśya*), fire is declared by Rudra; for paralyzing (*stambhana*), earth is praised; for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), space is proclaimed;
for eradication (*uccāṭana*), wind is remembered; and for killing (*māraṇa*), both earth and fire are considered appropriate.
That [should be performed] correctly at the rising of that respective [sign], conjoined with its corresponding maṇḍala.
That specific rite must be performed by a minister of resolute mind.

Thus, rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) should be performed during the flow of the left [channel], while fierce rites (*raudrakarma*) should not be performed during the flow of the right. Now follows the exposition of the rising of the lunar and solar breaths (*vāmadakṣiṇavāhabhūtodaya*). In the *Tripurāsāra*, it is said regarding the *iḍā*:

Thus the moon, garlanded with cool rays, moves; then the sun moves in the left channel (vāmā) which is designated as nectar (amṛta), while he moves in the piṅgalā [right channel], from which poison is said to flow on the right side by the lords of sages.
A wise man should know its rising in the belly of the Lord within the root-tube (kanda) of men.
The dissolution of the nostril-makara-finger occurs at both the morning and evening twilights;

its continuous arising and dissolution are downward-moving, while night and day are upward-moving. Likewise, when the moon has entered the channel of the makara situated above, it moves as the sun during the day.

A wise person, possessing sharp intellect, should perform rites such as those for peace (*āśāntika*) when the Sun is in its *vaṃśa*, *oka*, *mārtāṇḍa*, or *nāḍī* periods, and when it is not in conjunction with mixed (*miśra*) periods. The wise one should observe the rising of the elements (*bhūta*) in both fortnights; therein, at the beginning, he should note the rising of Earth (*vasudhā*).

For the subjugation (*vaśya*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is [auspicious] when touching the staff (*daṇḍa*). For the kindling of the gods (*devedha*), it is [auspicious] when touching water. When the deceased has departed, it is [auspicious] for those who move horizontally (*tiryak*) through contact.
For one who is touched on all sides by the two Rudras, [it is auspicious].
For subjugation and paralysis (*staṃbhana*), the rising of the earth is recommended; the rising of water is recommended.
In rites such as pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), [the fire] resides again within the heart; however,
for the performance of killing (māraṇa), rending (dāraṇa), and so forth against an enemy, it is in the anus (uccāṭana) and the genitals (chādayoḥ).

In the case of *śāntika* (pacification) and *vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugation), there is the destruction of what is unfavorable from the sky (*vyoman*). If [the planet] has arisen from the earth (*dharaṇi*) and approaches those afflicted by calamities here, then the afflictions arising from disease are indeed properly pacified. When there is an emergence from water (*jala*), the illness attains peace; however, in the case of destruction (*sūdaya*), death certainly occurs. Likewise, at the time of emergence...

The destruction of that disease of the wind (samīraṇa) and the sky (vyoman) occurs very quickly. Then, when a person situated on the right side of the deity is afflicted by disease, one should inquire: if the querent stands on the right and asks, that person will live with the disease for a long time; but if he stands on the left while the Lord is overwhelmed by pain on the left, [the prognosis is different].

If the querent asks while facing left and has come from the left, he will live for a long time; if he asks while facing right, his fortune is on the wane. Or if he comes from the right and then turns away, the wise say that even such a disease is curable. However, if the querent asks while moving inward (toward the center), [the prognosis is grave].
The lord of the gods lives free from disease; yet, when afflicted by that very same disease, he departs for the city of the King of the Departed.

In all undertakings, if this Lord is situated inside [the figure], there shall be the attainment of desired goals; if the auspicious Lord is outside, one should know that it is the fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious karma. Now, the seed-syllables are in the *Somabhujagāvalī*:
The moon, water, earth, ether, air, and fire are the qualities (varṇas) of the living beings within the machine;
their six activities are respectively as follows.

The meaning is that one should worship one's own respective deities, such as Rati and others, after having inscribed these seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the center of the mandala belonging to each [deity] in the sequence corresponding to the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. Now follows the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the mantras:
"Granthana, Vidarbha, Saṃpuṭa, and likewise Rodhana."
These, known as the "Yogapallava" arrangements, are for the six types of ritual actions.
One should interpose the name with the end of the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
one should know that this "stringing" (grathana) is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śāntika).
One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated in the middle of the mantra's syllables;
this is to be known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*).
When the mantra is at both the beginning and the end, with the name placed between them, it is known as the "encased" (saṃpuṭa) method;
this is declared by those who know mantras to be excellent for the purpose of paralyzing (saṃstambhana).
In the rites of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the mantra is considered to be at the beginning, end, and middle of the name;
however, in the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*),
one should write the letters of the name of the person to be acted upon situated in the middle of another mantra.
This Vidarbha is to be known as the foremost; this is declared to be the most excellent. At the end of the mantra, the application of the name is intended for eradication (uccāṭana).
With the name at the end, the mantra becomes a "sprout" (pallava), which is intended for killing (māraṇa).
Bhairavā is at the beginning of the ear (the mantra).
At the end of the name, the mantra becomes the "pallava" (sprout),
which is proclaimed for the purpose of killing, neutralizing poison, and expelling house-spirits.
In rites of eradication and inciting enmity, however, the word *pallava* is released;
at the end of the mantra, "my station" (*mama saṃsthānam*) is considered the ritual application (*prayoga*).
In rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, expiation and purification,
as well as for deluding and inflaming, the wise employ this yoga.

It is said that for the rites of paralyzing, expelling, cutting, and creating enmity, the mantra should be placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name; this is called the "wrathful" (kruddha) application.
It brings about the manifestation of mantras, wards off all evils,
and is awakened for the pacification of fevers, possession by spirits, and the effects of poison.
Furthermore, when the mantras and their syllables are intermingled,
that which is thus interspersed is proclaimed as "grathana" (interlacing).
When the mantra is placed at the beginning and the end near that [target],
it becomes a "casket" (saṃpuṭa), as prescribed for the rite of pinning (kīlana).

In the case of the *staṃbha* (paralysis) rite, the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra is preferred; in rites such as *lakṣaṇa*, the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) method is used, wherein the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are placed sequentially between each pair of mantra syllables.
That darbha grass is to be tied for the rites of subjugation, attraction, and nourishment;
such is the sequence of application declared by the wise for all desired objects.
Regarding the *saṃpuṭa* [interlocking] method: at the beginning there is the mantra, and at the end there is the mantra; thus, in both cases, it is indeed in direct order (*anuloma*). How so?

Because in the first section of the *saṃpuṭa*, there is direct order. True; even here, in the division of the sentence, in the phrase "the mantra at the beginning," there is direct order, whereas at the end, in the phrase "the lord of speech (*citpati*) at the end," there is reverse order (*viloma*). Otherwise, in the sixteen-fold arrangement (*ṣoḍaśī-prastāra*), [the sequence would not hold].
One should perform the *saṃpuṭī* (encasement) of the six peaks (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) with the five syllables beginning with *ājya*; this is because they are extracted here in reverse order.
This will become clear in the expansion (*prastāra*) of that mantra.
It is also stated in the *Yāmala*:
It is knotted, joined in a casket, composed of all the granthas, and likewise interlaced;
thus, having reached the end of the wheel, it is situated within the interior and surrounded on all sides.
Likewise, *mukti*, *vidarbha*, and *vidarbhagrathita*—
these mantras, when employed as one, grant all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
When each of the middle and ring fingers is joined with an interval between them and knotted together,
that is renowned as the supreme mudrā for subjugation and attraction.
One should first utter the mantra, then the name preceded by "sa" (sa-), and finally the mantra again;
this is known as the *saṃpuṭaka* (encased) mantra.
It should be known as bestowing peace and nourishment, and granting sovereignty over the three worlds;
the wise practitioner should perform the mantra by repeating it half and half, from beginning to end.
And in the center, the object of the rite (sādhya) should be placed within the mouth; this is called "devouring" (grasta).
One should employ this in all malevolent rites (abhicāra) and in acts of killing (māraṇa).
One should first utter the *abhidhāra* and then perform the mantra accordingly;
this entire procedure is said to cause the eradication of enemies.

Where two mantra-syllables enclose each single syllable of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), that is called a "thread" (*tantu*); it destroys evil and has the characteristic of subjugation (*vaśa*).
If the object to be accomplished stands on all sides, interspersed within the end of the mantra, [that is another form].
One should recognize that being "overpowered" (ākrāntatā) is the immediate means for accomplishing all goals.

In the dual practice of yoga, there is the conceptualization of desire. White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoky are proclaimed as the colors of the deities associated with mantras for the six types of ritual actions.
In the stream of existence (?),
for subjugation, attraction, and immobilization, one should visualize [the deity] as golden-colored;
for neutralizing poison, pacification, nourishment, and invigoration, one should visualize [her] as white.
One should visualize them as yellow for acts of immobilization, smoke-colored for eradication,
and black in color for killing.
Thus is the description of the colors. Now follows the arrangement of the deities:
one should always meditate on [the deity] as risen for killing, and as sleeping for driving away.
Seated and well-adorned, [one performs the rites] for subjugation and other purposes.
That which is situated on the path of *yāma* and is black is proclaimed to be *tāmasa*.
The *sāttvika* [mantra] is for those desiring enjoyment and liberation; the *rājasa* is for one wishing sovereignty;
and the *tāmasa* is for the destruction of enemies and the warding off of all diseases.

In rites for pacification she bestows nourishment; in subjugation, she is beautiful through her auspiciousness. All states of being arise within her, who fulfills the desires and aspirations of the heart.
The deity to be meditated upon correctly is the Daughter of the Mountain (*Nagātmajā*),
who is free from all worldly existence, devoid of ugliness and the fear of the unlovely.
When her desires have been fulfilled, she should be meditated upon in rites of incantation;
likewise, she is highly praised for the purpose of eradication and even for killing.
The state of being curable by others is excluded when attracting a medium, in cases of hatred, or when one is being threatened; likewise,
an enemy who is being threatened by wicked people, seized by a thief,
or possessed by an owl or one afflicted by *pāyasa* (milk-rice) is excluded in the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
One should meditate on the enemy as being trampled by a pillar, like grass or leaves,
and as being surrounded by thieves and royal officers like a beast.
Even by a tiger or a lion, the enemy is slain in this rite of killing;
and one should perform the recitation while mounted upon a corpse, with lips firmly pressed together in fury.
If one who is mounted upon a corpse performs the recitation while seated on a tooth, it means that the fruit is quickly obtained.
Now, the division of the mantra:
for the rite of fire, [the mantra is] "Obeisance to Parasvāna."
And in all self-worship—
whether for pacification, nourishment, hatred, eradication, or even killing—
the utterances *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, and *vauṣaṭ* are used in their respective order.

Now, the sequence: having first turned away from worldly involvement, being qualified [for the practice], having performed the ritual hand-washing as prescribed, having bathed as prescribed, having put on the garments as prescribed,
and facing the appropriate direction, one should first worship the presiding deity of each respective rite, and only thereafter [proceed].

Having worshipped one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevī) in each respective form, one should recite [the mantra] according to that specific occasion, with that specific yoga, in that specific number, and with that specific desire. This is the summary. Furthermore, one who seeks wealth through gambling should not perform the six rites (ṣaṭkarman), because of the scriptural condemnation: "There are not two fruits on a single tree. Now follows the exposition of the bali offering; its characteristics are as follows.

The *bali* prescribed for the specific deities according to their respective mantras is the *prāṇivadha-bali*. However, the *bali* beginning with the *kuṣmāṇḍa* is an extended (*ātideśika*) *bali*. This is because of the previously cited statement: "These are to be known as the *balis*. Now, one might object: "How can the killing of living beings produce merit? For, being an act of violence (*hiṃsā*), it should rather produce sin. Thus says the Śruti: 'Do not kill' (*mā hiṃsīḥ*)."

It may be that all beings [are to be protected]. In the *Gītā*, there is the statement regarding the renunciation of violence: "Non-violence, truth, non-stealing, and the protection of all. In the *Vāsiṣṭha*, there is the speech of the king to the Rākṣasī: "O lady, since your life must not be harmed by anyone, you shall obtain a monkey as your husband."

One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma; one should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Dhātr; Vāyu is indeed the swiftest mover—such statements would otherwise be rendered meaningless.

Therefore, because [the general prohibitions] such as "one should not harm any living beings" have a universal scope, a partial sublation (*bādha*) is postulated for them. And thus, regarding the killing arising from passion (*rāgaja-vadha*), the prohibitory injunctions [apply].

The scope of the prohibitions must be determined by considering their specific domain; therefore, a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) must be postulated. That is, while injury other than that which is sanctioned by Vedic injunction (*vaidha-hiṃsā*) produces sin, injury other than such [sanctioned] injury produces merit—this is the exclusionary negation. As for the fact that even Vedic injury is sometimes heard to be censured, as for example:
In the *Bhāgavata*, the Blessed Lord spoke these words to Mucukunda:
"Let there be for you, forever, undecaying devotion unto Me;
yet, remaining always established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, you have slain [enemies] by means of hunting and other such acts."
But he who, being composed through austerity, takes refuge in the water-born lotus,
O King, becomes the most virtuous among all beings in his very next birth.
"Having become an excellent brahmin, you will approach me alone;
[this was] the speech of Nārada to the assembly. In that very place:
"O King Prajāpati! Behold the sacrificial animals by you on the path."
Thousands of those who had been brought to life and possessed the notion of living were slaughtered by that pitiless man.
Having approached him, they wait while remembering their former excellence;
then, with their anger aroused, they strike the deceased with iron clubs.
That [killing] is indeed prohibited because it exceeds the restriction; for killing beyond what is prescribed lacks the nature of a sacrifice. And that restriction applies precisely there:
"At sacred fords (tīrthas) frequented by the Vedas, I shall seek cattle through meditation; I shall kill them only as much as necessary, being free from greed"—thus is one restricted.
O Indra among kings, the man who, knowing action to be thus determined, performs it, is not defiled by that action, for he is established in knowledge alone.
The meaning of this is as follows:
there is no rule regarding killing by one who possesses wisdom.
In that regard, these are the restraints concerning hunting.
The meaning is: at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), at sacrifices (*yajña*), and at those offerings of meat (*māsa-dāna*) prescribed by the Vedas (*śruti*) as seen in the scriptures.
This is one rule; [this is] the fifth [chapter], O King.
And others have two rules:
barren cows intended for sacrifice were prescribed by the Brahmins; they are indeed destroyers.
It should be performed; for the sake of the sacrifice, one who has fashioned [it] should drink it, having offered it.
He proceeded toward the city with humility.
This is its meaning:
bodily suffering such as beating and so forth... [for even one who has performed the vow of penance is indeed purified by it, through both internal and external cleansing].

Indeed, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) must be practiced regarding that which is to be avoided for the sake of sacrifice; however, violence must be practiced during times of famine and the like for the purpose of maintaining those who are dependent on one. For even the killing for sacrifice is [considered] Vedic because it is prescribed by the Vedas. Violence arising from passion (*rāga*) or hatred (*dveṣa*), when these are absent, is not Vedic.

Therefore, those who have turned away from the path of the Paramahaṃsas—the followers of the Buddha’s doctrine whose marks are cessation and wisdom—should avoid even twenty commoners who possess the signs of evil people; for this very reason, the mention of the word "greed" is a restrictive rule (*niyama*). If...

One who is greedy for action and deluded regarding worldly activity must perform that very violence enjoined by the Vedas even when seeking [other] results; for it is prescribed as an integral part of those respective rites. Since there is a rule that from Vedic action performed for the sake of mental purity, a result necessarily follows as an inherent part of the essence, their fruit is indeed the mind.

Purity alone is well-established; those very things established by the enemies—such as "whatever person," and so forth—are thus determined. In this context, one should perform the ritual action (*karma*) consisting of the various limbs (*śrāṅgaka*) according to the rule.
By that, knowledge is produced; by that knowledge, the state of being free from slaughter (*avadhajanya-prāgbhāva*) arises in the next life—this is the meaning.

Therefore, for that reason, it should be known that one must not [perform] it below human level. Thus, the offering of a *bali* [sacrifice] to Kālī—indeed, one should avoid all acts of violence toward the Goddess everywhere. For this very reason, Yudhiṣṭhira, it is heard in the *Prati-nārāyaṇīya* [section] regarding horses, goats, and so forth.

Thus, because the consumption of meat by Śrī Rāmacandra and others is observed, it is established that eating meat outside of scriptural injunction (*vaidha*) produces sin, whereas eating meat according to injunction produces merit; therefore, the act of eating meat should be avoided except when it is prescribed. As for those who are entitled to eat meat [under such injunctions], they may consume it.

"O Lord, those who eat what should be eaten at the proper time, yet cook for their own sake, partake of sin; whereas all those who subsist on the remnants of sacrifice are seen to be free from all taint. Therefore, one should not accept fish, meat, and the like created for the ancestors, as was declared by the Sun."

They are partakers of sin. According to the scriptural statement, "The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are prescribed for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*"), those who are *sāttvika* and compassionate abandon them; however, there is no sin in eating them when it is done according to scriptural injunction (*vaidha-bhojana*). For this very reason, Yājñavalkya also stated: "Among five-nailed animals, the porcupine, the iguana, the tortoise, the hedgehog, and the hare are to be eaten."

The *Kālikā Purāṇa*, concerning the autumnal worship (*śāradī-pūjā*), states: "The *siṃhatuṇḍaka*, *rohitā*, as well as the *pāṭhīna*, *rājīva*, and *saśalka*—these fish are permitted by the twice-born; thus one may dwell with them for six days."
The autumnal worship of Caṇḍikā is proclaimed to be of three kinds:
the sāttvika is indeed characterized by the sacrifice of recitation (japa) and by food offerings that are meatless.
The majesty of the Blessed Lady is celebrated in the Purāṇas and other scriptures;
the recitation of that [text] is declared to be *japa*, as is the *japa* of the Gaurī-mantra.
The recitation of the Devīsūkta, the muttering of mantras, sacrifice in the fires, and libations—
these constitute the rājasa mode through the offering of bali-oblations as well as meat-offerings and food presentations.
That [practice] is proclaimed here for those possessed of passion when performed without recitation-sacrifices;
however, that which is performed with the consumption of wine, meat, and so forth, without recitation-sacrifices, is likewise [for the passionate].
For those of a *tāmasa* nature and for those who employ weapons (*kirata*), [the rite] is considered acceptable even without mantras.

In this context, within the *sāttvika* worship, the offering of a sacrificial oblation (*validāna*) is neither enjoined nor prohibited; however, it enters as an ancillary part of the worship, for on the ninth day the oblation is performed according to rule. This is because of such scriptural statements as, "If the oblation is omitted, there will be famine," and so forth. By this, the *sāttvikas*...
Those who practice compassion should not offer abundant animal sacrifices (bali) for the sake of completing their ritual acts; rather, only a single offering should be given.
Regarding the phrase "with non-flesh offerings" (nirāmiṣaiḥ), it means that for those of a sattvic nature, the food offering (naivedya) as a limb of worship must be non-flesh;

for that purpose, one should certainly perform the slaughter [of a single animal]. However, for those of a rājasic nature, the offering of animal sacrifice (bali) consists of food offerings containing meat.

Those seeking specific fruits should offer worship, incense, and a single oblation; however, those desiring abundant results should offer a profuse oblation as a constituent part of the worship, and by the previously stated rule, they do not become partakers of sin. Even so, as long as no fixed rule is contradicted, those seeking various fruits should perform those respective rites consisting of the constituent part of offering a profuse oblation.

"Sinners do not [attain success] due to the previously mentioned rule; such is the general direction [of the teaching]. Now, regarding the prescribed offerings (valaya): in the Kālikā Purāṇa it is said:
'The goat, the buffalo, and the human, respectively, are proclaimed as the offering (vali), the great offering (mahāvali), and the supreme offering (ativali).'"
In the offerings of oblations by practitioners, these should be accepted by all the gods:
birds, tortoises, crocodiles, fish, and the five kinds of deer.
The buffalo, the gayal, the cow, the goat, the brown antelope, the boar, the rhinoceros,
the black antelope, the monitor lizard, the sharabha, and the lion.
The tiger, the man, and likewise the blood of one's own lineage are proclaimed as the sacrificial offerings (*valaya*) for Caṇḍikā, Bhairava, and the others.
Liberation is accomplished through offerings; heaven is accomplished through offerings.
By the giving of offerings, one may conquer all enemies, including kings and princes.
The mention of goats and the like at the outset was merely for the sake of illustration; now, regarding the calculation of folds (*vali*), there is no tautology even without further examples.
A *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourd, a stalk of sugarcane, liquor, and likewise meat—
These are to be known as the folds; the two dark ones are equal to a goat.

In the Vārāhī Tantra: "Even at a *saṃbhava* [conjunction], one should offer an animal; likewise for festivals and so forth, as stated by Cāmara: 'The black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*), fish, and the *matsya-madgura*.'"

The Rohita, the Sapi, the sheep, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, and the Madgura; the separate mention of the Rohita from the group beginning with Rohitā is for the sake of a greater reward. As stated in the Yāmala:
The yak, the black antelope, the fish, the sheep, and the tortoise;
the buffalo, the monkey, the rhinoceros, the man, the tiger, and the lion.
O beloved, rabbits, tortoises, and likewise birds [are to be avoided]; now, those who are to be excluded [from the rite] are mentioned.
This is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
One who is one-eyed, aged, lame, afflicted by disease, discharging phlegm,
impotent, deficient in limb, or possessing the characteristics of a pierced horn.
O King, one should not offer as a sacrificial victim (bali) a Brāhmaṇa, even if he is variegated in color, very short in stature, or likewise afflicted with a great skin disease, nor even a Caṇḍāla.
One should not give the remainder to the twice-born gods, nor likewise to the king’s son; one should not give it to a mortal, nor for long, without the recitation of mantras.
A mortal who gives [a gift] with the king's permission incurs sin;
one should give it after having conquered that enemy king from his realm in battle.
That refers to the *nada* (the river);
other [types of water] are those produced from wells and so forth.
One’s own son, or even a brother, or even a *piṇḍa* (funeral cake)—[these are the recipients].
One should offer that oblation and also [the sacrifice] to Bhānu and Mātula.
One should never give an animal with its tail or ears severed, nor one with fierce teeth, nor likewise one with fierce horns and the like.
The previously mentioned objection should also be applied,
as far as possible, to goats and other such animals. Furthermore, one should not offer an animal for the *śivā-bali* that is less than three months old.
One should give at least nine sets of three fortnights' worth of food to a bird of prey.
In the Hayamedha sacrifice, one should at times offer a horse as a tribute;
likewise, O lord of the city, one should offer an elephant to the guardians of the quarters.
One should never offer two elephants, nor a lion, a tiger, or a human, nor likewise one's own bodily blood to the Goddess.
"O Mahādevas, a Brāhmaṇa should never give me [human flesh];
having given a lion, a tiger, or a human, a Brāhmaṇa would go to hell."
He would surely be like a horse with its tail cut off, truly devoid of good fortune;
by giving his own body's blood, he would incur self-destruction.

By giving liquor to a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa indeed falls from his status as a Brāhmaṇa; Kṣatriyas and others, however, should not give even a *kṛmca* measure or an offering (*bali*) to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a black antelope, one incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin;
this applies especially to the killing of animals, birds, or human beings.

"One should give a woman as an offering; by giving such an offering, one would attain hell. [In the *Yoginītantra*: "One should not give a woman as an offering; by giving such an offering, one would attain hell."
But when given during the month of Mithuna, O beloved, no fault arises.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"During the collective offerings of oblations (bali), one should offer a woman among the animals and birds;
however, out of devotion, one should cast the human offering into that water."
Where the killing of a lion, a tiger,
or a man is ordained for the first caste and so forth, there the *vihikrada* [is performed] at the very beginning by the word of a Brahmin.
O Bhairava, having fashioned a tiger, a man, or a lion made of ghee,
or alternatively, one made of barley flour placed within the sun (pūṣan).

Now follows the pair of Āgrayaṇas: first the five [offerings] beginning with the Khaḍga, then the ram at the beginning; having offered the black goat as a sacrifice, one should afterwards eat the great offering (mahābali).
Now, the classification by color: white, black, brownish-red, tawny, variegated,
and pale— this sixfold goat is declared to be the great offering for householders.

For kings, the buffalo is the great offering (*mahābali*); for householders, the goat is the great offering; and the buffalo is the supreme offering. This is because, apart from kings, men have no authority over large animals. As for the ram, the lizard, and so forth, these are minor offerings (*kṣudrabali*) even for a king. The white and black ones are the best; the variegated and tawny ones are middling; and the red one is [the lowest].
And Kapila is proclaimed to be the youngest;
for as long as one year from three months onwards,
the wise man should avoid such a goat from afar.
A black or white horse that is young is praised;
it is considered excellent until it reaches its second year, provided it remains so beyond the first year.
That offering is declared to be the best; therefore, one that is inferior is considered the lowest. When the offering is black in color but has a white tail, it is so described.
A wise man should avoid such a goat from the doorway;
likewise, an intelligent person should avoid one that is white with a black tail.
If a goat is black in color and its backbone is white, one should recognize it as excellent; otherwise, one should reject it.
One who possesses all these marks is endowed with a crown; such a person is praised and called Vali.
Yet, one who is lame, one-eyed, humpbacked, or likewise possessed of sores or scars [is not].
One should carefully avoid that which lacks large teeth;
as long as it does not possess the fragrance of guggulu, one should likewise avoid such an offering.
Since it is equal to the gift of a bird, one should therefore avoid it;
a white buffalo five years old is proclaimed to be highly recommended.
That very same [being] is known as the middling Kṛṣṇa, while the Pāṇḍaka is considered the lowest;
that very same one is also known as Mahiṣa;
that very same one is indeed Mahiṣa.
And birds of all castes that are auspicious and beautiful should be present. [This is] the description of the openings at the non-severing points:
one should place a lion on the right and offer a buffalo in front.
One should offer a bird to the left and the blood from one's own body in front.

The meaning is "of the Goddess"; the other bracelets should be placed according to their availability—this is the meaning. Now, regarding the relative gradation of the bracelets, the *Yoginītantra* states:
"A single bracelet made of goat [bone] is distinguished as superior to ten chowries."
A goat also bites, and a tortoise alone is praised.
Even for a hundred tortoises, a single hare is praised;
even for a hundred hares, the blood from one's own body is esteemed.
O Maheśvarī, as long as the lotus petal remains full, it is of that same measure;
thereafter, the head of the hundred-fold folds is distinguished as superior.
The meaning is "of him" (tasya).
The word *tan* is the genitive plural form (*ṣaṣṭyāḥ*) derived from the suffix *tas* after all case endings.
And thousands of female disciples (*śiṣṇya*) distinguish themselves [from] Varāha.
Two thousand [cows] are for a boar, and the buffalo is distinguished [by being worth] more.
Of a thousand common deer, a single rhinoceros is superior;
and of thousands of rhinoceroses, a human being yields incomparable fruit.

Thus ends the section on Kāmākhyā. By means of a powerful man, the Goddess attains satisfaction after a thousand years; by means of ten men who follow the prescribed rite, she attains it in three hundred thousand years.
The meaning is that they are emitted one by one on a single day. Regarding the word "thousand" and so forth,
after a year [of practice], for twelve years or ten years, one effects [the result] through the years.

The three types of restraint are as follows: for killing a boar, [the penance lasts] fifteen years; for a yak, half of that; for a monitor lizard, one year; and for the blood of a limb, six months. This refers specifically to the blood from the limbs of another person;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement to be mentioned later. Thus, commodities such as meat yield minor results, whereas [other items] are more powerful.

Regarding "the excellent fruit": in the *Muṇḍamālātantra*, it is said: "One should offer an oblation of a head burnt by a lord (or fire), smeared with ghee, either at night or during the day; especially so during the dark fortnight, and most especially during the dark fortnight."
If a goat is given, one becomes eloquent; if a ram is given, one certainly becomes a poet;
if a buffalo is given, there will be an increase in wealth; and if a deer is given, the fruit of enjoyment shall arise.
From a bird, there will be great supernatural power; from a lizard, a great fruit;
from a Narendatta, there will be great prosperity; and from a rhinoceros, unsurpassed accomplishment.
On the forehead, hands, heart, head, and the space between the eyebrows—
having offered his own body-blood, he becomes another form of the liquid essence of Rudra’s body.
The fruit of that is explained in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"O Śiva, by means of the blood of fish and of those [beings] from bell-metal vessels, one attains satisfaction for one month; and by means of the flesh of crocodiles, for three months."
The Goddess does not attain satisfaction with the blood of deer, nor especially that of men, even for eight months; yet she is the bestower of auspiciousness.
With the blood of a lizard, one obtains for five years the satisfaction [of the goddess];
with the blood of a black antelope or the blood of a boar,
the Goddess obtains for twelve years a hundredfold satisfaction.
With the blood of Jāmbukās, one attains [the power] for twenty-five years.
With the blood of buffaloes and rhinoceroses, one attains supreme satisfaction lasting for a hundred years; likewise, with the blood of tigers and leopards.
Then, with the blood of the lion, the śarabha, and his own limbs,
the Goddess attained satisfaction for a thousand years.
Whatever pleasure one derives from the flesh or even the blood [of other beings],
[one may likewise offer] the black antelope, the rhinoceros, as well as the fish Rohita, when they have died.
Listen now to the separate fruits of the channels (nāḍīs) and the conjunctions (saṃyugas):
by means of the flesh of the black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra) and likewise by the rhinoceros (khaḍga), one pleases Caṇḍikā.
One obtains satisfaction for a mere thousand years by [offering] the flesh of the rohita fish;
and Caṇḍikā obtains satisfaction for three hundred years by the flesh of the vārdhrīṇasa.
In the Yoginītantra: "One should not give the flesh of a female animal to a paśu, except for that of a lizard, a doe,
or one possessing inferior characteristics."

In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "One who has lost the three [qualities], whose senses are decayed, who is white-haired, aged, and without a lord— such a person is called 'half-less' (arddhīnasa) when he is appointed to the offerings to the gods and ancestors."
Blue-necked, red-headed, with black feet and split wings,
this lord of birds, though devoid of speech, is dear even to Viṣṇu.
With human blood and flesh, Kāmākhyā Bhairava— who bears my own form— attains satisfaction for three thousand years.
Blood purified by mantras always becomes nectar;
O Sadāśiva, the head and the flesh are likewise always pleasing to you.
Therefore, in the worship of the Goddess, if strength, head,
or blood is offered without being purified by mantras, that which is thus given brings about the total destruction of the donor.
In the *bhojya-homa*, the wise practitioner should employ meats;
for the worship, he should offer meats under their own names, and occasionally, the practitioner may indeed give them.
But without the blood from the head, that [elixir] is not produced as nectar; O King, the Goddess must be worshipped according to the rules with a head containing blood.
Durgā shall be exceedingly satisfied for a full hundred thousand years.
Now follows the description of the sword.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Cutting with a sword (caṃdrahāsa) or a knife is indeed the primary method;
cutting with a sickle or a circular saw is middling; [cutting] with the fingers is [the lowest]."
A small dagger, a short sword, a pickaxe, a mechanical device,
and arrows such as the kṣurapra, kṣura, and bhalla— these are proclaimed to be the lowest [weapons].
This offering (bali) can never be cut by others, such as those possessing power or arrows;
if one attempts to seize the Goddess or that offering, the giver shall meet his death.
If a practitioner of the *suṣma* rite cuts a consecrated sacrificial animal or a bird with his hand,
that impetuous man incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
And in the Vārāhī Tantra:
"Now, O Maheśānī, I shall explain the determination of the sword and other weapons,
by which weapon the practitioner [cuts through obstacles] and attains success."
The Caṇḍahāsa vessel is proclaimed to be the most excellent;
it should be made fifty finger-breadths in size, or else three spans (tāla).
Is it in the shape of a human hero, or perhaps in the form of a lotus petal?
Or else, with a curved sword, he might strike with staff-like blades.
Among all the Valīs and those possessing great discernment, the Candrahāsa sword is preeminent;
it is proclaimed as the weapon of choice for all those of great strength.
One may cut with a razor, or indeed with a knife;
or with a pickaxe and an axe, or with a razor and a razor-sharp blade.
One should cut it with a sharp, flawless, and auspicious sword;
however, one must not cut it in the open air, but rather in a clean, secluded place.
The practitioner, facing north with his eyes fixed on himself, should cut the sacrificial offering (bali) situated upon the ground while facing east,
using the mantra alone.
Furthermore, for animals such as goats and others, as well as for the planets and the presiding deities, the faces are prescribed to be turned in the opposite direction.
The determination regarding the slayer is found in that very same [text]:
"Whether it be himself, a brother's son, a brother, or even a friend, he alone shall perform the severance of the *piṇḍas*; one should not join him to the lineage."
One should not employ an enemy, nor one who is deficient in a limb, nor one who is one-eyed, nor even one who is hunchbacked,
as an offering on the side of the foe in the rite of cutting.
Now, the determination regarding the falling of the head:
