If the head falls toward the northwestern direction, the southwestern direction, or the south,
one should predict loss for that person.
Listen now to the results in all the remaining directions and intermediate points:
if the head falls in the north-eastern quarter, [the following occurs].

One should know that this brings about all prosperity; it should be prescribed for kings seeking sovereignty. When the head indeed falls after having circled around the right ear, [that is a sign of success].
Then, there will be success for you through meat; however, misfortune may occur in your left ear. For kings, there will be great destruction, while for householders, there will be happiness.
If the head falls toward the northeast and the center as well,
then, through the power of that dream, all success will certainly be attained in due time.
Success occurs when there is a single emission; one should indicate eight [units] by means of the mouth.
One should recognize loss through three; therefore, one should avoid three or more.
Twenty-five [beads] are recommended for a small rosary, while one hundred and eight is for a medium one;
the best of practitioners should not provide more than this, nor less.
One should employ a vessel made of silver or gold;
some say that Viśvāmitra used a skull-bowl made of a human cranium.
One who gives the blood from one's own body as an offering of the filaments of a hundred-petaled lotus or a red water-lily shall obtain the fruit of the gift of a ram.
Alternatively, there may be one hundred dots, or thirty-two, or even twelve;
but never on the neck or the belly of the garland.
One should never offer milk, blood, or anything else;
rather, one should offer three applications of the Great Nectar using a brush made of sugar.
The practitioner, aiming for the fulfillment of desire, should cause rock salt, ginger, or even a plantain fruit to fall while pouring a stream of honey.
Blood remains on the ground until sunrise;
that which has fallen during the day or night does not defile one's own blood.
If a severed head is seen falling while still accompanied by a smile, it does not defile.
One should know his prosperity; for kings, one should designate it as sovereignty.
Success occurs once; on the second occasion, loss is seen. This should be understood for householders, while for kings it is the opposite.
When the eyes are seen to be closed, one should predict loss;
when a grinding sound occurs among the teeth at any time.
In that case, one should know it to be death; one should merely indicate loss.
Now, regarding the place of the shaven-headed (Muṇḍa):
the practitioner himself, having cut the sacrificial offering (bali), should give it in the direction of the Rākṣasas.
To its south is a red vessel; if it is inverted, one should not speak of it.
The best of practitioners should offer oblations to the great serpents in the northwest;
he should place the heads of those known as the "Excessive" (ati) serpents in the east.
One should offer the heads of carnivorous animals and birds on the left side,
and those of aquatic creatures entirely on the right side.
One should offer the black antelope, the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and the hare,
as well as the fish of the planets, at the very left front.
One should strike the back or the head of Bali with blood,
facing the deity, and thus fashion the portion to be severed.
One should know that very [state] as the "crown" (masta), and the "middle" is its opposite;
one should place the head at the end of the *kīlaka* when the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) does not arise.
One should offer a lamp burning atop the head, anointed with sandalwood;
by means of ghee one becomes a sovereign of the whole earth, and by means of oil one attains spiritual accomplishment.
One should provide a wick made of thread; a wick made of cloth is also recommended. Its thickness should be that of a thumb, and its length should be six finger-breadths.
It should be fashioned with twenty threads, beginning with the *vāda* [threads];
one should place fragrant substances within its interior, such as camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should not cause a lamp to be offered at the head of crocodiles, tortoises, especially monitor lizards, fish, or birds.
As long as the lamp burning upon the head continues to burn, for that long one shall vomit [the merit] in heaven; therefore, one should cause it to be given with great effort.
Having smelled the fragrance arising from the offering of space, the Goddess becomes pleased;
therefore, one should offer a lamp, and for that reason, one should avoid [using] a vessel.
One attains death in Nirvana as the lamp is extinguished. Now follows the opening of the limbs through the gift of blood, according to the Kālikā Purāṇa.
One should apply the previously mentioned rock salt and other substances to his blood;
likewise, one should use silver, copper, and tin in a threefold crucible.
A vessel made of māheya, kāśya, or even yajñadāru wood should be prepared for the offering of blood, according to one's means.

One should not give blood on iron, on a cloth, nor into the hand of a physician, nor likewise into the hand of a child; nor should one let it fall upon the ground, whether heard of in the scriptures or otherwise.
Neither in a jar nor on the ground, O Goddess,
should a man who desires prosperity offer blood for the consumption of the deity;
rather, for the sake of human vitality and for the sake of Maheśvara’s splendor, one should then offer fresh blood.
The king should give [the offering] there; never in a leaf-cup (puṭa) or similar vessel. Now follows the explanation of the sprinkling of the bali offering.
In the Vārāhī Tantra:
Having oneself first become facing east, one should offer the bali while facing north;
or else, it may be milk adorned with vermilion and other such substances.

One should sprinkle [the area] three times with pure water from the arghya vessel while reciting the root mantra, as well as the mantra beginning with "Oṃ Vārāhī... and the mantra beginning with "paśupāśa...".
One should sprinkle it with auspicious bilva-leaf water while reciting the Sahasraśīrṣā mantra, and worship that [liṅga] which has been encircled with sandalwood paste and perfumes.
Then, having gazed [at it], the practitioner should recite:
"O goat, you have appeared before me in the form of an offering through my good fortune."
I bow to him who possesses all forms and who takes the form of Bali;
he who, through the gift pleasing to Cāmuṇḍā, is the destroyer of the calamities brought by Datta.
O Cāmuṇḍā, to you who take the form of a sacrificial offering, salutations again and again;
we have been surrendered by the Self-born One himself for the sake of the sacrifice.
"Therefore, I shall cause you to be slain; thus, in this sacrifice, killing is not truly killing. Furthermore, in the *Kulārṇava*:
"This *piṇḍa* is the nectar of Śiva; having attained Śiva-nature through me, [partake of it]."
For while you are bound in the state of a limited soul (paśu), you are not Śiva; yet you are indeed Śiva.
O Dear One, one should quickly slay the sacrificial animal (paśu) with this mantra:
"Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ. With these three seed-syllables (bījas), one should cast a flower upon its head three times;
with the seed-syllables Vāṅ, Māyā, and Kamalā, one should cast the flower upon its head.
"I shall offer this according to the *prasūniti* Vedic meter.
Then, having offered the oblation (*bali*) and performed the optional rite (*kāmya*), the one of vast intellect [proceeded] as stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.

But when there is an abundance of offerings, the practitioner, having placed the foremost [deities] at the head, should worship all of them for two or three nights according to the *lājāgata* method using the general ritual procedure (*tantra*).
When a buffalo is offered to Bhairavī and Bhairava,
one should then worship that sacrificial offering (bali) with this very mantra.
Just as you hate me and just as you [hate] Caṇḍikā in secret, so do not harm my enemies; O Bahululaṅka, bring about what is auspicious.
O you who are indeed the vehicle of Yama, and who assume the form of a human; salutations to you, the embodiment of life-span, wealth, fame, and physical form!
When the gift of a sword is being made,
one should sprinkle the mandala there with water, reciting the mantra "guhājāte."
O son of the Mountain, you are the sword of fortune among the ancestors; you resemble a sword—cut through the obstacles, O highly fortunate one born from Guha! Salutations to you!
This mantra is proclaimed for the gift of a black antelope:
"O black antelope, embodiment of Brahman, increasing the splendor of Brahman!"
O wise one, composed of the four Vedas, grant me wisdom, O you of great renown!
Now follows the detailed exposition of the worship of the sword (khaḍgapūjā).
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Having consecrated it with mantras, the wise one should offer the auspicious oblation;
as many mantras as were previously declared for the consecration of the sword [should be used]."
The wise should employ the *mahāmāyā* mantra at the beginning of the ritual;
by this, meditation, worship, and salutation are indicated.
This authority will become clear from the statement in the Vārāhī Tantra: having uttered the word "Kālī" twice,
then "Vajreśvarī," and then "A-nu-lo-ha-daṇḍā-dyaiḥ," one should join "namaḥ" at the end.
Having grasped it with this mantra, one should take up the sword with the hand.
One should consecrate that sword with the mantra beginning with "Kālarātri" and employ the middle [part] by reciting the mantra of the Eye-seed (netrabīja) twice.
Even further, [one should address] Kālikālī, who has formidable fangs and carries a skull,
with the third vowel, namely the eleventh [vowel], preceded by *hāṃ*.
Having joined the two [mantras] for the purpose of cursing and subduing, one should subsequently employ them;
thereafter, one should add the words "phetkāriṇi," followed by "khādaya" (devour! and "chedaya" (cut!).
Then, [uttering] "sarva * * *," he twice made the lūlāpaka sound; then [he cried out] "chiṃdhi chiṃdhi" with his sword, and then "kilikili."
Then, with the sounds "ki-cit-ki-cit," then "pi-va-pi-va," and then "kālikāyai namaḥ"—this is the mantra for Kālarātri.
With this single mantra... [the ritual is performed].
Kālarātri herself [cuts] with a sword; she does not cut the sacrificial offering (bali) facing east. However, she herself faces east while the [victim's] face is turned upward and then downward.
The meaning is that one should sprinkle [it].
Having meditated upon [the deity] in the form described by "Kṛṣṇam" and so forth, one should worship with the mantra.
And you are the tongue of Caṇḍikā... [etc.]
O Vajreśvarī, then [worship] Lohadaṇḍā, Antā, and the word "namaḥ."
One should inscribe the seed-syllable *kūrca* on the sword with vermilion, sandalwood paste, and other substances:
"O sword, you who possess a sharp edge and are difficult to approach;
you whose interior is auspicious, you who are victory itself, and the support of dharma—salutations to you!"
Having taken that sword and empowered it with mantras,
the deity [assumed] a pair of illusory Kali-forms of terrifying appearance.

One should utter the word "daṃṣṭre," followed by "sphreṃ sphreṃ," and then the phrase "phetkāriṇīti khādaya" (O Phetkāriṇī, devour! twice. Then one should utter the word "chedaya" (cut! and "piba rudhiram" (drink blood!). [Then follows: "sphroṃ sphrāṃ...
araṇyā sarvadevatāḥ prokṣitāḥ... (The forest-dwelling deities are all consecrated...).
Wherever a favorable or even an unfavorable [mark] falls upon the tactile surface,
one should then indicate the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the directions starting with the west and so forth, in sequence: east, southeast, south, and northwest.

There is no doubt: whatever sentence he utters, that very thing comes to pass without delay. Through the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, the seizure of kingdoms, and so forth, one shall obtain incomparable splendor upon the head within six months.
But if, at the time of taking blood, one should discharge feces or urine,
or if the body moves either downward or upward, then death will be granted.
From the paralysis of the left foot, a great disease arises;
otherwise, from its twitching and movement, well-being is produced.
Listen to how the head of Mahiṣa fell, following the sequence starting from the north and ending at the northwest corner, out of sheer grief.
O Bhairava, know that fortune, loss, sovereignty, wealth, victory, fearlessness, the attainment of a kingdom, and the threefold increase follow in this sequence.
And for all animals, especially goats and the like, such is the fruit; from aquatic creatures, however, it is produced differently.

Water-born creatures, beasts, and birds are [associated with] the village and the Nairṛta [directions], while both are present elsewhere; however, the severed head falling down should be understood as being distinct from these.
When the sound *kaṭaka* occurs at the head of the dentals (*daṃtya*),
it brings disease to men, cattle, birds, and so forth, as well as to planets and the like.
If a large eye-mark is present on the head of a buffalo, and that eye-mark is severed or reported as damaged, one should predict the death of the enemy king.
Just as the forehead of others bears the fear-inducing mark of a line emerging from the side or elsewhere,
so too does it bear the supreme terror of a mole.
That man who, having taken with both hands the blood from the head of one with red limbs and wrinkles, meditates upon the Goddess, stands before her.
Having attained his desires with laughter, he is honored in the world of the goddesses.
Now, regarding the gift of one's own flesh:
he who himself [offers] a piece of heart-flesh the size of a black gram bean—
Therefore, one should not intentionally take even as much as a mung bean for the Goddess.
Within six months, one shall properly obtain all desired objects and meat;
those who give with the truth of their own flesh for the sake of their own prosperity, I grant them this.
"By that truth, grant me nirvāṇa! Hūṃ hūṃ namaḥ!
When this statement at the end of the root mantra has been uttered, this is the recitation of the mantra.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the independent *Kulavṛtti*, composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru.

Now, the procedure for the *cakra* (the ritual circle). First, regarding the determination of the time: according to the *Kulārṇava*, it is after the dismissal of the deities; according to other tantras, it is after the recitation of hymns of praise. The classification of the types of practitioners is as follows: the *divya* (divine) is established for those who are not *vīras* (heroes); drinking is performed by the *divya* while occupied with [other duties], whereas the *vīra* drinks on a soft seat. Drinking according to one's own desire is the drinking of the *paśu* (the bound soul).

It is stated [in the scriptures] thus: "So they declare. According to all systems (*sarvamata*), the worship of Śakti occurs immediately after the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇaka*). However, according to the *Kulārṇava-mata*, the worship of Śakti occurs even before the offering to Brahman. According to other Tantric systems, it occurs even before the placement of the water-pot (*ghaṭa*) and the arghya vessel. Thus, it should be understood according to the specific requirements of each case. Now...

The Sacrifice to Annapūrṇā: It has been stated by Tattvānanda: First, having fashioned the victorious Annapūrṇā who fulfills all causes—a lotus with petals made of food and adorned with nectar—one should meditate upon this limb endowed with the six long vowels and the source of *māyā*. One should meditate on the goddess Danneśvarī, the gracious goddess.

One should take refuge in her, who is in the bloom of youth, addressed with gentle words, adorned with all ornaments, and intent upon giving with her own right hand; she holds in her left hand a jewel-vessel filled with nectar from the ocean of milk, produced from pure gold.
*Tāra-māyā-ramā-kāmā namo bhagavati*.
At the end of the word *māheśvarī*, one should write the word *jālapūrṇe*.
This mantra, joined with the fire-born consort (*svāhā*), is the fulfiller of all desires.
Therein, one should perform the invocation according to the sequence to be described;
then, having recited "This food is nectar," one should fill the two vessels.
"Obeisance to Vahnipriyā and Ātodya"—this is remembered as the mantra for invocation.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the sandals of Annapūrṇā.
Then, in the Kulārṇava:
"Thereafter, having lifted the vessel with both hands, he should offer it to the second [recipient], who is the venerable Guru and is Paraśiva himself in visible form."
Also in the Bhairava Tantra:

"Having caused one's own Śakti or a Vīra-Śakti who has been initiated and has heard [the teachings] from the Guru to drink [first], one should then drink the substance; such is the determination of the scripture."
In the Kulārṇava: "Then, having taken a flower, one should offer it into the vessel of the Guru;
having offered it to the Guru and then given it to the Śakti, one should take it for oneself."
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "If the Guru is not personally present, then one should dismiss [the deity] into water. In the *Kulārṇava*:
The Śrī Devī said:
O Kuleśa, ocean of the nectar of compassion, O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear about the different types of spiritual exaltation (ullāsa), as well as the union of the substance and the vessel.
O Supreme Lord, tell me of the Śrīkrama, its very state, and the activity of the powers known as Ceṭṭāli.
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask me;
by the mere hearing of it, a divine disposition arises.
The stages are: commencement, youth, adolescence, maturity, its end, the state of being beyond the mind (unmanā), and the seventh is exaltation (ullāsa).
O Mistress of the Kula, the commencement of the three principles has been declared;
O Ambikā, the youthful effulgence and the youthful bliss have been described.
O beloved, when youth is fully blossomed for the mind and brings benefit,
yet there is still stumbling in sight, thought, and speech, one is called "mature" (prauḍha).
The falling and rising [of the breath] is called *prauḍhānta* (the culmination of maturity);
until the dissolution of the mind, it is designated as *unmanī* (the state beyond the mind).
Now, the sequence:

having performed the worship at the conclusion of the hymn of praise and offered [the oblation], one should worship Annapūrṇā; having presented the Guru’s vessel to the Guru, one should offer the purification and so forth. Having given the Śakti’s vessel to the Śakti, one should take that vessel into one's own vessel.

Having received the command from the power of the Guru, and having accepted the sacred site (tīrtha) according to the sequence to be described— beginning with the mantra of salutation and culminating in intense ecstatic joy— one should perform the assembly of the Kaulikas, as stated in the Jñānārṇava:
If one desires the union of vessels (pātramelana) in the supreme wheel of intense radiance (samullāsa),
one should never perform it in a lower wheel, even if that radiance is mature.
In that case as well, the blending of vessels (pātramelana) must be performed according to one's qualification;
however, those who are uninitiated and lack proper conduct [should not perform it] with mantras, gurus, or deities.
One should not form a gathering of ritual substances with those who are corruptors, those who have fallen from their commitments,
those who merely imagine themselves to possess supernormal knowledge, or those who observe vows for the sake of worldly display.

One should not form a collection of ritual materials with animals, those engaged in menial tasks, those hated by women, those who have offended their guru, those lacking power, or those who are devoid of devotion and of low character.
One should not form an assembly of worthy recipients with those who are devoid of noble lineage and instruction;
rather, one should associate with those who understand the authority of words and sentences, and who are guided by the Śruti and Smṛti.
O Pārvatī, if they are ignorant of the family traditions, one should avoid association with them,
even if they are beloved women, friends, or kinsmen.
O beloved, one should avoid association with those who are ignorant of family customs,
as well as with men who have not seen their parents or who reside in foreign lands.
Without the application of conventional signs, one should not perform the gathering of vessels.
O Dear One, those who know the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition, and who do not contradict the Śruti and Smṛti, should avoid such association.
One should not establish a connection with worthy recipients (pātras) who are strangers and reside in other lands, unless there is a prior agreement or arrangement.
One should not use a single vessel even if it belongs directly to the Lord of the Family;
otherwise, the mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step.
One should not offer the substance contained in one's own vessel to Bhairava;
if one were to offer it, O Mistress of the Kula, the deity would incur a curse.
One should never cause Śaṅkara to perform the preparation of the seat, the food, the vessel, the garments, the fire-offering, and so forth, by those who are ignorant or unworthy.
Or, according to the division of the currents (*śrota*), one should perform the "fusion of vessels" (*pātramelana*) with the Kaulikas:
the unification of the East and South, and likewise of the North and West.
In that [mandala], one should perform that worship with heroes who are devoted to sequential worship and are similar to oneself,
as well as with passionate women, within the fourfold white [squares].
In the Rudrayāmala:
"One should give the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and sandalwood paste to the practitioners who are devoted to Śakti.
O Goddess, the initiate (sāmayika) should partake equally in the drinking and eating along with them."
In the *Somabhujagāvalī*, it is stated:
"One should reside in the form of a wheel or in the shape of a row;
or one may also dwell joined with a Śakti according to the rule of pairs."
One should worship all [the deities] within the center of the wheel with the thought that they are Śiva and Śakti. As stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"The abode of women is one thing, and that of men is another, each being distinct."
Alternatively, O Dear One, having formed pairs, one should seat them properly either in a linear row or in a circular formation.
One should worship all [the deities] within the center of the wheel with the thought that they are Śiva and Śakti;
O Dear One, just as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa are inseparable beyond words.
Just as Vāṇī [is] Satānanda, so too is Vīra accompanied by Śakti;
neither Cakrāṅgī nor Padmāṅgī, nor Vakrāṅgī, is the Prajā.

The body is the *liṅga* and the female organ is the *bhaga*; therefore, the power (*śakti*) is of the nature of Śiva. A seeker of pleasure should not approach a woman who has not been initiated, even if she is purified by immediate consecration (*sadyaḥ-saṃskāra*). Having performed the ritual of rising [from the state of non-manifestation], he should meditate upon the mantra-body, the state of the Guru, and the goddess as the digit (*kalā*) consisting of consciousness.
Afterwards, one should offer an excellent vessel filled with *palāśa* leaves, joined with blazing lamps, and perfumed with incense and the like, consecrated by its own mantra;

it is sun-like and destroys delusion. Those who sprinkle [it] and purify [the area] go indeed to the divine nectar, attaining both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation. In the *Āgamārṇava*: "The body..."

Having remembered the mandala of the Guru according to the ritual of the mantra, one should contemplate the four seats upon the head and satisfy them with the nectar of the Śrīkula-vidyā and the Samaya-vidyā. Those who drink this divine nectar, which uproots the tree of suffering, attain the sequence of spiritual accomplishments (siddhi-krama).
Having applied vermilion as a tilaka on the forehead and wine upon the hand,
one should meditate upon Śiva as the Guru, as well as upon the Goddess who is composed of consciousness.
The unconditioned is the drink for the wise, while the conditioned is Bhairava himself;
it is praised in the ritual of wheel-worship as the auspicious, supreme accomplishment of mantras.
Now, regarding the filling of the vessel, it is stated in the *Kulasāra*:
"O Supreme Goddess, O lady with the face of a boar, one should perform the drinking for the sake of the cause by means of six pulls from the eyes."
Furthermore, practitioners must not consume more than this;
"karṣa" here means a worldly *tola*.
Thus it is stated in the Kuloḍḍīśa:
Twelve *guñjās* shall constitute one *māṣa*, and eight of those are said to be one *karṣa*.
Having established this conventional measure as the support, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
p.
165b) In *Tattvānanda*, one should then duly recite the root mantra eight times over that; [then] Ānandabhairavī and the venerable Guru.
Having performed the libation according to the rules for the Supreme Goddess, one should practice the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*).
As it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"The gods and sages desire an offering of food (*naivedya*) for the Goddess Tripurā."
Therefore, O best of gods, even to Viṣṇu who appears in the guise of a deer, [one should act thus].
Wine [is offered] to Sūrya, Śukra, Gaṇeśa, and Yama;
and to Agni, Varuṇa, Aṅgiras, Vāyu, and Dhanada.
One should cause the Great Goddess to be given to the practitioner for Īśāna;

the meaning is that one should offer her to the practitioner just as to the deity. One should worship her together with the attendants (āraiḥ), solely for the sake of accomplishing one's own spiritual lineage (svasaṃpradāya).
Having performed mutual salutations, one should drink with their permission;
having lifted the vessel with the left hand and formed the mudrā with the right hand.
According to the prescribed rite, while reciting the mantra, one should take with the second hand a quantity of the ground substance,
about the size of a masha or a hollowed palm.
Having made [the disciple] equal to one's own body, one should purify the three principles (*tattva*). As for the fragrance, it is that which is heard in the *Kaula* tradition.

Oṃ, he gives a golden vessel filled with honey; at one time, O Brahmin, he carries away the king's honeyed juices and bestows [the fruits] of the stations of longevity. Oṃ, I offer [this] for the sake of supreme bliss; may you, O Earth, become the delighter of Māyā for the practitioners of Brahman.
And in the Kulārṇava:
"Neither the creator nor the one who pierces [the mantra] is to be blamed; rather, an expiation is prescribed.
Therefore, the mantra must be performed according to the ritual rules for the sake of satisfying [the deity] in this worldly state. This...
I drink this purifying nectar, which is proclaimed by Bhairava as the cause for severing the bonds of the fettered soul through the recitation of mantras;
it is the equality of the consciousness’s sovereignty, which bestows bliss in its entirety.
Because all things consist of that [consciousness], one should dwell with all phenomena internalized within it.
The moon, which has become a deer-marked spot through a fragment of its own sovereignty, is drunk by him;
therefore, I offer this Goddess Surā as a complete oblation.
O Goddess of the gods, the knower of mantras,
with a mind free from agitation, should slowly perform the consecration of the offering vessel (balipātra) with this mantra.

In the triangular field rooted in the self, which is the peak of the sun and possesses the luster of fire, one should offer the substance accompanied by mantra into the fire of consciousness shaped like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
This offering, filled in the vessel of ego, is the nectar of the heated essence.
In the fire consisting of the destruction of the enemy, one performs oblations characterized by the act of acceptance.
One should indeed contemplate with the intellect the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra;
until the state of supreme bliss is reached, one should drink the nectar from one's own abode.
Caraka is said to bestow success, while initiation grants knowledge;
through drinking, one attains the supreme state—thus the triad is proclaimed in the Kaula tradition.
Now, immediately after receiving the vessel, there is the veneration of the vessel (*pātravaṃdana*).
As it is stated in the *Kulāmṛtasaṃhitā*:
"O Goddess of the gods, having received the command and having fully worshipped the vessel, one should venerate it."
It is made to flow with the nectar of the moon, which is the shimmering nectar of the glorious Bhairava-Śiva.

Having prostrated to the vessel, [saying]: "This ocean of bliss, the great-souled one, is worshipped by the lords of the fields, the yoginīs, the reciters, and the perfected ones; it is the direct manifestation of the Unbroken One (*Vikhaṇḍā*), the venerable first hand, the support of the world, and the bestower of purity. Thus, having paid homage to the vessel.

One should offer oblations into the sacrificial pit while reciting the mantra; one should worship the previous sacred sites and others as well. The beloved golden [offering], which brings forth the essence of fish, was given by her; and she partook of it along with drinks and other things.
Nothing moved for her whose eyes were like trembling red lotuses. To her, purity and supreme purification were revealed on the left.
Having performed the purification of the *pāśu* within the vessel,
I now salute the second vessel, which increases the bliss of the one without end. Oṃ, [to you who embody] all the traditions (*sarvāmnāya*).
I perpetually salute that Supreme Vessel, who is endowed with a multitude of arts, who illuminates all curiosity,
who is served by Candra, Upendra, Mahendra, Śambhu, Varuṇa, Brahmā, and others,
and who is meditated upon at all times by hosts of gods and groups of sages seeking liberation.

Now, the third [chapter] is the self-restraint which is appropriate: Oṃ! May the *pañcamakāra* protect [us]—that which brings the essence of wine and fish, filled by Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the others; devoted to the practices of mudrā and sexual union; consisting of the salty, sour, and bitter;
wherein the eightfold perfection of the Ācāryas is attained; and which is served with meat along with the *bhairava-kalā*.

The fourth [offering] is the vessel together with the reality; obeisance! Oṃ! Upon the foundation, encircled by the king of serpents, is the vessel, the orb of the earth; the wine is the water of the seven oceans, and the meat is the eight elephants of the quarters.
Thus, I worship Bhairava every day, while the hosts of stars and the sun and other planets provide protection.
At the time of the Wheel, the disciple stands present before the hosts of gods and asuras, who act as obedient servants; this is the specific instruction in the *Ākulārṇava*:
"O you whose face is serene, endowed with youthful radiance, be for a moment [present]."
O Dear One, the Guru, having summoned his disciples, should bestow upon them the three principles (tattvas).
Having taken the disciple’s offering— flowers and so forth— the pure-souled one,
being humble in spirit and free from deceit regarding his wealth, [presents it] according to his capacity.
Having prostrated outside with the eight limbs, O beloved, one should slowly enter within and,
with devotion, offer a drink to Śiva in the form of the Guru.
Having joined the two hands with the thumbs interlaced and the index fingers extended like spear-points,
the preceptor, having gone to the ground upon his knees, should perform the five-limbed prostration.
With the left thumb and ring finger,
having remembered the right hand extended, one whose heart is purified should remain as the destroyer of the most terrible [obstacles].

O Dear One, the venerable Guru, using the left thumb and ring finger, should perform the purification of the fettered soul (*paśu-śuddhi*) for the disciple, beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with *pṛthivī*, as previously stated in the *Prasthāna*. He should utter "Purify! and bestow the second *mala*. The Guru [should do so].
While uttering the words, "I purify," he should receive a handful from the Guru.
Bowing with devotion and proper conduct, the disciple should drink it three times slowly and silently;
then, as before, the purification of the reality (tattva) must be performed by the disciple.
The sequence, however, is exactly as previously stated.
Thus, having learned from the Guru the knowledge of the three principles (tattva), one should act accordingly;
by doing so, one shall live united with the gods—so it was spoken by Śaṅkara.
Then, having performed the auspicious rite, the Guru shall become the bestower of Śiva upon his disciples;
having received what was given by the Guru, that second [disciple] should drink it all.
O Mistress of the Kula, it is the firm conclusion of the scriptures that one should not sit down to drink wine in the presence of the venerable Guru, elders, or those worthy of worship.

He who practices without knowing the distinctions of the drink, its fruits, its splendor, its measure, its duration, and its characteristics, will become the abode of misfortune. Wine is poison at the end of a meal; food is poison at the end of wine.
One should know that food consumed together with liquor is nectar. Thus, O Divine Hero, drinking is said to be of three kinds.
Through the rites of the bound (paśu):
the divine drink is before the Goddess, while the hero remains on a soft seat;
having drunk according to his own will like a bound soul, it is called the "drink of the bound" (paśupāna).
The divine liquor for heroes bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
they know the fruit of drinking to be that it grants liberation even to the fettered (paśu).
As long as one’s pride of views does not move equally toward speech and body,
for that long one should not take life; therefore, one who kills a living being is a beast.
As long as there is no impairment of the sense organs and no distortion of the facial expression, one may drink the substance; otherwise, downfall occurs.

O Goddess, for those who have received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking is prescribed. Having lifted the vessel with both hands, one should recite the root mantra and the *pādukā* [mantra] while extending [the hands].
One who drinks the substance until it reaches the throat is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Having drunk it again and again, and having drunk it once more, he falls upon the surface of the earth.
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth is no longer found;
the Goddess Ānandā is satisfied, and Bhairava himself enters a state of ecstatic swoon.
Because of this delight, all the gods [attain their state]; therefore, one should practice this triad.
Indeed, the bliss that belongs to those devoted to divine drink is the same for the Kula-yogin.
Even for a king who rules over the entire earth, that happiness is not surpassed which belongs to those established in their lineage who do not squander the family wealth.
O King, that very bliss is indeed liberation; this is the truth.
This is the state bestowed by yogins and yoginīs with the full vessel.
O Dear One, he who possesses the sandals of his mother should drink that which has been consecrated by the root-mantra;
or, O Goddess, if at any time a vessel of wine is obtained by chance, he should take it with devotion, recite the mantra as before, and drink while remembering his Guru.
O Pārvatī, one should eat the remnants of food from the sons of the Guru’s Śaktis, from those younger than the Guru, and even from one’s own elder brother.
The elder should join with the younger, but should not cause him to receive [the teaching] again from that point.
One should drink the wine remaining from the capacity [of the teacher], and chew what remains from the hero.
One should not give what is left over from one's own meal, nor should one eat what belongs to another. One may eat the leavings of a woman, but one should not offer one's own leavings to her.
O Goddess of the gods, within the center of the wheel there shall be no other way of falling;
O Ambikā, one should give the remains of the meal to the most junior disciples.
If he gives [the remnants] out of affection to others, he shall suffer calamity at every step;
for that person of deluded intellect who takes up the vessel containing the remnants of the *āsava* [liquor].
Even a deity, out of affection or through delusion, may incur a curse;
therefore, one should not spit or discharge wind and other such excretions in the midst of the assembly.
One should not engage in excessive laughter during the gathering of yoginīs and vīras;
even if he is an initiated disciple, he must avoid neglecting the Kula worship.
Then the youngest, knowing the proper sequence, should perform the family worship (kulapūjā);
having understood that he is near [the teacher], he should pay homage just as one does to a guru.
O Pārvatī, having offered the remainder to him, one should eat everything;
this applies whether the worship is in progress or when the elder or the venerable one has arrived.
Having bowed, he should report his state; the remainder he should perform with their permission.

Having paid homage, he should report the remainder of the worship, meaning he should say, "This has been done; this remains. This applies whether the senior and junior disciples are together or alone.
In that regard, O Mistress of the Kula, the conduct has been described as before.
If [the time] has arrived when it is unknown, one should reflect upon the sequence of prior and subsequent events;
then, having honored one's respective gurus, one should satisfy the deity according to one's own specific path.
The meaning is that if one has multiple gurus, one should offer libations according to the instructions of each respective guru.
Whether one performs the daily (nitya) worship or not, the occasional (naimittika) worship should be performed at night;
the optional (kāmya) rite may be performed at either time—this is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
Whether standing, seated, having eaten, or even while applying ointments,
one should offer perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣatas) according to the ritual manuals and the requirements for a hundred thousand Brahmins.
One who stands outside the heroic state (avīrastha), whether in body or mind, should not perform the worship of the Kula;
nor should there be worship without mantra, or satiation (tarpaṇa) without meat.
O beloved, it is said that drinking without [the presence of] Śakti is fruitless;
one should not perform the worship of the Śrīcakra alone, nor should one worship in a single vessel.
One should not worship with only one hand, nor should one recite the Veda with only one hand;
nor should one worship the Goddess with fish and meat in the presence of animals.

Having prostrated, one should enter; and having prostrated, one should exit. O Dear One, one should not remain upon the Śrīcakra seat nor in the vīrāsana posture. O Goddess, the sight of the Śrīcakra destroys the sins of both [the teacher and the disciple]. If that [sight] is absent, then for the Kaulika, the pair of eyes is merely a pair of wounds.
Those of improper conduct and those of proper conduct, those established in the wheel, and the Śakti-kaulikās.

O Goddess, one should contemplate with the thought that [the vessel] is Śiva and Gaurī, but one should not consume it oneself; rather, the Kula-teacher should take that vessel, which has been empowered by their power, with devotion.
One should receive it after paying homage; otherwise, one would go to hell.
O Mistress of the Family, even if one eats without having bathed or without devotion, [the fault remains].
He who takes the property of a Śreṣṭhin shall incur poverty;
he shall be one with a turban, wearing a bodice, naked, with disheveled hair, and his neck covered.
One who is averse to others and a litigious disputant should not serve the nectar of the noble family;
for he has spat upon the nectar of yoga by blowing into a vessel of liquor.
One should not drink with the tail held upward, lest one incur the curse of the deities;
likewise, those seated on a single seat or eating from a single vessel [are subject to the same].
O beloved, those who drink from a single vessel go to hell;
likewise, he who uses the family property while the guru resides in the same village.
If one takes [the initiation] without permission from a knower of the lineage, his son, one's own elder brother, or the family preceptor, he shall go to an inexhaustible hell.
O Pārvatī, one should not touch the wheel with impure hands;
having washed both hands outside, one should offer the *kula* substances.
Having lifted up the vessel for liquor, one should not fill the cup;
nor should one ever cast the vessel of enjoyment into the jar of wine.
Indeed, that foolish-minded person who, with a pure mind, performs the washing and other rites within the center of the *cakra* shall become the abode of the state of the gods.
He who voids phlegm, excrement, urine, semen,
or wind within the center of the cakra shall become a beast for the yoginīs.
O beloved, when one eats from a vessel marked with a jar in the center of a *cakra*,
a wise person should ward off the *śrīcakra* with a lamp for the sake of quelling that fear.
The wise ones mutter, meditate, praise, bow down, awaken, inquire, and rejoice;
they wander about, roar, laugh, and speak.
O beloved, even the wise weep when they lose a woman they desire.
One should not engage in joking, idle chatter, caviling, excessive talk,
servility, fear, or anger within the center of the wheel.
O Great Goddess, those who stand in the midst of the circle should hold a vessel in their hands and remain bowed;
O Dear One, one should not stand for long with a full vessel in hand.
O Ambikā, holding the vessel in his hand, he should not break it through idle chatter;
he should not touch the vessel with his feet, nor should he let even a drop fall to the ground.
One should not give with only one hand, nor should one drink without the *mudrā*. One should move the vessel from its place, but one must never cause Śaṅkara to be moved.
He should drink the liquor without making noise, and likewise he should not fill [the vessel] to the brim;
he should not strike one vessel against another, nor should he set a vessel down on the ground.
One should not lift up the vessels together, nor should one scatter them while moving about;
one should not leave a vessel empty, nor, O beloved, should one wave the vessel about.
The wise one should not shake the vessel, nor should he let the vessel fall, O Dear One;
having washed it, he should conceal the vessel—thus say the ignorant ones, O Supreme Goddess.
When the Kaulika, radiant with the splendor of the inner light,
beholds a bound soul (paśu) who recites the scriptures of the bound or associates with the wife of a bound soul;
One may engage in the company of cattle or cause them to perform their duties;
however, even if the acquisition of cattle is for the sake of dharma, one's knowledge, happiness, and so forth will perish.
He who gives the kula-substances situated within the Śrīcakra to the uninitiated (paśus),
whether out of affection, greed, or even fear, shall become a paśu among the Yoginīs.
One should not engage in verbal dispute even with an enemy in the midst of the assembly;
one should endure such a person, regarding them as equal to one's father or mother, as it has been said.
Just as the mind rejoices upon seeing a woman, a son, or friends,
so too would he be dear to yogins if he were to see the Kaulikas.
Behold, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the lineage of my gurus;
for me, their disciple, they are the objects of Kaula worship upon this earth.
He whose mind is thus resolved shall be dear to us both;
whereas I am proud, thinking, "I am the guru," "I am the elder," and so forth.
Those Kaulikas who possess such a mindset pass beyond [all obstacles],
honoring the venerable Guru, the Kula scriptures, and the objects of worship.
O Goddess, having bowed down to her, one should recite her name preceded by "Śrī."
Now, regarding the dismissal of the *bali* offering, as stated in the *Kulārṇava*:
"O Maheśānī, one should perform the dismissal of the *bali* during the intense state of spiritual fervor (*prauḍhollāsa*).
One should draw a triangle within a square outside the house of worship."
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, one should meditate upon Ucchiṣṭabhairava,
who holds a mace, a trident, a hand-drum, and a vessel in his hands, and has three eyes.
One should meditate upon Bhairava, who has the luster of black [ink] and wards off all obstacles;
having first uttered the three *tāras*, one should then call out, "O Ucchiṣṭabhairava!"

"Ehi-yugmaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa-yugmaṃ hūṃ phaṭ dvi-ṭhāntakaḥ. With this, one should offer all the *bali* offerings. Then, immediately after the dismissal of the *bali*, one should recite the *Śāntistotra* as follows, according to the *Kulārṇava*:
Thereafter, one should recite the Śāntistava and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with drops of honey;
the preceptor, taking the vessel filled with the nectar of ritual substances in his hand, [should proceed].
One should sprinkle [the vessel] and recite the *Sāmayika-nimitta-śānti* mantra:
"Oṃ! Victorious are the Goddesses who have taken refuge at the lotus-feet of Hara, bestowing desire, immortality, and liberation.
I bow to this group of eight-times-eight Yoginīs, the awakeners of the infinite Siddhānta. Yoginī...

I bow my head to the Lord, who stands in the center of the wheel, surrounded by the circle of Mothers, the beloved of Bhairava and Bhairavī; salutations to Him who destroys the darkness of the beginningless and terrible cycle of existence. Salutations to the venerable Lord-Physician, the one who provides the medicine for the Kula, the remover of calamities, sins, diseases, and transgressions of the rules of conduct.

By leaping [over obstacles], one destroys all misfortunes; by the union with the divine wheel, there is long life, health, sovereignty, the attainment of fame, auspicious victory, peace, and the fulfillment of desires. May all the deities protect the worshippers, the guardians, the masters of yoga who have subdued their senses, the swift warriors, and the country.

May the Blessed One, the Lord of the Family, grant peace to the kingdom, the lineage, and the king. May he who beholds the sky [the void] praise the great lineage, the vehicle of the fourfold [truths], beginning with the eighth [state] and beyond, which is called the "Inexpressible" (anākhyam); may all those devoted to the families of beings rejoice in that supreme bliss.
May others, moreover, attain peace through the Śāmbhava state, which distinguishes the supreme from the particular.
May the Siddhas and Gurus, the elder and younger brothers of the lineage, the initiates (*samayins*), the *vaṭukas*, and the maidens rejoice!
May those born of the six Yoginīs and the noble clans of heroes rejoice! May kings, cattle, the twice-born, and the virtuous people rejoice!
May those who are skilled in ethics, free from pride and envy, devoid of physical form and worldly afflictions, eternally devoted to the stainless, the infinite Gurus— peaceful, with tranquil minds,
and having cast off all fear of disease— be joyful; may those devoted to yoga, joined with the Kula-yoga, and the teachers of the Samaya, be joyful.

May the practitioners and their spiritual sons, the cows, the twice-born, the young women, the ascetics, and the maidens who delight in dharma and are solely devoted to their gurus— all those established in the power of *siddhis* within the lineage of practitioners— may the curses of the Yoginīs fall upon the hater of the *samaya*. Today, may that indescribable state of Śambhu manifest clearly within me, in which...
The lotus-feet of the Guru alone are the goal to be attained by those who abide within the channels (nāḍīs) situated in the body, residing in the pores of the skin that have emerged from it;
they are those who dwell upon the waves of the wind of exhalation and whose abode is the breath of inhalation.
May the goddesses, devoted to consuming the side of the sacrificial offering and worshipped by the Kaulas, be satisfied! If this Bhairavī is the Power (Śakti), if this is the teaching of Bhairava,
and if this is the established Dharma, then may those who revile Śiva perish!
"Salutation to all those [goddesses] by whose great power the three worlds abide in well-being"— when this was uttered in the golden age, [the world was filled with light].

May those goddesses who have originated from the Kula, who reside on earth as deities of renowned splendor, who dwell eternally in the fire, and who are the Mothers and refuges; may they who consist of the nectar of the lunar orb in the sky,
who are omnipresent at all times, and who are intent upon protecting the path of all Kulas, grant me peace.
Whether above the cosmic egg in the celestial expanse, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, or in the netherworld,

in fire or water or wind, wherever they may be stationed; or having taken their place in sacred fields, seats, and secondary seats with incense, lamps, and the like, or with meat— may the Goddesses, always pleased by this rite of auspicious offerings, protect us.

Worthy of homage by the lords of heroes: Brahmā, Śrī, Śeṣa, Durgā, Guha, the Gaṇas, the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, Ādityas, the Planets (Grahas), Vasus, Munis, Siddhas, Apsarases, Guhyakas, and others; Bhūtas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, Kiṃnaras, Yakṣas, Rāgas, Yogīśvaras, and Cāraṇas. And who else? Kiṃ...
May all those with human faces who move upon wheels protect me; may all the deities residing within the body,

the elephant-faced ones, the lords of the fields, the Bhairavas, the Yoginīs, the Vaṭukas, the Yakṣas, the Pitṛs, the Bhūtas, the Piśācas, the Grahas, and other beings who roam the earth, the sky, and the night, as well as the Vetālas, the Cetakas, and the Cetiṅkas, be satisfied while this son of noble family drinks.
If the wine, the confection, the lamp, and the sacrificial oblation exist; if the gurus, the gods, the ancestors, the Vedas, the Agamas, and the Yoginīs exist;

if the mantra exists, and if the Supreme Deity exists; if the Vedas are indeed authoritative, and if the Śākta vision exists; if there is a command to be obeyed, and if the truth of the Kaulika tradition exists; and if there is always the power to conquer [the senses]—then [one may proceed].
All the Pitṛs, O best of lineages, reside as gods within my body;
all the Bhairavas likewise reside within my body.
All the Mothers, the oceans, and the lords of the hosts, as well as the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas, being satisfied, are established within my body.
May that which extends from Śiva down to the sacrificial offering (bali), including all from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
and from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) up to Śiva, be satisfied by this sacrifice.
In the Vāmakeśvara Tantra:

Oṃ! I bow to that pervasive Cintāmaṇi, the Lord of the Kula hosts, whose worship according to the prescribed rite brings about the accomplishment of all actions in this world and yields fruit; who is the essence of all the paths and the very activity of the mind.

I bow to Vaṭukanātha, the son of the Goddess, who is clad in red garments, whose mass of matted hair is tawny like blazing fire, who wears a fierce, curved crescent moon amidst garlands of flames, and whose complexion is like the color of molten gold from the mountain of minerals at the rising sun; may he, as the Lord of the Kula-gaṇas, destroy all remaining hosts of obstacles.

May that lineage be the fulfillment and perfection for practitioners; may Vaṭukanātha drink the blood of those who revile [the teachings]; may Gaṇeśa grant all desires to the Kaulikas. May Dharma triumph, bringing well-being to the entire world;
may all Adharma, the root of manifold suffering, perish. These are words of blessing.
May the drops of the night, resembling nectar, fall equally upon the yoginīs who have entered the state of the wheel-sequences (*cakrakrama-bhūmikā*).
May those [drops] which reside in the channels (*nāḍī*),
those situated in the body within the pores of the skin, those established in the elements (*dhātu*), and those dwelling in the waves of the breath like the horses of the ocean, [all descend].

May these goddesses, Niḥśvāsa, Vāsā, and Ayātā— who are intent on devouring enemies and the Makṣas— be satisfied, honored by the Kaulas. May the deities of the earth residing in the body, the elephant-faced Lords of the Fields (Kṣetrapālas), the Bhairavas, the Āyityas, the Vaṭukas, the Yakṣas, the Pitṛs, the Vetālakas, the Ceṭakas, the other excellent wanderers of the night, the Kharas, and the Piśācas [be satisfied].

The houses of the son of noble family may be satisfied; let there be fivefold drink for his father as well. If the word of the Guru is indeed true, if the parents are gods, if the Yoginīs are pleased, and if the Supreme Deity is [pleased]; if the Vedas are indeed authoritative, if the Śākta philosophy is the view, and if sacrifice is indeed sinless.
If there should be universal victory through both independence and the Kaulikas, may there be welfare for the entire world;
may the hosts of beings be devoted to the highest good; may faults go to peace everywhere, and may people be happy; and may the Yoginīs and the Kaulas rejoice.
May the family preceptors rejoice, as well as the others who protect the lineage;
may all practitioners rejoice, while the detractors perish.
May the state of Śambhu be attained; may the Guru always be gracious.

May those who abide within and outside the Kaulika-cakra—the many chambers of the Kulayoginīs—being gratified by the supreme nectar being drunk, be pleased, gracious, and granters of boons. [And likewise] those who are the enemies of sin...

Those who delight in finding fault, those who revile the worship [of the deity], those who destroy family traditions, those who are wicked-hearted, and those practitioners who have fallen away— having seen them as detractors of the Kaulikas during the ritual procedure for the sequential worship (*kramapūjana*),
their destruction shall occur at this moment by the command of Śrī Bhairava.
They are the enemies of practitioners and the defilers of the divine tradition;
O sons, they are satisfied by flesh in the mouths of the ḍākinīs.
In the *Yāmala*: "Having drunk [the water] together with the afflicted people, one should then recite the *Śāntistotra*:
'May the *preta* and *kuṣmāṇḍa* demons perish; may the defilers perish!'"
May the auspicious ones be favorable to the practitioners who protect the tradition.
All the Mothers are victorious; the hosts of Yoginīs are victorious.
Victorious are the Siddhi-Ḍākinīs; victorious are those who worship the Guru;
victorious are all practitioners, purified even while relying upon the worldly realm.

May the sages and Siddhas, perfected in the conduct of the Samaya, rejoice for the sake of the worshippers; may the protectors of the Kula rejoice! May the practitioners of mantra, purified by the eternal tradition, always have hearts full of joy; may the protectors of the Kula grant that joy!
May Indra and the others attain satisfaction; may the deities of the site (vāstudevatās) be satisfied.
May the gods beginning with Candra and Sūrya be satisfied through my devotion;
may the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the planets (grahas), diseases, the karaṇas, and whatever zodiac signs (rāśis) there are [be appeased].
May all the ancestors—the Samas, the Saṃvatsaras, and the rest—be satisfied;
may those who move in the sky and those who move upon the earth be satisfied through my devotion.
May those who move through the atmosphere, and whatever other divine beings there may be—
including serpents, rivers, and birds— be happy today.
May cattle, horses, mountains, caves, sages,
and all Brahmins grant me peace forever;
may the many sacred fords (tīrthas), cows, and other holy lands do the same.
May the trees and the chaste noble women always grant me peace;
may there be auspiciousness for me everywhere, regarding my sons, wife, wealth, and all else.
May those kings who abide by the path of forbearance protect the earth and enjoy happiness;
may my days be auspicious, and may my friends always remain steadfast for me.
May the practitioners of spiritual means be victorious; may the worshippers abide in auspiciousness.

As for those of sinful intellect who delight in grave faults and revile the worship, whose hearts are lost in straying from the path of divine conduct, and those practitioners who have fallen away—having seen them, O you of dull heart, according to the sequence of the transmission (krama)—
Those who defile the Kaulika [tradition], those who, by the command of Śrī Bhairava at this time of the mantra, bring about destruction,
those who hate practitioners, and those who defile the divine lineage (daivāmnāya)—
they are satisfied in the mouths of the Ḍākinīs with their flesh.
May those who cause my censure, as well as those enemies and haters of practitioners, meet their destruction; may they find peace by the command of Śiva.
The ritual duties following the recitation of the *Śāntistava* are stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Dear One, having recited [the hymn], the Guru should dismiss the vessel of worship."
Then, O Mistress of the Kula, one should bestow this grace upon a worthy disciple.
The performance of desired activities is proclaimed as the "mature end" (prauḍhānta);
O Goddess, when the circle of yogis is delighted, this occurs within the "mature end-play" (prauḍhāntallāsaka).
In the maṇḍala of the Yoginīs, the wheel is called bliss;
when the heroes have ascended that [wheel], there is neither "to be done" nor "not to be done."
The Supreme Goddess’s command is that their attainment is indeed dependent upon desire;
therein, whatever action is performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [is determined by it].

O beautiful goddess of the gods, all that arises for the pleasure of the deity; according to the tantras, talk is the fruit of recitation (japa), and meditative absorption (samādhi) is what is prescribed.
Transformation is worship, O Goddess; that which is vomited is the offering to Bhairava.
Liberation arises from union with Śakti, and praise is whatever is spoken at that moment.
O Īśānī, through the non-dual application [of mantras], eating, offering oblations, ritual action,
gazing, meditation, lying down, and salutation become [the Supreme].

That [state] is produced by its manifestation and drawn forth in various ways; it is that very [state] which is true compassion. But he who makes a distinction between what is to be done and what is not to be done is a sinner.
Those who have entered this wheel are to be known as heroes, supreme yogins,
by whom men attain the very form of Bhairava in person.
Having performed the sounding of flutes, lutes, and other instruments, as well as vocal recitations and the like, which describe the pacification of afflictions and the rising of heat;
Weeping, speaking, falling down, rising up, yawning, walking, and physical transformation— this is designated as the sacrifice to the Goddess (deviyāga).
In this wheel, O Goddess, the heroes and heroines, afflicted by passion,
act according to their delight and as it arises in their minds.
He asks those standing nearby slowly, his mind discerning through mindfulness;
having placed the bowl in his mouth, he dwells in states of nirvāṇa.
Having perceived that man as one intoxicated by his beloved, who is as radiant as an immortal,
the man likewise was refined by the intense joy of his own mature passion.
A woman, intoxicated and embracing her husband Puṣa, asks her lover: "Who are you? And who am I here?"
"What business brought you here? For what purpose have you stayed?
Alas, is this a garden, or has it become a house, or what indeed has happened?"
O beloved Śambhavī, having honored [the deity] in their mouths, the women make them drink wine;
having placed a morsel of food in their mouths, they cause it to be swallowed by the women's mouths;
and they take up other vessels and side-dishes, O Śambhavī.
Placing it upon their heads, the intoxicated yogins dance.
Unbeknownst to him, the inner song has reached the palm of his hand;
his steps falter, and the powers of his lineage dance.
The yogis become intoxicated with pride and fall into negligence;
and the yoginīs, agitated by passion, fall upon the men.
O leader of the clan, they fulfill each other's desires completely and perform various such actions.
When, having abandoned the fluctuations of the mind, the inner radiance (ullāsa) proceeds,
then the best of yogis perceive one who has attained the state of divinity.
O Kulanāyikā, the Yoginīs undoubtedly destroy that fool-minded person who reviles the Kaulikas who are possessed by Bhairava.
One should neither revile nor laugh at those who are intoxicated within the midst of the circle;
furthermore, one must never disclose to outsiders any news concerning those who have entered this circle.
One should not commit malice toward them nor perform any harmful act against them;
rather, one should protect them with devotion and guard them with great effort.
Then, having seen the Kulas, one should meditate upon them with the intellect focused on the deities; by enjoying them, one rejoices, pays homage, and attains the state of a Yoginī.
O Dear One, that Kaulika who beholds the Lord in this manner with devotion shall obtain the fruit of ten million vows,
pilgrimages, austerities, gifts, and sacrifices.
In the sixth [state] called Unmanā, which is accompanied by the Hero (Vīra), there is the repeated rising and falling from the state of Unmanā, as well as fainting.
O Mistress of the Kula, these two syllables, *tu* and *au*, which are beyond the reach of the senses, long remain present;
yet they desire union with the Supreme Brahman.
The instability of the body, the senses, and the mind is described;
this is the method for establishing stability, O beloved of the seventh [chapter], in this manifestation.
He becomes the nature of primordial bliss, arising from the *mūrcchanā*;
they know him as supreme when he is joined with the waves and roots of the proximity of the *mūrcchanā*.
With the internal focus and the external gaze, free from blinking or opening the eyes—
this is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, hidden in all the Tantras.
This Khecarīmudrā bestows equality with Śiva; it is my composition concerning that state of perpetual "I-ness" which transcends all and is characterized by aesthetic unification (sāmarasya).
These heroes, radiant with this [practice], are indeed Śivas themselves; of this there is no doubt.
Devoted solely to meditation on their own Self, they do not perceive anything else at all.
Then, a mutual happiness beyond the reach of mind and speech manifests of its own accord, like the drinking of sugar-water and milk.
Such and such happiness cannot be described;
that which is perceived through horripilation and other signs is called the meditation on Brahman.
That supreme state which exists spontaneously within meditative absorption and brings about the penetration of the body,
even one who is fully awakened cannot describe it through the power of samādhi.
Those supreme and noble ones, who were well-perfected and devoted to meditation on the bliss of Brahman,
grieved even for a moment when he had vanished, as if they themselves had been struck by a sword.
O Kuleśvarī, for those great-souled devotees of yours described in the seventh chapter,
there arise eight signs of realization born from the knowledge of time.
The eight stages, as well as the offerings of water for honor and water for the feet, arise; of this there is no doubt.
What is the use of saying more here? The eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), [are attained].
Having attained the status of female doorkeepers, they have long served the temple;
those auspicious qualities of the Supreme Lord are the embodiments of the five principles (pañcatattva).
O knower of the essence of the lineage, those qualities are fully established through the knowledge of reality;
[the stages] beginning with childhood, followed by youth, are called adolescence.
That which is called "the end of that" is said to be *unmanā*, and it is termed *svapna* (dream).
*Suṣupti* (deep sleep) is the state of non-abiding, joined with the three states.
He who knows the seven splendors (ullāsas) is disciplined and a true Kaulika;
when the wheel of Bhairavī is set in motion, all castes become twice-born.
When the Bhairavī-cakra has ceased, all castes are distinct from one another—
whether woman, man, neuter, outcaste, or the highest of the twice-born.
There is a distinction within the center of the wheel, yet all the gods are remembered as equal;
just as the Gaṅgā, having reached the city where the ages meet, attains oneness.
Even within the center of the Śrīcakra, those who are being cherished attain oneness,
just as water mixed with milk becomes milk itself.
Likewise, even within the Śrī-cakra, no distinction exists;
just as among the meritorious worlds such as heaven there is no one other than the gods,
so too within the Cakra, all human beings are deities.
The wheel of existence moves through differentiation, yet all are remembered as equal to Śiva;
for even in the Veda it is established thus, and it declares that "all is Brahman."
What is the use of saying more here, O Sovereign of the Gods? Within this wheel, O Beloved, all men are my forms and all women are your forms.
O Mistress of the Kula, the Yoginīs devour that deluded soul who even attempts to cause a schism within the Cakra.
One should arrange a separate place for each woman, and likewise a separate one for each man; or else, considering them as a couple, one should seat them together in order.
If there is a difference in capacity, they should be seated separately; this is the meaning.
O beloved, whether in the form of a row or perfectly in the form of a circle,
just as there is Nandī with a hundred voices, so too is that hero accompanied by Śakti.
Thus, after experiencing bliss, one should perform the dismissal of the Goddess;
however, the ritual of desire (kāma) therein has already been described in the Kulārṇava.
Then, preceded by water consecrated with mantras, the practitioner of mantras should offer all [the rites],
beginning with worship, to the Goddess, starting from the east and so forth, while reciting the mantra.

From here, there are three levels of intensity; first, the vital breath (prāṇa), then the intellect (buddhi), and thereafter, at the conclusion of the authority over the bodily functions, during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

One should speak of that Supreme with the mind, speech, and action; likewise with the two hands, then with the feet, then with the belly, and finally with the genitals— whatever has been remembered, whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done.
All that is offered at the end of the Guru and the Devas with the word "anvitam," and "svāhā" is said to be the mantra, O beloved one, consisting of twenty-one syllables.
O Śivā, whatever I do, whether with knowledge or even without it, consider all this to be your own work; therefore, forgive me.

Thus it is said in general. But for the southern [direction], on a slippery surface, one should extract the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* mantra; that is preceded by the letter *ka*, and immediately after that [is the letter *ra*].
The seed-syllable of Māyā, conjoined with the Self (Ātman) and united with the letter Kṛti (the letter Ṛ).
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, within your own self on the right, I have offered this state of oneness; O Mahādevī, "I" and "you" are of one single form.
O Great Goddess, when this has been performed, the practitioner becomes identical with your own nature;
for through this mantra of self-surrender, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [are attained].
The sages have indeed been fully described, and the three types of meters have been illustrated;
likewise, the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas] have been declared by the deity as pertaining to this time.
The application [of mantras] is proclaimed to be for the purpose of attaining the state of oneness through self-surrender;
O Goddess, once this nyāsa has been performed, the surrender of the self follows thereafter.
Having thus made this prayer and having praised and bowed with great devotion to the Goddess of Gods,
one should invoke the retinue within the form of the principal deity.
Thus it is said in the Bhairavatantra:
"Having duly offered the goddess both within the heart and externally,
one should then place the remains of the offering (nirmālya) in a pure place and thereafter consume the food offering (naivedya)."
After paying homage to the preceptor, one should then offer the *argha* nectar;
having turned one's own vessel face down, one should cast a flower into it.
Having washed the vessel, one should store it away and remain intent on the contemplation of reality (tattva). The procedure for that is as follows:
Having satiated the Root Goddess (Mūladevī) and having circumambulated the Śrīpātra three times around the head of the vessel facing away [from the deity],
the best of practitioners, having placed a flower upon the head of the Goddess with the mantra "Oṃ parāṅmukhārghaḥ svāhā," should prostrate before it after casting [the flower] upward.
One should place the vessel, together with the remaining substances, upon the support.
As it is said in the *Bhujagāvalī*:
"Having gratified the Root Goddess, the practitioner should lift up the vessel."
Having rotated it three times around the head, one should eat a little and leave some remainder.
The mantra for the offering of *argha* is considered to be "parāṅmukhārghasvāhā. And in the *Yāmala*:
"Having uttered the root mantra and [the name] 'Tripurasundarī'..."
The *parāṅmukhārgha* is declared to be the *svāhā* offering made with the face turned away.
May all the deities be dissolved into the body of the illustrious Tripurasundarī;
may they be united and placed within the limbs of the Goddess by means of the root mantra.
Then the practitioner, having meditated upon the form of Kāmakalā,
should dismiss the wheel of energies (śakticakra) of the Khecarī with the words, "Forgive me."
Regarding "by means of the Khecarī mudrā": in the case of Sundarī, it is the Yonimudrā; in other cases, the name of the respective goddess should be taken in place of that mantra.
And while reciting the root mantra, one should perform the installation of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the body of the goddess.
Having smelled the flower situated within the yantra, one should likewise perform the mudrā of withdrawal (saṃhāramudrā).
Having placed the upward-facing left hand upon the downward-facing right hand, and having interlaced the fingers of one hand with the fingers of the other, [one should perform] the *pari*... [mudrā].
And this is considered the *saṃhāramudrā* in the rite of dismissal:
"Go, go to the supreme abode, your own place, O Supreme Goddess!"
There, where the Brahmans and the gods know the supreme state,
one should then perform the filling of the breath with this mantra.
One should meditate upon that [deity] situated within the heart by means of the root mantra. Then,
with the mantra for the offering of the self (*ātmārpaṇa*) beginning with "Tattvānande," one should offer up the self.
Thereafter, one should dismiss the goddess into one's own heart with the *saṃhāramudrā*.
O Lord, one should worship the Goddess Nirmālyavāsinī with the remains of the offerings (nirmālya);
thereafter, one should partake of the entire nectar from the Śrīpātra with a spirit of devotion.
Whatever merit is found in all the sacred fords, and whatever merit is found in the holy lands,
by the touch of the nectar of the Śrīpātra, it becomes a hundred times greater than that.
From the consecration, one obtains that which bestows universal sovereignty;
and there are also things to be licked, drinks, betel, and ointments.
"I give you the offering of the remains (nirmālya) by the command of Śrī Śiva.
With this mantra, the practitioner should worship the beautiful Śeṣikā.
This, however, is the pledge-mantra (pratijñā-mantra).
But the root-mantra (mūla-mantra) is [found] in the Jñānārṇava:
"Then, having bid farewell to the goddess Sāvarṇī in the lotus of the heart..."
Then, having removed the remainder and offered it, one should purify it with the *sthūla-mantra*.
Having formed *syādvān* as *bhavam*, then *mucchiṣṭa cāṇḍāli*,
and finally *mātaṅgi* at the end—
this mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables is proclaimed as the *Eṣikā-manu*.
By means of this mantra, the remains of the offering (nirmālya) are absorbed into the remainder of the body.
I bow to the goddess Ucchiṣṭamātaṅgī, whose face bears a beautiful smile;
to the goddess who holds a parrot in her hand.
One should meditate upon her, the sole enchantress of the world, as she plays the lute within a triangle, a circle, and a square drawn in the northeast.

I bow to Mātaṅgī, who is intent on playful song, radiant in her blue silken garment; she with lips like the bimba fruit, whose hair and locks fall over her feet for Rudra; she of lovely limbs, wearing white conch-shell earrings, blazing with ornaments of rubies.

To the goddess Mukhī, who is dark as a parrot, [one should offer] in the northeast (Īśānī) direction. Having drawn a triangle, a circle, and the orb of the earth, and having recited the Pratijñā-mantra, one should take the foremost portion of the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering), meditate upon her as described, and uttering the prescribed mantra, one should present it. [The offering consists of: *avaṭu*, *taṭa*, *ghaṭita-kuṭī*, *tāḍita-āḍī*, and *palāśa-tā*.
"I bow to Mātaṅgī, whose head trembles at the moment of playing the ḍaṃkā drum and the lute"—thus is the hymn of praise. In the *Yāmala*:
"The remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) should be worn upon the head by all, and one should not smear them [on other parts of the body]."
And one should partake of the food offering after having given it to one who is devoted to Him.
Then, having offered flowers and other items, one should cast them down in a clean place;
thereafter, one should recite the birth-mantra while facing downward upon the ground.
Having placed [the vessel] above the flower-offering, the best of practitioners should prostrate;
then, having washed it and performed the concealment, he should deposit that sacred water (tīrtha) upon moist ground.
Having drawn Mahāmāyā,
the practitioner of mantra should apply a *tilaka* with the little finger while reciting this mantra beginning with "Yama."
Whatever he touches with his foot, whatever he beholds with his eye— always, if he should cross over, he approaches that which belongs to the virtuous.
This yoga of action has been described, by which one becomes free from impurity;
through its repeated practice, the giver of yoga becomes perfected.
Then the wise one should offer three prostrations to the guru,
as well as the water remaining from the worship of the deities that is held within the conch shell.
It removes the sin of killing a Brahmin from those who have it clinging to their limbs.

The water of the Śrīcakra-pīṭha is more pure than thousands of millions of baths in sacred fords within the vessel of the universe, such as the Revā, Sindhu, Sarasvatī, and others; it is superior to the Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, Narmadā, and so forth.
Perform your ritual bathing at the holy sites of the Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Gomatī, and at the cities of Prayāga and Vārāṇasī, and along the Sindhu rivers.
Śrī Durgā: Obeisance to You, the source of all auspiciousness, who hold the Vaijayantī garland upon the ground of hundreds of thousands of beauties;
I meditate upon Śrī Sundarī, who is adorned with the crescent moon and whose very essence is the overflowing stream of bliss.
[I bow] to those intent on the worship of Śrī Sundarī, whose eyes are tremulous with the intoxication of wine.
May the days pass for us, the devotees of Maheśvara, with our minds filled with joy—
days spent drinking sweet wine from the hollow of our necks while devouring pieces of horse-flesh.
"O dear one, by focusing our gaze upon the left-eyed woman, we shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

That place where even the suspicion of policy is crushed and where the five-syllabled mantra (the name of the Lord) is not found, and where there is the company of deer-eyed women— that very day I consider a day of ill-fortune, while drinking wine in the temples of the initiated."

The courtesan shall be his own wife in the houses; wandering from house to house, the sovereign adept (sādhaka-cakravartin) shall partake of food alone. Day by day let the vessel of the Siddhas be full; day by day let there be libation for the Goddess. Day by day let there be a second companion; day by day let there be union with the fifth state. [He shall] pour forth a stream of treasures.

Having extracted the Śrīcakra from the mouth of the gods according to the Kula tradition, and having tasted the freshly crushed [substance], those of wise intellect attain liberation by embracing the deer-eyed woman. Where there is enjoyment (bhoga), there is no liberation;
where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment. For those intent upon the propitiation of the venerable Sundarī, even enjoyment [becomes liberation].

Liberation is indeed already within one's grasp. The performance of sacrifices at the Bhāgīrathī, the visiting of Kedāra-tīrtha and other holy sites—these and others are merely the world’s [conventions]. O Śrī Sundarī, the Tantra itself is the true sacred site (tīrtha). For those who practice it, prosperity comes instantly to their home, while enemies are gradually eliminated.

May the calamities of those who practice the *sādhana* of Śrī Sundarī go to destruction; may leprosy afflict their limbs, poverty their homes, and their dwellings become like cremation grounds. To whatever extent people heap contempt upon the practitioners of Śrī Sundarī, [so shall it befall] even their own sons.

In such a manner, my wife, friends, and others quickly meet their destruction; thereafter, by the power of time, I too shall transcend [this state]—I have no despair. I bow to and praise that Lord Bhairava, the source of the births of the illustrious Sundarī and all other beings, who, standing on the banks of the pool of conceptualization, manifests as the sixfold senses.
The attraction [of the senses] is like a lotus; the state of form, the drinking of wine, and the movement of the breath are equal.

You have arrived through the path of departure into the heap [of existence], O Great Lord; my effort has now become great. Having made the Kaula path the bestower of the boon for the sake of the essence of liberation, I do not look elsewhere, nor do I praise any other who is free from exertion.

I shall not remember another, nor shall I take refuge in anyone else; never, by virtue of my realization of the ultimate truth, will I abandon the illustrious Sundarī. Having drawn the King of Śrī-cakras, composed of vermilion and nourished with nectars, I shall contemplate the illustrious Sundarī within my heart.

They bring people under their control with glances that inspire longing; the left side is skilled in the dalliance with the Beloved, as is the boar and the meat of this [pig]. Upon the shoulder is the lute, graceful and auspicious, the conduct of true gurus.
The Kaula Dharma is supremely profound, inaccessible even to yogis. The Left... [vāma]... [fragmentary].

The contemplation of the glorious [Guru] is the mental support for meditation upon the Blessed Lady; the tongue is the means for recitation through its beloved [mantra]; and by practicing the Kaula lineage, a person who is restrained in hand and deed attains both worldly success and liberation.
The vessel is in the hand, the hymn in the mouth, and bliss in the lotus of the heart;
the remembrance of the feet of the venerable Guru is upon the head— what could be beyond this?
If, with a single [offering], I do not present a jar of fermented gruel,
and if I drink from the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the ocean all at once,
then may the city of women smeared with unguents be honored with enjoyments... [and so forth].
I am the one whose feet are the Guru; I am Bhairava; I am Śiva. Thus ends the Maṅgalāstotra. 4.
In Nepal, [there are] the manifestations (*utpattayaḥ*) in Kāmarūpa;

the completion (*samāpti*) indeed occurs in Japtyā, for this is the way of the family lineage (*kulavṛtti*). The excellent disciple of the venerable and self-luminous Gurus, joined with the power of the venerable Durgā, [worships] the venerable Durgā...

A preeminent among brahmins, always a guest in the homes of the virtuous, beheld with reverence by the good, an eater of what is fit to be eaten, possessed of a gracious heart, and a refuge for the illustrious land of Vaṅga— he who is renowned as Kṛṣṇānanda, whose speech is established in the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*).

Known as Bhaṭṭācārya, he was a master of elegant speech residing in his native land; having learned the Dharma from Navachūsenya, he attained his own station as a venerable teacher (pīṭhanepālavīra) at Śrīdevī’s lotus feet. With a heart overflowing with the essence of tranquility, this venerable one has attained the spiritual state of the Śrīkaulikas.
Thus ends the Kaula conduct, which brings about welfare. In this independent *Kulavṛtti* composed by Śrī Pūrṇānandanātha out of devotion to his Guru, the thirtieth chapter has been declared.
The first section is complete. In the city of Ṇīyārika, in the presence of the feet of the Gurus, the first section was completed by the voice of Yaśodhara.
It is supreme through its devotion to the lineage of Gaṅgāvateta.

Having first bowed to the gurus upon his head and afterwards to the Goddess in the lotus of his heart, he has written this treatise named Kulavṛtti, which is approved by his teacher; [those who] recite it...
